text: The letter lay where I had left it the night before, on the kitchen table beside the ledger, and I opened it with the butter knife because the butter knife was what I had in my hand.
Stainforth's script was small and level.
He would do me the courtesy of calling today between the hours of ten and twelve, on a matter concerning the lease.
He remained my servant, et cetera.
Three lines.
He was not a man to squander ink on a leaseholder.
I read it twice.
Then I folded it along the creases he had already set into it, put it under the ledger, and went to find my apron.
"Nan," I called, "the taproom floor wants a second sweep.
He'll see dust if there's dust."
"Who will?"
"Mr.
Stainforth."
Nan came to the kitchen door with a cloth over her shoulder and looked at me the particular brief way she looks at me when she is deciding whether to say anything.
She decided against it.
"I'll do the floor," she said.
"Jem's out at the post."
"Leave the post to Jem.
The floor first."
She went.
I set the kettle over the fire, not because I wanted tea but because a kettle on the fire is a thing a woman does, and I wanted my hands occupied if my hands were going to shake, which they were not.
I had been up since five.
The bread was out.
The sideboard was wiped.
The ledger was on the table, open to the current quarter, because I was not going to hide my accounts from him, and I wanted him to see that I was not going to hide them.
I did not want this today.
I had not wanted it yesterday either, and I was unlikely to want it tomorrow.
That was not useful information.
I tied the apron, put a second clean one on the peg by the door for when this one went, and went through into the taproom to see what Nan had made of the floor.
She had made a good job of it.
She always did.
By half past ten the gig was in the yard.
One groom, left holding the reins, and Stainforth himself handing down his hat to no one because no one had been sent to take it.
I watched him from the kitchen window while I dried my hands, and then I stopped watching, because standing at a window waiting for a man is a posture and I was not going to receive him in a posture.
His boots came down on the flagstones.
I heard them before I saw him.
Good boots, unhurried.
"Miss Dale."
He stood inside the door of the taproom with his hat in his hand and his coat still on.
The wool was very good.
My grandmother would have priced it in seconds and told me in pence.
"I hope I find you well."
"You find me well, Mr.
Stainforth.
Will you come through to the parlour, or would you rather the kitchen?"
"The parlour, if it is no trouble."
"It is no trouble."
I led him.
The passage was narrower than his coat, and he adjusted his shoulders for it without seeming to notice he had.

Patience had received his father at this same door in the year before she died; she had given him small beer and a seat by the fire, and when he left she had said, that one is civil, and civil is the worst of them, because you cannot show a civil man the door.
I had been eighteen and had not understood her.
I understood her now.
"I trust the roads were dry," I said.
"Dry enough.
Your yard is in good order."
"Thank you."
"Your ostler is the Yorkshireman."
"Jem Bowker, yes."
"A soldier, I understand."
"He was."
Stainforth nodded, once, as though a small box had been ticked in a book I was not permitted to read.
He sat when I indicated the chair.
He declined the small beer I offered and accepted a glass of water, which he did not drink.
"I shan't keep you long, Miss Dale.
I thought it proper, before any formal communication, to see the inn for myself.
The lease comes up for renewal at Michaelmas, as you know, and the vestry has begun to raise certain questions about the house which I should like to be able to answer."
"I should like to answer them myself, if I may."
"Of course.
That is partly why I am here."
He set the glass down untouched.
"Perhaps you would be so kind as to show me the house."
He had not asked.
He had told me he would be shown, and dressed the telling in a question because he was a man who preferred his pressure upholstered.
I could have left him in the parlour with Nan to bring him more water he would not drink.
I did not.
Leaving Stainforth alone in my house was worse than walking him through it.
"By all means," I said.
"Shall we begin with the taproom?"
We began with the taproom.
He stood in the middle of it and looked at the ceiling beam above the bar.
Then he laid his gloved hand flat on the beam, briefly, and took the glove away.
I watched the glove, and I watched his hand, and I did not narrate to myself what I thought about either.
"A good beam," he said.
"It is the original.
Sixteen-ninety something.
My grandmother had it scarfed in eighty-four, on the west end, where the damp had got at it."
"Your grandmother."
"Ruth Soulden."
"Ah."
He moved on.
The cellar door is at the foot of the passage, set low, with a step down that catches strangers and a hinge that sticks in damp weather.
Jem had been meaning to look at the hinge for a fortnight.
Stainforth opened the door, and the hinge caught as it always caught, and he paused with his hand on it as though the catch were a piece of information he was adding to a column.
"This wants oil."
"It does.
It is on the list."
"Is the list long, Miss Dale?"
"A working inn has a long list, Mr.
Stainforth.
One works down it."
He let the hinge go and the door settled.

We went down the three steps and I showed him the cellar, which was clean, and the casks, which were full to the mark I had set on them on Monday, and the slate on which I recorded what went out and when.
He looked at the slate.
He did not touch it.
"You keep the cellar accounts yourself."
"I keep all the accounts myself."
"That must be a considerable labour."
"It is the labour I was raised to."
We came up.
He wanted to see the stair to the first-floor landing, so I took him up the stair to the first-floor landing.
He rested his hand, once, on the newel post at the top, and the newel post did not shift because Jem had re-wedged it in the spring.
He did not touch any of the doors.
He looked down the passage and counted, not aloud, the rooms to the right and the rooms to the left, and I could see him counting because his eyes moved in the small increments that counting uses.
"Twenty rooms."
"Twenty."
"And in what proportion, commonly, full?"
"At present, fourteen.
In the spring I ran eighteen for six weeks together.
The posting trade has been steady since the summer."
"Despite the year."
"Despite the year."
He nodded again.
The box again, ticked.
I had begun to find the ticking an interesting piece of theatre; a man in a good coat, in my passage, counting my hinges, and me following him because the alternative was worse.
Somewhere inside me an accountant was running a tally that had nothing to do with feeling, and the accountant was not yet losing.
We went down the back stair to the yard.
He wanted the yard.
Of course he wanted the yard.
"A question, Miss Dale, if I may."
"Please."
"The lease, as drawn, contains a clause permitting reassignment at renewal at the lessor's discretion.
You will have it to hand, I expect."
"I have it to hand."
"My concern, and the vestry's, is not with the house as it stands.
The house, as it stands, is well kept.
My concern is with the house as it will stand in five years, in ten.

An establishment of this size and position requires, I think you would agree, a firmness of hand that is not easily sustained by any single person, over time, and in circumstances which the present year has made difficult for every inn on this road."
That was his long sentence.
He did not make another one like it in the whole of the visit.
I let it stand in the air between us until he understood that I had heard it, and then I answered the part of it I was willing to answer.
"The house has been sustained by a single person, Mr.
Stainforth, for the better part of forty-four years.
First my grandmother, then my mother, now me.
The hand has been one hand on each occasion, and it has been firm."
"Indeed.
It is a remarkable history."
"It is a working history."
He crossed to the stable-yard fence, where the post on the end had gone crooked in the September rain; Jem had propped it with a wedge of oak until he could reset it properly.
Stainforth put his hand on the top of the post and pressed, lightly, and the post gave, lightly, as the post would.
He took his hand off.
"This wants resetting."
"It does.
It is on the list."
"My nephew, Miss Dale, has taken an interest in the coaching trade."
There it was.
I had been waiting for him to put it on the table, and he put it there the way he had put his glove on the glove: without looking at it, as though it had simply arrived.
I did not look at it either.
"Has he."
"He has a mind for business.
Were the lease to pass to a man of his age and capacity, with the capital the improvements would require, the house might be placed on a footing that would secure it for a generation.
These are matters for Michaelmas, of course.
I do not raise them now to press you."
"You raise them now, Mr.
Stainforth, but you do not press me."
"Quite so."
The faintest crease, at the corner of his mouth, that was not a smile.
"I should not wish to be misunderstood."
"I understand you exactly."
A pair of jackdaws went up off the stable roof, arguing.
He waited for them to settle.
I waited with him.
The accountant in me had begun, finally, to lose a little ground, and I set my weight against the feeling and did not let it show in my face.
"I shall write to you before the quarter," he said.
"I should be obliged if you would have the lease to hand at that time."
"I shall."
"Miss Dale.
A pleasure, as always."
"Mr.
Stainforth."
He put his hat on at the yard gate, not before, and the groom had the reins ready for him because the groom had been watching the kitchen window for the half-hour Stainforth had been in my house.
The gig went out of the yard at a walk and turned south at the road.

I stood where he had left me for the space of two breaths, because I was not going to give him a third, and then I went in to Nan at the bar and told her to draw a small beer for herself and another for Jem, because it was done.
Then I went up the stairs to Bridget.
There are fourteen treads.
The third from the top has a warp in it that sings a half-note under the right heel.
I have been climbing that stair since I could climb stairs, and the note was the same note now as it had been when I was four.
I did not rehearse what I would say.
Bridget does not want a speech, and she does not give one.
"Come in, Dinah, and close the door behind you."
She was in the chair by the window that looks down on the yard.
The yard from her window is the whole yard, gate to stable door, because she chose the chair for the view forty years ago and has not moved it.
The tea tray was already on the table between the two chairs.
The good china, because what were we saving it for.
She had set out two cups.
"You saw the gig."
"I saw the gig.
Sit down.
The tea's drawn."
I sat.
She poured.
Her hands are knotted at the knuckles and she has to steady the pot on the lip of the cup, and she does not spill; she has never in my life spilled tea.
"Was it the father's manner or his own?"
she said.
"His own.
The father's was worse."
"The father was a fool.
This one isn't.
Drink your tea."
I drank my tea.
She watched me over the rim of her own cup, and she did not say anything about my face, which was a mercy, because my face was not yet back under my hand.
"The nephew?"
"Mentioned.
Not named."
"He'll name him by Michaelmas."
"He will."
"Eat a biscuit."
I ate a biscuit.
There were six on the plate, three each.
She had counted them out, and she would count them back at the end, and if I had eaten four she would have eaten two, which was the arithmetic of Bridget's affection and always had been.
"Your mother," she said, "kept this place standing through worse than a letter and a visit."
"I know."
"She also kept herself standing through worse than she needed to.
There's a difference, Dinah, and it took me thirty years to see it, and I watched her every day of it."
I set my cup down.
The saucer was steady under it.
"She kept what was hers.
I'd not have had her do otherwise."
"Nor would I.
That isn't what I said."
"Bridget."

"I said holding on and holding back aren't the same thing, child, and your mother did them both, and called them both by the same name, and I loved her, and she died at that range with a ladle in her hand, and I'd rather you didn't."
The Wexford was on her tongue at the end of it, at *child*, at *loved her*.
It comes out when she is pressed.
It came out now and went away again.
I did not answer her straight.

I could not, because she had put the line down exactly where she meant to put it, and it had landed, and the landing was a small hard thing low in my chest that I was going to have to carry downstairs with me and work alongside for the rest of the day.
Not agreeing with her.
Not arguing either.
Only noting that she had said it and that I had heard it.
"I've a brewer's bill to settle before four," I said.
"I know you have."
"More tea?"
"A half cup.
Then go."
I poured her a half cup.
I finished my own.
I stood, and she did not stand, because standing is a negotiation for her now and we do not make her negotiate in her own rooms.
She watched me to the door.
"Dinah."
"Yes."
"The ledger's on the table downstairs."
"It is."
"Good girl."
I came down the stair.
The third tread sang its half-note under my heel and I did not stop on it.
Down in the kitchen, Nan had a fresh cloth on the table and the brewer's bill laid out square.

I sat and went at the column, and the column was as it had been and answered to what I could set against it, and the line Bridget had put down sat quietly under my ribs and did not interfere with the arithmetic, because I would not let it.
The afternoon ran on.
The weather came down early; a thin rain started before four, and the wind turned colder, and Nan lit the lamps in the taproom an hour before she usually did.
Jem came in from the post with his coat wet at the shoulders, swore mildly at the state of the yard, and went out again.
The London coach came through at six and went on at quarter past.
A farmer from Codicote took a bowl of stew in the taproom and paid in coin.
By eight the rain had thickened and the yard was quiet, and I was in the kitchen with a knife and a heap of onions for tomorrow's pie.
A knock at the yard door.
Not the taproom.
Not the main.
Two knocks, measured, the second a little lower than the first, like a man not sure whether he ought to knock at all.
I wiped my hands and took the lantern off the nail and opened the door.
A man.
Tall; taller than the lintel wanted him to be; he had to stoop a half inch coming into the light.
The coat had been a good coat once and had been walked in hard; the boots had been a good pair and were now the boots of a man who walked.
At his heel, close in, a lurcher, grey-brindled, keeping its head low out of the rain.
The dog did not whine.
It was too tired to whine.
The man smelled of a long road and wet wool.
"Missus," he said.
"I'm looking for work, or a night's shelter.
Either will do.
Both, if you can spare them."
He did not make it a plea.
He made it a proposition, flat, as though he were used to being answered no and did not want to make the no difficult for me.
"The stable's dry," I said.
"There's straw in the end stall and a blanket on the hook.
You can sleep there.
There's bread and a bit of cheese in the kitchen; I'll put it out.
Work's a question for morning."
"Thank you."
"The dog goes with you.
Not in the kitchen."
"Yes."
"What do I call you, if I want you in the morning?"
He gave me a name.
One word.
I heard it and set it aside; there would be time for names in daylight, if there was going to be any time for him at all, which I had not decided and did not need to decide tonight.
Vagrants turn up at this time of year as regular as the weather turns; most move on at first light.
I was too tired to hire a man and too tired to turn one away, and I had learned long ago that the decisions one is too tired to make are not improved by making them.
"The stable's through the arch on your left.
Pump's by the trough.
Don't light anything in there; there's dry straw."
"I know not to."
He said it without offence.
It was the tone of a man telling a stranger a small true thing because it would save them both a longer sentence.
I liked the tone.
I did not let myself notice that I liked it.
"Go on, then."
He went.
The dog went with him, one pace behind his left boot, as though it had been walking at that pace behind that boot for a long time.
I shut the door on the rain, hung the lantern back on the nail, and went to cut the bread and cheese.
When I brought the plate out to the stable doorway he was already inside.
I set it on the bench by the door and went back.
I did not go in.
It was not a night for going in.
Back in the kitchen I finished the onions and swept the peel into the bucket and wiped the board.
There was one more thing to do before I banked the fire: the sponge cloths wanted wringing out and laying for the morning.
The kitchen window faces the yard.

While I wrung them, and laid them, and wrung the next, I watched the yard, because the yard was there to be watched and because watching the yard at the end of the day is a habit my grandmother gave me and my mother kept and I have not broken.
He came out of the stable with the dog at his heel.
He settled the dog in the lee of the wall, on the dry side, and said something to it that I could not hear through the glass and the rain; the dog put its head on its paws.
Then he went to the stable door and worked the hinge.
The hinge that sticks.
He did something with his thumb at the pin, and something else at the lower bracket, and the door swung once, twice, true.
He closed it and opened it again to be sure.
He let it stand.
He crossed to the fence post at the end of the yard, the crooked one, and crouched to it.
I could not see what he did at the base; his back was to me and the lantern in the stable doorway threw his shape in one long flat line against the wet flags.
He worked at it for a minute, perhaps two.

When he stood up the post stood up with him, square to its neighbours, and he pressed the top of it once with the flat of his hand, the way Stainforth had pressed it that morning, except that when his hand came away the post did not give.
I wrung out the last cloth.
His hands moved at the latch on the stable door as he went back in, checking it a second time because a man who has travelled rough checks things twice.
I watched his hands at the latch.
Then I laid the cloth on the rail, and I turned back to the board, and I put the knife away.
The letter was short.
Stainforth's hand was neat, the kind of neat that never wasted itself on warmth, and I read it twice standing at the kitchen table with one hand still on the teapot.
*I shall call this morning upon a matter touching the lease.* A single hour named.
A promise, or a notice; he had not troubled to choose between them.
I set the letter down beside the ledger.
I did not want this today.
I had not wanted it yesterday either, when it had arrived and I had left it unopened on the dresser like a mouse I was too tired to kill.
Now it lay flat against the wood, and the wood was scrubbed, and the ledger was open to last week's takings, which were honest and tidy and would have to speak for me.
"Nan," I said, when she came through with the pot of tea I had abandoned.
"He's coming this morning.
Stainforth."
"I saw the hand on it last night."
She did not look up from the pot.
"Will you want the good cups or the kitchen ones?"
"The kitchen ones.
I'll not put on a show for him."
"No," she said.
"I didn't think you would."
I put my apron on.
I checked that the taproom had been swept, which it had, because Nan had done it at six.
I checked that the fire in the front parlour was laid and not yet lit, because a cold grate on a dry morning said *we are at work here* more clearly than any amount of hospitality.
I left the ledger on the kitchen table, turned to the page I meant him to see.
I did not hide it.
I did not set it out either.
It was where it always was, and I wanted him to know that it was where it always was.
My mother had received his father once, in the year before she died.
She had met him on the flagstones, not in the parlour, and had offered neither tea nor a chair.

*If he wants to stand in my yard and ask me questions,* she had said afterwards, scraping carrots with a cold hand, *he can stand.* I thought of that now, and I did not smile, but something in me took up its old shape.
The gig came into the yard at a quarter past ten.
I heard it from the scullery: the particular crunch of wheels on the packed gravel by the pump, the single horse, the groom's low word to the animal.
I wiped my hands on my apron and went to the front door.
Stainforth stepped down from the gig as a man steps down from a pew, carefully and without haste.
His coat was good wool, darker than it needed to be, cut two seasons behind London but cut well.
His hat was excellent.
The groom stayed at the horse's head.
Stainforth crossed the flagstones and inclined his head precisely the degree custom required.
"Miss Dale."
"Mr Stainforth."
I held the door.
"You'll come in."
"Thank you."
He took off his hat inside the threshold and stood a moment looking at the passage, the taproom door, the stair.
Not appraising, he would have said; only noting.
I said nothing.
I had learned a long time ago that the first person to speak in a room like this generally lost something by it.
"A dry morning," he said at last.
"Dry enough.
The road will be hard by noon."
"You have had a quiet week, I hope."
"Eleven up on last week's board," I said.
"Two carriages in last night, one out this morning.
We are holding."
"I am glad to hear it."
He turned his hat in his hands once, and stopped.
"I wonder if I might walk through.
A quarter of an hour, no more.
It has been some time since I was in the house proper, and I find it useful, at this season, to refresh my memory."
There it was.
Civil as cream.
*Refresh my memory* was not a phrase that wanted an answer.
"By all means," I said.
"I'll come with you."
He had not asked me to.
He did not look surprised.
We began in the taproom.
He stood in the middle of the flagged floor and turned once, slowly, the way a man turns in a barn he is thinking of buying.
He touched the beam above the bar with two fingers, lightly, as though testing for dust and finding none.
"Sound," he said.
"It was new when my grandmother took the lease.
It was sound then.
It is sound now."
"Your grandmother had an eye."
"She had a carpenter.
His name was Hoggard.
She paid him in full and on time, which was not the custom then and is not the custom now."
He smiled, a narrow movement of the mouth.
"Miss Dale, I do not mean to put you on the defensive."
"I am not defensive, Mr Stainforth.
You have asked about the beam and I have answered about the beam."
He inclined his head again and moved on.
In the passage to the cellar he paused at the door.

The cellar door had a wrought iron hinge on the lower edge that stuck in damp weather; Jem had been meaning to oil it for three weeks and had not, and I had not reminded him, because there were twenty other things and the hinge held.
Stainforth lifted the latch, let the door swing a quarter inch, let it swing back.
He pressed the hinge with his thumb.
"A little gone."
"It sticks in damp.
It closes."
"Your man should see to it."
"He will."
He did not go down the cellar stair.
He let the door fall to and moved on, and I registered the fact that he had touched the hinge and the fact that he had not descended, and I entered both on an invisible ledger of my own.
On the first-floor landing he stopped by the window that gave on to the yard.
The groom was still at the horse's head.
Stainforth looked down for a moment as though checking his own arrival, and then he turned.
"Miss Dale, I must be candid with you."
"Please."
"The lease comes up at Michaelmas."
"At Michaelmas next.
Fifteen months."
"Fifteen months.
Yes."
He nodded, as though I had confirmed something he had already known and was courteous enough to let me say.
"I have been giving thought to the renewal.
You will understand that a lease of this kind, on a property of this standing, is not a small matter to the estate."
"Nor to me."
"Nor to you.
Quite.
Which is why I should prefer to speak of it early rather than late."
He rested one hand on the window sill.
He did not lean.
"There is a question, Miss Dale, which the vestry has begun to raise, and which I am obliged to take seriously.
The question of whether a public house on the Great North Road, at this season, with the number of discharged men on the roads, is best held by a single woman."
"The vestry has been raising questions since my mother took the lease.
The house has been held by a single woman for forty-four years."
"I am aware."
"Then you will be aware that the accounts are in order, the parish rates are paid, and the parish constable has had no occasion to call."
"I am aware of all three."
He did not raise his voice.
He did not need to.

"I am also aware that my nephew is of an age to take a commercial interest, and that a man of his standing, holding the lease, would answer certain of the vestry's concerns without troubling you further."
*A man of his standing.* Not named.
Not yet.
A shape, a shadow, a possibility he was laying on the sill between us to see how I received it.
"I see," I said.
"I hoped you would."
We moved on.
I made myself breathe with the regular work of my lungs and not with the pulse at my throat.
He touched the banister at the head of the stair.
He touched the frame of the door to room six.
He did not open any of the bedroom doors, which was a courtesy, or a demonstration of courtesy; I could not tell which, and I did not need to.
In the passage to the stable yard he stopped at the crooked fence post by the pump.
The post had been leaning for a month.
Jem had been meaning to reset it, and I had been meaning to remind him, and the post had gone on leaning, because a leaning post does no harm until it falls and the post had not fallen.
Stainforth put two fingers against the top of the post and pushed, gently.
It gave a quarter inch and came back.
"Miss Dale."
"I know.
He'll see to it this week."
"A small matter."
"A small matter."
"It is the small matters, I find, that a prospective tenant notices on his first visit."
I did not answer.

I looked at his fingers on the post and I thought, with an accountant's exactness, *he has touched the hinge, he has touched the post, he has named a nephew he has not named,* and I added it up, and the sum was what I had expected the sum to be.
He let go of the post.
He turned, and we walked back through the passage to the front door.
At the threshold he put his hat on, and then took it off again for a courteous half-beat while he spoke.
"I shall write in the next fortnight.
There is a term in the lease touching on assignment which I should like to discuss before the quarter.
Good day, Miss Dale."
"Good day, Mr Stainforth."
The hat went back on.
He crossed the flagstones, took the reins from the groom, and was gone at the same measured pace he had come in at.
The yard was quiet.
The horse's hooves receded along the road and were replaced, after a moment, by the ordinary sound of a jackdaw on the stable roof.
I stood where he had left me.
I counted to five, which was a thing my grandmother had taught my mother and my mother had taught me, to stop a woman standing any longer than five.
Then I went inside, past the ledger, up the stairs.
The third tread from the top warps.
It gives a half inch under a full foot, and it has done since I was a girl.
I put my foot on it now and felt it give, and I climbed past it, and I came to Bridget's door, and I did not knock.
"Come in, child," she said, before my hand was on the latch.
She was at her window.
She was always at her window in the mornings; the chair fitted the sill like a thing grown there.
The tea tray was laid on the small table, and the good china was out, because Bridget uses the good china, and always has, and what, she has been asking me for fifty years, are we saving it for.
"Sit," she said.
"Sit down."
I sat.
She poured.
Her hands are twisted at the knuckles, but they do what she requires of them; the tea went into the cup and not the saucer, and she pushed it across without looking at me.
"He stayed a quarter hour," she said.
"I counted."
"You always count."
"I do.
It passes the morning."
She settled the pot.
"Was it the nephew?"
"He did not name him."
"He will.
What did he touch?"
"The cellar hinge.
The fence post."
"Ah."
She nodded, once.
"A man who has a list."
"He has a list."
"And you?"
"I have a ledger."
She smiled.
The smile went into her cheeks and stayed there.
We drank our tea.
The china was thin in the hand, painted with a small green leaf I had known all my life.
Outside her window a sparrow landed on the sill, considered us, and went.
"Dinah."
"Yes."
"Your mother," Bridget said, "was the stubbornest woman I ever knew, and I grew up in Wexford, which is a place that breeds them."
"I know."
"She held on to this house with her teeth.
She held on to it past the point where any reasonable person would have set it down to rest her jaw."
Bridget set her cup in its saucer.
"But there is a difference, child, between holding on and holding back.
Your mother never learned it.
I would be sorry to watch you not learn it either."
The line did not ring.
It sat on the table with the teapot and the small green leaves.
I finished my tea.
I could feel her watching me, patient in the way very old women are patient, which is not patience at all but a refusal to be hurried.
"I have the bar to see to," I said.
"You do."
"Thank you for the tea."
"Any time, child."
The accent came up in the last word, a soft burr I had not heard in a week.
"Any time at all."
I stood.

I kissed the top of her head, which smelt of lavender and a little of pipe smoke, though she had never smoked in her life; it was Jem's pipe, carried up the stairs on Sunday evenings with the draughts board.
I went to the door.
"Dinah."
"Yes."
"He'll come back."
"I know he will."
I went down the stairs.
The third tread from the top gave under my foot, and I set my hand on the rail at the turn, and by the time I reached the kitchen I was back inside the day.
There was the bar to see to.
There were the chops to order.
There was a bucket that needed mending and a lamp that needed a new wick and a letter to the brewery that had been waiting since Tuesday.
I wrote the letter first, because it was the smallest task, and small tasks are the ones that hold the rest of the afternoon in place.
The afternoon ran.
Nan worked the taproom.
Jem was somewhere in the yard; I heard him once speaking to a horse in the tone men use when they mean it.
The light changed early, a thin rain came on with a colder wind behind it, and I had the lamps lit by four.
Two carriages came in.
One went out.
A man ate a pie at the bar and left threepence over.
By seven the rain was steady and the yard was a slick of wet flagstones under the lantern at the kitchen door.
I was at the scullery window with a knife in my hand, taking the eyes out of potatoes for tomorrow's breakfast, when the knock came at the yard gate.
Not the front.
Not the taproom.
The yard gate, low and twice, the knock of a man who did not expect to be let in and was asking anyway.
I set down the knife.
I wiped my hands.
I took the lantern from the hook and went out.
He was tall.
That was the first thing, because the lantern reached his chest before it reached his face, and I had to lift it.
He wore a coat that had been good once and had been walked in hard.
The rain had gone through the shoulders.
A dog stood at his heel, long-legged, low-bellied, not moving.
Its ears came forward when I came forward, and went back when I stopped, and that was all.
"Ma'am."
"Yes."
"I'm looking for work.
A night's shelter, if you've it.
I can pay for the shelter.
I'd rather work for it."
His voice was low and educated and tired.
I could hear the tiredness in it more than anything else.
"I've nothing to offer tonight," I said.
"The yard's settled.
The kitchen's closing."
"I understand."
"The stable's dry.
There's clean straw in the end stall.
You and the dog can have it till morning.
I'll look at you again then."
He took that in.
He did not thank me too much, which I marked.
"I'm obliged."
"The pump's by the gate.
There's a trough for the dog."
"Thank you."
I did not ask his name.
He did not offer one, or if he did, the rain took it.
I stood aside and let him through, and he went past me towards the stable with the dog at his heel, and I shut the gate behind him.
I went back inside.
The kitchen was warm after the yard.

I hung the lantern on its hook and picked up the knife and went on with the potatoes, and through the scullery window I could see the lantern I had left on the stable post, and the shape of him moving in its light.
He settled the dog first.
I saw him crouch and put a hand to its back and stay there a moment, and the dog went down with a slow fold of its long legs.
Then he stood and went to the stable door.
The door has a hinge that sticks in damp weather; it is the same hinge Stainforth had touched that morning, lower, at the outside edge.
I watched him lift the door a half inch on its pin and work the hinge with his thumb, the way a man works a thing he has understood at a glance.
The hinge gave.
He set the door back.
He did not stop there.

He crossed the yard to the pump and put his hand on the crooked fence post, and he looked at it, and then he set his shoulder to it and pushed it upright, and held it, and scraped gravel in at its foot with the side of his boot, and pressed it with the heel, and stood back.
The post stood.
I watched his hands.
They were large and moved without hurry.
They had set the post and they had worked the hinge and now they were at his sides, and the rain was on them, and he was looking at the stable door as a man looks at work finished for the night.
I turned back to the potatoes.
The letter sat where I had left it last night, unopened on the kitchen table, the seal a neat dark coin against the white.
I had known the hand before I carried it upstairs.
I had known it again this morning, coming down.
I broke the wax and read.
Stainforth's letters were always brief.
A landlord does not waste ink on a leasehold tenant.
He would call today, between eleven and one, to discuss matters touching the lease and the inn's situation.
He trusted he would find me at leisure.
He remained, and so forth.
I read it twice.
I set it beside the ledger.
The ledger had been open since six.
"Nan."
She came through from the scullery with her sleeves rolled and a wisp of hair already escaping her cap.
"Ma'am."
"Mr Stainforth before one.
Sweep the taproom again.
The stones by the hearth, mind, not just the middle."
"Ma'am."
She looked at the letter, and at me, and did not ask.
I tied a fresh apron.
I checked the fire.
I set the kettle.
I did not open the letter again, because I had it by heart after the second reading and there was nothing in it that rereading would soften.
Between eleven and one.
A window of hours inside which a man of his class would arrive at the hour most inconvenient to me and call it civility.
I put my hands flat on the table for a moment.
Then I took them off it and went to find the broom Nan had not yet reached for.
By half past ten the taproom was swept twice, the tables wiped, the fire banked low and clean.
The ledger stayed on the kitchen table where Stainforth would see it if he came through.
I would not hide my accounts from him.
I would not tidy my kitchen for him either, beyond what I would tidy for any man who had sent a letter ahead.
My grandmother had received his father once, I had been told, in a stained apron and without apology, and the old man had not dared remark on it.
Patience had told me that story the way she told me everything worth knowing: dry, flat, as if she were describing the weather.
I put on a clean apron all the same.
Armour was not a metaphor I cared to examine.
A clean apron was a clean apron.
He came at twenty past eleven.

The gig turned in at the yard gate, a neat black thing with a single groom at the horse's head, and the light on the flagstones was the dry clear light of a November morning that had decided to behave.
Stainforth stepped down.
The wool of his coat was very good.
The brim of his hat sat exactly where a hatmaker had meant it to sit.

His boots met the flagstones with a small definite sound, one and then the other, and I heard them through the kitchen wall and was already moving to the front door before the groom had the horse's bridle.
I opened the door on him as he raised his hand to knock.
"Mr Stainforth."
"Miss Dale."
He inclined his head the precise degree a man inclines his head to a woman whose lease he holds.
"I trust I find you well."
"Well enough, sir.
Will you come in."
"Thank you."
He stepped past me into the passage.
He smelled faintly of bay, and of the cold outside, and of a house much better heated than mine.
He handed me his hat without looking to see whether I was the person to take it, and I took it because I was.
"A fine morning," he said.
"It is, sir."
"The road was dry from Hatfield.
One forgets, in a year like this, that such a thing is possible."
"We have been fortunate on our stretch."
"Indeed."
He looked about the passage with the civil, measured attention of a man assessing the pointing on a wall he expected one day to own.
"You keep the place in good order, Miss Dale.
As always."
"Thank you, sir."
I did not ask him to sit.
He had not come to sit.
"I wonder," he said, "if I might trouble you for a turn through the house.
A landlord's small duty.
I should not wish to seem remiss to the trustees at Michaelmas."
"Of course, sir."
I did not correct Michaelmas.
Michaelmas had been and gone.
The quarter he meant was Lady Day, and he had named the wrong feast on purpose, or he had named it by accident, and I was not, this morning, going to find out which.
"The taproom first, perhaps."
"As you like."
He walked ahead of me, which was its own small civility, and also its own small assumption.
In the taproom he laid two fingers on the oak beam above the hearth, as if testing for heat, and took them off again.
"Capacity?"
"Forty at the long table.
Thirty with comfort."
"And the upper rooms?"
"Twenty bedchambers, sir.
Sixteen let last week.
Fourteen the week before."
"Your book records it."
"On the kitchen table.
You may see, if you wish."
"Presently."
He moved to the cellar door.
The hinge on that door had stuck in damp weather since before I was born, and Jem had oiled it yesterday, and it opened under Stainforth's hand as if it had never stuck in its life.
He set his palm flat on the edge of the door and then let it fall.
"The cellar is dry."
"Tolerably, sir.
We lime-washed in September."
"Good."
He closed the door.
The hinge made its small true sound.
"One hears, Miss Dale, of inns along this road falling into difficulty this year.
The harvest.
The grain prices.
The number of men on the road who cannot pay for what they eat."
"One hears it, sir.
I have not found it so here."
"No."
He looked at me, briefly, and looked away.
"No, I observe that you have not."
We went up the stair.
He did not touch the banister.
On the first-floor landing he paused at the window that gave over the yard and stood a moment looking down at the groom and the horse, and then he turned.
"Miss Dale, forgive the directness.
The lease falls to be renewed at Lady Day."
"It does, sir."
"I have been considering the terms."
"Yes, sir."
"You will understand that a property of this size, at such a crossing, carries certain public consequences.
The vestry has had cause to note the number of discharged soldiers who have taken shelter here in the last twelvemonth.
Not, I hasten to say, a matter of reproach to yourself.
A matter of situation."
"I feed what I can feed, sir."
"Just so."
He did not say, *it is not your place to feed them*.
He did not need to.
The civility carried it.
"My concern, Miss Dale, is that the lease, in its present form, was drawn for your mother, and that a good deal has altered since.
There are clauses that a trustee would wish to see strengthened.
The question of succession, for example.
The question of a man on the premises with the authority to speak for the concern in the parish, at the vestry, at quarter sessions."
"I have spoken for the concern these four years, sir."
"You have.
Admirably."
The word sat in the air and did not warm it.
"But the lease as drawn does not name you.
It names my father's tenant, and her heirs.
The trustees will wish clarity.
I wish clarity also.
It has been put to me that my nephew might take the lease at renewal, and that the arrangement would be the tidier for it."
"Your nephew, sir."
"A steady man.
He would not disturb your position here."
I did not ask what my position was, in the mouth of a man who had just named the lease and the succession in the same breath as my not being on either.
I said, "I should wish to see any proposed terms in writing, sir.
At your convenience."
"Of course."
"And the timetable."
"Before Christmas, I should think.
The vestry meets on the twelfth."
"I shall look for your letter."
He moved on.
The passage to the stable yard.
He did not touch the rail of the back stair.

In the yard he stopped at the fence post by the loose-box, the one Jem had been meaning to reset since October, and he laid his gloved hand on the top of it and pushed, not hard, and the post moved the quarter inch it had been moving all autumn.
"This wants attention, Miss Dale."
"Jem is to it this week, sir."
"I am sure he is."
He took his hand off the post.

It was, I thought, an absurd thing to be frightened of, a man in a very good coat counting the hinges on my cellar door, and I registered the absurdity because if I did not register it I was going to register something else.
A fence post.
A hinge.
A clause.
A nephew.
The arithmetic of what he was doing was not complicated.
He was making a list, in my hearing, of the things a man might mend that a woman had been letting go.
I had not been letting them go.
Jem had a list of his own, longer than Stainforth's, and every item on it would be done by Christmas.
I did not tell him this.
He had not asked.
We returned through the kitchen.
He looked at the ledger without opening it, which was its own form of courtesy, and he looked at me.
"You will receive my letter within the week, Miss Dale."
"Thank you, sir."
"Good day to you."
"Good day, Mr Stainforth."
He took his hat from the peg where I had hung it.
He put it on.

He went out the way he had come, and the groom was already at the horse's head, and the gig wheels made a neat bright sound on the flagstones, and then the yard was empty, and the morning was what it had been before he came, except that it was not.
I stood in the kitchen doorway a moment.
Only a moment.

Then I picked up the ledger and carried it through to the scullery shelf where it lived between uses, because I would not do the afternoon's entries on a surface his sleeve had brushed, and that was the one small piece of him I refused to keep.
Then I went up to Bridget.

The stair to her rooms had fourteen treads and a warp in the third from the top, and I counted them going up as I had counted them since I was six, which was a habit my grandmother had given me against dizziness in the dark.
I did not rehearse what I would say.
Bridget had been at her window this morning.
Bridget was at her window most mornings.
The gig in the yard would have been the first thing she saw.
I knocked and went in.
"Come and sit down," she said.
"The water's just on."
She was in her chair, the one by the window, with her feet on the little stool Josiah had made her forty years ago and her hands folded on the black wool of her lap.
The good china was already on the tray.
Of course it was.
Bridget had been using the good china every day since 1799, because what, she said, were we saving it for.
"You saw the gig," I said.
"I did."
She poured.
Her hands shook a little on the pot these days, and the tea went into the cup without a drop on the saucer anyway, which was a skill I had not inherited and did not expect to.
"Sit, Dinah."
I sat.
"Well?"
"Lady Day.
He wants his nephew on the lease."
"Does he."
"He called it tidier."
"He would."
She pushed the cup across to me.
"Drink your tea."
I drank my tea.
The cup was one of the pair with the blue rim, and the blue had worn thin where her thumb sat, and the inside of the cup was the colour of bone.
"How was he?"
she said.
"Civil."
"Ah."
"He touched the cellar door.
And the fence post."
"Did he now."
"I should have liked to see him try the taproom floor.
I should have paid to see him try the taproom floor."
She smiled, briefly, on one side, the way I smiled.
"Your mother would have sent him out through the kitchen."
"I thought of it."
"I know you did."
We drank.
On her mantel was the small brass clock that had been Josiah's mother's, and the tick of it was a sound I had known longer than I had known my own name, and I let it do its work.
"Dinah."
"Yes."
"Your mother kept this house standing through more than you remember."
"I remember enough."
"You remember what a child remembers.
I remember what a sister remembers."
She set her cup down.
"Patience held on to this place with both hands for thirty years.
She was right to.
It was hers.

But she held back from everything else with the same two hands, and I watched her do it, and at the end she had the inn and she had you, and those were good things, and they were not all the things she might have had."
"She had what she wanted."
"She had what she would allow herself."
I looked at the clock.
"Holding on and holding back are not the same thing, child.
Your mother never learned the difference.
I should like you to."
I finished my tea.
"I'll think on it, Aunt."
"No, you won't."
"No," I said.
"I won't."
I stood.
She did not reach for me, which was a kindness, because if she had reached for me I would have had to say something I did not have in me today.
She only looked at me, her eyes pale with the cataract coming in the left one, and she nodded once, and I went out.
Coming down, I did not count the stairs.
I put my hand on the warp in the third from the top and went past it.

In the kitchen I took the ledger off the scullery shelf and opened it on the table and entered the morning's small receipts in the column where they belonged, and I carried Bridget's line with me while I did it, the way a person carries a stone in a pocket: present, heavy, not looked at.
The afternoon went as afternoons go.
Nan at the bar with the two carriers who came in at three.
Jem in the yard with the mare that had cast a shoe at Welwyn.
The rain came on thin at four, and the wind with it, and the lamps were lit before five.
The coach from London was late, as the coach from London had been late all month.
I opened the kitchen door to a knock at the yard gate a little after eight.
A man stood there.
Tall.
A dog at his heel, low and grey, the long rough kind that takes up less room than it looks as though it should.
The man's coat had been good once and had been walked in very hard.
The rain was on the shoulders of it, and on the brim of his hat, and on the dog, and on the lantern I lifted, and on all of them about equally.
"Ma'am," he said.
"Good evening."
"I was told you sometimes have work."
"Sometimes."
"Tonight I'd settle for the stable, if you've a corner.
And the dog quiet, I promise you."
His voice was low, and tired, and did not ask for anything more than the words.
I looked at him in the lantern's little yellow yard of light.
I could see the shape of him, the height, the coat, the dog at his knee.
I could not see his face under the hat brim, which suited me, because I had no use tonight for a stranger's face.
"The loose-box at the end," I said.
"The one with the lame door.
There's straw.
You can draw water at the pump.
I'll send out bread."
"I'm obliged."
"Come to the kitchen in the morning.
We'll see then."
"Ma'am."
He touched the brim of his hat.
The dog looked up at him, and then at me, and then went ahead of him across the yard as if the yard were already known to it.
I watched them as far as the loose-box door.
Then I shut the kitchen door and put the bolt over and set the lantern down.
November.
Of course it was November.

The vagrants always came in November, when the roads got hard and the parish got mean, and I had known there would be one at my door tonight the way I had known Stainforth would be at the front door this morning, and the predictability of the world was, in its dry way, almost a comfort.
I cut the bread and sent it out with Nan.
The last of the kitchen work was the dishes from the late supper, and the sponge on the dresser, and the kettle off the hook.
I did the dishes.
I set the sponge.
I took the kettle off the hook and put it by the hearth where it would be ready for the morning.

The kitchen window gave on the yard, and the yard lamp was still burning by the stable, and through the rain I could see the loose-box door propped open and the lantern he had set inside it throwing a square of light on the wet flagstones.
He was out in the yard again.
I saw him stop at the loose-box door and lift the hinge pin and set it a quarter turn the other way, and the door, when he swung it, did not catch.

Then he crossed to the fence post by the stall and took it in both hands and rocked it free of the soft ground and set it straight and tamped the earth around it with the side of his boot until it stood.
His hands moved in the lantern-light, wet and unhurried, knowing the work.
I turned back to the dresser and folded the cloth.

The letter sat where I had put it last night, on the kitchen table beside the ledger, and I picked it up now and broke the seal because the hour had come round to breaking it, and waiting longer would only mean doing the same thing later with less light.
Stainforth's hand was small and even.
He did not waste a line.
He would call at the inn this morning between ten and noon to discuss matters pertaining to the lease and to certain concerns lately raised in the parish.
He remained my obedient servant.
He was not.
I read it twice, folded it along the crease he had made, and set it back down against the ledger where he would see it if he looked.
"Nan," I said.
She was coming in from the passage with a basket of linens on her hip.
"He's coming this morning.
Stainforth.
Between ten and twelve."
"Today."
"Today."
She adjusted the basket.
"Do you want the dining room swept again, or is once enough."
"Once is enough.
Sweep the taproom.
And have Jem move the gig out of the near yard so there's room for his."
"It's already out."
"Then leave it out."
I put on my second apron, the clean one, over the working one, and tied it tight.
I checked the fire in the range and banked it lower; I did not want the kitchen hot when he stood in it, if he stood in it.
I set the ledger square on the table.
I did not hide it.
My grandmother had kept hers in a drawer when the brewer's man came; my mother had kept hers on the sideboard when the vicar called for his quarterly tithe.
I was keeping mine on the table, and if Stainforth wanted to read my sums upside down he was welcome to try.
I went through the taproom myself when Nan was done and looked at it the way a man who owned land and did not own this inn would look at it.
The benches were clean.
The floor was scrubbed.
A tankard had been left on the bar from last night; I set it under the counter.
The fire wanted a log.
I added one.
I stepped back.
A taproom.
Four years of my management, and every board in it paid for, and still not mine in a way the law would recognise if it came to that.
I went back to the kitchen.
The gig turned in at eleven, or near enough.
I heard it before I saw it: the single horse, the light wheel on the flagstones, the quiet that followed a quiet man pulling up reins.
I went to the front.
Stainforth came through the main door and removed his hat.
His coat was a dark wool of a kind I had seen pass through the inn on better-dressed travellers perhaps twice a year.
The groom stayed at the horse's head.
Stainforth looked at me and inclined his head.
"Miss Dale."
"Mr Stainforth.
Good morning."
"I hope I find you well."
"You find me working, sir.
Which is near enough to well.
Will you come through?"
"Thank you."
He stepped into the hall and glanced at the board where the coach times were chalked up.
My mother had received his father here once, on a matter of repairs to the yard wall; I had been ten and had watched from the stair.
Patience had stood exactly where I was standing and had used exactly the civility I was using now.
I did not need to think about what to say.
I had watched her say it.
"The road was dry, I hope."
"Dry enough.
The wind was easterly."
"It usually is, this time of year."
"So I find."
He laid his hat and gloves on the hall chair.
"If it is not an imposition, Miss Dale, I should like to walk through the house.

It has been some little while since I was last within its walls, and my solicitor suggests it would be well for me to refresh my acquaintance with the property before we turn to the question of renewal."
The question of renewal.
There it was, inside the second exchange, folded into the civility like a shilling into a handkerchief.
"Of course," I said.
"Where would you care to begin."
"The taproom, perhaps."
"This way."
He walked through the taproom slowly and stopped at the end of the bar and put the flat of his hand on the beam above the hatch.
He did not press.
He rested his fingers there, as a man might rest his fingers on the withers of a horse he was thinking of buying.
"Oak," he said.
"Yes."
"Sound."
"My grandfather put it in.
It's older than I am by fifty years."
"A good piece of work."
He took his hand away.
"You have how many rooms let at present?"
"Twelve of twenty.
We expect to be full by Friday, with the Edinburgh coach."
"And your quarterly takings have held."
"They have risen.
The figures are on the kitchen table if you care to see them."
"Presently," he said.
"The cellar first, if I may."
I took a candle from the hall and led him down.
The stair to the cellar turned once and the third tread had a warp I knew to step over.
He did not know it and did not stumble; he set his foot carefully, as men of his class do on stairs that are not their own.
At the foot of the stair he stopped at the cellar door and put his hand to the hinge.
The lower pin sticks in damp weather.
It was sticking this morning.
He worked it gently, watching it, and let it swing.
"This wants oil."
"Jem will see to it this afternoon."
"In damp weather, I imagine, it binds."
"It does."
"A small thing.
But small things, in a house of this size, compound."
"They do, sir.
Which is why we see to them."
He went down the length of the cellar counting casks with his eyes.
He did not touch them.

He came back and paused by the door and looked once more at the hinge, and I understood, standing behind him with a candle that was dripping tallow onto my thumb, that he was not looking at the hinge.
He was looking at the fact that he could stand in my cellar and put his hand on my door and count my ale.
A man in a good coat counting cellar hinges.
I should have laughed.
I did not.
We went up to the first-floor landing.
He walked the passage to the end and back.
He looked into one empty room, a corner one where the window catch had been replaced at Michaelmas, and did not comment.
He came back to the head of the stair.
"You manage the house alone, Miss Dale."
"I manage it with a staff of four within the house and two in the yard.
I manage it, yes."
"You have no partner in the enterprise."
"I have not."
"The lease, as it stands, runs to Lady Day."
"It does."
"You will be aware that renewal is at my discretion."
"I am aware, sir."
"A matter has been raised with me in vestry, which I feel I must put to you plainly, as I should not care for you to hear it from any other quarter."
He paused at the head of the stair, one hand on the newel.
"There is a feeling in the parish that an establishment of this kind, so near the road, ought in the ordinary course of things to be held by a man.
I do not say this is my own view.
I say it is the view put to me, and that it has been put with some energy."
"By whom, sir."
"By more than one."
"I should be glad of the names, if you will give them, so that I may answer them direct."
"That would not, I think, be useful."
"I think it would."
He smiled a very small smile, not unkindly.
"Miss Dale.
My nephew is of age this year.
He has means of his own and an interest in a house of this character.
Were the lease to come to him at renewal, the parish would be served by a proprietor of a kind it is accustomed to, and you, if you chose, would not be without a position within the house.
I raise it now because I do not care to raise it in March, when the question will be sharper and the time shorter.
I should like you to have the winter to think on it."
It was his longest speech of the morning.
I noted that he had not named the nephew, and I noted that he had not needed to; the nephew was any man of the right sort, and his not-yet-naming him was the whole of the point.
"I am obliged to you for your frankness," I said.
"You will think on it."
"I shall think on what needs thinking on."
"That is all I ask."
We went down through the kitchen.
He stopped at the table and looked at the ledger without touching it.
I watched his eye move down the right-hand column.
He did not ask to turn the page.
I did not offer.
"Your figures are good," he said.
"They are."
"The yard, then."
The stable yard was bright and cold.
The groom had walked the horse up and down.
Stainforth went to the fence post at the corner of the near paddock, the one that had listed since Lammas, and set two fingers against it.
The post gave, very slightly, against his hand.
He let it go.
He did not speak of it.
He put on his hat.
"I shall write to you before the quarter," he said.
"You will have my letter in ample time."
"I shall look for it."
"Good day, Miss Dale."
"Good day."
He climbed into the gig.
The groom passed up the reins.

The wheel turned on the flagstones, and the horse went out through the gate at a neat trot, and the yard was quiet as it had been before he came, except that I was standing in it alone with my hands at my sides, and I had not stood with my hands at my sides in the middle of a working morning for four years.
I went in.

I lifted the ledger from the table and set it back on the sideboard where my mother had kept hers, and then I moved it again to the table where I keep mine, because I would not rearrange my kitchen for a man who had left it.
Then I went upstairs to Bridget.
The stair to her rooms has fourteen treads and the third from the top warps where the roof leaked in '09 and was mended.
It creaks under a particular weight at a particular angle.
It creaked under mine.
Bridget's door was open before I had reached the landing, because Bridget's door is always open when she has been at her window and has seen what she has seen.
"Come in, child," she said.
"The tea is made."
She was in her chair by the window.
The good china was on the tray: the blue-and-white, the pot with the chipped spout she would not let me replace.
A pair of her stockings lay mended on the arm of the chair.
On the mantel was the small tin soldier my uncle had carved for her on their wedding journey, painted once and never painted again.
"Sit down."
I sat.
She poured.
Her hands were not steady at the wrist these days, but the pour was exact; she had poured tea for fifty years and her hands remembered what her wrists had forgotten.
She passed me my cup.
"He was forty minutes," she said.
"I counted."
"Forty-two."
"I have the cataract, not the clock."
"Forty-two," I said again, and took the tea.
"He touched the cellar hinge."
"He did."
"And the post."
"He did."
"Drink your tea, Dinah."
I drank.
The tea was strong, the way she takes it; she has not weakened a pot in my lifetime.

The window looked down over the yard, and the yard was empty, and beyond the yard the road ran south and was empty too, because the Edinburgh coach was not due until the evening and the light was flat and colourless as it gets in November when the sky cannot decide on rain.
"He wants the nephew to have it," I said.
"He has wanted that two years."
"He has said it now."
"Has he named the man."
"No."
"He will not, until the quarter.
Your mother's father used the same trick with a carter once, over a field.
Never name the buyer till the price is settled; the buyer is always a better man for not being named."
"I thought of her on the stair."
"You would."
She set her cup down.
"Dinah."
"Aunt."
"Your mother ran this house for twenty-two years and never let a man into her accounts.
She died of it."
"She died of an apoplexy."
"She died of what she would not put down."
Bridget's accent came up under the words, the Wexford in it surfacing the way it does when she is in earnest, softening the consonants and lengthening the vowels.
"There is a difference, child, between holding on and holding back, and your mother did not know it, and I have watched you these two years doing the thing she did and calling it by her name."
I set my cup on the saucer.
The saucer rang, very faintly, because my hand had not been steady when I set it down.
"I've the afternoon's orders to place," I said, "and Nan wants the linens sorted before the coach."
"I know you have."
"Thank you for the tea, Aunt."
"Sit a minute longer."
"I can't."
She looked at me with the look she has, which is not soft, which has never been soft, and she nodded once and let me go.
I stood.
I carried my cup to the tray and set it there with the handle turned out, the way she likes it.
I went to the door.
I did not look back at her, because I could feel her line sitting in the middle of the room behind me, and I was not going to pick it up today, and I did not want her to see me refuse it.
The stair creaked on the same tread going down.
The afternoon went as afternoons go.
Nan was at the bar by four and the first of the evening's drinkers were in by five.
Jem brought the dray horses in from the lower field and the lamps in the yard were lit earlier than they had been yesterday because a thin cold rain had come on after three.
The lamp in the kitchen was lit by half past five.
I placed an order with the butcher's boy for Friday.
I went through the takings for the week.
I ate a piece of bread standing at the sideboard, because I had forgotten to eat at noon.
It was near nine when the knock came at the yard gate.
Not the main door.
Not the taproom.
The yard gate, low and twice, the knock of a man who knew enough not to bang on the front of a strange house at night.
I took the lantern from its hook and went out.
He stood in the rain with a dog at his heel.
Tall.
The coat dark with wet at the shoulders.
Boots that had walked a long way and been good boots when they started.
The dog was low and quiet at his side and did not move when I lifted the lantern.
"Ma'am," he said.
"Yes."
"I'm looking for work.
Any there is.
I'll sleep in the stable if you'll let me.
I can pay for the dog's keep if you'd rather."
His voice was even.
He did not add to it.
I was tired.

I had been tired since before Stainforth's gig came up the road, and I had been more tired since Bridget's line had landed in her parlour like a cup set down too hard, and I was too tired tonight to take on a question I did not already know the answer to.
"The stable's dry at the south end," I said.
"There's clean straw in the last stall on the left.
The dog can go with you.
I'll not take a decision on work tonight; come to the kitchen at six and we'll see."
"Thank you."
"There's bread in the kitchen by the door.
Take a piece as you pass."
"Thank you."
That was all.
He touched his hat, which was sodden, and went through toward the stable with the dog at his heel as though the dog had been walking at his heel a long time and expected to go on doing it.
I did not watch him the whole way.
I went back into the kitchen and hung the lantern and stood at the range for a moment with my hands over the warmth because my hands had got cold in the rain.
The kitchen window looks out on the yard.
I went to it because the last of the day's work was there: the butter crock to be covered and set on the cold shelf, which stands under the window.
I covered it.
I did not turn away at once.
Through the wet glass I could see him at the stable door.
He had set the lantern down.
He was crouched, settling the dog on a folded something, his coat perhaps, against the wall.
Then he stood and went to the door itself and worked the hinge, the one Jem had been meaning to look at, the lower pin that sticks.
He worked it twice, found where it bound, and eased it, and the door swung clean.
He went to the corner of the near paddock then, and I saw him stop at the fence post, the one that had listed since Lammas, the one Stainforth's two fingers had tested at noon.
He set his shoulder to it and righted it and packed a stone at the base with his boot.
His hands were quick at the post.
His hands were quick at the hinge.
I watched his hands a moment longer.
Then I turned back to the butter crock and carried it to the cold shelf and set it down.
The letter lay on the kitchen table where I had set it down the night before, still folded, the red smear of Stainforth's seal facing up like a small accusation.
I had thought I might leave it until after breakfast.
I had thought a great many hopeful things in my life, most of them in the hour before dawn.
I broke the seal with my thumb.
Stainforth did not waste words on a leasehold tenant.
Two sentences inside the fold, in the dry copperplate of a man who pays a clerk to write plainly.
He would call today between eleven and noon to inspect the premises in the ordinary course of his attention to the parish lease.
He trusted the hour would prove convenient.
I read it twice.
I set it down beside the ledger.
I tied my apron.
"Nan," I said, when she came through with the bucket, "he'll be here before noon.
The taproom's to be swept and the cellar door left open.
And put the ledger on the kitchen table.
Not in the drawer."
"The ledger," she repeated.
"On the table.
Where he can see it."
She looked at the letter, then at me, then past me at the bread oven, which was her tactful way of asking no further questions.
She set the bucket down, picked up the broom, and was gone.
I checked the fire.
I checked the flour crock.
I did not, as my mother had taught me not to, stand still in the middle of a room while there was work to be done in it.
Patience had been very clear on the subject.

A woman who stood still in the middle of a room, she said, was a woman advertising that she did not know what to do next, and no one at a coaching inn could afford to be seen not knowing what to do next, least of all the woman who owned the place.
I opened the ledger to the current quarter and laid it flat.
The entries were in my own hand, neat and dated, four years of them.
I had no intention of hiding a column.
He came in at a quarter past eleven.
I heard the gig before I saw it, the particular clean roll of sprung wheels on dry flagstones, and then the single short word from the groom as he took the reins.
I was in the passage when Stainforth stepped through the main door, and I was already walking toward him when he removed his hat.
The coat was good dark wool, cut two seasons back and kept with care.
The hat was beaver.
The boots were country, not town.
He had left the groom with the horse and had not brought a man in with him.

All of this I took in during the three paces between the passage and the door, because my grandmother had taught my mother and my mother had taught me that you learn more about a visitor in the first ten seconds than in the hour that follows, and the first ten seconds are free.
"Mr Stainforth."
"Miss Dale.
A clear morning."
"It is.
You had a dry road."
"As far as Codicote.
There is standing water past the bridge.
Your yard, I see, drains well."
"My grandfather laid it."
"So he did."
He passed his hat to his left hand.
"Shall we begin?
I should not wish to keep you from your morning."
Which was civil, and which meant that we would begin.
He walked ahead of me into the taproom, not waiting to be shown, because a man of Stainforth's sort does not wait to be shown through a building he considers in some sense already his.
I followed a half-step behind.
I had received his father once, with Patience, when I was fifteen; Patience had walked a half-step behind that man too, and had taken exactly the tone I found myself taking now.
It came up out of the bones without being asked.
Stainforth laid one gloved finger on the beam above the taproom hearth.
Not a press; a touch.
"The timbers are sound."
"They are."
"When were they last looked at?"
"Two winters ago.
Jem went over them with a rule."
"Jem."
"Bowker.
My ostler."
"Ah."
He did not write the name down.
He did not need to; a man like Stainforth files a name the first time he hears it and does not misplace it afterwards.
"And the cellar?"
I led him through to the cellar door.
He waited, so I opened it.
The hinge caught, as it always caught in damp weather, and I lifted the door half an inch on its pin to free it, which was a small motion I had done so often I no longer thought about doing it.
He watched me do it.
Then he reached out and tried the hinge himself, opening and closing the door twice, as a man confirms an observation.
"It sticks."
"In wet weather."
"You have not had it reset."
"Not yet.
It has been on the list."
"A list I should be glad to see, Miss Dale, when we come to the renewal."
He said it with no change of tone at all.
He said it as he might have asked after the weather at Codicote.
I registered the sentence in the place where I kept figures, not feelings, and filed it there, and said nothing.
We went down the three cellar steps.
He looked at the casks, counted them, and did not pretend not to be counting.
He touched the shelf where I kept the better wine and withdrew his finger clean.
"Twenty rooms above."
"Eighteen in use.
Two kept for overflow and repair."
"Occupancy through the quarter?"
"Seventy-one per cent of beds taken.
Eighty-three of the stabling."
"You have those figures to hand."
"They are in the ledger on the kitchen table.
You are welcome to them."
"I shall look."
He paused at the foot of the cellar stair and turned to face me, which obliged me to stop on the step above him, which I did not like, and which I did not let show.
"Miss Dale.
I will be direct, as between tenant and landlord there is no profit in any other method.
The lease comes up at Michaelmas.
I am reviewing the terms in light of the parish's broader interests."
"The parish's."
"The road is busier than it was.
The class of trade is changing.
A house of this standing, properly managed, could command a different sort of custom altogether."
"It is properly managed."
"I did not suggest otherwise."
He inclined his head half an inch, which was the civilest form of the word *yet* I have ever heard.

"I suggest only that the parish's long interest may lie in considering whether a house of this size is best held by a single tenant of your situation, or whether a renewal might be better framed in the name of a man with the resources to expand the premises.
I have a relation who has expressed such an interest."
"A relation."
"My nephew.
He is not yet known to you.
He has been abroad."
"I see."
"I do not propose anything today.
I observe only that the question will arise at the renewal, and that the parish officers will take a view.
I should not like you to be surprised."
He said *I should not like you to be surprised* with the faintest warmth, as though he were doing me a kindness.
And it was a kindness, by his lights.
He was letting me see the blade before he drew it, because he was a reasonable man, and reasonable men gave fair warning.
I thought, with a clarity that surprised me, that there was a peculiar absurdity in a man in a ninety-guinea coat counting cellar hinges in my house and calling it the parish's interest.
I did not say so.
The wit was for me.
"I am obliged for the warning," I said.
"Not a warning.
A courtesy."
"A courtesy, then."
We went up.
He continued through the house as though he had not just said what he had said: the stair to the first landing, the long passage, the door to the yard.
At the yard he stopped at the stable fence and laid his gloved hand on the post that Jem had been meaning to reset since Lammas.
The post moved under his hand, which he had known it would, because he had seen it tilt from the kitchen window as he passed.
"This wants doing."
"It does."
"Before the renewal, one would hope."
"Before the frost, Mr Stainforth.
It is on the list."
He smiled very faintly, which was the nearest thing to a human expression he had shown me, and took his hand off the post.
The groom brought the gig round.
Stainforth settled his hat.
"I shall write again before the vestry meets."
"I shall look for the letter."
"Good morning, Miss Dale."
"Good morning."
He climbed up.
The gig rolled out under the arch.

I stood on the flagstones a moment longer than I meant to, because I could feel the post behind me and the hinge behind that, and I could feel the ledger inside on the table with every entry in my own hand.

Then I went in and took down the tea caddy, because Bridget would have seen the gig from her window, and there was only one thing in the world Bridget ever wanted done after she had seen something from her window.
The stair up to her rooms had thirteen treads and a warp in the third from the top that you had to step a little wide of if you did not want to hear about it for a week.
I stepped wide of it.
I carried the tray in both hands.
Bridget was in her chair by the window, which was the chair she had sat in for twenty-six years and which had taken the shape of her, or given her its shape; it was no longer possible to tell.
Her black dress.
Her white hair pinned flat.
On the mantel, the small wooden box that had been Josiah's, and a dish of pins, and nothing else, because Bridget had never seen the sense in clutter on a shelf she could not dust without help.
She looked at me.
She looked at the tray.
She did not ask.
"The good cups?"
I said.
"The good cups.
What else are they for."
I set the tray down.

She lifted the pot with both hands, because her wrists did not take weight on one side any more, and poured with the care of a woman who had decided a long time ago that she would not spill tea in her own room so long as she was alive to prevent it.
"You saw the gig," I said.
"I saw it.
And I saw him get out of it.
And I saw you standing in the yard after he left, which you never do."
"I was thinking."
"That I could see."
She handed me my cup.
The china was very thin and very cold against the finger before the tea warmed it.
I wrapped my hands around it and did not drink yet.
"He wants the house," I said.
"He has always wanted the house."
"He has a nephew now."
"He will have a nephew as long as it suits him.
What did you say?"
"I said the post wants doing before the frost."
She laughed, one small, dry sound, and the Wexford came up through it the way it did when she was amused or pressed.
"Ah, that's Patience on you."
"I take it as a compliment."
"You'd take anything as a compliment if it came from her."
I drank.
The tea was very hot and very strong, which was how Bridget made it, because she had given up on the English habit of weakness in a pot fifty years ago and had not looked back.
She watched me over her cup.
I could feel her watching.
Bridget did not watch idly; she watched the way a clockmaker watches a mechanism that has begun to tick in a way he does not quite like.
"Your mother," she said.
"Don't."
"Your mother kept this place the way a drowning woman keeps a plank.
With both hands and her teeth if she had to.
And I loved her for it, God rest her, and I will not hear a word against her from anyone including you.
But she would not put the plank down long enough to see that there was a boat."
"Bridget."
"Holding on and holding back are not the same thing, Dinah.
She held on.
She never stopped holding on.
But she held herself back from every other thing that might have been hers, because she had convinced herself that the holding on was the whole of it.
And it was not."
The words went in the way a cold draught goes in under a door you thought was shut.
I felt them settle.
I did not let my face move.
"The tea is very good," I said.
"The tea is the same tea it always is."
"Then it is very good as it always is."
She looked at me a long moment.
Then she nodded, once, the way she nodded at Jem when he took a bad move at draughts and she was not going to save him from it, and she let it go.
I finished the cup.
I stood.
"I have the ledger to close," I said.
"Go on, then."
"Thank you for the tea."
"Go on."

I came down the stair and stepped wide of the third tread from the top without thinking about it, and by the time I reached the kitchen I had the ledger open and a pen in my hand and was entering the morning's figures, because Bridget had said what she had said and I had heard it and I did not need to stand still in a room to prove I had heard it.
The afternoon went the way afternoons went.

Nan at the bar with the Baldock carrier and two commercial gentlemen who wanted their chops at four; Jem in the yard with a shoe to look at on the grey mare; the London mail through at half past three, four outside and three in, none of them stopping.
By five the sky had gone low and the wind had turned, and a thin rain began that was the sort of rain that did not fall so much as settle.
I lit the kitchen lamps early.
I lit the taproom lamps early.
I mended the fire.
By eight the yard was quiet.
The knock came at the kitchen door, not the front.

I took the lantern off its hook and opened the door a handsbreadth first, because a woman alone at an inn at eight on a wet night does not open a door the whole way before she knows who is on the other side of it.
A man stood on the step.
Tall.
A long coat dark with rain at the shoulders.
A dog at his heel, low and quiet, its head level with his knee.
"I'm looking for work," he said.
His voice was low and civil and very tired.
"Or a night's shelter, if there's no work.
I can pay for the shelter."
I lifted the lantern.
The light caught the wet of his coat and the edge of a jaw and nothing else I cared to register.
The coat had been good once.
The boots had walked a long way.
"I've no work tonight," I said.
"I've a stable with clean straw and a dry corner.
You can have that.
We'll speak in the morning about the rest."
"I'd be obliged."
"The dog stays with you."
"He does anyway."
"Through the arch.
Second door on the left.
Tell Jem I said so if he asks."
"Thank you."
He touched the brim of his hat, which was wet through, and turned.
The dog turned with him without being told.
I watched them as far as the arch and then I shut the door.
I thought, with the same dry clarity I had used on Stainforth in the cellar, that it was the season for tired men and I was a tired woman and there was nothing in this to puzzle over.
I hung the lantern back on its hook.
I went to the sink.
There was the last of the evening's work to do; the pots from the chops, two knives, the long wooden spoon.
