I had told Nan to wear her clean apron.
I had checked the state of every room we were currently letting—four out of twenty, a thin week—and found nothing wanting, and had gone back to the kitchen and made myself eat breakfast.
Stainforth arrived at half past ten.
A man who comes at half past ten has chosen an hour when the coaches have gone and the taproom is empty and there is nothing else claiming your attention.
He was tall, spare, and dressed in the kind of careful coat that costs twice what it looks like it costs.

I had seen him perhaps six times in two years: twice when the lease came up for review, once at the winter parish fair, twice when he had occasion to ride past on the road and decided the occasion required commentary on the inn's condition.
The sixth time had been the letter, which I had read three times and then put face down on my desk and not looked at again.
He stood in the doorway of the taproom and looked at the room the way a carpenter looks at a structure he suspects is not square.
"Miss Dale."
He inclined his head.
"I appreciate your making time."
I had not made time.
He had arrived and I had answered the door.
But I said, "Mr Stainforth," and stepped back to let him in, because arguing about who had made time for whom was not the battle I needed to win.
The taproom was clean.
The flagstones swept, the tables wiped, the glasses stacked behind the bar in their proper order, the fire built up against the November cold.
The White Hound smelled of woodsmoke and the morning's first pot of coffee and the faint clean smell of a house that was looked after.
Stainforth did not appear to see it this way.
He walked the length of the taproom slowly, hands clasped behind his back, and looked at the ceiling, the walls, the bar, the fire.
His eyes moved the way an appraiser's eyes move.
He didn't touch anything.
He didn't need to.
When he reached the far end of the room he turned and walked back the same way.
His civil manner, which was worse than anger.
I had prepared for anger.
"The place appears well-maintained," he said.
"It is."
"Business steady, through the autumn?"
"Adequate."
A pause while he studied the bottles behind the bar.
"And your staff.
The stable hand—Bowker, is it?"
"Jem Bowker.
He's been with us eleven years."
"Good."
He said it as though he had tested a beam and found it sound.
"And you have a young woman working the bar?"
"Nan Soulden.
She's been with me since she was fourteen."
"Good."
He turned from the bar.
"Miss Dale, I want to be straightforward with you.
I have had some concerns raised—by several parties in the parish—about the inn's recent custom.
The character of it."
I kept my hands flat on the bar top.
"The White Hound has served the Great North Road for forty years, Mr Stainforth.
The character of our custom is what it has always been: travellers in need of a meal and a bed."
"Demobilised soldiers."
He said it without inflection, as though it were a category of weather.
"A number of them, by some accounts.
Lingering on the road.
Making use of the inn's—generosity."
"Some of them need feeding and I feed them when I can.
I was not aware that was a condition of the lease."
"It isn't."
He smiled.
"No one would suggest that a woman of your good character would do otherwise.
What I would suggest is that an establishment that becomes known as a waystation for the dispossessed may attract—difficulties.
Of various kinds.
The parish has an interest in maintaining order on the road."
A cold feeling in the pit of my stomach, but I held it there.
"There has been no disorder at the White Hound."
"Not yet."
He let that sit for a moment.
"I have the highest respect for your mother's memory, Miss Dale, and for what you've accomplished here since her passing.
But an inn of this size, on a road of this importance, requires leadership of a particular kind.
Continuity.
Stability."
I heard what he meant.
He said leadership.
He meant a man.
"I believe the inn's ledgers demonstrate the quality of its leadership," I said.
"Ledgers tell one kind of story."
He moved along the bar, unhurried, trailing a finger across the wood without quite touching it.
"A woman of your age—twenty-seven, I believe?—might naturally be thinking about her future.
About arrangements that would allow the inn to thrive and also provide her with security of a more permanent kind."
"My future is the inn," I said.
"Yes."
He nodded as though I had confirmed something he had suspected.
"Which is precisely my concern.
The lease renews in March.
I would hate for its review to be complicated by circumstances that could easily be avoided with a little foresight on both our parts."
He moved toward the door, unhurried.
"I thought it courteous to speak with you directly, rather than routing the matter through a solicitor.
You have time to consider your options."
There it was.
Options.
Formal review.
March.
An entire machinery of law arranged against a woman holding a lease, and he was explaining it to me as though he were doing me a favour.
"I appreciate your courtesy," I said.
He nodded and left.
His horse was a grey, well-kept.
He mounted without looking back and rode south at an easy pace, as though he had completed an errand and was thinking about the next one.
I stood in the empty taproom listening to his horse on the road until I couldn't hear it anymore.
Then I went to the kitchen and put the kettle on, because I didn't know what else to do with my hands.
Nan found me there twenty minutes later, staring at the wall.
"He gone?"
"He's gone."
She set down the basket she'd brought from the village—eggs, dried herbs, a paper of nutmeg—and looked at me.
"Bad?"
"Not loud.
The quiet kind."
"Bloody hell."
She began unpacking onto the kitchen table, quick and matter-of-fact.

And to suggest that I consider my future."
I poured hot water into the pot.
"He said stability."
Nan set down the eggs with considerable care.

It startled a laugh out of me.
Not a large one.
Enough.
I poured two cups and pushed one toward her, and we stood in the kitchen and drank tea.
We had until March.
That was something.
Ninety-two days.
After a while she said, "Will you go up to Bridget?"
"Later," I said.
"After the lunch trade."
She nodded, and picked up the eggs, and went about the day.

The lunch trade was modest—two commercial travellers and a family of four going north, the children exhausted and cross, the mother not much better—and I ran the dining room and helped clear and kept a running tally in my head of what it came to and whether it was enough.
Adequate.
It was always adequate, just barely, this autumn.
I locked the dining room at half past two and went up to Bridget.

Her rooms were at the top of the back stair, three flights, which she navigated with considerable dignity and pain in both knees, though she would have sooner walked them on her hands than admitted it.

She was in her chair by the window, cards laid out in a patience.
She did not look up.
Through the window: the yard below, and beyond the yard fence the Great North Road—a grey stripe of churned mud running north toward Baldock, south toward London.

"He came, then," she said, to her cards.
"He came."
She turned over the nine of hearts and placed it with the satisfied precision of a woman who has been winning arguments for seventy-two years.
"How was he?"
"Civil."
"He's always civil."
She turned another card.
"That's what makes him dangerous.

Of the lease's terms."

"I'm not certain she was right."
The fire settled.

I stayed another quarter of an hour.

He arrived at half past nine.

We'd had no custom since the six o'clock post—a thin November evening, wet and cold—and I had sent Nan home an hour before and banked the kitchen fire and was about to go up to bed when I heard the knock at the side door.
The one facing the stable yard.
I opened it with a tallow candle in one hand.

Not young, but not old.
Thirty, perhaps.
Dark-haired.
Contained.
The dog sat down in the rain as though sitting in the rain were an entirely reasonable thing to do.

"I saw the light."
He didn't move toward me or away from me.
"I'm looking for work.
Anything you have."

"What can you do?"
"Horses.
Stable work.
Repairs."

The candle guttered in the draft and I held it steady and looked at him.
The coat was good, once.

His hands, when the candle caught them, were the hands of a man who worked.

The kitchen was cold when I came down at four.
Not the deep cold of January, when the flagstones bit through your stockings and the water in the basin grew a skin of ice overnight.
This was October cold — a thin, spiteful thing that crept in under the back door and settled into the joints of the building like damp into old wood.
I knelt at the hearth and scraped out the ash from last night's fire, rebuilt it with kindling and a twist of straw, and blew until my eyes stung and the flames caught.
The fire decided the rest.
Once it was lit, the kitchen had a centre, and everything else arranged itself around it: kettle on the crane, bread from the crock, the stubborn knot in my back loosening as the room warmed.
I checked the bread.
Still good enough if I wasn't fussy about it.
Filled the kettle, hung it, wiped my hands on my apron.
Clean.
It would not be clean by noon.
Two rooms above the kitchen.
Sitting room that doubled as a workroom.
Bedroom door that didn't latch.
View of the yard.
Mine.
But the kitchen was where I started every day and where I ended them, and I could not have explained why except that it was mine in a way the rest of the inn was not.
The rest belonged to the guests, to the coaches, to the road.
The kitchen answered to nobody but me.
I had the ledger open by the time the first grey light came through the window.
Candles down to fourteen.
Flour good for four days, five if I stretched it.
Ale enough for the week unless a full coach came through, which it would, because they always did.
Grain prices had doubled since spring.
The barley harvest had failed across three counties.
The summer that never came — no warmth, no sun, rain from April through September — had rotted the wheat in the fields and driven the cost of bread to a place that made my chest tight when I counted.
I wrote the figures and moved on.
By six the inn was stirring.

I could track it by sound: Nan's quick step on the back stairs, the scrape of the yard gate where Jem dragged it open one-handed, the distant complaint of the hens when Nan's younger cousin — borrowed twice a week for the rough work — failed to feed them on time.
The White Hound had twenty guest rooms, a taproom, a dining room that seated thirty, and stabling for forty horses, and it ran on four people and a borrowed girl of fifteen.
My grandmother had run it with six.
My mother had managed five.
I managed with what I had, which was not enough, and I managed anyway.
Jem Bowker came to the kitchen door at half six for his tea and his report.
He stood in the doorway because he never sat down during working hours, and because the kitchen was my territory and Jem understood territory.
"North road's soft," he said.
"Ruts from yesterday's rain.
The Doddington coach'll be late."
"How late?"
"Half an hour.
Maybe more."
I handed him his tea.
He took it with his right hand.
The left was gone below the elbow — Salamanca, a French cannonball, the earthwork he'd been sheltering behind.
He didn't discuss it.
I didn't ask.
"The bay in stall four is favouring her off hind," he said.
"Badly?"
"Stone bruise.
She'll be right in two days if we rest her."
"Rest her, then."
Jem nodded.
He finished his tea, set the cup on the windowsill, and went back to the yard.
Our morning conferences rarely lasted longer than the tea.
He said what needed saying and then went and did something about it, which put him ahead of most men I had met in twenty-seven years.
The Doddington coach came in forty minutes late.
I heard the horn from the kitchen and was in the yard before the wheels stopped turning.
Six passengers, cold, stiff, cross.
A woman with a child who needed feeding.
A clergyman who wanted a private dining room, which we didn't have, and settled for a corner of the taproom with poor grace.
A commercial traveller who argued about the price of a bed for the night.
I ended that one with a look that Nan later told me could have stripped paint.
Nan Soulden was behind the bar by the time the passengers came inside.
Twenty-one, small, quick, her hair already escaping its cap the way it did by seven every morning.
She had been at the White Hound since she was fourteen, and there was nothing about the running of an inn that she didn't know and very little about the running of people that got past her.
"Clergyman wants coddled eggs," she said as I passed through the taproom.
"I've told him we've got what we've got."
"Which is?"
"Boiled.
Or boiled."
I didn't smile.
But I wanted to.
The morning coach brought the post.
Three letters for guests, a bill from the brewer that I would deal with later, and nothing else.
The road brought what it brought — coaches, strangers, commerce, trouble — and the inn absorbed it all.
I dealt with the chandler at ten.

His name was Pollard, and he had been overcharging me for tallow candles since July, and I had let it go because he was the nearest supplier and the alternative was a man in Stevenage who wanted payment in advance.
But the latest invoice had him charging fourpence ha'penny a pound when the going rate was threepence, and I told him so in the yard with Jem nearby and the October wind cutting through my shawl.
Pollard was a round, red-faced man who smiled when he was cornered.
"Now, Miss Dale," he said.
"You must understand.
The tallow supply's been short since —"
"Since you decided to charge me a penny more than you charge the Red Lion."
His smile held.
"The Red Lion orders in quantity."
"The Red Lion orders twelve pounds a month.
I order fifteen.
You know this because I have the receipts."
He opened his mouth.
I waited.
He closed it.
"Threepence ha'penny," I said.
"Or I write to the man in Stevenage today, and you lose fifteen pounds a month for the sake of a penny you thought I wouldn't notice."
Pollard left at threepence ha'penny.
I would have taken threepence three-farthings.
He didn't need to know that.
Nan was watching from the kitchen doorway when I came back inside, her arms crossed.
"You enjoyed that," she said.
"I did not enjoy it.
I won it.
There's a difference."
"If you say so."
I say so.
The soldier came at noon.
He was the third that week.
They came down the Great North Road in ones and twos now, heading north or south or nowhere, wearing what was left of their uniforms and carrying what was left of their kit.
The army had discharged them with a handshake and a few shillings and pointed them toward a country that had no work, no food, and no patience for the men who had fought its war.
Some were decent.
Some were dangerous.
I could tell the difference inside thirty seconds.
This one was decent.
I knew it from the way he stood at the kitchen door — cap in his hands, waiting to be told what to do.
Young.
Twenty, perhaps.
Thin in the way that comes from weeks of walking on bad rations.
His coat had been red once.
"Sit down," I said.
He sat at the kitchen table, and I gave him bread and broth and the end of yesterday's cheese.
He ate steadily, without rushing.
I didn't ask his name.
I didn't ask where he'd served.
He looked up once.
"Thank you, miss."
"Finish your broth."
He finished it.
I wrapped two rolls in cloth and gave them to him for the road.
He stood, put his cap back on, and walked out through the yard toward the Great North Road.
I didn't watch him go.
I had the dinner to think about and fourteen candles to last the week.
I fed them when I could.
Bread and broth, never coin.
It was something my mother had done, and her mother before her, and I was not going to be the one who stopped.
By the time I cleared his bowl, my hands were rough and my back had settled into the low ache that would carry me through to evening.
I poured myself a cup of tea and stood at the kitchen window, looking out at the yard.
From her rooms above the inn, Aunt Bridget would be watching the same yard.
She sat there most days — small, white-haired, dressed in black, sharp-eyed, missing nothing.
She had lived above the White Hound for twenty-six years.
My mother used to say Bridget saw more of the inn from her chair than the rest of us saw running it, and my mother had been right about most things.
I thought about my mother twice a day.
Once in the morning, when I rebuilt the fire the way she had taught me.
Once at night, when I locked the back door and the empty kitchen sat around me.
She had died in this room.
Two years ago.
An apoplexy, mid-service, during the evening rush.
She had been ladling soup.
She fell, and the soup spilled, and Jem carried her upstairs while I served the rest of the dinner, because the coaches would not wait and if I stopped I would have to feel it.
I did not stop.
I served the dinner.
I cleared the tables.
I washed the pots.
I locked the doors.
And then I sat in this kitchen at this table and I allowed myself the space of ten breaths.
Then I was done.
I would not marry.
I had refused two proposals and stopped entertaining the possibility of a third.
If I married, the lease transferred.
The income transferred.
The business my grandmother had built — three generations, sixty years — would belong to a man because I'd stood in a church and signed a register.
I would sooner chew my own boot.
There were women who married well and kept what was theirs through the goodwill of decent husbands.
I didn't doubt such men existed.
I doubted the wisdom of betting the White Hound on one.
The afternoon was a broken hinge on the door of room six, a drayman who charged me for four casks and delivered three, and Nan losing her temper with a guest who pinched her arm.
She lost it quietly, with a smile that made the man back up two steps without understanding why.
I liked Nan's temper.
It got things done.
I was in the kitchen at five, rolling out pastry for the pies, when Nan brought the second post.
"Letter for you," she said, and set it on the table beside the flour.
I wiped my hands.
Good paper — heavier than anything I bought.
Dark red seal pressed with an insignia I didn't recognise.
The direction in a careful, clerking hand.
Miss Dinah Dale, Proprietress, The White Hound, Great North Road, Nr.
Stevenage, Hertfordshire.
I broke the seal.
Dear Miss Dale,
I write to request the courtesy of a meeting at your earliest convenience.
There are certain matters pertaining to the lease of the White Hound which I should like to discuss with you in person.
I am confident we can resolve them to our mutual satisfaction.
I remain, Madam, your obedient servant,
Phineas Stainforth
I read it twice.
I set it down on the table.
The pies would not make themselves.
Seven-forty-two, and there were six of them.
I counted from the window because counting was something I could do without committing to anything.
Six squirrels on the tree line, sitting in a neat row, all of them facing the cottage.
I'd had five yesterday.
Four the day before.
Three the day before that.
I'd been calling it coincidence, which was a thing I was getting good at.
I pressed my thumb into the windowsill.
Bare wood where the paint had worn down to fir.
I'd made that groove myself over the past year.
One of them blinked.
Not the way squirrels blink.

The whole animal went, a flicker like a frame dropped from a reel, and in the gap there was something with a narrow red snout and amber eyes, and then there was a squirrel again, sitting in exactly the same spot, flicking its tail at nothing.
I pressed my thumb harder into the wood and held it there.
"Okay," I said.
"That's new."
I turned away from the window.
My nails were clipped too short.
I'd done it yesterday, impatient, and now I couldn't do the palm thing.
I'd manage.
I went to check the salt.
Every windowsill, a thin line of it.
Every sill of every exterior door.
The water bowls I refreshed every morning: one by the front door, one by the back, one on the kitchen counter where I could reach it fast.
My mother had kept the same setup in every house we'd rented.
I kept them after her because the cost of not keeping them was a number I had no interest in learning.
Two rooms above Gail Torvik's converted garage.
Kitchen that was also the living room.
Bedroom with a door that didn't quite latch.
Shower that ran cold for the first minute no matter how long you ran it.
No mirrors.
Mine.

Three years and the place had grown around me the way places do when you stop paying attention: books against the baseboards, cold teas started and abandoned, the smell of salt that wasn't entirely the ocean.
The mirrors I'd handled early on.
Broke them and didn't replace them, and I told myself at the time it was practical, one less thing to keep clean, and after a while the explanation stopped mattering.
I knew the layout of this place well enough that I didn't need to see myself in it.
I stood at the window with my cold tea.
The squirrels watched me.
I watched them back.
The one on the far left shifted its weight and adjusted its tail.
The rest didn't move.
Six of them sitting in a line, patient in the way things were patient when they were waiting.

I tried to decide if squirrels were territorial enough to do this, if there was some legitimate ecological explanation for six of them facing the same direction at the same time of morning, if I was just another person seeing patterns in randomness.
The brain argument was less convincing every day.
I drank the tea.
It was cold enough to make my teeth ache.
I'd dreamed Lyle Evenson's face last night.

Not the fox, not the squirrels, not Margery Halloran's breathing — Lyle Evenson's face, and I'd woken up at two in the morning with it sitting there in the dark in front of me like it had always been there.
I'd filed it.
The fox was a genuinely new development.
Lyle Evenson's face in a dream was not new and was not, in any meaningful sense, a problem.
I made myself another tea.
This one would get cold too, but making it gave me something to do for three minutes.
I thought about the fox.
Red snout, amber eyes, there and gone in less than a second.
I'd seen slips before, a dog that was briefly too large, a bird that banked at the wrong angle, but always small and fleeting, the kind you could write off.
This one I couldn't write off.
This one had looked back at me.
Karen Halloran called at six.
I'd been awake since five, not sleeping, just lying in the dark cycling through the list of things I wasn't going to think about.
Karen H.
lit up my phone and I was already reaching for my coat.
"Her breathing changed," Karen said.
"I'll be there in ten minutes."
Margery Halloran was in her bed with the window cracked an inch.
The hydrangeas outside were visible from where she lay, the blue ones she'd planted the year her husband died, almost gray in the October morning.
Her breathing had changed.

I knew this shift by now, the way you knew something you'd learned in your body rather than your head: the pauses between breaths getting longer, each one stretched a little past the last, the body beginning to let go of what it had been doing for eighty-one years.
You didn't rush it.
You sat down, took their hand, and you stayed.
I sat beside her.
Her hand was cool and papery and light.
I knew it by now.

Four months, twice a week, and in that time I'd learned her medication schedule and the name of every plant in her yard and the fact that she found the phrase "passed away" insufferable and wanted "died" and would tell you so unprompted.
She had opinions about the neighbor's fence and the hospice organization's morphine supply and the only correct method for boiling an egg.
She offered these opinions without apology.
I'd liked that about her from the first visit.
"Hey, Margery."
I kept my voice low.
"I'm here."
She didn't answer.
She was already somewhere else, not gone but going, in that corridor they all moved through at the end.
I'd sat at enough of these to know the corridor was real.
You could feel it in the room when someone was in it: a pressure drop, a stillness that had nothing to do with ordinary quiet.
Not the quiet of a room that was empty.
The quiet of a room that was holding still on purpose.
The body had a rhythm at the end.
I'd learned this from sitting in rooms and paying attention until it stopped being something I thought and started being something I knew in my hands.
Each pause between breaths a little longer than the last, the body easing its grip on what it had been doing.
Tide going out.
The only job was to sit with your hand in theirs and not interfere.
Karen sat in the corner chair.
Hands flat on her thighs, back straight, watching her mother's chest.
She'd been crying before I got there.
She was steady now.
"Does she know you're here?"
Karen asked.
"I think so."
I didn't know.
Nobody did.
But it was the right answer and I'd learned to give it cleanly, without the half-second hesitation that made people feel worse.
The pauses between breaths stretched.
Karen's lips started to move and I realized she was counting.
I put my free hand on her arm, gently, and she stopped.
Counting wasn't the job.
We sat.
Outside the cracked window the hydrangeas shifted in a little wind.
The room held itself quiet.
The breaths came slower, and then slower, and the pauses between them grew until they were the main event and the breathing was what interrupted them.
"She looks peaceful," Karen said.
"She does."
True, and also a kindness, and it wasn't my job to sort out the difference.
At eight-twelve, the breathing stopped.
The last breath came and the pause after it just kept going, longer and longer, and that was it.
I kept Margery Halloran's hand.
The room stayed quiet.

I waited until the body had finished understanding what had happened to it — this took longer than people expected, always — and then I set her hand gently on the blanket, folded her fingers over each other, and stood.
Karen made a sound in her throat, small and bitten-off.
I handed her the tissue box from the bedside table and stepped into the hallway to call the hospice nurse.
One thing from the end, filed away: at the last moment, her hand had tightened around mine.
A real grip, deliberate, the kind that costs something.
Then it let go.
I had a place for things like that.
Gail Torvik was on my doorstep when I got back, holding a container of soup.
She was my landlord and my downstairs neighbor and the person who had decided sometime in my first year above her garage that feeding me was part of the arrangement.
I'd stopped arguing about it.

She was fifty-three, built like someone who'd carried her own furniture up too many staircases, and she had a talent for knowing which of her opinions to keep to herself that I considered one of her better qualities.
"Heard the van," she said.
"She went quietly.
She was ready."
Gail nodded.
I'd noticed over the years she always asked how the deaths went, never the medical details, just whether it was okay at the end.
She'd lost her own mother two years before I moved in.
She never mentioned it directly.
She didn't need to.
"Eat something," she said.
"I will."
"That means you won't."
"It means I'll take it seriously and then probably not."
She squinted at me.
Gail had a squint that had seen through a lot of things and wasn't impressed by most of them.
"You look terrible."
"Thank you, Gail."
"How long since you slept?"
I took the soup because it was easier than the math on that question.
She watched me take it and I could see her running the calculation on whether to push harder.
She decided not to.
This was why we worked, the two of us.
"Lentils," she said.
"Your favorite."
"My favorite is Thai food."
"Your favorite that I make."
"You've never made Thai food."
"Correct."
She looked at me a moment longer, the way she did when she was deciding something.
"You're not sleeping, Nell."
"I'm fine."
"You've still got your coat on."
I looked down.
She was right.
I'd come in from Karen Halloran's and stood at the counter and eaten half a container of soup and still had my coat on.
"I was cold," I said.
Gail made a sound that meant she didn't believe me but wasn't going to say so.
She went back downstairs.
I took my coat off.
Set it on the back of the chair.
Stood at the kitchen window and looked out at the tree line, which was empty now.
No squirrels.
Just the gray afternoon light doing what it always did on the coast in October, which was make everything the same flat color.
I reheated the soup and ate half of it standing at the counter.
I thought about Margery Halloran's hand at the end, the grip of it.
I thought about the corridor in that room, the stillness.
I thought about the fox blink at seven-forty-two, the amber eyes, the squirrel sitting back into place after like nothing had happened.
One thing and then the next and then the one before.
I didn't think about Lyle Evenson.
I'd been not-thinking about him for five years and I was fucking good at it.
The dream at two in the morning was nothing.
I filed it.
I held off sleep as long as I could.
Dishes first.
Then the herbs on the kitchen windowsill, reorganized by no system I could explain to anyone.
Then forty pages of a novel I'd been reading for two months, none of which I retained.
I refreshed the water bowls.
I walked each room and checked every salt line.
I stood at the kitchen window and looked out at the tree line, which was dark by then, the pines just shapes against the sky.
By eleven I was making another tea I had no intention of drinking.
I stood at the table with the book open and tried to get through the same paragraph for the sixth time.
The paragraph wasn't the problem.
Margery Halloran's hand was the problem.
The fox blink was the problem.
Lyle Evenson's face at two in the morning was the problem, filed and still sitting there like something that knew it had been misfiled.
I'd been keeping them moving all day, one and then the next and then the one before, so none of them had room to settle into the thing I was actually dealing with.
After midnight, I ran out of things to do standing up.
The bedroom was cold, the draft coming in under the door that didn't quite latch.
I lay in the dark and counted the things in the room: chair, dresser, the stack of books I kept meaning to sort, the bat propped against the wall by the bed because old habits die slow.
I counted them twice.
I started over.
At some point I stopped knowing what I was doing.
The dream: a gray beach, the sand the color of ash.
A woman with her back to me, walking toward the water.
Hair loose and dark, moving a little even though I couldn't hear any wind.
The ocean was wrong — too flat, too still, the surface of it not moving the way water moved.
I was at the tree line.
My legs wouldn't work.

She kept walking and the water took her, up to her knees and then her waist and then her shoulders, and I could see the back of her head and then just the top of it and then nothing, and just before the water closed over where she'd been I had sand between my teeth, gritty and fine and real, and then I was awake.
I lay still.
My chest was doing the tight thing.
I breathed until it stopped.
Outside, the window had gone pale with early light.
On the tree line, probably, six squirrels were sitting in a row.
Some things you don't look at.
You just keep moving.
I got up.
Six squirrels at 7:42 AM.
Same six, same row, same spot at the tree line where the scrub pine met the blackberry tangle and the morning mist hadn't burned off yet.
They sat with their tails curled over their backs and their faces pointed at my window like I owed them something.
I pressed my thumb into the windowsill.
One of them blinked into a fox.
Red fur, narrow snout, amber eyes.
Half a second, and then it was a squirrel again.
The others didn't react.
I pressed harder into the sill and counted the grain of the wood under my thumbnail and waited until my pulse did something reasonable.
"Okay," I said, to myself and the window and the six squirrels that were definitely just squirrels.
"That's new."
It wasn't, actually.
That was the problem.
I'd seen it twice in the past two weeks.
The flicker at the edge of right, something slipping through a gap in the normal order of things and snapping back before I could look at it straight on.
I was getting good at not looking at it straight on.
I pressed my thumb in one more time and then I let go and went to deal with the morning.
My nails were too short to do the palm thing.
I'd clipped them yesterday without thinking about it, and the bite wasn't landing the way it needed to.
I made a note to let them grow.
The front door bowl was still clear.
I checked it on the way past to the kitchen.
The back window one had gone cloudy overnight.
Dumped it in the sink, refilled it from the tap, set it back in its spot.
Then the rest: kitchen windowsill, bedroom, bathroom, living room.
Salt undisturbed on all four.
Lines unbroken, solid end-to-end.
No shortcuts.
Fingertip along each sill.
Twelve minutes, same as every morning.
The apartment was two rooms above Gail's converted garage.
Kitchen that was also the living room, bedroom with a door that didn't quite latch, bathroom with a showerhead that ran cold for the first sixty seconds.
No mirrors.
I'd broken those the first week, which had felt dramatic at the time and turned out to be practical.
The place didn't have much going for it besides the price and the landlady and the fact that nobody knew where it was.
That covered most of its sins.
I stood at the counter and drank my cold tea and looked at the tree line.
The six squirrels were still there, tails up, faces pointed toward my window.
I'd been watching them for eleven days.
Eleven mornings of six squirrels at the same spot at 7:42, and now this on top of it.
Those amber eyes that had looked at me, not the way an animal looked at movement but the way something looked at you when it already knew exactly what it was looking at.
The other five not reacting at all.
I had a couple of theories about what it meant and I was not going to think about any of them right now.
I put the cup down and rinsed it.
The fog was starting to thin at the edges of the tree line.
Not gone, just shifting.

The squirrels sat where they'd been sitting since I came to the window, and none of them moved, and I stood there looking at them for longer than was reasonable and then I stopped doing that and went to get dressed.
I had a client at nine.

Estelle Halloran, who had been in the process of dying for three weeks now and whose daughter Karen had been calling me twice a day, convinced every change in breathing meant it was happening right now, and most of the time it hadn't been.
But it would be soon.
I'd sat with enough people to know what the body looked like when it was getting close to done.
Estelle was close.
I made a second cup of tea I also wasn't going to drink and stood at the window again, not looking at the squirrels this time, just watching the fog pull back from the water below the hill.
November in Manzanita was fog and rain and cold that came off the ocean in the mornings and sometimes lifted by noon and sometimes didn't.
I'd been here almost two years and I knew the difference between the fog that was going to burn off and the fog that was just going to get lower.
This one was going to burn off.
My phone buzzed at six-oh-three.
"She's changing."
Karen Halloran had the flat voice she used when she was reporting instead of feeling.
Three weeks of waiting had burned through most of what she had.
"The breathing.
It changed about twenty minutes ago.
I don't."
She stopped.
Started again.
"I don't know if I'm reading it right."
"You're reading it right."
She'd asked me what to listen for, and I'd told her, and now she'd heard it.
"I'm on my way.
Ten minutes."
"Okay."
A shorter pause.
"Should I go in there?
While I wait?"
"If you want to be in there, be in there.
There's no wrong answer."
I was already pulling my jacket off the hook.
"Karen.
You called at the right time."
She didn't answer that.
I didn't need her to.
I went out the door and down the stairs and didn't look at the tree line on the way.
Estelle's house was four blocks downhill toward the water, a white craftsman with a garden that had been better maintained when she could still get down on her knees.
The fog sat thick over the ocean this morning.
You couldn't find the horizon anywhere, just gray water bleeding into gray air, the coastline gone soft at the edges.
Manzanita knew how to do this kind of morning.
Karen let me in without a word and pointed upstairs.
She'd been crying recently, the skin around her eyes still pink, but she wasn't now.
She had the look of someone who'd used up most of their grief in advance and was running on whatever was left at the bottom.
"Is she" Karen started.
"Still here.
Go get some water for yourself."
She went to the kitchen.
I went upstairs.
Estelle was in her bed with the window cracked the inch she'd always wanted cracked.
The hydrangeas were visible through the glass, the blue ones she'd planted the year her husband died, browning a little at the edges now that November had come in hard.
Her breathing had changed in the night.
The rattle of it was unmistakable now, the body doing the last slow work, each breath coming a little later than the one before.
I sat in the chair by the bed.
"Hey, Estelle."
Low and even.
"I'm here.
Karen called me.
You're okay."
She didn't respond.
She hadn't been responding much since yesterday.
I talked to her anyway, just a little, nothing important.
My voice in the room.
