So I stayed up.
I read until I stopped caring who did it.
Made tea and let it go cold, same as the morning.
At nine I checked the bowls again, not because they needed it but because it gave me something to do.
I washed up.
I organized the shelf above the counter by size, which was a thing I'd done before and which made me feel faintly ridiculous, but it took twenty minutes and twenty minutes was twenty minutes.

I sat on the edge of the bed at eleven-thirty and told myself I'd just close my eyes for a bit and that was obviously not going to work, so I got up and went back to the window and stood there until I couldn't anymore.
At some point I was looking at the tree line again.
Waiting for something to be there.
Nothing was.
I turned off the lamp.
I was already half under when I smelled it.
Salt and low tide and something cold underneath, mineral and sharp, the smell the ocean got right before a hard storm came in off the Pacific.
I knew that smell.
I tried to get ahead of it anyway.
Gray beach.
Sky the color of nothing.
A woman walking out into the water, and the waves weren't breaking around her, they were moving through her, or she was moving through them, the water not noticing her at all.
Getting farther out.
I was standing at the waterline and my feet just wouldn't—
Sand between my teeth when I woke.
Palms flat on the mattress, pressing down.
Heart doing something I needed it to stop doing.
I lay there and breathed until it settled.
Then I got up.
I didn't think about the dream.
The front bowl was still clear.
The back window one had gone cloudy again overnight.
I dumped it, refilled it, set it back.
I didn't think about the woman or the water or whose face she had when she turned around.
Some things you don't look at.
You just keep moving.
Six squirrels.
Same tree line as yesterday, same neat row along the lowest branch, watching my window with those small flat eyes.
I counted them because counting was something to do with my hands while the tea went cold.
The fog hadn't lifted off the water yet.
It wouldn't for another hour.
I pressed my thumb into the windowsill.
Old groove, my groove, worn into the paint above the sill plate where I'd been pressing it for fourteen months.
I'd clipped my nails too short yesterday.
Couldn't grip my palms without them, which meant I was down to the windowsill, which meant I was standing at the window again staring at six squirrels in a row.
One of them blinked.
Not at me.
Not in the way squirrels blink.
Its face went red, narrow snout, amber eyes, a muzzle where the round nose had been, and for half a second it wasn't a squirrel at all and then it was again and the branch didn't even tremble.
I took my thumb off the windowsill.
"Okay," I said, to no one.
"That's new."
I was getting good at finding new.
The crow last Tuesday that had dropped off a telephone wire and hit the pavement as a cat and then been a crow again before I'd finished blinking.
The shape in the morning fog off the beach two weeks ago that walked like a person for three steps and then didn't.
I wasn't making them up.
I'd stopped telling myself I was making them up around month four, which had not made anything easier, but at least I'd stopped arguing with myself about it.
I drank the cold tea at the window and checked the salt.
Kitchen sill, front door sill, back step.
Front door bowl still clean.
Back door bowl had gone cloudy overnight.
I emptied it, refilled it from the tap, set it back down.
Then I stood there looking at the squirrel tree again because apparently that was what I did now.
Still six of them.
None of them were a fox.
So that was fine.
My apartment was two rooms above Gail Torvik's converted garage on the north side of Manzanita.
Kitchen bled into the living room.
Bedroom door that didn't quite latch.
Shower that ran cold for the first minute exactly.
Fourteen months and I knew all of it by now — the rhythms, the sounds, the salt bowls by both doors, the water bowls.
No mirrors.
I'd broken the last one eleven months ago when I'd looked into it at the wrong moment and seen something looking back at me that had my face but wasn't quite right.
I hadn't replaced it.
You got used to things faster than you thought.
The squirrel thing had started three weeks ago.
One squirrel, then two, then this week six in a row every morning at the same time.
I'd been tracking them the way you tracked anything that might matter: quietly, without telling anyone, without letting myself decide yet what it meant.
I thought about the dream I'd had last night.
The gray beach, the woman walking into the water, and before the beach, the other one.
The one I'd been not-having for four years.
Lyle Evenson's face in my dream.
Again.
That was worse than the fox.
I thought about it for exactly the amount of time it took me to refill my tea and then I didn't.
I had to be at Mrs.
Halloran's by six-thirty.
Karen Halloran called at six.
"She's changed," Karen said.
"The breathing."
"I'll be there in ten minutes."
I'd been sitting with Mrs.
Halloran since August.
She'd found me through a hospice referral, a name on a list that one of the nurses kept for families who wanted something the medical team couldn't provide.
I'd gone over with my bag and my salt habit and the ability to sit quietly in rooms where people were dying, and Mrs.
Halloran had looked me over from her recliner with those flat brown eyes and said, "You'll do," and that had been the whole interview.
I'd liked her from that moment.
She was in her bed when I got there, the window cracked an inch, the curtain lifting with the onshore air.
The hydrangeas she'd planted the year her husband died were just visible through the gap, the blue ones, almost gray in the coastal morning.
I set my bag by the door and didn't turn on the overhead light.
Karen was in the chair by the window, ankles crossed, hands in her lap.
She'd been crying since sometime in the night.
She was steady now.
I nodded at her.
She nodded back.
I pulled the other chair close to the bed.
Mrs.
Halloran's chest moved, slow, uneven, the pauses longer than the pulls.
I knew this rhythm.
I took her hand.
Cool and dry, the skin loose over the knuckles.
I knew the feel of it by now.
"She's been like this since four," Karen said from her chair.
"Good," I said.
Karen looked at me.
"Better than the other kind," I said.
Not explaining it, just saying it.
Karen nodded once and looked back at her mother.
The room was quiet after that.
That was the job, mostly — being someone who could be in a room like this without needing to fill it.
Some families wanted music, or prayer, or someone to narrate what was happening as it happened.
I didn't do any of that.
I just sat.
I let the room be heavy.
The fog was against the cracked window and the hydrangeas outside were gray-blue in the early light and Mrs.
Halloran breathed and I held her hand and that was enough.
Karen got up once, quietly, and went down the hall.
Water ran.
She came back.
I said, quietly, to Mrs.
Halloran: "Your hydrangeas are still out.
The blue ones."
Because they'd been the last thing she'd asked about, three days ago when she could still ask things, and because people could hear longer than anyone gave them credit for.
Mrs.
Halloran's chest rose.
A long pause after.
"You did good," I said.
At the end her hand tightened.
Real grip.
I felt the bones of her fingers pressing into mine, deliberate, the kind that costs something.
Then she let go.
I stayed until there was nothing left to wait for, and for a few minutes after.
I counted the hydrangeas through the gap in the curtain.
Eleven heads, three going brown at the edges.
Then I set her hand on the blanket and stood up.
Karen was in the doorway.
"She was ready," I said.
"That's what mattered."
Karen made a sound that wasn't words.
I went to put the kettle on.
I stayed another hour.
I made the calls Karen couldn't make yet — the funeral home, the hospice coordinator, Karen's brother in Portland who cried on the phone for three minutes and then got very practical.
Karen sat at the kitchen table with her tea and I sat across from her and neither of us talked much, which was fine.
There was a rhythm to this part too.
You didn't push people through it.
You just stayed until they could breathe normally again, and then you left.
She walked me to the front door when I finally left.
"How do you do it?"
she asked from the step, one hand on the door frame, still in her cardigan.
"I couldn't do what you do."
"You'd be surprised what you can do when you do it enough times."
Karen looked at me carefully.
She had her mother's practical mouth.
"You looked like you hadn't slept before you even got here."
"I'm fine."
"That's a useless answer."
"I know.
It's still true."
I picked up my bag from the step.
"Call me about the paperwork.
Or whatever comes up.
Any of it."
"Nell."
She said my name the way her mother had, flat and direct.
"Are you actually all right?"
"I'm very good at this," I said.
"Go be with her."
She went inside.
I walked home through the fog.
Manzanita in the morning was quiet, no traffic yet, no dog walkers, just the muffled ocean three blocks west and the smell of it in everything.
Salt and cold and something older underneath.
My hands were in my jacket pockets and my boots were wet from the grass at the edge of Mrs.

Halloran's path and I walked past the bakery that wasn't open yet and the hardware store that was, lights on yellow in the gray, and a dog tied to a parking meter that watched me go by with a specific suspicion.
The fog was close enough to taste.
I didn't think about Lyle Evenson.
I was fucking good at that.
Gail Torvik was on her front step with a container of soup before I'd made it halfway up the outside stairs.
She was four foot eleven, sixty-three years old, and ran the bookshop below my apartment the way she ran most things: with opinions and without apology.
She appeared with food when food was needed.
I'd stopped trying to figure out how she knew.
"Soup," she said.
"I have food."
"This is better food."
She held it out and did not move.
I took the soup.
"How was she?"
Gail asked.
"Gone."
"Good death?"
"Yeah.
Good death."
Gail nodded.
She didn't try to hug me.
She'd figured out, early on, that I was not a contact-after person, and she'd never once pushed it, which was one of the things I liked best about her.
"Sleep," she said.
"I'm going to."
She looked at me with those ocean-gray eyes.
"You're going to sit up there staring at the squirrels again."
"The squirrels are doing some interesting things lately."
"Like what?"
"Like sitting in a row every morning watching my window."
"I've noticed that too," Gail said.
Not alarmed.
Just noting.
"You think they're—"
"I think they're squirrels," I said.
"I think I need sleep."
She held my eyes a beat.
"There's bread in the bottom bag," she said.
"Go with the soup."
"Gail."
"And there's butter on your counter.
I let myself in to leave it because yours was gone."
"You let yourself into my apartment."
"You gave me a key in case of emergencies."
"This wasn't an emergency."
"Margery Halloran died this morning and you haven't eaten since yesterday, which I know because I can hear your kitchen from mine.
That's an emergency."
She looked at me calmly.
"Eat the soup.
Sleep.
The squirrels will still be weird tomorrow."
I opened my mouth.
She pointed up the stairs.
I went upstairs.
Ate the soup at the counter, with the bread.
The squirrel branch was empty, the fog moving through the tree.
I washed the bowl and the mug from the morning and dried them and put them away.
Checked the salt on the windowsills.
Front bowl clean.
Back bowl clear.
I read for a while.
Didn't retain anything but the reading was a kind of company.
When that stopped working I made tea I didn't drink and stood at the dark window.
Nothing out there: fog and wet pavement and the bookshop sign swinging in the onshore wind.
I sat on the couch and pulled up Mrs.
Halloran's intake forms on my phone and filled in what I could and saved it and set the phone down.
Picked it back up.
I thought about calling Gail to tell her what I'd actually seen this morning — the fox-face and the amber eyes, the way the branch hadn't moved.
What it might mean.
Whether she'd know.
I put the phone down.
The slips were getting closer together.
That was the thing I hadn't let myself say out loud yet, not even to myself in the dark.
The crow had been two weeks after the fog-shape.
The fox today had been one week after the crow.
Whatever was bleeding through was bleeding through faster.
I'd been in Manzanita for fourteen months.
Left alone for fourteen months.
The slips were getting more frequent.
The squirrels were getting bolder.
New things had shapes you could read if you knew how, and I was choosing deliberately not to read them yet, because once I did, I couldn't unchoose it, and I wasn't ready for whatever came after.
I checked the time.
Past ten.
The apartment was quiet.
The salt bowls were clean.
The branch outside was empty and the fog was in the tree and there was nothing watching me right now that I could see.
I lay down on the bed in my clothes and stared at the ceiling.
Mrs.
Halloran's hand tightening on mine.
The bones of her fingers.
I turned that over once and set it down.
The squirrel with the amber eyes.
I didn't think about Lyle Evenson.
I was good at that.
Sleep came eventually.
For a while there was nothing at all.
Then: a gray beach.
Flat water, no color.
The sky the same gray as the sand with no line between them.
The smell of kelp cold and thick.
A woman at the waterline.
Her back to me.
Walking toward the water with that slow patient step, already decided, just carrying it out.
The surf came up around her ankles and she didn't stop.
I tried to call out to her.
My mouth was packed with sand, gritty on the back of my tongue.
The water was at her knees.
Her waist.
She didn't look back.
I woke with sand between my teeth.
I lay there with the gray late-afternoon pressing through the curtains and my heart doing something I told it to stop doing.
I stayed still until it did.
The room was exactly where I'd left it.
No beach, no woman, no water.
The dream was nothing.
I filed it under nothing and kept it there.
I'd been not-thinking about that beach for most of my life and I was fucking good at it.
Some things you don't look at.
You just keep moving.
Six squirrels in a neat row at the tree line, 7:42 AM.
I counted them from the window the way I counted the salt lines every morning and the water bowls and the forty-seven feet between the back door and the first tree.
The squirrels were new.
They sat too still.
Squirrels didn't sit still.
They sat in rows even less.
I'd clipped my nails too short yesterday, cut them past the quick in a mood, which meant I couldn't do the palm thing.
So the windowsill was what I had.
I pressed my thumb into the bare wood, old paint worn down to fir, rough and familiar, and held it until my pulse went somewhere reasonable.
I'd been awake since four.
The dream had done that.
I wasn't thinking about the dream.
The squirrel on the end blinked.
Red fur, narrow snout, amber eyes, fox, half a second, clear as anything, then squirrel again.
Same posture.
Same row.
I set down the mug.
"Okay," I said.
No one there.
"That's new."
I drank the cold tea standing with my back to the wall, eyes on the tree line.
Six squirrels.
None of them moved.
The fox didn't happen again.
I was glad, because the fox was manageable.
The fox was weird don't think about it, labeled and filed.
The dream was a different category.
The face in the dream was a different category still, which was why I wasn't thinking about it and was instead watching squirrels.
When the mug was empty I went to the front door first.
The water bowl I kept there was still full, undisturbed, positioned exactly where I'd left it.
I topped it off anyway because the ritual was the ritual.
Back door: same.
Kitchen counter bowl: same.
Then the salt.
I did the windowsills in order, kitchen first, then bedroom, then the bathroom window that didn't open but I treated it the same as the ones that did.
I ran my finger a half-inch above each line to feel for breaks.
Nothing.
Clean from end to end.
I'd been seeing slips like the fox for three weeks.
A crow on the power line with too many joints in its wings, gone ordinary when I blinked.
Gail's orange cat sitting in two places at once for three full seconds before resolving into just the one cat on the mat.
The fox blink this morning.
Each one filed as soon as it happened, tucked in next to the dream and the name and the rest of the things I wasn't thinking about.
I had a very organized filing system.
It was getting crowded.
The apartment had no mirrors.
I'd broken all three about eight months ago, bathroom and bedroom and the hall, and the compact in my bag as well, methodically, one after another over the course of a Tuesday evening.
I hadn't replaced them.
I didn't miss them.
The squirrels were still at the tree line when I left for Mrs.
Halloran's.
Karen Halloran's daughter had called at six, just before I'd have left anyway.
"The breathing's changed," Carol said.

She'd driven from Portland two days ago and I'd seen her at the house yesterday, standing in the kitchen with her hands around a mug and the closed-off look of someone who has made peace with something and can't stop resenting it.
"The long gaps.
Is that—"
"Yes," I said.
"I'll be there in ten minutes."
She exhaled.
Not relief.
The other thing, the one without a good name.
Mrs.
Halloran was eighty-one and had arranged everything herself.
The hospice paperwork done and filed before I'd even been called in.
The playlist on the tablet propped on the dresser, strings, slow, the kind of music she'd described to me once as the closest thing she had to silence.
The hydrangeas she'd planted the year her husband died, blue ones that went almost gray in the coastal morning light, in the window box exactly where she'd wanted them.
She'd shown me a photograph the first visit: herself in the garden, sleeves rolled, her husband's good trowel in her hand.
That trowel was on the windowsill beside the flowers.
She'd put it there herself, two weeks ago, when she could still put things places.
I sat in the chair beside the bed and took her hand.
Her breathing did what it did at the end: long and slow and then longer and slower, the tide going out.
You learned to hear the rhythm of it or you didn't, and once you heard it you couldn't stop.
There was a pull to it, patient, and you either understood that it had its own pace or you spent the whole time fighting it.
I'd stopped fighting it years ago.
This was what the work actually was, not the paperwork and the phone calls and the families who needed hand-holding, but this: sitting still while someone left.
"I've got you," I said, quiet.
"You can go."
She couldn't hear me, most likely.
The hearing went before the rest.
I said it anyway because it was the job and because I meant it.
The strings on the tablet were low and steady.
The hydrangeas were still in the window.
The trowel was still on the sill.
Her breathing spaced out to five seconds between.
Then eight.
Then I stopped counting and just held her hand.
It tightened around mine once.
Real grip, deliberate.
I felt the bones in her fingers.
Then it let go.
I sat with her a moment before I stood and turned off the playlist and checked the time.
Six fifty-three.
Then I checked her once more in the professional way, and then I went to the doorway.
Carol was a few feet back from the bed, arms crossed, jaw tight.
Her sister Margaret was in San Diego and hadn't made it, which both of them had understood when Margaret stopped calling with updated arrival times.
"She went quietly," I said.
"She was ready."
Carol's jaw worked.
She looked at her mother and then at the hydrangeas.
"How long were you with her?"
"Since six-fifteen."
She did the math.
I watched her do it: forty minutes in that chair without calling Carol back in, a judgment call, and she'd have to decide what kind.
That was the part of this work nobody warned you about.
You made those calls and you lived with them and most of the time you never found out if you'd gotten them right.
Her eyes went wet but she didn't cry.
"Thank you," she said.
"For being with her when I—" She stopped.
"She wasn't alone," I said.
"That's what mattered."
Carol nodded, the slow nod of someone filing something for later.
I told her I'd handle the hospice coordinator, that she should take all the time she needed.
I went to the kitchen and stood at the counter and dialed, keeping my voice even, because that was the job and I was good at it.
When I was done I made Carol a cup of tea she hadn't asked for and left it on the counter and let myself out.
I drove back to Manzanita with the windows cracked.
The coast road was empty, just the fog and the gray light and the sound of the water through the trees.
The work had its own weight and the drive home was how I set it down.
It was good work.
Mrs.
Halloran had been ready and I'd been there and the drive was when I let that settle, and I did, and for about thirty minutes I didn't think about anything else at all.
Gail was on my front step when I pulled up.
Tupperware in one hand, worried expression she was trying to hide behind a smile.
"I made the soup," she said.
"Gail."
"It's just soup.
It doesn't mean anything."
Gail made soup when she thought something was wrong and didn't want to ask directly.
I'd been her tenant for fourteen months and I could read her concern by the container size.
Small was minor.
Medium meant she'd been thinking about it.
Large with handle-grip impressions in the lid meant she'd worked herself into a state before I'd even pulled into the driveway.
This was a large container.
"I'm fine," I said.
"Death doula work.
You know how it goes."
"I know how it goes for tenants who sleep."
She was looking at my face with the blunt expression she got when she'd made a decision and wasn't going to be argued out of it.
"You don't look like you've been sleeping."
"I sleep a completely normal amount."
"Nell."
"Like a regular person.
In the bed.
Every night."
"The circles under your eyes are the color of a bruise."
"It's a lifestyle choice.
Very fashionable."
She made the sound she made when she'd decided to give up on something but needed me to know it was a decision and not a defeat.
Half laugh, half exasperated exhale.
I'd been hearing it since the second week of my tenancy and I was glad she hadn't stopped.
"The soup has actual noodles," she said.
"Not the rice things.
I know you think the rice things are sad."
"The rice things are objectively sad."
"I know that."
She pointed at me.
"Eat it before it gets cold."
I took the container.
She went back downstairs to her bookshop, which had been failing cheerfully for fifteen years and showed no signs of stopping.
I locked the door and looked at the Tupperware on the counter, then put it in the refrigerator.
I wasn't hungry.
I'd eat it later when no one was watching.
The rest of the afternoon I kept moving.
Carol's sister Margaret in San Diego needed the same calm voice walking her through the next forty-eight hours, and that was another forty minutes on the phone.
Then the documentation.
Then a grocery run because I'd been out of coffee since Tuesday.
Then a walk along the beach road in the fog.
The fog on the Oregon coast in October wasn't picturesque.
It ate everything, swallowed the ocean and the dunes and the parking lot at the trailhead, left only the road and the sound of the water somewhere past the gray.
I walked for an hour in it and my coat was damp when I got back and I felt marginally better, which was the most I was asking of a walk.
I counted the salt lines when I got home.
Refilled the bowls.
Stood at the back window and looked at the tree line.
Dark, ordinary.
No squirrels.
Nothing wrong with any of it.
I did not think about the fox.
I did not think about the dream.
Three nights ago I'd woken at four with sand between my teeth and a gray beach in my head: a woman walking into the water and not stopping.
I'd woken with a face in my chest that I wasn't going to name, the face I'd been not-thinking about for five years because I was good at it, I was excellent, I had a system.
Filed.
Done.
The fox was easier.
I'd been thinking about the fox all day on purpose.
I put off sleeping as long as I could.
Dishes.
The documentation a third time.
A book on my phone I read the same paragraph of four times.
I went through the bowls again, which I never did twice in one day, but I checked each level anyway and ran my finger over the salt lines a second time.
Everything clean.
Everything where I'd left it.
The soup eaten standing over the sink in the dark because I was hungry and it had the actual noodles and Gail had been right to be concerned, not that I was going to mention that to anyone.
Around midnight I ran out of reasons to be awake.
The apartment was cold the way it got on the coast, damp coming in through the walls, and I lay in the dark and listened to the fog and the distant water and waited.
When I went under it was fast, the way it always was when I'd been fighting it long enough.
Gray beach.
Driftwood in rows too neat for anything natural.
The water the color of a mirror laid face-up on the ground.
At the waterline, a woman walking in, not stopping when the water hit her knees, not stopping at her waist, not stopping at her shoulders, not stopping.
My mouth full of sand.
I woke standing at the window with my thumb jammed into the bare wood groove, already grinding.
My feet were cold on the floor.
I'd crossed the room in my sleep.
That was new.
I pressed my thumb into the wood and waited for my chest to settle.
The squirrels were gone.
The tree line was dark.
I didn't look at the clock.
Some things you didn't look at.
You just kept moving.
Chapter One
Six squirrels at the tree line.
I counted them twice because the first time I got five, and five was fine.
Five was Tuesday.
Six was something else.
They sat in a neat row along the edge of Mrs.
Peretti's overgrown laurel hedge, tails flat, ears forward, all of them watching my window.
I'd been watching them watching me for eleven minutes, which was nine minutes longer than any reasonable person would spend on squirrels before coffee.
I wasn't being reasonable.
I was being careful.
The sixth one, the one on the far left, blinked.
Not the way squirrels blink.
The whole animal flickered, just for a half-second, and in that half-second it was a fox.
Red fur.
Narrow snout.
Amber eyes that looked directly into mine with something worse than intelligence.
Then squirrel again.
Sitting there.
Tail flat.
Like nothing happened.
My thumb found the windowsill and pressed down hard.
The wood was soft from rain damage, and I could feel the grain denting under my nail.
I held it there until the pressure turned sharp, until my heartbeat stopped doing whatever it had been doing and went back to its job.
"Okay," I said to nobody.
"That's new."
It wasn't new.
I'd been seeing slips like that for three weeks.
A crow that was briefly a woman's hand.
A shadow under the porch that moved against the light.

The fox was the clearest one yet, and the clearest meant the worst, and I was not going to think about what it meant because I had things to do today and none of those things included losing my mind before breakfast.
I checked the salt on every windowsill.
All four.
Kitchen, bathroom, bedroom, the one narrow window in the hall closet that didn't open but still counted.
The lines were undisturbed, thin and white and even, the way I'd laid them three days ago.
I changed the water bowls by the front door and the back door, dumped the old water down the sink, filled them fresh from the tap.
Cold.
Always cold.
I didn't remember who told me that, which meant it was probably my mother, which meant I wasn't going to think about that either.
I drank my tea.
It had gone cold an hour ago, when I'd made it and then stood at the window instead of drinking it.
It tasted like what it was: punishment for not paying attention.
I drank it anyway.
My nails were too short.
I'd cut them yesterday, down past where I should have, and now I couldn't grip my palms the way I needed to when things got loud in my head.
The windowsill trick worked.
Mostly.
But my hands felt useless and blunt, like tools someone had filed down to keep me from hurting myself.
No mirrors in the apartment.
I'd broken the bathroom one in March and the bedroom one in April and told Gail downstairs that I was clumsy, which she believed because she wanted to.
The medicine cabinet had a piece of cardboard taped over where the mirror used to be.
I brushed my teeth looking at cardboard.
I got dressed looking at the wall.
I did my hair by feel, which meant I probably looked like I'd been sleeping in a ditch, but death doulas don't need to be pretty.
They need to show up.
The phone rang at six.
Mrs.
Halloran's daughter, Karen, who always called from the driveway because she couldn't make herself walk inside until someone else was already there.
"The breathing changed."
Karen's voice was flat, the way people get when they've been scared for so long it stops feeling like fear and starts feeling like furniture.
"It's—she's doing that thing you said.
The pauses."
"I'll be there in ten minutes."
"Is it—"
"Ten minutes, Karen."
I hung up, grabbed my bag, and walked the four blocks to Mrs.
Halloran's house without running.
Running would have been for me.
Mrs.
Halloran didn't need me winded and sweating.
She needed me steady.
The house smelled the way dying houses always smell: lavender someone plugged in to cover the other thing, and the other thing winning.
Karen was on the porch, arms crossed, jaw set like she was preparing to get hit.
I touched her shoulder on the way past.
Didn't stop.
Mrs.
Halloran was in the living room, in the hospital bed her insurance had fought for three months.
She was eighty-one and weighed maybe ninety pounds and her breathing was the thing I'd told Karen to listen for: long inhale, pause, long exhale, longer pause.
Cheyne-Stokes.
The body practicing for the stop.
I pulled the chair closer and sat down.
Took her hand.
It was cool and dry and her fingers didn't grip back, which was fine.
That wasn't what hands were for at this point.
"Hey, Mrs.
H.
It's Nell."
Her eyelids moved.
Maybe she heard me.
Maybe she was somewhere else already, halfway between the living room and whatever came after, and my voice was just weather.
Either way, I kept talking, low and even, the way you talk to someone who's doing the hardest work of their life and doesn't need your opinion about it.
I told her the squirrels were back.
I told her the rhododendrons in her side yard were blooming early this year.
I told her Karen was right outside.

I didn't tell her it was okay to go because that wasn't my call, and because people who are dying don't need permission from a thirty-two-year-old with chewed-down nails and no mirrors in her apartment.
They need company.
Quiet company.
Someone sitting close enough that the silence has a shape.
The body has a rhythm at the end.
I'd sat with enough people to know it.
A tide that pulls out slow, each wave a little thinner, a little further from shore, until the water just doesn't come back.
Mrs.
Halloran's tide had been going out all week.
Now it was almost gone.
She died at 7:14 AM.
One long breath, a pause that kept stretching, and then nothing.
No sound.
No drama.
Her face didn't change.
She just stopped being here and started being somewhere else, and the room got very still and very large around the empty space where she'd been.
I sat with her for another fifteen minutes before I went to get Karen.
That was for Mrs.
Halloran.
The fifteen minutes after death belong to the person who did the dying.
I don't know who taught me that either.
Karen cried, which was right and good and exactly what she should have done.
I made the calls.
Hospice.
Funeral home.
The neighbor who had a key.

I stripped the bed while Karen sat on the porch and called her brother in Medford, her voice going high and breaking on "this morning," and I folded the sheets into a tight square and set them by the door because someone would want to wash them later and it should be easy to find them when they did.
Professional.
That's the word people use.
Nell is so professional.
What they mean is: she doesn't fall apart where you can see it, and she knows where to put the sheets.
Gail was waiting on my doorstep when I got home.
She had a casserole dish covered in foil and the expression of a woman who'd been rehearsing a speech she knew wouldn't work.
"Before you say anything," she said.
"I'm fine."
"That is exactly what I was going to tell you not to say."
She held out the casserole.
"Chicken.
Rice.
Those little breadcrumb things on top.
You're going to eat some of it."
"I ate this morning."
"Tea doesn't count."
"It does if you believe in it hard enough."
Gail didn't laugh, which meant she'd noticed more than I wanted her to.

She was sixty-three and ran the bookshop below my apartment, the one that had been "about to close" for nine years and somehow kept not closing, and she looked at me now the way she looked at the shop's leaking roof: with affection and deep structural concern.
"You haven't been sleeping," she said.
"I sleep fine."
"Your light was on at three AM."
"I read."
"At three AM."
"It was a really good book."
She set the casserole on the step between us like a peace offering that also happened to be food.
"Mrs.
Halloran?"
"This morning.
It was peaceful."
Which was true.
It was also the only thing I was going to say about it.
Gail nodded.
She didn't hug me.

She'd learned, over the fourteen months I'd been renting the apartment above her garage, that I'd tolerate food and conversation but not contact, and that pushing got you nowhere except the other side of a closed door.
"There's enough for three days if you actually eat human portions."
"Your faith in me is staggering."
"My faith in you is extremely well-calibrated."
She pointed at the casserole.
"Eat."
She left.
I brought the casserole inside and put it in the fridge next to the last casserole she'd brought, which I hadn't opened.
I closed the fridge.
I sat on the kitchen floor for a while, not because I was sad but because the floor was cold and solid and didn't require me to decide what to do next.
Evening came the way it always does when you're trying to outrun it: fast and without asking.
I cleaned things that were already clean.
I reorganized the salt in the kitchen pantry by container size, which took eight minutes and accomplished nothing.

I stood at the window and watched the tree line go dark and the squirrels disappear into whatever squirrels disappear into, and I thought about going to bed the way someone standing at the edge of a pool thinks about cold water.
I didn't want to sleep.
Sleep was where things happened that I couldn't control, and today had been a day of controlling things carefully and well, and I wanted to stay inside that feeling for as long as I could.
Mrs.
Halloran had died the right way.
Quiet, attended, with clean sheets and someone holding her hand.
That was craft.
That was the work.
I could hold onto that for a few more hours if I just stayed awake.
I read until the words blurred.
I washed the mug I'd already washed.
I checked the salt lines again, all four windowsills, and the water bowls by the doors.
Everything in place.
Everything where I'd put it.

At some point, I sat down on the bed, and sitting became lying down, and lying down became that gray middle place where you're not awake but you're not gone yet, just drifting at the edge with your hands still gripping the sides.
Then the dream.
A gray beach.
No color anywhere, just ash-gray sand and pewter water and a sky that looked like the inside of a shell.
A woman walking into the surf, her back to me, her hair dark and wet against her shoulders.
She didn't look back.

The water was at her ankles, then her knees, then her waist, and I was standing on the sand watching her go and I couldn't move, couldn't call out, couldn't do anything except stand there with my feet sinking while she walked further in and the tide took her legs and then her chest and then her shoulders and then there was nothing but the flat gray water and the taste of sand between my teeth, gritty and cold, filling my mouth like someone had pressed my face into the beach and held it there.
I woke up choking on nothing.
Gail's light was off, which meant she'd stopped watching my window, which meant I could sit up in the dark and shake without anyone seeing it.
The sand taste stayed for ten minutes.
It always did.
I didn't think about the woman.
I didn't think about the beach.
I didn't think about Lyle's face, which had been there too, somewhere in the gray, just for a second before I'd shoved it down so hard and fast that it might as well not have happened.
Some things you don't look at.
You just keep moving.
I got up.
I checked the salt.
I made tea.
I drank it cold.
Seven forty-two and there were six of them today.
I counted twice before I let myself look away.
Six squirrels in a neat row along the tree line behind the garage, not eating, not moving, all of them watching the window where I stood with my cold tea.
Same spot as yesterday.
Five yesterday.
Four the day before.
I'd told myself I wasn't going to count.
The tally was at seventeen days.
One of them blinked, and for half a second it wasn't a squirrel at all: red fur, a narrow snout, amber eyes that were too still and too steady and too aware of me.
Then it was a squirrel again, sitting in its row with the others, watching the window the way squirrels apparently did now.
I pressed my thumb into the windowsill.

There was a groove worn into the wood where the paint had gone bare, rough and familiar under my thumb, and I held it there until the tree line was just a tree line and all six of them were just squirrels, sitting there being completely normal squirrels who were absolutely not watching me.
"Okay," I said.
"That's new."
I drank the rest of the tea cold and didn't look at the tree line again.
The salt on the windowsills was fine.
I checked it the same way every morning, working counterclockwise: front door bowl first, back door bowl second, then the sills.
The back bowl had gone cloudy overnight so I dumped it and refilled it from the tap.
The bathroom sill needed freshening the way it always did, the steam from the shower doing something to the line I'd never fully worked out.
I freshened it.
Everything else intact.
The bathroom wall had the ghost of a mirror on it, the outline where the frame had been, a rectangle of slightly cleaner paint.
I'd broken them eight months ago, the week I moved in.
I'd gotten used to doing my hair by feel.
My nails were too short to do the palm thing.
I'd cut them yesterday, which was not a great call, timing-wise, given the squirrels.
The fallback was pressing my thumb into something solid instead, which worked fine but left marks.
I'd manage.
I made a second cup of tea and stood at the kitchen window with it and watched the tree line and drank it before it went cold, which was a first.
The phone rang at six-oh-three.
Karen Halloran, Margery's daughter, calling from the same blocked number she always used.
"The breathing's changed," she said.
No hello.
"I'll be there in ten."
I was there in eight.

Margery was in her bed with the window cracked an inch, the hydrangeas she'd planted the year her husband died visible from where she lay, the blue ones that looked almost gray in the coastal morning light.
The room had the smell I'd come to know over six months of visits: lavender, old wood, clean linen, and underneath all of it something else I still didn't have a name for.
I'd been doing this work long enough to know it was the right smell to find in a room like this.
Not bad.
Just the threshold.
I did this work because I was good at it, and I was good at it because I didn't flinch.
You couldn't flinch in a room like this one.
People needed you steady and present and genuinely unafraid, somebody who had been here before and knew how it went.
I'd learned that early.

I'd learned it by sitting with my grandmother when I was nineteen and watching the hospice nurse work, how she moved through the room without disturbing the air, how she talked to my grandmother the way you'd talk to anyone, not lowering her voice into something hushed and significant.
Just normal.
Just there.
I'd decided that day that I wanted to do that.
Her breathing had the sound I knew.
Long pause, then a shallow pull, then a long pause again.
The tide going out slow.
You sat with it and let it find its pace because that was the only thing to do, and I'd made peace with that years ago, and I pulled the second chair over and sat.
Karen was in the chair by the window, her hands in her lap, past crying and into the still place on the other side of it.
"I didn't know if I should have called sooner," she said.
"You called at exactly the right time."
That was true.
I could hear it in Margery's breathing, the rhythm of it.
We had some time.
"She was talking last night," Karen said.
"About what?"
"Dad.
The house they had in Cannon Beach.
She kept asking about the dogs."
Margery hadn't had dogs in twenty years.
I didn't say that.
"That's good," I said, and I meant it.
Karen stood.
"I'm going to make tea."
"Okay."
She went.
I heard the kettle in the kitchen, the tap running, the particular knock of the old pot hitting the burner.
Outside, a gull called once.
The hydrangeas moved in the gap of the window.
I leaned in close enough for Margery to hear me.
"It's okay," I said quietly.
"You can go whenever you're ready.
Karen's here.
She's not going anywhere."
I waited a breath.
"You did everything right."
I'd learned that people heard at the end.
I'd learned it the way you learned things in this work, not from a manual but from being in enough rooms.
You watched faces.
You watched the breathing.
You learned which words did something and which ones were just sound you made to fill the air.
"You can go" did something.
It was the truest thing you could say to someone who'd been holding on, and Margery had been holding on for weeks, and I'd been watching her hold on, and I was glad Karen had called when she did.
Margery's chest rose and fell.
Rose.
Fell.
Didn't.
I sat with it for a moment.
The room went quiet in a way that was different from the quiet before, and I let that change settle before I noted the time and picked up my phone.
Karen came back without the tea, still holding the mug, steam rising from it.
She stood in the doorway and looked at her mother's face and already knew.
"She's gone," I said.
Karen set the mug down on the nightstand, very carefully, with a small precise click.
She crossed the room and sat on the edge of the bed and took her mother's hand in both of hers.
I stepped back to give her room.
That was the job too: knowing when I was done.
I went to stand on the front porch and wait for the hospice nurse.
It was still early, the street empty, the fog sitting low over everything the way coastal fog did in October, not burning off but just waiting out the morning.
I could hear Karen inside talking on the phone, her voice low and unsteady, doing the calls.
I'd offered to do them for her once and she'd shaken her head, said no, she needed to be the one.
I understood that.
Some things you needed to do yourself so you knew you'd done them.
The hospice nurse arrived at seven-forty.
I gave her what she needed, signed what needed signing, answered her questions.
I was good at the handoff too.
Gail found me twenty minutes later.
She lived four houses down and had some kind of landlord sonar that activated on hard days.
She came around the side gate with a container of soup and a look on her face that said she already knew and wasn't going to make it weird.
"Here," she said, handing me the soup.
"I made too much."
"You always make too much."
"I have a big pot."
She leaned against the railing.
She had her bookshop apron on over her coat, which meant she'd left mid-opening to come this way.
"You eat breakfast?"
"I had tea."
"Tea is not breakfast."
She looked at me the way she did when she was deciding whether to push, which she almost never did, which was one of my favorite things about Gail Torvik.
She had a gift for stopping just at the edge of the thing.
"I've got the open shift.
You going to be okay?"
"I'm always okay."
"I know you're always okay.
I'm just saying."
"I know you're just saying."
I held up the soup.
"Thank you."
"How was she?"
Gail asked, quietly, the way she asked when she actually wanted to know.
"Quiet.
She was ready."
I looked out at the street.
"Her daughter was there.
She got to be there for it."
"Don't thank me, eat it."
She pushed off the railing.
"Come by the shop later if you want.
Or don't.
Either way."
She left.

I stood there with the soup going warm in my hands and the sound of Karen moving somewhere inside the house and the street quiet the way it got mid-morning when everyone who had somewhere to be had already gone.
I was fine.
I was always fine.
I'd gotten good at it.
Back at the apartment I put the soup in the fridge and didn't eat it.
The afternoon had no appointments.
I walked the coast road for an hour, the wind off the water cold and sharp and smelling of salt and low tide, and watched the waves come in and break and pull back.
There were tourists on the beach with a big yellow dog that kept running at the water, ears flat, delighted and skidding back every time a wave came.
I stood at the guardrail and watched the dog figure out the waves until the tourists packed up and left, and then I headed back.
I didn't think about the fox.
The fox had been a slip.
I'd been seeing more of them lately, small wrongnesses at the edge of vision that my brain smoothed over before I could look too hard.
A shadow in the wrong place.
A bird flying the wrong direction.
The sense of something at the periphery that wasn't there when I turned.
I was watching the waves, and the fox was a slip, and I wasn't thinking about any of it.
I walked back along the coast road as the fog started to thin, not burning off but pulling back a little, the kind of halfway-clear that passed for good weather on the Oregon coast in October.
The ocean was gray-green and loud and doing its own thing out past the break, which was the thing I liked best about it.
It didn't care.
It was just the ocean.Back at the apartment I did laundry and sorted my kit for the week.
I refilled the travel salt case and checked the obsidian disc, held it for a moment the way I always did: cold, quiet, nothing active in it.

I nested it back in the cloth bag and set the bag in the kit case alongside the copper bowl I used for Veil clearings, the extra candles wrapped in cloth, the small notebook where I kept my client notes in the handwriting that was too small for anyone else to read.
I checked the windowsills again, which I'd already done that morning.
Then I checked them one more time.
The apartment was two rooms above Gail's garage, the kitchen folding into the living space, the bedroom door that didn't quite latch, the shower that ran cold the first minute.
Small and mine and exactly accounted for, and I was keeping it that way.
I made rice and ate half of it standing at the sink and threw the rest away.
I didn't touch Gail's soup.
By eight I was out of things to do that weren't sleeping, which meant I was in trouble.
Books helped.

The neighbor's TV through the wall helped, some home renovation show where the host talked about crown molding with a level of enthusiasm that made me think he'd never had to worry about anything worse than crown molding.
I made tea and drank half of it cold and held the mug even after it went cold because it was something to do with my hands.
The trick was to keep the hands busy.
The trick was to stay on the surface of things and not let the current take you under.
What didn't help was the part where eventually you ran out of tricks.

I'd been awake until midnight three nights running this week, lying there waiting for the current to take me somewhere I didn't want to go, and I was getting tired enough that I was starting to be angry about it, which meant I was probably close to actually sleeping, which was the closest thing to a system I had.
I didn't think about Lyle Evenson.
I'd been not-thinking about him for five years and I was fucking good at it.
He'd been in last night's dream and the dream could do whatever it wanted.
I picked up the book.
I picked up the book I'd been rereading for three weeks, got through four pages, put it down.
Turned the light out.
The beach was gray, the water flat and colorless and too wide, and the woman ahead of me had a dark coat and she was walking into it.
The water was up to her knees, then her waist.
I was walking after her because I always walked after her, sand cold and wet under my feet, the taste of it already at the back of my throat.
I called to her.
She didn't turn.
The water was at her shoulders now and I was still walking and my feet were still on the sand and the distance between us wasn't closing.
She never turned.
I woke up at two-seventeen.
The apartment was dark and the neighbor's TV was finally off and the only sound was the window over the sink where the seal had gone bad, the small tick of wind finding the gap.
I lay there for a moment with the grit between my teeth that wasn't there.
Some things you don't look at.
You just keep moving.
I got up and checked the salt.
The sixth squirrel sat down at 7:42.
I was at my window with cold tea when it happened: five already lined up at the tree line, and then this one dropped from the oak and took its place at the end of the row.
Six squirrels sitting perfectly still, watching my cottage.
I pressed my thumb into the windowsill.
Old groove.
I'd worn it in over the past year.
The third one blinked.
I saw it happen: red fur, narrow snout, amber eyes catching the morning light.
Then squirrel again, half a second, gone.
I pressed harder into the groove until I felt bare wood, rough under my thumbnail, and when I looked up they were just squirrels, fat and gray and doing nothing squirrels don't do.
Well.
That was new.
I drank my tea and watched them for another minute and a half.
They didn't move.
They didn't blink into anything else.
They sat there in their row with their flat black eyes and then, by the time I'd finished the tea and set the cup down, they were gone.
The tree line was just pines.
I did a slow circuit of the apartment: south sill, east sill, north sill, the bowl by the front door.
Everything where I'd left it.
I'd clipped my nails too short the night before, which meant I couldn't do the palm thing, which was why the windowsill was getting overtime.
I touched the bowl by the front door, checked the salt on the three sills I could reach without stepping into the bathroom, and went to get dressed.
My apartment was two rooms and a bathroom with no mirrors.
I'd broken them in the first week.
I hadn't liked what I saw, or maybe what I'd seen hadn't been quite what I was.
I had a small hand mirror in the drawer by the sink for when I needed it.
I didn't need it this morning.
I had clean clothes, the smell of salt and lavender from the bowls, and thirty-five minutes before I needed to be four blocks away.
My hands were steady.
My chest felt normal.
I hadn't shifted in four months.
My wolf was sluggish, half-hibernating, and sometimes when she was that quiet I started seeing things at the edges.
Shapes doing things shapes shouldn't.
That was probably it.
Tired brain, tired wolf.
I'd manage.
My phone rang at 6:02.
Karen Halloran had her mother's voice, thin and careful, the kind that apologized for taking up space.
"The rhythm changed overnight," she said.
"I've been sitting with her since three.
I didn't know if I should call you sooner, but —"
"You called at the right time," I said.
"I'll be there in fifteen minutes."
I drove the four blocks because I had my kit in the car: the lavender oil, the weighted blanket Mrs.
Halloran liked against her feet, the folder marked with Karen's name.
It had everything: hospice notification, the county death certificate request, the DNR she'd signed in three different places across two years because she kept forgetting she'd signed it.
The Hallorans were a family who wanted the paperwork ready before they had to think about it.
I'd learned that in October, the first afternoon I'd come to the house.
Mrs.
Halloran was in her bed with the window cracked an inch, hydrangeas coming through on the air.
Blue ones she'd planted the year her husband died, she'd told me that the first time we met.
She kept her hands folded on her chest even in sleep.
I'd sat with her in this room eleven times over the past four months.

I knew the squeak of the third floorboard from the door, the way the TV remote always sat beside her even though she hadn't touched it in weeks, the smell of the lavender sachets she kept in the pillowcase.
Her breathing had changed.
It was slower now.
The intervals were wider, open in the way that means the effort is going somewhere else.
There was a rhythm to the end.
I knew it by now.
Tide going out.
You didn't rush it.
I set my bag down quietly and took the chair Karen had left at the bedside.
"It's Nell," I said, just above a whisper.
"I'm here.
Karen's right outside."
She didn't respond.
She was past that.

But I'd learned early that the hearing goes last, so I kept talking, low and unhurried, the hydrangeas and the good weather expected later in the week and how I'd brought the weighted blanket she liked.
Just so there was a voice in the room.
Her hands were cool when I held them.
I knew the feel of them by now.
Karen came to the doorway once.
I heard her stop, heard her hand find the frame.
She didn't come in and I didn't turn around.
Karen's love sat heavy in any room she brought it into.
She knew that about herself, and she stayed at the door.
I'd told her that, two weeks ago, when we'd talked about what the end would look like.
Credit to her: she'd listened.
It took an hour and eight minutes.
When it was done I smoothed the blanket at her shoulders and closed her eyes and checked my watch for the paperwork: 8:49 AM.
The hydrangeas were still coming through the crack in the window.
I sat with her a few more minutes.
I always do.
Then I got up.
Karen was in the kitchen with her hands wrapped around a mug she wasn't drinking from, looking at the wall above the coffee maker.
"She went quietly," I said.
"She was ready."
Karen swallowed roughly, more than once.
Her eyes were dry but her jaw was working at something.
"She wasn't —" She stopped.
Started again.
"I keep thinking I should have stayed in the room.
Last night.
When she was still — when she could still hear things."
"She knew you were here."
"I fell asleep in the chair at two AM."
Her hands tightened on the mug.
"I woke up and I came and checked and she was still breathing and I thought I had time, so I went and lay down on the couch, and —"
"Karen."
She looked at me.
"She was ready for a long time.
She wasn't waiting for anything."
Karen's eyes spilled over then.
She put the mug down and covered her face with both hands, brief and contained, and then she straightened up and took a breath.
"You'll stay until they come?"
"Of course."
I made her sit.
I made the calls: the funeral home, the county office, her brother in Portland who she'd asked me to handle because she didn't trust herself on the phone with him right now.
I made Karen tea she didn't drink either and I sat at the kitchen table with her while she cried, the long quiet kind that comes after a long quiet waiting.
The funeral home came late morning.
I stayed twenty minutes past when the job ended, because Karen's hands were still shaking when she signed the forms and I wasn't going to watch her do it alone.
Gail was on her front step when I pulled up.
Foil-wrapped plates in both hands, her expression set the way it gets when she's decided to do something and already knows I'm going to be difficult about it.
"I made too much frittata," she said.
"You always make too much."
"I've been experimenting with a new egg ratio."
She held out a plate.
"There's vegetables in it."
I took it.
Arguing with Gail Torvik when she's in feeding mode takes more than I had left.
The plate was warm through the foil.
I was hungrier than I'd realized, which Gail had somehow clocked before I had.
She had an irritating gift for that.
She was watching me, though.
That careful look she gets when she's holding something back.
"You look tired," she said.
"I'm fine."
"I saw your lights on at four-thirty.
Through the ceiling."
My apartment sat directly above her back office.
She'd been tracking my insomnia by ambient glow for most of the eighteen months I'd lived here, and I'd meant to get blackout curtains since probably month three, and hadn't.
I liked that she knew.
"Early client," I said.
"Early."
She shifted her own plate to one hand.
"You've got the Mrs.
Halloran folder in your bag."
I glanced down.
The tab was showing above the zipper.
"How's your eyesight been lately?"
"Sharp."
She tilted her head.
"How is she?"
"She passed this morning," I said.
Gail went quiet.
She looked at the middle distance, then back at me.
"She was ready," she said.
"Yeah."
"Well."
She tilted her chin toward the plate in my hands.
"Frittata's better warm."
"I know."
She went inside.
I stood on the step looking at the tree line.
Just pines, same as always.
I went upstairs.
I ate the frittata.
She was right about the egg ratio.
I didn't tell her.
The afternoon ran sideways, the way it does after a death.
I filed the paperwork.
I called Karen twice about a form.
I washed Mrs.
Halloran's weighted blanket because Karen had asked me to return it and I didn't want to hand it back dirty.
I hung it to dry over the shower rod and sat on the couch with a book I didn't read.
I was not thinking about the squirrels.
The fox blink had been bad lighting.
I'd been up since four-thirty and the morning was gray and shapes do things when you're that tired and the light is that flat.
Nothing had touched the salt lines.
Nothing had moved the bowls.
My wolf had been half-asleep for months and I was fine.
I was getting good at fine.
The blanket dried by six.
I folded it and set it by the door.
I ate the rest of the frittata cold, standing at the counter.
I went over the week in my head: two more home visits, the county paperwork for Mrs.
Halloran, a referral call I'd been putting off for a client in Tillamook.
It was a normal week.
Outside the window the afternoon light went gray and then gray-orange and then dark.
I watched it happen, which was something I did sometimes instead of sleeping.
Night came fast off the water.
I turned on the lamp by the couch, not the overhead, because the overhead buzzes and I can't stand it, and the buzzing gets into the back of my skull and sits there.
I tried the book for another forty minutes.
I got through two pages that I'd read before and couldn't remember reading.
I gave it up.
I went to bed at ten.
The neighbor's cat was on the fence below.
Gail's shop light went off at ten-fifteen.
The street settled into the quiet that rolls in on weeknight evenings on this stretch of the coast: just the ocean and the wind and an occasional set of headlights passing on the 101.
I lay there and thought about the county form, whether I'd gotten Karen's address right in the third field.
I thought about the blanket by the door and whether it would still be dry in the morning.
I thought about the squirrels and how they'd sat in exactly the right interval between each other, like they'd practiced.
I stopped thinking about that.
I thought about Lyle's face.
It came up the way it had come up for the past three nights: not invited, nothing that triggered it.
Just Lyle's face.
The new scar along his jaw I hadn't seen yet in real life, and the fact that I knew exactly what it looked like anyway.
I put it somewhere else.

I pressed my thumb into the windowsill.
The groove was old.
I'd worn it in over the past year.

They didn't blink into anything else.

The tree line was just pines.

Everything where I'd left it.

I'd clipped my nails too short the night before, which meant I couldn't grip my palms for grounding, which was why the windowsill was getting overtime.

My apartment was two rooms and a bathroom with no mirrors.
I'd broken them in the first week.

My chest felt normal.

"She's changing."
Karen Halloran had the flat voice she used when she was reporting instead of feeling.
Three weeks of waiting had burned through most of what she had.
"The breathing.
It changed about twenty minutes ago.
I don't."
She stopped.
Started again.
"I don't know if I'm reading it right."
"You're reading it right."
She'd asked me what to listen for, and I'd told her, and now she'd heard it.
"I'm on my way.
Ten minutes."
"Okay."
A shorter pause.
"Should I go in there?
While I wait?"
"If you want to be in there, be in there.
There's no wrong answer."
I was already pulling my jacket off the hook.
"Karen.
You called at the right time."
She didn't answer that.
I didn't need her to.
I went out the door and down the stairs and didn't look at the tree line on the way.
Estelle's house was four blocks downhill toward the water, a white craftsman with a garden that had been better maintained when she could still get down on her knees.
The fog sat thick over the ocean this morning.
You couldn't find the horizon anywhere, just gray water bleeding into gray air, the coastline gone soft at the edges.
Manzanita knew how to do this kind of morning.
Karen let me in without a word and pointed upstairs.
She'd been crying recently, the skin around her eyes still pink, but she wasn't now.
She had the look of someone who'd used up most of their grief in advance and was running on whatever was left at the bottom.
"Is she" Karen started.
"Still here.
Go get some water for yourself."
She went to the kitchen.
I went upstairs.
Estelle was in her bed with the window cracked the inch she'd always wanted cracked.
The hydrangeas were visible through the glass, the blue ones she'd planted the year her husband died, browning a little at the edges now that November had come in hard.
Her breathing had changed in the night.
The rattle of it was unmistakable now, the body doing the last slow work, each breath coming a little later than the one before.
I sat in the chair by the bed.
"Hey, Estelle."
Low and even.
"I'm here.
Karen called me.
You're okay."
She didn't respond.
She hadn't been responding much since yesterday.
I talked to her anyway, just a little, nothing important.
My voice in the room.
I told her the fog was in this morning.
I told her the hydrangeas were still going, mostly.
I told her Karen was downstairs and was doing fine.
The room smelled like chamomile and something else underneath.
A sweetness that arrived near the end, the body releasing what it had spent a lifetime holding.
I knew that smell by now.
It wasn't a bad smell.
Just honest.
There was a rhythm to the end.
I'd come to understand that over four years of this work.
Tide going out.
You didn't rush it and you didn't hold it back.
Trying to do either only made it worse for everyone.
So I sat and I talked a little and I waited.
The slow rise and fall of her chest.
The hydrangeas through the cracked window.
The light coming gray through the fog outside.
At 8:47, her chest stopped moving.
I stayed another minute.
Just the stillness.
Her hand near mine on the blanket, cool now, the skin papery and familiar from three weeks of sitting beside her.
I knew the feel of it by now.
Then I went and got Karen.
She was sitting at the kitchen table with her water glass and her phone face-down in front of her.
She looked up when she heard my step.
"Yeah," I said.
She let out a long breath.
Then she got up and came upstairs with me.
She stood in the doorway and looked at her mother for a long moment without saying anything.
Her hands were at her sides and they were steady.
"Was it quiet?"
"Very quiet.
She wasn't in any distress."
She nodded.
"Was she scared?
At the end?"
"No."
Estelle had been more curious than afraid over the past few weeks, watching what her body was doing like it was something interesting happening to someone else.
"She was ready.
She'd been ready for a while."
Karen made a sound that wasn't quite a word.
Tears spilled over and tracked down her cheeks, and she let them.
She was looking at her mother's face.
"She talked about you," she said, after a minute.
"The last couple of weeks.
Said you made her feel like it wasn't some terrible thing she had to white-knuckle her way through."
She wiped her face with the back of her hand.
"Like it was just a thing that was going to happen.
Part of it."
I squeezed her hand once and told her I'd check in tomorrow and left her to make the calls she needed to make.
Gail was on my front steps when I got back.
She was holding a plate covered in foil and wearing the look she used when she'd had another reason to stop by.
There was always another reason.
"I made too much breakfast," she said.
"You always make too much breakfast."
"It's a genuine character flaw."
She held out the plate.
"There's also half a blueberry muffin from yesterday in there.
The muffin is a little sad.
Still structurally sound."
I took the plate.
Gail ran the bookshop below my apartment, had opinions about everyone's eating habits, and kept a garden that expanded into the backyard a little more every spring.
She didn't require anything from me in return for the food or the opinions.
Almost two years in and I was still working out the right response to that.
"You look tired," she said.
"I was with Estelle Halloran this morning."
Gail's face shifted.
She'd known Estelle.
Everyone in Manzanita knew everyone in Manzanita; it was one of the town's primary features and its primary limitation, depending on the day.
"She's gone?"
"Just before nine.
It was quiet."
"How's Karen holding up?"
"Better than some.
She'll need food this week."
"I'll take something over this afternoon."
Gail looked at me with the calculation she used when she was deciding whether to say a thing out loud.
She decided not to.
She'd gotten better at that.
"Did you sleep last night?"
"Some."
She looked at me.
I looked back.
Neither of us said anything about what some meant.
"Eat the muffin, Nell."
"I will eat the muffin."
"I'm serious about the muffin."
"Gail."
"I'm going."
She went back inside.
I stood on the steps for a moment looking at the ocean, visible from up here on the hill, the fog almost gone now, the water that flat gray-green it got on cold days, and then I went upstairs.
I ate the muffin at two in the afternoon, standing over the sink.
It was fine for being a day old.
I washed the plate and set it by the door to take back to Gail.
Did the water bowls again.
Checked the salt.
The front bowl was clear.
The back one had gone cloudy again, same as the night before and the night before that.
I was starting to develop theories about the back window bowl and I wasn't ready to develop any of them yet.
I refilled it and set it back and stopped.
I stood at the window and watched the tree line go dark as the light dropped.
The squirrels were gone.
I told myself that was fine.
Sleep was the problem.
It had been the problem for three weeks now, not the falling asleep part but what was waiting on the other side of it.
So I stayed up.
I read until I stopped caring who did it.
Made tea and let it go cold, same as the morning.
At nine I checked the bowls again, not because they needed it but because it gave me something to do.
I washed up.
I organized the shelf above the counter by size, which was a thing I'd done before and which made me feel faintly ridiculous, but it took twenty minutes and twenty minutes was twenty minutes.

I sat on the edge of the bed at eleven-thirty and told myself I'd just close my eyes for a bit and that was obviously not going to work, so I got up and went back to the window and stood there until I couldn't anymore.
At some point I was looking at the tree line again.
Waiting for something to be there.
Nothing was.
I turned off the lamp.
I was already half under when I smelled it.
Salt and low tide and something cold underneath, mineral and sharp, the smell the ocean got right before a hard storm came in off the Pacific.
I knew that smell.
I tried to get ahead of it anyway.
Gray beach.
Sky the color of nothing.
A woman walking out into the water, and the waves weren't breaking around her, they were moving through her, or she was moving through them, the water not noticing her at all.
Getting farther out.
I was standing at the waterline and my feet just wouldn't—
Sand between my teeth when I woke.
Palms flat on the mattress, pressing down.
Heart doing something I needed it to stop doing.
I lay there and breathed until it settled.
Then I got up.
I didn't think about the dream.
The front bowl was still clear.
The back window one had gone cloudy again overnight.
I dumped it, refilled it, set it back.
I didn't think about the woman or the water or whose face she had when she turned around.
Some things you don't look at.
You just keep moving.
The salt on my front windowsill had been disturbed.
I didn't figure that out right away.
What woke me was nothing — or nothing I could name — just my heart doing something urgent at two in the morning while the apartment sat dark and quiet around me.

I lay still and ran the inventory that I'd stopped calling an inventory because naming it made it sound like a system, and it wasn't a system, it was just what I did: sound, smell, the specific weight of the air.
The street outside was doing its usual nothing.
The dog three houses down that barked at eleven and again near three had already done its eleven.
No footsteps on the stair.
No creak of the door.
The cold tea on my nightstand smelled like cold tea and the salt bowls by the doors smelled like nothing because salt smelled like nothing, which was the point.
Nothing was wrong.
And yet.

My wolf — who had been a banked ember for seven months, so dormant I'd started to forget she was there, who I'd been avoiding shifting because shifting meant remembering how much I'd given up of both of us by not shifting — had come fully awake.
She was pressing at the inside of my chest with her nose, the way she did when she'd caught something I hadn't.
I reached for the bat before I sat up.
The perimeter check was automatic — feet on floor, moving the apartment's edge in the dark before I was fully conscious, touching each sill in sequence the way I'd done every morning for three years.
Front window, side window, the two in the kitchen.

The line I'd drawn three nights ago across the front sill, a half-inch of salt in a clean straight band, was broken in the middle, pushed aside like someone had run a finger through it slowly and deliberately.
Not wind.
The gap under the front door was enough to stir the curtains on a bad night; it had never touched the sill lines, not once.
These were set back four inches from the glass.
This was a finger.
Or something shaped like one.
Something had been inside my apartment.
Then the sounds from below started.
Low.
Shuffling.
The particular wet-friction sound of something moving through a space it didn't belong in.
I stood in my kitchen and listened and my wolf, who'd been a faint warmth at the base of my skull for seven months, went fully alert for the first time since I'd stopped letting her out.
That was enough.
The stairwell steps I'd oiled in September, an old habit I'd kept without examining it too hard, and they held their silence while I went down bare-footed with the bat across my chest.

The door to Gail's bookshop at the bottom was closed but not latched — she'd never latched it properly, three years of watching her forget and I'd never managed to care enough to fix it — and it swung in at my shoulder.
I had maybe two seconds of the room before the third one hit me from behind.
Two of them were already in the stacks.

One had Gail down against the front counter — her head at the angle that meant unconscious, not dead, blood from her hairline dark on the floorboards — and it was crouched over her, not tearing at her, not feeding, just holding her down with one hand while it watched the door with patient, specific eyes.
The one by the shelving behind it was half-shifted, hands too wide, jaw too long, blocking the back window.
And the third came from my left and caught me hard before I'd finished clocking any of it.
I got the bat up on reflex.
Wood took the hit instead of my skull.

My arms went numb from the elbows down and I crashed sideways into the nearest shelf, and a cascade of paperbacks rained down on all of us — Gail's organizational philosophy was aspirational at best, meaning she had stacked twelve paperbacks horizontally on top of a full upright shelf because she'd run out of room and hadn't gotten around to caring — and I used the half-second of chaos to plant my feet and swing back with everything I had.
Connected.
The one behind me hit the shelving hard and went down.
The problem with seven months of no shifting was that my wolf was supposed to be the part of me that got bigger and faster and meaner when the rest of me started failing.

Right now she was awake but not functional — a fire banked so long the heat was theoretical — and I could feel her straining at it while my arms were still half-numb and the two from the stacks had clocked me and were already moving.
What I had was a bat, fast hands, and the specific viciousness of a person with nothing to lose.
Which was slightly different from having something to protect, and I needed to not mix those up right now.
The two came at me together.

I dropped low, let the first one overshoot, brought the bat hard across the back of the second one's knees — not a kill shot, I wasn't going for kill shots, I was going for Gail — and got past them both while they were sorting themselves out.
I got her pulse under two fingers at her throat.
Quick, thin, present.
"Stay with me," I said.
"Stay with me, stay with me."
Her lashes didn't move.
I got one arm under her shoulders and started pulling her toward the front door, and that's when I stopped fighting and started watching.
The rogue I'd put into the shelving had gotten back up, and it wasn't pressing the advantage, wasn't coming at me — it was moving to the back exit, slow and deliberate, and parking itself there.
Blocking it.
The two from the stacks had broken off and taken angles, one near the shelving, one near the counter, and the triangle they'd made had me and Gail at the center of it.

My shoulder was heating up under the bruise that was going to be spectacular by morning, and my wolf was doing her useless best, and I looked at the shape of the three of them and felt the cold land in my stomach.
Rogues went feral.
That was the universal truth about rogues — they lost the thread of themselves, became all hunger and noise and impulse, as hard to direct as a fire.
You couldn't send a feral rogue anywhere.
You couldn't give one a position and expect it to hold.
These three had positions.
Someone had sent them.
I thought about that for about one second, which was all I had, because the one near the counter shifted its weight and I started moving.

I got Gail up by the shoulders and walked us toward the door and she made a sound against my neck, small and hurt and half-conscious, and I said "almost there" into her hair and kept my eyes on the rogue ahead of me.
It stepped aside.

They all stepped aside, the three of them pulling back in a slow, coordinated motion that was worse than if they'd attacked, because it meant they'd gotten what they came for or they were content to let me run wherever I was about to run.
Gail wasn't what they'd come for.
The Nguyens across the street had a light on.
I got Gail to their porch and knocked until Mrs.
Nguyen answered in her bathrobe, and I said the necessary things in the flattest voice I owned: head wound, unconscious, breathing, call 911.
She looked at me over her reading glasses and then at Gail and then back at me.
"What happened?"
"She fell."
Mrs.

Nguyen had lived across from Gail for eleven years and knew she was not a person who fell down her own stairs, but she also knew the voice I was using, the one that said there was no time, and she made the right call.
"Come inside."
"I can't."
I got Gail's arm settled around Mrs.
Nguyen's shoulders and stepped back.
"Someone needs to stay with her until the ambulance gets here.
I have to —" I didn't finish that sentence because I didn't have an ending for it that was true.
"Please."
Mrs.
Nguyen looked at me for another second and then said "go" in a tone that meant she knew I wasn't coming back and had already decided to let me.
I stood on the porch with Gail's blood drying on my hands and looked back at the bookshop.
One of the rogues had come to the doorway.
The other two were visible through the front window, not moving, not leaving.
Watching me with the specific patience of things that had been told to wait and were good at it.
Their eyes caught the streetlight the way animal eyes did in dark — too bright, held too still — and the intelligence behind them had a quality I hadn't expected from rogues.
Directed.
Purposeful.
The one in the doorway said my name.
"Nell."
Not a growl, not a challenge — my actual name, in a voice that had been mostly human once and kept the shape of it.
I stood on the Nguyens' porch and felt my stomach do something slow and cold.
They'd come to a specific address on a specific street in a specific town.
They'd known where I slept.
They'd crossed my salt lines without tripping them, which meant they'd been careful about it, which meant someone had told them about the lines.

Three years I'd built this life careful and invisible — the apartment above the garage, the job, the new name on the lease — and every precaution I'd taken had been a precaution against something that had apparently known exactly where I was the whole time.
I thought about that for about four seconds.
Then I went back upstairs.
Shoes first.
Then my mother's journal from the box under the bed, the emergency cash from the back of the kitchen drawer in its rubber-banded stack.
My phone.

The ziplock of salt by the door — not because I thought it would help wherever I was going but because packing without it felt wrong, the way leaving without your keys felt wrong even when you weren't planning to come back.
I stood in the middle of the apartment and did a slow turn.
The salt bowls by the doors.
The window whose rod I'd re-hung so it hung level, something the previous tenant hadn't bothered with.
A jacket I liked.

The kettle Gail had given me for my birthday because she'd noticed I drank cold tea and had decided, with the confident kindness of someone who collected lame ducks for a living, that this was a problem she could solve.
My copy of the tidal charts for the next six months, because old habit.
The broken mirrors I'd never replaced.
No photographs.
I'd built this carefully.
Three years of careful and invisible and it had turned out not to matter.
I left the jacket.
I left the kettle.
I took the bat to the door and then put it back — where I was going I couldn't walk around with a bat, and if I needed a bat it was already too late for a bat to help.
I didn't look at the broken salt line on my way out.
The rogues were gone from the street.
I didn't know if that meant they'd accomplished what they came for or if they were just ahead of me on the highway, and I didn't stay to figure it out.
My car was at the end of the block, and I was moving, and Manzanita started shrinking in the rearview before I'd made any actual decision to leave it.
