The ocean disappeared first.

I didn't notice it going until it was already gone — the sound cut off when I turned off the coast road, the smell a few miles after that, and by the time I hit the main highway it was just dark sky without the weight that ocean sky had, and the radio was off and the heater was on and I was somewhere else entirely without having chosen to be anywhere at all.
I'd forgotten I could lose it.
That was the thing about building a life slowly and carefully — you stopped seeing it as a thing you'd built.
The oiled steps, Gail's impossible shelves, the salt lines I drew every three days.
The kettle she'd given me because she'd noticed I drank cold tea and apparently decided this was a problem she had the power to solve.
None of it had felt like something I could lose.
It had just felt like texture.

Tuesday morning, three years of it, and now I was on a highway in the dark with Gail's blood under my fingernails and the ocean behind me and the rogues who'd known my name somewhere ahead of me, maybe, or everywhere.
They'd known my name.
They'd been inside my apartment while I slept, and they'd left the salt line broken on purpose, and I didn't know how long they'd known where I was.
I pressed my thumb into the steering wheel and drove east and didn't let myself finish any of the thoughts that were stacking up behind that.
Some things you didn't look at.
You just kept moving.
My hands were cold by the time I finished the salt.
Six this morning.
They were lined up along the base of the big fir: six squirrels facing the cottage, none of them moving, not foraging, not chasing each other.
Just sitting there at 7:42 in the morning watching me stand at my window with a mug of cold tea.
I pressed my thumb hard into the sill.
One of them blinked into something else for half a second.
Red fur, narrow snout, amber eyes catching the gray light all wrong.
Then it was a squirrel again, tail going.
I set down my tea.
"Okay," I said.
Nobody answered.
I got back to work.
I started on the windowsills, front to back, working left to right with the sea salt from the canning jar by the stove — thin lines, even coverage, same as every morning for eight months.
Then the bowls: front door, back door, kitchen counter.
The counter one had gone cloudy overnight and I dumped it, ran the tap until it was cold, refilled it, set it back.
That was the one I could reach in the dark without thinking, which was the only thing special about it.
My nails were clipped too short from the day before.
I'd done them without thinking and now I couldn't grip my palms the way I liked.

I pressed my thumb into the sill above the counter instead, holding it against the wood until I could feel the grain and my shoulders came down, and then I picked up my tea and drank it cold because reheating it took more optimism than I had at 7:52 in the morning.
There were no mirrors in the cottage.
I'd broken them in the first week and put nothing up in their place.
Eight months, and I still didn't miss them.
I'd been seeing the slips more often lately.

The fox that morning, and the way shadows moved sometimes when I wasn't looking directly at them, and two nights ago the water in the front bowl had been warm when I went to change it at midnight — warm when it should have been cold, sitting in a dark room in November all night.
I hadn't written any of that down.
I wasn't going to write any of it down.
That was a thought I was finished having.
I stood at the window for another minute with my cold tea.
The squirrels didn't move.
I made toast and ate it over the sink, looking at the side yard.
The phone rang at 6:12.
Joyce Halloran, and she didn't say anything when I picked up — just held the line, her breath catching slightly — and I already knew.
I'd learned to read the silence of people who'd been awake all night listening for a breathing change.
There was a quality to it, a kind of wrung-out stillness, that you recognized once you'd heard it enough times.
"I'll be there in ten minutes," I said.
"You really don't have to—"
"I'll be there in ten minutes, Joyce."
I was there in eight.
The house smelled like lavender and the close, stale warmth of rooms where someone has been dying slowly for weeks, windows kept shut against the cold because dying people got cold.
Joyce met me at the door in yesterday's clothes, still in her braid from the night before, dark circles, the hollowed-out look of someone who'd been running on adrenaline and had just run out.
I squeezed her arm on the way past and went down the hall without needing to be shown.
I'd been here four times in the last three months.
Mrs.
Halloran was in her bed with the window cracked an inch.
The hydrangeas were visible from where she lay, blue ones she'd planted the year her husband died, gone leggy now with nobody trimming them back.
The light on them was flat and gray.
She was still breathing.

That surprised me a little; the change Joyce had described on the phone had sounded close to done, but sometimes the body had more countdown than anyone expected and you couldn't do anything about that except pull up a chair.
I could hear a ceiling fan running somewhere in the house, the faint tick of an unbalanced blade.
I pulled up a chair.
"I'm here, Mrs.
Halloran," I said.
"It's Nell.
You're not alone."
She didn't respond.
She was past responding.

But I said it anyway because that was how the work went: you told them someone had shown up, even when you didn't know if they could hear you, because sometimes they could and you never got to know which times were which.
Her breathing was the shallow, spaced kind.
There was the labored kind that went on for hours and wore everybody down, and then there was this kind, which was quieter.
A tide going out, pulling slow.
I'd learned the difference between them the hard way, trying to anticipate it with my second client, sitting there checking my watch as if the number on it would tell me anything useful.
You didn't rush it and you didn't time it.
You sat down and kept them company and let the tide do what it was going to do.
I murmured to her while I sat.
Nothing important, just her name, just that the hydrangeas were doing well, just that Joyce was down the hall.
Not that Joyce was sitting in the kitchen with the look of someone who'd been awake too long waiting for something awful.
That was true but it didn't belong in here.
Joyce came in twice.
I shook my head both times and she went back out.
The light changed in the window.
The gray brightened slightly and then went flat again, clouds moving through.
At the end of the second hour, Mrs.
Halloran's hand tightened around mine.
Real grip — deliberate, the kind that costs something when you're that far down.
I felt the bones in her fingers.
I held on.
Then she let go.
I stayed a few minutes after.
I always stayed a few minutes after.
That was the least you could do.
Then I went and found Joyce at the kitchen table.
"She's gone," I said.
"It was quiet.
She was ready."
"Okay," Joyce said.
She didn't say anything else for a moment.
Then: "Thank you for staying."
"Of course," I said.
Joyce nodded and I watched her bank it.
Her hands were wrapped around a mug of coffee that had gone cold.
I made a fresh pot while she sat there — she probably wouldn't drink it either, but it gave us both something to do.
I called the funeral home from the kitchen while she stared at the hydrangeas through the glass.
I gave them what they needed, the standard information, the same language I always used, and when I hung up she was still looking at the hydrangeas.
"They'll be here within the hour," I said.
She nodded again.
I put a hand on her shoulder for a second and then let go and went to get my coat.
On the walk back to the cottage I let myself come apart a little.
Just for a moment, just until I reached the end of her block.
Then I straightened up and kept moving.
Gail was on her doorstep when I came up the drive, leaning against the frame with both arms folded.
She had on the enormous rust-orange knitted cardigan she'd owned since the nineties, roughly the size of a small tent, the one she broke out when she had feelings that needed managing.
She was holding a covered plate.
She had the look of someone who had timed this.
"I made too much pasta," she said.
"You always make too much pasta."
"I always make too much pasta because I know my neighbors."
She held out the plate.
I took it.
Arguing with Gail before nine in the morning was an investment that had never paid off and I'd stopped attempting it.
"How'd she go?"
Gail asked.
"Quiet.
She was ready."
Gail nodded slowly, the same nod she always gave it.

She'd asked me that question after every call for three years and I'd given her the same answer when it was true and a different answer when it wasn't, and she'd never pushed for more than what I gave her.
She was good that way.
"You look like absolute hell," she said.
"I look exactly how I always look."
"I know," she said.
"That's the problem."
She glanced at the plate in my hands.
"There's the sausage and fennel in there.
Don't leave it in the fridge until it's terrible and then throw it out."
"I would never."
"You absolutely would."
She glanced down at my hand.
"What happened to your thumb?"
"Windowsill."
She looked at me for a second longer than she needed to, then decided not to pursue it.
"Go eat.
Go sleep."
She went back inside before I could tell her I wasn't going to sleep, which she probably already knew.
The pasta was good.

She'd done the sausage and fennel, which she knew I liked, and I ate it standing at the counter instead of sitting down because sitting down would have meant accepting that the morning was over and I had thoughts I wasn't ready to sit still with yet.
I ate most of it and put the rest in the refrigerator and stood there with my hand on the door after I closed it, not quite ready to stop.
My thumb was still sore from the morning.
The skin at the tip had gone pink, a little tender.
I changed into clean clothes and sat down at the desk with the intake paperwork I'd been ignoring for a week.
I got through two forms before I stopped.

Red fur and amber eyes, there and then not there, a squirrel again before I'd even finished pressing my thumb into the wood — I'd been going through the salt and the bowls and drinking my cold tea and trying to decide whether what I'd seen was what I'd seen, and the answer was that I didn't know, and that was the answer I was going to have to live with.
I filed it under the same heading as the warm water in the bowl and the dream I wasn't thinking about yet and got back to the forms.
Some things you didn't look at.
You just kept moving.

By eight I'd finished the intake paperwork, made actual dinner from the eggs and the last block of cheddar and some spinach that was a day past optimal, done two loads of laundry, fixed the cabinet hinge that had been loose since October in three minutes with a screwdriver from the junk drawer, and moved all my books from alphabetical order to organized by color with the blue ones on the left.
There were more of them than I remembered.
I only ever did the books by color when I was trying to stay up, and I did it anyway because the alternative was going to bed.
I was avoiding sleep and I knew exactly why and I was finished thinking about it.
I kept the lights on until almost midnight.
When I finally turned them off I lay on my back in the dark and listened to the road outside.
A few cars going past, headlights sweeping the ceiling, the sound fading, and then no more cars and it was just me and the dark and the sound of the wind off the water two blocks over.
I dreamed of the beach.
The sand was gray and the driftwood was gray and the sky was the same flat gray, the color of something washed out.
The ocean the color of old iron.
A woman stood at the waterline with her back to me, walking in.
Just her silhouette, getting smaller as the water took her.

Up to her knees and then her waist and I couldn't move my feet, couldn't make any sound come out, could only stand there on the sand and watch until the ocean closed over where she'd been and went smooth again like she'd never happened.
I woke with sand between my teeth.
It wasn't there.
I knew it wasn't there.

I lay in the dark with my mouth closed and counted my breath until my heart stopped doing what it was doing, and the grit taste faded, and I was just a person lying in a bed in the dark with sore nails and a sore thumb.
I pressed my thumb into the mattress instead of my palm and felt nothing useful and eventually gave up and lay there watching the gray light start to come in around the curtains.
I didn't think about the woman.
I didn't think about the face I'd half-seen in the moment before she turned, the one I'd been half-seeing in this dream for three months, the one I kept not looking at long enough to confirm.
When it was light I got up and put the kettle on.
I did the salt and the bowls before anything else, front windowsills to back, all four bowls in order.
The counter bowl was cloudy again and I dumped it, and then I had a reason to stand at the window and I stood at it and looked out.
Seven today, one more than yesterday.
All of them in a row, all of them watching, the big fir behind them going dark and still in the no-wind morning.
I drank my tea before it went cold.
I almost managed it.
THE LAST RETREAT
Chapter One: The White Hound
The ledger had not balanced since Monday and it was Thursday now.

I knew this the way I knew the first coach from London would be late, and the fire in the taproom would need banking twice before noon, and Jem would forget to water the grey before nine if I didn't remind him.
Three days unbalanced meant either Nan had made a mistake or I had, and I knew my own hand well enough to know whose mistake it probably was.
I got up and went downstairs to confirm it.
The kitchen at half past five was mine and nobody else's.
Fire low, last night's ash not yet cleared, a smell of woodsmoke and yesterday's onions that had seeped into the plaster over the years and was now simply what the White Hound smelled like.
I took the ledger from the shelf above the bread crock and set it on the table with the tallow candle close.
Outside, the yard was still dark.
The cold came through the flagstones into the soles of my boots—wet and mean and already in the joints of the building, three weeks before November.
I'd felt it coming since August, which was when summer had stopped pretending to be summer and settled into the grey it had been wearing since April.
The error was mine.
A subtraction done wrong Tuesday evening, after the Norwich coach left us short two passengers and long one very drunk solicitor who knocked over a pot of stew.
I corrected it with the spare quill.
Sat back.
Still down six shillings on candles.
The chandler, again.
I wrote it at the bottom of the page and put the ledger back on the shelf.
Then I got the kitchen fire going properly and started the bread.
The day came up slowly—pale light edging in around the kitchen shutters, rooks starting up in the elm at the far end of the yard, the inn sign creaking on its chain.
Fields of mud where the barley should have been, from what I could see through the gate.
Frost on the ruts.
A sky that should have been blue and was not, not this year, not since April.
I had run this inn for five years.
Before that I had helped my grandmother run it, and before that I had watched her, from the time I was six, and the White Hound had always been there before me.
Good old red brick, and the rest of it held together by habit.
Nan came in at six with her hair half-pinned and her coat thrown over her shoulders and the expression of a woman who had slept badly and intended the morning to know about it.
She stopped inside the door, looked at me, looked at the bread, and said, "The Wickfield coach is early."
"How early."
"Jem says ten minutes."
Ten minutes meant passengers wanting breakfast at half past six instead of quarter to seven, which meant I had not yet started the eggs.
I stood up and got the pan.
Nan moved to the kettle without comment, which was how we worked.
"There's a soldier in the yard," she said.
I cracked an egg.
"Which kind."
She considered.
Nan Soulden had worked behind bars for fifteen years and she had a taxonomy of men I found reliable.
"Thin kind.
Young.
Ate the bread I gave him like he hadn't seen any in a while."
The thin ones had walked too far and eaten too little and wanted somewhere to sit out of the wind.
The broad ones—the ones bought out with a lump sum and through it by September—could go either way depending on the hour and whether any whisky was showing.
I had a rule about whisky before noon.
"Feed him whatever's left from last night.
Not the good bread."
"Already did."
Which was why I kept her.
Jem appeared in the kitchen doorway with mud on his boots and the grey's lead rope still in his hand.
I said nothing.
I looked at his boots.
"I'm going now," he said.
"Wipe your boots."
He wiped them on the mat, which he had not done the time before, or the time before that.

Jem Bowker had been at the White Hound since before I was born—he'd come with my grandmother's husband and stayed after, and he mentioned this when he thought it would be useful and I mentioned it never.

He knew every horse that came off the Great North Road by temperament, he kept the yard running without instruction, and he would give me his honest opinion on any matter I cared to raise and several I didn't.
He was fifty-three.
He had never wiped his boots before being asked.
A man was the sum of his qualities, and Jem Bowker's sum was very much in credit.
"East stable hinge is going," he said, from the doorway.
"I know."
"Going fast.
Before the hard freeze."
"I know, Jem."
He went.
I plated the eggs.
The Wickfield coach arrived in a clatter of hooves and a great deal of unnecessary noise from the coachman, a man named Gibbs who had never in his life arrived anywhere quietly.
Four passengers came down the step.
A wool merchant from Huntingdon who wanted coffee, which we did not have, and who wished to explain to me at some length why this was a shortcoming.
Nan listened to him with the expression of polite attention she'd spent fifteen years perfecting and then told him the tea was very good and would he like some.
He took the tea.
A clergyman who wanted nothing and sat in the corner with his hat in his lap looking chastened by the world.
A young woman with a hatbox and the eyes of someone who had been crying for most of Hertfordshire.
She sat next to the fire without asking and I did not ask her to move.
When I brought the merchant his tea she was still sitting there, hands wrapped around nothing, staring at the coals.
I set a cup in front of her on the way past.
She looked up.
"I didn't order—"
"No," I said, and went back to the kitchen.
Nan raised her eyebrows at me from across the bar.
I ignored her.
A large man with a good coat and a military bearing came last, pausing in the taproom doorway to look around it the way men who had been in charge of things looked around rooms.
He met my eye without surprise, which meant either he'd expected a woman running the place or he didn't care either way.
I thought the latter.
"Hot breakfast," he said.
Not a question.
"Bacon and eggs.
Bread.
Ale or tea."
"Tea."
"Sixpence."
A beat.
The look that men with good coats sometimes gave, working out whether the price warranted comment.
He sat down.
I went back to the kitchen.
Nan was already at the eggs.
"Military."
"Yes."
"Not trouble."
"No."
Trouble came in threes, loud, and smelling of cheap spirits.
That man would eat his breakfast, pay his sixpence, and be back on the road before ten.
Demobbed men came through in waves this year—officers, infantrymen, men who'd served as servants to officers, all of them washing back onto English roads now that the current had reversed.
I fed them when I could.
You could not run an inn on the Great North Road in 1816 and act as though the war had nothing to do with you.
The chandler came at nine.
Holt was a tidy man with a ledger of his own and an expression that said he'd decided before arriving how this conversation would go.
He stood in the kitchen doorway, because I had not invited him into the kitchen, and he held his hat in both hands.
"Miss Dale.
I've had to revise the candle prices.
Supply, as I'm sure you understand."
He put the sheet on the table.
The numbers were not last month's numbers.
They were considerably not last month's numbers.
"Tallow's up," he said.
"Tallow has been up since February.
You held the price."
"I can't hold it any longer, I'm afraid."
From the taproom: the clergyman scraping his chair back and leaving without a word, the merchant's voice raised at something, Nan's flat reply.
I did not send help.
"You understand supply," Holt said.
"The harvest—"
"I understand the harvest."
The spring had been grey.
The summer cold and wet from April to September.
The barley rotted in the fields and the cattle sickened and the price of everything climbed.
I put the sheet face down on the table, which was a mercy to my temper.
"I can't absorb this."
"I'm sorry—"
"Can you hold the October price for November and I'll pay on time rather than at month end."
He turned his hat.
"I'd have to—"
"Check."
"Perhaps six weeks.
If payment is by the end of the month."
"Done."
I held out my hand.
He shook it with the air of a man who had not expected to shake hands today, and left.

I sat down and thought about what a bad year compounded by another bad year looked like when you added them up five years running, and whether my grandmother had ever had three bad years together, and what she had done about it.
She had held on, presumably.
The inn was still here.
I got up and went to see about the east stable hinge.
The soldier was sitting on the mounting block with Jem's spare coat around his shoulders and a heel of bread in his hand, looking at the road.
Up close he was perhaps five-and-twenty, though the road aged men badly.
Grey eyes.
A jaw too sharp on a young face.
His boots had been good boots once.
At his feet, a small brown dog lay with its chin on its forepaws, watching me with the patient attention of an animal that had learned to go wherever it was taken.
"Where are you headed," I said.
"North.
More north."
He didn't look at me.
"I was in the Seventh Foot.
Peninsula, then Waterloo."
Three years since Waterloo and they were still coming through.
They would be coming through in ten years.
I looked at him.
His hands were steady on the bread.
He wasn't asking for anything—that was the thing I noticed.
He'd eaten what Nan gave him and he was sitting out the cold and he was not asking for anything.
"Can you do anything useful," I said.
He thought about it, which was better than the men who said yes immediately.
"Most things."
"Can you fix a stable hinge."
He glanced at the east stable door, which was hanging at its angle.
A brief assessment.
"Yes."
"Then do it.
Tool chest is in the east stable.
When you're done I'll give you supper and sixpence and the straw tonight, if you're decent to my staff."
He looked at me then.
Not at the inn, not at the road.
At me.
"I'll be decent," he said.
He was taller than I'd expected when he stood.
He went into the east stable without asking where the tool chest was.
The dog got up and followed him, and sat down outside the stable door and waited.
By noon the door was hanging straight and Mills—Nan had learned his name—was up on the corner of the roof replacing two split shingles he'd found without being asked.
Jem came and stood beside me and watched this.
"Hm," he said.
"Yes," I said.
"I'd have got to those shingles."
"I know you would."
Jem went back to the horses.
I went back inside.
The afternoon was the slow part, after the coaches and before the evening trade.
Four more came through between noon and four: the York mail, two private carriages going south, a carrier's cart from the north that bought three pints and the last of the cold beef.
Nan ran the taproom.
I did accounts and inventory at the kitchen table.
The flour merchant in Stevenage had not replied to my last letter about November prices.
I wrote him again in terms I hoped were clear without being hostile, which was a distinction that cost me two drafts.

The bread past the end of October was a question I needed answered before October was out—less than two weeks away—which meant either he replied promptly or I went in person, and half a day off the road in weather that had made its feelings about travel clear since September.
I wrote the letter.
Sealed it.
Through the kitchen window I could see Mills stacking wood on the south side of the stable.
He had split a good deal of it.
More than a sixpence worth.
The dog sat by the stable wall and watched him work.
Nan came in for the tea things.
She stood at the window alongside me.
"Good worker," she said.
"Yes."
"Dog too.
Wherever he goes it sits outside and waits."
She took the tea things.
"Very loyal sort of dog."
She went back to the taproom.
Down six shillings on candles, even with the chandler's concession.
The flour would go up.
The tallow would go up again after Holt's six weeks.
The accounts said what they always said in a year like this: possible, if nothing else went wrong.
I took the Stainforth letter out of my apron pocket and read it a third time.
He would call Friday at two.
He wished to discuss the terms.
The courtesy of the phrasing was the thing—the tone of a man who had already decided something and was making arrangements around the decision.
Everard Stainforth held the freehold on this building and most of the land between the village and the high road.
He'd left me alone for four years.
He took his quarterly payment and said nothing.
Whatever he wanted to discuss, it was not nothing.
I folded the letter and put it back.
Aunt Bridget came down at noon and again at supper.

She was seventy-one and small and she moved carefully but without apology, and she had lived in the two rooms above the taproom on an arrangement with my grandmother that I had not seen any reason to disturb.
She was not my aunt.
She was the closest thing I had to family on this side of the churchyard.
She sat in the kitchen chair by the fire while I cooked.
"You look tired," she said.
"The chandler came."
She already knew this.
"And the letter."
"And that."
She was quiet.
The fire moved.
Outside, the wind came off the north road with the cut it had been carrying since September.
I heard Mills bringing wood in through the kitchen passage and stacking it quietly against the inside wall.
"Your grandmother had a letter like that," Bridget said.
"Second year she held the lease.
His father, not him.
He wished to discuss the terms."
"What did she do."
"She went in with three years of quarterly receipts and laid them on his desk.
Said she kept her word and expected he would keep his."
A pause.
"He did.
But she'd had the receipts to hand."
"Mine are in order."
"I know they're in order."
Bridget looked at me over her cup.
"It's not the receipts he'll be looking at."
I did not ask what he would be looking at.
I knew.

He would be looking at an inn held by a woman alone, which had been true when my grandmother went in with her three years of receipts and which had been an unanswerable argument then because she had been my grandmother.
Thirty years in.
A dead husband too long gone for anyone to run her through him.
I had five years and twenty-eight.
Different arithmetic.
"She held it," I said.
"She did."
Bridget set her cup down and looked at me, straight.
"I just want you to go in knowing what room you're walking into."
I served supper.
Outside, Mills finished the wood and went to the stable, the dog at his heels.
By nine the taproom was half full and the fire had been banked twice and Nan's feet were hurting—I could tell from the set of her shoulders.
I took the second half of the evening so she could sit.
Jem was at the near end of the bar telling the two farriers from Baldock about the shingles in the tone of a man who had identified the problem himself.
I let it stand.
Mills had gone to the stable after supper.
Nan said he'd been decent.
Nan did not like easily, so I took this as the report it was.
I locked up.
I banked the fire.
I went through each room in the order I always did: taproom, kitchen, the two guest rooms above, the larder, the cellar door I always checked twice.
Bolts and windows and the back door.

The inn was quiet the way it went quiet after ten—not empty, just settled, the beam shifting, the sign chain, the draft under the east-facing window I had stuffed with rags in September and would again before November.
I went upstairs.
The Stainforth letter was in my apron pocket and I took it out and read it one last time by the candle I'd brought up from the landing.
Six lines.
Very courteous.
He would call Friday at two.

He wished to discuss the terms of my lease, which I had held for five years in good faith and on the quarter day and with the accounts in my own hand, the lease that had my grandmother's name above mine and the clause she'd argued for and won that specified female heirs, the lease that was mine in law and had been mine in practice since the morning I carried the strongbox up to Patience's room and she pressed my hand over it and told me she'd sooner leave it to the road than to a man who didn't deserve it.
The candle went out.
He wished to discuss the terms of my lease.
The inn sat in the flat grey centre of Hertfordshire, which had very little going for it besides the fact that it was mine.
I held it by a lease.
Both hands, one civil nod a week toward the landlord's solicitor, accounts balanced, yard clear, beds without lice.
Four years of that and I had not yet been dislodged, which was not nothing.
The morning coach from London was due at half-seven.
I was in the yard at six.
Cold out, the frost still white on the fence posts, my breath short in the raw air as I did my circuit.
Jem was already in the stable, talking to the horses in the low even voice he used when the weather changed and they felt it before he did.
I could hear him through the half-door as I passed: not words, just sound, the steadying murmur of a man who had been doing this since before I was born.
The pump handle wanted oil.
The gutter above the stable door had shifted half an inch overnight and would need seeing to before rain came in earnest; the sky had that flat sealed look that meant a serious day.
I wrote both in the ledger I carried everywhere, the leather worn soft at the corners.
"Gutter's off," I said, stopping at the stable door.
Jem looked up from the horse.
He looked at the gutter.
"I saw it."
"Before the rain."
"Before the rain," he agreed, and went back to the horse.
I went in to start the kitchen fire.
Nan was already behind the bar when I came through the taproom, setting out the mugs with the efficiency of a woman who knew every inch of that room and was still tired of it.
She had worked the White Hound since before I took the lease.
"Coach is on time," she said.
"Jem heard from the carter."
"Good."
I set the ledger on the kitchen table and put the kettle on.
"Two rooms wanted for the overnights.
Put them in the back."
"Those are cold."
"Those are ours."
The front rooms went to guests who paid the better rate.
I kept the back rooms for everyone else on the grounds that having something to give was better than having nothing, which it always was.
Above me, faint across the ceiling, the creak of Aunt Bridget's chair.
She rose early and went late to bed and in between she sat at her window with her book and her candle.
The light behind her curtain had been on since before I came down.
I did not need to knock to know she was up there.
She watched the road, and said nothing about what she saw, and I had learned to read the angle of the light under her door the way other people read a newspaper.
The chandler came before the coach.
He always came before the coach.
Mr.

Aldersham had a gift for arriving when I had my hands in something, and he opened the morning's dealings the way he had opened every dealing for eight months: by placing his case on the kitchen table I had just cleared and telling me that candles were dearer than they had been.
"Tallow's up," he said.
"Whole country's feeling it."
"Not your prices last quarter."
I dried my hands on my apron.
"What's your dozen at now?"
"Eleven and four."
"I paid nine and six last month."
"That was last month."
He had a way of saying it that made the recent past sound like a foreign country.
"There's shortage coming.
You'll not find better."
I knew his margin.
I had been keeping track since the second time he'd tried this, which was December.

By my calculation there was somewhere between a shilling and eighteen pence of air between what the tallow cost him and what he charged, and that gap had not shifted enough in the past month to account for what he was proposing.
"Ten and two," I said.
"I'll take two dozen."
"Eleven."
He began closing the case.
"Ten and three.
And you keep the account regular.
Every fortnight, as agreed."
"Regularity doesn't come free."
"It saves you riding out here twice a month on bad roads."
He kept the case closed a moment longer than he needed to.
"You know the price of everything, don't you, Miss Dale."
"That's why you come back."
He opened the case.
"Ten and four."
"Ten and three."
He took it.
He wrote the new figure on the account card in his neat cramped hand and signed without being asked.
He hadn't managed to irritate me into dropping the account yet and he knew it.
He was halfway to the door when the horn sounded from the north road.
Three passengers off the London coach, and the coachman wanting a word.
I met Fletcher in the yard.
He was a heavyset man I knew from the twice-weekly run, and he had the look of someone who had been saving a complaint for forty miles and was going to get his money's worth.
"Road from Hatfield's a disgrace," he said.
"Three inches of rut past the tollgate.
Whoever's meant to be maintaining that stretch hasn't been near it since summer."
"I don't maintain the road, Fletcher."
"No, but you'll write to whoever does.
You've done it before."
True.
Twice, with results best described as partial.
"I'll write again.
Before Thursday."
"Do it before Thursday, yes."
He nodded and went to see to the horses.

Jem was already there, left arm gone at the shoulder, settling the nearest horse with a voice and a hand and the economy of a man who had long since stopped needing two of anything to get the work done.
He caught my signal and tipped his chin toward the pile of luggage: he'd spotted it before me.
The trunk, as it turned out, was the problem.
One gentleman in a good hat had a trunk with a split hinge, and he had decided over the course of the journey that this was owed to the state of the roads, and the state of the roads was owed to me.
"The trunk is your property," I said.
"The road belongs to the county."
"I want it repaired before I continue north.
I have correspondence in there."
I looked at the split.
It had probably been cracked before Barnet.
"Jem can look at it."
"When?"
"Come inside.
Nan will bring you breakfast."
He began about the road again.
I waited until he was done and asked about breakfast and he said yes, and thanked me, which I had not expected.
The woman with the small child asked, very quietly, whether there was somewhere she could sit for a quarter of an hour.
She had the look of someone who expected to be told no.
I took her to the kitchen, poured her tea, and cleared the bench so the boy could lie flat.
He was asleep before she had finished thanking me.
I left them there and went back to the accounts.
The third passenger, the one who had gone straight to the taproom and sat with his back to the wall, needed nothing from me.
I appreciated this about him.
By mid-morning the kitchen smelled of soup and wet wool and the coal smoke the chimney threw back when the wind came out of the north.
The bread was gone before noon.
I sent Piers to the baker — the neighbour's boy, quick and reliable and good at not asking the wrong questions, which was what I needed from him.
Nan came through while I was at the ledger.
"Trunk's sorted," she said.
"Jem bodged the hinge.
Good enough to hold to York."
"He'll want paying."
"Already charged to the gentleman's account."
She washed a cup without being asked.
"Man tipped him sixpence.
Came out after to apologise about the cobble he chipped in the yard.
Very civil."
I looked up.
"Perfectly pleasant," she said, in the tone she used when she found human beings puzzling.
"Asked if there was good road north of Hatfield."
"There's not."
"That's what I told him."
She dried the cup.
Paused.
"Mrs.
Sefton's girl is looking for work."
"I know."
"She's quick."
"I know, Nan."
She put the cup back.
"We're running one short," she said, very carefully.
"I'm not complaining."
"A little."
"A little," she agreed.
She was heading back to the bar when she stopped in the doorway.
"The gentleman with the trunk.
When he was at his second round of complaints about the road, I told him you were in the cellar and couldn't be disturbed."
I looked up.
"When was this?"
"Noon."
She studied the doorframe with great interest.
"You were at the accounts."
We both knew where I had been at noon.
"And he accepted that."
"He accepted that."
She went back to the bar.
I went back to the numbers.
Six weeks before the next quarter's rent came due.
Six weeks of the inn running as it was, no shift to the income, no give in the costs, and then I would need to be in a different position than I was now.
I had been arriving at this same figure since September.
It had not improved.
I pressed my thumb into the ledger's binding.
Old groove there, rough where the leather had worn through to board.
Jem appeared in the kitchen doorway, wiping his hand on his trousers.
He looked at me.
He looked at the ledger.
He did not say anything, because he never said anything he didn't have to, which was one of the things I valued about him.
"Hinge'll hold to York," he said, which I already knew.
"Gate latch wants a new pin before winter."
"Add it to the list."
He looked at the list, which was pinned to the board above the fireplace and had seventeen items on it.
"Right," he said.
He went back out to the yard.
I closed the ledger and followed him.
The soldier came around eleven.
I saw him from the kitchen window: a young man on foot, coming up the south road, the kind of thin that is not illness but is near enough to it.
He stopped at the yard gate and stood there looking at the inn the way men did when they were working out whether they were welcome or not and had learned to check before walking in.
Boots coming apart at the welt.
Coat the colour of old service, the military cut faded past easy identification.
He had the posture of a man who had been told to stand straight long enough that he did it without thinking, even now.
He did not come to the front.
He came round to the kitchen door.
I had it open before he knocked.
"Are you eating?"
I said.
Young eyes in an older face; he was perhaps twenty-two and looked closer to thirty.
"I haven't any money on me."
"I didn't ask about money."
I brought him in and gave him bread and the end of the morning's soup and a cup of tea strong enough to stand a spoon in.
I put him in the kitchen, not the taproom.
The paying guests were in the taproom and some of them had views about certain kinds of company, and today I was not in a position to argue with views.
He ate without rushing.
"Thank you," he said, when he was done.
"The back road will take you to St Albans by dark," I said.
"Stay on the east side of the river.
There's a parish house on the High Street that doesn't ask too much."
He nodded.
He stood, and for a moment he held the empty cup in both hands as if uncertain what to do with it.
Then he set it down on the table, carefully, and went out the way he had come.
I watched him go down the back road until the hedgerow took him.
There was nothing more to do about it after that.
I did not know his name.
I had not asked and he had not offered, and I thought that was probably how he preferred it — one kitchen that did not require him to explain himself, one hour of sitting without being a problem.
The road south was empty after that, the frost burned off, the sky flat and grey and going greyer toward the west.
Above me the faint sound of Bridget's chair.
She had moved it to the window.
She had seen him.
She had not come down.
The near-altercation happened at half-past three.

A farm labourer who came in most afternoons, a commercial traveller who did not know the customs of the house, and the stool by the window the labourer had been sitting on for two years without anyone formally saying he could.
The traveller had sat down on it.
The labourer had expressed a view at some volume.

The traveller had expressed an opinion in return, and then the labourer's stool scraped back on the flagstones, and I heard that scrape from the kitchen and knew what it meant before I was through the door.
Nan had her arms folded in the way that meant this one was mine.
Both men were on their feet.
The labourer was broad through the shoulders and red in the face and had been drinking since two.
The traveller was younger and had the confidence of a man who had never been in a room he couldn't leave.
Neither of them had looked at the knife block yet.
I came to stand between them and did not say anything.
I waited until both of them had noticed where I was and where the counter was and where the light from the kitchen doorway fell.
It took about four seconds.
Then I looked at the traveller: "Window seat's free."
And at the labourer: "Sit down."
The traveller moved.
The labourer sat — the way men sit down when they are not certain they've lost but have decided not to find out: with deliberation, without looking at me.
I went back to the kitchen.
Nan followed.
"Decisive," she said.
"I didn't threaten anyone."
"You stood where the light caught the knife block."
"That's just where I was standing."
She gave me the look she kept for statements she found implausible.
Then she went back to the bar, and I heard the taproom resume its ordinary murmur, and nobody said anything else about the stool.
By seven the taproom was empty.
Jem had the horses settled and the yard locked.
Nan was finishing the bar.
She came through for her coat and found me at the accounts and stopped in the doorway.
"Go home," I said.
"You've been up since five."
"I know.
Go home."
She put her coat on.
Paused at the door.
"You could take Piers on regular," she said.
"He's good."
"I know he is."
She waited.
"Good night, Nan."
She went out.
I heard her cross the yard and the gate latch catch behind her.
Then it was quiet.
Above me, Bridget's light was still on.
It was always still on at this hour.

I thought about going up, and then I thought about what she would say — nothing direct, because she never said anything direct, but something about patience, or holding on, or the difference between stubbornness and sense, and I was too tired for the distinction tonight.
I poured the last cold inch of tea from the pot and drank it standing at the window, looking at the empty yard.
Jem had righted the fence post that had been leaning since October.
I had not asked him to.
He had done it at the end of the day, before the light went, without mentioning it.
I set the cup down and went to lock up.
I locked up alone.
Taproom first, chairs up, shutters bolted, checked twice because the left shutter had a bad latch and I had learned not to trust it.
The cellar hatch, padlocked.
The kitchen — fire banked, the good knife away, the ledger back in its drawer, the drawer itself pushed flush.
I went room to room with one tallow candle and the cracked clock the only sound.
The back door.
The storeroom, with its smell of old hops and vinegar and the particular cold of a room that never fully warmed.
The boot room where the south-facing window had never latched properly and the wedge I used instead had been in place so long it had its own groove in the sill.
The guest corridor, all four doors, pulling each closed until the latch caught.
Number three stuck, the way it had stuck since last February; I lifted the handle as I pulled and it caught.
Upstairs, Bridget's strip of light still showing under the door.
The stable yard gate.
The panel in my room.
The strongbox in its place behind it, the accounts folded inside, the key on the cord around my neck.
I knew every sound the inn made in the dark.
The creak on the fifth stair, always the fifth.
The way the taproom door settled back against its frame when the kitchen fire banked down and the air between the two rooms stopped moving.
The drip from the yard pump that was not quite rhythmic and had not been quite rhythmic since the mechanism was replaced in August.
I had learned all of it over four years.
When something sounded wrong, I knew it had sounded wrong before I had consciously registered what I was hearing.
It was the one thing about the place I did not worry about losing.

My hands were red from the pump and the cold water and the afternoon's work, and I had a cut on my right index finger where the chandler's invoice had caught me — a thin bright line that had stopped bleeding around noon and now just stung when it caught on anything.
I pressed it against my thumb going up the stairs.
The letter was on the kitchen table.
I noticed it when I came through for the candle.
I noticed it again when I went back for the matches.
I had a brief, entirely unnecessary errand to the boot room, and when I came back through the kitchen I did not look at the table at all, which was its own kind of noticing.
It had been there since the afternoon post.
It was from Stainforth.

I had known it was from Stainforth before I turned it over, because I had known it was coming since the last rent quarter, since September's conversation with his solicitor that had ended before I was finished talking.
I sat down.
The kitchen was dark except for my candle.
The fire had burned to embers.
Outside, barely a sound from the yard.
Above me, the thin line of light under Bridget's door.
Stainforth's seal.
Red wax, his initials.
His handwriting on the direction.
Six weeks before the next quarter's rent became a problem.
I had counted it three times this week and the number had not changed.
"All right then," I said, to the kitchen, to nobody.
I opened it.
Madam — I write to request the favour of a meeting at your earliest convenience, with a view to discussing the terms of your current lease arrangement.
I remain, &c.
The terms of the lease.
I sat with it in my hands for a while.
The candle burned down.
I did not get up to trim it.

My knees had gone stiff from the cold by the time I finally stood, and I stood carefully, the way you stand when you have been sitting in the same position long enough that your body has forgotten it agreed to move.
The letter went into the strongbox.
I went to bed.
I lay with the ledger on the table beside me and ran the numbers one final time, though I knew them exactly.
Six weeks.
Six weeks, and then I would need to be somewhere different than I was now, or that would be decided for me.
Six weeks was not long.
I turned onto my side.
The room was dark and quiet and mine, in the inn that was mine to lease, on the road that would be there in the morning as it had been today.
Six weeks was enough time.
It had to be.
I closed my eyes.
The ledger had not balanced since Tuesday, which meant I had been staring at the same column of figures long enough to memorise the ink blots and resent them personally.
I closed it.
Opened it.
Closed it again.
The morning coach from London was due at half past eight.
I had forty minutes, a kitchen that still smelled of last night's soup, a taproom that needed its chairs turned down, and a cellar delivery at ten.
The ledger was not going to fix itself in forty minutes.
The ledger had not fixed itself in three days.
The kitchen was mine at this hour.
No Nan yet, Bridget not down, Jem already in the yard by the sound of the bucket and the creak of the stable door that needed its lower hinge oiled and had needed it for three weeks.
I put the kettle on, checked the bread, found the heel of yesterday's loaf had gone soft in the damp and cut it anyway.
The candle on the mantel had a quarter inch left.
I made a note.
Candles were going to be a problem by Thursday.
This was the hour I was best at.

Before the yard filled up, before the first coach brought whatever it was bringing — broken axles, difficult guests, news I hadn't asked for — I could walk every room of the inn and know that every bolt was mine to throw, every fire mine to tend.
A kitchen that answered to nobody but me was everything, and I had learned not to be precious about saying so, at least to myself.
I set the fire higher, pulled on my second shawl, and went to see about the taproom.
It looked more or less as I had left it: chairs on the tables, floor swept, the smell of ale and cold ash that was simply the smell of the place and could not be helped.
The White Hound had been a coaching inn for forty years before I arrived and the smell had forty years of permanence to it.
Nan had been at it until nearly midnight.
I could see it in the damp mop propped in the scullery corner and the fact that the far table's leg was still ringed with wet from where she'd mopped around rather than through.
She'd been on her feet since seven that morning and I was not going to say a word about the leg.
I moved the table.
Mopped under it.

Checked that the fire irons were back where they belonged, which they were not, which was the kind of small disorder that accumulated when the last customer had finally gone and everyone involved had reached the end of their usefulness for the day.
Then I went back to the kitchen, poured the hot water over the last of the tea leaves, and stood at the window looking out at the yard in the grey not-yet-dawn.
The rooks were up already in the oak on the far fence.
A bite in the air that went straight through the glass, winter not here yet but close enough to taste — October doing what it had done all year, which was its worst.

The Year Without a Summer had rolled straight into autumn without the common decency of a warm September, and now here we were, frost on the ruts and dead growth in every ditch and the barley price up again and my tallow supply running two weeks ahead of schedule.
One misery after another, weather-wise, and all of it landing eventually on the ledger.
The forty-three shillings had not sorted themselves out in my absence.
I put the ledger on the shelf and went down to the cellar.
Counting the ale casks was a thing that could actually be completed, which I needed more than I needed one more session with the accounts.
The cellar was cold enough to see your breath and smelled of damp stone and old wood and the underground cold that came up through the flagstones no matter what the season.

I counted twelve casks against the delivery note, found eleven, found the twelfth behind the door where someone had left it for reasons I chose not to pursue, noted that the small beer would hold for three days and the dark ale needed topping up by the weekend, and came back upstairs feeling marginally more like a person who ran an inn rather than one who was being slowly eaten by a ledger.
My hands were cold from the cellar walls.
I wiped them dry on my apron and went to put the kettle back on.
Information I could act on.
The other kind could wait.
I had been keeping the White Hound's accounts since I took over the lease three years ago.

Patience had taught me the booking system before she died, and I had taught myself the rest from her old records and from the particular education of catching my own mistakes before they became disasters.
The numbers I was looking at were not a disaster.

They were the kind of numbers a woman with a husband absorbed through the household accounts, and a man with a lease absorbed through the bank, and that a woman holding a lease alone absorbed by knowing exactly how much tallow cost in Baldock and writing letters to surveyors who did not write back.
I had been writing those letters for three years.
I was very good at them.
They had not yet produced a single repaired drainage ditch, but I kept copies in case they ever became useful, and that was the whole of my legal position on the north road.
I made myself a second cup of tea and turned my attention to the things I could actually manage.
The coach arrived eight minutes late, which was fine, and with a split trunk hinge, which was not.
The coachman was a heavyset man named Birch who ran the London-to-Huntingdon route and had been doing it long enough to have opinions about every yard between here and both ends.
He told me about the ruts north of Stevenage while his horses were being watered.
"Sent a letter to the surveyor's office in October," I said.
"First week.
And the week before that, about the drainage ditch near the Bell."
"And?"
"And nothing yet.
I'll send another."
"Won't matter," he said.
"Same surveyor, same nothing."
"Probably not," I agreed.
"Go see to your horses, Mr Birch."
He went, still talking.
The two passengers who came inside were short-tempered in the way of people who have been cold and jolted for six hours and want someone to blame for it.
The first was a wool merchant from somewhere near St Albans who had a complaint about the state of the north road, which I had just heard in full from the coachman.
I settled him with hot tea and a table near the fire.
The second was a younger man with good luggage and the air of someone accustomed to private parlours, who wanted to know why we didn't have one.
"We have a very private corner of the taproom," I said.
"Quieter than most private parlours, and you'll have the window."
"Three shillings more?"
"Three shillings more."
He thought about it.
He took it.

By that point Nan had come in through the back and had the bar cloth in her hand and one eye on the door and had already, without a word to me, redirected the wool merchant onto his second cup and away from the topic of the north road.
Nan's talent for this was one of the main reasons the White Hound had not yet ground me to powder.

I gave her a look that meant the corner table was paid and she gave me one back that meant she'd clocked the younger man as a complainer and was going to be magnificently pleasant to him for the next hour.
Neither of us said a word about any of it.
Jem came in from the yard long enough to say the split hinge was a clean break and he could pin it with what he had in the stable.
"Get it done before the coach leaves," I said.
"Aye."
He was already turning round.
I did not worry about whether Jem would get it done.
There was an economy to the way he moved through the yard — one arm and no wasted motion — that I had learned to read as a guarantee.
There was a moment, mid-morning, when I stood in the kitchen doorway and watched the whole arrangement operate without a word from me.
The corner-table man had stopped complaining and started drinking his tea in the satisfied manner of someone who had got what he wanted.

The wool merchant was on his second cup and had begun, by the signs, to tell Nan about his wool business, which Nan was receiving with an expression of professional interest that I recognised as entirely manufactured and deeply respectful.
Outside, I could hear Jem in the yard with the easy unhurried sounds of the work going exactly as it was supposed to go.
The arrangement had taken four years to build.

Four years of learning which suppliers could be pushed and which needed handling, which regulars wanted a specific chair and which coachmen would complain about the road but still bring their custom back because the White Hound had better ale and a better yard and a landlady who didn't send them away wet.

Patience had built the first ten years of it and I had inherited it with the lease and the accounts and the complicated grief of walking into a dead woman's kitchen and finding it already shaped around you.
I did not stand in the doorway long.
Standing there long was how you started to believe in things.
The chandler arrived at eleven with an invoice I hadn't asked for and a new price I hadn't agreed to.
I set it on the kitchen table and read it twice.
The numbers did not improve.
"Mr Pickett," I said, with all the pleasantness I could manufacture.
"You've charged me fourteen shillings a dozen for tallow dips.
In September it was eleven."
"Tallow's up this month, Miss Dale.
Supply and demand.
Nothing to be done."
"I know what tallow costs.
I also know what your supplier in Baldock charges per stone, because he sells to the Bell too, and Mrs Pearce at the Bell and I have a long-standing arrangement to compare notes."
Mr Pickett's expression underwent a small recalibration.
"Be that as it may, my costs—"
"Twelve shillings.
I'll take four dozen, paid today.
Or I take my custom to Harrow and you explain to your Baldock man why your volume's dropped."
A pause.
His civil manner was worse than anger.
It meant he was deciding whether I was worth the trouble.
I kept my hands flat on the table and waited.
"Twelve and six," he said.
"Twelve."
"Miss Dale, I am trying to be reasonable—"
"Mr Pickett," I said, "you are trying to see how much I'll pay before I stop being polite about it.
Twelve shillings, four dozen, paid now.
Or I write to Harrow this afternoon."
He smiled.
I had learned that smile.
A man making a calculation, deciding it came out in my direction.
Not a friendly expression, whatever shape the mouth was in.
"Twelve," he said.
I wrote out the payment while he loaded the crates.
The chandler was managed.

The chandler would be managed again next month and the month after that, and I was good at managing chandlers, and I was good at managing coachmen and short-tempered travellers and drainage ditches that no one was ever going to fix, and none of it added up to anything if the lease went.
What could not be managed by small renegotiations was the rent at next quarter, the full weight of the lease on the ledger's far side, the thing I had been not-thinking about for three months.
I had known it was six weeks since the quarter before.
I had been moving faster ever since.
The soldier came round mid-afternoon, in the quieter hour between the luncheon traffic and the evening coaches.
He knocked at the kitchen door.
Not the front, not the taproom door, not the yard gate.
The kitchen door was the door for deliveries and for people who were not certain of their welcome.

Young — early twenties, maybe; it was getting harder to tell, they all looked older than they had before — with the kind of thin that came from missed meals rather than build, and boots coming apart at the welt.
Dark wool coat, no uniform, but the coat cut in a way that had once had something under it.
He had the soldier's way of standing: still, hands at his sides, taking up exactly as much space as his body required and not an inch more.
His eyes went to the yard before they came to my face.
"Beg pardon, miss.
Wondered if there was work going."
I looked at him properly.
Not threatening.
Not drunk.
Just used up, the way they all were, the men coming back down the London road who had done what was asked of them and found their place in the world had been filled in around their absence.
"Have you eaten today?"
I said.
He answered honestly.
"No, miss."
I told him to wait.
I kept him in the kitchen and not the taproom.
The paying guests did not need to see it and he did not need the inspection.
I put bread and cold mutton in front of him and a cup of something warm and went back to the cellar delivery list.
He ate without comment, which I respected more than I would have respected thanks.
When he was done he sat quietly for a moment, as though allowing the food time to land.
"There's nothing I can do in return for it," he said.
"I know."
"I'm sorry for that."
"Keep well," I told him.
He went.
Quietly, the way he had come.
I stood in the kitchen a moment, looking at the empty plate.
The post-war roads were full of men like him, young and thin-soled and going somewhere they weren't certain of, knocked loose from everything that had given them a shape.
They came through two or three a week in good weather, less in the cold.
Some of them asked.
Some just stood in the yard a moment and looked at the inn and decided not to bother.
I kept a few of them fed.
It was not enough and I knew it and there was nothing else to be done about it, and the ledger was not going to change itself and the cellar order was due.
I cleared the plate and went back to work.
The near-altercation in the taproom happened at half past five.

A drover who had been drinking since four had taken the chair that the commercial traveller from Cambridge — a man with a long chin and a longer list of complaints, three shillings in the private corner and two hours spent making it clear he had expected more for the money — considered his own.
The traveller said something.
The drover said something back.
The sound from the taproom changed in the way it changed before things got complicated.
I came out from behind the bar before Nan had to move.

I put a fresh pint in front of the drover and told the commercial traveller from Cambridge that I had just had a thought: the corner was in fact rather warmer in the evenings if he moved slightly, which would make it more genuinely private, and I could see he was a man who appreciated a genuinely private space for his work.
I moved his papers while I was saying it.
He was sitting somewhere else before he had decided to sit somewhere else.
The drover drank his pint.
The traveller worked his papers in his new corner.
Nobody had lost anything.
Nan watched the whole affair from behind the bar with the expression she kept for moments when she and I were thinking the same thing but one of us had got there faster.
She wiped down the bar.
By the end of her shift, the traveller from Cambridge had moved twice more: once of his own initiative, once at my gentle suggestion.
He had eventually settled into a corner that he believed he had chosen himself, which was as good an outcome as I could have hoped for.
"Efficient," Nan said, pulling on her coat.
"Go home, Nan."
"You were up since four."
"I know when I was up."
"Go to bed at a reasonable hour."
She pulled on her second glove.
"I mean it."
I told her goodnight.
She went out with the air of a woman who had said what she'd come to say and was satisfied regardless of whether it was going to be acted on.
I watched the yard door close.
Nan had been covering for me in the taproom more than I'd let myself notice.
More than I'd wanted to notice.
I bolted the door and went back inside.
By eight o'clock the taproom was closed, the fire banked, the last glasses washed and set to dry.
Jem had the stable settled before dark.
The creak of his room above the tack store had been quiet for an hour.
The yard was dark and cold, rooks somewhere in the oak, the inn sign doing its patient complaint in the wind.
Bridget's window above the courtyard had a light in it still — the reading kind, steady and warm.
She'd had a light every night this week.
Bridget read late when she was thinking, and she had been thinking more than usual.
I could not always tell what she was thinking about.
I had a suspicion about this week.
I checked each room before I locked up: taproom, private corner, scullery, the small back room we let out when anyone wanted it, which in November almost nobody did.
Hinges oiled, bolts checked, back door bar dropped, kitchen bar after.
I had done this every night for three years and I still did it twice over because the first pass settled the door and the second pass settled me.
Seven minutes, and I slept better for it.
The yard was dark and cold.
The inn sign creaked in a wind that had come up from the north since sundown, which was the kind of wind that promised nothing good about the week ahead.
The coal supply was going to be a problem by December.
The tallow was already a problem.

The forty-three shillings in the ledger were a problem I had been carrying since Tuesday, and behind all of it, quiet and patient, was the rent at next quarter and the fact that I had been running the place on my own for fourteen months and the money I was working with had margins that did not accommodate bad luck.
I came back to the kitchen.
The fire was down to a steady burn that would hold through the night.
I sat down at the table with the ledger and a new candle, opened it to the column that hadn't balanced, and added it up one more time.
The same answer.
It was always the same answer.
My hands were reddened from the cold water, a cut on my index finger from where I'd handled the chandler's invoice too sharply.
The paper edge had found the exact worst spot, as paper always did.
I pressed my thumb against the ledger's binding.
Bare board under the leather where the corner had worn through, old groove worn in over the past year.
Forty-three shillings short.
Six weeks to next quarter.

Patience had been dead for fourteen months and I had been running the place on my own for all of them, and I was good at it, and I had been good at it, and the margins I was working with were thinner than they looked from the outside.
One bad coach season, one bad winter, and the margins stopped existing.
I had known this since the quarter before.
I had been moving faster ever since and it had not yet been fast enough.
I closed the ledger.
I had not yet looked at the table's corner, where a letter was set squarely in the way Bridget set things she wanted me to see.
She had come down while I was seeing to the evening coal.
She had seen the seal.
She had said nothing, and said nothing was Bridget speaking volumes.
I looked.
Phineas Stainforth.
In his own hand, not his clerk's.
I sat with it.
The fire settled.

Old red brick and woodsmoke and cold stone — the smell of the bread I'd baked that morning, the smell of the place I had built into mine over three years and Patience had built into hers for ten before that.
I knew every creak of it.
I knew where the draught came under the kitchen door and where the plaster had a hairline crack above the taproom window and which stair on the back flight squeaked and which three didn't.
I knew how to feed it and hold it and keep it going on margins thinner than good sense recommended.
The letter was in his own hand, not his clerk's.
He had written it himself, and that told me something about how certain he was of the outcome.
What I did not know was how much longer I could do it alone, and I had been not-knowing that for three months.
"Right, then," I said, to the room and nobody in it.
I broke the seal.
Read it twice.
He wished to discuss the terms of my lease.
At my earliest convenience.
He remained, et cetera, et cetera.
I folded it back along its crease and held it in my reddened hands.
Six weeks.
CHAPTER ONE
Six squirrels sat in a neat row at the tree line, watching my cottage.
Seven forty-two in the morning, and they were already out there.
I pressed my thumb into the windowsill hard enough to feel the grain and counted them again.
Six.
Same as yesterday.
Same as the day before that.
Normal squirrel stuff, if you didn't think about it too hard, and I was excellent at not thinking about things too hard.
Then the one on the far left blinked into a fox.
Red fur.
Narrow snout.
Amber eyes that locked onto mine through the glass for maybe one second before the shape collapsed back into gray squirrel.
Just sitting there, tail flicking, like nothing had happened.
"Okay," I said to my empty apartment.
"That's new."
My nails were clipped too short — I'd hacked them down past the quick yesterday — and I couldn't grip my palms the way I needed to.
Pressing the thumb harder into the windowsill would have to do.
Wood is real.
The ache in your cuticles is real.

A squirrel turning into a fox for half a second is not real, because if it were real, that would mean the slips were getting worse, and if the slips were getting worse, then the salt on every windowsill and the water bowls by every door weren't doing a damn thing, and if the protections weren't working —
I stopped that thought, walked to the kitchen, and drank my tea cold.
It had been sitting on the counter since five AM when I'd given up on sleep.
Tasted awful.
I drank it anyway because routine was the only thing keeping me upright most days.
The phone rang at six twelve.
Mrs.
Halloran's daughter.
I knew before I answered because no one else called this early, and because I'd been expecting it for three days.
The breathing had changed on Tuesday — that slow, rattling downshift where you can hear the body quitting.
You hear it enough times, you stop needing a stethoscope.
"She's different this morning," Kathy said, her voice thin.
"She won't open her eyes."
"I'm on my way."
I grabbed my bag — lavender oil, soft cloths, the notebook I never wrote in but always carried — and checked the salt lines on the way out.
Windowsills: intact.
Front door bowl: full.
Back door bowl: full.
Everything where it should be.
Some things you don't look at.
You just keep moving.
Mrs.
Halloran's house was four blocks away, close enough to walk.
The morning was gray and wet, standard February on the Oregon coast.
I didn't own an umbrella.
Nobody in Manzanita owned an umbrella.
You just got damp and dealt with it.
Kathy met me at the door looking like she hadn't slept in a week, which she probably hadn't.
I squeezed her arm, said the things I always said — I'm here, she's comfortable, you did everything right — and went into the bedroom.
Mrs.
Halloran was eighty-three and had been dying for six weeks with the same stubbornness she'd apparently applied to everything else in her life.
Kathy had told me stories: Mrs.
Halloran refusing to sell the house after her husband died.
Teaching herself to fix the roof at seventy.
Telling the hospice nurse she could go to hell when the nurse suggested a facility.
She was dying the same way she'd lived — in her own bed, with the quilt her mother made pulled up to her chin, and absolutely no interest in anyone's opinion about it.
I sat down in the chair beside her and took her hand.
Cool skin, thin, the pulse barely there.
Her breathing had that long exhale thing, the one that goes out farther than it comes back in.
The body has a rhythm at the end, a tide that pulls out slow.
You don't rush it.
You just sit with it.
"Hey, Mrs.
Halloran," I said.
"It's Nell.
I'm here."
No response.
But the hand in mine twitched, just slightly.
I sat with her for two hours.
Kathy came in and out, bringing coffee I didn't drink, asking questions I answered honestly.
You don't lie to the family.
Even when the truth is that the breathing is going to stop soon and there's nothing to do except be in the room when it happens.
At eight seventeen, it stopped.
Her face relaxed.
The tension went out of her jaw and her forehead.
I checked for a pulse I already knew wasn't there, noted the time, and sat with her for another minute.
Then I went to find Kathy.
She cried.
I held her hand and walked her through the next steps — call the funeral home, call her brother, don't worry about the dishes.
She'd be fine.
Not today, but eventually.
I walked home through the same gray morning.
Four blocks.
A death doula coming home from work.
It had been a good death — quiet, not scary, someone holding her hand at the end.
I was good at this part.
I'd been doing it long enough to know that this was the best version of how it goes.
The rest of my life was a different story, but whatever.
Gail was on the front porch of the bookshop when I got back, which meant she'd been watching for me.
She was holding a plate covered in foil.
"Banana bread," she said before I could get past her.
"Don't argue."
"I'm not hungry."
"You're never hungry.
Eat it anyway."
She pushed the plate at me with both hands.
Gail Torvik had been running a bookshop in a town of six hundred people for thirty years.
She did not take no for an answer about books, baked goods, or whether you were eating enough.
"How was Mrs.
Halloran?"
"Peaceful."
"Good."
Gail looked at me.
That look she'd been giving me for weeks, the one that meant she was noticing things and didn't know what to do about them.
"You look tired, Nell."
"I'm fine."
"You look like you haven't slept in a month."
"Slight exaggeration."
I took the banana bread because it was easier than arguing.
"Thank you.
Really."
She wanted to push harder.
I could see it.
She'd noticed the salt on my windowsills — I'd told her it was for slugs.
She'd noticed I never had people over.
She'd noticed the flinching at sounds that weren't there.
She didn't say any of that.
She just watched me climb the stairs to my apartment with that worried look she was too polite to explain.
Good landlord.
Good person.
Deserved a tenant who had her shit together, but that wasn't what she got.
Inside, I put the banana bread on the counter next to the cold tea.
The apartment was small — kitchen, bedroom, bathroom, a living room that barely fit a couch — and I'd arranged it with the kind of precision that should probably concern someone.
No mirrors.
I'd smashed them all six months ago and told Gail I was clumsy.
She'd believed me because the alternative explanation — that I'd started seeing things in them that weren't my reflection — wasn't exactly something you brought up to your landlord.
Salt on every windowsill.
Water bowls by every door.
Nails clipped short so I couldn't claw at my own palms in my sleep.
A baseball bat by the bed.
I ate a piece of the banana bread standing up because Gail would ask tomorrow.
It was good.
She was a better baker than she was a businesswoman, which was saying something because the bookshop had been "almost profitable" for as long as I'd known her.
The rest of the day was just me trying to fill hours until dark.
I cleaned.
I organized my doula bag.
I did laundry.
I read a novel I couldn't focus on.
I made dinner I didn't eat.

I watched the tree line from the window and counted the squirrels, and none of them turned into foxes, which should have been reassuring but wasn't because I wasn't crazy and I knew what I'd seen that morning.
By ten PM, I was out of tasks.
The apartment was clean, the salt was fresh, the water bowls were full.
Nothing left between me and sleep except the fact that I really, really didn't want to go to sleep.
I brushed my teeth in the mirrorless bathroom.
Checked the locks.
Checked the salt lines again.
Got into bed with the bat in reach and the covers pulled up and told myself that whatever was waiting behind my eyelids couldn't actually hurt me.
I'd been telling myself that for months.
Hadn't been true for a while.
I fell asleep fast.
I always did.
It wasn't the falling asleep that was the problem.
The dream was already there.
Gray beach.
Flat, colorless sky.
Driftwood everywhere.
The ocean was wrong — too still, too dark, moving in a way that didn't match any tide I'd ever seen.
And there, at the waterline, a woman walking in.
I knew her.
I always knew her, even though her face was never clear.
Just the shape — thin, straight-backed, walking into the water like she'd already decided and wasn't looking for input.
The water took her ankles, her knees, her hips.
She didn't look back.
I tried to call out.
I always tried.
Nothing came out.
The sand was in my mouth.
Between my teeth, grinding against my molars, tasting like salt and something worse.
I couldn't spit it out.
I couldn't breathe.
The woman was waist-deep now, still walking, and the ocean was taking her.
I woke up gasping.
I ran my tongue over my teeth and there was no sand, but I could still taste it.
Three twenty-seven AM.
The apartment was dark.
The salt lines were intact.
The bat was where I'd left it.
I sat up, pressed my thumb into my palm where my nails should have been long enough to dig in, and breathed until the shaking stopped.
Some things you don't look at.
You just keep moving.
I didn't go back to sleep.
The ledger had not balanced since Tuesday, which meant I had been staring at the same column of figures long enough to memorise the ink blots and resent them personally.
I closed it.
Opened it.
Closed it again.
The morning coach from London was due at half past eight.
I had forty minutes, a kitchen that still smelled of last night's soup, a taproom that needed its chairs turned down, and a cellar delivery at ten.
The ledger was not going to fix itself in forty minutes.
The ledger had not fixed itself in three days.
The kitchen was mine at this hour.
No Nan yet, Bridget not down, Jem already in the yard by the sound of the bucket and the creak of the stable door that needed its lower hinge oiled and had needed it for three weeks.
I put the kettle on, checked the bread, found the heel of yesterday's loaf had gone soft in the damp and cut it anyway.
The candle on the mantel had a quarter inch left.
I made a note.
Candles were going to be a problem by Thursday.
This was the hour I was best at.

Before the yard filled up, before the first coach brought whatever it was bringing — broken axles, difficult guests, news I hadn't asked for — I could walk every room of the inn and know that every bolt was mine to throw, every fire mine to tend.
A kitchen that answered to nobody but me was everything, and I had learned not to be precious about saying so, at least to myself.
I set the fire higher, pulled on my second shawl, and went to see about the taproom.
It looked more or less as I had left it: chairs on the tables, floor swept, the smell of ale and cold ash that was simply the smell of the place and could not be helped.
The White Hound had been a coaching inn for forty years before I arrived and the smell had forty years of permanence to it.
Nan had been at it until nearly midnight.
I could see it in the damp mop propped in the scullery corner and the fact that the far table's leg was still ringed with wet from where she'd mopped around rather than through.
She'd been on her feet since seven that morning and I was not going to say a word about the leg.
I moved the table.
Mopped under it.

Checked that the fire irons were back where they belonged, which they were not, which was the kind of small disorder that accumulated when the last customer had finally gone and everyone involved had reached the end of their usefulness for the day.
Then I went back to the kitchen, poured the hot water over the last of the tea leaves, and stood at the window looking out at the yard in the grey not-yet-dawn.
The rooks were up already in the oak on the far fence.
A bite in the air that went straight through the glass, winter not here yet but close enough to taste — October doing what it had done all year, which was its worst.

The Year Without a Summer had rolled straight into autumn without the common decency of a warm September, and now here we were, frost on the ruts and dead growth in every ditch and the barley price up again and my tallow supply running two weeks ahead of schedule.
One misery after another, weather-wise, and all of it landing eventually on the ledger.
The forty-three shillings had not sorted themselves out in my absence.
I put the ledger on the shelf and went down to the cellar.
Counting the ale casks was a thing that could actually be completed, which I needed more than I needed one more session with the accounts.
The cellar was cold enough to see your breath and smelled of damp stone and old wood and the underground cold that came up through the flagstones no matter what the season.
