I counted twelve casks against the delivery note, found eleven, found the twelfth behind the door where someone had left it for reasons I chose not to pursue, noted that the small beer would hold for three days and the dark ale needed topping up by the weekend, and came back upstairs feeling marginally more like a person who ran an inn rather than one who was being slowly eaten by a ledger.
My hands were cold from the cellar walls.
I wiped them dry on my apron and went to put the kettle back on.
Information I could act on.
The other kind could wait.
I had been keeping the White Hound's accounts since I took over the lease three years ago.

Patience had taught me the booking system before she died, and I had taught myself the rest from her old records and from the particular education of catching my own mistakes before they became disasters.
The numbers I was looking at were not a disaster.

They were the kind of numbers a woman with a husband absorbed through the household accounts, and a man with a lease absorbed through the bank, and that a woman holding a lease alone absorbed by knowing exactly how much tallow cost in Baldock and writing letters to surveyors who did not write back.
I had been writing those letters for three years.
I was very good at them.
They had not yet produced a single repaired drainage ditch, but I kept copies in case they ever became useful, and that was the whole of my legal position on the north road.
I made myself a second cup of tea and turned my attention to the things I could actually manage.
The coach arrived eight minutes late, which was fine, and with a split trunk hinge, which was not.
The coachman was a heavyset man named Birch who ran the London-to-Huntingdon route and had been doing it long enough to have opinions about every yard between here and both ends.
He told me about the ruts north of Stevenage while his horses were being watered.
"Sent a letter to the surveyor's office in October," I said.
"First week.
And the week before that, about the drainage ditch near the Bell."
"And?"
"And nothing yet.
I'll send another."
"Won't matter," he said.
"Same surveyor, same nothing."
"Probably not," I agreed.
"Go see to your horses, Mr Birch."
He went, still talking.
The two passengers who came inside were short-tempered in the way of people who have been cold and jolted for six hours and want someone to blame for it.
The first was a wool merchant from somewhere near St Albans who had a complaint about the state of the north road, which I had just heard in full from the coachman.
I settled him with hot tea and a table near the fire.
The second was a younger man with good luggage and the air of someone accustomed to private parlours, who wanted to know why we didn't have one.
"We have a very private corner of the taproom," I said.
"Quieter than most private parlours, and you'll have the window."
"Three shillings more?"
"Three shillings more."
He thought about it.
He took it.

By that point Nan had come in through the back and had the bar cloth in her hand and one eye on the door and had already, without a word to me, redirected the wool merchant onto his second cup and away from the topic of the north road.
Nan's talent for this was one of the main reasons the White Hound had not yet ground me to powder.

I gave her a look that meant the corner table was paid and she gave me one back that meant she'd clocked the younger man as a complainer and was going to be magnificently pleasant to him for the next hour.
Neither of us said a word about any of it.
Jem came in from the yard long enough to say the split hinge was a clean break and he could pin it with what he had in the stable.
"Get it done before the coach leaves," I said.
"Aye."
He was already turning round.
I did not worry about whether Jem would get it done.
There was an economy to the way he moved through the yard — one arm and no wasted motion — that I had learned to read as a guarantee.
There was a moment, mid-morning, when I stood in the kitchen doorway and watched the whole arrangement operate without a word from me.
The corner-table man had stopped complaining and started drinking his tea in the satisfied manner of someone who had got what he wanted.

The wool merchant was on his second cup and had begun, by the signs, to tell Nan about his wool business, which Nan was receiving with an expression of professional interest that I recognised as entirely manufactured and deeply respectful.
Outside, I could hear Jem in the yard with the easy unhurried sounds of the work going exactly as it was supposed to go.
The arrangement had taken four years to build.

Four years of learning which suppliers could be pushed and which needed handling, which regulars wanted a specific chair and which coachmen would complain about the road but still bring their custom back because the White Hound had better ale and a better yard and a landlady who didn't send them away wet.

Patience had built the first ten years of it and I had inherited it with the lease and the accounts and the complicated grief of walking into a dead woman's kitchen and finding it already shaped around you.
I did not stand in the doorway long.
Standing there long was how you started to believe in things.
The chandler arrived at eleven with an invoice I hadn't asked for and a new price I hadn't agreed to.
I set it on the kitchen table and read it twice.
The numbers did not improve.
"Mr Pickett," I said, with all the pleasantness I could manufacture.
"You've charged me fourteen shillings a dozen for tallow dips.
In September it was eleven."
"Tallow's up this month, Miss Dale.
Supply and demand.
Nothing to be done."
"I know what tallow costs.
I also know what your supplier in Baldock charges per stone, because he sells to the Bell too, and Mrs Pearce at the Bell and I have a long-standing arrangement to compare notes."
Mr Pickett's expression underwent a small recalibration.
"Be that as it may, my costs—"
"Twelve shillings.
I'll take four dozen, paid today.
Or I take my custom to Harrow and you explain to your Baldock man why your volume's dropped."
A pause.
His civil manner was worse than anger.
It meant he was deciding whether I was worth the trouble.
I kept my hands flat on the table and waited.
"Twelve and six," he said.
"Twelve."
"Miss Dale, I am trying to be reasonable—"
"Mr Pickett," I said, "you are trying to see how much I'll pay before I stop being polite about it.
Twelve shillings, four dozen, paid now.
Or I write to Harrow this afternoon."
He smiled.
I had learned that smile.
A man making a calculation, deciding it came out in my direction.
Not a friendly expression, whatever shape the mouth was in.
"Twelve," he said.
I wrote out the payment while he loaded the crates.
The chandler was managed.

The chandler would be managed again next month and the month after that, and I was good at managing chandlers, and I was good at managing coachmen and short-tempered travellers and drainage ditches that no one was ever going to fix, and none of it added up to anything if the lease went.
What could not be managed by small renegotiations was the rent at next quarter, the full weight of the lease on the ledger's far side, the thing I had been not-thinking about for three months.
I had known it was six weeks since the quarter before.
I had been moving faster ever since.
The soldier came round mid-afternoon, in the quieter hour between the luncheon traffic and the evening coaches.
He knocked at the kitchen door.
Not the front, not the taproom door, not the yard gate.
The kitchen door was the door for deliveries and for people who were not certain of their welcome.

Young — early twenties, maybe; it was getting harder to tell, they all looked older than they had before — with the kind of thin that came from missed meals rather than build, and boots coming apart at the welt.
Dark wool coat, no uniform, but the coat cut in a way that had once had something under it.
He had the soldier's way of standing: still, hands at his sides, taking up exactly as much space as his body required and not an inch more.
His eyes went to the yard before they came to my face.
"Beg pardon, miss.
Wondered if there was work going."
I looked at him properly.
Not threatening.
Not drunk.
Just used up, the way they all were, the men coming back down the London road who had done what was asked of them and found their place in the world had been filled in around their absence.
"Have you eaten today?"
I said.
He answered honestly.
"No, miss."
I told him to wait.
I kept him in the kitchen and not the taproom.
The paying guests did not need to see it and he did not need the inspection.
I put bread and cold mutton in front of him and a cup of something warm and went back to the cellar delivery list.
He ate without comment, which I respected more than I would have respected thanks.
When he was done he sat quietly for a moment, as though allowing the food time to land.
"There's nothing I can do in return for it," he said.
"I know."
"I'm sorry for that."
"Keep well," I told him.
He went.
Quietly, the way he had come.
I stood in the kitchen a moment, looking at the empty plate.
The post-war roads were full of men like him, young and thin-soled and going somewhere they weren't certain of, knocked loose from everything that had given them a shape.
They came through two or three a week in good weather, less in the cold.
Some of them asked.
Some just stood in the yard a moment and looked at the inn and decided not to bother.
I kept a few of them fed.
It was not enough and I knew it and there was nothing else to be done about it, and the ledger was not going to change itself and the cellar order was due.
I cleared the plate and went back to work.
The near-altercation in the taproom happened at half past five.

A drover who had been drinking since four had taken the chair that the commercial traveller from Cambridge — a man with a long chin and a longer list of complaints, three shillings in the private corner and two hours spent making it clear he had expected more for the money — considered his own.
The traveller said something.
The drover said something back.
The sound from the taproom changed in the way it changed before things got complicated.
I came out from behind the bar before Nan had to move.

I put a fresh pint in front of the drover and told the commercial traveller from Cambridge that I had just had a thought: the corner was in fact rather warmer in the evenings if he moved slightly, which would make it more genuinely private, and I could see he was a man who appreciated a genuinely private space for his work.
I moved his papers while I was saying it.
He was sitting somewhere else before he had decided to sit somewhere else.
The drover drank his pint.
The traveller worked his papers in his new corner.
Nobody had lost anything.
Nan watched the whole affair from behind the bar with the expression she kept for moments when she and I were thinking the same thing but one of us had got there faster.
She wiped down the bar.
By the end of her shift, the traveller from Cambridge had moved twice more: once of his own initiative, once at my gentle suggestion.
He had eventually settled into a corner that he believed he had chosen himself, which was as good an outcome as I could have hoped for.
"Efficient," Nan said, pulling on her coat.
"Go home, Nan."
"You were up since four."
"I know when I was up."
"Go to bed at a reasonable hour."
She pulled on her second glove.
"I mean it."
I told her goodnight.
She went out with the air of a woman who had said what she'd come to say and was satisfied regardless of whether it was going to be acted on.
I watched the yard door close.
Nan had been covering for me in the taproom more than I'd let myself notice.
More than I'd wanted to notice.
I bolted the door and went back inside.
By eight o'clock the taproom was closed, the fire banked, the last glasses washed and set to dry.
Jem had the stable settled before dark.
The creak of his room above the tack store had been quiet for an hour.
The yard was dark and cold, rooks somewhere in the oak, the inn sign doing its patient complaint in the wind.
Bridget's window above the courtyard had a light in it still — the reading kind, steady and warm.
She'd had a light every night this week.
Bridget read late when she was thinking, and she had been thinking more than usual.
I could not always tell what she was thinking about.
I had a suspicion about this week.
I checked each room before I locked up: taproom, private corner, scullery, the small back room we let out when anyone wanted it, which in November almost nobody did.
Hinges oiled, bolts checked, back door bar dropped, kitchen bar after.
I had done this every night for three years and I still did it twice over because the first pass settled the door and the second pass settled me.
Seven minutes, and I slept better for it.
The yard was dark and cold.
The inn sign creaked in a wind that had come up from the north since sundown, which was the kind of wind that promised nothing good about the week ahead.
The coal supply was going to be a problem by December.
The tallow was already a problem.

The forty-three shillings in the ledger were a problem I had been carrying since Tuesday, and behind all of it, quiet and patient, was the rent at next quarter and the fact that I had been running the place on my own for fourteen months and the money I was working with had margins that did not accommodate bad luck.
I came back to the kitchen.
The fire was down to a steady burn that would hold through the night.
I sat down at the table with the ledger and a new candle, opened it to the column that hadn't balanced, and added it up one more time.
The same answer.
It was always the same answer.
My hands were reddened from the cold water, a cut on my index finger from where I'd handled the chandler's invoice too sharply.
The paper edge had found the exact worst spot, as paper always did.
I pressed my thumb against the ledger's binding.
Bare board under the leather where the corner had worn through, old groove worn in over the past year.
Forty-three shillings short.
Six weeks to next quarter.

Patience had been dead for fourteen months and I had been running the place on my own for all of them, and I was good at it, and I had been good at it, and the margins I was working with were thinner than they looked from the outside.
One bad coach season, one bad winter, and the margins stopped existing.
I had known this since the quarter before.
I had been moving faster ever since and it had not yet been fast enough.
I closed the ledger.
I had not yet looked at the table's corner, where a letter was set squarely in the way Bridget set things she wanted me to see.
She had come down while I was seeing to the evening coal.
She had seen the seal.
She had said nothing, and said nothing was Bridget speaking volumes.
I looked.
Phineas Stainforth.
In his own hand, not his clerk's.
I sat with it.
The fire settled.

Old red brick and woodsmoke and cold stone — the smell of the bread I'd baked that morning, the smell of the place I had built into mine over three years and Patience had built into hers for ten before that.
I knew every creak of it.
I knew where the draught came under the kitchen door and where the plaster had a hairline crack above the taproom window and which stair on the back flight squeaked and which three didn't.
I knew how to feed it and hold it and keep it going on margins thinner than good sense recommended.
The letter was in his own hand, not his clerk's.
He had written it himself, and that told me something about how certain he was of the outcome.
What I did not know was how much longer I could do it alone, and I had been not-knowing that for three months.
"Right, then," I said, to the room and nobody in it.
I broke the seal.
Read it twice.
He wished to discuss the terms of my lease.
At my earliest convenience.
He remained, et cetera, et cetera.
I folded it back along its crease and held it in my reddened hands.
Six weeks.
Chapter One
The ledger had not balanced since Tuesday, and I already knew it when I opened it.
I shut it anyway, pressed my thumb against the spine until the cover lay flat, and went to unbolt the kitchen door.
The yard was dark and cold and wet with last night's rain, the cobblestones shining under the stable lantern.
October had arrived in earnest the week before, all grey sky and teeth.
I tied my apron tighter and lit the kitchen fire.
The bread was in by half past five.

I used the wait to haul water twice, which the pump made difficult in the usual way, and to check the cellar latch, and to wipe down the kitchen table, which I did every morning because the mornings I didn't were the mornings someone found something to complain about.
By six the fire was properly up and the bread was proving and the kitchen smelled the way kitchens ought to smell, which was the best the day was going to offer for a while yet.
Jem appeared in the stable yard while I was hauling the second bucket.
He moved through the dark without a lantern, which he'd always done and which I'd stopped commenting on, and had the first team out, fed, and watered before the sky had properly lightened.
He worked with his back to the kitchen window.
This was his way of not looking at me.
I watched him for a moment through the glass.
He squared the wheelbarrow handles against the wall with a precision that meant he'd done it twice already, the handles level and parallel, the way he always left them.
Then he went back to the horses without looking up.
I went upstairs and aired the rooms.
There were seven guest rooms at the White Hound.

Three fit for a family, two for merchants, one for anyone sensible enough not to mind the view of the privy, and one at the far end of the passage that I let to long-term residents when they materialized and charged accordingly.
This morning they were all empty and cold and smelling of tallow and yesterday's boot mud.
I moved through them in order.
Opened windows, stripped linen where it needed stripping, and made a note in my head of what had to be brought up from the larder before the coaches arrived.
There was a crack along the ceiling of the fourth room that hadn't been there in September.
I stood on the bed in my boots to get a proper look at it.
It ran from the window corner toward the center beam, thin, plaster only, nothing worse yet.
I got down and looked at it again from floor level, which told me nothing new but which I did anyway, because the alternative was deciding it was a problem and I wasn't ready to do that yet.
I'd have Jem look at it from outside if the weather held.
It had been a foul summer, cold and grey from May onward, and October was settling in with the same temperament.
The north road was taking a beating.
The firewood was costing me more than I'd budgeted.
By half past eight I had two arguments with the chimney, a brief and losing engagement with the pump handle, and a working understanding with the back stairs about what we both owed each other.
They'd hold another season if I didn't press the point.
I wouldn't.
The inn was full of these arrangements.
The stairs and their opinion of cold weather.
The east window latch that wanted lifting before it would turn.
The cellar trap that only opened right if you lifted and shoved at the same time.
The low groan of the taproom settle that told you, if you knew how to listen, when the temperature had dropped enough to mean weather coming.
Nine years had taught me all of them.
The inn had finished learning me rather sooner than that.
Nan came in at seven for the taproom and we crossed in the passage, her coming up from the cellar with the first barrel of the day, me coming down with the linen.
"Quiet night?"
she asked.
"The fourth room ceiling's cracked."
She looked at me.
"How bad?"
"Not bad yet."
I shifted the linen.
"Jem will look."
She nodded and went on into the taproom.

By the time I came back through, she'd had the benches wiped and the fire fed and the two earliest risers from the overnight rooms settled with their eggs, and was standing at the bar wiping it down with one eye on the door, which was where she always had one eye when she was expecting the egg man to try the short-weight again.
He always tried.
She always caught it.
The morning coach from London arrived at quarter past nine.
It arrived twenty minutes late and seven passengers short of cheerful, the coachman in a black mood about the north road and the trunk situation.

The road past Welwyn had washed badly in the last rain, not impassably but badly enough that the coachman had taken the verge twice and lost twenty minutes doing it, and then the trunk had gone at the hinge on a rut near the first milestone, and the trunk's owner had spent four miles informing the coachman in detail about the nature of his professional failings.
I listened to all of it without visible impatience.
A coachman who felt unheard would find reasons to recommend a different inn at the next stop, and I couldn't afford a different inn this quarter or any quarter this year.
He had a legitimate grievance about the road.
The trunk situation wasn't his fault.
"I'll have Jem see to the trunk," I said, when he'd finished.
"And you'll want the good team for the next leg.
Not the greys."
He looked at me.
He'd been expecting to negotiate.
"The greys are soft in this cold," I said.
"You know that."
He did.
He nodded and went to get warm.
The trunk's owner was in the passage, arms folded, waiting to be the next problem.
A wool merchant from Finsbury, going by the smell of lanolin and the invoice edge-visible at his breast pocket, traveling north on business that had not improved his temper.
He had decided that the latch on his trunk was the inn's doing.
"The latch," he said.
"The road," I said.
He looked at me.
I gave him a moment.
"The road," he agreed, eventually, in a tone that meant he was conceding the point but retaining the grievance in reserve.
"Can your man do something with it?"
"If it can be done, he'll do it," I said.
He went inside.
I sent Jem to the trunk.

By the time the fire had done its work on the merchant's temper, Jem had the hinge braced well enough to hold to the next posting inn, which was all that was needed, and the merchant came back through the passage looking slightly less like a man who intended to write to someone about it.
"Better?"
I asked.
"Serviceable," he said, which was wool merchant for good enough.
He went to find his breakfast.
Nan had the taproom and had had it since before I'd come downstairs.
I could hear her moving between tables with the flat efficiency she used when her left knee was bad, which this morning meant it was damp.
She hadn't mentioned it.
She hadn't mentioned it in September either, when we'd lost the Grover boy to the harvest and not replaced him, and she'd taken on the south end of the room on top of her own section without a word.
I knew she was doing it.
She knew I knew.
Neither of us had found the moment to address it, which was both our faults and the fault of the quarter running tight.
I caught her eye through the passage door.

She had the egg man's table settled, the two overnight travelers in hand, and was already moving toward the three newcomers from the London coach with the kind of professional sympathy that would have them asking for more bread before she'd finished pouring.
She didn't need me.
She'd never needed me in the taproom.
That was the other thing I knew and had been finding it harder and harder not to say.
The egg man himself was on his way out as I came back through the passage, tucking the invoice into his coat with the air of a man who had recently lost an argument but was retaining his dignity.
"Short on the weight again?"
I asked.
He had the expression of a man who had learned that some arguments were not worth having before noon.
"Two dozen, same as agreed."
"Nan says otherwise."
"Nan has a very exacting scale."
"She does," I said.
"It's why I keep her."
He went out looking philosophical about it.
I kept moving.
The chandler arrived at eleven.
His name was Holt.
He had the build of a man who considered himself reasonable, which in my experience meant he considered himself reasonable and everyone else difficult.

He'd been supplying the White Hound with tallow candles for nine years, and every quarter we went through the same negotiation, and every quarter he was mildly surprised to find it ended the same way.
He set the invoice on the kitchen table.
I didn't look at it.
"Fourteen for the dozen," he said.
"Twelve."
"Cost of tallow's up since summer."
"You said that last summer.
And the summer before."
I picked up the invoice and ran my finger down the column.

The edge caught me along the index finger as I turned it over — a small thing, barely a mark, the kind of thing that would remind me of itself all day — and the dipping charge was there, third line, same as always.
"You've added the dipping charge again."
"Dipping's skilled work."
"I know it's skilled work.
I've been watching you add it to my invoice for nine years.
I've been taking it off for nine years and paying you twelve and sixpence, and you've been happy enough with twelve and sixpence to keep coming back."
I set the invoice down.
"Twelve."
He looked at the invoice.
Then at the good copper pot on the hob, which was old and well-made.
Then at the window where Jem was visible in the yard, moving the horses in without being asked.
"I've two other inns on this road," he said.
"You do.
The Hen at Woolmer runs eight rooms.
The Crown at Hatfield runs six."
I looked at him.
"I run twelve, and I've had your ledger for nine years.
You'd find it inconvenient to lose this account, Mr.
Holt."
"Thirteen, then.
That's the floor."
"The floor is twelve and six."
He had a face built for long consideration of unfair situations.
He considered this one, looking at the invoice and then at me, doing the arithmetic he always did at this point.
"Twelve and six," he said.
"Final."
"Done."
I took his pencil off the table and corrected the invoice before he could revisit it.
There was a cut along my index finger, just starting to sting now that I'd noticed it.
Holt clocked it and decided it wasn't useful.
He left at quarter past eleven.

I watched him go down the yard path and out the gate and turn north toward town, because I always watched the gate for a few seconds after a transaction to make sure nothing had been forgotten or reconsidered.
Nothing had been.
I wrote twelve shillings and sixpence in the ledger and looked at the column beside it.
Six weeks, approximately, before the next quarter's rent became a problem I couldn't work around.
Six weeks if nothing broke.

If the coaches kept running and the winter quarter came in on time and the barrel prices held and the ceiling in the fourth room turned out to be plaster only, which I believed and was choosing to continue believing.
A great deal was riding on nothing breaking.
I turned the page.
The soldier appeared at the kitchen door around two.
He knocked, which they didn't always.
Young, thin in the hollow way that wasn't the same as lean.
The kind of thin that happened over months, not days.
It sat differently in the shoulders.
His boots were coming apart at the welt.
He'd wrapped something around the left one, a strip of cloth bound tight at the ankle, doing what he could.

He had a regimental discharge paper in his hand, folded into quarters, and he held it out the way men held things they'd been told would serve as credentials, which was to say with a certain resignation about whether it would work.
"I can read," I said.
"Have you eaten today?"
He hadn't.
I could see it before he answered, in the set of his face and the way he'd braced himself in the doorframe without knowing he'd done it.
"The kitchen door's around the back," I said.
"Give me a few minutes."
He looked past me toward the passage, where I could hear voices from the taproom.
"Around the back," I said.
"It's warmer anyway.
The taproom fire smokes."
It did smoke.
He went.
I put a plate together myself because Nan's knee was bad and I wasn't going to ask her for this.
Bread and dripping, a heel of yesterday's cheese, the things that wouldn't show up missing against the accounts.
He was sitting at the kitchen table when I came through, spine straight, hands flat on the wood, perfectly still.
He ate without speaking.
I had the afternoon bread to shape and I shaped it.
We got on with our respective work.
I watched him.
His hands, mostly.
They were rough.
Capable.
Knuckles scarred in two places.
They shook when he set the bread down.
He folded them in his lap.
He looked about twenty-two.
He might have been younger.
His face had the look of someone who'd spent the last year trying to be older than he was and had mostly succeeded at it.
When the plate was empty he stood and folded the cloth off it with a precision that told me it had once been automatic.
He thanked me.
He looked at me when he said it, which I appreciated, and I nodded back.
"The road north is better from the ridge," I said.
"Stay on the high side past Stevenage."
He nodded and went out through the kitchen door.
I stood at the window for a moment after, watching the yard.
Jem was at the far fence post, the one that had been leaning since August.
He was fixing it.
No ceremony.
Just the work.
Then I went back to the bread.
Late afternoon, the near-altercation.

Two men from the northbound Manchester run, too much time and too much ale between York and here, and some dispute between them that had been simmering in the confined space of the coach and chose the taproom to arrive at.
I heard the change in noise from the kitchen, the drop in background conversation that meant everyone else in the room had gone quiet, and came through the passage door.
Nan had herself between the two men and the ale barrel.

She had her hand flat on the bar and was nodding slowly and speaking in a very even voice about the weather on the north road, which was what she did when she was buying time for someone's temper to come down.
It usually worked.
The larger of these two men wasn't interested in the weather on the north road.
His companion was looking at the door.
I came in from the far end and stood at the bar and waited.
The larger man looked at me.
He had somewhere to put it and I was nearest.
"There's a room," I said, "or there's the yard."
He held my eye.
I didn't give him anything else to work with.
He chose the room.
His companion followed, looking relieved in a way that said he'd been hoping for exactly this since York.
The remaining guests returned to their conversations with the careful normality of people who were not going to mention this later.
Nan raised one eyebrow.
I shook my head very slightly, which meant we'd handled it and no one needed to say so.
She turned back to the bar.
I went back to the kitchen.
The evening coaches cleared by half past seven.
The taproom emptied by nine.
Nan put her head through the kitchen door at half past eight, coat already on.
"Anything else?"
"Go home," I said.
"Thank you."

She looked at me the way she looked at me when I said thank you, which was a look that managed to convey simultaneously that the words were unnecessary, that she appreciated them anyway, and that she found the whole business slightly embarrassing.
"The fourth room ceiling," she said.
"Jem looked.
He says it's plaster only."
"I know.
I told him."
"He wanted to make sure you knew he'd checked."
She buttoned her coat.
"Goodnight, then."
"Goodnight."
She went, and I heard the back door close behind her, and then the kitchen was quiet.
Jem had gone at eight.
Aunt Bridget's window above the yard still showed a light.
It had shown a light since before supper, the lamp behind the glass steady and unmoving, the shape of her there in the frame.
She'd been at that window all afternoon.

I'd caught the shape of her twice when I'd come out to check the horses, her figure perfectly still, watching the yard with the patient attention of someone who had decided long ago that this was her work and she was going to do it.
She'd been watching from that window since before I'd taken the lease.
She'd watched my mother take it, and the woman before my mother, and probably the woman before that.
She watched and said nothing.
I went through the rooms in the order I always did.
Taproom first, the fire screen checked and the window latches seen to.
The passage and the snug.
The back parlour where nobody had been today.
The cellar stairs.
Kitchen.
Back door.
I walked the yard once in the dark, checking the stable latch and the gate bar.
The cobblestones were cold and wet underfoot.
The lamp in Bridget's window was still lit.
I stood for a moment with the smell of horse and woodsmoke and the rain that was coming again from the north, and listened to the yard settle.
The inn settled into its night sounds when I came back in.
The east beam contracting in the cold.
The wind working through the eaves.
I came back into the kitchen and stood for a moment with my hands at my sides.
They were reddened from the cold water, the way they always were by October.
The cut on my index finger had opened again.
I pressed my thumb against it and held it there until it stopped.
The ledger was on the table.
The letter was under it.
It had arrived in the afternoon post and I'd set it aside because I had bread in the oven.
Stainforth's seal.
His handwriting on the outer fold, or his clerk's — the clerk wrote for him in most things, but the seal was always his, pressed with the same ring, the same angle.
I'd known a letter was coming since September.

I'd known what it was about since the quarter before that, when he'd sent his man round to inspect the roof and his man had spent half an hour in the yard looking at the ground rather than the roof, taking measurements with his eye and writing nothing down.
I lifted the ledger and set it aside.
The letter lay on the kitchen table in the firelight, the wax unbroken, Stainforth's seal pressed clean into the red.
I picked it up and turned it over once.
Then I set it back down.
"Right," I said, to no one.
I didn't open it.
I knew what it said, and tonight that was enough.
Tonight I needed it to stay sealed a few more hours, while I could still believe there was something left to calculate.
I left it on the table and went to bed.
The ledger was still open to the page I'd turned.
THE LAST RETREAT
Chapter 1: The White Hound
The kitchen grate was cold.
I crouched in front of it with yesterday's ash on my hands and thought: there it is.

The fire had gone out sometime in the night, which meant the damper had stuck again, which meant Jem had forgotten to check it, which meant I had forgotten to remind him, which meant the fault was mine.
I laid the kindling anyway.
Small problems were still problems, and they didn't fix themselves while you stood there cataloguing them.
The White Hound woke up in a fixed order and I was always first.
Fire before light, light before Nan, Nan before the coaches.
The common room wanted sweeping.
The taproom floor had a puddle I was going to have to mop before it warped the boards.
The north-facing window above the stair hadn't latched properly since August.
The inn was mine, which covered most of its sins.

The law said otherwise, the law said a widow who remarried surrendered everything and a woman who didn't remarry held on by goodwill and the forbearance of her landlord, but the law had never carried a slop bucket up three flights of stairs at five in the morning, so the law could keep its opinions to itself.
The fire caught.
I stood up.
Nan arrived without knocking, which was her custom after seven years, and dropped her shawl over the back of the chair that no one ever sat in.
"Coach is early," she said.
"How early?"
"Jem says half an hour, maybe less."
She was already at the shelf, pulling down the cups.
"And he says the axle sounds wrong."
I looked at the bread.
Three loaves, enough for the regular morning trade, not enough for a coach-full of passengers stranded by a broken axle.
"How wrong?"
"His face when he said it."
She set the cups down.
"That kind of wrong."
I went to cut more bread.
The coach was not early by half an hour.
It was early by twenty minutes, which was worse, because it arrived before I'd had time to prepare myself for the passengers it contained.
There were six of them.
One was a clergyman who wanted hot water immediately.
One was a woman of about sixty who wanted her trunks carried in and would not specify where.
Two were commercial travellers who wanted ale and showed every sign of making themselves comfortable through the dinner hour.
One was a child of perhaps four years, unaccompanied, who wanted nothing visible but had opinions she expressed through volume.
The sixth was a young man in a military coat who sat on the bench by the door and looked at the floor and did not want anything at all.
I got the hot water.
I got the trunks moved to the east room, where there was a chair.
I told the commercial travellers the ale was half a penny the pint, which was what it was.
The child stopped crying when I gave her a heel of bread, which I had done before and expected to do again.
The young man by the door I left alone.
Jem appeared at my elbow while I was managing the trunk situation.
"The near-side wheel," he said.
"Can it make Stevenage?"
"Maybe."
He looked at his hands.
"Probably not."
I told the coachman.
The coachman said some things that would have distressed the clergyman if the clergyman had been within earshot.
We agreed that the wheel needed the wheelwright, the wheelwright was in the village, and the village was twenty minutes on foot or five minutes if Jem took a horse.
I told Jem to take a horse.
The coachman said he'd be wanting compensation for the delay.
I said that was between him and the coaching company, not between him and me.
He said he thought the White Hound ought to stand good for it.

I told him I'd been running this inn for six years and the coaching company's obligations were the coaching company's obligations, and if he wanted to take it up with Stainforth's agent the agent could usually be found at the Three Bells on Thursdays.
That ended the conversation.
The trunk with the split hinge was a separate problem.
The woman of sixty had not been informed of the split before the bags were loaded and was of the view that someone owed her an accounting.
I agreed that the hinge was split.
I agreed that the trunk had been in the care of the coaching company since York.

I could not agree that the White Hound was responsible for what had happened to it between York and here, but I could offer her twine and my sincere sympathy, and I could ask Jem, when he returned, whether he knew of a carpenter in the village who might look at it.
She said she supposed that would have to do.
I said it would.
Hartley, the chandler, arrived at nine.
He was a man who believed that arriving early gave him an advantage, which was a theory I had spent six years disproving.
I let him stand in the doorway of the kitchen long enough to notice that I had not looked up from the ledger, and then I closed the ledger and looked up.
"Mr.
Hartley."
"Miss Dale."
He had his sample case with him, which he always did when he intended to raise the price of something.
"I was hoping we might discuss the autumn order."
"We might."
I indicated the chair across the table.
"I have the accounts from last quarter."
He sat down.
He had the good grace to look at the ledger, though he didn't ask to see it.
He knew I kept good accounts.
He'd told me once, in a moment of candor he'd probably regretted, that I kept better accounts than three-quarters of the merchants he dealt with on the Great North Road.
"Tallow's gone up," he said.
"Cost of the rendering, the drought this summer affecting the cattle."
"The drought ended in July," I said.
"And the price you quoted me in June was two shillings sixpence the dozen.
I have it here."
"That was before."
"Before what, exactly?"
I opened the ledger to the right page.
"Because I have a letter from your counterpart in Hitchin who's quoting two and four for the same grade."
That was a slight exaggeration.
The Hitchin man had quoted two and four for a smaller run, which wasn't quite the same thing, but Hartley didn't need to know that and I wasn't going to tell him.
He looked at the table.
He looked at his sample case.
He looked, briefly, at the ceiling.
"Two and five," he said.
"For the full autumn order."
"Two and four," I said.
"And you include the half-dozen for the taproom sconces in the arrangement, same as last year."
He did the calculation I'd already done.
He arrived at the same place I had: that it was two and four plus sconces or it was nothing, and the White Hound was a better account than most on this road and he knew it.
"Right," he said.
"Two and four."
I wrote it in the ledger.
He watched me write it, which was the part I thought he resented most, not the price but the record of it, the permanence of having been outrun by a woman with good arithmetic.
I handed him the invoice to sign, and he signed it, and the corner of the paper was sharp enough that it caught the side of my index finger when I pulled it back.
A thin line of red across the top of the knuckle.
I pressed my thumb against it and didn't say anything, and he didn't notice, and that was fine.
He left.
I made a note in the accounts.
The cut stung more than it should have, that cold that meant rain coming, October's gift to everyone who worked outdoors or close to drafty windows.
I wrapped my finger in a bit of rag and got on with it.
The trouble in the taproom started at eleven and was over by a quarter past.
Two of the men from the stranded coach had been drinking since nine, which was their choice and my trade, and somewhere between the second and third round they had found something to disagree about.
By the time I heard it from the kitchen, a raised voice and then a chair, it had moved past disagreement into the territory where furniture became relevant.
I came through the door to find one of them on his feet with his hand on the other man's collar.
Nan was behind the bar with her face in the expression she used when she'd decided something was my problem rather than hers.
"Gentlemen," I said.
Neither of them looked at me.
The one on his feet said something I didn't catch, and the one in the chair said something I caught and wished I hadn't.
I walked to the table and put my hand on the standing man's arm.
He was perhaps thirty, travelling coat, ink on his fingers, commercial not military.
The kind of angry that was about something else and had attached itself to the nearest available target.
"Sit down," I said.
"Or find somewhere else to sit."
He looked at me.
He looked at the door.
He sat down.
The other one made a sound that was probably meant to be triumphant.
I looked at him until it stopped.
Then I took both cups from the table and brought them back to the bar.
"When they want more," I said quietly to Nan, "they can come ask for it."
"They'll be like that all afternoon."
She was already wiping down the far end of the bar, her back mostly to me.
"Road's full of it these days.
The ones coming back."
I didn't say anything.
She wasn't wrong.
The road brought back men who'd left one country and returned to find another, and some of them were carrying more than they'd packed for.
That was the world as it currently stood, and the world didn't ask whether I found it convenient.
I went back to the kitchen.
He was at the kitchen door at half twelve.
Young, younger than I'd thought from the bench, maybe nineteen or twenty.
The military coat was too large across the shoulders, cut for a bigger man or an earlier version of this one.
His boots were the detail.
The left one had a split along the welt, an old split that had been walked on until it separated, and the sole was held on in the front by determination and habit.
He didn't say anything at first.
Just stood there.
"You haven't eaten," I said.
"No."
Then: "I don't have means, I mean to say.
I wasn't expecting to be delayed."
I got up from the chair where I'd been going over the morning's accounts.
I cut a slice of bread, thicker than the ones I'd cut for the paying guests.
I put it on the table with a heel of cheese and the remains of the morning's butter.
"Sit down," I said, and went to check the fire.
He sat.
He ate the way I'd seen men eat when they were trying not to eat too fast and not quite managing.
I kept my back to him, because it struck me that what he needed was someone not watching him do it.
When I heard the plate shift I turned around.
"There's more bread," I said.
"I'm all right."
His colour was better.
"Thank you, miss."
He stood, tucked his coat, that gesture of straightening something that couldn't be straightened, and went out the back door into the yard.
I stayed where I was.
Through the small window I watched him go through the yard gate and onto the road, heading north.
The split boot on the left.
The coat too large.
The way he held his shoulders, like they'd been told to stay up and were still obeying orders no one had bothered to rescind.
I thought one thing, watching him.
I kept it to myself.
By four o'clock the stranded coach had been repaired and departed.
The commercial travellers had settled their tab and left.
The clergyman had taken his hot water and gone upstairs to write letters, which was fine with me.
The woman of sixty had had her trunk seen to by the village carpenter and departed in a hired vehicle toward Stevenage.
The child of four had gone with the carpenter's wife, who turned out to be her aunt, which answered a question I hadn't known I had.
Nan's end-of-shift came at half four.
"The Reeve boy's courting again," she said, pulling on her coat.
"Saw him walking past three times while I was doing the windows."
"Which one's the Reeve boy?"
"The one without the sense God gave a fence post."
She knotted her shawl.
"You'll be all right?"
"I'm always all right."

She gave me the look she reserved for statements like that one, not quite disbelief, not quite affection, something that had been deploying itself in my direction for seven years without ever resolving into one thing or the other.
Then she went.
I locked the taproom.
I locked the common room.
I did the bolts on the kitchen door and the yard gate and the small door at the east end that led nowhere anyone had ever needed to go, but which I checked anyway.
The inn settling around me, the creak of the floorboards upstairs, the tap from the water barrel outside, the rooks going in the elm at the edge of the yard.
Bridget's window above had a lamp in it, as it always did.
The shape of her behind the glass, not moving.
She'd been watching since before I had the inn.
She'd be watching after.
I sat down at the kitchen table with the ledger.
The accounts were what I'd known they'd be.
I was not surprised.

I had not been surprised since late July, when the harvest projections started coming in and I'd done the arithmetic and understood that the next quarter was going to be close, and the one after that was going to require something to change.
Six weeks, maybe eight, before the rent became the kind of problem I couldn't manage around.
I ran my finger down the column.
I closed the ledger.
My hands looked as they always did by end of day.
Reddened at the knuckles from the cold water, a cut on the index finger wrapped in rag, the old burn scar from the summer before last across the heel of the right palm.
They were good hands.
They'd done everything I'd ever needed them to do.
I pulled them into my lap and sat for a moment in the empty kitchen.
The letter was on the corner of the mantel where Jem had left it when it arrived.
I'd set it there myself, in fact.
I'd taken it from him, recognized the seal, and put it down.
Stainforth's handwriting on the outside, his clerk's careful copperplate: Miss D.
Dale, The White Hound, Great North Road, Hertfordshire.
The seal unbroken.
I knew what it said.
I'd known more or less since July, maybe earlier, maybe from the moment he'd ridden past on his inspection tour and looked at the inn the way a man looks at something he's already decided about.
I picked it up.
"Right," I said to the empty kitchen.
I set it back on the mantel and went to bed.
The grate was cold.
I'd banked it properly the night before, because I always bank it properly, but the ash had gone pale and the kitchen was close to freezing.
Sometime in the small hours the wind had shifted north.

I could tell by the ash, the way it lay flat on one side, scoured, and by the way the cold came in not from the walls but from the floor, which meant it had been below zero long enough to get under the foundations.
The cold was the sort that got into plaster and stayed there until spring.
I rebuilt the fire with the last of the dry kindling and crouched in front of it long enough to be sure it had caught.
My hands were already reddened from the pump.
Outside, the sky was the colour of tin.
By afternoon it would rain.
This was fine.
The White Hound had thirty-seven things wrong with it on any given morning.
I had catalogued them all.

The beam above the taproom door had been cracking for two years, not structurally (I'd had the carpenter look), but enough that I watched it every time I passed underneath, because the carpenter had also said it wouldn't last another decade and I didn't have a decade to be patient.
The east stable wall needed repointing.
The lock on the root cellar was held together by one rusty bolt and my consistent refusal to let it fail.
The window in the back bedroom hadn't seated properly since the last hard frost.
My name was not on the lease.
That was the one I came back to, always.

I had been running this inn for seven years, since my uncle died and my aunt lost what remained of her strength for it, and in those seven years I had stripped the wallpaper in the front rooms and replaced it with something that didn't embarrass me, and I had rebuilt the taproom shelving from scratch, and I had driven the coaching company agent down from ten percent to six on commission, and I had kept the thing alive through two bad winters and the worst harvest the county had seen in a generation.
I knew which floorboard in the taproom would take a man's weight and which wouldn't.
I knew the name of every driver on the Great North Road who'd cheat on the passenger count.
I knew that the well in the east yard ran two feet deeper than the one in the west, and that the west one tasted of iron in October and you had to know to switch over before the guests complained.
My name was not on the lease.
According to the law, the White Hound belonged to whoever held the paper, and the paper was in Stainforth's office in Hatfield.
Eleven miles away.
My uncle had held it.

When he died it had transferred, by the law's own logic, to Stainforth as the heir's executor, and it had stayed there because I had nowhere else to go and Stainforth had found it convenient to let the inn keep running on the strength of my labour while he collected the quarterly rent.
The law had a word for women like me.
I had a word for the arrangement too, and it was the same word I used for the east stable wall and the root cellar lock and the cracking beam.
Seven years of my labour and the lease was Stainforth's to extend or not as he chose.
There were mornings when I thought about this directly.
Most mornings I thought about the grate instead.
The fire caught.
I went to wake Nan.
She was already awake, pulling on her boots at the kitchen door, which meant she'd heard the cold too.
Seven years and Nan still had not stopped treating her morning arrival as an interruption of something private.
"Coach is early," she said.
"Jem sent word.
Axle trouble on the Barnet stretch."
"How bad?"
"Lame wheel, his word.
They'll need the spare.
He's put Dawson on it but Dawson's slow."
"How slow?"
"It's Dawson."
"Is it the nearside or the off?"
Nan looked at me.
"Does it matter?"
"It matters which spare we pull."
"Nearside," she said, after a moment.
"I think.
I can send Jem back to check."
"Do that."
I went to the sideboard and started on the bread.
The dough had risen overnight and the room smelled of it, warm under the cold, the one good thing about the morning so far.
Nan came to stand at the opposite counter and began slicing yesterday's heel into portions for the side table.
"Two passengers short-tempered," she said.
"One trunk with a split hinge.
Coachman already wanting a word."
"About what?"
"The north road, I expect."
"They always want a word about the north road."
"They do," Nan said.
"You could stop telling them about Brockett in Hatfield.
It winds them up."
"It's meant to."
She looked at me sideways.
I was already cutting the bread.
I heard the coach before I saw it — the drag of a reluctant wheel, heavier on the left, pulling the whole rig sideways on the ruts.
Lame wheel was right.
Also moving slower than it should be for the schedule, which meant the delay on the Barnet stretch had cost them more than Nan's estimate.
By the time it came into the yard I'd already decided.
Pull the spare from the west stable, send Dawson for the bolt-key, give them two hours and charge the coaching company for the delay, not the passengers.
I catalogued the passengers through the yard window while the horses were being changed.
Two clergymen, cold and put-upon, who would order the minimum and leave the smaller coin and ask whether we had any periodicals.

A woman with a trunk that had apparently generated its own argument about loading, currently standing beside it in the yard with her arms folded, waiting for someone to come and be wrong at — that one I'd have to manage, and the trunk was going to be a problem getting up the step.
A young officer in a coat that hadn't been brushed in a week, sitting alone on the far bench, looking at the ground.
That one I'd leave alone.
Jem appeared at the window, two fingers raised.
Two hours.
I gave him one back.
One hour.
He understood, and disappeared toward the stable.
Fletcher caught me in the doorway before I'd got as far as the taproom.
"Miss Dale."
He had the tone of a man who had prepared several opening remarks and was working down the list.
"I've got eleven miles of broken road behind me and a wheel that—"
"I know about the wheel.
Jem's handling it."
"It shouldn't want handling in the first place, is the point I'm making.
That road is—"
"The road is the company's road," I said.
"If you want compensation for the delay, the company's agent is in Hatfield on Wednesdays.
His name is Brockett and he keeps an office above the apothecary's.
I can write it down for you."
Fletcher's mouth did something complicated.
"That's not—"
"I can write it down," I said again, pleasantly.
"It's no trouble."
He decided not to push it.
They usually decided not to push it, once they remembered they still had forty miles to go and that I was the last hot meal before Peterborough.
I held the door open and he went in.
The trunk woman was next.
She wanted to know why her luggage had been left in the yard rather than brought inside.
I told her because it weighed more than any of us and we were waiting for Jem.
She told me what she thought of that.
I heard her out.
That satisfied something.
She came inside and ordered a pot of tea as if nothing had happened.
The chandler arrived at eleven, which was the part of the morning I'd been preparing for since the week before.
Hartley was a short man with the hands of someone who had not done his own work in several years.
He set his sample case on the kitchen table without asking whether he could set it on the kitchen table.
I'd been watching him do that for four years and it still cost me something each time.
"Quarter's turning," he said, as if I didn't know what month it was.
"Candles'll be at cost.
I can do you two dozen tallow at six for the shilling, same as last quarter."
"You did me two dozen tallow at seven for the shilling last quarter."
"Did I?"
He didn't blink.
"I may be misremembering."
"You're not."
I opened the ledger on the counter, to the page I'd marked three days ago.
"Seventh of July.
Two dozen at seven for the shilling, twice over."
Hartley looked at the ledger.
He had the expression of a man who'd been looking forward to this less than he'd let on.
"Season's turning," he said, as if the first time had not quite landed.
"Cold snap early this year.
Prices coming up all over."
"I know.
I've been getting quotes."

The quote from Hitchin was for a different quantity, but I had the name and the figure would hold if he didn't look too closely, which he wouldn't, because that was a four-hour round trip and he knew it.
"Rawson in Hitchin is at six and a half for the shilling.
I'd rather deal local."
He moved the sample case six inches to the left, which meant he was thinking.
"Six and a half's a stretch."
"Six and a half is six and a half."
"I can do six and three-quarters."
"Seven for the shilling and the same terms as last quarter."
He looked at the ledger.
Then he looked at the sconces hanging from the kitchen ceiling.
There were eight of them, and he'd supplied them all, and we both knew it.
I waited.
The kettle had begun to whistle.
I let it go on a little longer than necessary because it filled the silence better than I could.
"Seven for the shilling," he said finally.
"Same terms."
I wrote the invoice while he repacked his case.
As I folded the paper, the edge caught the base of my index finger — a clean slice, shallow enough that it took a moment to start bleeding.
I pressed my thumb to it and held.
Hartley didn't notice, or pretended not to.
He tucked the invoice under his arm and left looking like a man who'd had a better morning than he had.
I wrapped my finger in a scrap of linen and looked at the ledger for a moment.
Last quarter I'd had a surplus from a wedding party in September.
This quarter I had no wedding party.

What I'd have to open with next quarter depended entirely on what Stainforth decided to do about the lease, and I knew what Stainforth was going to decide, and that was the part I wasn't looking at yet.
I closed the ledger.
The altercation started over a seat.
The clergymen had gone on ahead with the southbound, which left the sort of passenger who develops opinions about taproom seating after their second ale.
I heard the voice change from the kitchen — not louder, but lower, with the flat quality that meant someone had decided to stop performing civility and start meaning it.
I came through the kitchen door with the bread knife still in my hand, which I hadn't planned but didn't mind.
One of them had his hand on the other man's collar and was explaining something at close range.
The other was leaning back against the bar, which is to say he was being held against the bar, and he had the look of a man who had decided that backing down would be worse than what was coming.
Nan was at the far end of the bar with the look of a woman who had already calculated the distances and decided the outcome wasn't her problem yet.
I set the knife on the bar where both of them could see it and put myself between them.
"Gentlemen."
I didn't raise my voice.
"Sit down, or I'll have you both in the yard."
One of them had the presence of mind to look embarrassed.
The other was still deciding.

I held his eyes until he decided correctly, and then I took the stool they'd been arguing over and moved it to the other side of the room, and by the time I turned back around they were both looking at their hands.
Nan came to stand beside me at the bar.
"Third one this week," she said quietly.
"Road's rough."
"It's getting rougher."
She wiped down the counter.
"Used to be they'd at least wait until dark."
She went back to the glasses.
I went back to the kitchen.

Something had changed on the road since the war ended, and I didn't know what to do with it except keep my knife visible and my voice flat and hope I didn't have to use either past what I already had.
Men who'd survived Waterloo were not the problem.

The problem was men who'd survived Waterloo and come home to find nothing waiting for them, and now they were on the roads with the tension of it all still in their shoulders, and the inns were where they ended up.
I fed more of them than I could count.
I'd stopped counting.
Which was how I nearly missed the boy in the yard.
I saw the boots first.
He was standing at the edge of the yard, and from the kitchen window the boots were the first thing that registered.
Left sole beginning to separate at the welt, the leather gone grey and cracked at the toe.
I read people by their shoes.
It was a habit you developed in this work.
These said: walking for months, nothing spare for repairs, not yet at the point of despair but not far from it.
The coat told a different story.
Military issue, from the cut and the buttons, but two sizes too large across the shoulders, the sleeves shortened badly at some point by someone who had no patience for the job.
It had been through worse conditions than him; the collar was stiff with old dirt, and the brass was tarnished to the point where it caught no light at all.
His or borrowed, it had kept him warm and that was the extent of what it was doing for him now.
He was standing very still, looking at the north road, not at the inn.
Not at anything in particular.
Just looking at the road the way men did when they weren't sure they were going to keep moving.
I went out through the back.
"Have you eaten today?"
He turned.
Twenty, perhaps.
Maybe younger — the road aged people, and the last year had aged everyone.
"Miss?"
"Have you eaten."
He considered whether honesty was safe.
"No, miss."
I took him in through the back door to the kitchen.
Not the taproom, where the paying guests would see him and one of them would say something, and then I'd have to deal with that too.
I put him at the small table in the corner, cut bread and the last of the morning's dripping, and set it in front of him along with the heel of cheese I'd been saving for my own supper.
"Sit."
He sat.
I turned back to the accounts.
Behind me I heard the bread go, quickly, without quite the desperation of someone who had been hungry for too long.
He had some dignity still, or some discipline.
When I heard the plate go down I waited another minute before turning around.
It was the decent thing.
He had stacked the plate and knife neatly at the corner of the table.
"Thank you," he said.
"Miss."
I nodded at the door.
He went.
I watched his boots on the north road until the road bent and he was gone.
I thought one thing, and then I chose not to think it, and I went back to the bread.
The house cleared the way it always did after the last coach of the afternoon — all at once, then completely.

The clergymen had gone on with the southbound, the smaller coin left in a neat stack under the edge of the saucer the way men who spent their lives judging other people's generosity sometimes left it, as if tidiness absolved them.
The trunk woman's trunk had been brought inside and she'd departed in a private carriage after a pointed conversation with someone I could only assume was her son.
Fletcher and his wheel had sorted themselves out behind schedule and lumbered north.
The young officer from the bench had gone at some point in the afternoon; I hadn't watched him go.
Nan put her coat on at half past six.
"I covered the bar from four," she said.
"You owe me."
"I know."
"Good."
She did up the top button.
"You're too thin.
You know that too."
"Goodnight, Nan."
"I'm just saying."
"Goodnight, Nan."
She went.
Her footsteps crossed the yard, steady and unhurried, and I heard the gate latch behind her.
From the yard came the sound of Jem settling the horses for the night, the stall doors and the low word he used when he wanted them to be still.
I didn't need to look.
I'd heard it every evening for seven years.
Above me, the shape of Bridget's lamp moved once behind the curtain, then held.
She'd been at that window all day.

She watched the road from that window, and the yard, and the post when it came, and she told me none of it until she decided I needed to know, which was her own system and not one I had ever broken her of.
I did the locking-up.
Taproom shutters.
Cellar door, back bolt, pump cover, front latch.
Bar cloth folded on the rail.
Pewter wiped and stacked.
Bread covered.
The side gate bolted last — I always did the side gate last, because that was the one that had been forced twice in three years, and I wanted to be awake and thinking clearly when I threw that bolt.
I knew the sequence so well I could do it in the dark, and most winters I did.

My hands were rough at the end of each day, reddened from the water and the cold — I noticed them now, in the candlelight, the skin tight over the knuckles, a cut on the index finger stiff under the linen bandage from this morning.
They were useful hands.
They had plastered walls and kept accounts and hauled kegs and negotiated invoices in languages that were not quite English and not quite not.
I didn't look at them often enough to mind them.
Tonight I minded them.
I brought the ledger to the kitchen table and opened it.
The numbers said I had approximately six weeks before the next quarter's rent became a problem.
They had been saying that for three weeks.

A wedding party in September had bought me into October with a small surplus; October had spent it on a new barrel hinge and Hartley's invoice and a farrier bill that Jem had apologised for with the air of a man who had not expected me to take it badly and had been wrong.
I hadn't found a new answer in three weeks and the numbers hadn't moved and sitting here in the cold kitchen was not going to change either of those facts.
I knew that.
I looked at them anyway, because looking at them was what I did instead of panicking, and it worked well enough, and then I closed the book.
The letter was on the sideboard.
Stainforth's seal.
His handwriting, the letters close and even.

It had arrived on the morning coach, which meant he'd sent it from Hatfield on Tuesday, which meant he'd written it over the weekend, which meant he'd been sitting with this decision for at least three days before he'd chosen to put it on paper and send it to me.
I had been expecting it since August.
I picked it up.
I held it.
The paper was heavy, the kind that cost money.
I put it back down on the sideboard.
"Well," I said to the empty room.
Then I went to bed.
The Last Retreat
Chapter One: The White Hound
The fire was sulking.

I'd banked it right — I always banked it right — but the grate had gone cold in the night, and now it was giving me the particular draught that meant either the chimney had a new blockage or the wind had turned easterly, and either way it was the sort of morning that started before you were ready for it.

I got on my knees and prodded at the ash until a grudging ember appeared, coaxed it along with a twist of paper, and watched the flame take hold with all the enthusiasm of a man being asked to work Sunday.
There.
Done.
The White Hound in late October smelled of tallow and damp wool and yesterday's stew, and I was fond of all three.

Not fond in the way people are fond of things they've chosen — fond in the way you get fond of a particular crack in the plaster above your bed because it tells you where you are at three in the morning when you've forgotten.
I had not chosen this inn.

It had come to me by way of my mother's second marriage and a year of legal wrangling that had left me exhausted and nearly broke and technically not the owner of anything, which was the law's position and not mine.
The law could think what it liked.
The White Hound answered to me.
Which was a more complicated thing than it sounded, when you sat down with it.
The inn had sixteen rooms, two of them habitually damp in the east corner where the guttering needed replacing and I hadn't had the funds for it since May.
The taproom held twenty-two at a push, the parlour eight in comfort and ten if no one complained.

The stable yard was large enough for the London coaches, the yard covered by an oak that had been there since before the coaching road, and the oak had opinions about what it would and would not allow to grow in its shadow, and it was right most of the time.
The back fence needed a new post by October and I kept meaning to ask Jem about it and kept not asking because the asking would mean admitting I hadn't got around to it myself.
I knew every fault in this building.
I'd made a study of them the way you study the weaknesses of something you intend to outlast.

The shutter sticking in the parlour, the third step on the back stair that gave under weight and needed to be taken at an angle, the kitchen pump that ran sluggish in cold weather and needed the handle worked six times before it caught.

The law said the inn was held in lease by my mother's estate, and the lease was administered by her solicitor, and the solicitor answered to Stainforth, who was the landlord, and none of that machinery included me in any official capacity.
Dinah Dale, manager.
Not Dinah Dale, owner.
Manager was the word you used when the real word wasn't available.
I'd been managing since I was twenty-three.

I was twenty-eight now and I was good at it, and the inn was better for my management than it had been under my stepfather, and Stainforth knew it, and none of that changed the legal position by a single inch.
I went through the rooms before anyone was up.
The front parlour had a sticking shutter I'd been meaning to fix since August.
The taproom floor was clean, which meant Nan had done the late sweep again without my asking.

The boot room had three pairs of gentleman's boots that wanted the mud knocked off them before the London coach arrived, so I knocked the mud off them myself and thought about what I'd charge for the extra service and decided a penny per pair was reasonable and that I'd rather have the penny than not.
The east window of the taproom looked out onto the yard.
Jem was already there, checking the horses.
He moved along the stall row with his hands running over each animal's flank, not speaking, just checking, and I watched him for a moment before the fire in the kitchen needed my attention again.
Jem had been with the inn since before my mother took it over.
He was not a man who required much management.
He was, in fact, a man who required almost none, which was fortunate, because I had limited management to spare.
I was counting stock in the dry larder — six wheels of cheese, two of them going — when Nan arrived.
"Coach is early," she said.
No good morning.
She hung her cloak on the hook by the door and retied her apron strings with the efficiency of someone who had been tying apron strings since childhood and hadn't improved her opinion of the task.
"Axle trouble on the north stretch.
They're coming in at least twenty minutes ahead and the coachman's in a temper about it."
"How bad?"
"The axle or the coachman?"
"Either."
"Axle's holding.
Coachman's the usual sort of bad."

She pulled a cloth from the shelf and started wiping down the bar without being asked, which was how Nan indicated she already knew what needed doing and would do it faster if I didn't get in the way.
"Two inside passengers short on patience and one outside box who looks like he's been up since before God.
There's a soldier on the back bench."
I was already cutting bread.
"Young or old?"
"Young.
Thin."
A pause.
"Boots."
We understood each other.
"I'll see to it," I said.
The coach came round the bend at a pace that said the driver was managing two problems at once: the cracked road and his own irritation.

I heard it from the yard before I saw it — the particular rhythm of a team pushing harder than the ground deserved, and underneath it the thin complaint of the troubled axle, which was not a sound I liked.
I got to the yard door in time to watch it pull in.

Two inside passengers emerged first: a merchant type in a good coat with a bad expression, the kind of man who travelled with the implication that his time was worth more than whatever delay had just occurred to it.
He looked at the inn, then at the yard, then at me, and I could see him deciding in real time whether any of this was going to meet his standard.
It was not going to meet his standard.
The second inside passenger was a woman in her forties with a travelling trunk bound with rope at the latch, the hinge having given up its commission some time back.
She emerged with the focused energy of someone who had been composing complaints in her head for three hours and was now ready to deliver them.

The outside box was a young man in a threadbare coat, the kind that had been decent once and wasn't any longer, and he held his hat and looked at the inn with the expression of someone calculating what he could afford, then recalculating, then getting down anyway.

There was a respectable woman somewhere in his life — mother, maybe, or a sister with opinions — because he had the careful manner of a man who knew how he looked and was trying to present the good side of it.
The soldier stayed on the back bench.
He was watching the yard with the look men come back with — not suspicious, exactly, just aware.
Taking inventory.
Jem appeared at the horses' heads before I'd crossed the yard.
"Near-side rear wants attention," he said, without looking up.
"Not the axle.
Pin's worn.
I can sort it, but it'll take an hour."
An hour.
I looked at the coachman, who had climbed down and was already searching for someone to be annoyed at.
He found me.
"There she is."
He planted himself in front of me, dust on his coat and grievance in his posture.

"The road coming out of Hatfield's got a new hole the size of my hat, and the company says that's not their concern, and I'm saying it very clearly is, and there's two passengers in there who've had three hours of rough coach and want to know what's to be done about it."
"Which company?"
I said.
"What's that?"
"Which coaching company.
I'll need to know when I write to the agent."
He blinked.
"Biggs and Morton."
"Morton's office is in Baldock on Tuesdays.
He's usually there by half nine."
I let that land.
"Your passengers can take breakfast in the parlour while Jem sees to the wheel.
I'll send bread and coffee out to the yard for your team."
I was already turning.
"Or you can stand here and we can discuss the road for another ten minutes, but the wheel wants the pin either way."
He didn't say anything.
That was the resolution.
The merchant came in looking for someone to complain at and found Nan, who was unimpressable, and he gave it up after two exchanges and sat down with his coffee.

The trunk woman found me in the boot room and told me at some length about the hinge: its previous integrity, its present failure, the quality of the rope she'd been forced to procure in Hatfield, the suggestion that the coaching road itself was responsible, and what she felt ought to be done about the situation as a general matter.
She wanted acknowledgment, not action.
I gave her the acknowledgment.
Her trunk went in the dry corner of the boot room and I told her so and she thanked me with the expression of a woman who had expected considerably less, which was gratifying in a small way.

The chandler arrived at half nine, which was earlier than I'd expected and later than I'd wanted, because I was still in the kitchen and the chandler always arrived ready to negotiate and I was better at that conversation when I had my hands free.
Hartley was sixty, stout, and had the manner of a man who had never once accepted the first offer he was given and intended to die that way.
He set his sample case on the kitchen table without being invited and looked around the kitchen with the specific attention of a man pricing everything he saw.
"Mrs Dale."
He had a habit of calling me Mrs Dale, which was not correct, which he knew, and which I suspected he did on purpose.
"Tallow's up this quarter.
The season, you understand."
"I understand the season," I said.
I put the kettle on, not because I was going to make him tea but because it gave me something to do with my hands.
"I also understand the margin on your last invoice, which was not the margin you showed me in July."
"Prices change."
"They do."
I opened the ledger on the table.
"Last quarter I was paying six and eight per dozen on the standard pillar.
March before that, six and four.
And now you're at seven and two."
"The price of tallow."
"The price of tallow has not moved twelve percent in four months, Mr Hartley.
The price of tallow has moved about three."
I turned the ledger to face him.
"There are the sconces in the front parlour and the taproom both.
That's nine dozen pillar a month through winter.
The woman at Hitchin quoted me six and ten last week."
He looked at the ledger.
He looked at me.
He had the expression of a man who had not expected to need to think this hard before his second coffee.
"Six and ten from Hitchin," he said, which was not an agreement but was a man buying time.
"She seemed to think it was reasonable."
"I'll tell you what."
He reached into the sample case and brought out a candle with the air of a conjurer producing something valuable.
"Six and eleven, and I'll throw in the church-grade wax on the parlour candles.
That's worth something."
"The parlour guests don't care about church-grade wax."
"You might."
He set the candle on the table between us.
"Seven and one.
Final."
"Six and ten," I said.
"Same as Hitchin.
And the delivery on Fridays instead of Wednesdays, because I'm short in the kitchen on Wednesdays."
He picked up the candle and put it back in the sample case and did up the clasp.
"Six and eleven and Fridays."

"Agreed," I said, which was one penny per dozen more than I'd wanted to pay and four fewer than he'd wanted to charge, and the delivery day was the thing I actually cared about, so the conversation had gone as well as it usually did.
I wrote up the invoice while he watched.
The paper had a sharp edge and I caught my index finger on it when I folded it over, a shallow cut that stung and bled a little before I pressed my thumb over it.
I kept writing.
The cut would close.

The invoice was two-thirds of what it would have been in September, and this was the third time this year I'd had to have this conversation, and the next time I had it I wasn't sure I'd have the Hitchin quote to back me up with because the Hitchin woman had been quoting me on the strength of a future order I'd implied was larger than it was.
I knew the math.
Approximately six weeks before the next quarter's rent became a problem.
This was not a new number; I'd been holding it in my head since the first frost.
I showed Hartley out through the back and saw him load his case onto his cart, and then I went to deal with the two men in the taproom who had been arguing since the coachman left.
I didn't know what it had started over.
By the time I pushed through the door, one of them — the merchant, of course — had the other fellow's collar and was using a voice that was carrying quite nicely all the way into the kitchen.
The other man, the one in the threadbare coat from the outside box, had gone red and was about to do something I would have to clean up.
I stepped between them.
I took the merchant's wrist — not the collar, the wrist, because that put me in charge of the contact — and I held it just long enough for him to feel the inconvenience of it.
"I'll need you to sit down," I said, to both of them but looking at the merchant.
He let go.
The coachman's passenger sat.
The merchant straightened his coat and looked at the ceiling and found something interesting there for a moment.
"Better," I said.
Nan appeared in the doorway behind me, wiping her hands on her apron.
