"That's three this week," she said, when the men had gone back to their separate corners.
She said it very quietly, for my ears.
"Used to be three a month."
I didn't answer that.
The soldier came round to the kitchen door mid-morning, while I was alone.
He knocked, which they didn't always do.

He was young — younger than I'd clocked from across the yard — with a face that was still trying to make up its mind between boy and man, and the large coat draped over his shoulders with the look of something he'd been handed in lieu of pay.
A sergeant's coat, maybe, or someone else's altogether — it fell past his hips in a way his own frame couldn't justify.
His boots had split at the welt on the left side, the upper separating from the sole in a smile that was going to admit water at the first puddle.
He'd tried to stitch it back, or someone had tried for him.
It hadn't held.
I read people by their shoes.
It was a habit I'd developed in the first year of managing the inn, when I'd learned that the state of a man's boots told me more about his situation than whatever he said about it.
Good boots, well-cared-for: he had something to come back to.
Boots in need of resoling but still maintained: he was on his way down but hadn't stopped fighting it.
Boots like these, with their careful improvised repair and their losing battle with the road: he'd been on his own for a while.
Long enough that he'd run out of the people who would have noticed.
He looked at me.
"Sorry to trouble you," he said.
"You're not troubling me."
I stepped back from the door.
"Come in."

He came in and stood just inside the threshold with his hat in his hands and looked at the kitchen the way people do when they want something and are trying to decide how to ask for it, or whether asking is the kind of thing they still did.

I turned back to the stove and ladled soup into a bowl — it was yesterday's, thicker than it should have been, but warm — and set it on the table with half a loaf and a heel of hard cheese I'd been meaning to deal with anyway.
"Have you eaten today?"
I said.
A pause.
"No, ma'am."
"Sit down, then."
He sat.
I turned away and gave him the kitchen.
Checked the larder, counted the tea, made some noise with the pots so he could eat without feeling observed.
I kept the parlour guests out by the front door being closed, which it was.
The taproom guests didn't bother coming to the kitchen.
He had the room.
When he was done, he sat quietly for a moment.
"Thank you," he said.
"I've nothing to—"
"I know."
I turned back and collected the bowl.
"There's more road north.
You'll want to get ahead of the dark."
He stood, pulled the coat around him, and nodded once, which was enough.
He went out the door and back across the yard and I watched his boots on the road until he was past the bend.
The left one was already darkening where the water was getting in.
I stood at the door until the road was empty.
Then I went back to work.

The afternoon passed in the way afternoons at the inn passed when there was no fresh crisis: complaints managed, rooms turned, bar stocked, Nan sent home with the promise of a day off she wouldn't take because she never took it.

The coachman's second journey came through at four and had no trouble except a passenger who wanted a room for the night and took a quarter-hour to understand there was none available, and by five the yard was quiet and the light was going and Jem was settling the horses for the evening with the particular silence of a man who preferred his work to conversation.
"Any trouble today?"
I called across the yard.
"Pin's sorted."
He didn't look up.
"Horses want the east stable reshod before the month's out."
"I know.
I'll arrange it."
He nodded and went back to the stall.
That was the whole of it.
Nan had done something affectionate on her way out, which was unusual enough that I noticed it.

She'd folded the clean bar cloths into a particular shape — a shape she only used when she was trying to tell me she was looking out for me without saying so, because saying so would require us both to pretend we hadn't noticed she'd been covering the late taproom shift since August.
I left the cloths where she'd put them.
The inn at seven in the evening, after the last coach and before anyone overnight needed anything, had a quality I couldn't explain to people who hadn't run one.
The building settled.
The fires banked right.
The bolts on the back door: shot.
The front: shot.
The cellar latch: down.
The shutters on the parlour window: closed.
I did this every night and it was the least interesting thing in my day and also, in some way I hadn't bothered to name, the most.
At the end of the round I was always tired and always calm and always briefly aware that what I was locking up was mine, legally or not.
I sat at the kitchen table with the ledger and added the day.
The chandler invoice.
The parlour breakfast.
The taproom ale.

The merchant who'd paid for both nights of a room I'd told him was available before I remembered it wasn't, and the subsequent negotiation that had cost me the second night's rate and a degree of credibility I was going to have to earn back.
The locking-up round had taken twelve minutes, which was two more than usual because I'd stopped at the stair cupboard to check the damp in the east corner and the damp had not improved.
I wrote that down too, in the margin, in the shorthand I used for things that needed money I didn't have yet.

My hands at the end of a day looked like someone else's: reddened from the cold-water wash, the cut on my index finger dried to a thin line, knuckles prominent in a way that hadn't been true five years ago.
I had my mother's hands.
She would have found that funny.
The numbers did not vary from what I already knew.
I closed the ledger on six weeks, give or take, and put it back under the bar with the invoices.
Somewhere above me I heard the creak of Aunt Bridget's chair, which meant she was settling in for the night.
She'd been up there all day.
I'd seen her window lit when I came in from Hartley's cart, and lit again at four when the afternoon coach passed through.
She watched the road from up there, which was how she knew things she didn't say she knew.
She hadn't come down today.
She would when she had something to tell me, or when she was ready, and Bridget operated on her own schedule and always had.
The letter was on the table when I came in from locking up.
I'd known it was there; I'd put it there myself after it arrived at four, tucked it under the sugar tin where I wouldn't have to look at it while I was doing the evening count.
Now the evening count was done.
Stainforth's seal.
His handwriting, neat as an invoice, the kind of handwriting that had learned its form at a good school and never revised its opinion of itself since.
I knew what it said without opening it.

I'd known what it said since the last rent quarter, when the numbers had come out the way they'd come out and I'd understood that the next conversation with Stainforth was not going to be about the rent.
I held it in both hands for a moment.
The fire was down to coals.
The inn was quiet.
"Right, then," I said to the empty kitchen.
I set the letter on the table and went to bed.
THE LAST RETREAT
Chapter 1: The White Hound
The kitchen grate was cold.
I crouched in front of it with yesterday's ash on my hands and thought: there it is.

The fire had gone out sometime in the night, which meant the damper had stuck again, which meant Jem had forgotten to check it, which meant I had forgotten to remind him, which meant the fault was mine.
I laid the kindling anyway.
Small problems were still problems, and they didn't fix themselves while you stood there cataloguing them.
The White Hound woke up in a fixed order and I was always first.
Fire before light, light before Nan, Nan before the coaches.
The common room wanted sweeping.
The taproom floor had a puddle I was going to have to mop before it warped the boards.
The north-facing window above the stair hadn't latched properly since August.
The inn was mine, which covered most of its sins.

The law said otherwise, the law said a widow who remarried surrendered everything and a woman who didn't remarry held on by goodwill and the forbearance of her landlord, but the law had never carried a slop bucket up three flights of stairs at five in the morning, so the law could keep its opinions to itself.
The fire caught.
I stood up.
Nan arrived without knocking, which was her custom after seven years, and dropped her shawl over the back of the chair that no one ever sat in.
"Coach is early," she said.
"How early?"
"Jem says half an hour, maybe less."
She was already at the shelf, pulling down the cups.
"And he says the axle sounds wrong."
I looked at the bread.
Three loaves, enough for the regular morning trade, not enough for a coach-full of passengers stranded by a broken axle.
"How wrong?"
"His face when he said it."
She set the cups down.
"That kind of wrong."
I went to cut more bread.
The coach was not early by half an hour.
It was early by twenty minutes, which was worse, because it arrived before I'd had time to prepare myself for the passengers it contained.
There were six of them.
One was a clergyman who wanted hot water immediately.
One was a woman of about sixty who wanted her trunks carried in and would not specify where.
Two were commercial travellers who wanted ale and showed every sign of making themselves comfortable through the dinner hour.
One was a child of perhaps four years, unaccompanied, who wanted nothing visible but had opinions she expressed through volume.
The sixth was a young man in a military coat who sat on the bench by the door and looked at the floor and did not want anything at all.
I got the hot water.
I got the trunks moved to the east room, where there was a chair.
I told the commercial travellers the ale was half a penny the pint, which was what it was.
The child stopped crying when I gave her a heel of bread, which I had done before and expected to do again.
The young man by the door I left alone.
Jem appeared at my elbow while I was managing the trunk situation.
"The near-side wheel," he said.
"Can it make Stevenage?"
"Maybe."
He looked at his hands.
"Probably not."
I told the coachman.
The coachman said some things that would have distressed the clergyman if the clergyman had been within earshot.
We agreed that the wheel needed the wheelwright, the wheelwright was in the village, and the village was twenty minutes on foot or five minutes if Jem took a horse.
I told Jem to take a horse.
The coachman said he'd be wanting compensation for the delay.
I said that was between him and the coaching company, not between him and me.
He said he thought the White Hound ought to stand good for it.

I told him I'd been running this inn for six years and the coaching company's obligations were the coaching company's obligations, and if he wanted to take it up with Stainforth's agent the agent could usually be found at the Three Bells on Thursdays.
That ended the conversation.
The trunk with the split hinge was a separate problem.
The woman of sixty had not been informed of the split before the bags were loaded and was of the view that someone owed her an accounting.
I agreed that the hinge was split.
I agreed that the trunk had been in the care of the coaching company since York.

I could not agree that the White Hound was responsible for what had happened to it between York and here, but I could offer her twine and my sincere sympathy, and I could ask Jem, when he returned, whether he knew of a carpenter in the village who might look at it.
She said she supposed that would have to do.
I said it would.
Hartley, the chandler, arrived at nine.
He was a man who believed that arriving early gave him an advantage, which was a theory I had spent six years disproving.
I let him stand in the doorway of the kitchen long enough to notice that I had not looked up from the ledger, and then I closed the ledger and looked up.
"Mr.
Hartley."
"Miss Dale."
He had his sample case with him, which he always did when he intended to raise the price of something.
"I was hoping we might discuss the autumn order."
"We might."
I indicated the chair across the table.
"I have the accounts from last quarter."
He sat down.
He had the good grace to look at the ledger, though he didn't ask to see it.
He knew I kept good accounts.
He'd told me once, in a moment of candor he'd probably regretted, that I kept better accounts than three-quarters of the merchants he dealt with on the Great North Road.
"Tallow's gone up," he said.
"Cost of the rendering, the drought this summer affecting the cattle."
"The drought ended in July," I said.
"And the price you quoted me in June was two shillings sixpence the dozen.
I have it here."
"That was before."
"Before what, exactly?"
I opened the ledger to the right page.
"Because I have a letter from your counterpart in Hitchin who's quoting two and four for the same grade."
That was a slight exaggeration.
The Hitchin man had quoted two and four for a smaller run, which wasn't quite the same thing, but Hartley didn't need to know that and I wasn't going to tell him.
He looked at the table.
He looked at his sample case.
He looked, briefly, at the ceiling.
"Two and five," he said.
"For the full autumn order."
"Two and four," I said.
"And you include the half-dozen for the taproom sconces in the arrangement, same as last year."
He did the calculation I'd already done.
He arrived at the same place I had: that it was two and four plus sconces or it was nothing, and the White Hound was a better account than most on this road and he knew it.
"Right," he said.
"Two and four."
I wrote it in the ledger.
He watched me write it, which was the part I thought he resented most, not the price but the record of it, the permanence of having been outrun by a woman with good arithmetic.
I handed him the invoice to sign, and he signed it, and the corner of the paper was sharp enough that it caught the side of my index finger when I pulled it back.
A thin line of red across the top of the knuckle.
I pressed my thumb against it and didn't say anything, and he didn't notice, and that was fine.
He left.
I made a note in the accounts.
The cut stung more than it should have, that cold that meant rain coming, October's gift to everyone who worked outdoors or close to drafty windows.
I wrapped my finger in a bit of rag and got on with it.
The trouble in the taproom started at eleven and was over by a quarter past.
Two of the men from the stranded coach had been drinking since nine, which was their choice and my trade, and somewhere between the second and third round they had found something to disagree about.
By the time I heard it from the kitchen, a raised voice and then a chair, it had moved past disagreement into the territory where furniture became relevant.
I came through the door to find one of them on his feet with his hand on the other man's collar.
Nan was behind the bar with her face in the expression she used when she'd decided something was my problem rather than hers.
"Gentlemen," I said.
Neither of them looked at me.
The one on his feet said something I didn't catch, and the one in the chair said something I caught and wished I hadn't.
I walked to the table and put my hand on the standing man's arm.
He was perhaps thirty, travelling coat, ink on his fingers, commercial not military.
The kind of angry that was about something else and had attached itself to the nearest available target.
"Sit down," I said.
"Or find somewhere else to sit."
He looked at me.
He looked at the door.
He sat down.
The other one made a sound that was probably meant to be triumphant.
I looked at him until it stopped.
Then I took both cups from the table and brought them back to the bar.
"When they want more," I said quietly to Nan, "they can come ask for it."
"They'll be like that all afternoon."
She was already wiping down the far end of the bar, her back mostly to me.
"Road's full of it these days.
The ones coming back."
I didn't say anything.
She wasn't wrong.
The road brought back men who'd left one country and returned to find another, and some of them were carrying more than they'd packed for.
That was the world as it currently stood, and the world didn't ask whether I found it convenient.
I went back to the kitchen.
He was at the kitchen door at half twelve.
Young, younger than I'd thought from the bench, maybe nineteen or twenty.
The military coat was too large across the shoulders, cut for a bigger man or an earlier version of this one.
His boots were the detail.
The left one had a split along the welt, an old split that had been walked on until it separated, and the sole was held on in the front by determination and habit.
He didn't say anything at first.
Just stood there.
"You haven't eaten," I said.
"No."
Then: "I don't have means, I mean to say.
I wasn't expecting to be delayed."
I got up from the chair where I'd been going over the morning's accounts.
I cut a slice of bread, thicker than the ones I'd cut for the paying guests.
I put it on the table with a heel of cheese and the remains of the morning's butter.
"Sit down," I said, and went to check the fire.
He sat.
He ate the way I'd seen men eat when they were trying not to eat too fast and not quite managing.
I kept my back to him, because it struck me that what he needed was someone not watching him do it.
When I heard the plate shift I turned around.
"There's more bread," I said.
"I'm all right."
His colour was better.
"Thank you, miss."
He stood, tucked his coat, that gesture of straightening something that couldn't be straightened, and went out the back door into the yard.
I stayed where I was.
Through the small window I watched him go through the yard gate and onto the road, heading north.
The split boot on the left.
The coat too large.
The way he held his shoulders, like they'd been told to stay up and were still obeying orders no one had bothered to rescind.
I thought one thing, watching him.
I kept it to myself.
By four o'clock the stranded coach had been repaired and departed.
The commercial travellers had settled their tab and left.
The clergyman had taken his hot water and gone upstairs to write letters, which was fine with me.
The woman of sixty had had her trunk seen to by the village carpenter and departed in a hired vehicle toward Stevenage.
The child of four had gone with the carpenter's wife, who turned out to be her aunt, which answered a question I hadn't known I had.
Nan's end-of-shift came at half four.
"The Reeve boy's courting again," she said, pulling on her coat.
"Saw him walking past three times while I was doing the windows."
"Which one's the Reeve boy?"
"The one without the sense God gave a fence post."
She knotted her shawl.
"You'll be all right?"
"I'm always all right."

She gave me the look she reserved for statements like that one, not quite disbelief, not quite affection, something that had been deploying itself in my direction for seven years without ever resolving into one thing or the other.
Then she went.
I locked the taproom.
I locked the common room.
I did the bolts on the kitchen door and the yard gate and the small door at the east end that led nowhere anyone had ever needed to go, but which I checked anyway.
The inn settling around me, the creak of the floorboards upstairs, the tap from the water barrel outside, the rooks going in the elm at the edge of the yard.
Bridget's window above had a lamp in it, as it always did.
The shape of her behind the glass, not moving.
She'd been watching since before I had the inn.
She'd be watching after.
I sat down at the kitchen table with the ledger.
The accounts were what I'd known they'd be.
I was not surprised.

I had not been surprised since late July, when the harvest projections started coming in and I'd done the arithmetic and understood that the next quarter was going to be close, and the one after that was going to require something to change.
Six weeks, maybe eight, before the rent became the kind of problem I couldn't manage around.
I ran my finger down the column.
I closed the ledger.
My hands looked as they always did by end of day.
Reddened at the knuckles from the cold water, a cut on the index finger wrapped in rag, the old burn scar from the summer before last across the heel of the right palm.
They were good hands.
They'd done everything I'd ever needed them to do.
I pulled them into my lap and sat for a moment in the empty kitchen.
The letter was on the corner of the mantel where Jem had left it when it arrived.
I'd set it there myself, in fact.
I'd taken it from him, recognized the seal, and put it down.
Stainforth's handwriting on the outside, his clerk's careful copperplate: Miss D.
Dale, The White Hound, Great North Road, Hertfordshire.
The seal unbroken.
I knew what it said.
I'd known more or less since July, maybe earlier, maybe from the moment he'd ridden past on his inspection tour and looked at the inn the way a man looks at something he's already decided about.
I picked it up.
"Right," I said to the empty kitchen.
I set it back on the mantel and went to bed.
The grate was cold.
I'd banked it properly the night before, because I always bank it properly, but the ash had gone pale and the kitchen was close to freezing.
October had decided to skip the rest of autumn and go straight to something worse.
The cold was the sort that got into plaster and stayed there.
I rebuilt the fire with the last of the dry kindling and crouched in front of it long enough to be sure it had caught.
My hands were already reddened from the pump in the yard.
Outside, the sky was the colour of tin.
By afternoon it would rain.
This was fine.

I had handled worse mornings than this one, and I would handle worse mornings than this one, and the fire was lit now and the kettle was on and the taproom benches needed wiping before the first coach, which was due at half past eight unless the north road was giving trouble again, which it usually was.
The White Hound was mine.
My name was not on the lease.
My name was never on anything.

But I had been running this inn for seven years, since my uncle died and my aunt lost what remained of her strength for it, and in those seven years I had learned every drip and creak and groan of the building, every fault in the cellar steps, every penny the coaching company owed me and hadn't paid.
The beam above the taproom door had been cracking for two years.
The east stable wall needed repointing.
The lock on the root cellar was held together by habit and one rusty bolt.
I knew all of it.
Every bolt and hinge and groaning timber of it.
The fire caught.
I went to wake Nan.
She was already awake, pulling on her boots at the kitchen door, which meant she'd heard the cold too.
Seven years and Nan still had not stopped treating her morning arrival as an interruption of something private.
"Coach is early," she said.
"Jem sent word.
Axle trouble on the Barnet stretch."
"How bad?"
"Lame wheel, his word.
They'll need the spare.
He's put Dawson on it but Dawson's slow."
"How slow?"
"It's Dawson."
I went to the sideboard and started on the bread.
The dough had risen overnight and the room smelled of it, warm under the cold, the one good thing about the morning so far.
Nan came to stand at the opposite counter and began slicing yesterday's heel into portions for the side table.
"Two passengers short-tempered," she said.
"One trunk with a split hinge, Jem said.
Coachman already wanting a word."
"About what?"
"About the north road, I expect.
They always want a word about the north road."
"They can want all they like.
The coaching company built the north road."
Nan looked at me sideways.
She did that when she thought I was going to start trouble before I'd had my tea.
She was usually right.
The coach pulled in at ten past nine, which was eleven minutes late by my count and forty minutes late by the coachman's count, and he said so before he'd climbed down from the box.
His name was Fletcher, I'd had him three times before, and he had a face that arrived already grieving about something.
The passengers I catalogued through the yard window while the horses were being changed.
Two clergymen who looked cold and put-upon and would order the minimum.
A woman with a trunk so large it had generated its own argument about loading, currently standing beside it in the yard with her arms folded, waiting for someone to come and be wrong at.
A young officer in a coat that hadn't been brushed in a week, sitting alone on the far bench, looking at the ground.
Fletcher caught me in the doorway before I'd got as far as the taproom.
"Miss Dale."
He had the tone of a man who had prepared several opening remarks and was working down the list.
"I've got eleven miles of broken road behind me and a wheel that—"
"I know about the wheel.
Jem's handling it."
"It shouldn't want handling in the first place, is the point I'm making.
That road is—"
"The road is the company's road," I said.
"If you want compensation for the delay, the company's agent is in Hatfield on Wednesdays.
His name is Brockett and he keeps an office above the apothecary's.
I can write it down for you."
Fletcher's mouth did something complicated.
"That's not—"
"I can write it down," I said again, pleasantly.
"It's no trouble."
He decided not to push it.
They usually decided not to push it.
I gave him a moment to remember he still had another forty miles to go and that I was the last hot meal before Peterborough, and then I held the door open and he went in.
The trunk woman was next.
She wanted to know why her luggage had been left in the yard rather than brought inside.
I told her because it weighed more than any of us and we were waiting for Jem.
She told me what she thought of that.
I heard her out.
That satisfied something.
She came inside and sat down and ordered a pot of tea as if nothing had happened.
The chandler arrived at eleven, which was the part of the morning I'd been preparing for since the week before.
Hartley was a short man with the hands of someone who had not done his own work in several years.
He set his sample case on the kitchen table without asking whether he could set it on the kitchen table.
I'd been watching him do that for four years and it still cost me.
"Quarter's turning," he said, as if I didn't know what month it was.
"Candles'll be at cost.
I can do you two dozen tallow at six for the shilling, same as last quarter."
"You did me two dozen tallow at seven for the shilling last quarter."
"Did I?"
He didn't blink.
"I may be misremembering."
"You're not."
I opened the ledger on the counter, to the page I'd marked three days ago.
"Seventh of July.
Two dozen at seven for the shilling, twice over."
Hartley looked at the ledger.
He had the expression of a man who'd been looking forward to this less than he'd let on.
"Season's turning," he said again, as if the first time had not quite landed.
"Cold snap early this year.
Prices coming up all over."
"I know.
I've been getting quotes."

The quote from Hitchin was actually for a different quantity, but I had his name and the figure I'd cited was defensible if Hartley didn't look too closely, which he wouldn't, because that was a four-hour trip and he knew it.
"Rawson in Hitchin is at six and a half for the shilling.
I'd rather deal local, but I'd rather deal cheaply more."
He moved the sample case six inches to the left, which meant he was thinking.
"Six and a half's a stretch."
"Six and a half is six and a half."
"I can do six and three-quarters."
"Seven for the shilling and the same terms as last quarter."
He looked at the ledger again.
He looked at the sconces hanging from the kitchen ceiling.
There were eight of them, and he'd supplied them all, and we both knew it.
I waited.
The kettle had begun to whistle, which I let go on a little longer than necessary because it filled the silence better than I could.
"Seven for the shilling," he said finally.
"Same terms."
I wrote out the invoice while he repacked his case.
As I folded the paper, the edge caught the base of my index finger — a clean slice, not deep, but enough.
I pressed my thumb against it until it stopped.
Hartley didn't notice, or pretended not to.
He took the invoice and left the kitchen the same way he'd entered it, sample case tucked under his arm, looking like a man who'd had a better morning than he had.
The price was going to be worse next quarter.
I knew that already.
Seven for the shilling today because I had a ledger and a name in Hitchin and the patience to wait through his silences.
What I'd have next quarter was harder to say.
I closed the ledger.
The altercation started over a seat.
Two men from the stranded coach.
The clergymen had gone on ahead, which left the type of passenger that tended to develop opinions about taproom seating after their second ale.
I heard the voice change from the kitchen, the shift from loudness to intent.
I had learned to tell the difference.
By the time I came through, one of them had his hand on the other's collar and Nan was standing at the far end of the bar with the look of a woman calculating distances.
I put myself between them.
I had good timing for that.
You developed it.
"Gentlemen."
I didn't raise my voice.
There was no need to raise it.
"Sit down, or I'll have you both in the yard."
One of them had the presence of mind to look embarrassed.
The other was still deciding.

I held his eyes until he decided correctly, and then I took the contested seat and dragged it six feet to the left so there was nothing to argue about anymore, and by the time I turned back around they were both looking at their hands.
Nan came to stand beside me at the bar.
"Third one this week," she said quietly.
"Road's rough."
"Road's been rough for three years.
It's getting rougher."
I went back to the kitchen.
She wasn't wrong.

Something had changed on the road since the war ended, a tension that didn't resolve — men with nowhere to be and not enough reason to behave, and Waterloo already far enough behind them that the civility of the returned soldier had worn off.
I fed more of them than I could count and I'd stopped trying to count them.
Which was how I came to notice the boy in the yard.
He'd been there for half an hour before I looked up from the bread and placed him.
Young, thin enough that the military coat looked borrowed, which it might have been.
His boots were the thing — coming apart at the welt on the left, the sole beginning to separate.
He was standing at the edge of the yard with his hands in his pockets, looking at the road, not at the inn.
I went out through the back.
"Have you eaten today?"
He turned.
Twenty, perhaps.
Maybe younger.
"Miss?"
"Have you eaten."
He considered whether honesty was safe.
"No, miss."
I took him through the back door to the kitchen.
Not the taproom, where the paying guests would see him and one of them would say something, and then I'd have to deal with that too.
I put him at the small table in the corner and cut bread and the last of the morning's dripping and set it in front of him.
"Sit."
He sat.
I turned back to the accounts.
Behind me I heard the bread go, quickly but not desperately, the sound of someone who had learned not to let on how hungry they were.
When I heard the plate go down I waited another minute before turning around.
It was the decent thing.
He had stacked the plate and knife neatly at the corner of the table.
"Thank you," he said.
"Miss."
I nodded at the door.
He went.
I watched his boots on the north road until the road bent and he was gone.
I thought one thing, and then I didn't think it anymore, and went back to the accounts.
The house cleared the way it always did after the last coach of the afternoon.
All at once, then completely.
The clergymen had gone on with the southbound.
The trunk woman's trunk had finally been brought inside and she'd departed in a private carriage after a pointed conversation with someone I could only assume was her son.
Fletcher and his wheel had sorted themselves out two hours behind schedule and lumbered north.
Nan put her coat on at half past six.
"I covered the bar from four," she said.
"You owe me."
"I know."
"Good."
She did up the top button.
"You're too thin.
You know that too."
"Goodnight, Nan."
She went.
Her footsteps crossed the yard, steady and unhurried, and I heard the gate latch behind her.
Jem came in from the stables at seven, face red from the cold.
"Horses settled.
South box latch is still going.
I've got a piece of iron that'll hold it till morning."
"That's fine."
He looked at me the way Jem always looked at me.
He'd noticed things.
He'd decided not to raise them.
That was Jem.
"Night, then," he said.
"Night."
The yard went quiet.
From the window I could see the shape of Bridget's lamp behind her curtain on the floor above, the light steady and unchanged.
She had been up there all day.
She watched the road from that window and she watched the yard and she watched the seal on letters that came through the post, and she told me none of it unless she decided I needed to know.
I did the locking-up sequence from memory.
Taproom shutters.
Cellar door, back bolt, pump cover, front latch.
The bar cloth folded on the rail.
The pewter wiped and stacked.
The bread covered.
All the small tasks that meant the day was ending and the inn was mine in the way it was only mine after dark, when there was no one to witness it.
I brought the ledger to the kitchen table and opened it.
The numbers said I had approximately six weeks before the next quarter's rent became a problem.
They had been saying that for three weeks.
I had not found a new answer and the numbers had not changed, and sitting here looking at them again was not going to produce either.
I knew that.
I sat here and looked at them anyway, because it was what I did, and then I closed the ledger.
The letter was on the sideboard.
Stainforth's seal.
His handwriting, the letters close and even, the address written with the confidence of a man who had never needed to wonder whether the post would reach him.
I'd known it was coming since August, if I was being honest, and I had been many things that autumn but I had not quite been honest about that.
I picked it up.
I held it.
I put it back down.
"Well," I said to the empty room.
Then I went to bed.
THE LAST RETREAT
Chapter 1: The White Hound
The grate was cold when I came down.

Not banked cold, not last-coals-not-quite-out cold, but dead-out-since-midnight cold, which told me two things: Jem had been up past when he should have been, and the temperature had dropped hard in the night.
My breath hung in the kitchen.
The flagstones were cold enough to come through my boots.
I got the tinder box from the shelf and crouched on the hearthstone and got on with it, hands stiff, the flint throwing sparks that went nowhere for a good half-minute before the char cloth caught.
There are people who read tea leaves.
I read fires.
This one said the day was going to be difficult.
The White Hound was mine in every way the law declined to acknowledge.
I had run it for seven years, kept the accounts, managed the yard, renegotiated the chandler contracts, and replaced the east stable's listing wall twice.
My name was on nothing that mattered.

The lease was in my late husband's name, administered by his former solicitor, a man named Stainforth who came by twice a year to inspect the premises and remind me, in his pleasant paragraphs, what my situation was.
The inn was his client's asset.
That I had turned it from a coaching house with three regulars and a rat problem into something that made a quarterly profit was noted in the ledger as evidence of good management.
It was noted nowhere else.
Very little going for it, besides the fact it was mine.
And the law was working on that.

I had ten things that needed doing before the first coach arrived and I did them in the order that would save the most time: fire, bread, water, lamp oil, taproom chairs off the tables, the bar wiped down, the necessary account in the pantry checked against what I'd need for today's ordinary.
The White Hound had an opinion about every task.
The back-door lock had been stiff since April and communicated its displeasure each morning.

The east stable wall had developed a new lean sometime before August and I had been shoring it with a timber brace since then, which was a solution that fell somewhere between adequate and wishful thinking.
I had priced the proper repair twice and both times the number had been enough to make me close the ledger and think about it later.
Later had been going on for three months.
What I was proud of: the yard, which Jem ran with the same methodical steadiness he brought to everything, clean and ordered, the horses settled before dark without being asked.

The kitchen, which was mine in a way no other room in the building was, warm and particular, with bread that the village women had started buying off me on Wednesdays, which was not something I had planned but had decided to treat as revenue.

The accounts, which balanced when they had no right to, and which I had kept for seven years through two bad harvests, a road that was harder on coaches every winter, and a year in which the summer had been no summer at all.
What I was not proud of: the east stable wall.
The back-door lock.

The way the taproom had got rougher in the past year, the post-war mood on the road having migrated indoors, as though the men were still waiting for the orders that would tell them what to do with themselves.
I had no solution for that last one and I had stopped pretending I might.
The inn was mine in the way that a thing you've built with your hands is yours, which the law would tell you at length is not the same as owning it.
The law had strong opinions about women and leases.

Those opinions lived in a drawer in Stainforth's office in Hitchin, and twice a year he brought them to my kitchen table and laid them out with all the courtesy of a man who believed he was doing me a favour.
I had six weeks before the next quarter's rent was due.
I knew what six weeks meant.
I had been moving faster since I worked it out, in the way you move faster when you can hear something gaining on you and have not yet decided what to do when it gets here.
I put a loaf in to prove and went to wake Nan.
By the time Nan arrived, the kitchen was warm enough to stand without your coat on.
"Coach is late," she said, not as a greeting, because after seven years we were past greetings.
She hung her cloak on the peg and tied her apron and reached past me for the bread knife.
"Or early.
Depends on your outlook.
Came through Stevenage with a cracked axle."
"How cracked?"
"Cracked enough to make Jem look worried."
She began cutting.
"He's not telling you how worried because he knows you'll just fix it before he's done explaining what's broken."
I cut bread alongside her for a moment.
That was the thing about Nan: she told you the situation in two sentences and then let you do the thinking.
"The spares are in the side store."
"I know where the spares are."
"The coachman's going to want something."
"I know that too."
She looked at me sideways.
"You're going to give it to him."
"I'm going to let him think he's getting it," I said, and went out to the yard.
The coach was already in, pulled to the side to take the weight off the damaged wheel.
Jem had it up on the block and was crouching beside it with a lantern, which at this hour meant he'd been up since well before five.
He was a solid man, Jem — a head shorter than me and twice as wide, with hands that could bend iron and a temper that never surfaced.
He had a solid man's way of not complaining about the inconvenience of anything, which I valued more than I paid him for it.
"Bad?"
I said.
"Manageable."
He tilted his head at the wheel.
"Spoke's split but not through.
Brace it and she'll hold to the next stop."
"Good.
How long?"
"Hour," Jem said, without turning round.
Then: "Cold.
Hungry."
I went back inside.
The passengers were already out, pacing the yard with the particular irritation of people who have concluded that delay is being done to them personally.

I catalogued them on my way to the coachman: a stout woman in a green travelling coat who had supervised her trunk off the roof and was now standing over it as though it might make a run for it; a clergyman writing in a small notebook as he paced — composing a complaint, probably, or possibly a sermon, the handwriting too urgent to be devotional; two men in coats that had come off a demobilization allowance, with the careful posture of soldiers in civilian dress who have not yet decided what soldiers in civilian dress are supposed to do with their hands.
One of them glanced at me as I passed.
Young.
Thin.
I had already seen his boots in the yard earlier and registered them and filed them.
He was not on my immediate list.
The coachman was at the water trough, watching Jem work with the expression of a man who has calculated what the delay will cost him and decided someone else should pay it.
"Miss Dale."
He was large and red-faced and smelled of wet wool.
"North road's a ruin past Baldock.
That cobble repair they did in August has not held and now I've got a spoke that could've killed someone—"
"Are you in need of breakfast, Mr.
Falconer," I said, "or are we settling something first?"
He drew himself up.
"I'm saying the road—"
"Is maintained by the turnpike trust, whose agent has an office in Baldock and takes meetings on Wednesdays.
I have his schedule, if you'd like it."
I let him absorb that.
"The spoke will be braced.
You'll be on the road in an hour.
Breakfast is included."
Falconer looked at me for a long moment.
He had the kind of bluster that worked on women who were frightened of it.
I was not, and he had worked that out by now, which was why we spent thirty seconds each time performing this particular ritual before he backed down.
"An hour," he said.
"An hour," I said.
He went inside.

The trunk woman informed me that her trunk had been improperly loaded in London and any damage to the contents fell entirely on the coaching company, as she had taken the precaution of informing the guard at the point of departure.
Her evidence was a label she had written herself, in pencil, which specified FRAGILE and the date, which was today's date written this morning.
I thanked her for the information and said I would note it.
She went inside satisfied.
Most people were, if you noted it with sufficient gravity.
The noting was almost the point, as often as not.
Hartley the chandler arrived at half past nine with his sample case and his new price list, which was higher than last quarter's by fourpence per dozen.
He set his case on the kitchen table with the air of a man delivering good news and began explaining the cost of tallow, the difficulty of the season, the rising price of everything along the road.
I let him talk.
I opened the ledger to the November page and let it lie there.
"Miss Dale, I understand the last quarter's arrangement was—"
"Last quarter was two and eight per dozen for the sconces and two and four for the table stock."
I did not look up from the ledger.
"What are you asking now?"
"Three shillings is not unreasonable, given—"
"I had a quote from Hitchin in September."
This was somewhat true; I had spoken to a man who knew Hitchin's chandler, which was close enough.
"Two and ten across."
Hartley sucked air between his teeth.
"Hitchin's stock is inferior.
The wick quality alone—"
"I have twelve sconces and want forty pounds of table tallow to last me through March," I said.
"At last quarter's price."
He looked at his case.
He looked at the ledger, which was open to a page that showed, coincidentally, the last three months of chandler expenditure in clear columns.
He looked at the twelve sconces, which were visible from where he was standing, and perhaps performed the calculation of whether I might have overstated my count.
I had not.
"Two and eight," he said, "and I'll throw in the tapers."
"Two and six and the tapers, and you have my custom through spring."
The silence lasted perhaps four seconds.
"Two and six," he said, in the tone of a man being drained.
I wrote up the invoice myself, which was faster and kept my margins visible to no one.
The pen caught on the edge of the paper as I tore it along the fold and dragged a small cut across the tip of my index finger — not deep, not worth noting, but present.

I handed Hartley his copy and sent him on his way with the understanding that next quarter he would open at two and ten and I would close at two and seven, and so it would go until one of us found a better arrangement.
The negotiation was getting harder each quarter.
Not impossible.
Just harder.
The margins on everything had been tightening since the harvest failed, and I could feel it the way I felt weather coming in from the north: not yet a problem, but the air was changing.
The taproom altercation happened before noon.
Two men from the stranded coach, at the window table, voices rising with the concentrated urgency of people who have been made to wait and have decided to make use of the time.
A bottle between them, one man on his feet and leaning, the other with his jaw set.
I did not need to know the cause.
The cause, in my experience, was almost never the thing.

Some anger was about whatever it was about and some anger was about three years of war and coming home to a bad harvest and a country that had spent its goodwill on bunting and was now busy with other things.
I came through the door from the kitchen, crossed the room without hurrying, stepped between them, and removed the bottle from the table in a single motion I had developed through repetition.
My body knew the geometry of it by now.
"Gentlemen," I said.
The voice I used was not a shout and not a request.
I had found it in year two, when I understood that authority is mostly a matter of performing certainty that there is no alternative to what you're about to say.
"This is handled."
The man on his feet looked at me.
He was working out whether I was something he could push past.
I held his gaze and waited for him to finish working it out.
He sat down.
Nan appeared at my elbow as I walked away.
"Three this week," she said quietly, not loud enough to carry.
"They're all off the London road.
I don't know if it's the wait or what they're coming back to."
She meant the soldiers.
She did not have to say more than that.

The road had been moving them through since summer, ones and twos, men with plans and men without, all of them with the same look — still half somewhere else, still waiting for orders that would clarify what to do with themselves now that nobody needed them to be dangerous.
I managed it as it came.
There was no other policy available to me.
The young man from the coach appeared in the kitchen doorway around midday.
I had clocked his boots in the yard that morning.
Shoes first, always — they show you what someone's life has been doing to them.
His were infantry issue, good leather once, the welts splitting now at the front, the right one repaired at the heel with what appeared to be boot-black and considerable optimism.
The coat was infantry, hung loose on him, the shoulders set for someone broader and heavier than he was now.
He had lost weight he hadn't had to start with, and his face was young — twenty at most, with the thinness that meant he was still finding out what his own bones looked like.
He stood in the doorway and said nothing.

He had positioned himself where someone might notice him without him having to speak, which was the calculation of a man who had learned that asking directly either worked badly or cost more than he had.
I knew the calculation.
I had watched it performed on my doorstep enough times to recognize it from thirty feet.
"Have you eaten today?"
I said.
He looked at the question for a moment before answering, as if checking whether it was genuine or a prelude to something.
"No."
"Sit down."
I did not take him into the taproom.
The paying passengers were in the taproom and I did not want him drawing their notice, and beyond that I did not want him eating under observation.
There was a way to feed a man with some dignity and a way to feed him as a demonstration of your own generosity, and the difference was a closed door and whether you watched.
I put bread and cold beef and the end of the morning's ale on the table in front of him without ceremony, and then turned to the window.
The herb jars on the sill needed rearranging.
They required a good deal of focused attention, the sage in particular having shifted toward the left in a way I found troubling and corrected at some length.
Behind me I heard the scrape of the bench, then a brief settling silence, and then the sounds of eating — steady, deliberate, without the self-consciousness of someone performing gratitude.
I was glad of that.
Some of them arrived with the gratitude already prepared, the speech, the looking up.
This one just ate, which was the thing a man needed to do, and I let him do it, and I found a great deal to occupy me along the windowsill.
When the sounds stopped I counted to ten and turned around.
He was standing, straightening the coat with a formality that cost him something.
It was the coat of a man who had once known how to wear a uniform properly and had not quite abandoned the habit.
"Thank you," he said.
"Safe road," I said.
He went out the kitchen door.

I watched through the window until his boots reached the bend in the road and the oak took him behind it, and I had one thought about the whole of it — about what the war cost and who paid and where the bill kept showing up — and I kept it to myself.
What I could do was a kitchen door and a plate of bread.
The thought was not useful.
I put it where I put most of my useless thoughts and went back to the taproom.
The afternoon moved through its ordinary paces: the stranded passengers away when the spoke was braced, two local men in for the midday ordinary, the draper settling an old account.
Jem worked the yard.
Nan worked the bar with one eye on the door and her usual economy of motion, the kind of efficiency that comes from seven years of covering more ground than she'd been hired to cover.

Above the first floor, a light had come on in Bridget's window sometime in the morning and stayed steady through the afternoon, a lamp-glow behind the glass that I did not look at directly and did not need to.
She was watching.
She had been watching all day.
Bridget had that talent: a first-floor window, a view of the yard, and seventy-three years of practice at reading a house by what it sounded like.
I had stopped finding it disconcerting some time around year three.
By four the light was failing and I sent Nan home.
"You'll be up till midnight," she said, in the coat phase, which was always when the observations arrived.
"I'm always up till midnight."
"You were up till midnight the night before that too."
She looked at me with the expression that stood in for the concern she was too practical to perform.
"You're running this place on no sleep and spite."
"The spite is load-bearing," I told her.
"Don't touch it."
She made a sound that was somewhere between a laugh and a reprimand, and went.
I heard her boots on the road for a moment and then the wind took it.
I went through the closing sequence: taproom chairs up, bar wiped, spigots closed, the cash box to the strongbox in the pantry, the door bolts checked, every window latched.

The back-door lock caught on the first try, as it always did, and yielded on the second, as it always did, and I made a note in my head that I had been meaning to replace it since April and had not and might not this quarter either, given how things were going.
The east stable wall still had its lean; the timber brace still held.
The kitchen fire banked.
The lamp on the hall table turned low.
I sat at the kitchen table with the ledger open on the numbers I already knew by heart.
The chandler contract would hold through spring.

The axle repair had come out of the contingency I kept for the east stable, which meant the east stable's contingency was now smaller, which meant I was back to hoping the timber brace held through to February.

The October takings would balance if December was reasonable, and December on the Great North Road depended on weather and traffic and the mood of travelling men, which this year had all been unpredictable.
The numbers said six weeks, approximately.
After six weeks the next quarter's rent became a conversation I would need to have with Stainforth.
The conversation would go like this: I would ask about the terms.
He would express concern.
He would note that the lease was due for review.
He would suggest, in his pleasant paragraphs, that there were arrangements to be considered, alternatives to the current situation that might benefit all parties.
The alternatives would benefit Stainforth's client.
I already knew this.

I had known it since the last rent quarter when the numbers first told me what was coming, and I had been moving faster since then, in the efficient and largely futile way you move faster when you can feel something closing in.
I closed the ledger.
My hands at the end of a day like that: reddened from the cold water, dry at the knuckles, the cut from the invoice sharp when I flexed my finger.
I looked at them for a moment in the lamplight, then got up and took the lamp to go up.
The letter was on the hall table.
It had been there since the afternoon post, and I had spent the better part of five hours developing a working relationship with it based on mutual avoidance.
Stainforth's seal.
His handwriting on the direction — thin, precise letters, the hand of a man who wrote for legal purposes and had seen no reason to soften his correspondence for personal ones.
The wax was dark red.
The handwriting did not slope.
I picked it up.
I turned it over.
The weight of it was nothing, one sheet folded, less than an ounce.
A lease had no weight when it was paper.
The weight was somewhere else.
I knew what it said.
Not the words — those I would learn when I opened it — but the shape of the news inside.

I had known it since last quarter, when the numbers had first arranged themselves into their current uncomfortable pattern, and I had been moving faster since then, in the way you move when you can hear something gaining ground behind you and have not yet decided whether to turn around and face it or keep going and see how far the running gets you.
"Well," I said, to the empty hall.
To the dark house and the banked fire and the bolts I had just drawn.
I put the letter in my apron pocket and took the lamp and went up to bed.
The grate was cold.
I'd banked it properly the night before, because I always bank it properly, but the ash had gone pale and the kitchen was close to freezing.
Sometime in the small hours the wind had shifted north.

I could tell by the ash, the way it lay flat on one side, scoured, and by the way the cold came in not from the walls but from the floor, which meant it had been below zero long enough to get under the foundations.
The cold was the sort that got into plaster and stayed there until spring.
I rebuilt the fire with the last of the dry kindling and crouched in front of it long enough to be sure it had caught.
My hands were already reddened from the pump.
Outside, the sky was the colour of tin.
By afternoon it would rain.
This was fine.
The White Hound had thirty-seven things wrong with it on any given morning.
I had catalogued them all.

The beam above the taproom door had been cracking for two years, not structurally (I'd had the carpenter look), but enough that I watched it every time I passed underneath, because the carpenter had also said it wouldn't last another decade and I didn't have a decade to be patient.
The east stable wall needed repointing.
The lock on the root cellar was held together by one rusty bolt and my consistent refusal to let it fail.
The window in the back bedroom hadn't seated properly since the last hard frost.
My name was not on the lease.
That was the one I came back to, always.

I had been running this inn for seven years, since my uncle died and my aunt lost what remained of her strength for it, and in those seven years I had stripped the wallpaper in the front rooms and replaced it with something that didn't embarrass me, and I had rebuilt the taproom shelving from scratch, and I had driven the coaching company agent down from ten percent to six on commission, and I had kept the thing alive through two bad winters and the worst harvest the county had seen in a generation.
I knew which floorboard in the taproom would take a man's weight and which wouldn't.
I knew the name of every driver on the Great North Road who'd cheat on the passenger count.
I knew that the well in the east yard ran two feet deeper than the one in the west, and that the west one tasted of iron in October and you had to know to switch over before the guests complained.
My name was not on the lease.
According to the law, the White Hound belonged to whoever held the paper, and the paper was in Stainforth's office in Hatfield.
Eleven miles away.
My uncle had held it.

When he died it had transferred, by the law's own logic, to Stainforth as the heir's executor, and it had stayed there because I had nowhere else to go and Stainforth had found it convenient to let the inn keep running on the strength of my labour while he collected the quarterly rent.
The law had a word for women like me.
I had a word for the arrangement too, and it was the same word I used for the east stable wall and the root cellar lock and the cracking beam.
Seven years of my labour and the lease was Stainforth's to extend or not as he chose.
There were mornings when I thought about this directly.
Most mornings I thought about the grate instead.
The fire caught.
I went to wake Nan.
She was already awake, pulling on her boots at the kitchen door, which meant she'd heard the cold too.
Seven years and Nan still had not stopped treating her morning arrival as an interruption of something private.
"Coach is early," she said.
"Jem sent word.
Axle trouble on the Barnet stretch."
"How bad?"
"Lame wheel, his word.
They'll need the spare.
He's put Dawson on it but Dawson's slow."
"How slow?"
"It's Dawson."
"Is it the nearside or the off?"
Nan looked at me.
"Does it matter?"
"It matters which spare we pull."
"Nearside," she said, after a moment.
"I think.
I can send Jem back to check."
"Do that."
I went to the sideboard and started on the bread.
The dough had risen overnight and the room smelled of it, warm under the cold, the one good thing about the morning so far.
Nan came to stand at the opposite counter and began slicing yesterday's heel into portions for the side table.
"Two passengers short-tempered," she said.
"One trunk with a split hinge.
Coachman already wanting a word."
"About what?"
"The north road, I expect."
"They always want a word about the north road."
"They do," Nan said.
"You could stop telling them about Brockett in Hatfield.
It winds them up."
"It's meant to."
She looked at me sideways.
I was already cutting the bread.
I heard the coach before I saw it — the drag of a reluctant wheel, heavier on the left, pulling the whole rig sideways on the ruts.
Lame wheel was right.
Also moving slower than it should be for the schedule, which meant the delay on the Barnet stretch had cost them more than Nan's estimate.
By the time it came into the yard I'd already decided.
Pull the spare from the west stable, send Dawson for the bolt-key, give them two hours and charge the coaching company for the delay, not the passengers.
I catalogued the passengers through the yard window while the horses were being changed.
Two clergymen, cold and put-upon, who would order the minimum and leave the smaller coin and ask whether we had any periodicals.

A woman with a trunk that had apparently generated its own argument about loading, currently standing beside it in the yard with her arms folded, waiting for someone to come and be wrong at — that one I'd have to manage, and the trunk was going to be a problem getting up the step.
A young officer in a coat that hadn't been brushed in a week, sitting alone on the far bench, looking at the ground.
That one I'd leave alone.
Jem appeared at the window, two fingers raised.
Two hours.
I gave him one back.
One hour.
He understood, and disappeared toward the stable.
Fletcher caught me in the doorway before I'd got as far as the taproom.
"Miss Dale."
He had the tone of a man who had prepared several opening remarks and was working down the list.
"I've got eleven miles of broken road behind me and a wheel that—"
"I know about the wheel.
Jem's handling it."
"It shouldn't want handling in the first place, is the point I'm making.
That road is—"
"The road is the company's road," I said.
"If you want compensation for the delay, the company's agent is in Hatfield on Wednesdays.
His name is Brockett and he keeps an office above the apothecary's.
I can write it down for you."
Fletcher's mouth did something complicated.
"That's not—"
"I can write it down," I said again, pleasantly.
"It's no trouble."
He decided not to push it.
They usually decided not to push it, once they remembered they still had forty miles to go and that I was the last hot meal before Peterborough.
I held the door open and he went in.
The trunk woman was next.
She wanted to know why her luggage had been left in the yard rather than brought inside.
I told her because it weighed more than any of us and we were waiting for Jem.
She told me what she thought of that.
I heard her out.
That satisfied something.
She came inside and ordered a pot of tea as if nothing had happened.
The chandler arrived at eleven, which was the part of the morning I'd been preparing for since the week before.
Hartley was a short man with the hands of someone who had not done his own work in several years.
He set his sample case on the kitchen table without asking whether he could set it on the kitchen table.
I'd been watching him do that for four years and it still cost me something each time.
"Quarter's turning," he said, as if I didn't know what month it was.
"Candles'll be at cost.
I can do you two dozen tallow at six for the shilling, same as last quarter."
"You did me two dozen tallow at seven for the shilling last quarter."
"Did I?"
He didn't blink.
"I may be misremembering."
"You're not."
I opened the ledger on the counter, to the page I'd marked three days ago.
"Seventh of July.
Two dozen at seven for the shilling, twice over."
Hartley looked at the ledger.
He had the expression of a man who'd been looking forward to this less than he'd let on.
"Season's turning," he said, as if the first time had not quite landed.
"Cold snap early this year.
Prices coming up all over."
"I know.
I've been getting quotes."

The quote from Hitchin was for a different quantity, but I had the name and the figure would hold if he didn't look too closely, which he wouldn't, because that was a four-hour round trip and he knew it.
"Rawson in Hitchin is at six and a half for the shilling.
I'd rather deal local."
He moved the sample case six inches to the left, which meant he was thinking.
"Six and a half's a stretch."
"Six and a half is six and a half."
"I can do six and three-quarters."
"Seven for the shilling and the same terms as last quarter."
He looked at the ledger.
Then he looked at the sconces hanging from the kitchen ceiling.
There were eight of them, and he'd supplied them all, and we both knew it.
I waited.
The kettle had begun to whistle.
I let it go on a little longer than necessary because it filled the silence better than I could.
"Seven for the shilling," he said finally.
"Same terms."
I wrote the invoice while he repacked his case.
As I folded the paper, the edge caught the base of my index finger — a clean slice, shallow enough that it took a moment to start bleeding.
I pressed my thumb to it and held.
Hartley didn't notice, or pretended not to.
He tucked the invoice under his arm and left looking like a man who'd had a better morning than he had.
I wrapped my finger in a scrap of linen and looked at the ledger for a moment.
Last quarter I'd had a surplus from a wedding party in September.
This quarter I had no wedding party.

What I'd have to open with next quarter depended entirely on what Stainforth decided to do about the lease, and I knew what Stainforth was going to decide, and that was the part I wasn't looking at yet.
I closed the ledger.
The altercation started over a seat.
The clergymen had gone on ahead with the southbound, which left the sort of passenger who develops opinions about taproom seating after their second ale.
I heard the voice change from the kitchen — not louder, but lower, with the flat quality that meant someone had decided to stop performing civility and start meaning it.
I came through the kitchen door with the bread knife still in my hand, which I hadn't planned but didn't mind.
One of them had his hand on the other man's collar and was explaining something at close range.
The other was leaning back against the bar, which is to say he was being held against the bar, and he had the look of a man who had decided that backing down would be worse than what was coming.
Nan was at the far end of the bar with the look of a woman who had already calculated the distances and decided the outcome wasn't her problem yet.
I set the knife on the bar where both of them could see it and put myself between them.
"Gentlemen."
I didn't raise my voice.
"Sit down, or I'll have you both in the yard."
One of them had the presence of mind to look embarrassed.
The other was still deciding.

I held his eyes until he decided correctly, and then I took the stool they'd been arguing over and moved it to the other side of the room, and by the time I turned back around they were both looking at their hands.
Nan came to stand beside me at the bar.
"Third one this week," she said quietly.
"Road's rough."
"It's getting rougher."
She wiped down the counter.
"Used to be they'd at least wait until dark."
She went back to the glasses.
I went back to the kitchen.

Something had changed on the road since the war ended, and I didn't know what to do with it except keep my knife visible and my voice flat and hope I didn't have to use either past what I already had.
Men who'd survived Waterloo were not the problem.

The problem was men who'd survived Waterloo and come home to find nothing waiting for them, and now they were on the roads with the tension of it all still in their shoulders, and the inns were where they ended up.
I fed more of them than I could count.
I'd stopped counting.
Which was how I nearly missed the boy in the yard.
I saw the boots first.
He was standing at the edge of the yard, and from the kitchen window the boots were the first thing that registered.
Left sole beginning to separate at the welt, the leather gone grey and cracked at the toe.
I read people by their shoes.
It was a habit you developed in this work.
These said: walking for months, nothing spare for repairs, not yet at the point of despair but not far from it.
The coat told a different story.
Military issue, from the cut and the buttons, but two sizes too large across the shoulders, the sleeves shortened badly at some point by someone who had no patience for the job.
It had been through worse conditions than him; the collar was stiff with old dirt, and the brass was tarnished to the point where it caught no light at all.
His or borrowed, it had kept him warm and that was the extent of what it was doing for him now.
He was standing very still, looking at the north road, not at the inn.
Not at anything in particular.
Just looking at the road the way men did when they weren't sure they were going to keep moving.
I went out through the back.
"Have you eaten today?"
He turned.
Twenty, perhaps.
Maybe younger — the road aged people, and the last year had aged everyone.
"Miss?"
"Have you eaten."
He considered whether honesty was safe.
"No, miss."
I took him in through the back door to the kitchen.
Not the taproom, where the paying guests would see him and one of them would say something, and then I'd have to deal with that too.
I put him at the small table in the corner, cut bread and the last of the morning's dripping, and set it in front of him along with the heel of cheese I'd been saving for my own supper.
"Sit."
He sat.
I turned back to the accounts.
Behind me I heard the bread go, quickly, without quite the desperation of someone who had been hungry for too long.
He had some dignity still, or some discipline.
When I heard the plate go down I waited another minute before turning around.
It was the decent thing.
He had stacked the plate and knife neatly at the corner of the table.
"Thank you," he said.
"Miss."
I nodded at the door.
He went.
I watched his boots on the north road until the road bent and he was gone.
I thought one thing, and then I chose not to think it, and I went back to the bread.
The house cleared the way it always did after the last coach of the afternoon — all at once, then completely.

The clergymen had gone on with the southbound, the smaller coin left in a neat stack under the edge of the saucer the way men who spent their lives judging other people's generosity sometimes left it, as if tidiness absolved them.
The trunk woman's trunk had been brought inside and she'd departed in a private carriage after a pointed conversation with someone I could only assume was her son.
Fletcher and his wheel had sorted themselves out behind schedule and lumbered north.
The young officer from the bench had gone at some point in the afternoon; I hadn't watched him go.
Nan put her coat on at half past six.
"I covered the bar from four," she said.
"You owe me."
"I know."
"Good."
She did up the top button.
"You're too thin.
You know that too."
"Goodnight, Nan."
"I'm just saying."
"Goodnight, Nan."
She went.
Her footsteps crossed the yard, steady and unhurried, and I heard the gate latch behind her.
From the yard came the sound of Jem settling the horses for the night, the stall doors and the low word he used when he wanted them to be still.
I didn't need to look.
I'd heard it every evening for seven years.
Above me, the shape of Bridget's lamp moved once behind the curtain, then held.
She'd been at that window all day.

She watched the road from that window, and the yard, and the post when it came, and she told me none of it until she decided I needed to know, which was her own system and not one I had ever broken her of.
I did the locking-up.
Taproom shutters.
Cellar door, back bolt, pump cover, front latch.
Bar cloth folded on the rail.
Pewter wiped and stacked.
Bread covered.
The side gate bolted last — I always did the side gate last, because that was the one that had been forced twice in three years, and I wanted to be awake and thinking clearly when I threw that bolt.
I knew the sequence so well I could do it in the dark, and most winters I did.

My hands were rough at the end of each day, reddened from the water and the cold — I noticed them now, in the candlelight, the skin tight over the knuckles, a cut on the index finger stiff under the linen bandage from this morning.
They were useful hands.
They had plastered walls and kept accounts and hauled kegs and negotiated invoices in languages that were not quite English and not quite not.
I didn't look at them often enough to mind them.
Tonight I minded them.
I brought the ledger to the kitchen table and opened it.
The numbers said I had approximately six weeks before the next quarter's rent became a problem.
They had been saying that for three weeks.

A wedding party in September had bought me into October with a small surplus; October had spent it on a new barrel hinge and Hartley's invoice and a farrier bill that Jem had apologised for with the air of a man who had not expected me to take it badly and had been wrong.
I hadn't found a new answer in three weeks and the numbers hadn't moved and sitting here in the cold kitchen was not going to change either of those facts.
I knew that.
I looked at them anyway, because looking at them was what I did instead of panicking, and it worked well enough, and then I closed the book.
The letter was on the sideboard.
Stainforth's seal.
His handwriting, the letters close and even.

It had arrived on the morning coach, which meant he'd sent it from Hatfield on Tuesday, which meant he'd written it over the weekend, which meant he'd been sitting with this decision for at least three days before he'd chosen to put it on paper and send it to me.
I had been expecting it since August.
I picked it up.
I held it.
The paper was heavy, the kind that cost money.
I put it back down on the sideboard.
"Well," I said to the empty room.
Then I went to bed.
THE LAST RETREAT
Chapter One: The White Hound
The fire was low again.

I'd laid it generous the night before, banked it the way my father had shown me before he died and left me with his inn and his debts and his opinion of how coal should be stacked, and still it had burned down to ash before the cold could be bothered to wait for morning.
October.
I crouched in front of the grate with my hands already aching and thought: well.
That settles the question of how today will go.
I got the fire up by the time the yard clock struck six.

Then I started on breakfast, then on the list of everything that needed doing before the London coach arrived, a list I could recite the way other women recited prayers and that served roughly the same purpose.
The White Hound was mine.
That was the first thing I thought every morning, and I let myself think it, because by midday there were always sufficient reasons to think the opposite.

The taproom floor needed new rushes, and I'd been putting it off because the rushes cost money and the floor was still serviceable if you kept the fire hot and didn't let the rushes get wet, which you couldn't always manage given that men came in off the road with mud up to their knees.
The sign above the front door had faded to the point where the white hound on it looked more like a dirty goat.
I was proud of the sign anyway, the way you're proud of a thing that's seen too much weather but is still standing.
The chimney in room four drew badly.

The second, fourth, and seventh stairs on the back staircase announced anyone who tried them after midnight, which had twice this year deterred men I did not want in my corridors and once had also announced Nan sneaking out to meet the blacksmith's nephew.
That was her business.
I told her the next morning which steps to skip.
There were things I was proud of.
The kitchen, which was large and clean and mine in a way that no other room in the building was.
The yard, which Jem kept in a state that turned heads on coaches from London, the gravel raked and the water troughs full and the stable doors hung true.
The accounts, which were in my handwriting in my ledger and added up correctly, which was more than could be said for the accounts when my husband had kept them.
The beds, which were dry.
The ale, which was good.
The table in the private parlour, which had a decent cloth and candles that were the proper length.
I'd sourced those candles myself, negotiated the price myself, and would do so again this morning.
I'd been running the inn for six years.
I knew how to fix everything that could be fixed and I knew, with the precision of long acquaintance, everything that couldn't.
The taproom floor was serviceable.

The room-four chimney was a problem I had quoted to three different masons and received three different prices for, none of which I could currently afford, which meant I smiled at guests in room four and reduced their terms and absorbed the difference.
The sign above the door I would fix in spring, when there was cash left after the winter accounts.
Maybe spring.

Legally, the White Hound belonged to my husband's estate, which meant it belonged to his creditors until the debts were cleared, which meant that in the eyes of the Crown I ran an inn I did not own, negotiated leases on property I could not legally hold, and was subject to the pleasure of one Mr.
Stainforth of Lincoln's Inn, who managed the estate and who had, for six years, allowed me to conduct myself as though none of this were true.
The law called what I did management on behalf of the estate.
I called it keeping the place standing and did not examine the distinction too closely.
Coverture was the word.
My husband had been dead four years and the law had not updated its opinion of our arrangement.

I had been a feme covert when he was alive and I was apparently still a feme covert now, which meant that anything I signed, I signed as agent of a dead man's estate, and anything I built, I built on ground that didn't legally have my name on it.
The inn ran because I ran it.
The accounts balanced because I balanced them.
None of that gave me the standing, in a court of law, of a woman who owned the building she was standing in.
The arrangement had suited Stainforth well enough.
He received his percentage without any effort of his own and the estate stayed solvent, which reflected well on his management.

I received the fiction of ownership, which was worth considerably more to me than any legal reality because it meant I could still get out of bed in the morning and act like a woman with something to protect.
I knew, without having been told directly, that the arrangement was changing.
Nan arrived at half past six, the way she'd arrived every morning for the past seven years: without announcement, without ceremony, already in her apron.
She took the bread from me and started slicing.
"Coach is late," she said.
"Which?"
"London.
Chapman stopped at the Goat last night, told Jem the offside wheel's going.
They might limp it in or they might not."

I thought about the three guests waiting on the London coach, about the chandler's order that was also coming down from London, about a stranded coach and what it meant in terms of guests who needed to eat and rooms that needed to be ready and passengers who would want compensation that I was not in a position to offer because the wheel was not my wheel.
"How bad?"
"Bad enough he told Jem."
Nan set the loaf down and looked at me directly, which she only did when she thought I was about to miss something.
"He's got a full box.
Seven passengers."
Seven passengers and a lame wheel.
I pulled the second kettle onto the fire and started cutting bread myself.
"Right," I said.
"Get the back rooms aired."
I heard the coach before I saw it, the way you learn to hear things when your livelihood arrives on wheels.
A good coach sounds like a coach.

This one came in with a skip in the rhythm that told me the wheel was worse than Chapman had told Jem, and it pulled up in the yard at three minutes to eight listing slightly to the offside, which meant the problem was not just the wheel but the axle tree and Chapman was lucky to have made it at all.
I was in the yard when it arrived.

The two women descended first, the way women always descended first when there was no one of consequence to insist otherwise: they were sisters by their matching good coats and the identical expression they wore, which was the expression of people who expected better and had been disappointed in this expectation for several hours.
Behind them came a clergyman who descended blinking into the October light, stood a moment taking his bearings, and reached instinctively for a bag that Jem had already moved without being asked.
He looked surprised, which told me he wasn't used to inn yards where the ostler was faster than he expected.
