The merchant's wife came next with a trunk that Jem had to carry two-handed, the lid held shut by nothing but a combination of luck and the way it was packed, the hinge split clean along one side.
She watched him carry it the way people watch their property when they're calculating whether to argue.
I met her eyes and she looked away.
Behind her came a family of three, the children attached to the mother and the mother attached to her husband's arm.
The youngest child had a high colour that wasn't the cold.
I looked at her and made a note of it.
And last, on the box beside Chapman, a young soldier who climbed down without being told and went immediately to the horses' heads.
He was nineteen, maybe twenty.
His uniform coat was too large in the shoulders, which told me it hadn't been issued to him.
His boots were going at the welt on the right foot.
He stroked the near horse's nose and spoke to it in a low voice and kept his eyes on the animal rather than the crowd unloading around him.
I marked him and moved on.
Chapman wanted a word.
"Miss Dale."
He descended from the box with the deliberate heaviness of a man preparing to be aggrieved.
"I'll need to speak with you about compensation."
"For the wheel."
"For the delay.
My passengers—"
"Your passengers are at the White Hound and not in a ditch on the north road, Mr.
Chapman, which is a distinction I'd encourage you to appreciate."
I kept my voice pleasant.
"If you want to discuss compensation, I'd suggest starting with Rogers at the coaching company.
He's in Ware on Thursdays.
Today is Thursday."
Chapman drew breath.
"He'll be easier to reach," I said, "if you start now."
He closed his mouth.
Then he went to see about the axle.
The merchant's wife wanted to know where her trunk was going.
I told her Jem would have it in her room by the time she'd had breakfast, which was true because Jem was already halfway up the stairs with it.
The clergyman was travelling to a living in Newcastle and had not eaten since yesterday; I put him at the good table in the parlour with a full pot and left him to it.
The family needed rooms and hot water and something for the child's fever.

I sent for Nan's boy to go to the village for the apothecary's draught, got the family into the largest guest room, and had the fire in there going properly before the mother had finished unpacking the children's coats.
By the time all seven passengers were settled it was gone nine, and Hartley, the chandler from Hitchin, was waiting in my kitchen doorway with his sample case.
I'd known Hartley eight years.

He was a careful man who liked to think he was cleverer than he was, which meant every negotiation followed the same shape: he opened high, I opened my ledger, and somewhere in the middle we landed on a number that was lower than he wanted and higher than I needed, and we both pretended this was a satisfactory outcome.
Last quarter I'd held him to one and five per dozen tallow.
He was back now with October turned cold early, which he believed gave him the advantage.
He set his case on the kitchen table and looked around the kitchen the way he always did, as though pricing it.
"Miss Dale.
Autumn's turned cold early."
"It has," I said.
I didn't move from the fire.
"Season like this, everyone's burning through their stock."
He opened the case and laid out his samples with the methodical care of a man who had rehearsed this.
"I've had three inns on the road this week alone.
Supply's short."
"I'd heard something similar."
I went to the dresser and came back with the ledger.
"From Millar's, in Hitchin.
He's got last quarter's stock still on hand and is looking to move it before the new shipment comes in.
One and two per dozen, to a steady buyer."
Hartley looked at the ledger.
His samples were good tallow, better than Millar's, and he knew I knew it, and he was calculating whether I'd actually take the inferior stock to save tuppence.
"One and two," he said.
"He was quite specific."
"Millar's tallow is soft.
Burns fast."
"My guests don't sit up long enough to notice the difference."
"Your guests in the private parlour might."
"My guests in the private parlour are charged accordingly."
I turned a page in the ledger.
"One and two, Hartley.
Millar's is keen."
He was quiet.
I let the quiet sit there and did not help him with it.
"One and three," he said finally.
"One and three for the full winter order, same delivery terms as last quarter, and you include the tapers for the front hall sconces."
I turned another page, as though confirming something I'd written there.
"The sconces take the long taper.
Millar's doesn't stock them."
He knew I'd been holding that back.
I watched him understand that I'd been holding it back specifically for this moment, and then I watched him decide that the long tapers were not worth the argument.
"One and three," he said again, resigned this time.
"Including the tapers."
"I'll have Jem ready on Thursday."
He wrote out the invoice with the particular care of a man who has lost a negotiation and wants to at least have neat handwriting to show for it.
I took the invoice when he offered it and the corner caught the side of my finger, a paper cut clean and immediate, the kind that doesn't hurt until a moment later.
I blotted it on my apron without looking at it.
When he was gone I stood in the kitchen with the invoice in my hands.
One and three.
Six months ago it had been one and four.
One and four was what I needed to run the inn at a profit through winter.

One and three was what I could manage if everything else stayed level, and everything else was not staying level, had not stayed level in two years, was in fact moving in one direction at a pace I could calculate and did not enjoy calculating.
I put the invoice in the ledger and closed it.
The cut on my finger had stopped bleeding.
I got on with the rest of it.
The altercation in the taproom happened at half past eleven.
Two of the stranded passengers had been at the ale since ten, which I'd allowed because they'd paid for their rooms and ale was profit and I needed the profit.

By eleven they had moved from argument about the road to argument about something that had started with one of them accidentally stepping on the other's coat, which was draped over a chair in a way that made it impossible to avoid, and had escalated from there with the efficiency of men who had been uncomfortable for six hours and needed somewhere to put it.
I heard the raised voices from the yard and came in through the kitchen.
By the time I reached the taproom the younger of the two had his hand on the older one's collar and the older one had his hands up and wasn't looking at the younger man's fist.
The chair had gone over.
I walked between them and picked up the chair.
"Sit down," I said.
Not loudly.
Loudly would have made it a challenge.
The younger man looked at me.
His jaw was still set.
I held the chair with my hand on the back of it and looked at him and waited.
He sat.
I looked at the older man, who righted himself and took his ale and moved to the far end of the bar without being asked.
Nan was wiping down the bar with one eye on the door.
"Third one this month," she said, when I passed her.
"Road's full of men with nowhere to go and too much pride to admit it."
I set the fallen chair against the wall.
"Post-war.
They'll settle."
"Aye."
Nan looked at the younger man, who had his head down over his ale now, the anger gone and something tireder in its place.
"Or they won't."
The soldier appeared at the kitchen door at about noon.
He knocked.
I knew it was him before I turned around because he knocked the way soldiers knock when they've learned that you don't enter someone else's territory without asking, and most men hadn't learned that.
I turned around.
His cap was in his hands.
He was thinner than he'd looked on the coach.
He'd been making himself useful in the yard all morning, keeping out of the way but there when hands were wanted.
"Have you eaten today?"
I asked.
He looked at the floor between us.
"Not since yesterday, ma'am."
"Sit down."
I fed him at the kitchen table, not in the taproom.
There was cold mutton from breakfast and bread and a pot of tea I'd just made, and I set it in front of him and turned back to the fire.
He ate.
When I heard his fork go down I turned back.
"The coach goes tonight," I said.
"It'll be repaired by six."
He stood and put the cap back on.
His hands were steady.
"Thank you, ma'am."
He went out through the yard.
I watched from the kitchen window until he turned onto the north road and was gone from sight.
From the back, his right boot was worse than I'd thought.
The welt had pulled entirely away from the sole at the toe, and he was walking with the slight list of a man who knows it and is compensating.
He had fifty miles to Newcastle on those boots, give or take.
I thought what I thought.
I didn't say it to anyone.
The wheel and axle were done by four.
The merchant's wife left, her trunk roped shut and her opinion of the establishment mostly intact.
The clergyman had a second pot and finally departed for Newcastle.
The family stayed; their room was paid through Sunday and the child's fever had broken by evening, which Nan told me with the satisfaction of a woman who had been keeping score.
By five the taproom was quiet.
By six it was mine.
Nan wiped the bar a final time, put on her coat, and stood in the kitchen doorway.
"You need another pair of hands," she said.
"Mornings especially."
"I'll think about it."
"You've been saying that since August."
"Nan."
She tied her bonnet.
"Dinner's on the range.
Don't leave it."
"Good night."
"Good night."
She went.
Jem was in the stable another quarter-hour.
I heard the big doors latch.
Upstairs, Bridget's window lit.
I bolted the back door.
The front door.
Checked the taproom candles, swapped out the stubs, checked the office strongbox.
Room four was empty; its chimney could wait.
The fires in the occupied rooms were banked.
That was the list done.
In the kitchen I sat down at the table with the ledger and wrote the day's numbers.
I already knew what they said.
One and three per dozen tallow.
Rent at December quarter unchanged.
The family in room three would leave Sunday, which meant two days of room income against the reduced rate I'd given them for the child's illness.
The stranded coach passengers had all eaten and three had taken rooms, which was better than I'd had any right to expect.
The cut on my index finger had a crust over it.
My hands at end of day: reddened from the cold water, ink along the outside of the right.
The ledger columns were even.
I closed it.
Sat a moment with my hands in my lap.
Then I got up.
The letter was on the hall table where I'd put it that morning.
Stainforth's seal on the red wax, his tall copperplate on the face of it.
The handwriting he used when he'd dictated something to a clerk and reviewed it before sending.
Not a casual letter, then.
Not that I'd thought it was.
I'd known since August that it was coming.
I'd been moving faster ever since.
I picked it up.
Heavy for a short letter.
I set it back down.
"Damn you," I said, to Stainforth and his tall copperplate and his percentage of a dead man's debts.
I went upstairs to bed with my boots still half-laced and the letter still on the table, sealed, in Stainforth's hand.
I did not take it with me.
I counted the squirrels at seven forty-two AM, same as every morning.
Six of them.
Sitting in a neat row at the tree line behind Mrs.
Torvik's converted garage, which was technically my apartment now.
The "apartment" part was generous.
It was a studio with delusions of grandeur and a toilet that ran all night.
Six squirrels.
Staring at me.
They'd been doing this for three weeks, ever since I moved to Manzanita.
Living above a failing used bookstore was exactly the kind of anonymous I needed.
What was new was the third one from the left blinking.
When it opened its eyes again, it wasn't a squirrel.
Red fur.
Narrow snout.
Amber eyes that locked on mine.
A fox.
Then it blinked again, and it was a squirrel.
Gray tail.
Black eyes.
Sitting perfectly still like the other five.
"Okay," I said out loud to my empty apartment.
"That's new."
I pressed my thumb into the wooden windowsill, hard.
Focused on the grain of the wood, the splinter I'd gotten yesterday.
Grounding.
Real.
The squirrels were still squirrels.
I counted again.
Still six.
Still staring.
I stepped back from the window.
Checked my hands.
Nails clipped too short—I'd done that yesterday and now I couldn't grip my palms the way I used to when things got weird.
Couldn't dig in and feel the sting that said yeah, you're awake, this is real.
The salt lines on my windowsills were intact.
I'd checked them last night before bed and I checked them again now.
Ran my finger along the thin white line.
Unbroken.
The water bowls by both doors were full.
Clean.
Doing whatever the hell water bowls were supposed to do when you kept salt on windowsills and told yourself it was just a habit.
My phone buzzed.
Mrs.
Halloran's daughter.
I didn't have to look at the screen.
There was only one reason Denise called at six in the morning.
I answered.
"How's the breathing?"
"Changed."
Denise's voice was tight.
She'd been preparing for this.
"Can you come?"
"Twenty minutes."
I hung up.
Grabbed my bag—the one I kept packed for when someone I'd been sitting with was finally letting go.
Walked out without finishing my coffee.
The cold tea could wait.
Mrs.
Halloran couldn't.
Mrs.
Halloran's house was four blocks from the bookshop.
Close enough to walk if the Oregon coast weather cooperated, which it never did.
I drove.
Denise met me at the door, her face doing that thing where you're trying to hold it together and failing.
"She asked for you," Denise said.
I nodded.
That's what Mrs.
Halloran and I had agreed on two months ago.
She wasn't afraid of dying, she just didn't want to do it alone.
The house smelled like lavender.
Something sharper underneath.
The particular scent of a body beginning to shut down.
Not decay.
Just the body starting to close up shop.
Mrs.
Halloran was in her bed, propped up on pillows.
Her breathing was shallow.
Uneven.
The rhythm had changed.
I'd heard it enough times to recognize the pattern.
The body deciding.
The mind letting go.
The space between breaths getting longer.
She opened her eyes when I sat down.
"Nell."
"I'm here."
"Took you long enough."
Her voice was thread-thin but the sharpness was still there.
Even dying, Rita Halloran was a pain in the ass.
"Traffic was hell," I said.
She made a sound that might have been a laugh if she'd had the breath.
I took her hand.
Cold.
Papery.
Bones too close to the surface.
She squeezed once, weak, and then her eyes drifted shut.
I sat with her.
This was the part people didn't understand about death doula work.
Most of it was just sitting.
Being present.
Not fixing, not saving.
Just witnessing.
The body did what it did at the end and you couldn't stop it.
Mrs.
Halloran's breathing slowed.
Longer gaps.
I counted without meaning to.
Twelve seconds.
Fifteen.
Twenty.
When she stopped breathing, it wasn't dramatic.
No gasping.
No struggle.
Just a final exhale that didn't have an inhale to follow it.
Gone.
I sat for another minute, holding her hand.
Then I stood and went to find Denise.
"She's gone."
Denise nodded like she'd already known.
Maybe she had.
I stayed while she called her brother, while the hospice nurse arrived.
The house filled with the usual chaos of death.
Paperwork.
Phone calls.
Who to notify.
I slipped out when no one was looking.
Gail Torvik was waiting on the steps outside the bookshop when I got back.
She'd been watching for my car.
She had a casserole dish in her hands and an expression that said she was about to mother me whether I wanted it or not.
"Heard about Rita," Gail said, standing up.
"Denise texted."
Of course she did.
Manzanita was small enough that everyone knew everyone's business.
That's why I'd chosen it.
You couldn't disappear in a city, but you could absolutely disappear in a town where people were too busy gossiping to notice the quiet woman who paid rent on time and never caused trouble.
"She went easy," I said.
"No pain at the end."
"You need to eat."
Gail thrust the casserole at me.
"Don't tell me you already ate.
I know you didn't."
She wasn't wrong.
I took the dish.
It was warm.
She'd been planning this.
She cared.
Something in my chest tightened.
"Thanks, Gail."
"You look like hell, Nell.
When's the last time you slept?"
"Last night."
"Liar."
I shrugged.
Gail studied me with that attention that came from twenty years of running a bookshop and learning to read people.
She was in her sixties, sharp as hell.
The only person in Manzanita who'd rented to me without asking questions when I'd shown up three months ago with cash and no references.
"You're not eating," she said.
"You're not sleeping.
You want to tell me what's going on?"
"Just work.
Death doula hours are weird."
"Bullshit."
But she didn't push it.
One of the reasons I liked her.
"Eat the casserole.
Get some sleep.
And for god's sake, Nell, take a day off."
"I will."
Another lie.
We both knew it.
Gail headed back into the bookshop—which was definitely failing, based on the dusty shelves and the fact that I'd seen maybe two customers in three months.
I climbed the stairs with the casserole and the bone-deep exhaustion that came from sitting with someone while they died.
I put the casserole in the fridge.
Didn't eat it.
Evening came fast.
Gray.
I avoided sleep as long as I could.
Paced the apartment.
Rechecked the salt lines.
Changed the water in the bowls even though it didn't need changing.
Sat at the window and watched the tree line.
The squirrels were gone.
I didn't want to think about the fox.
I didn't want to think about the fact that I'd seen slips like this before.
Small ones.
Easy to dismiss.
They'd been getting worse.
More frequent.
I didn't want to think about the dreams.
The ones that left me tasting salt when I woke up.
My teeth gritty like I'd been chewing sand.
Some things you didn't look at.
You just kept moving.
I lasted until midnight before my body gave up.
The dream was waiting.
Gray beach.
Overcast sky.
Kelp smell.
Cold water.
A woman walking into the ocean.
Her back to me.
Her hair the same color as mine.
Dark, with a streak of gray at the temple.
I tried to call out.
My mouth filled with sand.
The woman kept walking.
Water rose to her knees.
Her waist.
Her shoulders.
She didn't stop.
Didn't turn around.
When the water closed over her head, I woke up gasping.
Sheets tangled.
My mouth tasting like salt and grit.
I didn't think about it.
I got up.
Checked the salt lines.
Changed the water in the bowls.
Watched the tree line until the sun came up.
Six squirrels.
All of them gray.
All of them watching.
I counted them twice to be sure.

The kitchen, which was large and clean and mine in a way that no other room in the building was.
The yard, which Jem kept in a state that turned heads on coaches from London, the gravel raked and the water troughs full and the stable doors hung true.
The accounts, which were in my handwriting in my ledger and added up correctly, which was more than could be said for the accounts when my husband had kept them.
The beds, which were dry.

The table in the private parlour, which had a decent cloth and candles that were the proper length.
I'd sourced those candles myself, negotiated the price myself, and would do so again this morning.

I knew how to fix everything that could be fixed and I knew, with the precision of long acquaintance, everything that couldn't.
The taproom floor was serviceable.

The room-four chimney was a problem I had quoted to three different masons and received three different prices for, none of which I could currently afford, which meant I smiled at guests in room four and reduced their terms and absorbed the difference.
The sign above the door I would fix in spring, when there was cash left after the winter accounts.
Maybe spring.
Everything in the White Hound answered to me.
That was the useful fiction I'd kept going for six years, and it was useful enough that I had stopped thinking of it as fiction most days.

Legally, the White Hound belonged to my husband's estate, which meant it belonged to his creditors until the debts were cleared, which meant that in the eyes of the Crown I ran an inn I did not own, negotiated leases on property I could not legally hold, and was subject to the pleasure of one Mr.
Stainforth of Lincoln's Inn, who managed the estate and who had, for six years, allowed me to conduct myself as though none of this were true.
The law called what I did management on behalf of the estate.
I called it keeping the place standing and did not examine the distinction too closely.
Coverture was the word.
My husband had been dead four years and the law had not updated its opinion of our arrangement.

I had been a feme covert when he was alive and I was apparently still a feme covert now, which meant that anything I signed, I signed as agent of a dead man's estate, and anything I built, I built on ground that didn't legally have my name on it.
The inn ran because I ran it.
The accounts balanced because I balanced them.
None of that gave me the standing, in a court of law, of a woman who owned the building she was standing in.
The arrangement had suited Stainforth well enough.
He received his percentage without any effort of his own and the estate stayed solvent, which reflected well on his management.

I received the fiction of ownership, which was worth considerably more to me than any legal reality because it meant I could still get out of bed in the morning and act like a woman with something to protect.
I knew, without having been told directly, that the arrangement was changing.
Nan arrived at half past six, the way she'd arrived every morning for the past seven years: without announcement, without ceremony, already in her apron.
She took the bread from me and started slicing.
"Coach is late," she said.
"Which?"
"London.
Chapman stopped at the Goat last night, told Jem the offside wheel's going.
They might limp it in or they might not."

I thought about the three guests waiting on the London coach, about the chandler's order that was also coming down from London, about a stranded coach and what it meant in terms of guests who needed to eat and rooms that needed to be ready and passengers who would want compensation that I was not in a position to offer because the wheel was not my wheel.
"How bad?"
"Bad enough he told Jem."
Nan set the loaf down and looked at me directly, which she only did when she thought I was about to miss something.
"He's got a full box.
Seven passengers."
Seven passengers and a lame wheel.
I pulled the second kettle onto the fire and started cutting bread myself.
"Right," I said.
"Get the back rooms aired."
I heard the coach before I saw it, the way you learn to hear things when your livelihood arrives on wheels.
A good coach sounds like a coach.

This one came in with a skip in the rhythm that told me the wheel was worse than Chapman had told Jem, and it pulled up in the yard at three minutes to eight listing slightly to the offside, which meant the problem was not just the wheel but the axle tree and Chapman was lucky to have made it at all.
I was in the yard when it arrived.

The two women descended first, the way women always descended first when there was no one of consequence to insist otherwise: they were sisters by their matching good coats and the identical expression they wore, which was the expression of people who expected better and had been disappointed in this expectation for several hours.
Behind them came a clergyman who descended blinking into the October light, stood a moment taking his bearings, and reached instinctively for a bag that Jem had already moved without being asked.
He looked surprised, which told me he wasn't used to inn yards where the ostler was faster than he expected.
The merchant's wife came next with a trunk that Jem had to carry two-handed, the lid held shut by nothing but a combination of luck and the way it was packed, the hinge split clean along one side.
She watched him carry it the way people watch their property when they're calculating whether to argue.
I met her eyes and she looked away.
Behind her came a family of three, the children attached to the mother and the mother attached to her husband's arm.
The youngest child had a high colour that wasn't the cold.
I looked at her and made a note of it.
And last, on the box beside Chapman, a young soldier who climbed down without being told and went immediately to the horses' heads.
He was nineteen, maybe twenty.
His uniform coat was too large in the shoulders, which told me it hadn't been issued to him; he'd got it from someone else, which told me something more than that if I cared to follow the thought.
His boots were going at the welt on the right foot.
He stroked the near horse's nose and spoke to it in a low voice and kept his eyes on the animal rather than the crowd unloading around him.
I marked him and moved on.
Chapman wanted a word.
"Miss Dale."
He descended from the box with the deliberate heaviness of a man preparing to be aggrieved.
"I'll need to speak with you about compensation."
"For the wheel."
"For the delay.
My passengers—"
"Your passengers are at the White Hound and not in a ditch on the north road, Mr.
Chapman, which is a distinction I'd encourage you to appreciate."
I kept my voice pleasant.
"If you want to discuss compensation, I'd suggest starting with Rogers at the coaching company.
He's in Ware on Thursdays.
Today is Thursday."
Chapman drew breath.
"He'll be easier to reach," I said, "if you start now."
He closed his mouth.
Then he went to see about the axle.
The merchant's wife wanted to know where her trunk was going.
I told her Jem would have it in her room by the time she'd had breakfast, which was true because Jem was already halfway up the stairs with it.
The clergyman was travelling to a living in Newcastle and had not eaten since yesterday; I put him at the good table in the parlour with a full pot and left him to it.
The family needed rooms and hot water and something for the child's fever.

I sent for Nan's boy to go to the village for the apothecary's draught, got the family into the largest guest room, and had the fire in there going properly before the mother had finished unpacking the children's coats.
By the time all seven passengers were settled it was gone nine, and Hartley, the chandler from Hitchin, was waiting in my kitchen doorway with his sample case.
I'd known Hartley eight years.

He was a careful man who liked to think he was cleverer than he was, which meant every negotiation followed the same shape: he opened high, I opened my ledger, and somewhere in the middle we landed on a number that was lower than he wanted and higher than I needed, and we both pretended this was a satisfactory outcome.
Last quarter I'd held him to one and five per dozen tallow.
He was back now with October turned cold early, which he believed gave him the advantage.
He set his case on the kitchen table and looked around the kitchen the way he always did, as though pricing it.
"Miss Dale.
Autumn's turned cold early."
"It has," I said.
I didn't move from the fire.
"Season like this, everyone's burning through their stock."
He opened the case and laid out his samples with the methodical care of a man who had rehearsed this.
"I've had three inns on the road this week alone.
Supply's short."
"I'd heard something similar."
I went to the dresser and came back with the ledger.
"From Millar's, in Hitchin.
He's got last quarter's stock still on hand and is looking to move it before the new shipment comes in.
One and two per dozen, to a steady buyer."
Hartley looked at the ledger.
His samples were good tallow, better than Millar's, and he knew I knew it, and he was calculating whether I'd actually take the inferior stock to save tuppence.
"One and two," he said.
"He was quite specific."
"Millar's tallow is soft.
Burns fast."
"My guests don't sit up long enough to notice the difference."
"Your guests in the private parlour might."
"My guests in the private parlour are charged accordingly."
I turned a page in the ledger.
"One and two, Hartley.
Millar's is keen."
He was quiet.
I let the quiet sit there and did not help him with it.
"One and three," he said finally.
"One and three for the full winter order, same delivery terms as last quarter, and you include the tapers for the front hall sconces."
I turned another page, as though confirming something I'd written there.
"The sconces take the long taper.
Millar's doesn't stock them."
He knew I'd been holding that back.
I watched him understand that I'd been holding it back specifically for this moment, and then I watched him decide that the long tapers were not worth the argument.
"One and three," he said again, resigned this time.
"Including the tapers."
"I'll have Jem ready on Thursday."
He wrote out the invoice with the particular care of a man who has lost a negotiation and wants to at least have neat handwriting to show for it.
I took the invoice when he offered it and the corner caught the side of my finger, a paper cut clean and immediate, the kind that doesn't hurt until a moment later.
I blotted it on my apron without looking at it.
When he was gone I stood in the kitchen with the invoice in my hands.
One and three.
Six months ago it had been one and four.
One and four was what I needed to run the inn at a profit through winter.

One and three was what I could manage if everything else stayed level, and everything else was not staying level, had not stayed level in two years, was in fact moving in one direction at a pace I could calculate and did not enjoy calculating.
I put the invoice in the ledger and closed it.
The cut on my finger had stopped bleeding.
I got on with the rest of it.
The altercation in the taproom happened at half past eleven.
Two of the stranded passengers had been at the ale since ten, which I'd allowed because they'd paid for their rooms and ale was profit and I needed the profit.

By eleven they had moved from argument about the road to argument about something that had started with one of them accidentally stepping on the other's coat, which was draped over a chair in a way that made it impossible to avoid, and had escalated from there with the efficiency of men who had been uncomfortable for six hours and needed somewhere to put it.
I heard the raised voices from the yard and came in through the kitchen.
By the time I reached the taproom the younger of the two had his hand on the older one's collar and the older one had his hands up and wasn't looking at the younger man's fist.
The chair had gone over.
I walked between them and picked up the chair.
"Sit down," I said.
Not loudly.
Loudly would have made it a challenge.
The younger man looked at me.
He was angry and embarrassed and looking for somewhere to put both, and for a moment he looked at me as though I might do as a destination.
I held the chair with my hand on the back of it and looked at him steadily.
He sat.
I looked at the older man, who righted himself and took his ale and moved to the far end of the bar without being asked.
Nan was wiping down the bar with one eye on the door.
"Third one this month," she said, when I passed her.
"Road's full of men with nowhere to go and too much pride to admit it."
I set the fallen chair against the wall.
"Post-war.
They'll settle."
"Aye."
Nan looked at the younger man, who had his head down over his ale now, the anger gone and something tireder in its place.
"Or they won't."
The soldier appeared at the kitchen door at about noon.
He knocked.
I knew it was him before I turned around because he knocked the way soldiers knock when they've learned that you don't enter someone else's territory without asking, and most men hadn't learned that.
I turned around.
His cap was in his hands.
He was thinner than he'd looked on the coach, the way people always looked worse when they stopped moving.
He'd been making himself useful in the yard all morning, I'd noticed that, keeping out of the way while still being where hands were wanted.
"Have you eaten today?"
I asked.
He looked at the floor between us.
"Not since yesterday, ma'am."
"Sit down."
I fed him at the kitchen table, not in the taproom.
There was cold mutton from breakfast and bread and a pot of tea I'd just made, and I set it in front of him and turned back to the fire.
He ate with the careful restraint of a man who had learned not to show hunger, and the restraint showed anyway, in the deliberate pace of it.
When I heard his fork go down I turned back.
"The coach goes tonight," I said.
"It'll be repaired by six."
He stood and put the cap back on.
His hands were steady.
"Thank you, ma'am."
He went out through the yard.
I watched from the kitchen window until he turned onto the north road and was gone from sight.
From the back, his right boot was worse than I'd thought.
The welt had pulled entirely away from the sole at the toe, and he was walking with the slight list of a man who knows it and is compensating.
He had fifty miles to Newcastle on those boots, give or take.
I thought what I thought.
I didn't say it to anyone.

The afternoon ran: the wheel and axle repaired by four, the stranded passengers dispersed, the merchant's wife departing with most of her good opinion of the establishment intact, the trunk tied shut with cord from Jem's stable and loaded without further incident.
The clergyman lingered over a second pot and finally left with the air of a man who had eaten enough to face Newcastle.
The family with the sick child stayed.

Their room was paid through Sunday and by evening the child's fever had broken, which Nan reported with the satisfied precision of a woman who had been monitoring the situation and was pleased with the outcome.
By five the taproom was quiet.
By six it was mine.
Nan's end-of-shift followed its usual shape: the bar wiped down a final time, coat on, bonnet tied, a pause in the kitchen doorway.
"You need another pair of hands," she said.
"Mornings especially."
"I'll think about it."
"You've been saying that since August."
"Nan."
She tied her bonnet ribbon with the particular firmness of someone concluding an argument.
"Dinner's on the range.
Don't leave it."
"Good night."
"Good night."
She went, and I heard her footsteps in the yard and then on the road and then nothing.
Jem was in the stable for another quarter-hour after that, the yard settling into its evening sounds: horses fed, straw down, the particular creak of the big doors pulled to and latched.
Then quiet.
Upstairs, the light in Bridget's window came on, the shape of her moving behind the glass.
I bolted the back door.
The front door.
Went through the taproom checking candles, taking down the ones that had burned to stubs and replacing them from the box in the hall cupboard.
Room four was empty, which meant its chimney was room four's chimney to sort when someone was in it.
I checked the office: strongbox locked, ledger on the shelf where I'd left it, nothing disturbed.
I checked the private parlour, the two guest rooms currently occupied, confirming both fires were banked and neither guest would freeze in the night.
The family's youngest child was asleep when I went past.
The mother was awake.
I put my head in and she nodded, and I nodded back, and I went on.
In the kitchen I sat down at the table with the ledger and wrote the day's numbers.
I already knew what they said; I'd known since Hartley left.
But writing them was different from knowing them.
Writing them made them fixed, and fixed things could be planned around, and planning was the only instrument I had.
One and three per dozen tallow.
Rent at December quarter unchanged.
The family in room three would leave Sunday, which meant two days of room income against the reduced rate I'd given them for the child's illness.
The stranded coach passengers had all eaten and three had taken rooms, which was better than I'd had any right to expect.
The cut on my index finger had a crust over it.
My hands at end of day: reddened from the cold water, ink along the outside of the right.
The ledger columns were even.
I closed it.
Sat a moment with my hands in my lap.
Then I got up.
The letter was on the hall table where I'd put it that morning.
Stainforth's seal on the red wax, his tall copperplate on the face of it.
The handwriting he used when he'd dictated something to a clerk and reviewed it before sending.
Not a casual letter, then.
Not that I'd thought it was.
I'd known since August that it was coming.
I'd been moving faster ever since, in the way that you do when the direction you're heading is clear and the destination isn't somewhere you can choose not to arrive.
I picked it up.
Felt the weight of it, which was heavier than a short letter, which meant there was more in it than a single paragraph.
Which meant he had made a decision and wanted me to have the full argument rather than just the conclusion.
I set it back down.
"Damn you," I said, to the hall, to the inn, to Stainforth and his tall copperplate and his percentage of a dead man's debts.
The words went nowhere.
The inn absorbed them the way it absorbed everything.

I went upstairs to bed with my boots still half-laced and the fire banked and the letter sitting on the hall table, sealed, unchanged, waiting for the morning the way everything I couldn't fix waited for the morning.
When I got there, it would still be there.
It always was.
THE LAST RETREAT
Chapter 1: The White Hound
The grate was cold.
I had banked it before bed, or I thought I had.
The ash was still warm when I pushed a finger in, but the kitchen was dark and the fire was out and the morning was already wrong.
I got it going again with the last of the good pine kindling and stood over it with my hands out until the feeling came back to my fingers.
Outside, frost.
The yard was silent.
October had arrived in Hertfordshire the way it always did — without apology and ahead of schedule.
The fire told me something every morning.
This morning it told me I had gone to bed too tired to do the banking properly, which meant yesterday had been harder than I'd admitted.
I filed that and went on.
The White Hound was not a beautiful inn.
I had never pretended otherwise.

The eaves wanted repair on the north side, the taproom ceiling had a stain that Jem had plastered twice and which came back every winter regardless, and the upper passage smelled of damp wool no matter how often I aired the rooms.
The single pump in the yard ran slow when the temperature dropped, which it had been doing since September.
The sign above the door showed a white hound that had faded, over the years, to the approximate colour of old bone.
What it had was: a yard big enough for a six-horse change, a kitchen I could find my way around blindfolded, and a road that brought coaches through whether the weather was fit for it or not.
That was the thing about coaching inns on the North Road.
They did not require charm or beauty or a proprietress who had made better choices at twenty-two.
They required a working kitchen, a yard, and someone who got up before dawn to bank the fire.
I had been that someone for seven years.
The inn was mine in every sense except the one that would hold up in a court of law, but I had learned not to dwell on that.
The lease was in my name, which was better than nothing, and Stainforth had not yet found a reason to move against it, which was better still.
I kept the books carefully.
I kept Jem and Nan paid on time.
I kept the place running.
That was the plan.
Keep it running.
I was very good at the plan.
I checked the bread from last night — still good — and put the kettle on.

The accounts from the previous week were on the table where I had left them, the column for October looking thin in the way it always did when the summer coaches stopped and the winter ones had not yet committed to a regular schedule.
I had been carrying the numbers in my head since Tuesday.
They were not better for being written down.
Nan came in without knocking, which she had not bothered doing in five years.
She was already wearing her apron, and she had two loaves from the baker's wrapped in cloth under her arm.
"The axle went on the Leeds coach," she said, unwrapping the loaves on the board beside mine.
"Jem heard it last night.
Driver says he needs a wheel-wright before he goes further."
"When did it happen?"
"Sometime after eleven.
He came in on three wheels, more or less."
"How many passengers?"
She set the loaves on the board.
"Six inside, two up.
Including a woman who has opinions about trunks."
"What sort of opinions?"
"The expensive sort."
I cut the bread.
"Who's the wheel-wright?"
"Haverstock, if he's sober."
"He's never sober before noon."
"Then it'll be a long morning."
Nan pulled the kettle before it boiled over.
"The coachman wants a word."
"I'm sure he does."
"He's going to want something for the delay."
"He can want."
I put the bread on a board and carried it through to the passage.
Behind me I heard Nan begin to set the tables, the precise efficient sounds of someone who had done it ten thousand times and was not going to rush on anyone's account.
The coach was already in the yard when I got outside, sitting at an angle that explained the axle.
It was a heavy vehicle, the kind that took the North Road at speed and paid for it.

I read it before I reached it: one passenger already complaining from the window — a woman in a green travelling coat, head turned toward someone inside, which meant she was directing her complaints at a companion rather than the window, which was marginally better for the yard — luggage strapped on top in a configuration that suggested a hasty departure, a bandbox tied on with someone's belt rather than a proper strap.
A gentleman in a brown greatcoat was already out and stretching his back.
Two younger men — brothers, by the look of them — stood near the rear wheel examining the damage with the authority of people who knew nothing about axles.
An older woman with a reticule stayed in the coach door, not committing to the yard.
The near lead horse was favouring a foreleg.
Jem was at the horse's head, running a hand down the leg with the economy of motion that meant he had already decided what needed doing and was waiting for me to catch up.
"Foreleg?"
I said.
"Stone bruise.
She'll be right in two days."
He did not look up.
"The axle's worse."
"Haverstock."
"I already sent the boy."
He glanced at me then.
"Eight o'clock.
Later, probably."

Which meant the six inside passengers and two up would be eating my bread and wanting my fire and asking Nan where the privy was until at least ten, and the woman in the green coat would have more opinions about more things, and the two brothers near the wheel would want ale before anyone had earned it.
Fine.
I had bread and fire and answers to all of those questions.
That was what the morning was for.
"Right," I said, and went back to the kitchen to cut more.
The coachman found me by the door.
He was a heavyset man in a many-caped greatcoat and he had the look of someone composing an argument on the walk over.
"Miss Dale."
He did not remove his hat.
"I'll want compensation for the delay.
The company has a standard arrangement."
"The company also has an agent," I said.
"Mr.
Pitt, out of Hitchin, Tuesdays and Thursdays.
He handles the road contracts."
"It's your yard."
"It's your axle."
He looked at me.
I looked at him.
He had perhaps ten years on me and twice my weight and none of that was relevant to the question of whose name was on the road contract.
"The standard schedule compensation — "
"Take it up with Pitt."
I handed him the cutting board with the bread.
"In the meantime, your passengers are welcome in the taproom.
The fire's been going an hour."
He took the board.
The hat came off, eventually.
Not happily, but it came off.
The woman with the trunk cornered me while I was directing the boy to bring it in from the roof.
She had a great deal to say about how it had been loaded in London, what had happened to the brass fitting on the left side, and whose negligence had caused it.

I listened for as long as was useful and established that the fitting had come loose on its own — the thread was already stripped before she'd boarded; I could see the damage — and that no one owed her anything except the use of a screwdriver and five minutes.
She did not agree with my assessment but she took her trunk inside, which was the relevant outcome.
Hartley, the chandler, came at half past nine.
He always came on Wednesdays.
Same sample case, same opening number, same patient expression.
He was not a bad man — he had a family and a margin the same as I did — but he came in every quarter knowing he was going to lose and he had never once adjusted his opening offer to account for this.
I had given up trying to understand it.
Some people's hope was eternal.
"The season's turning," he said, setting the case on the kitchen doorway threshold.
"Tallow's up from last quarter."
"How much up?"
"Threepence the dozen."
I opened the ledger.
"Last quarter I paid ninepence.
Threepence up is a shilling the dozen."
"Supply and demand, Miss Dale.
The cold came early."
"It came early for everyone."
I ran my finger down the column.
"Including Bridwell and Sons in Hitchin.
They quoted me tenpence-halfpenny last week."
I looked up.
"In writing."
He went still in the way that meant he was doing his own arithmetic.
He knew I might be exaggerating the quote by a penny.
He could see that I might.
The trouble was, if he pushed the point, he had to be right, and he was not certain he was.
"Tenpence-halfpenny's Bridwell's quoted rate," he said.
"Delivered costs more."
"Hitchin's sixteen miles.
The delivery charge would be approximately — " I looked at the ledger — "sixpence on the haul, divided across twenty-four dozen.
That's one-quarter of one penny per dozen.
Your threepence is still more expensive."
Hartley looked at the case.
He looked at the ledger.
He looked at the cut on my finger and then away from it.
"Ninepence-halfpenny," he said.
"Ninepence."
A longer pause this time.
Then: "Invoice on delivery."
"As always."
He signed his ledger.
I signed mine.
When I handed it back, the cut on my index finger caught on the paper edge — I had got it earlier, helping with the trunk woman's luggage — and I pressed my thumb over it until it stopped.
The thing about the chandler was that this negotiation was harder than last year.
Not by much; Hartley had not grown sharper or bolder.
The problem was that the margin had moved.

Between October last year and October this year, the gap between what came in and what went out had narrowed by enough that I had started running the arithmetic in my head before I had finished my morning tea, and I had been doing it more days than not.
A shilling on candles.
Three shillings on coal if the winter ran cold.
The Stainforth quarter coming up in November.
The axle on the Leeds coach had cost me nothing today because Haverstock charged the company, not the inn, but the next one might go differently.
One bad quarter on the road and the October numbers went from thin to something I had not yet named.
I put the ledger away.
The altercation in the taproom started while Nan was still clearing the breakfast plates.
Two men from the stranded coach — both inside passengers, both going north, both apparently of the opinion that the window seat was rightfully theirs.
By the time I heard it from the kitchen, it had gone past words into the preliminary shoving stage, which was the stage I had least patience for.
I came through the taproom door and stepped between them.
The larger man's elbow caught my shoulder; he had not seen me coming and pulled back immediately, which gave me approximately two seconds of his attention before he composed himself.
"The coach goes as far as Stamford tonight," I said, looking past them both.
"You'll be sitting next to each other again in four hours."
The smaller man's jaw worked.
The larger one had the decency to look embarrassed.
"Think on it," I said, and walked back to the kitchen.
Behind me, I heard Nan say: "This is the fourth time this week."
Not to the men.
To me, through the door.
Loud enough for them to hear, quiet enough to make them think she had not meant them to.
She had meant them to.
She had also not been wrong about the count.
The road had been rougher this past year than any since I had been running the inn.
The men coming down it were rougher too, or tireder, or carrying things they had brought back from the continent that did not show up in their luggage.
I did not know what to do about that.
I stepped between when I had to and I kept the kitchen stocked and I tried not to look too hard at any of them.
He was in the yard by the stable wall, trying to be small.
He was young — younger than I had expected — with the hollowed-out look of someone who had been walking on less than he needed for long enough that he had stopped noticing it.
The coat was army issue, or had been once; it was a size too large across the shoulders and the sleeves came past his wrists.
His boots were coming apart at the welt, the leather cracked at the toe and the left heel wrapped with cord to hold the sole on.
I clocked the boots before anything else.
You could learn a great deal about the last month of a person's life from their boots.
He had not asked for anything.
He was simply standing there, near enough to the kitchen door to be visible, far enough away that he could not be accused of asking.
I went back inside and cut bread.

More than he would want to be seen eating in one sitting, but I cut it anyway and added cold beef from the morning and the end of the cheese from yesterday because the cheese was nearly done regardless.
"You can sit in the kitchen," I said when I came back out.
He looked at me carefully — not with suspicion, exactly, but the way a person looks when they have been offered things that came with conditions and have learned to read the offer first.
"I'm not going to charge you."
"I can pay."
He said it quietly, without argument, the way people say it when it might not quite be true but they need it to be said.
"Sit down," I said.
He sat at the kitchen table and I turned to the fire.
I did not want to watch him eat.
He deserved that much — to eat without someone looking at him doing it.

I busied myself with the fire and the kettle and a pot that did not need stirring, and I kept my eyes on the coals and listened instead: the scrape of the plate, the sound of the cup set down, a long breath that had nothing theatrical about it, just lungs doing their work after a meal when they had not been sure of one.
When the sounds stopped I set a second mug beside him without looking at his face.
He said, very quietly: "Thank you."
"Road to Stamford's clear at this time of year.
If you keep to the verge when the coaches go past."
He stood.
He wrapped the last of the bread in his handkerchief, which I had not seen him do but which I noted.
The door opened and closed.
I watched his boots on the road from the kitchen window until the lane turned and I lost him.
What I thought, I kept.
The post-war world was full of men with boots like that and there was nothing to do about it except cut bread and look away when they needed you to.
