They were not better for being written down.
Nan came in without knocking, which she had not bothered doing in five years.
She was already wearing her apron, and she had two loaves from the baker's wrapped in cloth under her arm.
"The axle went on the Leeds coach," she said, unwrapping the loaves on the board beside mine.
"Jem heard it last night.
Driver says he needs a wheel-wright before he goes further."
"When did it happen?"
"Sometime after eleven.
He came in on three wheels, more or less."
"How many passengers?"
She set the loaves on the board.
"Six inside, two up.
Including a woman who has opinions about trunks."
"What sort of opinions?"
"The expensive sort."
I cut the bread.
"Who's the wheel-wright?"
"Haverstock, if he's sober."
"He's never sober before noon."
"Then it'll be a long morning."
Nan pulled the kettle before it boiled over.
"The coachman wants a word."
"I'm sure he does."
"He's going to want something for the delay."
"He can want."
I put the bread on a board and carried it through to the passage.
Behind me I heard Nan begin to set the tables, the same quick unhurried sounds she made every morning.
The coach was already in the yard when I got outside, sitting at an angle that explained the axle.
It was a heavy vehicle, the kind that took the North Road at speed and paid for it.

I read it before I reached it: one passenger already complaining from the window — a woman in a green travelling coat, head turned toward someone inside, which meant she was directing her complaints at a companion rather than the window, which was marginally better for the yard — luggage strapped on top in a configuration that suggested a hasty departure, a bandbox tied on with someone's belt rather than a proper strap.
A gentleman in a brown greatcoat was already out and stretching his back.
Two younger men — brothers, by the look of them — stood near the rear wheel examining the damage with the authority of people who knew nothing about axles.
An older woman with a reticule stayed in the coach door, not committing to the yard.
The near lead horse was favouring a foreleg.
Jem was at the horse's head, running a hand down the leg with the economy of motion that meant he had already decided what needed doing and was waiting for me to catch up.
"Foreleg?"
I said.
"Stone bruise.
She'll be right in two days."
He did not look up.
"The axle's worse."
"Haverstock."
"I already sent the boy."
He glanced at me then.
"Eight o'clock.
Later, probably."

Which meant the six inside passengers and two up would be eating my bread and wanting my fire and asking Nan where the privy was until at least ten, and the woman in the green coat would have more opinions about more things, and the two brothers near the wheel would want ale before anyone had earned it.
Fine.
I had bread and fire and answers to all of those questions.
"Right," I said, and went back to the kitchen to cut more.
The coachman found me by the door.
He was a heavyset man in a many-caped greatcoat and he had the look of someone composing an argument on the walk over.
"Miss Dale."
He did not remove his hat.
"I'll want compensation for the delay.
The company has a standard arrangement."
"The company also has an agent," I said.
"Mr.
Pitt, out of Hitchin, Tuesdays and Thursdays.
He handles the road contracts."
"It's your yard."
"It's your axle."
He looked at me.
I looked at him.
He had perhaps ten years on me and twice my weight and none of that was relevant.
"The standard schedule compensation — "
"Take it up with Pitt."
I handed him the cutting board with the bread.
"In the meantime, your passengers are welcome in the taproom.
The fire's been going an hour."
He took the board.
The hat came off, eventually.
Not happily, but it came off.
The woman with the trunk cornered me while I was directing the boy to bring it in from the roof.
She had a great deal to say about how it had been loaded in London, what had happened to the brass fitting on the left side, and whose negligence had caused it.

I listened for as long as was useful and established that the fitting had come loose on its own — the thread was already stripped before she'd boarded; I could see the damage — and that no one owed her anything except the use of a screwdriver and five minutes.
She did not agree with my assessment but she took her trunk inside, which was the relevant outcome.
Hartley, the chandler, came at half past nine.
He always came on Wednesdays.
Same sample case, same opening number, same patient expression.
He was not a bad man — he had a family and a margin the same as I did — but he came in every quarter knowing he was going to lose and he had never once adjusted his opening offer to account for this.
I had given up trying to understand it.
Some people's hope was eternal.
"The season's turning," he said, setting the case on the kitchen doorway threshold.
"Tallow's up from last quarter."
"How much up?"
"Threepence the dozen."
I opened the ledger.
"Last quarter I paid ninepence.
Threepence up is a shilling the dozen."
"Supply and demand, Miss Dale.
The cold came early."
"It came early for everyone."
I ran my finger down the column.
"Including Bridwell and Sons in Hitchin.
They quoted me tenpence-halfpenny last week."
I looked up.
"In writing."
He went still.
He knew I might be exaggerating the quote by a penny.
He could see that I might.
The trouble was, if he pushed the point, he had to be right, and he was not certain he was.
"Tenpence-halfpenny's Bridwell's quoted rate," he said.
"Delivered costs more."
"Hitchin's sixteen miles.
The delivery charge would be approximately — " I looked at the ledger — "sixpence on the haul, divided across twenty-four dozen.
That's one-quarter of one penny per dozen.
Your threepence is still more expensive."
Hartley looked at the case.
He looked at the ledger.
He looked at the cut on my finger and then away from it.
"Ninepence-halfpenny," he said.
"Ninepence."
A longer pause this time.
Then: "Invoice on delivery."
"As always."
He signed his ledger.
I signed mine.
When I handed it back, the cut on my index finger caught on the paper edge — I had got it earlier, helping with the trunk woman's luggage — and I pressed my thumb over it until it stopped.
The thing about the chandler was that this negotiation was harder than last year.
Not by much; Hartley had not grown sharper or bolder.
The problem was that the margin had moved.

Between October last year and October this year, the gap between what came in and what went out had narrowed by enough that I had started running the arithmetic in my head before I had finished my morning tea, and I had been doing it more days than not.
A shilling on candles.
Three shillings on coal if the winter ran cold.
The Stainforth quarter coming up in November.
The axle on the Leeds coach had cost me nothing today because Haverstock charged the company, not the inn, but the next one might go differently.
One bad quarter on the road and the October numbers went from thin to something I had not yet named.
I put the ledger away.
The altercation in the taproom started while Nan was still clearing the breakfast plates.
Two men from the stranded coach — both inside passengers, both going north, both apparently of the opinion that the window seat was rightfully theirs.
By the time I heard it from the kitchen, it had gone past words into the preliminary shoving stage, which was the stage I had least patience for.
I came through the taproom door and stepped between them.
The larger man's elbow caught my shoulder; he had not seen me coming and pulled back immediately, which gave me approximately two seconds of his attention before he composed himself.
"The coach goes as far as Stamford tonight," I said, looking past them both.
"You'll be sitting next to each other again in four hours."
The smaller man's jaw worked.
The larger one had the decency to look embarrassed.
"Think on it," I said, and walked back to the kitchen.
Behind me, I heard Nan say: "This is the fourth time this week."
Not to the men.
To me, through the door.
Loud enough for them to hear, quiet enough to make them think she had not meant them to.
She had meant them to.
She had also not been wrong about the count.
The road was harder this year than it had been before the war, and the men on it were rougher, or tireder, or both.
I stepped between when I had to and I kept the kitchen stocked and I tried not to look too closely at any of them.
He was in the yard by the stable wall, trying to be small.
He was young — younger than I had expected — with the hollowed-out look of someone who had been walking on less than he needed for long enough that he had stopped noticing it.
The coat was army issue, or had been once; it was a size too large across the shoulders and the sleeves came past his wrists.
His boots were coming apart at the welt, the leather cracked at the toe and the left heel wrapped with cord to hold the sole on.
I clocked the boots before anything else.
You could learn a great deal about the last month of a person's life from their boots.
He had not asked for anything.
He was simply standing there, near enough to the kitchen door to be visible, far enough away that he could not be accused of asking.
I went back inside and cut bread.

More than he would want to be seen eating in one sitting, but I cut it anyway and added cold beef from the morning and the end of the cheese from yesterday because the cheese was nearly done regardless.
"You can sit in the kitchen," I said when I came back out.
He looked at me with the careful attention of someone reading an offer before accepting it.
"I'm not going to charge you."
"I can pay."
Said quietly, without argument.
The kind of thing that needed to be said.
"Sit down," I said.
He sat at the kitchen table and I turned to the fire.
I did not want to watch him eat.
He deserved that much — to eat without someone looking at him doing it.

I busied myself with the fire and the kettle and a pot that did not need stirring, and I kept my eyes on the coals and listened instead: the scrape of the plate, the sound of the cup set down, a long breath.
Nothing theatrical.
When the sounds stopped I set a second mug beside him without looking at his face.
He said, very quietly: "Thank you."
"Road to Stamford's clear at this time of year.
If you keep to the verge when the coaches go past."
He stood.
He wrapped the last of the bread in his handkerchief, which I had not seen him do but which I noted.
The door opened and closed.
I watched his boots on the road from the kitchen window until the lane turned and I lost him.
Then I went back to the bread board.
By four o'clock the Leeds coach was fixed and gone.
Haverstock had sobered up enough by half past ten to do the job, charged the coaching company twice what it was worth, and left before I could congratulate him.
The yard had spent the rest of the afternoon being a yard again.
I cleared the taproom, wiped the tables, and banked the fire for the evening trade.
By the time I came back through, Nan was folding the last of the cloths and had her coat on already.
"That'll do me," she said.
She had her coat on already.
"My feet have opinions about the flagstones."
"Go."
"Mrs.
Bowker brought a chicken broth round for the supper trade.
It's on the range."
"Thank you."
She paused at the door.
Nan had a pause for practical things she'd forgotten and a different pause for things she'd noticed and hadn't decided whether to say.
I knew them both.
This was the third kind.
"You should sleep past six, one of these mornings."
"I'll put it in the diary."
She looked at me for a moment with the expression she had been perfecting since before I could honestly remember — the one that weighed whether I wanted to hear the rest of it — and then she left.
The taproom went quiet again.
Outside, Jem was talking low to the horses in his evening voice, the sounds of someone letting an animal know they were not alone.
Bridget's window above showed a strip of light at the shutter's edge, which meant she was reading.
She had been in her window when the Stainforth letter arrived.
I had not looked up to check, but I knew she was watching.
She always watched.
Bridget's talent was observing things that were none of her business and then not saying a word about them.
I locked up room by room, top to bottom.
Taproom first: chairs up, fire banked, the sticky latch on the window by the fireplace checked twice.
Then the kitchen, the back passage, the office, the strongbox under the floorboard checked by touch.
Up the stairs and down.
The back door last, both bolts home.
The kitchen window latch still stuck.
I lifted the frame, turned the latch, set the frame back down.
Three years I had been meaning to have Jem file it.
I no longer mentioned it.
The ledger was on the kitchen table.
I sat down and opened it.
The numbers had not improved since this morning.
The October account was thin, the October rent was six weeks out, and fourteen shillings was the margin between them.
I knew the figures by heart; I had known them since Tuesday.
Writing them down in ink did not tell me anything new.
I closed the book.
My hands were raw from the cold water, a line of red along each knuckle.
The cut on my index finger had stopped bleeding but left a brown crescent on the page.
I would trim the corner in the morning.
I was very good at this.
Seven years and I was very good at all of it, and the numbers in the ledger were still what they were.
I stood up.
The letter was on the shelf where I had left it this morning, propped against the wall with Stainforth's seal facing out.
I had put it there when it arrived, which was before eight o'clock, and I had looked at it every time I walked through the kitchen since, and I had not opened it because I already knew what it said.
Or I knew the shape of it.
I knew the shape of these things.
Stainforth owned the inn.
He owned the building, the yard, the stables, the kitchen I had just cleaned, the ledger I had just closed.

He owned it the way men like him owned things — with papers signed in offices, at a remove from the daily work of it, through agents who came round in October with politely worded letters when the quarter rent was coming up and a woman running a coaching inn alone looked more like opportunity than tenant.
I had known this letter was coming since July, when I heard from a man in Stevenage that Stainforth had been asking after the market rate for coaching inn leases on the North Road.
I had started moving faster in August.
I was still moving.
I stood at the shelf for a moment with the letter in my hands.
The wax was Stainforth's red.
His handwriting on the outside.
His signature on what was inside, whatever it said.
"Well," I said to the room.
Outside, the frost was settling on the yard again, the same as every night this week.
The road was empty.
I took the letter upstairs and set it on the nightstand, still sealed.
Morning would do.
The White Hound
The grate was cold and I was not in the mood for it.
I crouched on the kitchen flags with my hands already going numb, because the fire never lit on the first attempt in October and I did not know why I kept expecting otherwise.
The tinder caught.
I held it there until I was sure, then added the kindling in order, smallest to largest, the way I had learned not to rush.
You could not hurry the White Hound's kitchen grate.
It had been here longer than I had.
It had been here longer than the road, or so Jem claimed, and Jem was wrong about most things but occasionally right about grates.
I held the tinder and waited, and by the time the blaze was taking properly I had enough feeling back in my fingers to be useful.
The kettle went on.
I put the bread to prove beside the fire.

I did the accounts in my head while I waited — the way I had gotten into the habit of doing, because the numbers didn't change between the ledger and the waking hours before anyone else was about, but it helped to know them again in the cold and the quiet, when there was no one to perform anything for.
The White Hound was mine in the sense that I ran it, kept it, lost sleep over it, and could name every board that needed replacing on the south-facing eaves.
Mine in the sense that I had been here seven years and the guests knew my face and the chandler came to me directly when the tallow price went up.

Mine in the sense that I knew the cellar's damp corner, and the particular creak of the third stair, and which of the taproom regulars needed handling carefully and which needed telling once and that was that.
It was mine in every sense except the one that mattered to a solicitor.
The lease was in the name of my late husband.

A widow on the Great North Road had no standing to change that — not without a man to counter-sign, not without permission from the estate, not without navigating the kind of legal machinery designed by men who assumed a woman managing a coaching inn was a temporary arrangement while she found somewhere better to be.
Mr Stainforth of Stainforth & Croft had the original in his office in Hitchin.
I had a copy, filed in the strongbox under the kitchen counter.
The copy had Abel Dale's name where mine ought to be, and above it, in the particular cramped hand of Stainforth's secretary, the date of execution: the twelfth of March, 1806.
A document that had nothing to do with the woman standing in this kitchen at five in the morning getting her hands warm, except that it governed whether she could stay.
I was not going to dwell on the arithmetic of it.
I had the fire.
I had the bread proving.
I had the day.
There were things wrong with the inn and I knew them all intimately.
The east stable wall had developed a lean that Jem called cosmetic and I called a warning.
The second guest room window latch was loose enough that a determined child — or a determined adult with no better options — could work it from outside.

The taproom floor near the entrance had gone soft in a patch three feet wide; I had put a chair in front of it and told myself I would deal with it before March, which was optimistic if the ground froze early.
The flue above the taproom hearth pulled badly on east winds.
The well rope wanted replacing.
I had a list.
I kept it in the ledger, in the column I called 'eventual,' which was polite for 'when I can afford it.'
There were things right with the inn as well.
I was not going to list them.
I knew them; that was enough.
The ledger was on the kitchen table where I always kept it.
I did not open it.
I knew what was in it the same way I knew what was wrong with the eaves: intimately, against my will, in the particular way of things that required your attention whether you gave it or not.

The number in the rent column had been sitting there since I last tallied, and it had not improved in the night, and it would not improve between now and the quarter day unless the coaches ran well and the taproom stayed busy and the chandler stayed reasonable, which two of those three were currently doing.
Nan came in without knocking, which she had never done in seven years and I had stopped waiting for.
"London coach," she said, hanging up her coat and not looking at me, because she did not need to.
"Running behind.
Axle trouble at Welwyn, or so they're saying at the Lion."
"How far behind?"
"Hour.
Maybe more.
Jem says the road's bad past Baldock — the ruts froze overnight."
She looked at the bread I hadn't started cutting.
"They'll be hungry when they arrive."
"They're always hungry."
"And cross.
Axle trouble does that."
She reached past me for the knife.
"There was a woman at the Lion last night going south.
Said three passengers argued the whole way from Barnet.
Trunk fell off somewhere."
"Whose trunk?"
"Woman travelling alone.
The arguing was other people's."
I moved to the fire to check the proving loaf.
Nan cut bread the way she did everything: with absolute conviction and a noise level that suggested personal grievance with the bread itself.
"I'll handle the passengers," I said.
"You take the bar."
"I always take the bar."
"Then nothing's changed."
She said something under her breath that I chose not to hear.
I heard the London coach before it rounded the bend from the north: the rhythm of iron-shod wheels on frozen ruts changing as the road curved, then the coachman's horn, two short blasts.
A scheduled stop.
I was already in the yard when the first passenger stepped down.
I sorted them before they'd found their footing.

The merchant in the port-wine cravat wanted a private parlour and would settle for the taproom bench nearest the fire if I handled the introduction correctly — and I would, because handling people correctly was the only tool I had that worked every time.
The two women travelling together wanted tea and something warm and someone to sympathise about the journey; I could give them the first two.

The older gentleman with the walking stick needed the step, which Jem was already moving toward because Jem saw these things the way he saw everything: without being told, without being thanked, without making anything of it.
There was a woman behind them with a trunk that was not going to fit up the stairs without damage, and she already knew it and was preparing her objection.
I let her get to the end of it before I said anything, because interrupting women with objections took longer than letting them finish.
And there was the young soldier on the outside bench, thin in the way that had nothing to do with the journey and everything to do with the months before it.
I clocked his boots.
I set him aside.
I had the paying guests first.
"The wheel," said Jem, appearing at my shoulder in the particular way he had of materialising when there was news I didn't want.
"How bad?"
"Wants looking at.
Spoke's cracked, maybe two.
An hour's work."
"Then look at it."
He went.
He had already been going.
He had told me as a courtesy, not a question, and I appreciated that about Jem, which was most things about Jem when I was being honest about it.
The coachman caught up with me near the pump.
He was a large man with the air of someone who had been right about everything all his life and found it exhausting.
"Two hours we've lost," he said.
"Two hours at minimum.
I want something for the passengers — a reduction on the stop fee."
"You want to speak to Mr Aldridge about the stop fee, you'll find him at the Red Hart in Hitchin.
Tuesdays and Thursdays before noon."
I shifted the bucket I was carrying to my other hand.
"He's very accommodating to coachmen with documented delays."
A pause.
He reassessed.
"The wheel's your job to inspect."
"The wheel is my stableman's job to repair, at no charge to the coaching company.
I'd call that a fair arrangement."
He looked like he wanted to continue.
He did not continue.
"I'll be speaking to Aldridge," he said.
"I know you will."
I moved toward the inn.
"Tea's on inside."
The woman with the trunk was exactly what Nan had described: a woman with a large trunk and the absolute conviction that the inn's storeroom was an insult to her luggage.

I covered the ground in under two minutes — the storeroom had a lock, I had the key, the key would be placed in her hand personally at eight o'clock this morning and again tonight when she collected it, and the trunk was going in the storeroom because the alternative was in the yard and I did not think she wanted the yard.
She did not want the yard.
She wanted it noted that this was unsatisfactory.
I noted it.
Hartley the chandler arrived at mid-morning with his sample case and the expression of a man who had a number in mind and intended to get there.
He opened with the season.
They always opened with the season.
"Miss Dale, I can't hold last quarter's price.
The tallow market's moving, and with the harvest the way it's been—"
"Last quarter was four shillings the dozen."
"The cost of—"
"I had a conversation last week with a supplier out of Hitchin.
He quoted me four and four for sconce candles.
The good ones, double-wick."
I opened the ledger on the kitchen table to the candle column, turned it so he could read it.
"I told him I had an existing arrangement and I'd prefer to keep it."
Hartley looked at the ledger.
He looked at his sample case.
"Four and six is—"
"You've got sixty sconces in this inn," I said.
"Sixty sconces, lit every evening from October through March, plus the taproom and the kitchen.
I buy more tallow candles than anyone on this stretch of road between Hitchin and Stevenage.
I know your margin, Mr Hartley.
I know it down to the penny.
And I know the Hitchin man's margin, which is why I told him I preferred my existing supplier, which was the truth, but it is not a truth that will survive another conversation like this one."
"Four and two," he said.
"Four shillings flat."
He looked at the ceiling.
He was doing arithmetic.
I had already done the arithmetic, some time ago.
"Four shillings flat," he said, with the tone of a man surrendering to the weather.
"God help me."
"He generally does."
I took the invoice from him.
"Same schedule as last quarter.
I'll have payment ready."
He picked up his sample case with the dignity of a man who had gotten less than he came for and was going to find a way to believe it was what he'd wanted all along.
The kitchen door closed behind him.
I put the invoice in the ledger and found, when I was putting it back, the cut from the paper edge: a thin line across the pad of my index finger, not deep, just present.
I pressed my thumb against it until it stopped.
The numbers in the ledger said what they said.
The negotiations were done for this quarter.
Next quarter would be harder.
I closed the book and went to start the midday bread.
It started the way it always started: raised voices from the taproom, the particular pitch that meant two men who did not know each other deciding they had a grievance.
I was across the room before Nan had to move.
Two men from the coach, both standing, a spilled ale between them on the table.
The taller one had his jaw set in a way that said he'd already decided how this ended.
I stepped between them.
I picked up the pewter mug from the table.
"Gentleman on the left," I said.
"Sit down."
I looked at the taller one.
"Gentleman on the right.
Sit somewhere else."
The one on the left sat, because he'd been waiting for a reason.
The one on the right assessed his options — the mug in my hand, my expression, the room watching — and found that his dignity was better served by the bench near the window.
Neither of them said thank you.
That was fine.
"Third time this week," Nan said, when I got back behind the bar.
"The road's rough this autumn."
"Road's been rough since Waterloo."
She said it the way she said most things: plain, without particular feeling, as an observation rather than a complaint.
"More of them coming through.
Hungrier.
Angrier than they should be at each other when the thing they're angry at isn't in this room."
She reached under the bar for the cloth.
"They don't fight at home.
They come here and they fight here."
"They pay for the ale either way."
"They do," she said.
"Doesn't make it easier."
When the coach was loaded and gone and the yard was quiet, the young soldier was still on the bench.
I'd been watching his boots since he got off the step.
They were army-issue, or had been: standard-pattern leather, or what was left of it.
The right welt was splitting at the toe, the leather dark and cracked in the way it went when it dried wrong repeatedly, which was everywhere at once once it started.
The coat was regulation too — I'd seen enough demobilised men come through in the past year to know the shape of an army coat on a man who'd put weight on going in and lost it coming out.
This coat had been made for someone broader in the shoulder and longer in the arm.
It sat on him with the mute persistence of a thing that no longer fit and had nowhere else to go.
He was looking at the road.
He had been looking at the road for an hour.
"Have you eaten?"
I said.
He looked up.
Young.
Twenty, maybe twenty-two, with the face of someone who had been outside in all weathers for long enough that the weather was in there permanently now.
"Not today, ma'am."
"Kitchen, then.
Come round the back."

I put him at the kitchen table, where the taproom couldn't see and the guests wouldn't wonder, and I put bread and cold beef in front of him and found the mustard and the heel of the game pie from last night and a cup of the good tea that I kept for myself.
Then I turned to the sink and got on with the midday pots, because a man eating after hunger did not need to be watched.
That was the kindness that cost nothing: turning your back.
I knew when he was done by the sounds: the scrape of the plate being set down carefully, and the particular quiet that followed when someone had finished eating and didn't know what to do next.
"Thank you," he said.
He stopped.
"I haven't—" He tried again.
"Thank you, ma'am."
"North or south?"
I said, without turning from the sink.
"North.
Leeds."
"Road's straight from here.
No trouble past Biggleswade if you keep to the main."
"Yes, ma'am."
I heard him stand, heard the bench scrape back on the flags.
I heard him cross to the door and pause.
"The pie was—" he said.
"I hadn't had pie in—"
"Travel well," I said.
He went.

I stayed at the sink until I heard his boots on the yard stones, then crossed to the kitchen window and watched him go out through the gate and onto the road, north-facing, his coat too large on him, his right boot working loose with every step.
I watched until the road bent and he went with it and I couldn't see him.
There was one thought.
I kept it.
Then I went back to the pots.
The inn emptied in the late afternoon the way it always did: gradually, then with a rush.

The merchant got his private parlour in the end, because the taproom thinned after four o'clock and it cost me nothing to move him, and men who felt they'd gotten something extra tipped more generously and complained less.
The two women left on the Stevenage coach with their tea drunk and their sympathy exhausted.
The older gentleman took a room for the night on account of his knee, which was honest and meant he'd be up for the early coach and I'd need the bread started an hour sooner.
"Nan," I said, when the last regular left.
"Go home."
"I'm fine."
"Your feet are not fine.
I've been listening to you shifting weight for the past hour."
"I always shift weight."
"Not like that."
She pulled on her coat with the energy of someone who was not admitting anything.
"I'll be in at six."
"Seven.
Coach doesn't come through until nine."
"Six and a half."
"Good night, Nan."
"You'll check every room before you lock up," she said, from the door.
"I always do."
"Check the second guest room too.
The latch."
"I know about the latch."
She looked like she was going to say something else, then decided against it.
The door closed behind her.
I heard her in the yard for a moment, then the gate, then nothing.
Above me, the light was on in Bridget's window — the shape of it through the glass, steady.
She had been up there since mid-afternoon.

I had seen her cross to the window once when the carrier came with the post, and she had stood there for a moment longer than the carrier warranted, and then she had gone back to whatever she was doing.
I had not asked.
Bridget did not ask me things, and I did not ask Bridget things, and this was an arrangement that had worked for three years and showed no signs of requiring revision.
The inn was quiet in the way it only got after a full day: a particular kind of emptiness that was different from morning-empty, heavier, like a room after a long conversation.
I liked it.
I would not have said so to anyone, but I liked it.
I locked up in order.

Taproom door, front door, back door, cellar hatch, the window above the sink that had never in seven years decided to close properly and tonight was no exception — I propped the loose latch with the bit of folded card I kept there for this purpose, which was not a solution but was a practice.

I checked every room: the occupied guest room first, quiet and dark with the old gentleman's snoring already audible through the door; the unoccupied rooms, including the second guest room, including the latch, which gave exactly as much as it always gave.
I moved the chair back over the soft spot in the taproom floor.
I blew out every candle except the one I was carrying.
In the kitchen I sat down with the ledger one more time.
The numbers were the same numbers they had been this morning.
The chandler quarter was managed.
The wheel repair was Jem's time and Jem's wage, which was money I had.
The rent was due in six weeks and three days, and the number in the rent column said what it had been saying since August, and I had been listening to it since August.
Six weeks.
Possibly five, if the coaches ran light.
I spread my hands flat on the kitchen table and looked at them.
Red from the cold water, the cut on my index finger already going to a thin line.
The knuckle of my right thumb where I'd caught it on the pump handle last Tuesday.
I had good hands for this work — that was what Bridget said.
What she meant was that they were capable and not delicate and she intended it as a compliment and it was, mostly.
The trouble with capable hands was that they were capable of earning something and not owning it.
The hands on the lease document, the ones that had signed the paper in the office in Hitchin in the spring of 1806, had belonged to Abel Dale.
Abel Dale was three years dead.
His hands were not working.
Mine were.
Mine.
I closed the ledger.
The letter was on the shelf where Jem had put it when the carrier came mid-afternoon.
I had known it was there since I passed the shelf at four o'clock and saw the seal.
I had known whose seal it was then and I knew whose seal it was now.
I crossed the kitchen.
I picked it up.
Stainforth & Croft.
Solicitors, Hitchin.
The paper was heavy — Stainforth always used heavy paper, the kind that cost more than necessary and was meant to signal that.
The handwriting on the front was his secretary's, not his own: a formal hand, addressed to the occupant of the White Hound, which was the correct legal phrasing and also, in its way, the point.
I turned it over.
His seal, in good red wax.
I held it.
I had known since the last rent quarter, when the number in the ledger had been smaller than it should have been and I had looked at it for a long time and understood what it meant.
I had known when the summer harvest failed across three counties and the ale price went up and the coaches came through hungrier and with less coin.
I had known when Stainforth's man came in September asking questions about the inn's accounts — the kind of questions that were not about the accounts.
I knew what was in this letter.
"Well," I said to the kitchen.
The kitchen had nothing to say.
I put the letter back on the shelf.
I took the candle upstairs to my rooms, the two rooms above the kitchen that made up the bulk of my life.
I sat on the edge of the bed with my boots still on for a moment and looked at the ceiling, then thought better of sitting like that, and took the boots off.
The letter could wait until morning.
I already knew what it said.
THE LAST RETREAT
Chapter 1: The White Hound
The kitchen was dark when I came down.
I had forgotten to bank the fire.
The hearth was cold and grey, which told me everything I needed to know about yesterday: too long, too much, not enough sleep.
I did not dwell on it.
I went for the kindling.
The rake first, clearing ash down to bare grate.
Then kindling in a pyramid the way my mother had shown me, the small stuff at the centre.
I knelt on the flagstone and struck the flint and watched the spark catch.
The cold was in my hands.
Late October and the frost had already got inside the window glass, a skim of ice on the inside pane that the coming fire would not touch for another quarter-hour at least.
I pressed my palm flat against the stone and then I got up and went to work.
The morning checks ran through my head while the fire caught.
Twenty letting rooms, two of them drafty enough that I kept the price low and hoped no one would ask why.
Taproom with twelve tables, four of them preferred.
Dining room that seated thirty at a pinch.
Stabling for forty horses, though we rarely ran to more than twenty since the war ended and the coaching trade had not come back to what it was before.
The White Hound's reputation was for reliability and cleanliness, not for fashion.
We fed people well.
The linen was laundered.
The horses were not mistreated.
That was the whole of the offering, and it was enough.
This inn was not grand and it had never tried to be.
My grandmother had bought it for practicality: the Great North Road ran past the front door, the well was good, the stabling yard could handle four coaches at once.
She had not cared about fashion and neither had my mother and neither did I.
Three women and eighty years of clean sheets and honest accounts, and I intended to be the last only because I intended to run it until I died.
The kitchen was the seat of all of it.
The table in the centre, scarred deal wood, big enough to seat eight.
The range along the north wall.
The door to the yard.
The window that showed me the road.
Every important conversation I had happened at this table.
Every account I kept was balanced here.
When I needed to know what to do next, I came here.
The harvest had failed and the price of bread had followed it upward and I did not need a pamphlet to tell me what that meant for an inn that fed forty people a day.
I put the kettle on and stood at the window.
The Great North Road was dark and empty in the grey pre-dawn, mud and ruts and dead growth along the verge.
Cold since June.
The wheat had come up wrong and the barley worse, and the sky had been the colour of dirty wool for four months running.
Someone in a York newspaper had written about a volcano in the Dutch East Indies, ash in the upper air, the sun filtered through something it could not get past.
I did not know if that was true.
I knew the cold was real, and I knew the wood bill was real, and I knew I had burned through half again what I had burned in October the year before.
The groove in the counter caught my thumb as I reached for the tea.
My mother's groove.
She had rested her right hand there for fourteen years, the side of her palm finding the same channel every morning.
The ledger was in her hand through 1814, a cramped and precise script.
Mine since.
The handwriting had changed; the channel had not.
She died in this room.
Two years ago last March.
I thought of it the way I thought of the cold: it was a fact of the house, and the house needed managing.
I cut away from it and went back to the accounts.
I had refused two proposals of marriage since my mother died.
I thought about them the way I thought about everything I could not afford to examine too long: briefly, in the terms that mattered.
Thomas Alcott, who ran the millinery in Stevenage, had been first.
A decent man.
What he had not understood was that everything my grandmother had built would belong to him the moment I said yes.
The inn, the lease, the income, the name above the door.
All of it transferred by law, immediate and complete, with nothing held back for the woman who had been managing it for two years without a single quarter's deficit.
I wished Thomas Alcott well.
I had declined.
The second had been less decent and the analysis shorter.
I brought my tea to the table and opened the ledger.
The morning coach was forty minutes late.
This was not unusual.
The roads between London and Edinburgh had been worsening since June, the mud deepening with every frost and every rain, and the coaches ran them on stubbornness.
I was in the yard when I heard the horn, standing in the grey grudging dawn with my coat buttoned to the throat.
Jem had already had the lead pair standing in the cold for half an hour and he had the traces in his hands before the wheels stopped.
Jem Bowker had come with the inn when I inherited it, which meant he had come from my grandmother's time and knew more about running a stable yard than anyone I had ever met.
His left sleeve was pinned at the elbow and had been since Badajoz.
He worked the yard with the focused economy of a man who had spent three years working out how to do everything one-handed, and he was better at it now than most two-armed men I had employed.
Broad, weather-beaten, with the face of someone who had decided a long time ago not to be surprised by anything.
He had the lead pair changed out before the coach door was fully open.
"Late," I said.
"Roads."
He did not look up from the traces.
The inside passengers came out stiff and cold and wanting breakfast immediately, which was fair enough.
The outside passengers came out half-frozen and furious, which was also fair enough.
One of them, a red-faced man in a coat that had been good fifteen years ago, turned to me with the gravity of a man delivering a formal verdict.
"The north road," he said, "is a disgrace."
"It is," I said.
"Breakfast is ready inside."
He looked as though he wanted to say more.
I looked as though I had already moved on, which I had, so there was no performance required.
Inside, Nan had the dining room running at full pitch.

She was quick and freckled and twenty-one years old, and she worked as hard as I did without any of the standing that should have gone with it, which was a problem I thought about more the longer she stayed.
She caught my eye across the room and tilted her head toward the outside passengers.

I nodded: she had seen the coat and read the situation and was already steering the man toward the table nearest the fire, which was the warmest table and the one I held back for guests who needed soothing.
Behind the bar she had a novel tucked flat between the port bottles.
I noticed it.
Filed it.
Moved on.
I glanced up at the window above the yard.
Bridget was at her post: the chair, the window, the view of the gate and the road beyond.
Small and white-haired and dressed in black the way she had dressed since her second husband died twelve years ago, which was how long I had known her.
She missed nothing from that window.
She had survived two husbands, five monarchs, and my mother's cooking, and she had not in all that time been surprised by anything that arrived on the Great North Road.
I raised my hand.
She nodded once, slowly, with the authority of a woman who had outlived everyone who might contradict her.
That was her morning greeting and it was sufficient.
The chandler came at half past nine.
His name was Fenn, and he had been supplying the White Hound with candles for three years.
This was the third time this year the price had gone up.
"It's the tallow," he said.
He had the expression of a man who was embarrassed about something he was going to do anyway.
"Cost of it, Miss Dale.
Can't help the market."
"The price went up in March," I said.
"And in July."
"As I say.
The market."
I knew the tallow market the way I knew the grain market and the coal market: through the invoices and the ledger and every conversation I had with every supplier who came through the yard.
The wholesale price of tallow had been difficult since the war; it had not been this difficult.
There were three chandlers in this part of the county who could supply what I needed.
Fenn was the only one who ran up the road from Hatfield on a Tuesday.
The other two were more expensive by sixpence a dozen already, and Fenn knew this.
Fenn knew this.
We both knew this.
The conversation we were having was not really about the market.
Three times this year.
I could not prove it was deliberate.
I got a partial concession, a penny in the shilling, and I took it and thanked him and let him go.
I paid from the strongbox.
I wrote the amount in the ledger.
I looked at the column of figures and thought about the winter ahead, the coal delivery that was due next month, the cost of flour, the cost of firewood.
The margins were thin.
They had been thin before and I had managed.
If nothing else went wrong.
I closed the ledger.
I went back to the taproom.

The altercation happened just after the dinner hour, when the taproom was at its worst: the coach traffic done, the local men in for their afternoon pint, and two commercial travellers who had been drinking since eleven.
I heard the chair go over from the kitchen.
I came through the door at a walk.
Not a run.
Running told a room there was something to panic about, and a room that decided to panic was harder to manage than two drunk men with a grievance.
I had learned this at nineteen, my first week managing the taproom alone, and I had not forgotten it.
Two men, both on the heavy side of middle age.
There had been a card game.
The upended chair told me how recently it had stopped.
I walked to the centre of the room and stood there.
"Sit down," I said.
"Both of you."
The louder of the two: heavyset, green coat, face red before the ale and redder after it.
He pointed across the upended chair at the other man.
"He owes me—"
"Sit down," I said again, the same pitch, the same nothing in it.
He looked at me.
I looked at him.
The room had gone quiet in the way rooms did when they were waiting to see what would happen.
He sat.
I set the chair upright.
I poured them each a half-measure of ale from the bar, placed one in front of each of them, and told them the card game was over for the day.
The man in the green coat opened his mouth.
I looked at him.
He closed it.
Nan was watching from behind the bar.
One eyebrow, just slightly raised.
I picked up the cloth and began wiping the spilled ale from the table.
My hands were occupied with the cloth and the table.
That was the thing about hands: if they were busy, they could not shake.
I worked the cloth across the wood in steady circles and when I had finished I straightened up and went back to the kitchen.
My hands had been occupied.
The soldier came to the back door at half past four, in the fading light.
Not the front.
The men who came to the front door wanted lodging and could pay for it.
The men who came to the back wanted food and could not.
I had the door open before he knocked a second time.
I looked at him the way I had learned to look at them, which was quickly and completely, reading everything the posture and the eyes gave away before he had to say a word.
Thin, recently discharged, not dangerous.
He had the empty, bewildered look of a man who had walked out of the army and into nothing and had not yet found his footing in the world that had replaced it.
Some of them were dangerous.
This one wasn't.
I held the door wider.
He sat at the kitchen table.
I put bread and broth in front of him and went back to the evening preparations.
He said almost nothing.
I did not ask questions.
The fire was well up by then and the kitchen was warm, and after a while the set of his shoulders changed.
Not much.
Just enough.
There were more of them every week.
The war was over and the men it had used up were walking home, and most of them had no home to walk to.
His boots were army-issue and nearly worn through, the soles separating from the uppers at the toes, the leather cracked grey with road mud.
I noticed boots on everyone who came in from the road.
They told me more than faces did, most of the time.
These had done a hundred miles since they were last resoled and they had perhaps twenty left in them.
He would need to sort that before the real cold came.
He ate steadily and without looking up, and when the bowl was empty he sat for a moment with his hands flat on the table.
He was looking at the door to the yard, through it, at something else entirely.
I did not interrupt him.
I had a tray of glasses to polish and I polished them.
He left at dark.
I watched him go back down the track toward the Great North Road, growing small against the grey verge, until he reached the road and turned north without looking back.
He walked like a man with a destination, even if he didn't have one.
That was the army in his feet.
It would take years to leave him, if it ever did.
I went inside and washed the bowl and the spoon and set them to dry on the rack.
I fed the men who came to the back door because hungry, desperate men near a coaching inn were a problem I would rather manage before it arrived than after.
Bread was cheaper than a broken window.
I had done the arithmetic in the first winter and I had not reconsidered it.
The house was quiet by ten.
The closing was the same route every night.
Taproom bolts, both of them, the iron cold in my hands.
Dining room shutters latched.
The yard door locked and the key on its hook above the lintel, where my grandmother had always kept it.
I carried the candle through the upper corridor, listening at the occupied rooms for the quiet of sleeping guests, checking that every window was latched against the October wind.
The inn breathed around me in the way I had come to know: the last creak of a floorboard settling upstairs, Jem coughing once in the stable, the rooks in the oak behind the yard wall.
The oak was older than the inn and the inn was older than the road, or near enough.
I counted the evening's takings.
I locked the strongbox.
I carried it to the back cupboard and set it on the shelf where my grandmother had kept it and where my mother had kept it after her.
Then I sat at the kitchen table and did the figures by the last candle.
The numbers were not good and not ruinous, which was the best I could honestly say.
My boots were pinching and I thought about it briefly — new boots, the cost, the spring — and wrote it in the margin and moved on.
The table.
One chair pulled out, the others pushed in around it.
The ledger open.
One candle burning down toward the holder.
The window showed me the road: dark and empty, the mud hardening in the frost.
My mother had done this.
She had sat at this table after the house was quiet and counted the earnings and planned tomorrow's provisions.
She had done it alone for fourteen years, from the time my grandmother died until the March that took her.
I had done it for two.
It was not the same and I did not think about why.
The draught from the back door made the candle dip.
I steadied it.
Nan appeared in the doorway.
She had been in the sitting room sorting the evening post from the last coach.
She held out a letter.
Her expression was pleasant.
Neutral.
But her hand lingered on the paper a moment before she let it go, and I had known her long enough to know the difference between a neutral expression and a managed one.
I took it.
The seal was Stainforth's.
My thumb pressed the corner of the paper too hard.
I felt the fold of the wax, the slight depth of the stamp.
I held the letter for a moment and then I set it on the table beside the ledger.
I knew what this was.
I did not need to open it tonight to know what kind of letter it was.
Stainforth wrote to discuss the terms of the lease when he meant to change them.
He was always polite about it, unfailingly and carefully polite, in the way of a man who held every advantage and saw no reason to be otherwise.
He had a solicitor in London and a land agent in Hertford and the letter would be in one of their hands before it was in mine.
I had the ledger.
I had the accounts.
I had a lease that ran to next Michaelmas.
I knew the shape of this.
Not tonight.
Not when I was this tired.
"Good night," I said to Nan.
She went.
The kitchen was cooling at the edges, the fire down to coals, the warmth pulling back to the centre of the room.
I sat at the table and looked at the letter for a moment without touching it again.
The seal was red.
The wax was good quality, which was the kind of thing I noticed about Stainforth without intending to.
I left it there.
I took the candle and went upstairs.
Behind me, in the kitchen: the table, the ledger, the letter.
Stainforth's seal in the last light.
The fire going out.
The inn held its breath.
I counted the squirrels at seven forty-two AM, same as every morning.
Six of them.
Sitting in a neat row at the tree line behind Mrs.
Torvik's converted garage, which was technically my apartment now.
The "apartment" part was generous.
It was a studio with delusions of grandeur and a toilet that ran all night.
Six squirrels.
Staring at me.
They'd been doing this for three weeks, ever since I moved to Manzanita.
Living above a failing used bookstore was exactly the kind of anonymous I needed.
What was new was the third one from the left blinking.
When it opened its eyes again, it wasn't a squirrel.
Red fur.
Narrow snout.
Amber eyes that locked on mine.
A fox.
Then it blinked again, and it was a squirrel.
Gray tail.
Black eyes.
Sitting perfectly still like the other five.
"Okay," I said out loud to my empty apartment.
"That's new."
I pressed my thumb into the wooden windowsill, hard.
Focused on the grain of the wood, the splinter I'd gotten yesterday.
Grounding.
Real.
The squirrels were still squirrels.
I counted again.
Still six.
Still staring.
I stepped back from the window.
Checked my hands.
Nails clipped too short—I'd done that yesterday and now I couldn't grip my palms the way I used to when things got weird.
Couldn't dig in and feel the sting that said yeah, you're awake, this is real.
The salt lines on my windowsills were intact.
I'd checked them last night before bed and I checked them again now.
Ran my finger along the thin white line.
Unbroken.
The water bowls by both doors were full.
Clean.
Doing whatever the hell water bowls were supposed to do when you kept salt on windowsills and told yourself it was just a habit.
My phone buzzed.
Mrs.
Halloran's daughter.
I didn't have to look at the screen.
There was only one reason Denise called at six in the morning.
I answered.
"How's the breathing?"
"Changed."
Denise's voice was tight.
She'd been preparing for this.
"Can you come?"
"Twenty minutes."
I hung up.
Grabbed my bag—the one I kept packed for when someone I'd been sitting with was finally letting go.
Walked out without finishing my coffee.
The cold tea could wait.
Mrs.
Halloran couldn't.
Mrs.
Halloran's house was four blocks from the bookshop.
Close enough to walk if the Oregon coast weather cooperated, which it never did.
I drove.
Denise met me at the door, her face doing that thing where you're trying to hold it together and failing.
"She asked for you," Denise said.
I nodded.
That's what Mrs.
Halloran and I had agreed on two months ago.
She wasn't afraid of dying, she just didn't want to do it alone.
The house smelled like lavender.
Something sharper underneath.
The particular scent of a body beginning to shut down.
Not decay.
Just the body starting to close up shop.
Mrs.
Halloran was in her bed, propped up on pillows.
Her breathing was shallow.
Uneven.
The rhythm had changed.
I'd heard it enough times to recognize the pattern.
The body deciding.
The mind letting go.
The space between breaths getting longer.
She opened her eyes when I sat down.
"Nell."
"I'm here."
"Took you long enough."
Her voice was thread-thin but the sharpness was still there.
Even dying, Rita Halloran was a pain in the ass.
"Traffic was hell," I said.
She made a sound that might have been a laugh if she'd had the breath.
I took her hand.
Cold.
Papery.
Bones too close to the surface.
She squeezed once, weak, and then her eyes drifted shut.
I sat with her.
This was the part people didn't understand about death doula work.
Most of it was just sitting.
Being present.
Not fixing, not saving.
Just witnessing.
The body did what it did at the end and you couldn't stop it.
Mrs.
Halloran's breathing slowed.
Longer gaps.
I counted without meaning to.
Twelve seconds.
Fifteen.
Twenty.
When she stopped breathing, it wasn't dramatic.
No gasping.
No struggle.
Just a final exhale that didn't have an inhale to follow it.
Gone.
I sat for another minute, holding her hand.
Then I stood and went to find Denise.
"She's gone."
Denise nodded like she'd already known.
Maybe she had.
I stayed while she called her brother, while the hospice nurse arrived.
The house filled with the usual chaos of death.
Paperwork.
Phone calls.
Who to notify.
I slipped out when no one was looking.
Gail Torvik was waiting on the steps outside the bookshop when I got back.
She'd been watching for my car.
She had a casserole dish in her hands and an expression that said she was about to mother me whether I wanted it or not.
"Heard about Rita," Gail said, standing up.
"Denise texted."
Of course she did.
Manzanita was small enough that everyone knew everyone's business.
That's why I'd chosen it.
You couldn't disappear in a city, but you could absolutely disappear in a town where people were too busy gossiping to notice the quiet woman who paid rent on time and never caused trouble.
"She went easy," I said.
"No pain at the end."
"You need to eat."
Gail thrust the casserole at me.
"Don't tell me you already ate.
I know you didn't."
She wasn't wrong.
I took the dish.
It was warm.
She'd been planning this.
She cared.
Something in my chest tightened.
"Thanks, Gail."
"You look like hell, Nell.
When's the last time you slept?"
"Last night."
"Liar."
I shrugged.
Gail studied me with that attention that came from twenty years of running a bookshop and learning to read people.
She was in her sixties, sharp as hell.
The only person in Manzanita who'd rented to me without asking questions when I'd shown up three months ago with cash and no references.
"You're not eating," she said.
"You're not sleeping.
You want to tell me what's going on?"
"Just work.
Death doula hours are weird."
"Bullshit."
But she didn't push it.
One of the reasons I liked her.
"Eat the casserole.
Get some sleep.
And for god's sake, Nell, take a day off."
"I will."
Another lie.
We both knew it.
Gail headed back into the bookshop—which was definitely failing, based on the dusty shelves and the fact that I'd seen maybe two customers in three months.
I climbed the stairs with the casserole and the bone-deep exhaustion that came from sitting with someone while they died.
I put the casserole in the fridge.
Didn't eat it.
Evening came fast.
Gray.
I avoided sleep as long as I could.
Paced the apartment.
Rechecked the salt lines.
Changed the water in the bowls even though it didn't need changing.
Sat at the window and watched the tree line.
The squirrels were gone.
I didn't want to think about the fox.
I didn't want to think about the fact that I'd seen slips like this before.
Small ones.
Easy to dismiss.
They'd been getting worse.
More frequent.
I didn't want to think about the dreams.
The ones that left me tasting salt when I woke up.
My teeth gritty like I'd been chewing sand.
Some things you didn't look at.
You just kept moving.
I lasted until midnight before my body gave up.
The dream was waiting.
Gray beach.
Overcast sky.
Kelp smell.
Cold water.
A woman walking into the ocean.
Her back to me.
Her hair the same color as mine.
Dark, with a streak of gray at the temple.
I tried to call out.
My mouth filled with sand.
The woman kept walking.
Water rose to her knees.
Her waist.
Her shoulders.
She didn't stop.
Didn't turn around.
When the water closed over her head, I woke up gasping.
Sheets tangled.
My mouth tasting like salt and grit.
I didn't think about it.
I got up.
Checked the salt lines.
Changed the water in the bowls.
Watched the tree line until the sun came up.
Six squirrels.
All of them gray.
All of them watching.
I counted them twice to be sure.
THE LAST RETREAT
Chapter One
The kitchen was dark when I came down.
I had forgotten to bank the fire again.
The hearth was cold, so I had slept past the point of managing it, and that told me everything I needed to know about yesterday.
I did not dwell on yesterday.
I raked the ash, laid the kindling, struck the flint, and by the time the first coach from London was due I had the fire going and the kettle on and the bread proving beside the range.
Late October, 1816.
The harvest had failed and the price of bread had climbed after it, and I did not need a pamphlet to tell me what that meant for an inn that fed forty people a day.
The frost on the inside of the window said it was wrong for the season.
I had grown up knowing October cold, and this was something else entirely — the summer refusing, quietly, to arrive.
It had been doing it since June.
The barley fields north of the road had gone to mud in August and not recovered.
I had raised the price of bread by a penny in September and lost three regular families from the taproom.
I had spent three days deciding, which was two and a half days more than the decision deserved.
I lit the tallow candle on the mantel and began my check.
Twenty rooms.
Six occupied last night, which was better than the week before.
Taproom: bolts drawn, chairs on the tables, the smell of old ale hanging in the cold air.
Dining room: set for breakfast, the cloth straight, Nan's work from the night before.
The strongbox in the office behind the bar: locked, as it should be.

# THE LAST RETREAT
## Chapter One: The White Hound
The grate was dead.
I rebuilt it.
Whoever had let it go out overnight had done so with such thoroughness that I suspected malice, which was uncharitable and probably accurate.
Forty years of coaching traffic had worn the flagstones uneven.
Forty years had smoked the ceiling beams to the colour of old bone.
Forty years, and the place still stood, which was more than I could say for the hinge on the cellar door.

The taproom smelled of last night's tallow and the particular sour warmth of spilled ale that had soaked into the boards so deeply that no amount of scrubbing would shift it—not that I had stopped scrubbing.

I ran my hand along it now from habit.
Still good.
The damp patch above the third window had crept another half-inch toward the beam since October.

The beam would need tarring before the hard frost came, and I had already written it in the house book, and there was no reason to think about it further except that thinking about necessary tasks that could not yet be done was something I did in the small hours when the inn was quiet and the part of my mind that managed the inn by day had nothing to occupy it and turned instead to managing everything else.
Behind the bar, on its nail, the lease.
Stainforth's name at the top in his solicitor's clean hand, and below it the terms and conditions of our occupation, and nowhere on it, in any hand, mine.

I was weighing the merits of the tarring versus the cellar hinge—which was the more pressing catastrophe—when the kitchen door opened and Nan came in already talking, her cap half-tied and one hand reaching for the apron on the peg.
"There's a gentleman been outside since before light," she said, pulling the apron over her head and not looking up from the bow she was tying, "or something like a gentleman.
Jem says he came on foot and he's got a dog."
"Which room did he take last night?"
"He didn't.
He slept in the yard, Jem thinks.
Or didn't sleep.
He was just there when Jem came out."
"Has he been to the door?"
"No."
Nan looked up then.
"That's what I thought was odd."

The morning coach was the six o'clock from London, running to York, and it came in hard and fast and loud the way the York coaches always did, the coachman working on the assumption that enthusiasm compensated for chronically bad timekeeping.

Jem was already in the yard when I came out, the lead pair standing ready and the gate open and the yard swept, and the water bucket at the trough, and the ostler's boy stationed at the far gate, and the luggage rack cleared of the night's accumulation of boxes and forgotten parcels, which was everything that needed doing, done.
I counted passengers as they descended.
Seven, plus a woman with a child who had been riding inside and emerged blinking and pale in the thin October light.
I marked it in the book.
Seven, one infant, southbound luggage forwarded to the Red Lion at Welwyn, northbound bag for collection at the desk.

The coachman dropped from the box still complaining—the roads past Potters Bar, the wheel that wanted attention, the passenger in the third seat who had been sick twice—and I let him finish before I handed him the ostler's receipt and said: "You can speak to Mr.
Hadley at the Hatfield office.
Tuesdays and Thursdays, nine until noon.
He handles the road complaints for this section."
He looked at me.
"I can write it down if you prefer," I said.
He picked up the trunk.
The woman with the child wanted a private room for an hour.

She said this in a way that suggested she was braced for argument, so when I simply showed her to the back parlour and told Nan to bring hot water and a clean cloth, she stood in the doorway for a moment as though she had prepared a speech and I had taken away the occasion for it.

She gathered herself—there was really no other way to describe it, as though composure were a physical thing she had misplaced and needed to locate under the furniture before she could proceed—and went inside.
Nan shot me a look as she passed with the water.
I let it go.
The chandler arrived at half past eight.

He was a man named Collinson from Welwyn, who had been supplying the inn's candles for eleven years and who had, in that time, twice attempted to raise his prices to levels I would not accept and twice retreated when I opened the house ledger and named his margin.
He set his sample box on the bar with the deliberate care of a man who is trying not to show that his hands are uncertain.
He looked at the samples.
He looked at a point somewhere past my left ear.
He placed one hand on the counter, then moved it to his lapel.
"Mrs.
Dale," he said, though I was Miss Dale and he knew it—the Mrs.
was a courtesy he extended as a form of apology for whatever came next.
"I'm afraid I find myself in a difficult position."
"How much?"
He told me.
It was sixpence above the winter rate I had paid for the last three years.
"The tallow cost has risen.
It's not only your account—all my customers are seeing the same—"
I opened the ledger.

I turned it to face him and set my finger on the column that showed his November delivery to the Woolpack in Baldock, which was a larger inn than mine and a less loyal customer and which paid, as I had established through the simple method of asking the Woolpack's housekeeper over a glass of cider at the autumn fair, four shillings per gross less than I did.
"The Woolpack," I said.
He looked at the column.
He looked at me.
"I understand costs have risen," I said.
"I'll meet you at last winter's rate plus two shillings per gross."
"Miss Dale, Mr.
Stainforth has—"
"Two shillings, Mr.
Collinson."
He said nothing for a moment.

He was a decent enough man in most respects and the Stainforth business clearly caused him some genuine discomfort—I could see it in the set of his shoulders and the way his hand had gone back to the sample box as though the wax might offer him support.
I waited.
I had learned, over years of negotiation, that the silence after a fair offer was the other person's problem, not mine.
"Two shillings," he said finally.
"Good."
I closed the ledger.
"Delivery as usual.
I'll have the cellar cleared by Friday."
He left.
The ledger went back on the shelf.

I was angry—a clean, impersonal anger, the kind that didn't cloud the thinking, because anger at a system was useless unless you used it—and then I was already checking the bar stock for the afternoon, which was the next thing, and that was how it went.
That was how it always went.

The trouble in the taproom started just after noon, when two men who had been drinking since the first coach came in decided to conduct their disagreement about who had precedence at the trough—a matter that had apparently been festering since Baldock—in the middle of my taproom floor, using their voices and then, briefly, their bodies.
I let it go one exchange.
Two men working themselves up to something that might or might not become worth stopping was a judgement call, and a premature intervention created more resentment than a late one.
The second exchange settled it.
"Enough," I said.
Jem was at the edge of the room.
He hadn't moved.
He didn't need to move.

He was positioned, which was different, and both men clocked it at the same moment they clocked me, and one of them sat down and the other, after a pause of the kind designed to suggest that sitting was his own idea, sat down too.
One of them muttered something.
I chose not to hear it.
The table by the window needed clearing, and I took the glasses, and by the time I had set them on the bar neither man was looking at me anymore.
I glanced across at Jem.
He looked back at me.

Seven years, and we had an entire language for this—the frequency of it, the specific exhaustion of it, the particular quality of men who had walked to France and back and then walked through my door and found, to nobody's surprise, that whatever they'd left behind to fight was still here, waiting.
He was at the kitchen door just before three, when the afternoon coaches had settled and the yard had gone quiet.
I had seen him from the window: the man Nan had mentioned.
He stood in the doorway—not leaning, standing—with his weight distributed evenly and his hands at his sides in a way that told me what he was before I could have said why I knew it.
His coat was a soldier's coat, the cut of it several years old, the wool still sound but the colour gone to a brown-grey that had nothing to do with the dye.
His boots had been repaired, carefully, with different leather at the toe.
His posture was the posture of a man who had stood very still in worse places than this and was not frightened of standing still.
He did not ask for charity.
He asked if there was work.
"Stabling," I said.
"The afternoon horses need brushing out and Jem's got the colic case to manage.
Two hours, maybe three.
I pay in supper and a bed."
He nodded once and went to find Jem, and the dog—a long grey thing with the look of permanent mild worry—followed at his heel.
I put the broth on.
I had already put the broth on, but I checked it, and I cut more bread than the evening would require, and I didn't think about why.
He came in at five, after the last of the afternoon horses were done.
I was at the range.

He sat at the kitchen table without being asked—not with presumption, but with the ease of a man who understood that the kitchen table was where the working people sat—and I set the bowl in front of him and went back to the stockpot.
After a while, he said, "Road was frozen past Stevenage."
"It'll be worse by the week's end," I said.
He ate.
I turned the stockpot.
The fire had settled to a good even heat and the kitchen smelled of broth and woodsmoke and the bread that was cooling on the rack, and neither of us said anything else.
It was not uncomfortable silence.
It was the silence of people who are doing what needs to be done and do not require commentary on the doing of it.
He finished the bread and thanked me and went.
I watched his boots cross the yard through the window—the repaired toes, the careful heel, the even deliberate pace of a man going somewhere with no destination—until the dark took him.
I went back to work.
By nine the taproom was cleared, the fire banked, the last guest accounted for.

I locked up in the order I always locked up: the yard gate first, then the stable door, then the back passage bolt—which stuck unless you lifted the door on its frame, a trick that required a specific combination of pressure and angle that I had learned from my mother and that I had never written down and that only I and Nan knew—then the taproom shutters, their iron latches cold now, the left one always stiffer than the right.
The strongbox clicked shut under the bar.

The kitchen window latch had a gap where the wood had warped, and I wedged it with the same folded piece of card I had been wedging it with since July, which was not a solution, and I made the note in the house book, again, and it would be addressed when I had the carpentry money, which I would have in the spring if Collinson held his price and the February coaches ran to schedule.
I wiped down the bar.

It was already clean—Nan had done it before she went up—but I wiped it again, the way I always did at the end of the night, the cloth going in slow circles from the near end to the far, following a path I had followed so many times that my arm knew it without instruction.
There was a gouge in the wood near the centre, old and darkened, that had always been there.
I ran my thumb across it.
A keg, I thought.
Or a chair leg—no.
A keg.
Thursday's delivery, the big ones that Jem could only just manage now.
I'd have to get the boy to help, next week, if Jem's shoulder was no better.
The hook was one my mother put in.
It was iron, set into the beam above the hearth, driven there in—I did not know exactly.
Before I was born.

My mother had hung her good apron on it at the end of each night, the same motion, the cloth catching the firelight as it settled, her hands moving to the bow at her back and then up and then the apron was on the hook and the night was done.
I had stood in this kitchen and watched her do it ten thousand times.

The last time I saw her do it was the night before she died, though of course I didn't know it was the last time, which was the way of such things—they only became the last time afterward, when you were no longer in a position to have paid proper attention.
I wrung out the cloth now.
Hung it on the hook.
Felt nothing, which was not the same as there being nothing to feel.
The letter was on the shelf beside the ledger, where I had put it that afternoon when it came.
Stainforth's seal.

I had known what it was when I saw the seal and I had put it on the shelf and I had gone back to the afternoon's work, and I had known all evening, the way you know a thing that is waiting for you at the edge of the firelight.
I had let it wait.
I was letting it wait now.
I set the candle on the bar and looked at the letter and the ledger side by side, the seal and the columns, Stainforth's name and my figures, and I thought: not tonight.

Not because I was afraid of what it said—I knew what it said; I had known for six weeks what it said—but because I was tired, and because the fire was going down, and because there was nothing I could do about it before morning.
I took the candle and went to bed.
The grate was dead.
I rebuilt it.
Whoever had drawn the early watch — Piers, it would have been Piers, who had not yet learned that a banked fire needed tending at three in the morning and not only at bedtime — would hear about it.
Not today.
I had too much else to do today.
Forty years of coaching traffic had worn the flagstones uneven.
Forty years had smoked the ceiling beams to the colour of old bone.
Forty years, and the place still stood, which was more than I could say for the hinge on the cellar door.
I had mended that hinge twice.
I would mend it again.

I knew every crack in the bar top, knew which window stuck in the rain and which stuck in the dry, knew that the third step on the back stair would report any weight above eight stone and so I had learned to step to the left of it, which preserved the sleep of guests who deserved their sleep and prevented the departure of guests who did not.
The damp patch above the third window had spread since August, which meant the lead flashing above it was failing, which meant money I did not have.
The bar top I had sanded myself in June, which is not a pleasant undertaking in June, and the grain had come up well.
I was proud of it.

The lease was on its nail behind the bar, Stainforth's name at the top, a king sitting on a throne he had done nothing to deserve, and the irritation of that sight was old and familiar enough to be almost companionable.
Almost.
Nan came in knotting her cap with both hands and said, before she had cleared the doorway, "The Baldock coach sent word — they're running twenty minutes late and Mr.
Hollis wants his boots at the door by six not seven, he said seven yesterday but now it's six."
"Hollis said seven.
I heard him."
"He says six now."
Nan reached past me for her apron, already moving.
"And the grey cob's gone lame, Jem thinks it's the left fore."
"How lame?"
"Lame enough he said so."
She tied the apron strings with a sharp tug.
"Which means the Alderton party hasn't got a third horse for their hire."
That was the morning, then.
I filled the kettle and set it on the newly rebuilt fire and went to find Jem.

He was already in the yard when I came out, the lead pair standing ready and the gate open and the yard swept and the water trough full and the lanterns lit, which was everything that needed doing, done.

The Baldock coach rolled in at a quarter past the hour, horses blowing steam into the October dark, the coachman's voice preceding him by thirty yards, three passengers descending before the steps were properly down, Nan appearing from the side door with the speed and accuracy of a woman who has been counting coach arrivals for seven years and knows exactly how long she has before the third passenger asks for hot water.
I counted five passengers.
I had been told four.
Jem appeared at my shoulder.
"The grey won't do more than a walk."
"I know."
"Thought you'd want to hear it from me."
"I did."

The fifth passenger was a woman of about sixty with a bandbox under each arm and the expression of someone who has been on a public coach for longer than she had expected and intends everyone around her to be aware of it.
"Is Wheeler's cob still sound?"
"Was last Tuesday."
We went about our business.
The coachman found me at the luggage boot while I was directing the unloading of a trunk that was considerably heavier than the passenger had declared.
"Three shillings above the agreed rate," he announced, in the tone of a man who had been rehearsing this.
"On account of the road conditions north of Hatfield, which have materially—"
"You'll want to speak to Mr.
Granger about that.
He's the posting agent.
He's at the Falcon in Hatfield every Tuesday and Thursday between nine and noon."
I looked at him.
"Today is Thursday."
He opened his mouth.
"The trunk," I said.
He picked up the trunk.
The woman with the bandboxes had, in the meantime, established that the inn's upstairs rooms lacked a southern aspect and that this constituted a species of fraud.

I reported her complaint to no one, because there was no one to report it to, and noted that she would require approximately three hours before she forgave the building for its orientation and began to enjoy her breakfast.
I have found that almost everyone does.
Griggs the chandler arrived at half past eight with his sample box and his new prices, both of which I had been expecting since September.
He set the box on the bar top with the deliberate motion of a man who wishes to appear casual and is not.
He looked at the window.
He put his hands in his coat pockets and took them out again.
"Mrs.
Griggs well?"
I asked.
"Very well, thank you, Miss Dale."
"Good."
I opened the ledger.
"Your tallow has gone up four shillings the gross since June."
"Costs have risen across the—"
"Your margin on that order in June was eleven percent."
I turned the ledger to face him and put my finger on the column.
"The chandler in Baldock is presently quoting me nine and six the gross for the equivalent weight.
I've been patient with you through summer because the road to Baldock is inconvenient and your delivery is reliable."
I waited.
"I'd like it to remain convenient not to go to Baldock."
He looked at the ledger.
He was, I noted, calculating.
"Eight and nine," he said, finally.
"Eight and six."
"Eight and eight."
"Eight and six and you keep the quarterly account, which the Baldock man won't extend me because he doesn't know me yet and I don't know him."
I let that sit.
"His loss.
Possibly yours."
Griggs looked at the ledger for another moment.
