He had the expression of a man arriving at a conclusion he had known he would reach from the moment he walked in.
"Eight and six," he said.
The ledger went back on the shelf.

The anger at what the increase had been — what it had already cost me through the summer months, quietly, while I waited, while I paid it — I named once, to myself, and then I was already pulling on my coat because the Alderton party needed to be told about the grey cob and that conversation would require my full attention.
By two o'clock the taproom had the particular quality of midafternoon — a lull, not a peace, the difference being that peace is something you can trust.
I was clearing glasses when it started.
Two men at the far table, neither of them drunk enough to be unreasonable and both of them drunk enough to try.
It was about a seat.
It is always about something equally small.
"Enough," I said.
The standing man sat down.
The other one looked at his hands.
Jem caught my eye from the doorway.
There was nothing in the look that needed saying and we did not say it.
He came to the kitchen door at half past four, when the light was nearly gone.
His coat was an army coat worn to a colour that had once been red, with new stitching at the left cuff and boots that someone had resoled not long ago with leather that didn't quite match the uppers.
He stood in the doorway with his shoulders square, the way men stand when they are trying not to look as though they need anything.
He did not ask for charity.
He asked if there was work.
I gave him the chicken coop to latch, which wanted latching and which Piers had not yet got to.
When he came back I had broth on the table and bread beside it.
He sat.
He ate.
I was covering the bread for the morning when he said, after a while, "Road was frozen past Stevenage."
"It freezes early up there," I said.
He was quiet again.
I moved the stockpot to the cooler end of the range.
He finished the bread and thanked me and went.
I watched his boots cross the yard, the mismatched soles, until the gate blocked the view.
I went back to work.
By ten o'clock the inn had emptied down to its bones.
I drew the bolt on the main door, the iron stiff with the cold.
I pulled the front shutters and latched them, the wood's edge sharp against my palm.
I did the side passage door, which requires lifting the handle as you pull or it will drag, a fact I have known for fifteen years and still have to remember.

I locked the strongbox — the click of it familiar and solid — and checked the taproom fire, and snuffed the wall sconces, and did the cellar door, whose hinge I wedged with the folded cloth I keep there for the purpose, and which I will replace when I have time and money enough in the same month.
I wiped down the bar though it was already clean from the last hour's end-of-service.
There was a gouge near the middle I'd never satisfactorily accounted for — too narrow for a keg, too short for a chair leg.
Boot heel, possibly.
Thursday last, when the Alderton party's manservant had been rather more forceful with the luggage than was warranted.
I made a note to mention it, though I would not, because there was no point.
The wood would carry the mark now.

The bar would carry it the way it carried the ink stain at the north end from 1809, and the ring from a glass that must have sat there for the length of a very long conversation sometime before my mother's time, worn into the grain like a permanent record of a meeting I would never know about.
The hook was one my mother put in.

The letter was on the shelf next to the ledger, where I had set it when it arrived at three and where it had waited with the patience particular to things that are not required to do anything but be opened.
Stainforth's seal.
I had known what it was when Nan brought it in, and I had set it down and attended to four other things before I allowed myself to come back to it.
I knew what it said without reading it.
I had been knowing since afternoon.
I set it on the shelf next to the ledger, where the two of them could keep each other company.
In the morning there would be a fire to rebuild and a grey cob to rest and a lame horse's hire to apologise for and the bread already covered and waiting.
I took the candle and went to bed.`;
THE LAST RETREAT
Chapter One: The White Hound
The grate was cold.
I knelt and rebuilt it—ash out, kindling laid, the tinder caught on the second strike—and I had one thought about whoever had let it go out, and the thought was not generous.
The inn was the inn.
Twenty rooms, a taproom, a dining room, stabling for forty horses, and a reputation I had inherited and not once let slip.

What needed fixing that morning: the shutter on the second-floor east room, which had come off its upper hinge and would not last another storm; the pump in the yard, which had been stiff for a week and which I had told Jem about and which had not yet been attended to; and the smell of damp in the linen store, which was the smell of money slowly leaving.
What I was proud of: the floors, scrubbed and even; the larder, which was full; the accounts, which balanced.

The lease on the inn was held in my name, Dinah Dale, which was also my mother's name in the records and my grandmother's before that, and which would cease to be my name the moment I signed a marriage register, at which point it would become a man's name, and the inn along with it.

I had seen this fact written in the lease itself, in the cold language of the law—in the event of the lessee's marriage, all interests in the property shall vest in the lessee's husband—and it had not surprised me.
It had clarified things considerably.
Nan came in through the kitchen door with her cap already tied and her face already decided about something.
"Coach is late," she said.
"Axle trouble outside Hatfield, they're saying.
Hour behind at least."
I filled the kettle.
"They're saying, or you know?"
Nan tied her apron.
"I know.
Bill Pryce came through on horseback half an hour ago.
Said the lead horse lost a shoe outside Hatfield and they've had to wait for the farrier from the village, only the farrier from the village has gone to his sister's wedding in St Albans."
She set the cups on the table.
"The farrier's sister's wedding is today."
"So it's not an axle."
"It is not an axle," Nan said.
"It's a wedding."

When the coach finally came in at half past ten it came in at speed, the horses blowing and the coachman leaning forward as though the delay were a debt he was settling against the road, the wheels throwing mud up over the step, the passengers already pushing at the door before the yard boys had the block down.

I counted them as they descended: a clergyman with a hat box, two ladies who appeared to be related and equally displeased about it, a young man in a coat too thin for the weather, a merchant of some kind with a trunk that required three separate declarations about its contents, and one more behind him—a woman with a child on her hip who had not been on the booking.
Seven, where the manifest said six.
One more than expected.
Jem had the yard already set: fresh water in the troughs, three horses brought out from their stalls and the next four ready, hay down and the block positioned.
This was what I saw when I came out: everything in its place, nothing waiting on a direction.
Jem at the head of the lead horse, talking to it in the low, particular way he talked to horses, which I had never heard him use with people.
The coachman climbed down last.
He had the bearing of a man who had been composing remarks for the last hour.
"Miss Dale."
He pulled off his hat and put it back on again.

"I'll tell you plainly, the road between here and Hatfield is in a condition that no reasonable person would call fit for traffic, and I have three passengers in that coach who've told me they intend to write to the posting agent, and I can't say I'll dissuade them."
"The posting agent," I said, "is Mr.
Hartley, and he's at the Crown in Stevenage on Tuesdays.
He keeps office between ten and noon."
He opened his mouth.
"It is Tuesday," I said.
"He's there now."
He looked at me.
He looked at the yard.
He put his hat back on his head with a firmness that had no further application.
"The trunk," I said.
The one belonging to the merchant, which was still in the boot.
He went to it.

The woman with the extra child had established, by the time I reached her, that she had been sold passage on a coach that had advertised itself as a comfortable conveyance and that this representation was fraudulent and she intended to say so.
Her child was asleep on her shoulder.
I told her the room rate and showed her the stairs.
She went up them without saying anything else, which was the correct response.
The chandler arrived at eleven.
He set his sample box on the bar with the particular deliberateness of a man who has been considering the placement for some time.
He looked at the window.
He put his hands in his pockets.
He took them out and put one on the box.
"Miss Dale."
He opened the box.
"I'm afraid I've some unwelcome news about the autumn pricing.
Tallow's up across the board—Suffolk, Essex, everywhere—and I can't in good conscience offer you last summer's rate."
I put the ledger on the bar.
"Last summer's rate was twelve shillings the gross.
I have it here in June and again in August."
I turned the ledger so he could read it.
"I also have the rate from Aldrich in Baldock, who wrote to me in September and whose figure was eleven and six."
He looked at the ledger.
"Aldrich is a smaller operation."
"He has access to the same Suffolk market you do."
He calculated.
"I could manage twelve and three."
"Twelve and one," I said, "and I stay with you through spring."
He was quiet for a moment.
"Twelve and one," he said.
"Through spring."
The ledger went back on the shelf.
I pulled on my coat.
Outside, the yard wanted attending.
The trouble in the taproom started at four o'clock and was about a threepence, which is what taproom trouble is always about.
Two men, not drunk enough to be unreasonable, drunk enough to try.
I came through the door and said, "Enough."
The standing man sat.
The other one looked at his hands.
Jem was in the doorway, and we looked at each other, and then I went back to the kitchen.
He was at the kitchen door at half past five.

His coat was the colour of a road that had been rained on for six months—a brown that had once been something else—and the cut of it was military, the collar and the set of the shoulders, though whatever regiment had issued it was long since past recovering from the dye.
His boots were down at the heel, the left one split along the welt.
He stood in the doorway with his shoulders square.
"Any work going?"
he said.
"The wood wants splitting.
Round the back.
There's a cord's worth that hasn't been touched."
He went.
He came back when it was done and the light was going.
I put broth on the table and bread beside it.
He sat down.
He ate.
After a while he said the road from Hertford had been bad since the rains—two washouts between the milestone and the bridge—and I said I'd heard the same.
The kitchen was warm.
The fire had come up properly by then.
He broke the bread in half and ate the second piece more slowly.
Neither of us said anything else.
I watched from the kitchen window when he went.
His boots crossed the yard in the particular flat-heeled way of a man who has walked a long way on bad roads and has more of it ahead of him.
The gate swung shut.
I went back to work.
I locked up in the order I always locked up: the taproom bolt, the kitchen shutters, the strongbox in the back office.
I wiped the bar though it was already clean.
There was a gouge in the wood near the pump end—old, dark at the edges—that had been there since before I could remember it not being there.
On the wall beside the back shelf was the hook my mother put in, iron, bent slightly to the left.
She had put it in herself with a hammer and a nail punch and had hit her thumb twice.
I had been six years old and watching from the stool by the door.
I remembered the thumb but not the words she said about it, which was a pity, because they had been considerable.
The letter was on the shelf above the bar where I had put it when it arrived that morning.
Stainforth's seal in red wax, the S clear enough.
I had known what it was when I saw it.
I had not opened it.
I took the candle and went to bed.
The grate was cold.
I rebuilt it.
Whoever had banked it the night before had done it badly, and the coals had died to ash while I slept.
The inn stretched around me in the grey light before dawn.
The kitchen smelled of yesterday's bread and the soot that never quite cleared from the chimney.
I walked through the taproom, checking the tables for damage from the night's custom.
One chair had a loose leg that would need mending.
The front windows showed clean, though the left pane had a crack running from corner to corner that I'd been meaning to fix for a month.
Upstairs, the floorboards creaked under my feet as I checked the rooms.
Three were let, two empty, one with a broken latch that stuck when you tried to open it from the inside.
The beds were made, the washbasins clean, the chamber pots emptied and scoured.
The lease was on its nail behind the bar.
My name was on it, which was also my mother's name, which was also my grandmother's.
If I married, it would belong to my husband by law.
The kitchen door opened and Nan came in, tying her apron as she walked.
"Coach is late," she said, not looking at me.
I filled the kettle and set it on the hob.
"How late?"
"Hour, maybe two."
"They're saying, or you know?"
Nan stopped tying and looked at me properly.
"Coachman's wife sent word.
Axle snapped outside Hitchin, and they're waiting on a wheelwright who's drunk and won't sober up till noon."

The coach came in at half past eight instead of seven, the horses lathered and the passengers sour-faced from the delay, and when I counted heads as they climbed down, there were six instead of the four the manifest promised.
Jem had the yard set.
He'd moved the water troughs, laid fresh straw, and cleared the traces from yesterday's coaches before I'd finished dressing.
The coachman climbed down last.
"Need a word about the manifest," I said.
He pulled off his hat and wiped his forehead.
"Posting agent changed the route.
Nothing I could do about it."
"The posting agent is Mr.
Hartley, and he's at the Crown in Stevenage on Tuesdays.
He keeps office between ten and noon."
He opened his mouth to speak.
"It is Tuesday," I said.
"He's there now."
He looked at me.
He looked at the yard.
He said nothing.
"The trunk," I said.
One of the extra passengers wanted breakfast in her room because her child was fretful from the journey.
I carried the tray upstairs, listening to her complaints about the roads, the other passengers, and the quality of the inn's butter.
The chandler arrived at eleven.
He put his sample box on the bar.
He kept his hands in his pockets, looked out the window, then opened the box with the careful movements of a man checking his wares.
"Prices have gone up," he said, not meeting my eyes.
"Everywhere, I'm afraid.
Can't be helped."
I put the ledger on the bar.
"Last summer you charged fourpence per pound for tallow.
This says sixpence."
"Costs are up across the trade.
Everyone's paying more."
I turned the page and found the entry I wanted.
"Mr.
Whitmore in Baldock charges fourpence halfpenny."
He looked at the ledger.
I waited.
"I could do fivepence," he said.
"But I'd need payment on delivery, not monthly terms."
"Fourpence threefarthings.
Monthly terms as before."
"Fourpence threefarthings," he said.
"Monthly it is."
The ledger went back on the shelf.
I pulled on my coat.
The trouble in the taproom started at four and was about a threepence.
Two men, not drunk enough to be unreasonable, drunk enough to try.
One stood up, knocked his chair back, and reached for the other man's collar.
"Enough," I said.
The standing man sat.
The other looked at his hands.
Jem was in the doorway, his good hand resting on the frame.
I nodded to him and went back to the kitchen.
He was at the kitchen door at half past five.
His coat was army issue, old, the colour gone.
His boots were down at the heel, the left one split along the welt.
He stood in the doorway with his shoulders square.
"Any work going?"
he said.
"Stalls want mucking.
I'll give you supper and a bed in the stable loft."
He sat down.
He ate.
I ladled broth from the pot and cut bread thick enough to fill a grown man's stomach.
The kitchen was warm from the fire, and he didn't speak until the bowl was empty.
"Long road from London," he said.
"Longer still ahead."
"Aye."
I watched from the kitchen window when he went.
His boots crossed the yard, the broken sole flapping against the cobbles.
The gate swung shut.
I went back to work.
I drew the bolt on the front door, latched the shutters, locked the strongbox.
I wiped the bar.
There was a gouge in the wood near the corner where someone had carved initials ten years ago and I'd sanded them out badly.
The hook was my mother's.
She'd put it in herself with a hammer and hit her thumb twice.
The nail had gone black and she'd cursed in ways that would have shocked the vicar.
The letter was on the shelf where I'd put it that morning.
Stainforth's seal.
I had not opened it.
I took the candle and went to bed.
Chapter 1: The White Hound
The grate was cold that morning.
I rebuilt it while the kitchen smelled of yesterday’s grease and tallow smoke.
Nan had let it go out again, and I made a note to speak with her about banking the coals properly before she went to bed.
The taproom needed sweeping.
Crumbs scattered the floor where yesterday’s passengers had eaten their bread and cheese.

I walked through to the dining room where six chairs remained pushed back from the table where the Leeds coach passengers had taken their dinner, the cloth stained with gravy and a wine ring no one had wiped.
The stairs wanted mopping where someone had tracked mud up to the first landing.
My room above held the accounts ledger and the strongbox with yesterday’s takings.
The guest rooms on the second floor were empty, still warm from bodies, their doors standing open to air.
The lease was on its nail behind the bar.
My name was on it, which was also my mother’s name, which was also my grandmother’s.
Under the law of coverture, if I married, it would belong to my husband.
Nan pushed through the kitchen door, tying her apron strings behind her waist.
“Coach is late,” she said.
“How late?”
I filled the kettle from the pitcher and set it on the hob.
“They’re saying, or you know?”
I dried my hands on my apron.
“I know.
Driver’s got the ague and they’re running a replacement who doesn’t know the road.
He’s taken the wrong turn at Stevenage and gone toward Hitchin instead.”

The coach came in at nine instead of seven, passengers spilling out in a tangle of complaints and confusion, boxes tumbling from the roof as the guard threw them down, horses stamping and blowing in their traces, and two more people than the manifest had promised.
Jem had the yard set.
He’d moved the water troughs, checked the harness hooks, and laid fresh straw in the boxes for the change of horses.
The coachman climbed down last.
“Where’s your posting master?”
he said.
“I’ll have words with him about the state of this road.
Ruts deep enough to snap an axle, and that’s if the highwaymen don’t get you first.”
“The posting agent is Mr.
Hartley, and he’s at the Crown in Stevenage on Tuesdays.
He keeps office between ten and noon.”
He opened his mouth.
“It is Tuesday,” I said.
“He’s there now.”
He looked at me.
He looked at the yard.
“The trunk,” I said.
A woman in a green pelisse complained that her seat had been given to someone else’s child.
The child in question was sick on the stairs.
I carried the child up to the water closet myself and cleaned the mess with a rag that had seen worse.
The chandler arrived at eleven.
He put his sample box on the bar.
He smelled of tallow and the road.
His hands went to his pockets, then to the window, then back to the box.
“I’m afraid there’s been an increase,” he said, sounding genuinely sorry about it.
“Costs are up everywhere, Miss Dale.
The war, you understand.”
I put the ledger on the bar.
“Last summer you charged me two shillings threepence for a dozen tallow dips.”
“The chandler in Baldock charges two and eight,” I said, and waited.
“Well, perhaps we could manage three shillings even,” he said.
“Two and sixpence,” I said.
“And you’ll throw in the rushes.”
“Two and sixpence it is.
And the rushes.”
He looked at the ledger.
I waited.
The ledger went back on the shelf.
I pulled on my coat.
The trouble in the taproom started at four and was about a threepence.
Two men, not drunk enough to be unreasonable, drunk enough to try.
“Enough,” I said.
The standing man sat.
The other looked at his hands.
Jem was in the doorway.
I went back to the kitchen.
The light was going when he came to the kitchen door at half past five.
His coat was army issue, old, the colour gone to something between grey and nothing.
His boots were down at the heel, the left one split along the welt where the stitching had given way.
He stood in the doorway with his shoulders square.
“Any work going?”
he said.
“Stable wants mucking out,” I said.
He sat down.
He ate.
He didn’t talk while he ate, which I noticed.
I gave him broth and bread, the heel from yesterday’s loaf softened in the pot liquor.
He told me he’d walked from London.
The kitchen was warm.
I watched from the kitchen window when he went.
His boots crossed the yard.
The gate swung shut.
I went back to work.
The taproom was still.
I drew the bolt on the front door, latched the shutters, locked the strongbox.
I wiped the bar.
There was a gouge in the wood where someone had dragged a pewter mug too hard across the surface.
The hook was my mother’s.
She’d put it in herself with a hammer and hit her thumb twice.
The nail had gone black and she’d cursed in a way that would have scandalized the vicar.
The letter was on the shelf where I’d put it that morning.
Stainforth’s seal.
I had not opened it.
I took the candle and went to bed.
THE LAST RETREAT
Chapter One: The White Hound
The grate had not been raked properly since I did it myself three days ago.
The ash lay packed against the bars like mortar, and the kindling would fight it, and everything in this kitchen fought me if I gave it half a day’s neglect.
I had given it three.
I knelt on the flagstones and scraped the bars clean with my fingernails because the rake had gone missing again—probably to the stable yard, where tools went to be borrowed and never confessed to.
The cold bit through to the knuckle.
The first flame caught, held, and I fed it a twist of straw until the heat pressed back against my palms.
It would do.
Not well.
But it would do.
The White Hound had twenty rooms, a taproom, a dining room, and stabling for forty horses.
It was not grand.
It was not fashionable.
It was mine in every way that mattered and in none of the ways that counted at law.
I checked the hinge on the cellar door.
Jem had oiled it without being asked, which saved me the asking and him the pretence that he had not noticed it squealing for a fortnight.
The bolt was smooth and the hinges silent, and I ran my thumb across the join the way my mother used to, testing whether the metal sat flush.
It did.
The dining-room shutter I’d been meaning to rehang since August still hung crooked, catching the frame when the wind came from the north.
I added it to the list.
The list did not get shorter.
It grew in the night like something with roots.
The fourth stair creaked as I passed it.
That creak was a dependable thing; it told me when someone was coming down for breakfast before they had finished deciding they were hungry.
I let my hand trail the banister and felt where the wood had gone smooth from a century of palms.
In the taproom the chairs were still up on the tables from last night’s sweeping.
The fire was dead.
The smell of old ale and wet wool hung in the air like a guest who had overstayed.
I pushed the windows open and let the October cold cut through it.
Downstairs, the ledger lay open on the kitchen table where I had left it last night.
The numbers said what they always said.
Six weeks before the quarter’s rent became a problem I could not solve by moving faster.
I turned the page.
The name on the lease was my mother’s.
The name on the lease was always a woman’s in this family, and the law had always hated that, and the law was patient.
I closed the ledger.
The leather cover was cracked at the spine from my mother’s hand and her mother’s before that.
We wore everything in this place down to the bone and kept using it.
Nan came through the kitchen door with her cap already escaping her hair and her apron tied before she’d cleared the threshold.
She was working before I could assign her anything—wiping the flour from the table edge, setting the kettle back over the flame, checking the bread in the crock with two fingers pressed to the crust.
I noticed this the way I noticed the hinge and the shutter: with a satisfaction I did not name.
“The man in number seven left before dawn,” Nan said.
“Without settling.”
“How much did he owe?”
“Four shillings and the candle he took from the sconce.”

I could have asked which candle, because I knew the sconces, all forty-six of them, and I would have known from the sconce which room he’d passed through and whether he’d helped himself to anything else on his way out.
But Nan’s face already held the rest of the answer.
“Just the candle,” she said.
“I checked.”
That was Nan.
She checked because she knew I would, and she would rather have the answer ready than watch me go looking for it.
Seven years she had been doing this.
Seven years of answers ready before I had finished forming the question.
The morning coach from London came in at half ten with two passengers short-tempered from the road and one trunk split clean at the hinge.
I heard the wheels before I saw them—the particular grind of an overloaded axle, the coachman’s shout that meant he was behind time and wanted everyone to know it was not his fault.
My hands were already on the bar towel and my feet were already moving toward the yard before I had finished hearing the complaint.
The woman with the trunk wanted someone to blame.

She had the voice for it—pitched to carry, trembling with a fury that was mostly about the road and the weather and the hours she had spent with her knees pressed against a stranger’s valise, and the trunk was simply the nearest injustice to hand.
I had seen a thousand split trunks.
The leather was always cheaper than the owner pretended, and the hinge was always the first thing to go.
I told her we had twine and a quiet corner where she could sit while it was mended, and I said this in the voice that did not invite further discussion.
She discussed it further.
I nodded at the parts that needed nodding at and mended the trunk.

Around me, the yard was its own species of chaos: horses being unhitched and led steaming to the trough, luggage hauled down from the rack, a hatbox rolling under the dray and a child I did not recognise chasing it on hands and knees.
The ostler’s boy ran a bucket and managed to splash the coachman’s boot on the return trip.
The coachman said something about the boy’s parentage that I chose not to hear.
The second passenger wanted to know if the beef was good.
The beef was always good.
I did not say this.
I said the beef was fresh this morning, which was a different kind of answer and a more useful one, and I said it while steering the child out from under the dray with my knee.
Jem had the yard straight before I’d finished with the trunk.
He worked with the pitchfork braced against his right side, the hook on his left arm holding the stable door while his hand did the rest.
He did not look as though he were managing.
He looked as though this was how pitchforks were meant to be used, and the rest of us had been doing it wrong with our unnecessary second arms.
“Dray wheel’s cracked,” he said as I passed.
“Need it by Thursday.”
I nodded.
Thursday was the Baldock delivery.
We both knew this and neither of us needed to say it.
The coachman found me in the taproom.
He wanted compensation for the delay.
He said the word delay as though I had personally manufactured it, and he dropped the name of the coaching agent in London the way a man drops a card he thinks will win the hand.
“Mr Harding, is it?”
I said.
“Mr Harding of the Highflyer Company, whose schedule gives you forty minutes at this stop and whose contract gives you no right to compensation for delays caused by passenger luggage.
If you’d like to take it up with Mr Harding, I can give you his direction.
I can also tell you that there is no other inn with stabling for forty between here and Baldock, so I expect we’ll be seeing each other again on Thursday.”
He said he’d take it up with Mr Harding.
He said this at a lower volume than he had used for anything else, and he took his ale with him when he went.
Above the yard, the curtain in the first-floor window moved and then was still.
I did not look up.
I knew who watched from there the way I knew the fourth stair creaked.
The chandler came after midday with his cart and his prices and the expression of a man who has rehearsed his argument on the road and is half in love with his own reasoning.
I had been expecting him since September.
I knew his margin better than he knew it himself, because I had been tracking tallow prices in the London papers that the coaches left behind, and he had not thought to wonder whether I would.
I put down the cloth I was holding.
I did not hurry.
The refusal to hurry was the first move.
“The price has gone up,” he said.
He put his hands on the counter as though the counter were the last word.
“Tallow’s risen everywhere between here and London.
You can check with any chandler on this road.”
I opened the ledger.
I turned it so he could see the column of figures, though I was not certain he could read them as quickly as I could.
“Tallow has risen threepence the hundredweight since Midsummer,” I said.
“Your candles have risen sixpence the dozen.
That’s not tallow, Mr Parrish.
That’s margin.”
He shifted his weight.
His hand came off the counter.
“Costs have gone up everywhere,” he said again, because repetition is what men do when they have run out of evidence.
“The haulage alone—”
“You buy your tallow from Jessop in Ware,” I said.
My finger was on the column now.
“At ninepence the hundredweight less than what you’ve written on this invoice.
I know this because your cousin George sells the same tallow to the Lamb in Welwyn at the price you used to charge me, and George will deliver to the Great North Road for a penny a mile.
I wrote to him last week.”
He looked at the ledger.
He looked at me.
I could name every sconce in this building—all forty-six—and the hours each candle burned, and the rate at which the tallow sweated in a warm room versus a cold one.
I had done the arithmetic.
The arithmetic was my weapon, and he was looking at it now.
“Last quarter’s price,” he said.
Not a question.
He said it the way a man sets down a heavy thing he is tired of carrying.
“Fourpence ha’penny the dozen,” I said.
“Same as August.”
He wrote the figure on the invoice.
He did not look at me while he wrote it, and I did not watch him write it, and neither of us said anything further because the conversation was over and we both knew it.
He went.
I closed the ledger.
There was a cut on my index finger from the invoice edge that I had not felt until now, a thin bright line like a whisper from the paper.

The trouble in the taproom started the way it always started: two men, enough drink to make them stupid, and a disagreement about something that did not matter—a bet, a horse, a woman who was not present and would not have thanked either of them for the attention.
The larger of the two had his fist on the table and his voice pitched to fill the room.
The smaller one was standing, which was worse, because standing meant he had decided to do something with his hands.

The room had gone quiet in the way rooms go quiet when men are about to do damage—the conversations thinning, the heads turning, the particular quality of silence that is not peace but the held breath before the breaking.
I walked between them.
I did not hurry and I did not raise my voice, because hurrying and volume were concessions to the idea that they were in charge of what happened next, and they were not.
I was.
“You can settle this outside,” I said, “or you can settle your tab and leave.
But you will not break my furniture, and you will not raise your hand under my roof.
Choose now.”
The larger man looked at me.
He looked at the smaller man.
He looked at Nan, who was behind the bar with one hand on the tap and the other resting on the stoneware bottle she kept beneath the counter for exactly this purpose.
She did not look alarmed.
She looked like a woman standing behind a bar on a Tuesday afternoon, which is what she was, and the fact that she was also ready to swing a bottle at his head was simply part of the same Tuesday.
He sat down.
The smaller man sat down after him, which was the right order and told me everything I needed to know about which of them had started it.
The room went back to its murmuring.
The fire cracked.
Someone asked for another pint.
Tuesday.
“One of these days,” Nan said from behind the bar, “they’ll notice you’re half their size and then you’ll actually have to hit someone.”
I did not smile.
Nan saw me not smiling and looked satisfied.
He came to the kitchen door, not the front.
Young—twenty, perhaps, or a hard twenty-five that had worn him past his years.
Thin in the way that meant weeks, not constitution.

His boots were coming apart at the welt, the sole peeling back from the upper where the stitching had rotted, and he stood the way soldiers stand when they are trying not to look like they are begging: straight-backed, eyes level, hands at his sides, as though they were still on parade and someone might inspect them.
I knew what he was inside thirty seconds.
Decent.
Hungry.
Not dangerous.
I could tell the difference the way I could tell a cracked beam from a sound one—by looking, and by knowing what to look for.
His hands were empty and open.
His eyes moved once across the kitchen and settled on the pot over the fire with a steadiness that was not greed but recognition.
I fed him in the kitchen, not the taproom, because paying guests who see vagrants fed for free become guests who question their bill.
This was not sentiment.
This was the arithmetic of keeping the doors open, and I did not apologise for it, not to him and not to myself.
“When did you eat last?”
I asked.
“Day before yesterday, ma’am.
A woman in Hatfield gave me bread.”
“There’s broth on the range and bread in the crock,” I said.
“Sit by the fire until you’re warm.”
He sat.
He ate the way hungry men eat—steadily, without haste, as though hurrying would remind his body how long it had been and the knowing might undo him.
I did not sit with him.
I did not watch him eat.

I was at the table behind him, working through the bread order for tomorrow, close enough that the warmth of the kitchen held us both but far enough that he was not a project or a cause or any of the other things that let a person feel virtuous about feeding a hungry man.
He was a man having a meal.
The fire ticked.
His boots steamed where he had set them near the grate, and the leather was so thin I could see the shape of the nails through the sole.
The laces were knotted where they had broken and been retied, twice on the left and once on the right.

The broth was the same broth I made every day—bone stock and whatever root vegetables the garden had offered up that week, an onion, two parsnips, the end of the carrots—nothing particular, nothing anyone would remark on.
But he held the bowl in both hands and drank it as though it were the most serious thing he had done in weeks, and the kitchen was quiet around him, and I let it be quiet.
The bread he tore carefully, not crumbling, the way a man eats who knows the value of what he is holding.
“Thank you, ma’am,” he said when the bowl was empty.
He said it the way he had stood at the door: straight, level, without performance.
I nodded.
There was nothing else needed between us.
He left by the kitchen door.
I said something about the road north being better than the road east at this time of year, which was true and also the kind of thing you say instead of the thing you mean.
He thanked me again.
He did not linger and I did not ask him to.

I watched his boots on the path until they reached the road, and then I watched the road until I could not tell his shape from the hedgerow and the grey October light had swallowed the distance between us.
Then I went back inside and wiped the table where he had sat, and the cloth came away warm.

The day ended the way days end at an inn: slowly, then all at once, then in the silence that follows when the last voice has gone and the building settles back into its beams and remembers it is only wood and stone.
I checked the doors—front, side, kitchen, cellar.
I banked the fire and watched the coals settle into their orange geometry.

I swept the taproom floor, working the broom into the corners where the sawdust caught, and counted the candles—the new candles, the chandler’s candles, fourpence ha’penny the dozen—and stacked the mugs and wiped the bar until the wood showed its grain in the last of the firelight.
The room smelled of ash and tallow and the ghost of the evening’s ale.
The bolt on the front door was new.

Jem had replaced it in September, which meant the old one had lasted eleven years, which meant my mother had put it on, standing where I stood now, with her hand on this same frame, in the year the inn’s roof needed repointing and the hay harvest failed and she managed both without raising her voice or asking for help from anyone who was not already helping.
She had a talent for that—for making people want to help without being asked.
She had another talent, too, which was dying without warning on a Tuesday evening in the middle of the dinner service.
Apoplexy, the surgeon said.
I finished serving dinner.

I cleared the plates and closed the kitchen and sent Nan home and then I sat on the floor beside my mother’s body and allowed myself the luxury of falling apart, which I did quietly, because the guests were sleeping upstairs and it would not do to wake them.
I had inherited the stubbornness.
Whether I had inherited the rest was a question I did not let myself finish.
The ledger was still open on the kitchen table.
Six weeks.
The number had not changed since this morning, but it felt different at night.
Everything felt different at night, when there was no task left to stand between me and the looking.
I closed the ledger.
The work never left.
That was the thing about the work.

My hands were reddened from the cold water and the scrubbing, and the skin across the knuckles had cracked the way it always cracked in October when the weather turned and I had not yet remembered to use the tallow salve.
The cut on my index finger from the chandler’s invoice was still there, a thin bright line across the pad.
I noticed it the way you notice a thing only when you stop moving.
It did not hurt yet, but it would.
The paper had been sharp, that was all.
I had used my hands all day and the paper had been sharp.
From the kitchen I could see the window above the yard.
The light in Bridget’s room went dark.
The inn was quiet.
The inn was mine, for now.
The letter was where I had left it that morning, on the shelf by the kitchen door where I set things I intend to deal with and then walk past all day.
Stainforth’s seal, pressed deep into the red wax.
Stainforth’s handwriting on the direction—that careful, clerk-taught script that always looked as though it had been written by a man who believed neatness was a form of authority.

I had known the letter was coming since the last rent quarter, the way you know a storm is coming from the weight of the air, and I had been moving faster ever since, as though speed could outpace what was in the envelope.
The seal was unbroken.

I had not opened it this morning, and I had not opened it at midday when I passed it on my way to the chandler, and I had not opened it this evening when I came back from the taproom with the sound of the altercation still ringing in my hands.
I had been choosing, all day, not to open it, and now the inn was quiet and there was no task left to stand behind.
I broke the seal.
The paper was good—heavier than a bill, lighter than a summons, exactly the weight of a man who wishes to discuss terms.
His words were polite.
They were civil.
They were the worst kind of threat, because they did not sound like a threat.
They sounded like a reasonable man making a reasonable enquiry, and that was how Stainforth always sounded, and it was the thing about him that frightened me most.
He wished to discuss the terms of my lease.
He hoped I would find it convenient to call upon him at my earliest opportunity.
He remained, as ever, my obedient servant.
He had signed his name in a hand that gave nothing away.
I set the letter down on the kitchen table.
The wood was still warm from the soldier’s meal.
He had sat here an hour ago, perhaps two, and the fire had been close, and the oak held heat the way oak does—slowly, grudgingly, giving it back only when everything else had gone cold.
I had fed a hungry man at this table today.
Stainforth wanted to take the table.
I folded the letter.
I did not put it away.

I set it on the ledger, where the numbers were, because that was where it belonged—with the arithmetic, with the evidence, with the weeks that were not six any longer but five, perhaps four and a half, because a day had passed and the number only ever moved in one direction.
“Right,” I said to the empty kitchen.
“Right, then.”
The candle on the table guttered in a draught I could not find the source of.
The letter sat on the ledger.
My hands were in my lap, and they were very still, and the cut on my finger had begun to sting.
# Chapter 1: The White Hound
The grate held yesterday's ash like a grudge.
Someone had banked the fire without clearing the spent coal first.
Nan, most likely.
The tinder would catch slow and the morning would start cold.

I crouched before the hearth, my knuckles already stiff from the October air that crept through every crack in the White Hound's bones, and began the daily argument with flame and fuel that kept the inn breathing.
The kindling was damp.
Everything in England had been damp since June, when the rains came and refused to leave.
I struck the flint twice before the spark caught, three times before the flame held long enough to matter.
The fire would sulk for another quarter hour before it gave proper heat, but it would give heat eventually.
Like everything else in this place, it only needed the right sort of stubborn coaxing.
I stood, brushing ash from my hands, and surveyed my kingdom of cracked plaster and questionable joints.
The White Hound had been standing on this stretch of the Great North Road for sixty years, and every one of those years showed in its bones.
The taproom floor held a loose board that caught every second heel.
I'd asked Jem to plane it three times, and three times he'd found more pressing work with the horses.
The dining room still carried yesterday's tallow smoke, thick and greasy in the corners where the draught didn't reach.

The window at the stair landing let in a finger of cold air that I'd stuffed with rags since September, because proper glazing cost more than the quarterly rent and Stainforth's name was already on enough of my business.
The lease document lived in the kitchen drawer, beneath the good napkins Mother had saved for occasions that never came.
Stainforth's signature sprawled across the bottom in the kind of hand that expected to be obeyed, while my name appeared nowhere at all.
Not Miss D.
Dale, leaseholder.
Not even Miss D.
Dale, occupant.
Just Stainforth, landlord.
The ink itself declared ownership of every board and stone.
I knew exactly where that document waited, the same way I knew where every loose hinge and cracked pane lived in this building.
It was part of the inventory of things that needed fixing and probably never would be.
"Brewer's cart was late again."
Nan's voice arrived before she did, cutting through the kitchen's morning quiet as she pushed through the back door with her apron already half-tied.
A hairpin caught between her teeth, her cap askew from hurrying, she delivered the morning's first crisis without preamble.
"Half-and-half will run short by evening if we pour the usual measure."
I turned from the stuttering fire.
"How short?"
"Short enough to matter."
She pulled the hairpin from her mouth and stabbed it into the unruly curl that had already escaped her cap.
"Unless you want to water it down and pretend we didn't."
"Have you counted the casks yourself, or are you taking Jem's word?"
Nan's hands stilled on her apron strings.
She'd known me long enough to recognize the question beneath the question.
"I counted.
Two and a half barrels left from last week's delivery, and the usual trade means we'll pour through one and three-quarters by closing time.
That leaves us three-quarters of a barrel for tomorrow, assuming the brewer's boy remembers where we are."
I nodded.
Stretch what we had, or send someone to Stevenage for emergency supplies that would cost twice the usual rate.
"We'll pour light until midday, then normal measure for the evening trade.
If anyone complains about weak ale before noon, send them to me."
"Right."
Nan tied the final knot in her apron and moved toward the taproom, already cataloguing the morning's work in the efficient way of women who had learned to count hours like coin.
"I'll set the tables and check the stock behind the bar.
Fire's drawing better today.
Might actually see some proper warmth before Christmas."
The rumble of wheels on packed earth announced the London coach before I saw it, but the sound carried the wrong rhythm.
Too fast, too urgent, the kind of pace that meant trouble for someone.
I was in the yard before the four-horse team came properly to a stop, reading the situation from the coachman's face and the sharp voices spilling from the passenger box.

Two passengers today: a merchant's wife whose traveling trunk had split at the hinge, spilling silk stockings and complaints across the coach's interior, and a clergyman who'd missed his breakfast in London and seemed determined to blame everyone between here and Scotland for the oversight.
Hartwell ran this route three times weekly and usually kept his temper better than his passengers.
He swung down from the box and looked like he'd been managing unreasonable demands since Hatfield.
"Road's clear to Baldock," he said without preamble, "but there's talk of a washout past the village.
Nothing I can confirm, but thought you'd want to know."
The merchant's wife emerged from the coach clutching her damaged trunk like evidence of personal persecution.
"This is intolerable," she announced to the yard at large.
"Simply intolerable.
I cannot arrive at my sister's wedding with my belongings scattered like...
like refuse."
I approached the trunk, which had indeed split along its brass-bound edge but remained fundamentally intact.
"Jem can tie it with rope," I told her.
"It'll hold for the rest of your journey, and your sister's probably too distracted by wedding preparations to notice a bit of wear on your luggage."
"Rope?"
She said the word like I'd suggested binding it with pig's entrails.
Behind her, the clergyman cleared his throat with the particular irritation of men accustomed to being the center of attention.
I glanced at him.
His mouth was a thin line and he checked his pocket watch.
One passenger whose problem had a solution, one passenger whose problem was his own character.
"Rope it is," I said to the trunk woman, then turned to Hartwell.
"Twenty minutes to change the team.
Ale if you want it."
He nodded, already reaching for the tankard I hadn't yet fetched but would.
We'd danced this particular negotiation enough times that the steps had worn smooth.
Jem was at the fresh team before I'd finished with the passengers.
He unhitched the blown horses and had been managing four-legged complaints longer than I'd been breathing.
The pinned sleeve of his left arm caught briefly on a harness buckle, but he worked it free without breaking stride or acknowledging the delay.
He never acknowledged delays.
He never acknowledged the dozen ways he managed horse and tack and heavy lifting with one arm.
The arrangement was the most natural thing in the world.
He'd been Mother's man before he was mine, hired the spring after Waterloo when the roads filled with discharged soldiers and most of them wanted something other than honest work.
Jem had wanted work, and Mother had given it to him, and he'd been straightening what didn't need straightening ever since.
Today he had the fresh team watered and harnessed before the clergyman finished complaining about the temperature of his coffee.
"Road trouble?"
Jem asked as he led the blown horses toward the stable.
"Nothing confirmed.
Washout past Baldock, possibly."
I handed Hartwell his tankard.
"You'll hear about it before I will if there's anything to it."
Hartwell drank, wiped his mouth with the back of his hand, and glanced toward the merchant's wife.
She was directing Jem's rope-work and getting it wrong.
"Compensation for the delay," he said.
"Trunk business put us behind schedule."
I'd heard this particular song before, usually from coachmen who'd discovered that blaming passengers was easier than explaining poor time management to their employers.
"Mr.
Farris will be at the Hatfield office Thursday," I said mildly.
"He'll want to hear about any irregularities in the schedule.
I'm sure you'll give him a complete account."
Hartwell's expression shifted.
He knew Farris, and he knew I knew him, and he knew that my version of today's events would carry more weight than his if it came to a dispute.
He finished his ale without mentioning compensation again.
The trunk woman departed in a cloud of indignation and rope-bound luggage.
Jem loaded it onto the coach without comment, received no thanks for his trouble, and returned to the stable.
Difficult passengers were weather.
Unpleasant, unavoidable, and best endured without complaint.
Mr.
Pennick arrived with his cart and his prices just as the London coach disappeared around the bend toward Baldock.
I saw him from the kitchen window, adjusting his hat and checking his coat buttons in the particular way of men working up courage for unpleasant business.
His cart's left wheel squeaked with each revolution.
He'd been promising to grease the axle for three months and never seemed to find time for it.
He approached the kitchen door with the shuffling gait of the reluctantly dutiful.
Pennick wasn't a bad man, merely a man caught between his supplier's demands and his customers' coin, and I was the customer who paid attention to arithmetic.
"Miss Dale."
He touched his hat brim.
"Fine morning."
"Is it?"
I glanced at the grey sky, heavy with the promise of more rain.
"What's your price for tallow candles this quarter, Mr.
Pennick?"
His face colored slightly.
"Well, now, there's been some...
adjustments to the wholesale rates.
War's ended, but costs haven't settled the way we'd hoped.
My supplier's raised his prices across the board, and I'm afraid I'll need to pass along a bit of that increase.
Tuppence more per dozen, I'm sorry to say."
I went to the kitchen dresser and removed the ledger from its drawer.
The binding was worn smooth from handling, but the columns inside remained admirably clear.
I opened it on the table between us and turned to the current quarter's accounts.
"Tuppence," I said.
"That would put your candles at..."
I ran my finger down the column.
"Seven shillings per dozen.
Which is curious, because Barrett in Stevenage is charging the posting house at five and six for the same quality tallow, and the ordinary at Welwyn pays five and eight."
I looked up from the ledger.
"Your supplier must have raised prices quite significantly to justify such an increase."
Pennick's eyes flickered to the open ledger, then to my face, then back to the ledger.
His hat turned slowly in his hands.
well, that is...
circumstances vary from shop to shop, Miss Dale.
Quality, quantity, terms of payment..."
"Quality."
I turned back a page.
"Last quarter you delivered forty-three dozen candles.
I tested the burn time on six of them.
Roughly four hours each, which matches your usual standard.
Shall I assume this quarter's batch burns longer?
Or perhaps brighter?"
"No, miss.
Same quality as always."
"Then we come to quantity and terms."
I closed the ledger with a soft thump.
"I pay on delivery, in full, no credit required.
Barrett's rate for my usual order would be six pounds, four shillings.
Your new rate would be eight pounds, fourteen shillings.
That's a difference of two pounds, ten shillings.
Enough to buy half a barrel of ale or a week's worth of bread for the kitchen."
Pennick's knuckles whitened where he gripped his hat.
"Miss Dale, I've known your mother, known this inn, always dealt fair and square..."
I let the words hang in the air between us.
Outside, Jem's hammer rang against the anvil where he was straightening a bent horseshoe, each blow steady and purposeful.
The kitchen fire crackled behind me, finally drawing properly now that it had finished sulking.
"Six shillings per dozen," I said at last.
"Same as last quarter, plus a halfpenny for good faith.
Barrett can have my custom if that doesn't suit your margins."
Pennick stood silent for a long moment, turning his hat in slow circles.
His cart's squeaking wheel had gone quiet.
The horse stood patient in the traces, probably hoping its master would finish his business and return to the familiar rhythm of roads and deliveries.
"Six and a half per dozen," he said finally.
"I can manage six and a half."
"Good."
I opened the ledger again and wrote the price beside his name.
"Forty dozen this quarter, same as usual.
I'll take delivery Friday morning if that suits your schedule."
He nodded, settled his hat back on his head, and departed looking like a man who'd have to explain the shortfall to someone else.
I watched from the doorway as he loaded his cart and guided the patient horse back toward the main road.
By Christmas, he'd try to raise the price again, and next time he might not fold so easily.
But Christmas was eight weeks away, and today's candles were ordered at a price that wouldn't break the household budget.

The taproom filled with the midday trade: coach passengers taking their dinner, local farmers escaping wives who'd found morning work for idle hands, and a handful of men with familiar faces but no names I could place.
The room held that particular energy of people who'd come together by accident but settled into temporary community over ale and conversation.
Near the fire, tension simmered between two men.
Hadley, whose farm lay three miles south, and a younger fellow whose coat marked him as a former soldier looking for work.
Their voices hadn't risen yet, but their shoulders had set in the familiar pattern of men preparing to make their points more forcefully.
I crossed the room without hurrying, stopping at the table nearest the potential combatants to collect empty plates and wipe down surfaces that didn't strictly require attention.
"Mr.
Hadley," I said as I worked, "how's your wife's cough?
Last time you were here, she was having trouble with the night air."
Hadley's attention shifted from the younger man to me.
"Better, thank you for asking.
Dried coltsfoot helped settle it, just like you suggested."
"Glad to hear it.
Nothing worse than a cough that won't clear."
I continued wiping the table, moving closer to where the ex-soldier sat nursing a half-empty tankard.
"You look like a man who's walked some distance today.
Road from London treating you well?"
The younger man's shoulders dropped a fraction.
"Well enough, miss.
Thank you."
The moment balanced, then shifted.

Whatever disagreement had been building dissolved into the broader conversation of the room, defused by the simple reminder that this was a place where people knew each other's names and asked after each other's troubles.
I poured fresh ale without being asked, distributed it to both men, and returned to the bar where Nan was polishing glasses with mechanical precision.
From the window above, light shifted behind glass.
A shadow moved across the frame, then stillness.
Someone watching the yard, the room, the careful choreography of an inn at midday.
The light held steady for a moment, then moved away, leaving only the reflection of grey sky against the pane.
The afternoon had nearly spent itself when the young man appeared at the kitchen door.
He knew which entrance to use.
That told me something about how many inns he'd tried and how many times he'd been turned away from the public rooms.
He stood straight despite the exhaustion that lined his face, and his eyes met mine directly when I looked up from the stockpot I was tending.
His coat was army surplus, too large across the shoulders.
It had belonged to a bigger man and would outlast its current owner by years.
His boots were coming apart at the left welt, the sole flapping with each step like a mouth trying to form words it couldn't quite manage.
Young, perhaps twenty, with the particular thinness that came from irregular meals rather than natural build.
"Begging your pardon, miss," he said.
"Wondering if there might be work.
Nothing permanent required.
Just enough for a meal and a place to sleep rough."
His hands weren't steady, but his voice was.
He wasn't performing need; he simply carried it, the way other men carried pocket watches or walking sticks.
"When did you last eat?"
"Yesterday."
He paused, reconsidered.
"Day before, if I'm honest about it."
I ladled broth from the stockpot into a wooden bowl and set it on the kitchen table beside a heel of bread and a wedge of cheese that had been destined for tomorrow's scraps.
We were already standing at the kitchen door.
No need to parade him through the public rooms where paying guests might take exception to vagrant soldiers sharing their air.
"Sit," I said, and returned to stirring the pot.
He ate without comment, efficiently but not desperately.
He'd learned to manage hunger with patience and careful attention to what was actually available.
I continued working, chopping carrots for tomorrow's stew, checking the bread rising under damp cloth near the fire, letting the silence settle between us like a familiar thing.
When he finished, he set the bowl down carefully and looked up.
"Thank you."
I nodded.
He stood, straightened his too-large coat, and walked back toward the road without lingering or looking back.
I watched from the doorway until the bend hid him from sight.
His left boot flapped with each step.
He kept his shoulders straight and walked with the steady pace of someone who'd covered a lot of ground without knowing where the road would end.
The stockpot bubbled softly behind me.
Tomorrow there would be another pot, another ladle of broth for whoever needed it, another young man or old woman or child whose need was simpler than the world's willingness to meet it.
Tonight there was only the pot, and the slowly fading sound of footsteps on packed earth.
The evening guests departed by degrees.
Coach passengers continuing north, local men returning to wives and suppers and the comfortable complaints of home.
Nan finished wiping down the bar, counted the day's receipts, and disappeared into the October dusk with a tired wave and the promise to return early tomorrow for the London coach.
I moved through the building alone, following the nightly ritual that had shaped my evenings since Mother died.
Bank the taproom fire to coals that would hold warmth until morning.
Check the front door's bolt and the window latches, test the lock on the strongbox where the day's takings waited to join the rest of the quarter's slim accumulation.
Wipe the bar one final time, not because it needed wiping but because the motion was part of the rhythm that carried me from day's work to night's rest.
The building settled around me, creaking and sighing in the familiar language of old wood and older stone.
Every sound belonged—the soft thud of a settling beam, the whisper of wind through the chimney, the distant stamp of a horse shifting in its stall.
I knew the inn's nighttime voice as well as I knew my own heartbeat.
I paused at the bar, running my fingers along its surface to check for problems the day might have left behind.
A new gouge marred the wood near the tap, deeper than I'd noticed before—probably from the keg Jem had dropped last Thursday when the rope slipped.
The rope wanted replacing; I should have ordered new line along with the candles.
The ledger waited on the kitchen table, open to this week's accounts.
Numbers that had seemed manageable in the morning's bustle now stared back with uncomfortable clarity.
Six weeks, perhaps seven, before the next quarter's rent became a crisis rather than a concern.
The arithmetic was relentless as winter: expenses that wouldn't bend, income that couldn't stretch, and Stainforth's name signed to every legal document that mattered.
I closed the ledger without adding anything up again.
The numbers wouldn't change for being studied.
At the kitchen basin, I washed the day's grime from my hands with water that bit cold against my skin.
My fingers were reddened, roughened, marked with the small cuts and burns that came from a life spent managing fires and knives and the thousand sharp edges of keeping house on a commercial scale.
A paper cut from Pennick's invoice decorated my index finger—I hadn't noticed it until now, but the chandler's bill had drawn blood along its edge.
My mother had hands like these.
The thought arrived without invitation, and I put it aside without examination.
Some comparisons led nowhere useful.
I found the letter under the front door—slipped through the gap while I'd been banking the fires and checking the locks.
Stainforth's seal, red wax pressed with the family crest I'd seen on a dozen documents over the years.
His handwriting addressed the direction: Miss Dale, the White Hound.
Not Mrs.
Never Mrs., no matter how many years I ran the place or how many quarterly rents I paid on time.
The paper was heavy, expensive, folded once and sealed with the precision of a man who expected his correspondence to be treated as important.
I didn't open it.
I knew what it said—not the exact words, but the meaning underneath.
He wished to discuss the terms of my lease.
Terms that had been perfectly acceptable when Mother was alive but had somehow become negotiable since her death.
Mother had received a letter like this once, from Stainforth's father, back when I was still young enough to believe that owning a business meant it belonged to you.
Patience had laughed and said that man couldn't pour his own wine without a servant to hold the glass.
I didn't laugh.
The current Stainforth poured his own wine just fine—he simply preferred to have other people's hands do the work while his signature claimed the credit.
I stood in the hallway with the letter in my hands and the inn dark around me, feeling the weight of good paper and bad news.
"Well," I said to the empty air, "at least he has decent handwriting."

Then I walked to the kitchen and placed the letter on the table beside the ledger, because that was where it belonged—next to the numbers that would determine whether Stainforth's discussion would be a conversation or a decree.
# Chapter 1: The White Hound
The fire had not been banked properly.
I could tell from the colour of the ash—grey where it should have been white, cold where it should have held heat until morning.
Nan, most likely, or one of the travelling men who'd lingered too late in the taproom and thought himself helpful.
I crouched before the grate and built it back the way it should have been done the first time, muttering words my mother would have boxed my ears for using in the presence of decent coal.
The White Hound complained at me through every timber and stone as I moved through the morning.

The hinge on the cellar door had worked loose again—I'd told Jem about it twice, and twice he'd nodded and done nothing, which meant I'd be crawling under there myself with a screwdriver before the week was out.
The damp patch above the third window had reappeared right on schedule, October faithful as sunrise, spreading across the plaster like a bruise I couldn't heal.
I'd had that wall resealed after the spring floods, paid good money for it, and still the rain found its way in.
The bar top bore the scars of twenty years' hard use, rings from ale mugs and scratches from coins, but I'd sanded and sealed every inch of it myself after Mother died.
It gleamed now in the weak morning light, better than it had any right to look.
Behind it hung the lease, rolled tight and tied with Stainforth's ribbon, his name at the top in the solicitor's careful script.
Not mine.
Never mine.
Three generations of Dale women keeping this place standing, and still we held it on a man's sufferance.
The thought sat in my chest like week-old bread, heavy and sour.
"Morning, Dinah."
Nan appeared in the doorway with her arms full of clean linens and her cap already askew.
"Chandler's coming up the lane.
Looks like he's brought samples."
I looked up from polishing a glass that was already clean.
"What's he brought samples for?
We settled on tallow candles for the quarter not three weeks past."
"Perhaps he's got better ones to offer."
But Nan's voice carried the particular doubt of a woman who'd lived through too many price increases to believe in unexpected improvements.
"Perhaps he's got reasons to think we'll pay more for the same ones."
I set the glass down harder than necessary.
"What else?"
Nan shifted the linens to one arm and shrugged.
"Mrs Hartwell in room seven says the washstand's loose.
Wobbles when she pours water in the basin."
"And?"
"And nothing else worth mentioning."
The admission came with the resigned sigh of someone caught holding back the worst news for last.
"Except the coachman from yesterday's asking after compensation for the delay.
Says his passengers complained to the company about arriving late to Baldock."
I closed my eyes briefly.

The delay had been caused by a horse throwing a shoe two miles south of Stevenage, which was neither my fault nor my concern, but coachmen had a way of making their problems everyone else's responsibility.
"I'll deal with him when he comes round for the return journey.
Get those linens upstairs before the morning coach arrives."
The sound of the horn reached us first—two long blasts that meant the Baldock coach, right on time despite yesterday's dramatics.
I counted passengers by habit as they descended: four inside, two on top, all looking rumpled and eager for breakfast.

The yard came alive with the precision of a military exercise: Jem appearing from the stables to take the horses, Nan threading between the passengers to collect their requirements, myself managing the luggage and the coachman's complaints and the delicate arithmetic of getting everyone fed and watered and back on the road within the appointed hour.
"Neat bit of work with that near-side leader," I told Jem as he led the horses toward the water trough.
The animal had been favouring its left front foot since pulling into the yard.
"Stone bruise," Jem said.
"Day or two of rest and he'll be sound."
"Will they rest him, or will they run him lame?"
Jem's single shoulder lifted in the barest suggestion of a shrug.
"Not our horses."
He was right, of course.
The coaching company's animals were the coaching company's concern.
But I'd seen too many good horses destroyed by owners who valued schedule over soundness, and it never sat well with me.
Jem managed the yard with the efficiency of a man who'd made his peace with having one arm and no patience for anyone who felt sorry for him about it.
I assigned him tasks according to what I knew he could do, and he did them without comment or complaint.
It was an arrangement that worked.
The coachman approached with the swagger of a man preparing to win an argument.
"Miss Dale, about yesterday's delay—"
"Take it up with Hewitt at the Swan in Baldock," I said, naming the coaching agent and the day he'd be making his rounds.
"He's there every second Tuesday.
I'll write you a note explaining the circumstances if you'd like."
The coachman's bluster deflated visibly as he realized I knew the system better than he did.
"Well.
I suppose.
If you think he'll listen."
"He'll listen."
I watched him pick up the trunk he'd set down in preparation for his demands.
"Hewitt's got sense, which is why they put him in charge of the route."
The woman who owned the trunk made some remark about the inconvenience of delays and the impossibility of maintaining a schedule when every small problem brought the entire enterprise to a halt.

I nodded and made appropriate sounds of sympathy while thinking that if she'd ever tried to run anything more complicated than a drawing room, she might have more appreciation for the difficulties involved.
The chandler set his sample box down on the bar with the particular care of a man who knew he was about to ask for something he wasn't entirely entitled to.
I recognised the signs—the way he avoided meeting my eyes directly, the unnecessary attention he paid to arranging his wares just so.
William Marsh had been selling me candles for three years.
I knew his manner when he was confident in his prices, and this wasn't it.
"Miss Dale."
He opened the box with a flourish that didn't quite mask his nervousness.
"I've brought the finest tallow we've seen this season.
Clean-burning, long-lasting, perfect for an establishment of your calibre."
I opened the ledger and turned it toward him.
"Three weeks ago you sold me a quarter's worth of tallow candles at fourpence the dozen.
Same quality, same supplier, same season."
I ran my finger down the column of figures.
"What's changed?"
"Costs have risen, I'm afraid.
Nothing I can do about it—the tallow merchants are asking more, and I can't absorb the difference indefinitely."
"Tallow's selling for the same price it was in August.
I checked at Baldock market not five days past."
I named the price per pound and watched his face.
"What you're adding is margin, not cost."
He shifted uncomfortably.
"There are other expenses to consider.
Transport, storage, the risks of dealing with smaller establishments—"
"Smaller establishments?"
I closed the ledger with a snap.
"Harwick in Baldock sells the same candles at threepence ha'penny the dozen.
Shall I send him my custom instead?"
The negotiation continued for another few minutes, but I could see in his face that he knew I had him trapped between his greed and my arithmetic.
We settled on fourpence ha'penny—higher than I wanted to pay, but lower than he'd hoped to charge.
His agreement came with the faint whiff of apology that told me the price increase hadn't been his idea.
After he left, I closed the ledger and allowed myself one moment of pure irritation.
The squeeze was tightening, and I could feel it in every transaction, every supplier who suddenly found reasons to charge more for goods that had cost the same for months.
Someone was making it worth their while to press me, and I had a fair idea who.
The altercation in the taproom started, as these things usually did, with something perfectly ridiculous.
Two men, neither of them sober enough to be drinking at midday, had taken exception to each other's opinions about the relative merits of their respective horses.
The argument escalated from disagreement to insult to the suggestion that one man's mare wouldn't be fit to pull a rag-and-bone cart.
"Gentlemen."
I stepped between them before either could stand up properly.
"You're welcome to settle your differences outside, or you're welcome to finish your ale in silence.
Choose now."
The larger of the two men looked ready to argue with me as well, but something in Jem's posture at the far end of the room suggested that would be an error in judgment.
Both men subsided into muttered complaints about the other's character and ancestry, but they stayed in their seats and kept their hands on their mugs instead of each other's throats.
Jem and I exchanged a look across the room.
Neither of us spoke, but the message was clear enough: this was happening more often, and we both knew why.
Near evening, a man appeared at the kitchen door.
He wore a coat that had been military issue before someone removed the buttons and insignia, and boots held together with leather strips and optimism.
He didn't ask for charity.
He asked if there was work.
There wasn't, but I gave him bread and broth anyway, and set him to stacking wood while he ate.
He did the work with the careful attention of a man who understood the value of earning what he received, even if the task was worth considerably less than the meal.
"Good broth," he said, scraping the bowl clean.
Not about the war, not about his circumstances, nothing that required me to feel sorry for him.
Just an ordinary observation about ordinary food.
"My mother's recipe."
I watched him finish the last of the bread.
"Road's dry as far as Baldock, if you're heading north."
He thanked me and left.
I watched his boots disappear into the gathering dusk and thought something I kept to myself.
Then I went back to banking the fire properly for the night.

The routine of closing the inn was as familiar as my own breathing: checking the guest rooms for forgotten belongings and unlatched windows, testing the bolts on the doors, counting the day's takings and locking them in the strongbox behind the bar.
The bolt on the back door stuck, as it had every night for the past month, requiring the precise combination of lifting and turning that I'd learned through repetition.
The window in the third guest room still wouldn't close completely, leaving a gap just wide enough to admit cold air and my persistent irritation.
With the inn locked and empty, I found myself alone in the taproom for the first time all day.
The silence settled around me like a familiar coat, comfortable and confining at once.
I wiped down the bar one more time, though it was already clean, and noticed a new gouge in the wood I hadn't seen before.
The keg Jem had dropped last week, most likely, or a guest's boot, or simple wear from twenty years of coins and mugs and elbows.

Jem would need to manage the new barrel delivery on Thursday—his arm made the work slower but not impossible, and I'd learned to allow extra time rather than wound his pride by suggesting he needed help.
The lease was in Stainforth's name and always had been.
My mother knew that.
My grandmother knew that.
Three women running a business on a man's sufferance, and none of them with the wit or the option to change it.
I wrung out the cloth and hung it on the hook.
The hook was one my mother had put in.
Her hands had polished this same bar the night before she died, using this same motion with the same careful attention to corners and edges.
The memory arrived without warning and left without being processed.
The letter lay on the bar where someone had left it during the day.
I saw Stainforth's seal before I saw my name in the direction—his coat of arms pressed into red wax, as unmistakable as a brand on cattle.
The weight of it in my hands told me nothing I wanted to know and everything I feared to learn.
I set the letter on the shelf behind the bar, next to the ledger and the strongbox key.
It would be there tomorrow.
I would deal with it then.
Nell counted squirrels at seven forty-two AM because that's when they showed up.
Six today, sitting in a neat row at the tree line like someone had arranged them there.
She pressed her thumb into the windowsill.
The squirrels didn't move.
They just watched her cottage.
One of them blinked.
Except it wasn't a squirrel when it blinked.
Red fur, narrow snout, amber eyes—a fox.
Half a second, then squirrel again.
Same spot.
Same tree.
"Okay," Nell said.
"That's new."
Her hands shook.
She gripped the windowsill but her nails were too short—she'd cut them yesterday, couldn't stop herself—and she couldn't dig into her palms.
The fox had been there.
She'd seen it.
Six squirrels instead of five.
That was wrong.
She'd been counting for three weeks.
Always five squirrels, always seven forty-two, always the tree line.
Not six.
She was keeping count, which meant she was expecting something to change.
The thought made her cold.
She forced herself to keep watching instead of turning away.
The squirrels didn't move.
A crow landed near them and they still didn't scatter.
Just sat there watching her back.
She needed to check the salt.
The salt on the kitchen windowsill was fine—clean white line, no breaks.
She checked it anyway.
Ran her finger through it.
The water bowls by the doors were still full.
No dirt.
No scratches.
Everything looked fine, which made the fox worse because there was no threat inside.
The wrongness was outside.
Or in her.
She drank the tea she'd made earlier.
It was cold.
She drank it anyway because her morning was already fucked and wasting tea felt wrong.
No mirrors in the apartment.
She'd broken them when she moved in six months ago.
Wrapped the shards in newspaper, drove them to a dumpster three towns over.
Gail had asked once—why no mirrors—and Nell said something about vanity.
Gail laughed.
The lie worked.
Nell did the ritual anyway.
Every salt line.
Every water bowl.
Every windowsill.
By the time she was done it was past seven and the ritual hadn't done anything except prove she was faking it now.
The phone rang when she was rinsing her mug.
Mrs.
Halloran's daughter.
Scared voice.
"The breathing's different."
Nell switched to her work voice.
Calm.
Steady.
"I'll be there in twenty minutes."
She hung up.
Her hands were still shaking.
The fox was still in her head.
She had a job now.
The morning was over and nothing had held.
The chair was in the wrong place when Nell got there.
Mrs.
Halloran's daughter—Carrie—was pacing by the bed with her phone, making calls she didn't need to make yet.
Nell moved the chair where she wanted it.
Six inches from the bed.
Angled toward Mrs.
Halloran's face.
She sat down and took Mrs.
Halloran's hand.
The hand was cool.
Papery skin over bones.
The breathing had gaps in it now.
Long spaces between breaths.
This was hours, not days.
Nell knew what it looked like.
"You're doing fine, Margaret," she said.
She put her thumb on Mrs.
Halloran's wrist.
The pulse was thin.
"Overcast this morning.
No rain.
Your daughter's here."
Carrie made another call by the window.
Nell let her.
The vigil had started.
Her own shit—the fox, the squirrels, the dream—didn't matter now.
The light through the window did something weird.
Nell looked up.
It didn't look like a cloud.
More like something pressing close and then pulling back.
The Veil.
She didn't let herself think the word but she felt it.
Too close.
She pressed her thumb into the chair arm.
Wood grain.
Solid.
Mrs.
Halloran's breathing changed again.
Longer gaps now.
Nell stayed still.
Talked about the weather.
About the garden.
Nothing important.
She held Mrs.
Halloran's hand and kept her face steady when the breathing stopped for seven seconds and then started again.
