The wood caught clean — he'd split it dry, which meant he'd been thinking ahead, which he always was.
She did not remark on it to herself.
It was simply the condition of the morning, the same as the cold striking up through the flagstones and the grey light at the east window and the smell of last night's tallow thinning in the new air.
Bar stock next.
She moved through the taproom with the lamp held low, not trusting the early light, checking the level in each cask by the sound a knuckle made against the side.
Two needed rotating to the front of the cellar before midday.
She noted it.
The spigot on the third needed attention — there had been a slow seep for three days now, barely a drip, but she had watched it long enough to know it would not correct itself.
She added it to the list she carried nowhere but in her head.
The taproom chairs were stacked, the hearth cold and swept.
She built the fire here with last night's coals and new wood, working quickly, not because anyone was watching but because there was no reason to be slow.

By the time guests came down for breakfast the room would be warm and would smell of nothing worse than oak smoke and ale, which was the smell the White Hound had always had and which she associated with a particular quality of rightness that she would not have named to anyone.
She went through the kitchen door to the back.
Jem was in the yard, working at a length of harness across his knee.
He didn't look up.
She hadn't expected him to.
His single hand moved with the patient economy she had stopped noticing years ago, the leather bending to the pressure he applied through the crook of his arm.
Two horses stood in the open stable, already brushed, their coats dark in the morning damp.
She looked at them, looked at the harness, looked at Jem's bent head, and went back inside.
Nan came through the kitchen door six minutes later.
She was still pushing pins into her hair, but her apron was already tied, and she went straight to the bar without speaking.
There was nothing to say.
The morning had its shape; they had both been inside it long enough to know where each piece of it fell.
The London coach came in at half past ten, which was forty minutes late and three passengers short of what she'd arranged for.
Two passengers, and one of them was standing in the middle of the yard before the wheels had properly stopped, addressing the space in front of her as though the air owed her an explanation.
The trunk was the first thing.

Jem appeared from the stable door, moving before she had a chance to call for him, and she could see from where she stood that the hinge had given on the left side — the lid lifting crookedly, the strap the only thing keeping it closed.
She crossed the yard.
"Jem will take it to the storeroom," she said to the woman, who turned on her with an expression that had been sharpened by forty minutes of bad road.
"There's cord in the storeroom.
He'll have it re-strapped before you leave."
The woman drew breath.
Dinah held her gaze.

Something in it — not warmth exactly, but certainty, a sense that the thing would simply happen because it had been said — transferred across the yard air, and the woman let the breath out without the argument she'd been assembling and turned toward the inn door.
Jem took the trunk.
The coachman was down from the box, handing off the reins.
He was a man she knew slightly, ran the northern route out of the Blue Boar, had a way of picking at his teeth with his thumbnail when he was preparing a complaint.
He was picking at his teeth now.
"Road above Hatfield," he said.
"The surface is gone, north of the turnpike."
"Coming down?"
"Potholed out.
Lost a quarter of an hour to it.
If it freezes tonight it'll be worse tomorrow."
"I'll send word to the parish."
She wouldn't.
The parish wouldn't act before Christmas, and they both knew it.
"The teams I have are rested.
Do you want the near-side leader swapped out?"
He looked at her, recalibrated.
Swapping the leader would save him time and the horse the bad stretch.
He nodded, and that was the end of the conversation.

She left him to settle the swap with Jem and went inside to see about the second passenger, who had taken himself quietly to the dining room and appeared to require only tea and bread, which was the most useful thing a traveller could do and she silently credited him for it.
The yard cleared.
Nan had been wiping down the bar with her back to the window since the coach arrived.
Dinah noticed the set of her shoulders, the way she hadn't once turned to look at the door.
She said nothing.
Whatever it was, it wasn't her business yet.
It would become her business if it interfered with the work, and until then it was Nan's to carry.
The chandler came just before noon with two boys and a cart and the carefully arranged expression of a man about to say something he expected to argue about.
She saw him cross the yard and met him at the kitchen door.
"Miss Dale."
He set down his sample basket.
"Good price on the tallow this month.
Better wick quality, the half-dozen at two-and-six."
"You were at two shillings in September."
"Cost of tallow's up.
Can't be helped."
"Your supplier on the Stevenage road has been at the same price since July."
She knew because she had asked.
It had taken one question and a walk of half a mile, which was a small investment against the six pence per dozen that had migrated from her account to his since May.
"And I know what you charge at the Antelope in Hatfield, because their landlord and I had occasion to speak last quarter."
He looked at his sample basket.
He looked at the boys on the cart.
He looked at Dinah.
"Two-and-two," she said.
"Same wick quality.
I'll take the full order."
"Two-and-three," he said.
"It's a fair margin."
"Two-and-two, and I'll pay on receipt rather than at month's end.
Which saves you the bother of the book."
A pause.
The boys on the cart studied the middle distance with great attention.
"Two-and-two," he said.
She stepped back from the door to let the boys through with the first crate.
He left without anything further being said on either side.
The door closed.
She took the delivery note and wrote the adjusted price in the margin in her own hand, then filed it in the kitchen drawer with the others.

Somewhere between replacing the pen and pulling out the invoice for the week's grain, a thought moved through her the way a working thought does, without ceremony: if she married, this conversation would not be hers to have.

The negotiation, the account, the lease — all of it would pass out of her hands into the hands of a husband the moment the church finished with them, and there would be nothing left of what her mother had built and what her grandmother had built before her mother except a legal transfer of ownership dressed up as a sacrament.
She had done the arithmetic on this before, more than once.
The answer was always the same.
She moved on to the grain invoice.
She saw him through the kitchen window before he knocked.

He was young — younger than the boots suggested, because the boots were old enough to have creased through their own weather rather than his, the welts coming apart in the way leather came apart when it had done too much in too little time.
He stood at the corner of the door, not quite at it.
His coat hung without any body behind it.
He had a soldier's way of standing that hadn't left him yet, chin up, heels together, which made the thinness worse to look at because it put the structure of him in relief against the posture.
He was deciding whether to knock.
She watched him make the decision and then knock anyway, and there was something in that — the deliberateness of choosing to ask — that settled something in her chest.
She opened the door.
He was perhaps twenty.
His eyes, when they found hers, were careful.
"I'm not looking for trouble," he said.
"I didn't think you were.
Have you eaten today?"
A beat, honest and brief.
"Not recently, no."
"Then come in."
She stepped back.
"Kitchen, not taproom.
That's the arrangement."
He understood.

He sat where she pointed, at the far end of the worktable, and she put bread and the remains of the morning's soup in front of him without ceremony, because that was what there was and there was no point in presentation.
He ate steadily, not fast, with the control of a man who had learned that speed was a mistake and had taught himself out of it.
She worked at the other end of the table while he ate.
When he had finished she cleared the bowl.
"Where are you headed?"
she asked.
"North," he said.
"Toward Lincoln, I think.
I've a brother there, maybe."
"Maybe," she said.
"The last letter was two years ago."
She said nothing.
He stood, and she could see it cost him something to do so cleanly, some stiffness in the left leg that he'd learned to conceal.
"Thank you," he said.
"I'm obliged to you."
"The privy's round the side if you need it before you go.
The road north is in poor repair above Hatfield.
Keep to the verge."
He nodded and went out through the back.
She cleared the bowl into the washing basin and dried her hands and moved on to the next thing.
The two men in the taproom had been at it for twenty minutes by the time it reached the point of voices.
She heard them from the hall — not the words, just the pitch of it, that particular rise that went nowhere good.
She came through the door without hurry and stopped at the end of their table.
"Not in here," she said.
That was all.
The particular quality of it — flat, not unfriendly, entirely without doubt — landed in the space between them and took the argument's air.
The older one looked at his ale.
The younger one looked at her, thought better of what he'd been about to say, and looked at his ale.
Nan, behind the bar, resumed wiping the counter.

The afternoon ground through its middle hours the way the middle hours always did, flat and grey and full of the ordinary labour that didn't announce itself: accounts to reconcile, rooms to reset for the evening's likely arrivals, the kitchen to provision for dinner, the second barrel of ale to rotate up from the cellar.
Jem came in once for rope.
Nan went up to see about the linen in room four.

Dinah moved through it all with the steady attention of a woman who had learned that the only way to finish a day's work was to be present in each piece of it, not to stand back and look at the whole, because the whole was always too much and the piece at hand was always manageable.
The afternoon gave way to evening in the gradual way it did in late October, light withdrawing from the windows not all at once but in increments, until the lamps became necessary.
She locked up alone.

This was always the last hour's work and she had done it so many times that it had become a kind of ritual without being named one, the same route through the same rooms in the same order, each check a completion in itself.
Taproom: fire taken down to coals, guard set, the two chairs left pulled in by the last guest pushed back to their places.
Bar: the till tallied and locked, the bottles returned to their shelf positions, the last rag hung to dry.
Cellar: hatch locked, key on the ring.
She went through the kitchen to the back door and checked the yard.
Jem would have settled the horses; the stable was quiet, no sound but the shift of weight and the occasional soft exhale.
The November air cut at her wrists where her sleeves had ridden up.
She pulled them down.
Her hands at the end of the day were the same as they always were: reddened at the knuckles, rough at the palm, a small cut at the base of the index finger that she hadn't noticed happening.
She turned the hand in the lamplight and found the culprit — the edge of the chandler's delivery note, of all things, the corner sharp enough to have caught her without her feeling it.
The invoice that cut her.
She thought, briefly and without sentiment, that there was something typical about that.
She looked up to the second floor on the return circuit.
A light behind Bridget's window, a shape in the chair where the shape always was — she'd have the small lamp on and her cards or her complaints about the cards, the same as every evening.
Dinah did not slow her pace or direct her attention to it with any particular intention.
Bridget was there.
She was watching.
These were facts of the White Hound at night the way the cold stones were a fact and the smell of spent coal and tallow was a fact, and noting them cost nothing.
She went inside.
Last lamp check.
Last bolt.
The letter was on the kitchen table where she had put it that morning, face down.
She hadn't forgotten it.
She had set it there and moved around it all day the way you moved around a thing in a room that you had decided not to deal with yet, and she had dealt with everything else instead.
She picked it up now.

The direction was in Stainforth's hand: she knew it from the Michaelmas correspondence, from the notice about the drainage assessment two summers ago, from the politely intractable letter about the north fence that she had answered with equivalent politeness and no concession.
The seal was his too, pressed deeply, a man who believed in the weight of his own mark.
She turned it over once.
She felt its weight.

She had known since the last quarter, since the chandler began adjusting his prices and the parish began finding small reasons to inconvenience the coach road outside her door, that this letter was coming.
She had been moving faster ever since.
She set it back down on the table, face up this time, and stood with her hand flat beside it.
She would open it tomorrow.
Tonight there was nothing to be done with it that couldn't be done in daylight, and she was too tired to read bad news with any clarity, and clarity was what bad news required.
She picked up the lamp.
"Well," she said, to the empty kitchen, to no one in particular, to the letter on the table and the walls around it and the three generations of women who had stood in this room before her.
"There it is."
She went upstairs and left the letter to wait.
Chapter One: The White Hound
The ledger lay open on the kitchen table.
I had done the calculation twice, which was not a habit of mine, and the number was the same both times.
Six weeks, near enough, before the next quarter's rent became a problem.
I closed the book.
The kitchen was cold.
I'd built the fire up an hour before it was properly light, but the heat was still pooled low near the grate and the rest of the room held the night's chill in the flagstones.

I pulled my sleeves down over my wrists and stood for a moment looking at the ledger's cover, at the brass clasp that had needed replacing for two years and that I had not replaced because there was always something that needed doing more urgently.
I would replace it in the spring.
I had said this before.
The taproom was dark and smelled of last night's ale and the close dampness of a room that has been breathed in by a great many people and then left to itself.
I moved through it without a candle.
I knew every table, every chair, the loose board three steps from the door and the one that caught at the bar corner if you didn't lift your foot.
The fire I'd laid last evening had burned down to nothing.
I set it fresh -- kindling first, properly laid, not bunched -- and had it going in four minutes.
The windows were rimed at the edges.
October, and a hard one so far.
Through the glass the yard was still dark, only the faintest separation of sky from roofline to say the morning was coming at all.
Bar stock: the gin was low, delivery expected Thursday.
I'd need to check the invoice before I signed for it.
The last delivery from Hoskins had come up a bottle short and he'd told me I was mistaken.
I had not been mistaken.
I noted the gin in the stock book.
I noted the port, which was fine.
I noted the condition of the second tap handle, which had been stiff for a week and which Jem needed to look at before it went entirely.
Three items for the morning list, and that was only the taproom.
I did the dining room and found it properly laid, which meant Nan had done it before she left last evening, which was what I had expected.
I adjusted one place setting that had been knocked slightly in the night and went back through to the kitchen to start the fire properly.
The coals I'd banked were still alive underneath.
I built it up, put the water on for the first pot, and went out to the yard.
Just after six.
The sky above the stable roof was the colour of old pewter, the kind of light that comes before light, when you can see things but they don't yet cast a shadow.
My breath went out in front of me in a short, visible puff.
The ground was hard underfoot.
Through the stable wall I could hear the sound of horses that have been watered and fed -- a settled sound, a sound that means work has already been done.
I went in.
Jem was at the tack wall, straightening the harness with his one good hand and the stump of his left braced against the wooden bracket, steadying the weight while he worked.
He didn't look up.
I didn't expect him to.
We had done this before, many times: him at the tack before I'd got there, me at the door running the yard-check.
Nothing between us required saying.
I moved down the row of stalls, checked the water buckets, noted the muck in the far stall that wanted clearing before the first coach, and went back past him toward the door.
"Hinge wants replacing on the third stall," I said.
He nodded without turning around.
Inside, Nan arrived through the kitchen door twenty minutes later, her cap on but the pins not yet properly set, her apron already tied.
She came through without knocking.
She never knocked -- she had worked here since she was fourteen and knocking would have been like a guest knocking.
She moved directly to the bar, and from the kitchen I heard the steady progress of the morning check: glasses first, working left to right, then the bottles, then the measures.
I had hired her because she was family, which was a reason that had nothing to do with merit, and she had proved herself worth keeping a dozen times over on merit alone.
She caught errors in supplier invoices that I sometimes missed.
She knew which guests needed watching and she never named them outright, only positioned herself so she could see the door.
We did not discuss feelings.
We discussed the running of the inn, and the feelings lived somewhere inside that, unexamined and sufficient.
I went back to the ledger and stayed with it until I heard the first coach.
The London coach was late, which was not unusual for October when the road above Hatfield turned into something better suited to a river.
It was running short, which was more unusual: two passengers where there should have been four, and both of them in a bad temper.

I could hear the quality of the arrival before I got to the yard -- the coachman's voice had a compressed, end-of-the-day flatness to it, the horses were blowing hard, and when the first passenger descended she was gripping the handrail with the kind of force that means she had been gripping something for a long time.
I had Jem by the coat before he turned around.
He was already moving.
The trunk came out of the carriage on a broken hinge, the leather strap hanging loose and one end of the lid unable to seat properly.

The woman -- perhaps fifty, grey-haired, wool coat of good quality and a face that told you she had not got to fifty without developing opinions -- told me about the trunk, about the road, about the unreliability of the coaching service in general, and about several other matters that were the fault of no one in particular but that wanted saying aloud.
I listened until she had finished the portion that required a response.
"I'll have the trunk seen to," I said.
"Jem will take it.
There's a fire in the dining room and I can offer you bread and beef from the kitchen."
She opened her mouth and then closed it again.
"This way, if you please," I said, and she came.
The coachman caught me when I came back out.
He had a square, weathered face and the resigned expression of a man who has been delivering complaints up and down the Great North Road for twenty years and knows none of them will change anything.
"Road wants attention above the Hatfield turn," he said.
"Ruts deep enough to lose a wheel.
I lost half my load last January to a rut not half so bad as what I came through this morning."
"I know it," I said.
"Has been written to."
"Written to doesn't fix a rut."
"Neither does telling me," I said.
"The parish surveyor is who wants to hear it.
My letter doesn't carry the same weight as twenty coachmen all writing at once."
He was quiet for a moment.
He did not appear to disagree with this.
He had a schedule to meet and I had a yard to clear and the road north of Hatfield was going to stay the way it was through the winter regardless of the conversation we were having in my yard.
He tipped his chin and went to see to his horses.
The second passenger had gone upstairs without speaking to anyone, which was the kind of guest I preferred.
Jem had taken the trunk.
Nan was back behind the bar.

I stood in the empty yard for a moment, listening to the sound of the coach moving on down the road -- the particular diminishing rumble of it, which could tell you a great deal about how loaded a coach was and how hard the driver was pushing the horses, and which today told me only that it was a thin morning.
I went in to do the accounts.
The chandler came just before midday.
His name was Pruett.

He had been delivering tallow candles to the White Hound since before my mother died, at a price she had set, and he had been quietly and systematically raising it ever since I had taken over the account.
First time, I asked him to explain the increase.
He explained it.
I paid.
Second time, I questioned it harder and the number came down before I agreed.

Third time, I sat across this same kitchen table from him and told him exactly what I knew: what he was paying per hundredweight for tallow from his supplier in Hatfield, what he was charging the Crown and Bell two miles north, what he was charging the posting house at Baldock, what he was charging the rectory, and what he was now proposing to charge me.
He had listened to all of it with the steady, slightly affronted expression of a man watching his own hand of cards being turned face-up on the table.
Then he named a price halfway between what he had asked and what I had paid the time before.
We shook hands on it and he left.
That had been four months ago.
Today he set the boxes down on the kitchen floor and named a price a shilling above last quarter.
I didn't say anything.
I let him straighten up and set his hands in front of him and wait.
Outside the kitchen window the yard was cold and ordinary.
I let the silence do its work.
"Fourth adjustment since April," I said.
"Tallow's dear," he said.
"Tallow was dear in August.
You charged me less for it in August."
"New supplier."
He spread his hands in the manner of a man who is the innocent victim of large and indifferent forces.
"Had to renegotiate.
Prices change."
"They do," I said.
"Yours change in one direction."
"Miss Dale."
His voice shifted into something more formal, the register of a man preparing to be reasonable on his own terms.
"I've the Crown and Bell.
I've the posting house at Baldock.
I've the rectory and the school and the Dunnage farm.
I can take my candles anywhere along this road and find a house glad to have them at a fair rate."
"You can," I said.
"The Crown and Bell is two miles further north, which puts four miles on your round each time.
The posting house is three beyond that, and their yard gate is on the wrong side of the building for a loaded cart, which you know already.
The rectory pays quarterly, which means you're carrying them for three months at a stretch.
I pay on delivery, same day, every time."
I looked at him.
"So take your candles where you please.
Only work out what it costs to get there first."
He stood with that.
He was a fair man, Pruett, not a dishonest one -- he was simply doing what any supplier did when the buyer was a woman on her own and the arithmetic was in his favour.
The arithmetic was not in his favour this morning.
"A penny less than you've named," I said.
"Same terms."
He left with the money.
The candles stayed.
I noted the adjusted price in the margin of the delivery note and set it with the morning's receipts.
I picked up the delivery note to file it and felt the small bite at the edge of my finger -- a paper cut, just above the first knuckle, the index finger of my right hand.
I hadn't noticed it happen.
I looked at it for a moment, then put it from my mind.

Somewhere in the tallying that followed -- invoices, stock count, the note I needed to write to the brewery about the last barrel of porter, which had been off and which they were going to hear about -- the thought came and went the way working thoughts do when your hands are occupied.
The ledger.
The rent.
Pruett and his tallow, the road getting worse, the coach running short, all of it resting on the same underlying fact, which was that if I married, this would not be my negotiation to have.
Not the candle price, not the beer invoice, not the lease itself.
The inn that my grandmother had built and my mother had kept and that I had been running since I was twenty-five would belong to a husband on the day I said yes to one.
I had thought about this before.
I would think about it again.
I moved on to the next column of figures.
I saw him through the kitchen window before he knocked.

He'd come around to the back, the way the signs asked, and he was standing at the kitchen door with his hat in both hands, looking at the window with the specific expression of a man who is working out whether the answer is already no before he commits to asking.
Young -- twenty, perhaps, or a younger man who had been aged hard.
His coat was thin for October and his boots were coming apart at the welt, the right one worse than the left.
He was not threatening.
There was nothing in his posture that said he was calculating anything except the question of welcome.
He stood still.
He did not knock immediately.
He gave himself time to read the place.
I went to the door and opened it.
He knocked the air where the door had been.
"When did you last eat?"
I said.
He looked at me steadily, the kind of look that is deciding whether the question is a real one or the preamble to a refusal.
He decided it was real.
"Day before yesterday," he said.
"More or less."
"Kitchen," I said.
"Not the taproom.
Bread and broth, and then you're on your way.
Those are the terms."
"Yes, ma'am."
He came in and sat at the end of the table I pointed to, away from the fire, and I set the bread and the morning's leftover broth in front of him and left him to it.
He ate without speaking.
He did not look around the room in the restless, measuring way that sometimes told you a man was scouting the place.
He was just hungry.

I worked at the kitchen end of the table getting the evening prep started -- the salt pork from the brine crock, potatoes to peel, the dried herbs from the shelf -- and he finished the bread and tipped the bowl and worked at the last of the broth with a seriousness that I recognised as the hunger of a man who has not known when the next meal was coming.
He sat for a moment after, his hands flat on the table.
"Thank you," he said.
He meant it simply.
"Where are you headed?"
I asked.
"North," he said.
"I've got a cousin in Durham.
Had, anyway."
I nodded.
He stood, put his hat on, and went to the door.
I heard his boots on the yard stones, the uneven sound of the loose sole slapping slightly on the right -- one more day's walking, maybe two, before that boot was finished entirely.
Then nothing.
I cleared the bowl.
I set the kitchen back.
The trouble in the taproom came just after three, while the afternoon light was still flat and the second fire hadn't caught yet to its evening warmth.
I heard it from the kitchen -- the particular shift in a room's noise when two voices are pushing against each other and the rest of the room has gone quiet around them.
I came through the door.

Two men, both settled in from the midday and both with the irritable, compressed look of men who have been sitting too long in a room that's too cold and have found each other at exactly the wrong moment.
They saw me come in.
The calculation was visible: the authority of the room versus the momentum of whatever they had worked themselves toward.
The room won.
"Lower your voices," I said, "or lower them outside.
Your choice."
A pause.
"Inside is fine," said one.
"Right," said the other.
I went back to the kitchen.
Behind the bar, Nan had been watching with one eye on the door, and she set down the glass she was holding and got back to work without a word between us.
She had not needed to intervene.
She never needed to intervene when I was there.
I sometimes wondered if she preferred it that way.
The afternoon went as afternoons do in a coaching inn when there are no coaches: quiet, and full of work.
I tallied the morning receipts and wrote the brewery letter and noted the items that wanted ordering before the week was out.

I went up to check the four empty rooms that Nan had made up, noted that the window latch in the second room was not catching properly -- another thing for Jem's list, and it was getting to be a long list -- and came back down.
There was a delivery of potatoes from the farm up the road that I had to count and sign for and that came in right, which made a change.
I gave the boy who'd brought them a penny and he left at a run.
Jem was in the yard when I crossed for the coal, doing something to the harness arrangement that I trusted him to have a reason for.
Neither of us spoke.
In the kitchen I saw Nan's back as she went upstairs with the linen for the evening service.
The work moved through the inn the way it always did, the way my mother had set it moving thirty years ago, and her mother before that.
The day was nothing I could not handle.
This was the point of the day -- to be nothing I could not handle.
By eight o'clock the last guests were settled and I started the final circuit.
Taproom fire down to a good bed of coals, fire guard set.
Bar tallied, locked, key in my apron pocket.
Dining room: chairs up, fire out, windows secure.
Back through the kitchen to the cellar hatch, which I tested twice -- the lock was still stiff, still unresolved, still on the list.
Yard: quiet, horses settled.
The gate, which Jem would have bolted and which I bolted anyway.
Not a question of trust.
Just the gate.
I came back through the kitchen and took the candle I'd left on the table and stood for a moment before going up.
I looked at my hands in the candlelight.

They were reddened from the cold water I'd used on the kitchen at close-down, dry along the knuckles in the way of October, and there was the cut on my right index finger from the chandler's delivery note -- a small clean line, the particular sting of paper edge.
I hadn't felt it happen and had barely thought of it since.
I looked at it now in the low light.
It was nothing.
It was the invoice that had done it.
On the final yard circuit I looked up at the second floor.
Bridget's window was lit, the lamp behind the glass casting a soft yellow square against the dark.

Her shape was in the chair -- white hair, the slight lean forward, the familiar arrangement of a woman who has kept vigil at that window so many times it has stopped being a vigil and become simply a place she is.
She was watching the yard the way she watched it every evening: steadily, without urgency.
She had lived above this inn for twenty-six years.
She had watched the yard when my mother was alive and she watched it now.
I did not look long.
I had seen it too many times to require acknowledging.
I bolted the kitchen door.
The letter was on the kitchen table.
I had passed it going to the door and known it was there without looking at it.
Now I turned and looked.
Stainforth's seal.
His handwriting on the direction, careful and even -- Miss D.
Dale, The White Hound Inn, Great North Road, Hertfordshire -- the kind of hand that has been taught to convey authority by its own evenness.
I picked it up.
The paper was stiff, heavier than ordinary correspondence paper.
He always used heavy paper.
It was the kind of thing you noticed about Stainforth: everything done to a specification that reminded you of his position, just in case you had for a moment forgotten it.
I turned the letter over once.
The seal was intact.
I knew what it was about.

I had known it was coming since the last quarter, perhaps since the spring, when his man had come round asking questions about the cellar capacity and the room count and the terms of the stable yard, questions that had no legitimate reason to be asked and no answer I was prepared to give.
I had thought about it since.
I had moved faster since, keeping the accounts right, paying on time, keeping the inn in order that no one could look at it and say it was poorly run.
Moving faster did not fix a problem of this kind.
It only meant you arrived at it with the place in good repair.
I set the letter down on the table.
I did not open it.
The fire had gone to coals.
The candle threw a low, unsteady light across the kitchen table, across the letter, across my own hands.
The inn was very quiet, the particular quiet that I knew as well as I knew anything -- the quiet of a space that has been used hard all day and is now at rest.
I stood with my hands on the table and looked at Stainforth's seal.
"Well," I said to the empty room.
"There it is, then."
Counted the column twice before I trusted it.
Six weeks, or thereabouts, before the next quarter's rent became a problem.
Thereabouts was doing a great deal of work in that sentence.
I closed the ledger.
The kitchen fire needed building up.
I did that first, then the taproom — dragging the grate forward, breaking the night's crust of ash, coaxing the coals into something that would hold.
October had come in hard this year and the inn windows were rimed at the edges, that particular frost that means the cold has been sitting for hours, settled and certain of itself.
I pulled my sleeves down over my wrists and went back to the kitchen for the bar-stock check.

Last night's accounts were tallied against the day-book: two tables of dinner, four overnight guests, and a party of three who drank through to closing and left without settling the last round, which I had noted in the margin and would not forget.
Bar stock: low on Madeira, out of Holland gin entirely, which was a nuisance I could not afford.
I added both to the order list.
The kitchen had enough in it for the morning.
Barely.
This was the ordinary work.
I had done it six days out of every seven for better than eleven years and I knew the shape of it the way I knew the shape of my own hands.

Jem was in the stable yard when I checked out the back — straightening tack, hanging it on the proper pegs in the proper order, not because I had asked him to but because the morning required it and he knew as much.
He did not look up.
A few minutes later Nan came through the kitchen door with the pins in her hair not yet set and her apron already on.
She took her place behind the bar without a word.
We had done this before.
Many times.

The London coach was late, which was not unusual on the north road above Hatfield in October, but it was also running short — two passengers instead of the expected four, and both of them in a temper that had had several hours to mature.

The first passenger was a woman of middle years with an opinion on everything and a trunk with a split hinge, and the two things together had brought her to a pitch of agitation that she was disinclined to set aside simply because she had arrived at her destination.
The second passenger was a clergyman who had apparently decided that silence was the correct response to every provocation and was sitting with it like a man in a box.
Jem appeared in the yard without being called — he always did — and I directed him to the trunk with a look.

The woman was already halfway through an account of exactly when the hinge had given, which suggested it had given at the beginning of the journey and she had spent the intervening time composing her remarks.
I let her compose them at me while I checked the latch she was indicating.
The hinge was split but not beyond mending.
I told her as much and told her where Jem would bring the trunk once it was seen to, and something in the directness of the answer surprised her into stopping.
She went inside.

The coachman had jumped down from the box and was waiting with the particular patience of a man who has been waiting in this particular spot on a great many mornings and expects to be dealt with soon.
"Road above Hatfield's gone to pieces again," he said.
"Lost an hour above Welwyn."
"Stone's been ordered."
"Ordered last quarter too."
He was not wrong on that point and I did not argue it.
"Worse below the village than above.
Right side of the road.
You'll want to tell your guests."
"I'll tell them.
Are you stopping for the return?"
"Feed and water.
Twenty minutes."
"Twenty minutes," I said, and turned back to the inn.
He was satisfied with that or he was not — there was nothing else I had to offer him on the matter of the road — and he went to see about his horses.
The yard cleared.
The passengers went upstairs or to the dining room.
Jem took the trunk to the corner of the stable where he kept his tools, moving without hurry because he never moved with hurry and there was no point in asking it of him.
Nan had been wiping down the bar with one eye on the door through all of it.
I noticed.
Said nothing.

Fallow came at half past ten with his cart and his monthly delivery of tallow candles, price per dozen, and a figure he named with the particular confidence of a man who has decided in advance that he is not going to be argued with this time.
I let him finish the figure.
Then I said: "That's four above what you charged me in March."
"Tallow's up.
You'll have seen it."
"I've seen what you charge the Crown at Stevenage."
He paused at that.
The pause was informative.
"Different arrangement there," he said.
"Different how?"
He moved the delivery note from one hand to the other.
The Crown at Stevenage took twice what I took, which meant he could afford to do them at a better rate and still come out, and he knew I knew this because I had made it my business to know it.
He knew the Crown's rate because he had told me once, in a moment of complaint about their payment terms, and I had not forgotten.
He was working out whether to contest the point.
"You're asking me to carry it," I said.
"You do this every quarter and I carry it because I don't have another supplier who can match your delivery schedule.
But I know your margin and I know what you paid for this batch and I know what I'm prepared to pay per dozen."
I named the figure.
He said nothing for a moment.
Then he said, "That's barely worth my time."
"It's ten dozen candles at a price that covers your costs and leaves you something.
If it's not worth your time I'll make arrangements elsewhere, but you'll lose the account and you'll lose it at the beginning of winter, which is a poor time to lose an inn account."
He picked up the delivery note.
He set it down.
He named a figure two below where he had started, one above where I had put it.
I took it.
He left.
The candles stayed.
I tallied the adjusted price in the margin of the delivery note with the stub of pencil I kept behind the bar, and put the note in the order file.

Sometime in the middle of the day's work — I could not have said exactly when, between the chandler leaving and the kitchen needing me for the midday arrangements — I ran the numbers in my head the way I sometimes ran them.
The ledger.
The rent.
The chandler's adjusted price, which was better than he had wanted but still higher than March.
All of it added against the same fact, which was that if I married, the inn would not be mine to negotiate for.
I had made this calculation before.
It was not a new one.
I moved on to the next thing.
He came around the back, as the sign asked.
The signs were at both gates and at the turn off the road, not rudely worded but plain enough: tradesmen and those seeking charitable relief to the rear.
Most did.
Some didn't bother reading them.
He had read them.
I saw him through the kitchen window before he knocked.
Young — twenty, perhaps twenty-one, no older.
Thin in the way that is not a man's natural shape but has been arrived at over time.
His coat had been a good one at some point and was now doing the work of a coat that was no longer good.
His boots were coming apart at the welt on the left foot, the sole beginning to separate from the upper so that each step must have been wet in this weather.
He stood outside the kitchen door without knocking immediately.
He was not threatening.
He was assessing whether he was welcome enough to knock.
He was not sure.
He knocked.
I went to the door.
"Have you eaten?"
I said.
"Not recently."
He said it honestly, which I appreciated.
Some of them said they had when they hadn't and then you could see it in them.
"Kitchen, not the taproom."
I stood back from the door.
"Sit there."
He understood the terms and sat where I indicated, at the end of the kitchen table nearest the door, which put him away from the fire and away from the pass-through to the taproom and the bar.
He held his hands still in his lap, which told me something, and he did not look around the kitchen with the calculating assessment of a man who is thinking about what might be taken.
He looked at the table.
I put bread down and went to the pot for broth.
There was bread enough and the broth was yesterday's, which was better than today's would have been at this hour.
I set it in front of him.
He ate.
He did not eat quickly or desperately, which surprised me, and then it didn't surprise me — a man who eats quickly has never learned not to, and this one had had time to learn.
When he was finished he said, "Thank you."
"Where are you headed?"
"North," he said.
"Sheffield, if I can make it."
He picked up his hat from where he had set it on the table and stood up.
I took the bowl.
He went to the door, opened it, and then looked back for a moment with the particular expression of a man who wants to say something else and knows that there is nothing else to say.
He went.
I cleared the bowl.
Nan would need me in the bar.
Two men at the corner table had been sitting too long over a half-empty jug and had found something to disagree about — the specific thing didn't matter, these things never did.
I heard the shift in the room before anything was said loudly enough to require attention, the particular lowering of other conversations that meant people were beginning to watch.
"That's enough," I said.
I didn't raise my voice.
I looked at them both.
"You'll settle up and either sit quietly or you'll go."
Nan was watching from behind the bar.
She did not need to do anything.
Neither of them said another word.
The afternoon gap.
The coach gone, the morning guests either settled in their rooms or gone on, the taproom quiet in the way it went quiet between one and three before the road trade began again.
Nan at the bar.
Jem somewhere in the yard.
I did the upstairs rooms that had been vacated, stripped the linen and stacked it for the laundress, checked for damage, which there wasn't, and made up the nearest of them for the evening.
Then the accounts for the chandler and the morning delivery and the dinner order and the kitchen arrangements for the evening service.
There were no incidents.
There was the work.
The last guests settled by half past nine.
I checked the taproom fire — coals still, no need to bank it further, it would be out by midnight.
The bar tallied and the takings in the lockbox.
The kitchen closed: fire down to coals, the last of the pots scrubbed and stacked, the pantry door pulled and latched.
The cellar hatch locked, which I had to do myself because I was the only one who held that key.
The ground floor done.
I went through to the back and out into the yard for the last circuit.
Jem would have seen to the horses — the stable was quiet, a warmth and a soft sound of breathing from behind the closed doors.
The yard gate was bolted.
The coal store locked.
I looked up at the second floor.
Bridget's window had a light behind it, a low steady one, not a candle guttering but the lamp she kept by the chair.
The shape of her behind the glass, watching the yard the way she watched it.
I had seen it too many times for it to need acknowledgment.
I turned back toward the inn.
The cut on my index finger had opened again — the edge of the chandler's delivery note, that morning, a small thing I had not noticed until now.
My hands at the end of a working day: reddened from cold water and the cleaning, the knuckles dry.
The cut was not deep.
I went inside.
The letter was on the table in the kitchen, where Nan had put the afternoon's post when it came.
I had walked past it twice in the evening's business without looking at it properly, which was a choice of a kind, though not one I would have admitted to at the time.
I looked at it now.
Stainforth's seal.

His handwriting on the direction, the particular way he made the capitals — the D of Dale with a hard downstroke and a loop that showed a man who had learned to write from a clerk who valued formality.
I had seen that handwriting on three letters in the past eighteen months.
I knew what each one had said and I knew what the pattern of them meant.
I picked it up.
It was heavier than the previous ones, which meant either enclosures or more pages, and I could not decide which of these was worse.
I turned it over.
The seal was unbroken, red wax, the small crest he used for correspondence he considered formal.
He considered all correspondence with me formal.
I had known this letter was coming.

I had known it since the last rent quarter, when his man had come in person rather than by post to collect and had spent slightly longer than necessary in the taproom — long enough to count the tables, assess the custom, look at the state of the yard.
I had been moving faster ever since.
The ledger, the chandler's margin, the half-dozen small savings of the past six weeks: all of it directed at the same thing, which was the question of what I could show him and what I could not.
I set the letter back on the table.
I would not open it tonight.
I knew what I knew and tomorrow I would know the rest of it.
Tonight there was no more to be done and opening it would not change any calculation I had not already made.
I looked at it sitting there on the table with its seal up and his handwriting facing the ceiling.
"Well," I said to the empty kitchen.
"There it is, then."
The fire had gone to coals.
I went upstairs to bed.
THE LAST RETREAT
Chapter One: The White Hound
The range took the kindling well.
I added coal, adjusted the damper, and had the first kettle on before the light outside had done much more than suggest itself through the kitchen window.
October had come in cold this year -- the kind that settled into the flagstones before dawn and stayed all day, working up through the soles of your boots while you went about your business.
I had learned not to remark on it.
The guests did enough of that for everyone.
Jem was already in the yard when I went out to check the bread delivery.

He was working along the near wheel of the post-chaise that had come in late the previous night, running his one hand slowly around the rim, and the set of his jaw told me everything I needed to know about the axle pin before he'd said a word.
He looked up when he heard the yard door.
"Before it goes out again," I said.
"Aye."
He turned back to the wheel.
That was settled.
The bread had been left on the step rather than in the cool-box, which meant the delivery boy had come before full light and been in a hurry to be somewhere else.
Two of the four loaves had gone soft at the bottom from the wet cobbles.
I carried them inside and stood them near the range to firm up, which was not the same as fresh but was better than nothing, and better-than-nothing was most of what the day was made of.
The larder: cream enough for the morning round, salt beef that would stretch through a full dinner service if the noon coach ran half-empty, three dozen eggs, a round of hard cheese still good.
I pulled the ledger from under the bread crock -- where I'd left it the night before after the last figures -- and looked at it for thirty seconds.
The numbers were exactly what they'd been at midnight, which was to say not what I needed them to be.
I put the ledger back and went to wake Nan.
She was half-dressed, sitting on the edge of her cot with one boot on and the other in her hand, eyes open but not particularly engaged with anything.
Seven years, and she still woke badly.
I'd stopped expecting otherwise.
"Noon coach may run early," I told her.
Whether it would or not, I didn't yet know.
But it was easier to give her the extra lead than to have her still blinking when the first passengers came through the door wanting hot water and someone to agree that the roads were a disgrace.
"Mm," she said, and fitted on her boot.
The morning had its own momentum after that.
I had the porridge up, the dining room set, and the first water carried before any of the overnight guests stirred.
The inn ran best when it was a little ahead of itself -- when there was already bread on the board and the fire laid before anyone thought to ask.
My mother had called it being ready before the need.
She'd never quite explained how you developed the instinct for it.
I'd worked it out on my own eventually: the need always arrived; the only question was whether you arrived first.
It was a coaching inn on the Great North Road, which meant the day ran on other people's schedules and not its own.
The White Hound sat at the point where southbound coaches began to think about London and northbound coaches began to think about everything London wasn't.

This put it in the position of serving travellers who were either relieved to have come this far or anxious to go further, and who expressed both emotions through complaints about the roads and the quality of the ale.
The roads were the roads.
The ale was good.
I had said both things so many times that they had stopped feeling like sentences and become something more like general policy.
At half past nine the morning coach from London came through the gate.
It was twelve minutes late by the yard clock and a full twenty minutes late by the coachman's estimate of what twenty minutes meant to his afternoon schedule.
He told me this at some length while I oversaw the unloading.
His name was Burrell.
I knew him by sight -- a capable, practical man who ran a clean vehicle and had never in four years given me cause for complaint, which I kept in mind while he finished.
"I'm not disputing the road," I said.
"The section past Woolmer Green was seen to last week.
You'll make the time up."
He looked at me, deciding whether to argue about it.
He decided not.
"Aye, well.
Twenty minutes, then."
"Fifteen," I said.
"The horses are rested and it's dry from here."
He went to see about his horses.
Jem, who had materialized near the mounting block in the way he had of appearing where he was needed without anyone having asked him to be there, caught my eye and did not quite smile.
The trunk situation was separate.

One of the passengers -- a thin man in a good coat and an expression suggesting the world had recently arranged itself against him -- was standing at a careful distance from the luggage, watching the unloading as though proximity might make things worse.
His trunk had split at the right hinge, not from any negligence on this yard's part but from age and damp and the particular violence of the Hatfield road after a night of rain.
"The contents," he said, in the direction of no one in particular.
"Will be fine," I said.
"The trunk needs tying.
It'll hold till your destination.
If it won't, I'll tell you before you leave."
He opened his mouth.

"I will tell you before you leave," I said again, pleasantly, and turned back to where Jem was already producing rope from somewhere about his person with the efficiency of a man who'd done this before.
The other short-tempered passenger was a woman travelling with three bandboxes and a conviction that the morning had been personally organised to inconvenience her.
She required hot tea, a warm room, and someone to agree that the roads were a disgrace.
Nan handled this.

I could hear her from the yard: patient, agreeable, delivering the tea and the room and the agreement in a tone so steady it was impossible to tell whether she actually concurred or had simply declined to provide resistance.
She was very good at that.
I had wondered occasionally whether she'd been born with it or whether the inn had made her.

By the time I'd seen the coach off, reset the dining room, and made a note of the smithy trip Jem had made at his own expense to replace the axle pin -- these things vanished from the week's reckoning if you didn't write them down immediately -- it was past eleven, and Heddle was coming down the lane.

He had supplied tallow candles to the White Hound for eleven years, three under my mother and eight under me, and every quarter he arrived with his invoice and a face arranged in an expression of regret about the prices, as though the prices were something that happened to him rather than something he set.
He put the invoice on the kitchen table with the air of a man delivering news he'd had no part in creating.
I looked at it.
I had a fair idea what it would say.
"Price per dozen is up again," he said, before I could speak.
"Tallow's been dear all quarter.
I'm told it'll ease come—"
"It was dear last quarter," I said.
"And the quarter before."
I turned the invoice to face him.
"At your current price, I'm paying a third again what Fowler's is charging the Goat at Royston."
He went still.
"Fowler's."
"I had their invoice in my hand Tuesday week."
This was true.
A guest had left it behind in room seven, and I had, in fact, held it.
"Fowler's candles aren't the same quality.
Their wick sits crooked in the mould -- anyone who's burned one will tell you.
The burn rate alone—"
"Heddle."
I waited.
"I'm not disputing your quality.
I'm telling you what the market bears, which you know as well as I do.
Better, probably."
I slid the invoice back toward him.
"One shilling and four a dozen.
Same as July.
That's what I'll pay."
He looked at the invoice.
He looked at me.
He had a particular way of calculating that I'd watched him do for years -- working out whether the principle of the thing was worth what it would cost him in custom if I started sending to Fowler's.
"One and five," he said.
"Can't do it for less."
"One and four, Heddle."
A silence.
He folded the invoice.
Put it back in his coat.
"You're a hard woman, Miss Dale."
"My mother was harder," I said.
"Candles on Thursday, if you please."
He went.

I stood at the kitchen window for a moment and watched him cross the yard, and thought about the ledger, and about the quarter-rent due at the end of November, and about six weeks being exactly as long as it needed to be and not much longer.
Then the kitchen door opened and Nan came through with a stack of clean glasses.
"The woman in room four wants to know if we do laundry," she said, setting them on the side table.
"We don't."
"I told her."
She picked the glasses back up.
"Also the gentleman in room two has lost his boot hook and would like to borrow one."
A pause.
"And he asked if I was local."
"What did you say?"
"That the boot hook was in the stand by the door."
She went back out.
I heard her in the corridor, and I heard the particular rhythm of her footsteps that meant she was privately amused.
The afternoon went as afternoons went.

The ledger gained seven more entries by two o'clock: rooms let, a dinner booking for six at the large table, a bottle of port charged at full rate to a gentleman who'd had the air of expecting a reduction and hadn't been offered one.
I found Jem straightening the hitching rail in the yard for no reason anyone had given him, noticed Nan wiping down the bar with one eye consistently on the door.
This was how the inn worked when it was working: without instruction, without ceremony, each person doing slightly more than their stated role and none of them drawing attention to it.
I had built nothing, I sometimes thought.
I had simply not let it fall apart.
My mother would have had a better answer for what the place was.
She had words for most things.
I had been in such a hurry to learn the work itself that I had not always listened carefully enough to the rest, and then there was no one left to ask.
The noon coach came through at twenty past twelve and ran six passengers, which was reasonable for October.
Nan had the dining room ready before they were through the door.
I watched her work for a moment from the kitchen passage -- the way she could track three separate requests without writing anything down, the way she refilled a cup before the guest thought to ask.
My mother had taught her that.
Or possibly the inn had, which was the same thing.
Outside, from the upper corridor window, Bridget's rooms were quiet.
The lamp near her window made a steady light behind the glass.
In the taproom, at half past three, there was a moment that required my presence.
Two men at the bench nearest the chimney.
One of them -- stout, red-faced, not a man given to fighting but not opposed to it either, in the right circumstances -- had taken exception to something the other had said.
The other was younger, with the particular alert look of someone who found other people's irritation useful entertainment.
Whatever had passed between them had reached the point where the first man's shoulders were up and his cup was in his hand rather than on the table.
I walked to the end of the bar and stood where both of them would see me without having to look for me.
Neither of them said anything for a moment.
"Another pint," I said to the first man, making it a practical observation rather than a question.
"And then the road, I'd think.
Light goes early now."
His shoulders came down a fraction.
"Aye," he said.
"Road."
The younger man found something to look at on the wall.
I poured the pint, set it down, and went back to the kitchen.
I didn't hear anything more from that end of the taproom for the rest of the afternoon.
He came to the back door just before four.

I heard the knock and thought it was the delivery boy back for the basket, but when I opened the door it was a young man -- twenty, perhaps, or younger -- in a coat that had done two or three years' more service than it should have, with boots that had come apart at the right welt and been wrapped round with rag to hold them together.
He was thin in the way that comes from weeks of it rather than constitution.
He held his hat in both hands and looked at me without saying anything.
"Have you eaten today?"
I asked.
"This morning."
"What did you eat this morning?"
A slight pause.
"Not much."
"The kitchen door is around the back of the yard," I said.
"I'll leave it on the latch.
Come in through there and sit at the table on the near side -- not the taproom."
I stepped back from the door.
"Two minutes."

I went back in through the dining room, told Nan I'd be in the kitchen for a quarter-hour, and put together what there was: bread, a good heel of the cheese, a bowl of the midday broth that was still on the back of the range.
I set it at the table by the back door and found a reason to busy myself with the larder hinge, which had been wanting attention since Tuesday and was not improved by waiting.
I wasn't ignoring him.
Men who'd been on the road that long ate better when there was no one watching.
When I came back to the table, the bowl was half-empty and he was eating the bread the way you do when you're trying not to finish everything at once.
His coat was on the peg behind him.
There was a regimental button still on the cuff -- just the one, which was what they left a man when they mustered him out.
He looked up when I came to refill the bowl.
"There's no need—"
"There's broth going to waste," I said, and went back to the hinge.
He finished.
I heard the chair, the peg as he lifted his coat.
He'd straightened himself to something close to attention by the time I turned around.
"Thank you," he said, and he meant it the way you only mean things when you've had to say them more often than you'd like.
"The road goes easier on a full stomach," I said.
"Keep to the main turnpike past Stevenage -- not the old track.
It's drier this time of year."
He filed this as directions, with a brief nod that was almost a salute.
Then he went out through the back.
I listened to his footsteps cross the yard -- steady, even, a man who knew how to keep a pace going -- and then fade toward the road.
I stood for a moment in the kitchen.
Then I went back to the taproom.
Nan was behind the bar with the cloth she kept under the ledge, one eye on the door as she always kept it.
She said nothing about the broth and the bread.
She knew the arithmetic as well as I did -- what the kitchen could spare and what it couldn't -- and she had never once commented on the soldiers I fed when I was able.
This was how Nan showed she agreed with something: by not mentioning it.

The dinner service ran for two hours and was as uneventful as a dinner service ever was, which meant there was only one genuine difficulty -- a dispute at the far table over the Rhenish versus the claret, settled in the way these things always settled, which was to bring both and charge for the one consumed.
Nan managed the floor; I managed the kitchen.

By the time the last cover was cleared it was past eight, and the taproom had settled to its end-of-day register: fire low, three men finishing their last cups, the sound of Jem putting the yard to bed outside.
I came through with the last of the cloths and found Nan at the bar pulling on her coat.
"Feet?"
I said.
"Done for since half six."
She was tying her cap.
She looked at me, and something in her face softened the way it sometimes did at the end of a long day -- the professional surface worn through to what was underneath it.
"You should eat something," she said.
"Not just the standing and looking at things."
"Same tomorrow," I said.
She went up.
I bolted the bar.
The locking-up took forty minutes.

My body knew the route without my having to direct it: taproom bolts, back door bolts, the latch on the yard gate that needed a lift and a push before it caught, the cellar hatch, the kitchen window that had swelled in the damp and required the flat of my hand to seat properly.
The dining room shutters.
The three ground-floor rooms that would sit empty tonight.

Upstairs, the corridor lamp turned low, and then the listening pause outside each occupied room -- nothing, nothing, nothing -- which I didn't truly believe was necessary but did anyway, because my mother had done it and her mother before her, and some habits were not worth breaking even after you'd forgotten why you'd started them.
At the top of the stairs I stopped.
Down the corridor, behind the door at the end, Aunt Bridget's light was still on -- the thin line of it under the door, steady and orange in the draught.
She would be in her chair by the window.

She would have heard the last coach leave and the sequence of locks going round, and she would know I was standing at the top of the stairs, and I would know she was there, and that was the whole of the exchange between us most nights.
It was enough.
I went back downstairs.
My hands, in the last of the kitchen lamplight, looked their age.
The right index finger had a paper cut from Heddle's invoice -- I hadn't noticed it in the afternoon, but it was making itself known now in the cold.
Reddened at the knuckles, rough at the palms, the kind of hands that came from this building and this work and no other life.
I looked at them the way you look at a familiar thing when you're too tired to look away.
Then I dried them and put the cloth to dry.
I opened the ledger to today's page one more time: the rooms, the service, the private lets, what I'd recovered from Heddle on the candles.
On the credit side, it was a reasonable day.
On the other side was the quarter-rent, due at the end of November.
Six weeks, more or less.

Six weeks in which nothing could go wrong that I couldn't fix before it got expensive, in which the inn needed to run at full rate or near it, in which I needed to find a version of the answer to the Stainforth question that I did not yet have.
I closed the ledger.
The letter was on the corner of the table.
I'd set it there when the afternoon post came in, meaning to open it before dinner, and then the dinner service had started and there it had sat.
Four hours now.
Stainforth's seal.

I knew it without looking closely -- the particular dark red of the wax, the impression of the signet ring, the handwriting on the direction precise and unhurried in the way of a man with time to write carefully and who wanted you to know it.
The letter was heavier than a single sheet.
He had things he wished to put into words.
I already knew what he wanted to discuss.
I had known since the last rent quarter.
Since the meeting in Stevenage, since the look that had passed between his steward and his man of business before anyone had said anything to me directly.
I had been keeping the knowing at arm's length -- the way you hold a bad tooth, not pressing on it except when you forgot to be careful.
I pressed on it now.
The letter was in my hands.
I turned it over.
The seal intact, the wax unbroken.
Stainforth's handwriting on the front: Miss D.
Dale, The White Hound Inn, Great North Road, Hertfordshire.
He wished to discuss the terms of her lease.
He wished to meet at a time of her convenience to discuss the terms of her lease.
"Well," I said, to the kitchen, to the dark window and the dying fire and no one at all.
"There it is."
I put the letter in my apron pocket and took the lamp to the stairs.
In the morning I would read it -- or tonight, after an hour's sleep, when I was better prepared to keep my face from doing anything I'd later regret.

Either way the contents would be the same, and either way the inn would open tomorrow, and the range would want banking, and the delivery boy would leave the bread on the wet step if I didn't watch for him.
The work would still be there.
It always was.
That had always been the part I could count on.
I went upstairs.
In the yard below, the gate latch held.
The stable doors were shut.
Somewhere on the road going north, a man with a rag-wrapped boot was putting miles behind him.
I did not open the letter that night.
CHAPTER ONE: THE WHITE HOUND
The coaching house wants to be up before you are.
My mother said this so often it stopped being instruction and became something else -- a sound the inn made, telling you what it needed.
By five in the morning I had the taproom fire stoked, the tap handles wiped of the condensation that October nights leave on metal, and the kitchen range drawing clean.
Jem was in the yard.
Not his words -- I never heard his words at that hour -- but the low register of sound that meant settle, and the horses were settling.
I don't know when he sleeps.
I've never asked.
By half past five the bread was proving.
The kitchen smelled like something worth getting up for, which is more than could be said for a good deal else in late October 1816.
I opened the ledger from the previous day -- eleven guests, three private suppers, taproom trade slightly down on last Tuesday -- and added the coal.
We were running lower than I'd like.
In the margin I wrote stable wall?
because Jem had said something about it settling, and then I closed the ledger because the numbers were the same as yesterday and looking at them a second time was not going to make them better.
The inn in the early morning is a different place from the inn at noon.
At noon it is performing.
Before six it is simply itself: cold flagstones, the smell of last night's tallow and yesterday's fire, every room doing what rooms do when there is nobody in them.
I have been up at this hour since I was old enough to carry a tray, and I have come to the conclusion that the White Hound does not particularly need me before six.
It is managing perfectly well.
But the fire needs banking, and the range needs drawing, and if I am not there to do these things then Nan will do them, and Nan has enough to do.
Nan came down at six, still pinning her cap, her hair mounting its usual early-morning protest.
"The man in room four wants his breakfast brought up," she said.
"Room four eats in the dining room."
"I told him.
He said it had been a long journey."
"They all say that."
I handed her the bread knife.
"Send him down."
She didn't argue.
Seven years had shown her what an inn run on exceptions looks like, and she didn't like what it looked like.
The man from room four came down and ate his breakfast in the dining room with everyone else, though he gave me the look of a man composing a letter to someone.
I wished him a pleasant stay and went to see about the deliveries.
The morning settled into its working shape.

By eight I had seen the butcher, revised the linen count, spoken to the laundress about Thursday, and walked the ground floor with the eye I give it every morning: not looking for something wrong, exactly, but maintaining the kind of familiarity that means wrong announces itself before it becomes expensive.
The front stair had a loose tread.
The parlour window had started to rattle in the east wind -- sash cording going.
The kitchen tap dripped with particular emphasis when the cold came.
None of these were disasters.
All of them were on my list.

Outside, the yard was straight and swept, and Jem was straightening it further -- a length of rope coiled and hung, a bucket pushed flush against the wall, small adjustments nobody had asked for and that would have gone undone if they had been.
He worked like a man who has decided the world requires a certain order and has taken personal responsibility for enforcing it.
I have never told him I notice this.
It would embarrass him, and there is something in the noticing that feels private, the way it's private to watch someone who doesn't know they're being watched do something honest.
Above the yard, the window on the second floor had been lit since before I came down.
Bridget was up there.
She didn't sleep early -- she sat in her chair by the window and watched, and I had long since stopped wondering what she made of what she saw.
I knew she was there by the light: a pale square in the upstairs dark, steady, neither inviting nor dismissing.
She had her reasons for most things.
She usually declined to explain them.
The London coach came in at half past nine, late, and loud about it.
The coachman was named Fawkes, and I had dealt with him three times a week for four years.
He came off the box with the deliberate movement of a man who has been rehearsing a grievance since Welwyn and is ready to deliver it.
"North road's bad past Baldock.
Ruts want filling before the frosts or I'm writing to the company about the route."
"Write to them," I said.
"How many stopping?"
"Two.
The Southwick party's going through to York, fresh horses only.
The rest -- woman with a bad back and a gentleman with something to say about his luggage."
The luggage was a trunk on the ground, its hinge split along the brass fitting.
The man standing over it had the compressed expression of someone deciding whether he had been wronged.
"The road does that," Fawkes said.
"I'll have Jem look at it."
I said this to close the conversation, which is most of what an innkeeper does -- close conversations before they expand into things that take up the afternoon.
The gentleman was watching to see whether he was going to be attended to, and the answer was yes, because the alternative was him standing in my yard composing that letter.
I called Jem over.
He spent thirty seconds examining the hinge, another thirty producing rope from somewhere about his person, and had the trunk lashed in a way that would hold to London and probably back again.
The gentleman did not thank him.
He picked up his bag, said something to the woman with the bad back about it being perfectly simple, and went inside.
Fawkes was watching.
"Cheerful party," he said.
"Fresh horses at two.
Go and eat, Fawkes."
He went.
The woman with the bad back turned out to be a Mrs.
Carver, from Sleaford, who required tea, a room, and a listener for the road.
I provided the first two.
For the third I positioned Nan, who can arrange her face into the expression of a woman genuinely interested in road conditions between Hatfield and Baldock.
I cannot make this face.
I have tried.
"How do you do that?"
I asked Nan afterward, when Mrs.
Carver had been installed with her tea.
"I think about supper," she said.
"It's not difficult."
Hodges arrived at ten.

The chandler came three times a year with his invoice tucked into his coat and his hat in his hand, and every time he came we had the same negotiation, which was not exactly the same negotiation because every time I had done more preparation for it than the time before.

My mother had first caught him in a short measure the winter I was twelve, in front of his assistant, which had done nothing for our warmth but had established the terms: he knew I counted everything, I knew what a tallow candle cost him to produce, and neither of us wasted the other's time pretending otherwise.
"Two shillings the dozen," he said, when we were settled at the kitchen table.
"Same as last quarter."
"One and ten," I said.
"Six-month agreement."
"I can't do one and ten.
The tallow's up."
"The tallow price from Stevenage market dropped in September.
I had it from the merchant last week."
This was true.
I had made a point of having it from the merchant, specifically so I could say it now.
Hodges turned his hat in his hands, which was his way of buying time while he worked out how much he needed the White Hound's account.
It was considerable.

We buy more candles in a quarter than he sells to most customers in a year, and he knew it, and I knew he knew it, and we both understood that we were performing a calculation that had already been done.
"One and eleven," he said.
"One and ten, six months."
He put his hat on.
"Done."
Not graciously, but done.
I walked him to the door.

He held out the invoice and I took it from him, and the corner of the paper was sharp enough to catch the knuckle of my index finger where the nail meets the skin -- a thin bright line of red, immediate.
I folded the invoice and put it in my apron pocket without looking at him.
"Good morning, Mr.
Hodges," I said.
He said good morning, and left.
I held my hand under the kitchen pump until the cold water stopped the bleeding.
The water was very cold.
October does this to everything -- the pump, the cellar stones, the metal fittings on the doors.

By the end of the day my hands would be reddened from it, from the pump and the cellar and the washing up, and the cut would open again if I pressed on it, which I would do occasionally without thinking.
I dried them and went back to work.
The chandler had agreed to one and ten.
I wrote it in the margin of the accounts next to where I had written his name, and below it I wrote: six months.
This was the morning's work.
There would be an afternoon's work after it, and an evening's after that, and tomorrow would want the same things today had wanted, and I would give them.
The taproom ran hot between noon and two.

There was the regular trade -- two carriers, the solicitor's clerk who came Tuesdays and Thursdays and ordered the same meal both days, a merchant who wanted the private room and settled for the corner -- and a near-altercation that began as a remark about the northbound service and was looking to become something involving furniture if I didn't cross the room.
I crossed the room.
"Gentlemen."
Neither of them looked at me.
I said it again in the other voice -- the one my mother used the night she turned two drovers back from the kitchen with six words and a look.
I practiced it for years before I trusted it.
When I trusted it, I stopped needing it quite as often, which I expect is how these things work.
The carrier looked at me.
The gentleman looked at me.
"Your horses will be ready in twenty minutes," I told the gentleman.
To the carrier: "Your next drink is on the house.
Sit down."
The carrier sat.
The gentleman deliberated for a moment about whether to be offended by being managed, decided against it, and went back to his table.
Nan, who had been watching from the bar with one hand on a pewter jug of perfectly serviceable weight and dimension, put the jug down.
She didn't say anything.
Neither did I.
We moved on.
The soldier came to the back door at three.
I saw him through the kitchen window before he knocked.

He was young -- not as young as he looked, probably, but the kind of thin that makes a man look younger, the kind you get from being marched lean and not having had enough time since to become anything else.

His coat had started out decent -- the cut was military issue, or had been -- and his boots were cracked along the welt in the particular way that means another few weeks and no cobbler will touch them.
He stood straight as a post and knocked and then stepped back to wait, which told me he had been doing this long enough to know you wait; you don't lean.
I opened the door.
"I'm not begging," he said, faster than he had intended to.
"No one said you were."
He had a scar along his jaw, fine and pale.
Healed at least a year.
I put him at twenty-two, possibly twenty-three, with the eyes of someone who has decided not to ask for anything and is holding to this with some effort.
"I thought there might be work," he said.
"Any kind."
There wasn't.
Jem had the yard and the stable, and the accounts didn't have room for labour we didn't need done.
I told him this plainly, because he was not a man who would be served by softening it.
"Right," he said.
He said it the way men do when they've been told the same thing enough times that surprise has stopped seeming worth the energy.
"Go around to the kitchen door," I said.
"I'll have someone bring you something."
"I told you I wasn't--"
"I heard you."
I was already turning.
"Go around."
I fed him in the kitchen, not the taproom.
This was a practical decision -- the paying guests don't need to see a vagrant soldier at the table, and the soldier doesn't need to eat in front of men who have decided he is a problem.
He ate quickly and thanked the girl who brought it without being asked, and left without taking anything that wasn't given.

I watched him cross the yard through the kitchen window, this slight figure in the cracking boots, walking toward the road at the pace of a man who has somewhere to be even if he doesn't yet know where it is.
There had been more of them since the summer -- since before the summer, since the year before that.
They came down the Great North Road in ones and twos and sometimes groups, the men the army had finished with.
They had the same quality about them regardless of how they looked or what they said: they took up slightly less space than they were entitled to.
Not cringing.
Not beaten.
Just adjusted.
Calibrated to an expectation of nothing, and managing, mostly, and occasionally not.
I fed them when I could.
