I said nothing about it to anyone except Nan and Jem, both of whom knew and both of whom said nothing about it, which is what understanding looks like when it doesn't need explaining.
My mother would have said: never trust a man who helps without being asked -- he's after something.
But she said this about a great many people, and she also died in the middle of ladling soup, so I don't hold her the final authority on all of it.
I went back to the coal order.
The cut on my index finger opened again when I pressed it against the pen.
I pressed my finger against my apron instead and let it be.
By five the light was gone and the taproom was evening trade: three farmers, a couple from the overnight stopping till morning, two locals whose names I had known for years.
Nan worked the bar.
I moved between the dining room and the kitchen -- managing the space between things, which is most of what the job amounts to.

Jem came in through the side door at his usual hour and took his usual chair by the kitchen fire and ate his usual amount without ceremony, because we had long since established that neither of us required the performance of invitation.
"Stable wall's moving," he said, when his plate was clear.
"More than last week?"
"Not more.
But it's moving."
I added it to the margin of the ledger: stable wall, watch.

The ledger was not the proper place for stable walls, but the money was in the ledger, and the stable wall would eventually become a question of money, and I found it useful to have the structural concerns and the figures in the same document so I could see the whole picture at once.
Nan's shift ended at seven.
"The couple in room three will want a warming pan," she said, collecting her things.
"She mentioned it twice, which means she'll come down and ask if nobody moves."
"I'll see to it."
She paused at the door.
"Good day?"
she said.
"Adequate.
Go home, Nan."
The door closed quietly behind her.
She does this -- leaves without a bang, without a pointed silence, just the soft click of a woman who has decided I am tired enough to be left to my own company.
She is usually right.
I locked up at nine.
Taproom door, back door, cellar hatch, stable yard gate, kitchen fire banked, front door.
The warming pan for room three, which I had nearly forgotten -- I had to backtrack to the kitchen, fill the pan, carry it up the back stairs and leave it at their door as promised.
Then the final walk through: dining room chairs pushed in, candle stubs cleared from the corner table where Nan had left them when the bar got busy, the last lamp turned down in the hall.
My mother did it in the same order.
Her mother probably did too.
There is something in the sequence that settles the day -- not into peace exactly, but into its proper shape.
Done.
The inn is what it is, and tomorrow it will need the same things, and I will provide them.
I sat down at the kitchen table with the ledger.
The numbers were the same as they had been in August.
Six weeks, give or take, before the quarter's rent became something other than a question of degree.

I had been knowing this for three months without giving it a name, which is to say I had been moving faster for three months -- cutting a price here, filling a room there, doing the laundry myself on Sundays, not replacing the serving girl who left for Hatfield.
Three months of moving faster without telling anyone, because telling someone would have made it a conversation, and conversations require the time I had been spending on the laundry.
I had not married.
This requires explanation only to people who do not understand how an inn is held.

If I married, the lease passed to my husband under coverture -- the lease, the income, the business my grandmother had built, the business my mother had kept standing through a war and a bad harvest and my father's best efforts to drink the cellar dry.
Two proposals I had declined, and the third man had not asked when he worked out why the first two had been.
I did not consider this a tragedy.
I considered it the terms of the situation.

But the terms of the situation meant that if I needed capital -- needed it the way you need it when the rent comes due and the numbers are six weeks and the weather is turning -- there was no husband to borrow it from, no family money beyond what the inn produced, and the inn produced what it produced and not more.
My grandmother ran this inn alone for twenty years.
My mother ran it alone for fourteen.
The fact of having run it alone for eleven did not feel like a number I was adding to; it felt like a fact about what I was.
The way the breed of a horse is a fact about the horse.
The inn was quiet.
Above me, to the left, the pale candlelight in Bridget's window.
She would be in her chair.
Earlier, passing her door, I had heard the small sounds of a woman entirely at ease with her own company -- the rustle of a page, the faint clink of her glass.
She had not called for me.
I had not knocked.
There was an understanding between us about evenings, which was that the evenings were mine.
I was writing the coal order figure into the margin when I remembered the hall table.
I had not looked at the post since eleven o'clock.
It was sitting on the hall table where the boy had left it in the morning -- a small stack held down by the brass weight my mother kept there for this purpose.
I picked it up on my way back from checking the front door lock and brought it to the kitchen and sorted it at the table: butcher's bill, a note from Mr.
Gaines about a December booking, two circulars, and then the last one.
The seal was Stainforth's.
I knew it before I turned the letter over -- the weight of the paper, the quality of it, the seal pressed deep.
Phineas Stainforth, our landlord, had been writing to this address since before I was born, and I had been reading his letters for eleven years.
I knew his handwriting the way I knew the sound the stable gate made in the east wind.
I set the other letters aside.
I held his letter for a moment without opening it.
The fire had burned down to coals.
From somewhere in the house, nothing -- just the sound an inn makes when it's asleep, which is not silence but a settled, working quiet.
He wished, the letter said, to discuss the terms of her lease.
I read it twice.
I didn't need to.

I had been expecting this letter since August -- since the last rent quarter, since the summer when I had noticed Stainforth in longer conversation with the estate agent from St Albans than the usual business between landlord and agent required.

I had been knowing it was coming the way you know a bad winter from the way October feels in your hands: not proof, exactly, but a particular weight in the air that keeps informing you of its intention.
I had been moving faster since August because of it.
I had not given it a name because naming it would have made it real in the way it was now real -- his handwriting, his seal, the paper in my reddened hands.
The inn was quiet around me.
Eleven years of evenings at this table, with this ledger, in this kitchen.
My grandmother's kitchen before it was my mother's and my mother's before it was mine.
The floor flagstones were worn in the same places they had been worn when I was a child carrying trays across them: a path from the range to the table, a path from the table to the door.
The weight of three women's working days, ground into stone.
Stainforth wished to discuss the terms of her lease.
"Right," I said.
To the kitchen.
To the empty chair across the table.
To nobody at all -- just to hear something in the quiet that wasn't the quiet.
I folded the letter and slid it under the ledger.
I put out the lamp.
I went upstairs to bed.
The fire had died overnight.
I knew what that meant before I was fully awake.
Too tired yesterday to bank it properly.
I did not dwell on yesterday.
The kitchen was dark and cold when I came down the back stairs, boots already on, hands already moving toward the hearth.
The flagstones were cold enough that I felt them through the leather soles.
Frost on the inside of the window — the second time this month, and it was only October.
The cold had been wrong since June.
I had learned not to comment on it.
I raked the ash and laid the kindling.
My hands were rough and reddened, the skin along my knuckles split where it always split when the temperature dropped.
I struck the flint twice before the tinder caught.
Good.
One thing working.
While the fire built itself, I did my scan.
Twenty rooms, all occupied at present — twelve regulars, five commercial men stopping over, three families working their way north.
The taproom hadn't been cleared properly last night, which meant Nan had been run off her feet and I hadn't noticed, which meant I needed to notice better.
Dining room serviceable.
Stabling for forty horses; we had twenty-three at the moment, Jem's domain and running cleanly.
Reputation: dependable, not grand.
Not fashionable.
Clean.
My grandmother had built it on those three words and my mother had kept it there and I intended to do the same.
The harvest had failed and the price of bread had followed it upward and I did not need a pamphlet to tell me what that meant for an inn that fed forty people a day.
The fire was drawing well now — it always did when the wind came from the north.
My mother had taught me that.
Read the sound, she'd said.
Listen to how it pulls.
She had sat at this hearth every morning for fourteen years before she sat here for the last time, and I had learned every trick of it from her.
The ledger on the table was in her hand through 1814, and mine since.
There was a groove in the edge of the counter where she had rested her thumb while she worked.
I pressed my thumb into it now without thinking about it, checking the morning's flour supply, and then I moved on.
She had died in this room.
I knew that and I used it and I did not stop to examine it the way a person might stop to examine a bruise.
I had refused two proposals in the past three years.
Both decent men.
I did not think of them as lost possibilities.
I thought of them as near misses.
One yes and the lease, the income, the business — everything my grandmother built would have belonged to a man the moment I said yes.
I was not prepared to test whether either of the two decent men would have been decent about it.
I was not prepared to test the law I did not name to myself, the one that would have handed them everything without their even asking for it.
I was aware of it the way I was aware of the cold.
A fact of the landscape.
I worked around it.
The kettle was on.
The fire was drawing.
The frost was retreating from the lower half of the window.
Upstairs, a guest coughed, turned over, went quiet.
The house was still waking.
I put the kettle on and went to see what yesterday had left me.
Dawn was grey and grudging, the sky the particular colour of old pewter, no sun visible and none expected.
I had stopped expecting sun in June.
The yard was already swept.
Jem Bowker had the lead pair harnessed and ready, moving between them with the efficiency of a man who had somewhere to be.
The right sleeve of his coat was pinned at the elbow.

The arm had been gone long enough that the work had rearranged itself around him — he had rearranged himself around the work — and it would not have occurred to me to say anything about it, and so I did not.
He had the yard swept and the horses ready and that was more than I could say for myself at this hour.
"Coach is late," he said, without turning.
"Roads."
I stood at the gate to the road.
The Great North Road stretched north and south, empty in the grey morning light.
It was not beautiful.
It was useful.

It brought everything to the inn — news, commerce, strangers, trouble — and this morning it was bringing the London coach, which was coming in late, which was fine, because I had twelve guests to get through breakfast and the kitchen girl had only just come down, and late was better than early when you were short a pair of hands.
When it came, it came fast, the driver pushing hard to make up time.
I heard it before I saw it — the rattle and the horse-noise and the particular complaint of wheels on the frozen ruts — and then it was in the yard, and the passengers were down, and we were busy.
The outside passengers were half-frozen and the first one to speak told me the road was a disgrace, as if I had laid it myself and ought to be ashamed of the work.
"Inside, please," I said.
"There's a fire."
He went.
They all went.
Jem had the horses and I had the passengers and Nan appeared at the taproom door with the look on her face that meant the kitchen was already behind.
Nan Soulden was twenty-one, quick and freckled and sharp-eyed, and she was the only other person in this building who worked as hard as I did.
She would have run her own establishment, if the world had been otherwise.
I had thought this before and I thought it again and filed it where I filed all the things I could not presently fix.
She deserved better than running herself ragged in someone else's kitchen before sunrise.
There was a novel tucked behind the bar — I caught the spine of it as I came through the taproom with a party of four and a request for hot breakfast.
Borrowed, by the look of it, the cover worn soft.
I noticed it.
I moved on.
I had three tables to seat and the fire in the dining room needed banking and there was no time for anything that was not immediately on fire.
I looked up at the window above the stable as I crossed back through the yard.
Bridget was at her post.
She was always at her post.

Small and white-haired and dressed in the black she had worn since her second husband died and showed no signs of abandoning, she sat in her chair at the upper window with the stillness of a woman who intended to observe everything and judge most of it.
I raised a hand.
She did not wave back.
She nodded, once, with the deliberate authority of a woman who has outlived everyone who might contradict her.
Bridget had survived two husbands, five monarchs, and my mother's cooking.
If anyone was going to outlast this winter, it was her.
The chandler came at mid-morning, when the breakfast service was winding down and I had a moment to breathe.
He was a small man, apologetic by nature, and this morning he was more apologetic than usual, which told me what the invoice would say before he handed it over.
I read the figure.
I did not let my face show anything.
"The tallow," he said.
"The supplier—"
"Has raised his price."
"I'm afraid so, Mrs.
Dale."
"Miss Dale."
"Miss Dale.
Yes.
I'm sorry."
He was sorry.
He had been sorry the last time, and the time before that.
Three increases this year.
I could not prove it was deliberate.

I had nothing to prove it with, only the pattern of it, which was the kind of evidence that would not stand in a courtroom and would not interest a magistrate and would not help me get through the winter on what was left in the strongbox.
I haggled.
He was apologetic but firm — costs were costs, his margins were thin, what could he do.
I got him down sixpence per dozen on the best wax tapers and a promise on the next delivery, which was not enough but was something.
He left.
I paid from the strongbox and recorded the amount in the ledger.
The column was not going in a direction I liked.
I had done this arithmetic before, in the summer, when I'd thought I understood how thin the margins were.
The summer had since disabused me of that notion.
The harvest failure had driven up every cost — flour, tallow, firewood, fodder.
I could survive the winter if nothing else went wrong.
The if sat in the accounts column like a debt I hadn't finished paying.
I put the ledger away.
The taproom needed wiping down and there was a delivery of firewood expected before noon.
The trouble started at half past one.
I heard the chair go over from the kitchen.
A very particular sound — not the slow tip of a chair that someone is leaning in, but the sharp crack of furniture moved by sudden force.
I was through the taproom door before the second shout.
Two commercial men.
Red-faced, both of them, one standing and one who had been in the knocked-over chair and was now getting up from the floor.
Cards on the table.
Ale cups.
A small pile of coins that was apparently the point of dispute.
I walked into the middle of it.
"Sit down," I said.
My voice was flat and certain and did not leave room for debate.
I had been doing this since I was old enough to carry a tray.
I had learned the voice from my mother, who had learned it from hers.
Both men sat.

The one who'd been standing — large, red-neckclothed, the kind of man who expected his size to do most of his arguing for him — looked at me with an expression that suggested he was deciding whether I was actually in charge here.
He had a nose that had been broken at some point and reset badly.
I looked back at him.
He decided.
"The card game is over," I said.
I poured them each a half-measure of ale, set the cups down.
"On the house."
The red-neckclothed man opened his mouth.
I waited.
He closed it.
I collected the cards, tapped them into a neat stack, and put them under the bar.
Neither of them would ask for them back.
They knew, and I knew they knew, and that was the end of it.
Nan caught my eye as I came around the bar.
One eyebrow.
I read it as something like: good, and also: that was faster than yesterday's.
I was not trembling.
My hands were busy with the cloth and the spilled ale, and that was the thing about hands — if they were busy, they could not shake.
I worked the cloth along the bar and did not look at them, and when I was done my hands had not shaken once, and that was what mattered.
The taproom went back to its ordinary noise.
He came to the back door at half past four, when the light was already failing.
That told me what I needed to know before I saw his face.
The men who came to the front door wanted lodging and could pay.
The men who came to the back door wanted food and could not.
I read the door.
Thin, dirty, recently discharged.
Not dangerous.
I could tell — I had been doing this for two years, since Waterloo had ended and the men it had used up had started appearing at back doors all over England.
Some had the coiled look of men you didn't turn your back on.
This one had the empty, bewildered look of a man who had walked out of the army and into nothing, and found nothing very difficult to navigate.
I did not sentimentalize him.
I fed him.
Bread and broth from the kitchen pot, which was yesterday's and still good.
I sat him at the kitchen table — the scrubbed oak table where I did my accounts and ate my meals and had sat with my mother while she taught me the books — and I let him eat.
He did not speak much.
I did not ask him questions.
The fire was good by then, the kitchen warm, and the steam from the broth went up in the good quiet way of a room doing its work.
His boots were army-issue and nearly worn through, the stitching along the left sole coming apart.
I noticed boots.
It was a habit.
He left when he'd eaten, thanking me in a way that suggested he was not used to having to thank people for things and found it uncomfortable.
I watched him walk back toward the Great North Road until the grey swallowed him.
There were more of them every week.
The war was over and the men it had used up were walking home, except most of them had no home to walk to.
I went back inside.
I washed the bowl.
The last guest settled just after ten.
I did the rounds: each room, door handle checked, fire banked.
Tap on the door of Room Four, where the family with the young children were staying; quiet inside.
Room Eight, the commercial man who snored; already at it.
I counted twelve rooms occupied and eight empty and locked the corridor doors at both ends.
The evening takings were counted twice, once at the bar and once at the kitchen table.
I recorded them in the ledger.
The figure was adequate.
Not good, not bad — the word I kept reaching for was adequate, and adequate was what I had.
My boots were pinching.
They had been pinching since July, the left heel particularly, the leather going at the seam.
I considered whether I could afford new ones.
I could not.
I shifted my weight and moved on.
The inn settled into itself.
The last creak of a floorboard, somewhere on the first floor — a guest turning over, nothing more.
Jem coughing once in the stable, the deep productive cough of a man who had been coughing the same cough every winter for the twelve years I had known him.
The rooks settling in the oak behind the yard, quarrelsome and loud and then suddenly quiet in the way they went quiet, all at once, as if someone had given a signal.
I stood at the kitchen window for a moment before I sat down with the ledger.
The Great North Road was empty and dark.
No coach due until morning.
A half-moon struggling through the clouds gave enough light to show the mud ruts and the bare hedgerows and the stretch of nothing that went north until it got somewhere worth going.
Winter was not here yet but close enough that I could taste it in the air, the particular bite of it, the smell of frost coming.
I sat down at the table.
It was a good table.

My grandmother's table — solid oak, the top worn smooth by decades of accounts and meals and elbows, one end darker where the morning light came through the window, one leg replaced some years ago with a slightly lighter wood that had never quite matched.
My candle threw a circle of light that reached the ledger and the ink pot and not much further.
The room went dark around the edges.
My mother had done this.
Sat here, after the house was quiet, and counted the day's earnings and planned tomorrow's provisions.
She had done it alone for fourteen years.
I had done it for two.
It was not the same and I did not think about why.
I closed the ledger.
I banked the kitchen fire.
I put the ink pot away.
Nan found me before I could get to the stairs.
She came through the taproom door with the last of the evening post in her hands, the letters that had come in on the late coach and waited for sorting until there was a moment.
She had been sorting them, her expression neutral and businesslike, until she reached the last one.
Her hand lingered on the paper.
She knew the seal.
I took the letter from her.
"Good night, Nan."
"Good night, Miss Dale."
She left.
I did not look at the letter until she was gone.
Stainforth.
The impression of the seal in red wax, his family crest, the S I could have identified at forty paces.
My body registered it before my mind had time to construct a useful thought about it.
Something went flat and cold in my chest, settling like a stone.
My thumb pressed the edge of the paper, too hard, and I felt the corner crease under it.
I did not open it.
I was too tired.
I knew — not the contents, but what it would contain.
Stainforth wanted to discuss the terms of my lease.
Discussing the terms of my lease was what Stainforth did when he meant to take it.
Not tonight.
I would not read it tonight.

I would read it tomorrow, when I had slept and could think clearly, and I would make a plan, and the plan would work because it would have to work, and there was nothing to be gained by standing in a cold kitchen in the dark staring at a piece of paper I had decided not to open.
I set the letter on the table, beside the ledger.
I went upstairs.
The kitchen held the quiet.
The fire was banking down, the embers going orange and then darker, casting their slow uncertain light across the table.
The ledger in its place.
The letter, unopened, Stainforth's seal showing dull red in the dying light.
The candle guttering in the draught from under the door.
The inn breathed around it.
Waiting.
The coach arrived twenty minutes behind the hour and two passengers short.
I counted heads at the door, adjusted the room list in my head, and turned to the coachman before the horses had stopped stamping.
"Late above Hatfield?"
I said.
"Road's broken past the mill.
Stone's gone into the ditch on the east side."
He pulled off his hat and turned it in his hands.
"Someone'll lose a wheel before January if it isn't filled."
"I'll send word to the surveyor."
It was the second time he had told me; the surveyor had done nothing the first time either, but that was not Holt's concern.
"Thank you."
He nodded and went to the horses.
I moved to the passengers.
The first, a stout man in a blue coat, came off the step without difficulty and went straight past me toward the dining room, which was his right.
The second came down more slowly.
He was somewhere near thirty and his expression had been set into displeasure long before the coach had pulled into the yard.
He stood on the cobbles and watched his servant lift a trunk from the boot.
"The hinge is split," he said.
"I see it."
One corner had come apart and the lid sat crooked.
"Is the lock holding?"
"For now."
"Jem," I said, without looking behind me.
Jem was already there.
He took the trunk from the servant, shifted it upright, and looped a length of rope twice around it from his coat pocket, without being asked and without hurrying.
The passenger watched this.
Some of the displeasure left his face.
"That will hold it until we can have the hinge properly fixed," I said.
"Depending on how long you're staying, I can have the smith look at it this afternoon."
"I'm stopping two nights."
"Then it will be done before you leave.
We'll bear the cost."
He looked at me.
"The hinge cracked on the road."
"It cracked on one of our roads.
Good enough."
He said nothing more.
Jem took the trunk up the back stairs.
I went inside.
The dining room settled.
The blue-coated man went to a table without asking where.
The younger passenger followed at a slower pace and chose the seat nearest the fire and sat with his coat still on.

Nan moved behind the bar with her cloth, doing what she always did when something was still in the process of resolving—wiping the same foot of counter, again and again, her eyes held low enough to see everything.
I noticed it and said nothing.
There was nothing to say yet.
The chandler came just past ten.
Ferris was a civil man and I had no quarrel with him personally, which made the conversation easier in some ways and harder in others.
He set his invoice on the bar and named his price.
I looked up from the account book.
"That's fourpence a dozen above September."
"Tallow's up at market."
He spread his hands.
"The whole road's paying it."
"The Crown and Bell at Ware is not."
A pause.
"I wouldn't know what they're paying."
"Threepence above last winter is what they're paying, and they take a larger order than I do."
I closed the account book.
"September's price."
He looked at his invoice.
He looked at me.
He named a figure two pence below what he had opened with.
"September's price," I said again.
He wrote the figure.
He turned the invoice toward me to initial.
"I'll be back the first of December."
"I'll be here."
I initialed and handed it back.
He carried the crates through to the cellar himself, as he always did, and let himself out the side door.
The candles were stacked and tallied by half past ten.
I stood at the end of the bar with the account book open and found my place.

Every figure on the page was mine to hold or lose; that would not be true if I were married, because the inn would pass to a husband and with it the rent, the ledger, and the right to send the chandler away with a lower price than he had named.
I found my column and went on.
Outside in the yard, Jem was hauling water for the afternoon.
I could hear the creak of the pump handle and the slap of water against the bucket.
The younger passenger came down from upstairs with his coat off now and asked for a newspaper.
"On the table by the window," I said.
He thanked me and went.
I corrected a figure I had carried wrong from the previous week, turned the page, and began the next column.
The London coach came in forty minutes late and short by two.
Dawes called it before he had pulled the horses to a full stop.
"Picked up two at Barnet but lost the same at Hatfield," he said.
"Road's the matter above the town.
You'll want to know."
I would, but not yet.
There were passengers to settle first.
The first two came down irritable—a Mr.

Fitch, who said the road had shaken a filling loose from his back tooth, and a woman in grey wool who said nothing at all but communicated displeasure through every movement she made, from the way she descended the step to the way she looked at the yard as though it had offended her.
I gave Fitch the name of a surgeon in the town who kept decent hours and told the woman in grey that the dining room was warm and that there was a good fire and a decent ordinary.
She went without speaking.

The third passenger had a trunk with a split hinge and he came down last, holding the lid shut with one hand and wearing the face of a man who had held it shut for thirty miles and intended to hold someone responsible for that.
"This hinge was sound when I left London," he said.
I looked at the trunk.
The hinge had been pulled half off its screws, the wood around the fitting cracked through.
"Was it packed to the top?"
I said.
He looked at me as though that were beside the point.
"I can have it looked at," I said.
"There's a man in the village does good work with iron fittings.
If the wood's sound enough underneath, it's half an hour's work.
I'll send for him today.
Your belongings will be safe in the meantime—the room has a bolt."
He drew a breath to continue the objection and found he had nothing to object to.
I saw Jem come round the side of the coach—I hadn't called him, but he'd heard enough—and he took the trunk from the passenger's hands, steady and sure, and turned toward the house.
The passenger watched him go.
"Today, you said."
"Before this evening."
He went inside.
Dawes came round to me then.
He was a reliable man, had been running this road for twelve years, and he did not waste my time with preliminaries.
"Mud's got bad above Hatfield," he said.
"The rise by the old brickworks.
A coach ahead of me went to the rut to the axle and lost two hours."
"I'll write to Fairfax," I said.
Fairfax kept the road on the northern stretch.
It would do no good for three weeks but it was the right thing to do.
"Any grit laid?"
"None.
And it'll ice in another fortnight."
"All right," I said.
"I'll write today."
He nodded and then he was up and gone, and the yard was emptying.
Fitch had gone toward the town.
The woman in grey was in the dining room.
The man with the trunk was upstairs with Jem.
The horses were being walked.
I stood a moment in the yard.
Through the bar window I could see Nan moving behind the counter, wiping down glasses, restacking them on the shelf.
She had been there the whole time.
I had not called her out and she had not come.
She had watched, and that was the shape of things between us now—her watching, me handling, neither of us saying anything about it.
I went back inside.
The chandler came at eleven.
Brewster, a thin man who kept good candles and knew it, and who had raised his price three times in the past seven months.
He set his book on the bar and named his figure.
I looked at the number.
It was eight shillings more than last month.
"You're charging Whitmore at the Crown sixpence less per dozen," I said.
He did not look surprised that I knew this.
"The Crown takes a larger order."
"I take more than the Crown does between October and March, and you know it.
My winter order alone brings you two days' profit."
I moved one of the candles to look at the base.
Good tallow, tight wick, even pour.
I set it down.
"Six shillings over last month's price.
That's what I'll pay."
"Eight is fair," he said.
"The tallow's dearer."
"Six.
And I settle immediately rather than at month's end."
He picked up his book.
He looked at the entry.
He put the book down.
"Six," he said.
I wrote the amount in the ledger and he left.
The candles stayed.
I wrote the price down next to the three before it and closed the book.
The rent was due at Christmas, the ledger had to balance to the shilling, and every supplier on this road knew what a lone woman could and could not do about prices.
If I married, there would be a man's name on this ledger and a man's hand on this business and it would no longer be mine to manage as I managed it.
That was the fact at the bottom of every number in the book.
I put the pen away and went to see about the linen.
The morning coach from London arrived forty minutes late, which was twenty minutes better than the week before.
I was in the yard when I heard it on the road.
The roll of iron on stone told me: full coach, not empty.
Jem was at the gate already.
He'd worked this yard for twelve years under my mother and two under me, and he never needed telling what to do.
I went back inside to see about the fire.
The kitchen had been going since four.
Nan had laid the first breakfast sitting before I came down, which she always did and never mentioned, and the smell of the bread was thick enough that I could judge the hour by it.
I pulled the nearest loaf from the rack, weighed it, put it back.
Good.
The second needed another ten minutes.
I moved it.
"Twelve passengers," Nan said from the doorway.
She had her apron on, her dark hair tucked under her cap, the look she wore when she was counting and did not want to be interrupted.
"Driver wants something hot.
Guard's tooth has been at him since Hatfield."
"What does he expect me to do about it?"
"He expects you to care, at least."
"Send him to the kitchen."
She went.
I got the bread knife out.
The White Hound had stood on the Great North Road since my grandmother put it there.

Not strictly accurate: she had inherited a failing alehouse from a husband who hadn't known what to do with it, and turned it into a coaching inn by force of will and thirty years of four o'clock mornings.
But the effect was the same.
Twenty rooms above stairs.
A taproom that held thirty when polite and sixty when necessary.
Stabling for forty horses, though Jem preferred twenty-five and had opinions about every one of the remainder.
A kitchen that ran from four until the last coach stopped.
It was late October 1816, and the harvest was dead.
The summer had broken in June.
Frost where there should have been sun, rain where there should have been dry, a cold that had settled over England with no intention of leaving.
Every farmer between here and St Albans had said the same thing by July: failed.
Barley, wheat, turnips.
All of it.

Bread prices had gone up in August and up again in September, and the men coming down the Great North Road without work, without regiments, without anywhere to be, were thinner than they'd been even a month before.
I had not raised my prices.
I had thought about it.
The guard's tooth was bad enough that he had stopped pretending it wasn't.
He sat at the kitchen table with his jaw in his hand.
"Cloves," I said.
I put them on the table along with a measure of brandy he hadn't asked for.
"Pack it in.
It won't fix it, but it'll manage until St Albans."
"Is there anyone decent in St Albans?"
"A barber-surgeon who does teeth.
Whether he's any good at it I can't say."
He took the cloves.
He took the brandy.
He went back to his coach without saying thank you, which was fair enough.
The twelve passengers ate eggs and bread and complained about the road, which was honest of them.
The coach company had been promising repairs since spring and would not deliver until someone with the right surname made noise about it, which had not happened.

I brought bread and refilled cups and listened without appearing to listen, and by the time the last passenger was back in the coach I had three names I wanted to remember and two I wanted to forget and a headache from the woman in the corner seat who had been worried about highwaymen since Barnet.
I wrote the names I wanted in the margin of the morning accounts and let the rest go.
The chandler came just before noon.
Bradwell was sixty, round-shouldered, with the pleasantness of a man who'd kept it up so long it had set like lacquer.
He sold me tallow candles by the gross and had been doing so for fifteen years, first to my mother and then to me, and in all that time his counts had been accurate to the last unit.
Until August.
When they'd stopped being accurate.
He sat down at the kitchen table with his hat in his hands and we looked at the order sheet together.
"Six dozen short," I said.
"Second month running."
"Supply's been difficult."
His eyes moved across the sheet without landing.
"Prices going up everywhere.
I've had to make some allocations —"
"To whom?"
A pause.
Not a long one, but long enough to matter.
"I have other customers," he said.
"You have four customers in this parish who order in bulk.
The Plough in Knebworth, the Rising Sun, the Stevenage factor, and me.
I'm your largest.
If you're pulling from my order to fill someone else's, I want to know whose."
His pleasantness shifted, the way a floor does when there's something moving underneath it.
"I'm sure we can come to an arrangement for next month," he said.
"The arrangement is the full order," I said.
"Which is what we agreed.
If I'm short again in December, I'll go to the Stevenage supplier and send you a note explaining why."
He left.
The pleasantness left with him.
I wrote Bradwell.
Third month.
Why in the accounts margin and let it sit.
Something had changed.
I didn't know what yet.
Bradwell had been selling to my grandmother in 1790 and he'd never shorted her.
Never shorted my mother either.
The only thing that had changed in the past three months was me.
Or rather: not me.
The lease.

Geoffrey Stainforth had taken over his father's estate in 1814, the year my mother died and I took over the inn, and for two years we had been politely ignoring each other across four miles of Hertfordshire.
The White Hound's lease was not mine.
The building was not mine.
The land was not mine.

They belonged to the Stainforth estate and had done so for forty years, and I held the lease on terms my grandmother had negotiated and my mother had maintained, and the terms were good terms, and good terms lasted until someone decided they didn't.
I could not buy the lease outright.
I did not have the capital.
I could not borrow against it.
It was not collateral.
I could not marry without losing it entirely.

Coverture: the law that had been explained to me by two different men who had found the explanation charming, as if the news that I had no legal existence once married was a mildly interesting historical footnote rather than the reason I had refused two proposals and was not entertaining a third.
If I married, the lease became my husband's.
The income became my husband's.
Everything my grandmother had built, everything my mother had held, everything I had been running on four hours of sleep and sheer stubbornness would transfer to a man the moment I said I do.
So I did not say I do.
I ran the inn.
The accounts were honest and I kept them that way.
The margin was thin.
It had always been thin; my mother had said a coaching inn on a good road was excellent fundamentals on slightly damp paper.
What she hadn't told me was what happened when the roads got bad and the harvests failed and the soldiers came down in numbers not seen since the regiments were full.
I knew what happened.
I was managing it one week at a time.
Good terms.
Until someone decided they weren't.
I closed the ledger and went to find Nan.

She was in the taproom, wiping down the bar with the focused efficiency she applied to tasks she found beneath her, which was most physical tasks, but which she performed flawlessly because Nan found being bad at anything more objectionable still.
"Rutland coach is an hour out," I said.
"I know.
Jem saw it on the road."
She wrung the cloth without looking up.
"Bridget's asking about the salt cod."
"Tell her November."
"I've told her November three times."
"Tell her again."
I leaned on the bar.
"How are we on ale?"
"Fine if the Rutland's not all men."
"It'll be all men."
She set the cloth down and gave me the look she reserved for situations where I was right and she would have preferred me not to be.
"I'll see about the next barrel," she said, and went.
The Rutland arrived twenty minutes early.
Eighteen passengers, all of them men, cold and bad-tempered and with six hours of each other already behind them.

I put them in the taproom and got Tom on plates and managed the kitchen myself while Nan managed the room, which she did with the efficiency and implicit threat that kept the rowdy ones from becoming a problem.
We were short a kitchen maid.

We had been short one since September, when the girl from Hertford decided that her cousin's dressmaking shop in London was a better prospect, which it probably was, and I had not replaced her because the arithmetic said wait.
We could manage with three of us and Tom if no one got ill and the coaches kept to schedule and nothing broke.
I filled plates.
Nan filled glasses.
Tom carried both and spilled neither, which was an improvement on last month.
By the time the Rutland had loaded back up and gone, I was running on the cold half-cup of tea I'd had at eleven.
The taproom was my grandmother's work, more than any other room.
She'd put in the oak counter and the hooks on the beams and the arrangement of barrels that Jem had never altered because it was, as he said, correct.
The portrait of King George above the fireplace was older than any of us.
I touched the frame as I passed.
The fire was low.
I built it up.
The soldier came in the back way just after one, during the gap between coaches.
He was at the kitchen door rather than the taproom entrance, which told me he'd been on the roads long enough to learn which door to try when you had nothing to spend.
His coat had been red once.
His boots were sound, which meant recently discharged rather than long adrift.
I was at the basin.
I turned and looked at him.
"I'm not asking for coin," he said.
"I've some left.
But if there's work —"
"Hauling water and washing pots," I said.
"You'll eat at the servant's table."
He hauled water and washed pots.
He was quiet and thorough and he stacked the crockery without being shown the system.
Nan came through, looked at him, said nothing.
He ate at the servant's table with Jem, who said little, and with Tom the pot boy, who said too much, and with Nan, who said exactly what was needed and stopped there.
I ate standing at the counter.
I always did.
After, I wrapped three thick slices of bread in cloth and put them in his hand.
"Beds in Hitchin," I said.
"Tell them the White Hound sent you.
The landlord owes me a favour."
He looked at the bread and then at me.
He nodded, thanked me, and went.
I stood in the doorway and watched him get small on the road north.
Jem came up beside me.
"Third this week," he said.
"Mmm."
"North roads are flooding out above Huntingdon.
More'll come."
"I know."
He turned and went back toward the stable, moving the way he always moved in the yard: steady, a little sideways, the empty coat sleeve pinned up where his left arm had been since Salamanca.
He had never said the word Salamanca to me.
I knew it because my mother had written it in the accounts margin the day he came to work for her: Jem Bowker.
Stable hand.
Lost left arm in the Peninsula.
Good with horses.
She had not said what she thought about the rest of it.
He picked up a pitchfork with his right hand and got to work on the nearest stall.
I watched him a moment longer than I needed to, then went back inside.
Bridget came down in the late afternoon, later than usual.

She was seventy-three and climbed stairs at the pace she had decided was right for seventy-three, and she arrived in the kitchen with the look she wore when she'd been sitting with a thought long enough to have an opinion about it.
She was my mother's aunt.
She had a room above the kitchen and a small allowance and the right to have opinions, and she had been at the White Hound since before I was born.
I put the kettle on without being asked.
"You're thin," she said.
"I'm the same as I was last month."
"Then you were thin last month too."
She settled into the chair by the fire.
Her hands were warm and papery when she folded them in her lap.
Her eyes were grey and missed approximately nothing.
"How are the accounts?"
"Fine."
"How are they really?"
"Honest.
Near enough."
She made a sound that was not agreement.
She looked at the fire.
"Bradwell was here," she said.
Not a question.
"He was."
"He looked worried when he left."
"He looked pleasant."
"Yes," she said.
"That's what I mean."
I poured the tea.
She took her cup with both hands, not because she needed both but because she liked the warmth of the whole circumference.

I sat down across from her, which I did not always do, and we drank tea and let the kitchen settle around us the way it did in the late afternoon when the coaches had gone and the next ones hadn't come.
"Your mother would have been glad of October," she said.
"She hated August."
"Everyone hated August."
"She hated it more."
She turned her cup in her hands.
"You're working too hard."
"I'm working the right amount."
"There's no right amount in a place like this.
There's what it takes and what's left of you after."
She looked at me steadily.
"Eat a proper dinner."
"I'll eat after the Edinburgh mail."
"That's nine o'clock."
"Yes."
She looked at me a moment longer.
Then she looked back at the fire and let it go.
"There's a good chapter in the Scott," she said.
"If you want something to take upstairs."
"I'll manage without Scott."
"That's what I thought."
She stood, careful, and put her cup in the basin.
She looked out the kitchen window at the yard, where the last of the daylight was doing what it could with the October cold, which was not much.
"Send Nan up with supper," she said.
"If you can spare her."
"I can spare her."
She went upstairs.
I heard each step, slow and even.
Her door.
Then nothing.
The Edinburgh mail came in at nine and left at half past.
Nan and I counted the takings at the bar, Nan on the coin, me on the notes, and by ten the house had gone quiet in the way that meant tomorrow was already starting.
I checked the fire.
I checked the bolts.
I went through the kitchen one last time.
Bread laid for morning.
Fire banked right.
Jem's lamp was out in the stable loft, which meant he'd gone down earlier than usual, which meant his knee was at him.
The cold always did it.
I was washing my hands at the basin when I heard the post slot click.
Late for the post.
I dried my hands and went through.
The letter was on the mat, one candle's worth of light from the sconce above the entry.
I picked it up.
The handwriting was careful and formed.
The seal was one I knew: the Stainforth estate, wax the dark red of old port.
Geoffrey Stainforth.
Who held the lease on the White Hound.
I broke it open.
Dear Miss Dale,
I hope this letter finds you in good health.
I write to request the convenience of a meeting at your earliest opportunity, in regard to certain matters concerning the current terms of the lease on the White Hound.
I intend no alarm by this correspondence — the meeting is a routine one, of the kind that good management of an estate requires — but I believe a conversation in person would be mutually beneficial.
I remain, &c., G.
Stainforth
I read it twice.
Certain matters concerning the current terms of the lease.
I folded the letter along its creases and set it on the mantelpiece where I would see it in the morning.
There was nothing to do about it tonight, and I was too tired to be frightened of it properly, which was perhaps the best time to stop being frightened of things.
I went upstairs.
The inn settled around me as I climbed.
All its old sounds.
The creak on the fifth step.
The draught under Bridget's door.
The smell of tallow smoke and cold stone and bread.
Mine.
For now.
I blew out the candle and went to sleep.
The coach was late by forty minutes.
I had the count from Jem, who had been standing at the gate since half past eight with his breath making clouds in the cold air.
I was crossing the yard when it came in—the horses blowing hard, the coachman working his brake on the gravel, the whole rig leaning slightly on the turn as if the road had tilted it.
Two passengers.
Not four.
The door swung open and a woman of middle years came down the step with her hat askew and her mouth already moving.
Behind her, a gentleman in a damp greatcoat stepped onto the gravel and looked at nothing in particular.
He had the face of a man who had not slept.
The woman reached me before I reached her.
"There is damage to my trunk.
The hinge is split and the coachman claims no knowledge of it."
"Let me see it."
The trunk came down from the boot.
I went down on one knee beside it.
The hinge had pulled half away from the wood—old screw holes, the timber bruised around them, working loose long before today.
But there was no good to come from saying so.
"Jem," I said.
He was already there, standing at the far corner of the trunk.
He took hold of the good end and lifted without waiting for direction.
"Take it through the side door," I said.
"The small parlour, not the hall."
He went.
"The hinge will be seen to today," I told the woman.
"I'll have word for you before the afternoon coach."
She drew breath.
I looked at her directly.
"Before the afternoon coach," I said.
"You'll be comfortable in the dining room."
She closed her mouth.
She went inside.
The gentleman in the greatcoat had already gone through the door without speaking to anyone.
The coachman came down from the box.
His name was Hurst—I knew him by his scar and by the particular way he wrapped his reins around the brake handle.
He pulled his hat off.
"The north road above Hatfield," he said.
"Bank's come down across the ditch.
You won't get a coach through in under a week, maybe two."
"How far past the milestone?"
"Half a mile.
Between the oak and the old stone wall."
"I'll send word to the inn at Welwyn this afternoon.
Thank you, Hurst."
He nodded and went to see about the horses.
The ostler had already taken two of them by the head.
The yard was clearing fast—gravel settling, voices falling away, the cold air coming back in around the spaces where the coach had been.
I turned toward the house.
Through the open bar door I could see Nan behind the counter, her cloth moving in slow circles over the wood, her eyes on the yard.
She had been watching the whole of it.
I did not say anything and she did not speak.
The chandler came at eleven.
His name was Ferris and he had been supplying the White Hound for six years.

He came in through the kitchen entrance with his boy behind him carrying a half-crate of tallow and set it down on the table with a small satisfied sound, as if he had delivered something I would be glad of.
He opened his book.
"Good morning, Mrs.
Dale.
I'll need to put the price up a ha'penny the dozen."
"You put it up in March," I said.
"Tallow's dearer again this quarter.
I can show you the—"
"I know what tallow is trading at.
And I know what you charge the Crown and Anchor at Essendon."
I kept my voice even.
"I take eight dozen a month.
They don't take that much in a quarter.
I'll pay sixpence the dozen."
He looked at his book.
He pressed his pen nib against the page without writing anything.
"Sixpence ha'penny," he said.
"Sixpence.
And I'll take ten dozen this month."
He was quiet for a moment.
Then he wrote it down.
He did not look pleased, but his pen moved and the number was there.
He tipped his hat, said good day, and went out with his boy.
The candles stayed on the table.
I carried the first box through to the storeroom.
The ledger was open on the shelf beside the door, a week's figures running down the page in my own hand.
The rent came due at the end of the month and the tallow price would go up again by spring—I knew Ferris well enough to know that.
I could work all of it because the inn was mine to work: the rent, the ledger, Ferris and his book and his halfpennies.
If I married, that would end.
The law would give the inn to a husband and I would have no more standing to speak to a chandler than a maid does.
I thought of that, and then I put it down and went back for the second box.
The coach was forty minutes late, which I had expected.
What I had not expected was it arriving two passengers short of the manifest, with a trunk roped shut at the back where the hinge had given.
I was in the yard when it came through the gate.
Jem appeared behind me before I had turned, which was his way.
The coachman called down from the box that the Marchmont party had not boarded at the Bell and Crown.
I nodded and made the note in my head.
The two who had boarded were a stout man in a wool coat and a younger woman who descended before her luggage, which was a habit I had learned to watch for.
"That trunk," the stout man said.
"I see it," I said.
"Jem."
Jem was already at the boot.
The stout man followed me with his eyes in a way that meant he had things to say about the trunk and had been saying them since Barnet.
"The hinge gave at Welwyn," he said.
"Your man will want to mind the contents."
"Jem minds everything," I said.
"Mrs.
Oakes will see you settled.
There is a fire in the dining room."
He opened his mouth once more.
I met his eye.
He closed it.
The coachman came down from the box while Jem worked the trunk free.
He had the manner of a man who had driven a bad road and would rather talk about it than not.
"The road above Hatfield," he said.
"Above the second milestone.
There's a rut across the full width of the north lane that wasn't there a fortnight ago."
"How deep?"
"Deep enough.
I took it slow.
A night coach coming fast would feel it."
"I'll send word to Holliday.
He'll see it patched before the week's out, or I'll ask why not."
He gave me a short nod and went to water his horses.
Jem took the trunk across the yard at a careful angle, his shoulder to the load.
I did not watch him do it because there was no need.
The stout man appeared again in the doorway to the passage, not quite willing to let the trunk go without another word.
I walked toward him, which brought him back inside.
I followed him in.
"The clasp has held," I said.
"We will have it up to your room.
If anything inside is damaged, I'll want to know before this evening."
He looked at the trunk, then at me.
"And what would you do about it?"
"Determine who was at fault," I said.
"And proceed from there."
He looked at me a moment longer.
Then he went upstairs.
I went back through to the bar.
Nan was behind it, wiping down the taps with a cloth, her eyes on the window that gave onto the yard.
She had been watching the whole of it.
I did not say so.
She said nothing either.
I checked the ledger entry I had made that morning and corrected the passenger count.
The Marchmont party would need rescheduling.
I wrote a note for the afternoon post.
The chandler came at half past ten.
Mr.
Birch, who had supplied the White Hound since before my time here.
He set his invoice on the bar without being asked, which was how I knew, before I looked at it, that the number had gone up.
"Six shillings the gross," he said.
"Tallow's dear this quarter."
"You charged four and six in March," I said.
"Four and eight in May.
Five in August."
"Tallow's dear," he said again.
"I know what tallow costs, Mr.
Birch.
I also know what you charge the Swan at Hatfield and what you charge the Red Lion."
I set the invoice back on the bar, facing him.
"Five and two is fair to both of us."
He looked at the ceiling.
He looked at his invoice.
He had the expression of a man calculating what he could still sell to someone who knew exactly what he was doing.
"Five and four," he said.
"Five and two," I said.
"And I pay on delivery, same as always."
He took the invoice and tucked it into his coat.
"Five and two," he said.
He left.
The candles stayed.
I entered the amount in the ledger.
The rent ran through my head, the coal for the north stable, the supplier prices, the repairs I had been putting off since September.
All of it ran through me because I was the one who held the inn, and if I married, I would not be — the inn would pass to a husband, and I would be negotiating nothing on anyone's behalf.
I did not sit with the thought.
I closed the ledger and went to see about the luncheon coal.
The London coach came in twenty minutes late with two outside seats empty and the coachman already climbing down before the wheels had settled.
I had the yard boys standing.
Two passengers descended stiff and out of temper.
The first, a man in a brown greatcoat, did not look at me and went directly for the door.
The second was a woman in good wool who surveyed the yard with the expression of someone who had decided in advance to disapprove of everything.
"You'll want the dining room," I said.
"Fire's lit, there's cold beef and bread, and I can send up hot tea in the quarter hour."
She looked at me.
"I had expected a room."
"There is a room.
I'll have it set while you eat."
That was enough.
She went in.
Saul Priddick, the coachman—I had known him three years—handed off the reins and came toward me pulling his hat off.
"Short by two.
Missed their place at the Bell."
"I know it."
"North road above Hatfield's gone to stones again.
Evening run cracked an axle there Tuesday.
I kept wide of it but it cost me time."
"I'll note it," I said.
He put his hat back on and that was that.
Behind me came the scrape of a trunk being dragged, and when I turned, Jem was already there—crouched over the damaged hinge, testing the gap with both hands.
The man in the brown greatcoat had come back out.
"That is my trunk," he said.
"I know it.
He's making sure nothing falls out before it goes upstairs."
"I want it delivered intact."
"So do we all.
Jem will bring it up and I'll have the hinge looked at.
If it can be repaired here I'll have it done before you leave.
If not, I'll tell you what we found."
He opened his mouth and then decided it was not worth his energy.
He went back inside.
Jem looked up at me from behind the trunk.
I gave him nothing.
He knew what to do.
The yard quieted.
The horses were led off to the stable.
The luggage went in.
The woman in wool appeared briefly in the window above the dining room, looked out at something she could not have seen, and moved away.
I watched Jem disappear through the door with the trunk slung over one shoulder, the bad hinge held against his chest with one hand.
I went in.
Nan was behind the bar working through the morning bottles, and she did not look up as I passed.
But she had been watching the yard all along—I could see it in how carefully she was not watching me now.
I said nothing about it.
There was nothing to say.
Thomas Meek the chandler arrived at half past ten with his cart boy and three crates of candles.
He had been supplying the White Hound since before I had it.
He named his price.
It was four shillings over what I had paid him in March.
"You've raised the price four times since April," I said.
"Tallow's up.
You'll have heard."
"I've heard.
But you charge the Blue Boar at Ware eight shillings less per gross than you're asking me now.
Your tallow is the same tallow."
He had not expected me to know about the Blue Boar.
I watched him understand that I did.
"The Blue Boar takes a larger order."
"I take a comparable order and I pay within the fortnight.
You've told me yourself you wait six weeks from them."
He looked at the crates.
"I can hold at last month's rate."
"Last month's rate was already over March.
Hold at last month's rate and take the full delivery today."
He said done, with the shortness of a man who is annoyed but not damaged.
He would come back.
I had made sure of that.
The crates went into the storeroom.
His boy loaded the empties.
Meek himself did not linger.
I stood at the passage desk and entered the figure in the ledger.
The candles, the rent due on the fourteenth, the coal order at the end of the month.
Every number resolved to the same fact: the inn was mine to negotiate for because there was no husband.
If I married, the ledger would be his—the supplier accounts, the keys, the whole of what I had made here—and he would not need to ask my view on any of it, in law or in practice.
I set the pen down.
It was not a thing worth dwelling on.
It never was.
The bell rang from the dining room.
I went to answer it.
The London coach came in forty minutes late and two passengers short.
I was in the yard when it turned under the arch, and I could see from the set of Dobbins's shoulders that it had been a hard run.
He brought the team down and called to me before he was properly stopped.
"Road above Hatfield's cut up bad, Mrs.
Dale.
Three inches of mud and worse where it narrows past the mill."
"How far past the mill?"
"Half a mile, then it eases.
But loaded, you'll feel it."
"I'll send word to the Hare."
That was enough.
He nodded and turned back to his team.
Two of the four passengers got down in a temper.
The first, a heavyset man in a damp coat, wanted to know why the journey had taken three hours longer than advertised.
I told him the road was responsible, and the road was not mine.
He wanted to complain further and I let him have his say, then asked whether he required a room or the dining room.
He required the dining room.
I sent him in.
The second passenger had a trunk.
It came down from the boot badly, one of the leather hinges split along the strap, the whole side of it gaping.
The passenger, a woman of perhaps forty with a good wool travelling dress and a look that suggested she had learned to expect things to go wrong, stood over it and waited.
"We can bind that today," I told her.
"There's leather and rivets in the tack room.
Jem will see to it before you travel on."
"And if it opens on the road?"
"It won't.
Not with a rivet through both sides."
I met her eye.
"I've had trunks mended here before.
This is a straightforward repair."
She looked at the trunk, then at me.
"Very well."
Jem was already there.
I hadn't called him.
He crouched beside the trunk and had his hand on the hinge before the woman had finished speaking, and she went indoors, and that was the end of it.
The coachman came round once more before he took the team through to the stables.
"One more thing, Mrs.
Dale.
Coming through Hatfield we passed two men on horseback asking whether anyone had seen a young woman travelling alone.
Couldn't say what she looked like, only that she had a bandbox and a green cloak."
I thought of the two missing passengers.
"Where did they ask?"
"At the toll.
Constables, they looked like.
Or close to it."
"Thank you, Dobbins."
He touched his hat and went.
The yard took perhaps ten minutes to clear after that.
The ostlers finished with the horses.
Jem took the trunk through to the tack room.
The cobbles were wet and the yard smelled of horse and cold mud and the particular sharpness of October mornings when the wind comes off the north fields.
I went back through the main door.
Nan was behind the bar, wiping glasses.
She had been there when the coach came in and she was there still, working through the rack with her back half-turned, but I had seen her watching.
I said nothing.
There was nothing to say.
The chandler came at ten.
Norris, who had been supplying the White Hound since before I took over the lease, and who had a workshop in the town and supplied four other inns on this road that I knew of.
He set his ledger on the bar and named his price before he had properly taken off his hat.
"Seven shillings the dozen for the tallow," he said.
"And eight and six for the wax."
"Last month you charged six and four for the tallow," I said.
"And eight even for the wax."
"Cost has risen.
It's the same for everyone on this road, Mrs.
Dale."
"I know what you charge at the Hart," I said.
"Six and nine for tallow.
Eight and two for wax.
This morning."
He had his pen out.
He set it down again.
"I need forty dozen tallow and eight dozen wax," I said.
"I'll pay six and nine for the tallow and eight and two for the wax, same as the Hart.
If that's not agreeable you're welcome to take the order back to your cart."
He looked at his ledger.
He did not look at me.
"That's a fair price," I said.
"It's the going price.
You know it and I know it."
He picked up his pen.
"Six and nine for the tallow," he said.
"Eight and two for the wax."
"Good."
He wrote out the bill and I signed it and he took his hat and went.
The candles stayed.
I was halfway back to the office with the copy of the bill when the thought came, the way it sometimes did between one thing and the next.
The rent, the ledger, the price of candles—all of it resting on my own name in the accounts, my own signature on the bill.
If I married, the inn would not be mine to negotiate for.
I noted it the way I noted the state of the north road, and moved on.
I sat down at the desk and opened the ledger.
The coach was late by forty minutes and arrived with six passengers instead of eight.

I had the yard swept and the horse trough filled before the wheels came through the gate, which meant I stood in the cold for ten minutes doing nothing, and cold October mornings at the White Hound do not run short of things that want doing.
The coachman pulled up short and set the brake.
Two passengers descended with the tight-lipped quiet of people who had spent three hours choosing not to speak to each other.
A third climbed down and stood in the yard looking at the sky as though it had wronged him personally.
The fourth and fifth followed without incident.

A woman came last, and behind her, stepping down carefully, a man in a merchant's coat with a trunk that was fighting him—lid askew, hinge sprung, the whole thing held together by one leather strap and his grip on the handle.
"Hinge is split," he said, to no one and everyone.
I could see that.
The latch had gone and the lid sat crooked, liable to pitch open if the angle changed.
"Jem," I said.
Jem was already halfway across the yard.
He took the trunk from both ends, shifted his weight, and bore it level through the door without a word spoken.
The merchant looked at me.
"I'll want that secured before anyone touches the latch."
"Jem will see to it," I said.
"He'll knock when it's done."
That was enough for him.
The two silent passengers had already gone inside without looking at me, which was fine—they wanted warmth and food, not conversation, and I was glad to provide both without providing the other.
The man who had studied the sky paused at the door.
"Is the dining room open?"
"It is."
He went in.
I crossed to where the coachman was walking his lead horse in a slow circle near the trough.
"Road above Hatfield's breaking up," he said.
"Past the second mile marker.
Ruts like that will be twice as deep by Christmas."
"I'll send word to the surveyor's office."
He nodded once, the nod of a man who has said the same thing at the same inn on the same road before.
"Not the first time."
"No," I said.
"But I'll send it today."
He looked at me a moment, then turned back to his horse.
I left him to it.
The yard cleared by degrees.
Bags went upstairs.
Horses went to the stable.
The two quarrelsome passengers found their room and the door closed behind them.
Jem vanished with the trunk.
The coachman brought his team around and went on toward London.
I came inside through the entrance passage and stopped to let my eyes settle.
Nan was behind the bar polishing glasses, her back mostly toward me, her cloth moving in steady circles.
She had been watching the yard—I knew this the way I know most things about this inn, which is not by looking directly but by knowing where things are when I look away.
I said nothing.
There was nothing yet that needed saying.
Thomas Greaves arrived at half past ten with the monthly delivery and his ledger open in his hand.
"Twelve shillings the gross, Mrs.
Dale."
Last month it had been eleven.
The month before, ten and sixpence.
I looked at the page long enough to make sure he knew I was looking at it.
"That's the fourth increase since March," I said.
"Tallow's up.
Everyone on this road is paying the same."
"The Lamb at Brookmans pays ten and four."
He had the decency not to blink.
"The Lamb takes half your volume."
"And the Bell at Welwyn takes twice mine.
You charge them ten and eight."
A pause.
He smoothed the ledger page with two fingers as though it needed smoothing.
"Eleven and six," he said.
"Eleven and two."
He looked at me.
I looked at him.
Outside, Jem said something in the yard.
A horse moved.
"Eleven and four," Greaves said.
"And I won't shift further."
"Eleven and four," I said.
"And the same rate through December."
He folded the page.
"Aye."
He left.
The candles stayed.
I stood at the counter a moment longer than I needed to, running figures.
The chandler, the tallow, the rent due at the end of the month, the linen account I owed before November was out.
All of it turning on margins small enough that a broken hinge or a late coach left a mark in the ledger.
The thought came the way it always came—plainly, without complaint.
If I married, this would not be mine to argue over.
The inn, the accounts, the chandler's price: all of it would become a husband's property under law, and what I had built by paying close attention would pass out of my hands and into his.
I did not dwell on this.
There was nothing to be done about the law before the linen account came due.
I took up my pen and made the entry.
The London coach came in forty minutes late and two passengers short, which meant the coachman was already talking before the wheels had stopped turning.
I went out to meet it.
The yard was cold, the cobbles dark from last night's rain, and my breath came in short clouds as I crossed to the step.
Jem was at the horses before I reached the coach door, which was where he was supposed to be and where he always was without being told.
"Road above Hatfield," the coachman said, climbing down.
His name was Aldous.
He'd been running this route four years and never wasted a word.
"Three inches of mud from Welwyn to the toll gate.
We took twenty minutes off the schedule and still came in behind."
"Same stretch as September?"
"Worse."
"I'll note it."
He nodded and went to his horses.
The two passengers who had made it were a woman of middle age in a grey travelling cloak and a younger man whose hat was pulled low and whose jaw was set tight.
The woman went straight toward the door without looking at me.
The man came last and then stopped and looked back at the boot.
"That trunk," he said.
I looked.
The hinge on the near corner had split, and the lid stood open a finger's width, held only by the rope the guard had lashed across it.
"I'll have Jem see to it," I said.
"It was locked when I handed it over in London."
"The road above Hatfield is three inches of mud.
Your trunk is intact.
You've lost a hinge."
He looked at me.
He was waiting for something—an apology, or an argument.
I offered neither.
"I'll want a room with a bolt," he said.
"You'll have one."
He went inside.
Jem was already there, hands on the rope, working it loose without being asked.
The guard had the mail bag down.
Aldous was at the trough.
The woman in grey was through the door.
I stayed until the last of it was settled.
Aldous came back around the rear of the coach, hands in his coat pockets.
"Same stretch will be impassable by December.
Tell Barker if you see him."
"Barker came through Tuesday.
He knows."
He nodded once.
That was the end of it.
The yard cleared in the way it always did: not at once, but in pieces, one thing finishing and then the next until there was only mud and wheel ruts and the smell of horse.
Jem went through the door with the trunk balanced on his shoulder.
The passengers were upstairs or headed to the dining room.
The coachman was gone.
I went back inside.
Nan was at the bar.
She had been pulling a cloth across the same length of counter for longer than the wood required, which was how I knew she had been watching the yard.
I did not say anything about it.
She did not say anything about anything.
I went through to the office.
Hollis came an hour later, earlier than his usual Monday, and that alone told me something.
He had his delivery cart outside and his boy with him, and he set the first box of candles on the counter before he had said good morning.
"Prices have come up," he said.
"Tallow's dearer now than it was at summer."
"How much dearer."
"Sixpence the dozen above what we agreed in March."
I knew what he paid for tallow.
I knew what he charged at the Falcon in Hatfield and the Cock at Welwyn, because Barker talked and the girl from the Cock came in on Sundays.
This was the fourth time since March he had arrived naming a new price.
Sixpence above our agreed rate was not the market.
It was what he wanted to see if I would pay.
"You charged the Falcon fourpence above March in September," I said.
"You're asking me sixpence."
"Different quantities."
"Same quantities.
I've kept the record."
He looked at the box on the counter.
He looked at me.
"Fourpence and a half."
"Fourpence," I said.
"Same as the Falcon.
And you'll be back next month."
He left the candles and went out to his boy.
I carried the first box through to the storeroom and set it on the shelf above the October account.
Four increases since March.
This one I had held.
The rent was due in eleven days.
The ledger balanced, barely, because I had managed every line of it myself.
If I had a husband, the inn would be his.
The ledger, the candles, the argument with Hollis, the note about the Hatfield road—all of it would pass from my hands by law and by the ordinary course of things.
I set the second box on top of the first and went back out to the bar.
Nan had stopped pretending about the counter and was drawing ale for the man from the coach, who had come down from his room and apparently found his temper somewhere on the stairs.
There was the dining room to check and the afternoon coach to account for.
I went to the dining room.
The London coach came in twenty minutes late and two passengers short, which I already knew from the yard boy's face before the wheels had stopped turning.
I was at the door before the coachman had handed down the second passenger.

There were four in all: a wool merchant I recognised from the autumn run, his face dark with something that had nothing to do with the cold; a woman in grey travelling alone who descended carefully, testing each step; a clergyman who went straight past me as though I were a post; and a young man in a new coat who stood looking at his trunk with an expression that prepared me for trouble.
The trunk had a split hinge.
One corner of the lid had buckled outward, and the strap across it was doing work the hinge should have done.
The young man said, "Your man dropped it."
"Let's see what we have," I said.
Jem was already there.
He had not been there a moment before and I had not called him; he was simply there, with his hands on the trunk before the young man could say anything further.
I watched him test the hinge with his thumb.
"Came to it already split," Jem said, not looking up.
"The leather's dried clear through.
See how it's cracked along the fold?"
The young man looked.
The cracking was there, plain enough.
"I'll have Watts look at it this afternoon," I said.
"He'll have it right before the evening.
If the goods are undamaged, the repair costs nothing."
He wanted to argue.
I could see it gathering in him.
But there was nothing in what I'd said to argue with, and after a moment he let it go and turned toward the door.
Jem lifted the trunk and took it toward the back passage.
The coachman caught me before I turned back to the others.
His name was Briggs and he was a careful man, not given to complaint.
"North road above Hatfield," he said.
"There's a section coming loose before the Stanborough turn.
Six feet, maybe eight.
I took it slow but the next rain will finish it."
"I'll send word to the surveyor's office today."
"Aye."
He looked at his horses.
"That's all."
The yard emptied by degrees.
The wool merchant went to the dining room still wearing his dark expression.
The woman in grey went upstairs with the chambermaid.
The clergyman had already vanished.
The young man followed when he saw Jem carry his trunk through the back.
The horses went to the stable in pairs, their breath hanging white in the cold air.
Briggs climbed back to his box and the coach went through to the far yard.
The silence after a coach arrival is not a quiet silence.
It is the silence of a room that has just stopped being loud.
I stood a moment in the doorway and watched the last of the mud settle in the wheel-ruts.
Behind me I heard Nan moving at the bar, the clink of a glass set down and taken up again.
She had been watching the whole of it through the serving hatch, her cloth going in slow circles on the counter.
She did not say anything and I did not turn around.
The chandler came just before eleven.
His name was Perrin.
He had held the account six years, and in that time I had paid him on the first of every month without exception.
He set his delivery down in the passage and named his price, and the price was higher.
I said, "That's the fourth rise since March."
"Tallow's up across the county.
I'm not the only one."
"You're charging the King's Arms at Welwyn sixpence less per dozen."
A pause.
He had not expected that.
"Different quantities," he said.
"I take more than they do."
I let that sit for a moment.
"I pay on time and I don't send things back.
That's worth something to a man carrying three accounts that don't."
I knew two of the three by name.
He knew I knew.
"I'll pay what I paid in September."
He looked at the candles.
He looked at me.
"Split the difference," he said.
"September's price," I said.
He left the candles.
I carried the tally book through to the back room and wrote the figure down.
The rent had gone up in August.
The coal price had gone up before that.
Every number I wrote came back to the same fact: every lease, every account, every supplier on this road would belong to a husband if I had one, and the inn along with them.
I would have no more standing to negotiate than the hall table.
I noted the figure and closed the book.
In the passage, Watts was already at the young man's trunk with a strip of new leather and a pot of paste.
The hinge, as Jem had said, had been dry for months.
The coachman brought it down in short order: two passengers short, the road above Hatfield broken since the last rains, and a trunk on the boot with a hinge split at the pin.
Four passengers climbed down instead of six, and two of the four were not disposed to patience.
The trunk belonged to a Mr.
Pryce — a dry little man in a bottle-green coat who told me twice that it was new.
I looked at the hinge.
The leather had pulled clean away from the wood.
"I can have it repaired in town," I said.
"In the meanwhile Jem will store it safely, and you'll have whatever you need from it tonight."
"I paid to have it carried intact," he said.
"And I'm sorry it wasn't.
The road is bad above Hatfield."
I said it plainly and waited.
He looked at me and then looked away, and that was the end of it.
Jem was already crossing the yard.
I had not sent for him.
He took the trunk and carried it toward the back stairs balanced against his shoulder, moving carefully on the wet stones.
Pryce watched him go and seemed somewhat less aggrieved.
The second difficult passenger was a woman travelling with a maid, whose complaint was that she had paid for a private compartment and ridden in company.

That was between her and the coaching office in London and I told her so, but I offered her the private parlour until her room was ready and she accepted it, which settled the matter without requiring either of us to remain dissatisfied in the hall.
Then Watkins.
He had driven this route since before I kept the inn and he was not a man who wasted words.
