"Road's bad above Hatfield," he said.
He meant worse than bad.
"Dug out in two places before Essendon.
I lost twenty minutes on the last mile."
"How bad through November?"
"It won't hold without repair.
You'll want to warn your guests going north.
Add half an hour at least."
"I'll note it," I said.
"Will you eat before you go back?"
He would.
I sent him through to the kitchen.
The yard cleared quickly after that.
The passengers went upstairs or to the dining room.
Jem came back through and checked the yard gate without being asked, because in wet weather it swung on its hinge and caught the post-boy's trap when he came in at an angle.
The sky was low and white.
October had been wet since the third.
Nan was behind the bar when I came back inside.
She had been standing at the window while she wiped the glasses, watching the yard, which she had been doing since before the coach arrived.
She said nothing and I said nothing.
The chandler arrived at half past ten.
His name was Frith and he had been supplying the inn for four years, long enough that he knew my habits and I knew his margin.
He named his price.
I looked at the invoice.
It was four shillings per gross above what I had paid in March.
"That's the fourth increase in seven months," I said.
"Tallow's dear," he said.
"It's dear all along this road."
"It is," I said.
"I know what you charge at the Crown in Hatfield and at the Red Lion in Welwyn.
Yours is a fair business, Mr.
Frith, but this rate is not a fair price for this inn."
He was quiet for a moment.
He was not a dishonest man.
He had named the price he thought I might accept.
"I'll take the March rate plus sixpence a gross," I said.
"That accounts for your cost increase fairly and leaves you something for your trouble.
That is my offer."
He looked at the delivery in his cart.
The weather was worsening and he had other calls to make and we both understood that he was not driving back with the candles.
"Done," he said.
The candles went into the storeroom.
I recorded the price in the ledger — the new price, the one I had arrived at, not the one he had named — and noted the date and the quantity and closed the book.
I was standing at the ledger when I thought of it, the way I sometimes did when I had just finished writing down what I had paid for something.
The rent came out of the inn's account because the inn was mine to run.
The ledger was mine to keep for the same reason.

Frith's candles, Pryce's trunk, Watkins and the road above Hatfield — all of it mine to manage, mine to decide, mine to answer for, until the day I married, at which point it would belong to whoever I married and not to me.
I wrote the figure in the margin, closed the ledger, and went to see about the afternoon fire.
The morning coach from London arrived forty minutes late, which was twenty minutes better than the week before.
I was in the yard when I heard it on the road.
The roll of iron on stone: full coach, not empty.
Jem was at the gate already.
He'd worked this yard for twelve years under my mother and two under me.
I went back inside to see about the fire.
The kitchen had been going since four.
Nan had laid the first breakfast sitting before I came down, which she always did and never mentioned, and the smell of the bread was thick enough to judge the hour by.
I pulled a loaf from the rack, weighed it, put it back.
Good.
The second needed another ten minutes.
I moved it.
"Twelve passengers," Nan said from the doorway.
She had her apron on, her dark hair tucked under her cap, the look she wore when she was counting and did not want to be interrupted.
"Driver wants something hot.
Guard's tooth has been at him since Hatfield."
"What does he expect me to do about it?"
"He expects you to care, at least."
"Send him to the kitchen."
She went.
I got the bread knife out.
The White Hound had stood on the Great North Road since my grandmother put it there.

Not strictly accurate: she had inherited a failing alehouse from a husband who hadn't known what to do with it, and turned it into a coaching inn by force of will and thirty years of four o'clock mornings.
But the effect was the same.
Twenty rooms above stairs.
A taproom that held thirty when polite and sixty when necessary.
Stabling for forty horses, though Jem preferred twenty-five and had opinions about every one of the remainder.
A kitchen that ran from four until the last coach stopped.
It was late October 1816, and the harvest was dead.
The summer had broken in June.
Frost where there should have been sun, rain where there should have been dry, a cold that had settled into the ground and meant to stay.
Every farmer between here and St Albans had said the same thing by July: failed.
Barley, wheat, turnips.
All of it.

Bread prices had gone up in August and up again in September, and the men coming down the Great North Road without work, without regiments, without anywhere to be, were thinner than they'd been even a month before.
I had not raised my prices.
I had thought about it.
The guard's tooth was bad enough that he had stopped pretending it wasn't.
He sat at the kitchen table with his jaw in his hand.
"Cloves," I said.
I put them on the table along with a measure of brandy he hadn't asked for.
"Pack it in.
It won't fix it, but it'll manage until St Albans."
"Is there anyone decent in St Albans?"
"A barber-surgeon who does teeth.
Whether he's any good at it I can't say."
He took the cloves.
He took the brandy.
He went back to his coach without saying thank you.
The twelve passengers ate eggs and bread and complained about the road, which was honest of them.
The coach company had been promising repairs since spring and would not deliver until someone with the right surname made noise about it.

I brought bread and refilled cups and listened without appearing to listen, and by the time the last passenger was back in the coach I had three names I wanted to remember and two I wanted to forget and a headache from the woman in the corner seat who had been worried about highwaymen since Barnet.
I wrote the names I wanted in the margin of the morning accounts.
The chandler came just before noon.
Bradwell was sixty, round-shouldered, with the pleasantness of a man who'd kept it up so long it had set like lacquer.
He sold me tallow candles by the gross and had been doing so for fifteen years, first to my mother and then to me, and in all that time his counts had been accurate to the last unit.
Until August.
He sat down at the kitchen table with his hat in his hands and we looked at the order sheet together.
"Six dozen short," I said.
"Second month running."
"Supply's been difficult."
His eyes moved across the sheet without landing.
"Prices going up everywhere.
I've had to make some allocations —"
"To whom?"
A pause.
"I have other customers," he said.
"You have four customers in this parish who order in bulk.
The Plough in Knebworth, the Rising Sun, the Stevenage factor, and me.
I'm your largest.
If you're pulling from my order to fill someone else's, I want to know whose."
His pleasantness shifted.
Not broke — Bradwell did not break — but the floor moved.
"I'm sure we can come to an arrangement for next month," he said.
"The arrangement is the full order.
Which is what we agreed.
If I'm short again in December, I'll go to the Stevenage supplier and send you a note explaining why."
He left.
The pleasantness left with him.
I wrote Bradwell.
Third month.
Why in the accounts margin and let it sit.
Something had changed.
Bradwell had been selling to my grandmother in 1790 and he'd never shorted her.
Never shorted my mother either.
The only thing that had changed in the past three months was me.
Or rather: not me.
The lease.

Geoffrey Stainforth had taken over his father's estate in 1814, the year my mother died and I took over the inn, and for two years we had been politely ignoring each other across four miles of Hertfordshire.
The White Hound's lease was not mine.
The building was not mine.
The land was not mine.

They belonged to the Stainforth estate and had done so for forty years, and I held the lease on terms my grandmother had negotiated and my mother had maintained, and the terms were good terms, and good terms lasted until someone decided they didn't.
I could not buy the lease outright.
I did not have the capital.
I could not borrow against it.
It was not collateral.
I could not marry without losing it entirely.

Coverture: the law that had been explained to me by two different men who had found the explanation charming, as if the news that I had no legal existence once married was a mildly interesting historical footnote rather than the reason I had refused two proposals and was not entertaining a third.
If I married, the lease became my husband's.
The income became my husband's.
Everything my grandmother had built, everything my mother had held, everything I had been running on four hours of sleep and sheer stubbornness would transfer to a man the moment I said I do.
So I did not say I do.
I ran the inn.
The margin was thin.
It had always been thin; my mother had said a coaching inn on a good road was excellent fundamentals on slightly damp paper.
What she hadn't told me was what happened when the roads got bad and the harvests failed and the soldiers kept coming.
I knew what happened.
I was managing it one week at a time.
Good terms.
Until someone decided they weren't.
I closed the ledger and went to find Nan.

She was in the taproom, wiping down the bar with the focused efficiency she applied to tasks she found beneath her, which was most physical tasks, but which she performed flawlessly because Nan found being bad at anything more objectionable still.
"Rutland coach is an hour out," I said.
"I know.
Jem saw it on the road."
She wrung the cloth without looking up.
"Bridget's asking about the salt cod."
"Tell her November."
"I've told her November three times."
"Tell her again."
I leaned on the bar.
"How are we on ale?"
"Fine if the Rutland's not all men."
"It'll be all men."
She set the cloth down and gave me the look she reserved for situations where I was right and she would have preferred me not to be.
"I'll see about the next barrel," she said, and went.
The Rutland arrived twenty minutes early.
Eighteen passengers, all of them men, cold and bad-tempered and with six hours of each other already behind them.
I put them in the taproom and got Tom on plates and managed the kitchen myself while Nan managed the room, which she did with the efficiency and implicit threat that kept the rowdy ones quiet.
We were short a kitchen maid.

We had been short one since September, when the girl from Hertford decided that her cousin's dressmaking shop in London was a better prospect, which it probably was, and I had not replaced her because the arithmetic said wait.
We could manage with three of us and Tom if no one got ill and the coaches kept to schedule and nothing broke.
I filled plates.
Nan filled glasses.
Tom carried both and spilled neither, which was an improvement on last month.
By the time the Rutland left, I was running on the cold half-cup of tea I'd had at eleven.
The taproom was my grandmother's work, more than any other room.
She'd put in the oak counter and the hooks on the beams and the arrangement of barrels that Jem had never altered because it was, as he said, correct.
The portrait of King George above the fireplace was older than any of us.
I touched the frame as I passed.
The fire was low.
I built it up.
The soldier came in the back way just after one, during the gap between coaches.
He was at the kitchen door rather than the taproom entrance, which told me he'd been on the roads long enough to learn which door to try when you had nothing to spend.
His coat had been red once.
His boots were sound, which meant recently discharged rather than long adrift.
I was at the basin.
I turned and looked at him.
"I'm not asking for coin," he said.
"I've some left.
But if there's work —"
"Hauling water and washing pots," I said.
"You'll eat at the servant's table."
He hauled water and washed pots.
He was quiet and thorough and he stacked the crockery without being shown how.
Nan came through, looked at him, said nothing.
He ate at the servant's table with Jem, who said little, and with Tom the pot boy, who said too much, and with Nan, who said exactly what was needed and stopped there.
I ate standing at the counter.
I always did.
After, I wrapped three thick slices of bread in cloth and put them in his hand.
"Beds in Hitchin," I said.
"Tell them the White Hound sent you.
The landlord owes me a favour."
He looked at the bread and then at me.
He nodded, thanked me, and went.
I stood in the doorway and watched him get small on the road north.
Jem came up beside me.
"Third this week," he said.
"Mmm."
"North roads are flooding out above Huntingdon.
More'll come."
"I know."
He turned and went back toward the stable, moving the way he always moved in the yard: steady, a little sideways, the empty coat sleeve pinned up where his left arm had been since Salamanca.
He had never said the word Salamanca to me.
I knew it because my mother had written it in the accounts margin the day he came to work for her: Jem Bowker.
Stable hand.
Lost left arm in the Peninsula.
Good with horses.
She had not said what she thought about the rest of it.
He picked up a pitchfork with his right hand and got to work on the nearest stall.
I watched him a moment longer than I needed to, then went back inside.
Bridget came down in the late afternoon, later than usual.

She was seventy-three and climbed stairs at the pace she had decided was right for seventy-three, and she arrived in the kitchen with the look she wore when she'd been sitting with a thought long enough to have an opinion about it.
She was my mother's aunt.
She had a room above the kitchen and a small allowance and the right to have opinions, and she had been at the White Hound since before I was born.
I put the kettle on without being asked.
"You're thin," she said.
"I'm the same as I was last month."
"Then you were thin last month too."
She settled into the chair by the fire.
Her hands were warm and papery when she folded them in her lap.
Her eyes were grey and missed approximately nothing.
"How are the accounts?"
"Fine."
"How are they really?"
"Honest.
Near enough."
She made a sound that was not agreement.
She looked at the fire.
"Bradwell was here," she said.
"He was."
"He looked worried when he left."
"He looked pleasant."
"Yes," she said.
"That's what I mean."
I poured the tea.
She took her cup with both hands, not because she needed both but because she liked the warmth of the whole circumference.
I sat down across from her and we drank tea and let the kitchen settle around us the way it did in the late afternoon when the coaches had gone and the next ones hadn't come.
"Your mother would have been glad of October," she said.
"She hated August."
"Everyone hated August."
"She hated it more."
She turned her cup in her hands.
"You're working too hard."
"I'm working the right amount."
"There's no right amount in a place like this.
There's what it takes and what's left of you after."
She looked at me.
"Eat a proper dinner."
"I'll eat after the Edinburgh mail."
"That's nine o'clock."
"Yes."
She looked at me a moment longer.
Then she looked back at the fire.
"There's a good chapter in the Scott," she said.
"If you want something to take upstairs."
"I'll manage without Scott."
"That's what I thought."
She stood, careful, and put her cup in the basin.
She looked out the kitchen window at the yard, where the last of the daylight was doing what it could with the October cold, which was not much.
"Send Nan up with supper," she said.
"If you can spare her."
"I can spare her."
She went upstairs.
I heard each step, slow and even.
Her door.
Then nothing.
The Edinburgh mail came in at nine and left at half past.
Nan and I counted the takings at the bar, Nan on the coin, me on the notes, and by ten the house had gone quiet in the way that meant tomorrow was already starting.
I checked the fire.
I checked the bolts.
I went through the kitchen one last time.
Bread laid for morning.
Fire banked right.
Jem's lamp was out in the stable loft, which meant he'd gone down earlier than usual, which meant his knee was at him.
The cold always did it.
I was washing my hands at the basin when I heard the post slot click.
Late for the post.
I dried my hands and went through.
The letter was on the mat, one candle's worth of light from the sconce above the entry.
I picked it up.
The handwriting was careful and formed.
The seal was one I knew: the Stainforth estate, wax the dark red of old port.
Geoffrey Stainforth.
Who held the lease on the White Hound.
I broke it open.
Dear Miss Dale,
I hope this letter finds you in good health.
I write to request the convenience of a meeting at your earliest opportunity, in regard to certain matters concerning the current terms of the lease on the White Hound.
I intend no alarm by this correspondence — the meeting is a routine one, of the kind that good management of an estate requires — but I believe a conversation in person would be mutually beneficial.
I remain, &c., G.
Stainforth
I read it twice.
Certain matters concerning the current terms of the lease.
I folded the letter along its creases and set it on the mantelpiece where I would see it in the morning.
I went upstairs.
The inn settled around me as I climbed.
All its old sounds.
The creak on the fifth step.
The draught under Bridget's door.
The smell of tallow smoke and cold stone and bread.
Mine.
For now.
I blew out the candle and went to sleep.
Chapter 1
The squirrels came out of the tree line at 7:42 AM, same as yesterday.
Same as the day before.
I stood at my window with a cold cup of tea and watched them gather at the edge of my yard.
Six of them today.
They sat on their haunches in a neat row, black eyes fixed on my cottage, tails flicking in unison like a single organism pretending to be many.
I wasn't sure if they could see me through the glass.
I wasn't sure it mattered.
One of them turned its head, a sharp, mechanical movement, and I blinked.
For half a second, it was a fox.
Red fur, narrow snout, eyes like amber coins.
I blinked again.
Squirrel.
"Okay," I said to no one.
"That's new."
My nails were clipped too short to dig into my palms properly.
I'd cut them yesterday, distracted, gone too close on three fingers.

Now I pressed my thumb against the windowsill until the wood grain bit into skin, until I was certain I was awake, until the squirrels were just squirrels, until my breath fogged the glass and obscured them entirely.
When the fog faded, they were gone.
Mrs.
Halloran was dying today.
Probably.
Her daughter had called at six to say the breathing had changed, and I knew what that meant.
I'd sat with enough of them to know.
The body has a rhythm at the end, a tide that pulls out slow and doesn't come back in.
I finished my tea.
I checked the salt on the windowsills.
I did not look at the beach in last night's dream, or the woman walking into the water, or the fact that I'd woken with sand between my teeth.
Some things you don't look at.
You just keep moving.
The apartment above Gail's old converted garage wasn't much.
One bedroom, a bathroom where the hot water worked about sixty percent of the time, and a kitchen with a window that faced the ocean.
I'd lived here for three years and I hadn't hung anything on the walls.
Not a picture, not a calendar, nothing.
Gail had asked about it once and I'd told her I liked minimalism.
That was a nicer word for what I actually liked, which was being able to leave in under four minutes.
I got dressed.
Dark jeans, a gray sweater that had seen better decades, boots I'd resoled twice.
I pulled my hair back and caught sight of the gray streak at my left temple.
Twenty-seven years old with a skunk stripe.
Stress, my doctor said.
I didn't bother telling her my stress was a little more complicated than her chart could handle.
No mirrors in the apartment.
I'd taken them all down eight months ago after I saw something in one that wasn't my reflection.
Wasn't not my reflection either.
I didn't want to think about what it was.
I grabbed my bag—herbs, essential oils, the small leather case with the tinctures I mixed myself—and headed downstairs.
The salt on the front doorstep was undisturbed.
The bowl of water beside it was still full.
Good.
Fine.
Everything fine.
Manzanita, Oregon, population six hundred on a generous day, was the kind of town where people came to disappear.
Retirees.
Divorcées.
Women running from men who hit them.
I fit right in, except I was running from an entire pack of werewolves and the memory of the boy who'd stood in front of three hundred of them and told me I wasn't enough.
But sure.
Minimalism.
Mrs.
Halloran's house smelled like lavender and old books and the faint, sweet undertone that meant her body was already letting go.
Her daughter, Karen, met me at the door with red-rimmed eyes and a coffee she'd made too strong.
"She's not responding anymore," Karen said, her voice cracking on the last word.
"That's okay."
I set my bag down and took the coffee because refusing would've been cruel.
"That's where she's supposed to be right now."
I'd been doing this for two years.
Death doula.
Fancy title for what basically amounted to sitting with people while they died and making sure the dying part went as smoothly as possible.
Herbs for pain.
Oils for calm.
My hands on theirs so they knew someone was there.
I was good at it.
Practiced at thresholds.
I knew how to stand at the edge of something and not fall in.
Most of the time.
Mrs.
Halloran was eighty-six, and she'd had a good life.
Husband dead ten years.
Three kids, seven grandkids, a garden that still bloomed in November because she'd planted it stubborn.
Her breathing was the slow, rattling kind that meant hours, not days.
I sat beside her bed and held her hand and didn't say anything because there was nothing to say that her body didn't already know.
Karen cried in the kitchen.
I could hear her trying to be quiet about it, which was worse somehow.
People always tried to be quiet, like death needed manners.
Like if they cried too loud, they'd disturb the process.
They wouldn't.
I'd learned that early.
The dying don't care about your noise.
They're busy.
I rubbed a drop of lavender oil between my palms and held them near Mrs.
Halloran's face.
Not touching.
Just close enough for the scent to reach her.
Her eyelids fluttered once.
Maybe she was dreaming.
Maybe she was already somewhere else entirely.
I didn't reach for the Veil to check.
That wasn't what this was for.
This was the waking world, and she deserved to leave it on her own terms, in her own time.
My mother hadn't gotten that.
Nobody sat with her.
Nobody held her hand while the tide pulled her out.
She walked into the ocean on a Tuesday morning while I was at school and by the time anyone thought to look for her, the water had already won.
I pressed my thumb into my palm hard enough to hurt.
Focus.
At 11:47 AM, Mrs.
Halloran's breathing changed.
That last long exhale, the one that stretches out and out and doesn't turn around.
I felt it happen.
Not just heard it.
Felt the shift, the threshold crossing, the exact moment she went from here to not-here.
If I let myself, I could almost see it.
A thread, thin as spider silk, pulling loose from the world.
Snapping free.
I didn't let myself.
"Karen," I called softly.
She came in.
She knew.
The sound of someone not breathing is louder than you'd think.
I stayed for another hour.
Made tea.
Helped Karen call the funeral home.
Packed my bag and left through the garden because Mrs.
Halloran would've wanted someone to notice the roses one more time.
They were beautiful.
Still blooming.
Stubborn as hell.
I liked that about the dead, actually.
They left things behind that kept going.
Gardens.
Books.
Kids who cried in kitchens and made coffee too strong.
The living thought death was an ending, and it was, but it was also just a door.
I'd stood next to that door enough times to know.
Standing next to it was fine.
Walking through it voluntarily was a different thing entirely.
That was the part my mother hadn't seemed to understand.
Or maybe she'd understood it perfectly and chosen it anyway.
I really needed to stop thinking about my mother today.
The walk home took me along the beach, which was a mistake I made at least three times a week.
The Oregon coast in November was gray on gray on gray—gray sky, gray sand, gray water churning itself into foam that looked like static.
I kept my head down and walked fast and absolutely did not think about my mother walking into water that looked exactly like this.
Twelve years old.
Siltwater Pack, the coast.
Mom walked into the ocean one morning and didn't come back out.
Drowned, they said.
Or maybe she slipped into the Veil during one of her episodes and couldn't find her way back.
Nobody knew which version was true.
I'd spent fifteen years trying to decide which one was worse.
I still hadn't figured it out.
My phone buzzed.
Gail.
New shipment of romance novels at the shop.
I saved you the ones with the shirtless guys on the cover because I know you have standards.
I almost smiled.
Almost.
My standards are exclusively shirtless guys, I texted back.
Home in ten.

Gail Torvik was my landlord, my only real friend in Manzanita, and the owner of a bookshop that was hemorrhaging money so fast I was genuinely concerned she'd have to sell the building and I'd lose my apartment.
She was thirty-four, human, had no idea werewolves existed, and made the kind of grilled cheese that could make a grown woman weep.
She was also the only person in three years who'd made me feel like maybe I wasn't completely unfixable.
Not that I'd ever tell her that, because feelings were a trap and hope was just disappointment wearing a nice dress.
She didn't know about the salt on my windowsills or the bowls of water by the doors.
She didn't know I hadn't slept through a full night in five years.
She thought I was a light sleeper.
She thought the herbs were for clients only.
She thought the gray streak in my hair was edgy.
Gail thought a lot of things about me that weren't true, and keeping it that way was the only reason our friendship worked.
The second she found out what I actually was, what I could actually do, she'd look at me the way the Ridgeline Pack had looked at me.
Afraid first.
Disgusted second.
Gone third.
Been through that enough times.
No thanks.
I turned off the beach and cut through town.
Past the coffee shop that closed at two.
Past the post office.
Past the little grocery where everyone knew my name but nobody knew what I was.
That was the deal with Manzanita.
People didn't ask questions.
You showed up, you were polite, you bought your groceries, and whatever you were hiding was your own business.
Worked perfectly for me.
I was halfway up the stairs to my apartment when I felt it.
A prickle at the back of my neck.
Not danger, exactly.
More like being watched by something that wasn't a squirrel and wasn't pretending to be one.
I turned.
Nothing.
Street was empty.
Wind pushed a paper cup along the gutter.
Somewhere down the block, a dog barked twice and stopped.
The prickle didn't stop.
I went inside.
Locked the door.
Checked the salt.
Checked the water.
Stood in my kitchen with my back against the refrigerator and breathed until my hands stopped shaking, which took longer than I wanted to admit.
At 3:17 AM tonight, whether I liked it or not, I would slip into the Veil.
I would walk through someone's dreams.
Probably his.
Because apparently I was the kind of pathetic ex-mate who couldn't stop visiting the dreams of the man who'd rejected her in front of his entire pack five years ago.
Lyle Evenson.
Alpha of Ridgeline Pack.
The man who'd looked me in the eye at our mating ceremony and said the words that severed everything I thought I was.
I remembered it in pieces.
The bonfire.
Three hundred wolves in a circle.
His father's hand on his shoulder.
The pack council watching from the dais like judges at a sentencing.
And Lyle, twenty-five years old, jaw set, eyes on mine, saying the formal words of rejection while his wolf howled so loud I could feel it in my own chest.
He'd made a choice.
The pack council told him a Tide Walker as Luna was dangerous, unpredictable, a threat to everything they'd built.
His father was dying—I didn't know that then—and Lyle was terrified and alone and he chose them over me.
Fine.
People made choices.
I'd made mine.
I'd walked out of Ridgeline with one bag and no plan and I hadn't looked back.
Except the bond hadn't severed.
Not properly.
I knew that now.
I could feel it, this thin bleeding thread between us that wouldn't die no matter how much I wanted it to.
Five years and it was still there, leaking power from both of us like a wound that refused to close.
I should hate him.
I did hate him.
I also walked through his dreams every single night and watched him sleep and that was so fucked up I couldn't even think about it without wanting to throw something.
Some things you don't look at.
I put the kettle on.
I unpacked my bag.
I wiped down the tincture bottles and lined them up on the counter.
I pressed my too-short nails against the edge of the sink and breathed.
Outside, the ocean sounded like static.
The sun was going down.
In approximately ten hours, I would close my eyes and slip into the space between waking and sleeping and I would go to him because I always went to him.
Five years.
Every night.
Like my mother walking into the water.
I really needed to get my shit together.
The kettle screamed.
I poured the water.
I didn't look at the window because the squirrels would be back at dusk and I wasn't sure what I'd see this time.

I sat on my kitchen floor with my tea and I didn't think about the dream and I didn't think about the thread and I didn't think about the static figure I'd been seeing at the edges of the Veil for the last three months, the one that watched me with a hunger I could feel in my teeth.
I thought about Mrs.
Halloran instead.
Her garden.
Her last breath.
The way the thread of her life had pulled loose and snapped free, clean and complete, the way a death was supposed to go.
Not like the thread between me and Lyle, which refused to snap.
Which just bled and bled and bled.
Not like whatever was watching me from the Veil, which had no thread at all.
Just static.
Just hunger.
Just the sense that something very old and very wrong knew my name and was getting closer.
Some things you don't look at.
You just keep moving.
That had worked for five years.
I was starting to think it wasn't going to work much longer.
The letter lay where I had put it the night before, unopened, on the scrubbed deal table beside the ledger.
I had thought about it through the small hours the way one thinks about a tooth that will have to come out.
I opened it now, standing up, because sitting down to read a letter from Phineas Stainforth was a concession I was not prepared to make to my own kitchen.
His hand was what it always was: upright, unhurried, economical of ink.
He would do me the courtesy of calling at the inn this morning, between ten and noon, on a matter pertaining to the lease.
He remained my obliged servant.
That was the whole of it.
Seven lines.
He had never needed more.
I read it twice.
I set it down next to the ledger, squared the edge against the wood, and went to the range to feed the fire.
"Was that the one from last night?"
Nan said.
She was at the dresser with a stack of breakfast plates and had the decency not to look at me while she asked.
"It was."
"And?"
"He's coming between ten and noon."
Nan set the plates down without a rattle.
"I'll do the taproom floor, then, if you're doing the bar."
"Please."
She did not ask the rest of it, for which I was grateful.
Nan had a gift for not asking.

I tied my apron, checked the water in the kettle, and went through to sweep the hearth myself because if I gave myself nothing to do I would sit down and think, and thinking was not the morning's work.
By nine the taproom smelled of soap and damp boards and the kitchen smelled of yesterday's bread.
I put the ledger on the kitchen table, open at the current quarter, and left it there.
He would want to see it eventually.
He could see it on my table, in my hand, with my figures in the margins.
I had not hidden an account from a man yet and I was not going to begin with him.
I put out a clean cloth, a jug, two cups.
Then I took my second apron off its peg, the good linen one, and tied it over the first.
My grandmother had worn two aprons on days she expected trouble.
She said it saved the under one and gave you something to untie when you wanted a second to think.
I had not understood her until I was twenty.
Nan, coming back from the yard with her broom, looked at the apron and said nothing, which was how she said a great deal.
He came at ten minutes past eleven.
I heard the gig before I saw it, the particular quick wheel of a gentleman's rig on the flags, and a single groom's voice calling the horse to stand.
By the time I was at the door he was already on my threshold, hat in hand, the morning behind him very clear and cold.
"Miss Dale."
"Mr Stainforth.
Good morning."
"A bright one."
His coat was dark blue wool, cut close, good at the shoulders, two years old and cared for.
His boots had been done that morning.
"The road was hard enough.
I expected mud."
"We've had the wind from the north three days.
It dries a road faster than sun."
"So I am told."
He stepped in as I stepped back, and handed me the hat without asking, which was the first thing he did and also the whole of what I needed to know about how he meant the visit to go.
"I won't keep you long.
I know mornings here are not idle."
"They are not.
Will you take tea?"
"Thank you.
A little."
I showed him into the small parlour off the taproom, which was clean and cold, and went to the kitchen for the tray.
Nan had already put the kettle back on the fire.
She lifted an eyebrow at me and I gave her the small nod that meant everything is as it should be, which was not true and also not her business.
I had received him before, twice, in my mother's time, standing at her elbow while she did the talking.
I had watched her pour his tea with a steady hand and ask after his sister's health and give him nothing at all.
Patience had a way of answering a question that made the questioner feel answered without having been told anything.
I did not have her way.
I had my own way, which was shorter.
I carried the tray in.
He had not sat down.
He was standing at the window with his hands behind his back, looking at my yard.
"Your stable boy," he said, without turning, "keeps the cobbles well."
"Jem is my ostler, not my stable boy.
He keeps the whole yard."
"My mistake."
"It's a common one."
He turned then, and the corner of his mouth moved in what a more hopeful woman might have read as a smile.
I poured.
He took his cup with a small bow of the head and did not drink.
"Miss Dale, I shall be frank, since frankness is a kindness between neighbours."
"I prefer it."
"The lease on the White Hound comes up for renewal at Lady Day."
"March the twenty-fifth.
Yes."
"Quite."
He set his cup back on the tray untouched.
"I have been reviewing the terms at some length.
There are clauses in the original agreement, drawn up in your grandmother's time, which have not been strictly observed in the years since.
The covenant as to repair.
The provision against lodgers of indeterminate character.
The matter of the tenant's standing in the parish."
"My grandmother's lease was granted to a widow.
My mother's was renewed to a widow.
I do not think the covenant as to repair has been neglected, Mr Stainforth.
I can show you a roof that doesn't leak and a cellar that keeps."
"I do not doubt it.
I should like to see them, if you will indulge me."
There it was.
He had not asked.
He had arrived at the asking as a man arrives at the last step of a staircase he has already climbed.
"Of course," I said.
"When you have finished your tea."
"I have finished, thank you."
I untied the outer apron and hung it on the hook by the door.
He watched me do it and said nothing, which was also an answer.
We went through the taproom first.

He touched the long oak beam above the bar with the flat of two fingers, looking up, and I watched him do it and did not feel anything in particular about it except a small, cold arithmetic in the back of my head.
He asked after the capacity at supper.
I told him: forty at a push, thirty in comfort.
He asked what I paid in parish rates.
I told him that, too, to the shilling.
He nodded each time as though confirming what he already knew, which was probably the case.
A man like Stainforth does not walk into a house unprepared.
The cellar door was next.
It had swelled in the damp of the autumn and sticks in its top corner; Jem had been meaning to plane it, and I had been meaning to let him.
Stainforth lifted the latch and found the resistance and did not force it.
He crouched, examined the hinge, and laid his gloved finger along the pin.
"Damp," he said.
"It sticks in wet weather.
Jem will see to it this week."
"Small things," he said, straightening.
"They tell one a good deal."
"They tell one there is always a small thing needing seeing to.
Yes."
He inclined his head.
I went down the cellar steps ahead of him with a candle and showed him the casks, and the slate where I kept the draw, and the iron-bound chest in the corner that holds the spirits.
He looked at everything and touched nothing down there, which I noted.
A man who touches the beams upstairs and not the casks below is a man whose interest is the building, not the trade.
Up the stair to the first floor.
Along the passage.
He paused at the linen press, and then at the door of the long room, and asked about the rooms that faced the road, whether they were let at present and at what rate.
I told him.
He asked whether I kept the rooms full through the winter.
I told him I did not; no one does, between Michaelmas and Candlemas, and the accounts showed it.
He said he was glad to hear I kept good accounts.
"I keep them because I must," I said.
"Not because I am glad to."
"A necessary virtue is still a virtue, Miss Dale."
"Is it."
He let that go, which was his decision, not mine.
We came out into the stable yard by the back passage.
The wind was sharp.
Jem was at the far end with a gelding's off-hind up on his knee, and did not look round, which is how Jem greets gentry.
A hen crossed the yard between us.
Stainforth walked to the corner where the rail meets the fence, and put his hand on the corner post, and gave it the smallest sideways push.
The post moved.
It always moves.
Jem had been saying for a month that he would reset it.
I had told him twice it could wait.
"A loose post," Stainforth said.
"Yes."
"Your man will see to it."
"He will."
He stood with his hand on the post and looked at me directly for the first time since he had come in the door.
His eyes were a pale, clean grey, and there was nothing in them I could take hold of.
"Miss Dale.
I wonder whether I may speak plainly about the renewal."
"Please."
"You have run this house for four years to a high standard.
I have no complaint to make of your management.
But you will understand that a coaching inn on the Great North Road is not a private concern.
It is a matter of parish interest.
The magistrates hear of it.
The vestry hears of it.
I hear of it."
He paused, and did not lift his hand from the post.
"It has been suggested to me, by parties I cannot name, that the house has of late offered shelter to men who cannot account for themselves.
Discharged soldiers without papers.
Vagrants.
Persons likely to be a charge upon the parish."
"I feed hungry men bread when they come to my door.
I do not lodge them upstairs."
"I make no accusation.
I note a concern."
"Noted."
"The lease, at renewal, carries a clause as to the character of the tenant and the public order of the house.
It is within my discretion."
He lifted his hand from the post at last.
"I have a nephew, as you may know, who takes an interest in property of this kind.
A man of sound habits.
It has been represented to me that a house of this standing might be steadier in a man's hands."
I counted the breaths in and the breaths out, the way I count a till.
It cost me nothing to count them.
Counting is not feeling.
"Mr Stainforth.
I have held the lease four years.
I have paid the rent to the day.
I have kept the roof, the stabling and the accounts.
The house is steadier in my hands than it has been in a generation, and you know it, because you have just walked through it."
"I do know it."
"Then we understand one another."
"I think we do."
He said it gently, which was the chill of the thing.
He was not threatening me.
He was telling me what he had decided, and allowing me the courtesy of being present while he decided it.
Somewhere behind my sternum the accountant's part of me was already writing down the figures: Lady Day, the clause, the nephew, the timetable.
Write them down.
Put them in the ledger.
Do not feel them yet.
"I shall write to you before the quarter," he said.
"There will be particulars to discuss.
I should not like there to be surprises on either side."
"Nor should I."
He inclined his head.
I walked him back through the yard, through the taproom, to the front door, and handed him his hat.
His groom brought the gig round.
He mounted without hurry.
He lifted the hat an inch as the horse took the weight.
"Good morning, Miss Dale."
"Good morning, Mr Stainforth."
The gig went out under the arch and turned south on the road, and the yard was suddenly quiet, the way a room is quiet after a clock has stopped.
I stood on the flagstones a moment.
Then I went back inside, because standing still is a thing I do not do in my own house when someone has just told me he means to take it.
I went up the stairs to Bridget.
There are fifteen treads, and the third from the top is warped, and sings a particular note under any weight heavier than a cat.
I did not count them.
I did not need to.
My feet have known them since I could climb.
Her door was on the latch.

She was in the chair by the window, where she is always in the chair by the window, with her work basket at her elbow and the blue bowl of apples on the mantel where it had been since my mother had set it there.
She did not turn her head when I came in.
She had been watching the yard.
"Sit yourself down," she said, "and put the kettle over.
I saw him come in and I saw him go out, and I've a decent notion of what went on in between."
"Have you."
"I have.
Cups are in the press."
I set the kettle on, and took down the good china, because she always used the good china, because what in the mercy of God were we keeping it for.
She poured when the water was ready.
Her hands are knotted at the knuckles now, and she does not hurry them, and the tea came out of the spout in a clean unbroken line, the way it always had.
"Drink that," she said.
I drank.
She watched me drink, and did not ask.
"He wants the lease for his nephew at Lady Day," I said at last.
"He was civil about it."
"He would be.
His father was civil to your grandmother when he raised the rent in eighty-nine.
It runs in the blood with them."
"He touched the hinge on the cellar door."
"Did he now."
"And the corner post in the yard."
She made a small sound in her throat, not quite a laugh.
"A man in a good coat counting the hinges of a house he means to have.
There's a thing your grandmother would have liked to see.
She'd have fed him a scone with the flour short in it and watched him eat it."
Her accent had come up on her a little; it does when she is amused, and when she is pressed.
"I didn't feed him anything.
He didn't drink his tea."
"No.
His kind don't."
I set my cup down.
My hand was steady.
I had known it would be steady.
That was not the part of me I was worried about.

She was looking at me across the rim of her own cup, and then she was not looking at me at all; she was looking at the yard again, at the line of the wall my mother had whitewashed the year before she died.
"Your mother," she said, "kept this place standing through worse than him.
Through a bad year and a worse man, and she did it on her own two feet."
"I know."
"She kept it because it was hers, and she would not be parted from what was hers.
That was her strength.
It was also the thing she starved for.
There is a difference, girl, between holding on to what is yours and holding yourself back from what might be.
Your mother never quite worked out where the one stopped and the other began.
It would be a great pity if her daughter didn't either."
She said it the way she said everything, without heat, the cup still in her hand.
She did not look at me while she said it.
That was the kindness in it.
I sat with it.
It sat with me.
I did not agree, and I did not argue, and I felt the shape of it settle somewhere I would have to deal with later and not now.
"I'll want the kettle on again at four," I said.
"There's a parcel coming from Hatfield and I've Jem to speak to about the yard."
"Go on with you, then."
I stood.
I stacked the cups on the tray, because she could not carry a tray down those stairs any more and would not let me say so.
At the door I stopped, because it seemed wrong to leave without saying something, and I had nothing to say.
"Go on," she said again, more gently.
"It'll keep."
I went down the fifteen treads, and the third from the top sang under me, and I carried her line down with me without looking at it directly, which was all I could do with it for the moment.
The afternoon ran as afternoons do.
Nan was at the bar by three, Jem in the yard with the gelding and then with the parcel from Hatfield, the rain coming on thin and cold with the early dark, the lamps lit before five.
I did not stop.
I did not sit down.
The wind turned and the lamps guttered in the passage and I trimmed them one by one as I went past.
It was full dark and after nine when I heard the knock at the yard gate.
Not the front door.
Not the taproom.
The yard.
I took the lantern off its hook by the kitchen door and went out.
The rain had set in properly; it ran off the gutter above the scullery in a thin rope.
At the gate stood a man, taller than the gate's top bar, with a dog at his heel, low and grey and wet through.
His coat had been good once.
His boots had been better.
He had walked a long way in them.
I could smell the walk on him from three paces off, the wet wool and the road.
"I'm sorry to trouble you, missus."
"Miss," I said.
"What do you want?"
"Work, if you've any.
A night's shelter if you've none."
He did not say it as a man begging.
He said it as a man stating the case.
The dog sat when he stopped speaking, without being told.
I was too tired for this.
I was too tired to set a question I already knew the answer to, and too tired to pretend I did not know it.
I held the lantern up.
He did not shy from the light.
His face was in shadow under the brim of the hat, and I did not try to make it out.
"The stable's dry at the north end.
There's clean straw in the last stall but one.
You can sleep there tonight.
The dog with you, if he's quiet."
"He's quiet."
"Come and see me in the kitchen in the morning.
Not before seven."
"Thank you."
"Don't thank me yet.
I haven't said I'd keep you."
"No, miss."
He touched the brim of the hat, the way a man does who has done it for years without thinking.
The dog got up when he moved.

They went across the yard together, and I shut the gate behind them, and went back into the kitchen with the lantern, and set it on the table, and did not think about him because there was the dough to set for the morning and I had not set it.
I set it.
I covered it with the cloth.
I wiped down the board.
The window over the sink gives on to the yard.
I did not mean to look.

I was rinsing the cloth, and the lamp in the stable doorway was lit, which meant he had found the flint box where Jem keeps it, which meant he had been in a yard like mine before and knew where such things lived.
The dog was settling itself on the straw outside the stall.
He was at the stable door with his back to me, doing something with the hinge, the one that sticks in damp weather, the one Stainforth had laid his finger along at noon.
He had his knife out.
He worked at the pin, eased it, set it back.
The door swung.
He tried it twice.
He set his shoulder to the corner post of the yard fence, the loose one, and lifted, and settled the foot of it in the hole, and packed stones round it with his boot.
His hands moved quickly and without fuss in the lamplight.
They were large hands and they knew the work.
I stood at the sink with the wet cloth in mine and watched his hands finish the post.
Then I turned back to my board and wiped it down again, because it did not need wiping down, and that was what I had to give it.
The letter was still where I had set it down the night before, face up on the kitchen table next to the ledger, as though leaving it in plain sight would make it smaller by morning.
It had not.
Stainforth's hand ran the usual four lines, and the four lines said the usual four things.
He would call today.
He trusted the hour between eleven and noon would suit.
He wished to walk the premises.
He remained my obedient servant, which was the part that always made me want to laugh.
I read it twice, because I had read it twice last night and wanted to see whether a third reading changed anything.
It did not.
I folded it, set it under the ledger's corner so the draught from the range would not lift it, and went to find my apron.
Nan was already at the bread.
She looked up, saw my face, and did not ask.

"I'll put the good cups out."
"Don't.
He's not a guest.
He's a landlord."
"All the more reason."
She went back to the dough.

I almost smiled.
My mother had a rule about cracked china and men who deserved it, and Nan had picked it up the way she picked up everything, by standing near and paying attention.
I did not say so.

I took down the broom instead and swept the taproom myself, which was Piers's job on a proper morning, because sweeping a room you have swept a thousand times is the kind of work that lets the mind settle.

I pinned my hair tighter than it needed to be pinned.
These were the small decisions.

The groom stayed with the reins.

"Miss Dale.
A fine morning."
"Mr Stainforth.
Will you come in."
"I thank you."
He removed his hat inside the door, which was a courtesy due any roof, and looked about the taproom as a man looks who has been in a room before and wishes you to know he remembers it.

I had feared otherwise."

She set her cup down.

Keeping the books.
Waiting."

"My mother ran the house."

It was not loud.

It landed.
I did not say so.

"I have the afternoon's provisions to see to."
"Of course you do."
"Thank you for the tea."
"You are welcome to it."
I went to the door.

Her hand did not reach for me; she was not that kind of aunt, and I was not that kind of niece, and the line had been said and the tea had been drunk and that was how women who had known each other fifty years arranged a morning.

"The fence post," I said.
"I shall speak to Jem."
"Do."

Two dozen eggs.
The chimney in the blue bedroom.
The fence post, which I underlined once and did not look at again.

I worked.
That was the answer.

"Understood."

She passed the cup.
I took it, and my hand was steadier than I had expected it to be, which was something.
The window behind her looked down into the yard, where Jem was bringing a grey out of the second stall and the crooked fence post stood as it had stood.

The mantel held three things: a silver cross that was my grandfather's, a wooden box with cards in it, and a small chipped plate that had come from Wexford in 1760 with a girl who had not yet been Bridget.
"He walked the house," I said.
"Did he."
"The cellar.
The landing.
The yard."
"And the fence post?"
I looked at her.
"Yes."
"That post has been crooked since your mother's time.
I have watched three men touch it for three different reasons and not one of them set it right."
"Jem means to."
"Jem means a great many things."
I drank the tea.
It was the proper tea, not the kitchen blend; she had a small canister she kept for occasions, and she had apparently decided this was one.
The cup was the one with the blue rim that had been her wedding china, which she used because what, she had once said to me, were we saving it for.
"He will not renew the lease," I said.
"He has not said so."
"He will not renew it in my name."
She set her cup down.
Her accent had come up on her a little; it does when she is amused, and when she is pressed.
"And what will you do about it, then."
"What I have been doing."
"Which is."
"Running the inn.
Keeping the books.
Waiting."
"Ah."
She looked at me, and I watched her decide something, and I braced myself the way I had braced myself in the yard half an hour before.
"Your mother waited."
"My mother ran the house."
"Your mother ran the house, and she waited, and she buried herself in the ledger every night of her widowhood because the ledger would not ask her anything she could not answer.
And one morning she dropped in the kitchen with a ladle in her hand.
There is a difference, Dinah, between holding on and holding back, and she did not know the difference, and I do not want to bury you the same way."
It was not loud.
It was not a speech.
She picked up her cup again after she said it, and she drank, and she did not look at me to see if the line had landed.
It landed.
I did not say so.
I set my cup down carefully on the saucer, because I did not trust my hand to set it down without care, and I finished the tea, and I stood.
"I have the afternoon's provisions to see to."
"Of course you do."
"Thank you for the tea."
"You are welcome to it."
I went to the door.

Her hand did not reach for me; she was not that kind of aunt, and I was not that kind of niece, and the line had been said and the tea had been drunk and that was how women who had known each other fifty years arranged a morning.
At the door I stopped.
"The fence post," I said.
"I shall speak to Jem."
"Do."
The stairs going down creaked on the same tread.
I registered it the way I had registered it going up.
I went into the kitchen and put the apron back on, and I picked up the list I had begun before the letter, and I wrote the afternoon's work into it.
Flour from Hitchin.
Two dozen eggs.
The chimney in the blue bedroom.
The fence post, which I underlined once and did not look at again.
Nan came through with the empty basket and did not ask about Bridget.
She saw the list and added hops in her own hand, because we were low, and went back out.
I worked.
That was the answer.
I had been given the answer a long time ago, and it had served me through worse mornings than this, and it would serve me through this one.
The afternoon went.
The lamps were lit early; the light went out of the sky by four, and a thin rain came in from the east, not hard enough to drum but steady enough to darken the yard stones.
Nan carried the bar.
Jem came in and out.
Two coaches came through, one late, one on time, and neither wanted trouble.
By eight the taproom had thinned and by nine it was quiet enough to hear the kettle.
I was at the kitchen sink with a pan in my hands when the knock came at the yard door.
Not the main door.
Not the taproom.
The yard door, which opened onto the stable yard, and which people knocked on only if they had come in past the gate and did not want to present themselves at the front.
I took the lantern.
I opened the door one-handed, with the pan still in the other, because I had been about to set it on the board and had not.
A man stood in the rain.
Tall enough that he had to incline his head a little under the lintel.
The coat was soaked dark at the shoulders.
A dog sat at his heel, long-legged, brindled, the kind that takes up less room than a dog its size ought to.
The man's face was half in shadow and half in the lantern's yellow.
I did not look at his face long.
I looked at the coat, which had been a good coat once, and the boots, which had been good boots and had walked too far, and the dog, which was not thin but was not fed that day either.
"Evening," he said.
"Evening."
"I'm looking for work.
Stable work, or any work.
I can pay for the night if I've to, but I'd rather earn it."
His voice was low, level.
Not a begging voice.
Not a practised voice either.
A tired voice.
I had been tired for fourteen hours and I was not going to hire a stranger at the yard door in the rain, and I was not going to turn a man and a dog back into the road at this hour either.
The predictable traffic of the year did not stop at November; I had fed six men already this autumn who would not remember my name by Christmas.
"The stable's dry," I said.
"There's hay in the far stall and a blanket on the peg.
You can sleep there tonight.
Come to the kitchen in the morning and we'll see about work then."
"I'm obliged."
"The dog with you?"
"He is."
"He sleeps where you sleep.
Not in the kitchen."
"Understood."
"Have you eaten."
A pause.
"Today, yes."
Which meant not much, and not recently, but it was the answer of a man who would not take more than he had asked for.
I went to the board and cut bread and cheese and wrapped it in a cloth and brought it to him at the door.
He took it with a small nod.
The dog's tail moved once against his leg.
"In the morning," I said.
"In the morning."
I closed the door.
I heard his boots go across the yard stones, and then nothing, because the rain took the rest of it.
I went back to the pan.

I finished it and set it on the rack and wiped my hands and began on the board, and as I worked I could see out the kitchen window into the yard, because the kitchen window looked out that way and there was nothing to be done about it.
The lantern he had been given from the stable peg moved across the yard in the rain.
He set it on the mounting block.
He was doing something at the stable door; I saw the shape of his shoulder against the wood and then heard the small creak of a hinge being worked.
The hinge that stuck.
He worked it twice and it stopped sticking.

Then he crossed to the far end of the yard, where the crooked fence post stood, and he crouched at the base of it, and his hands moved around the foot of the post in the lantern-light, packing something, stone or earth, I could not see which from where I stood.
The post straightened under his hands.
He stood up and tested it with a push.
It held.
I watched his hands at the post.
They were large and they moved without hurry, and they had set the thing right.
I turned back to the board and picked up the cloth.
The letter sat on the kitchen table where I had left it the night before, still folded, still sealed, still inarguably there.
I picked it up.
I put it down.
I picked it up again and broke the wafer with my thumb.
Stainforth's hand was what I expected: the long loops, the tidy spacing, the absence of anything warm.

*Miss Dale — I shall do myself the honour of calling upon you tomorrow between the hours of ten and twelve, upon a matter concerning the lease.* That was the whole of it, barring his name and the date.
He did not waste ink on people who held their property at his pleasure.
I read it twice.
Then I set it down beside the ledger and went to find my apron.
"Nan," I said, when I passed her on the stair.
"He's coming today.
Between ten and twelve."
"Lord help us," said Nan, who had been told enough about Mr Stainforth over the past two years to save me the trouble of explaining who *he* was.
"Shall I hide the soldiers?"
"The soldiers left at first light.
Sweep the taproom twice.
The ledger stays where it is."
"On the table?"
"On the table."
She gave me a look I knew and did not answer.
I had decided last night that he would not walk into my kitchen and find my accounts tucked out of sight like a secret.
The ledger was my work.
If he meant to question it, he could question it in front of the book itself.
I checked the fire.
I checked the fire again, because I had not seen it the first time.
I took down the good tea and then put it back, and took down the ordinary tea and kept it.
A landlord inspecting property is not a guest.
I would not offer him my best leaves.
My grandmother had received his father once, in the year before she died.
Patience had told me about it when I was fifteen, in the way she told me most things, while we were turning a mattress.
*Ruth gave him ordinary tea and let him wait in the taproom with the drovers.
He never called again.* My grandmother had been bolder than I could afford to be.
But the tea, at least, I could manage.
The gig came into the yard at twenty minutes past ten.
A single groom, a single horse, a coat of good wool the colour of wet slate.
I heard the boots on the flagstones before I saw the man, and I thought, absurdly, that he walked as though the flagstones belonged to him.
Perhaps, in some accounting, they did.
"Miss Dale."
"Mr Stainforth.
Good morning."
"A fine morning.
Drier than yesterday."
"The road will be easier for it."
"Just so."
He removed his hat.
"I trust I find you well."
"Well enough, thank you.
Will you come through?"
He came through.
I took him to the taproom because the taproom was where I received people who had not come as guests, and he registered the choice without remarking on it.
His eyes moved along the beams, the settle, the window into the yard, and then came back to me with the same composure with which they had left.
"I shall not detain you long," he said.
"I should like to look at the house, if you have no objection."
I had objections.
I had a great many.
"Of course," I said.
"This way."
He walked through the taproom first, then the passage to the cellar stair.
At the cellar door he paused and put his hand to the hinge, and the hinge, which sticks in damp weather and had been sticking yesterday, stuck now.
He worked it gently, twice, as if testing the weight of the thing, and then let it settle.
"The damp," he said.
"It eases in summer."
"Mm."
He looked at the hinge a moment longer than was needed for a hinge.
"Your casks?"
"Forty barrels in the lower cellar at present.
Porter, small beer, and two of brandy.
I can show you the cellar book if you wish."
"Not necessary."
He moved on.
I followed him, because leaving him to walk my house alone was worse than walking it with him.
He went up the stair to the first-floor landing and looked along the passage, counting doors without appearing to count.
A man in a good coat counting doors.
I kept my face still and thought, quite clearly, that I was watching a sum being done.
"Twenty rooms above," he said, not asking.
"Twenty."
"All let at present?"
"Seventeen.
Three held for tonight's mail."
"And your rate?"
I gave him the rate.
He nodded as though he had known it and was simply confirming that I knew it too.
He turned at the end of the passage and came back toward me.
"The parish, Miss Dale.
There has been some concern."
"Concern, Mr Stainforth."
"The number of discharged men at your door.
It has been remarked upon."
"By whom?"
"By those whose business it is to remark."
"I feed them bread and broth when I have it.
I do not take them in unless they have coin."
"Quite.
The point is that they come."
He said this in the tone of a man pointing out a draught in a window.
"An inn acquires a character, Miss Dale.
Once acquired, characters are slow to alter."
"The inn has been here ninety years.
Its character has altered several times."
He smiled, a small courteous smile that did not touch his eyes.
"Indeed."
He moved past me and down the back stair toward the yard.
I followed.

My grandmother had a way of standing at the top of a stair when she meant to remind a man whose house he was in; I used it now, two treads above him, and he did not turn, and the lesson went where lessons without an audience tend to go.
In the yard he went to the fence along the stable side.
Jem had been meaning to reset the post at the near end, which had lifted out of true in the autumn wet.
Stainforth put his hand to the post.
He rocked it, an inch, two inches, and then released it.
"A man's work, this," he said mildly.
"The post."
"It is on Jem's list."
"Mm."
He did not look at me.
He looked at the post.
"Miss Dale.
I shall be frank.
The lease comes up for renewal at Michaelmas."
"I am aware of the date."
"I have been giving thought to its terms.
The inn has been competently held these four years.
I make no complaint of that."
"Thank you."
"However."
He turned.
"A lease of this size, in a house of this custom, is a considerable undertaking.
It has been suggested to me, by those with an interest in the parish, that the terms might be better fulfilled by a tenant of broader resource.
A man, for instance, with access to capital for the repairs that time will demand.
A man whose standing would ease the concerns I have mentioned.
I have a nephew who has expressed some interest.
I mention him only as a possibility.
The decision is mine."
He said it without heat, as he had said everything.
He might have been remarking on the weather.
I was aware, in the way one is aware of having put one's hand too near a flame, that my face had not moved.
Four years of numbers sat on the kitchen table behind me.
The house was paid to the week.
I had made improvements he could see if he turned his head.
I said none of this.
Instead I said: "The lease's terms are in the document, Mr Stainforth.
I have kept to them."
"You have.
I do not say otherwise."
"Then the question at Michaelmas is whether you renew."
"The question at Michaelmas," he said, "is what best serves the house."
"The house is served."
"So it appears."
A silence.
Absurd, I thought, the arithmetic of this: a man in a fifteen-guinea coat standing in my yard counting my fence posts, and I am to believe he is thinking of the house.
"I shall not trouble you further this morning," he said.
He replaced his hat.
"You will hear from me before the quarter.
Good day, Miss Dale."
"Good day, Mr Stainforth."
He crossed the yard to the gig.
The groom handed him up.
The wheels turned on the gravel and the gate swung to, and the yard was quiet after, with the hens in the shed, and a wind in the elm by the wall.
I stood where he had left me.
Then I moved, because standing still on his schedule was a thing I would not do.
I climbed the back stair to Bridget's rooms.
Bridget's stair has seventeen treads and a warp in the third from the top that has been there since I was a child.
It creaks under weight and it does not creak under mine, because I have known how to place my foot on it since I was nine.
I placed my foot on it now and it made no sound at all.
She was in her chair by the window.
She had seen the gig, of course; her window is exactly the window for seeing gigs.
The good china was already on the tray.
"Sit down," she said, without turning round.
"The kettle's been and gone twice waiting on you."
"He kept me longer than I meant."
"Aye, he would."
She poured.
Her hands are not steady now, but they are exact, and the tea went into the cup without a drop on the saucer.
"Sugar?"
"No."
"You never do.
I ask because I hope."
She handed me the cup.
"Drink your tea."
I drank my tea.

The window faced the yard and I could see the place the gig had stood, and the post at the near end of the stable fence, and a sparrow on the post that had not been there when Stainforth had his hand upon it.
"He went through the house," I said.
"I know he did."
"He touched the cellar hinge."
"Mm."
"And the fence post."
"Yes."
"He spoke of his nephew."
"Did he name him?"
"No."
"He will."
She took up her own cup.
"In his time."
We sat.
A clock I could not see was ticking somewhere in the far room.
I had not realised, until I sat down, that my shoulders had been up near my ears for the better part of an hour.
I set them down.
"Your mother," Bridget said, "would have given him ordinary tea."
"I did."
"Good girl."
A small silence.
I thought she would leave it there.
She did not.
"Dinah."
"Yes."
"There is a difference," she said, "between holding on to a thing and holding back from every other thing for its sake.
Your mother never learned it.
She held on with both her hands, and she kept the house, and she died on her feet in the kitchen with a ladle in her grip.
I loved her.
I am telling you what I watched."
The Wexford came up into her voice at the end, the way it does when she is tired or pressed, and then it went again.
I set the cup down.
The saucer was louder than I meant.
"I have the inn to run," I said.
"You have."
"I am not my mother."
"You are not."
She looked at me over the rim of her cup.
"I am saying that the holding on is a thing you have, and the holding back is a thing you do, and they are not the same, and I should like you not to confuse them."
"I shall think on it."
"You shall not.
You shall go down those stairs and not think on it for a fortnight, and then one night you shall think on it for half a minute while you are doing something else, and that will be the beginning.
I know you, child."
I stood up.
I finished the tea standing, which was rude, and she let me be rude, which was how she let me love her back when I could not say so.
"I am going down," I said.
"Go down, then."
At the door I turned.
"The tea was good."
"The tea is always good.
It's the company that wants work."
I came down the seventeen treads and the third from the top creaked this time, because I was not attending, and I let it.
In the kitchen the ledger was where I had left it and the letter was where I had left it, and I took the letter and put it into the drawer with the others, and I went back to the day.
The afternoon took what afternoons take.
Nan at the bar through the coach change at three.
Jem in the yard with the mail horses.
A barrel up from the cellar that had wanted shifting since Tuesday.
The sky lowered by four, and a thin rain began, and I sent Nan to light the lamps early.
By seven the wind had come round and turned colder, and the taproom was full of damp coats and the smell of wet wool and tallow.
It was near ten when the knock came at the yard gate.
Not the main door.
Not the taproom.
The yard gate, which is where men come who do not expect to be let through the front.
I took a lantern and went out.
The rain was fine, almost a mist, and the lantern's light went a little way and stopped.
A man stood on the far side of the gate.
Tall.
Travel-worn.
A dog at his heel, low and grey in the wet.
"Ma'am," he said.
His voice was low and not servile.
"I'm looking for work.
Or for shelter for the night.
Either will do."
I lifted the lantern a little.
The coat had been a good coat once and had been walked in hard.
The boots were Peninsular boots, or their cousins.
I could not see his face past the brim of his hat, and I did not try.
"We're full in the house," I said.
"I don't need the house."
I was tired.

I had been tired before Stainforth and I was tireder now, and the predictability of a man at my gate on a wet night in October was not lost on me, and neither was the fact that I had fed three such men that week and taken none in.
My grandmother had a rule about strangers at the yard gate after dark, which was to shelve the question until the morning, because the morning had better light and a steadier head.
"The stable's dry," I said.
"There's straw in the far stall.
You can sleep there.
The dog with you."
"Thank you."
"I'm not hiring tonight.
We'll talk in the morning, if you're still here."
"Understood."
He touched his hat.
Not a flourish; a small motion, done once.
He said something to the dog that I did not catch, and the dog went at his heel toward the stable.
I held the lantern until he had the stable door open, and I saw him stop and work the latch, which was not stiff, and then he went in.
I came back into the kitchen and set the lantern on the table.
Nan had gone to bed.
Jem had gone to bed.
The fire was down to its red.
I had one task left, which was the bread set for tomorrow, and I did it because it was there to do.
The kitchen window gave on the yard.
I could not help that; it had been put there for the purpose.
While I knocked the dough back and turned it I could see the stable door and the lantern he had lit in there, a soft square of yellow through the crack at the hinge.
He came out once.
He settled the dog, who had followed him out, under the eave where the straw was dry.

He went to the cellar side of the stable wall and put his hand to the hinge of the stable door, which sticks the same way the cellar hinge sticks, and he worked it twice and lifted the door a fraction on its pin and set it back, and the sticking was gone.
Then he went to the fence and the post at the near end, and he knelt, and he set the post true, and packed the earth at its foot with the side of his boot.
I covered the dough and laid the cloth over it.
His hands moved at the post, steady, and then he straightened, and then he went back into the stable, and the lantern inside went out.
I turned from the window to bank the fire.
The letter was on the table where I had left it the night before, face down, a corner caught under the lip of the ledger.
I had meant not to open it until the taproom was swept.
I opened it instead with my thumb still smelling of tea and read Stainforth's hand twice: he would call this morning, between ten and noon, on the subject of the lease.
He did not waste words on a leasehold tenant.
He did not need to.
I set the letter down next to the ledger and found my apron on the peg.
"Is he coming today, then," Nan said from the hearth, not looking up from the kettle.
"Between ten and noon."
"I'll do the taproom."
"You'll do the taproom and the first landing.
I'll see to the cellar myself."
Nan set the kettle on the hook without argument.
She had been fourteen when I hired her and she had learned early when I wanted answers and when I wanted the next thing done.
I was grateful for it most mornings.
This morning I was grateful for it the way a person is grateful for a wall behind her back.
I went through the taproom with a cloth and a practical eye.
The brass on the tap-handles, which would catch any light he brought in with him.
The ledger, left open on the kitchen table in plain sight.
I had no intention of hiding my accounts from a man who had come to question whether I could keep them.
If he wanted numbers he could have numbers.
I put out the good cups because the good cups said this was a house that received callers, and not a kitchen where a woman stood alone.
I did not change my dress.
I had thought about it for the length of time it took to lift my eyes to the press, and then I did not.
The grey wool was clean.
I was the woman who ran this inn.
A silk would have said I was a woman pretending to receive him on his terms.
At a quarter past ten the gig turned in at the gate.
One groom, a good bay in the shafts, and the dry clear light of a Hertfordshire morning over all of it.
Stainforth stepped down without hurry and looked up at the sign as a man does who has decided he will own the post it hangs from.
His coat was dark blue superfine, cut two years ago and kept well.
The hat was new.
I stood in the doorway as I had stood for my mother's callers, and before hers, for my grandmother's, and I did not fold my arms, which would have been the thing I wanted to do.
"Miss Dale."
He took his hat off as he came up the step.
"A fine morning for the road."
"It is, sir.
Will you come through to the kitchen?
The fire's laid there."
"Thank you."
He inclined his head precisely the way his father had inclined his to Patience, twenty years ago, at this same door.
I remembered it because I had been nine and had been sent with the tray.
"I hope I find you well."
"Well enough, sir.
And yourself?"
"Tolerably.
The roads are hard going above Welwyn; they want mending."
He stepped inside.
"I shan't keep you long."
He would keep me as long as he liked, and we both knew it.
I said, "You'll take tea, Mr Stainforth."
"Thank you, no.
I had rather see over the house first, if you've no objection."
I had every objection and no standing to make one.
"Of course."
*A man in a good coat, counting my hinges,* I thought, and led him into the taproom.
He walked it end to end once without speaking.
He laid his hand flat against the main beam above the hearth, looked up, and took the hand away.
He crossed to the bar and put one finger on the copper, which I had done myself at six.
He did not comment on the copper.
He went to the cellar door and lifted the latch.
"The hinge has a catch in it," he said.
"It sticks in damp weather.
Jem has the pin out once a quarter."
"Ah."
He tried the door a second time, as if to confirm the first impression.
"I take it the cellar is dry."
"Dry as Michaelmas.
You can see for yourself."
He did not go down.
He was not a man who went down cellar stairs in a new hat.
He closed the door again and turned, and his eye went to the ledger on the kitchen table without pausing on it.
"How many beds let this last quarter, Miss Dale."
"Four hundred and eleven."
"And in the quarter before."
"Three hundred and ninety-six.
I've the book here if you'd like the months separately."
"No, no.
I accept your figures."
He said it as if the accepting were a courtesy.
"And the stabling."
"Full most nights between Thursday and Saturday.
We turned away a post-chaise on the fourth of last month and two the Friday before."
"Turned away."
He considered the words.
"A pity."
"The yard holds forty.
I've no wish to keep horses worse than they arrive."
He permitted himself the smallest lift at the corner of his mouth.
"Quite."
We went up the stair to the first-floor landing.
He laid his hand on the newel post at the top and looked along the passage without walking down it.
Number six wanted papering and I had not papered it because I had not had the money this side of the harvest, and he knew this as surely as if I had said it aloud.
He did not mention number six.
He turned instead toward the window at the end and looked out at the yard.
"The lease comes up in the spring, Miss Dale."
"At Lady Day, sir.
Yes."
"I have been giving the matter some thought."
He was still looking at the yard.
"A house of this size, on this road, in this condition, is a considerable concern.
Your mother kept it well.
You have kept it well."
"Thank you, sir."
"It has occurred to me, however, that the parish's interest, and I confess my own, might be better served by a tenancy held in a name less liable to the ordinary interruptions of a woman's life."
"A man's name," I said.
"A man's name, yes."
He turned from the window.
The turn was unhurried.
"I have a nephew who has expressed an interest.
He is a sober young man of some capital.
He would retain your staff, I imagine, and he would not turn you out of doors."
"How kind."
"I thought you would prefer to hear it from me, and early, rather than at the last.
The vestry meets in February.
I should like to take the matter to them then."
*He is telling me the timetable,* I thought.
*He is telling me the timetable because he wants me to hear how short it is.* "I am obliged to you, Mr Stainforth, for the warning."
"Not a warning, Miss Dale.
A courtesy."
"A courtesy.
Yes."
We went down and through the passage to the stable yard.
I kept my hands at my sides.
He stopped at the fence on the far side, where the post leaned a thumb's breadth out of true.
Jem had been meaning to reset it since Michaelmas; there had been the roof above the kitchen first, and then the wheel on the brewer's cart.
Stainforth put his hand on the top of the post and gave it the lightest push, as if testing whether a man might lean on it.
"This wants setting."
"It does.
Jem has it in hand."
"Yes.
He is a good servant, I believe."
"He is."
"One-armed, though."
