"You have.

And you've also got the Crown at Welwyn paying you ninepence the dozen on a standing order of eight gross a quarter, which I happen to know because Mrs Parrish told me so last week when I complimented her candles."
Garvey's mouth opened and closed.
"Tenpence," I said.
"Same as last time.
And I'll take four dozen now and four dozen on the fifteenth."
"I can't do tenpence for split deliveries."
"You can.
Because the alternative is I buy from Jessop in Stevenage, and you lose this stop entirely.
Jessop's candles are worse than yours, and we both know it, but they burn and that's all I require."
He held his ground for perhaps three seconds.
Then he unloaded the four dozen from his cart and set them inside the kitchen door.
I counted them, signed the delivery note, and handed it back.
"Fifteenth," I said.
"Fifteenth."
He took the note, turned his cart, and left through the yard gate.
The gate banged shut behind him.
I stood in the kitchen with the delivery note's carbon still in my hand.
Tenpence the dozen.
I wrote the adjusted figure in the margin beside the last entry and set the note with the others in the box on the shelf.
The ledger, the rent, the candles.
Every figure pressed against the same calculation, the one I had made so many times it hardly registered as thought anymore: that if I married, none of it would be mine to negotiate for.
I wiped my hands on my apron and went through to check on the dining room.
The midday trade was thin.
Two local men took their ale in the taproom and ate the ordinary.
Nan served.
I stayed in the kitchen preparing the stock for the evening's broth and listening for trouble through the open door between kitchen and taproom.
There was none.
The afternoon was the kind that accumulated without event, one task following the next with the steady weight of hours that were neither good nor bad but simply used.
I saw the soldier through the kitchen window before he knocked.
He came around the back, as the board on the gate directed, and stood outside the kitchen door.
Young -- twenty, perhaps, or a year either side -- thin in the particular way of someone who had been thin for some time, not just today.
His coat had been army issue once, though the regiment markings were gone.
His boots were coming apart at the welt, the sole of the left one separating from the upper in a line I could see from six feet away through glass.
He stood there looking at the door.
Not knocking.
Assessing whether the kind of place this was would let him knock.
I opened the door.
He straightened.
"Ma'am.
I don't mean to trouble you."
"Have you eaten today?"
A pause.
He was deciding whether to lie.
"Not since yesterday."
"Kitchen," I said.
"Not the taproom.
Sit there."
I pointed to the bench against the wall.
He came in and sat where I pointed, his hands on his knees.
I cut bread from the loaf and ladled broth from the pot that had been simmering since morning.
I set the bowl and bread in front of him and put a cup of water beside it.
He ate the way hungry men eat, steadily and without pausing, but he did not snatch at it.
Someone had taught him his manners, or the army had.
When the bowl was empty he set his spoon down and looked at me.
"Thank you, ma'am.
That was kind."
"Where are you headed?"
"North," he said.
"There's work at the brickyards past Biggleswade, I was told."
I took the bowl from the table and set it in the washing-up basin.
He stood, ducked his head, and went out through the kitchen door.
I watched him cross the yard and pass through the gate.
The broken sole of his left boot caught on the cobbles as he went.
I turned the tap and rinsed the bowl.
Then I dried my hands and went through to the taproom.
The two local men had been joined by a third, a carter I knew by sight, and the conversation at the near table had turned loud.
Not violent -- not yet -- but the kind of loud that precedes loud, the pitch rising as two men discovered they disagreed about something too small to matter and too large to abandon.
I crossed the room and stood at the end of their table.
"Gentlemen.
If you want to continue this discussion, you're welcome to do it in the yard.
If you want to continue drinking, you'll do it quietly."
The carter looked at me.
The other man looked at the carter.
Nan, behind the bar, had her hand flat on the counter and her eyes on the table.
She did not need to move.
The noise settled.
I went back to the kitchen.
The afternoon wore on in the way of coaching inn afternoons when the road was quiet: stock to be checked again, rooms to be turned, the kitchen prepared for whatever evening trade came.
Nan cleared the taproom.
Jem was in the yard seeing to the horses.

I worked the accounts at the kitchen table, corrected an error in the week's column, moved through to check the upstairs rooms, came back down and counted the remaining candles against what Garvey had delivered.
The numbers held.
They always held, just barely, for now.
The evening came early, as October evenings did, the light going grey by five and dark by half past.
The last guests settled -- the woman with the trunk had taken supper in the dining room and gone upstairs; the man in the brown coat had eaten nothing and retired before seven.
I let the fires burn down to their banking height and moved through the closing routine.
Taproom first.
The chairs pushed in, the tables wiped, the fire raked and screened.
The floor wanted sweeping, but it could wait until morning.
I locked the cellar hatch and checked the bolt.
The taproom fire was down to a low orange crawl in the grate.
Through to the front.
Door bolted, windows latched.
The cold was sharper now, pressing against the glass from outside, and the frost had started again on the lower panes.
I crossed the yard.
The stable was quiet -- Jem would have settled the horses an hour ago, and I could hear nothing from inside but the occasional shift of weight and the sound of an animal breathing.
Above the stable, on the second floor of the wing that looked over the yard, there was a lit shape at Bridget's window.
The lamp behind the curtain, the outline of her sitting in the chair where she always sat.
I did not look long.
I turned and went back in through the kitchen door.
The kitchen was dark except for the low fire.
I moved through the last of it: banking the fire, checking the range, locking the back door.
My hands at the end of the day were reddened from the cold water and the scrubbing, and there was a small cut on my index finger that I had not noticed getting.
I looked at it.
The edge of Garvey's delivery note, I realized.
The paper had been rough-cut.
It was the invoice that had done it.
The letter was on the kitchen table.
It had not been there when I left the kitchen twenty minutes ago, which meant Nan had brought it in from wherever the afternoon post had left it and set it here before she went up.
The seal was dark red, pressed deep.
Stainforth's seal, his initials in the wax.
His handwriting on the direction, the same careful slanting hand I had seen on every quarterly communication for the past two years.
I picked it up.
Turned it over once.
The wax was cold and slightly ridged under my thumb.
I set it down on the table beside the ledger and did not open it.
I had known it was coming.

I had known since the last quarter, since the conversation at the gate when he had mentioned his nephew's name for the first time and I had understood what was being assembled behind the reasonable language and the measured voice.
I had been moving faster ever since.
The ledger, the margins, the chandler, the coach passengers counted and recounted -- all of it pressing against the same approaching wall.
The kitchen was quiet.
The fire ticked as it settled.
Outside, the yard was dark and still.
"Right, then," I said.
No one heard it.
I turned down the lamp and went upstairs.
I checked the ledger twice because the first time I did not believe my own arithmetic.
The kitchen was dark except for the single tallow candle I had carried down.
The fire was not yet built up.
The flagstones drew the cold through the soles of my boots and held it there, patient and absolute, the way cold is in a stone building before anyone has fought it back for the day.
I turned the page and ran my finger down the column again.
Tallow, flour, coal, the chandler's account, the brewer's account, Jem's wages, Nan's wages, the farrier for the off-side leader's shoe last Tuesday.
The figures were not wrong.
They were simply not enough.
Six weeks to the quarter, and the margin between what the inn would earn and what the rent required was a gap I could see but not yet close.
I shut the ledger.
The fire first.

I riddled the grate, cleared the ash into the pail, and laid the new fire the way my mother taught me: paper, then kindling split fine, then two pieces of coal set at an angle so the draught could get beneath them.
I struck the flint three times before the spark caught.
The paper flared and the kindling took, and I stayed crouched there a moment with my hands held out, waiting for the heat to reach me.
It did not, not yet.
The fire was too young.
I stood and left it to its business.
The taproom fire next.
The same procedure, though the grate was larger and the ash heavier, and the room smelled of last night's ale and the faint sourness of a tallow stub that had guttered into its dish.
I checked the bar stock by touch as much as sight: the ale cask near the tap had perhaps two days left in it, the gin was low, the brandy sufficient.
I lined up the clean tankards Nan had set out the night before and found one she had missed -- a smear of dried foam along the rim.
I wiped it with my apron and set it back.
The accounts from last night were on the shelf behind the bar where I always left them: three sheets of paper in my own hand, the figures small and tight.
I did not check them now.
I had checked them before I went up to bed, and they were correct then, and nothing would have altered in the night except my willingness to look at them again.
The windows in the taproom were rimed at the lower edges.
I pulled my sleeves down over my wrists and crossed to the front door to draw the bolt.
The door opened onto a morning that was grey and still.
The road was empty.
The inn sign -- the white hound, painted by a man in Stevenage eleven years ago and touched up twice since -- hung motionless.
No wind, which meant no coach dust, which was a mercy for the front windows.
I closed the door and went out through the kitchen to the yard.
Jem was already in the stable, which I expected.
He had the big grey's bridle off its hook and was checking the bit, turning the metal joint between his hand and the flat of the leather pad he wore strapped over his stump.
He did not look up when I appeared in the doorway.
The hay had been forked into the stalls.
The water buckets were full.
The saddle Nan's sleeve by the time she reached the bar and took up her cloth and began to wipe down the wood.
I watched her work for perhaps five seconds -- no more -- and then went back through the kitchen to check the bread delivery, which had not come, and the milk, which had.
The morning settled into its shape.
The London coach was late.
This was not unusual.

It was late more often than not since the roads north of Hatfield had worsened through the autumn, the parish having declined to repair a stretch of rutted ground near Welwyn that every coachman on the north road had a view about.
By the time I heard the horn and the rattle of wheels on the approach, I had the front door open and Jem was in the yard.
Two passengers instead of four.
Both women, both in poor temper.
The first descended from the coach unaided and stood in the yard with her mouth set in a line that promised complaint.
The second required the coachman's hand and had opinions about the trunk he swung down after her, which had a split hinge and gaped like a broken jaw.
I directed Jem to the trunk with a look.
He was already moving.
He took it by the handle and the base, bracing it against his hip with the ease of long practice, and carried it toward the door.
The woman with the trunk opened her mouth to instruct him further, but I stepped into her line of sight.
"The hinge can be mended before your departure.
There's a fire laid in the dining room and breakfast in half an hour.
Through the door and to your left."
She blinked.
She went.
The second woman followed without prompting, which was a relief.
The coachman -- a heavy man named Barlow whom I knew from his Wednesday route -- climbed down from the box and stretched his back with both hands pressed to his kidneys.
"That stretch above Hatfield is getting worse," he said.
"I know it."
"Near broke the axle on a rut the size of a drainage ditch.
Someone's going to lose a wheel before Christmas."
"I'll mention it to the parish again.
It won't do any good, but I'll mention it."
He grunted.
"You'll want to know the afternoon coach may run late as well.
They're saying there's a blockage on the road south of Stevenage -- a carter overturned."
"Thank you, Mr Barlow."
He touched his hat and went to see about the horses, and I went inside.
Two passengers instead of four meant half the coaching income for the morning stop.
I did not calculate the figure.
I did not need to.
I already knew it.
The passengers went upstairs.
Jem took the trunk.
The yard cleared.
Through the doorway to the taproom I could see Nan at the bar, her cloth in one hand, her eyes on the front door.
She had watched the whole arrival without moving from her position.
I noted it.
Said nothing.
The inn has its rhythms, and Nan knows hers.
The chandler arrived at half past ten.
He was a neat, compact man named Slade who carried his delivery box on one shoulder and his revised prices in his head, and who had been nudging both upward since March.
He set the box on the kitchen table and named his figure.
"Fourpence ha'penny the dozen."
I did not answer immediately.
I took the lid off the box and counted the candles.
Three dozen, as agreed.
Tallow, not beeswax.
The quality was adequate -- no better, no worse than the last delivery.
"It was fourpence last month," I said.
"Tallow's up.
The renderer in Hatfield has raised his price."
"The renderer in Hatfield charges you tuppence a pound for raw tallow, which is what he charged you in June.
I buy soap from the same man.
He talks."
Slade's expression did not change, but he shifted the empty lid from one hand to the other.
"There's the cost of carriage."
"You carry your own deliveries.
You are carrying them now.

Fourpence the dozen, Mr Slade, which is what I paid last month, and the month before that, and which is more than the Red Lion pays you, because Mrs Calder told me so last Thursday when she thought she was complaining about your service."
A pause.
He looked at the candles in their box, and then at me, and then at the kitchen door through which he had come and through which he could leave, taking his candles with him.
He would not.
I knew he would not.
I was his most reliable account on this stretch of road, and punctual with payment, and he knew that I knew he knew.
"Fourpence," he said.
"Fourpence."
He left the candles and took the empty box.
I heard the kitchen door close behind him.
I picked up the delivery note he had left on the table, found the figure he had written, struck through it, and wrote the corrected price in the margin.
The edge of the paper caught the side of my index finger as I set it down.
A thin line of blood rose but did not drop.
I entered the adjusted figure in the ledger and closed it.
The candles needed putting away.
The midday preparations needed starting.
Between one task and the next, in the pause where my hands were still and my mind was not, the thought came as it always did: a plain calculation, flat and familiar.
If I married, the lease would pass to my husband.
The income.
The negotiation.
The right to say fourpence and have it be fourpence.
All of it transferred, by law, to a man -- any man -- the moment I stood in a church and said the words.
I had done the sum before.
The answer had not changed.
I picked up the candles and carried them to the storeroom.
He came around the back, as the sign on the gate asked.
I saw him through the kitchen window before he knocked -- standing outside the door with his arms at his sides, looking at the handle as though measuring whether he had earned the right to touch it.
Young.
My age or younger -- it was difficult to say.
Thin through the coat, which was army wool, much worn.
His boots were coming apart at the welt, the left one separating from the sole so that I could see a line of grey stocking beneath.
He stood a moment longer, and then he raised his hand and knocked once.
I opened the door.
He was taller than he had looked through the window.
His face had the scrubbed, wind-raw look of a man who has been walking in open weather for some time.
"Have you eaten?"
I said.
He met my eyes.
It took him a moment.
"Not since yesterday, ma'am."
"Kitchen, not taproom.
Sit there."
I pointed to the bench by the range.
He came in and sat where I told him.
I cut bread from the loaf and ladled broth from the pot that had been warming since morning.
He ate without haste, which told me more about his hunger than speed would have.
A man who bolts his food has been hungry for a day.
A man who eats steadily, not looking up, not speaking, wrapping his hands around the bowl as though it might be taken -- that man has been hungry longer.
When he had finished, he set the bowl down and looked at me.
"Thank you, ma'am."
"Where are you headed?"
"North," he said.
He did not elaborate.
I held the door open for him.
He went through it, and I watched him cross the yard and pass through the gate without turning back.
His left boot flapped with each step.
I closed the door and cleared the bowl and the plate, washed them, and set them on the rack to dry.
The afternoon was quiet, and then it was not.
Two men in the taproom -- commercial travellers who had been sitting since noon -- found a disagreement between them about something I did not trouble to identify.
One of them had risen from his chair.
The other had raised his voice.
I crossed the room.
"Sit down, or finish your drinks and leave.
Those are the choices."
They sat down.
Nan, behind the bar, had not put down her cloth.
The hours between the midday trade and the evening settled over the inn like dust.
Nan at the bar, polishing what did not need polishing because idleness discomforted her.
Jem in the yard -- I could hear the slow scrape of his rake over the cobbles.

I worked through the afternoon's accounts at the kitchen table, then went upstairs to check the rooms the morning passengers had used, stripped the linens, brought them down, started the evening preparations.
Turnips to peel.
The remains of a mutton joint to be stretched into something that would serve.
Coal to be brought in for the taproom fire.
I carried, I chopped, I counted.
The work was the work, and it did not require my opinion of it.
Evening came on early as it does in late October.
The light outside the kitchen window turned from grey to a darker grey, and then to the colour of old pewter, and then it was gone.
The last guests settled or departed.
The last fire I checked was the taproom's -- I raked the coals flat and set the guard before them.
The bar was tallied, the figures entered, the cashbox locked and put away.
Nan had gone upstairs an hour earlier, her good night a nod and nothing more.
The kitchen I closed down by feel as much as by sight: the range banked, the surfaces wiped, the morning's bread set covered on the shelf.
I stood in the taproom doorway and listened.
The building made its settling sounds -- a beam contracting, a window frame ticking in its housing.
From the cellar, the slow drip of the tap I would need to re-seat in the morning.
I checked the cellar hatch: locked.
The front door: bolted.
The yard door: bolted.
I went out through the kitchen door and stood in the yard.
The cold was immediate and total.
Jem had settled the horses -- I could hear nothing from the stable except the occasional shift of weight and the sound of an animal breathing.
I looked up.
The second-floor window above the yard had a light behind it: the thin, steady glow of a single candle seen through old glass.
Bridget's shape was there, or the suggestion of it -- a stillness behind the pane.
I did not look long.
I went back inside and locked the kitchen door behind me.

My hands, when I turned the key, were red from the cold water and the cleaning, and the cut on my index finger from the edge of Slade's delivery note had opened again and left a thin rust-coloured line along the side of the key.
I wiped it on my apron.
The letter was on the kitchen table.
It had not been there before -- or it had, and I had not seen it, though I did not believe that.

Someone had put it inside the door while I was in the yard, or it had come with the afternoon delivery and Nan had left it and said nothing because the seal on the envelope was not the sort of thing Nan would remark on without being asked.
It was there.
That was what mattered.
The envelope was heavy paper, cream-coloured, the direction written in a hand I knew.
The seal was dark red wax, pressed with an initial I did not need to hold to the candle to read.
Stainforth.
I picked it up.
I held it.
I turned it over once and felt the weight of it, which was slight -- a single sheet, most likely, folded twice.
The wax was smooth under my thumb.
I set it down on the table beside the ledger and did not open it.
I had known it was coming since the last rent quarter.
I had known it the way I knew when the ale cask was nearly empty -- not because I had checked, but because I had been counting without counting, tracking the weight of what remained.
The chandler's prices.
The short coaches.
The gap in the ledger I had checked twice this morning because I did not believe my own arithmetic.
I had been moving faster ever since, and here was the reason, sealed and addressed and sitting on my kitchen table at the end of a day in which I had done everything right and it had not been enough.
I looked at the envelope.
The candle on the table guttered once and steadied.
"Well then," I said.
I checked the ledger twice because the first time the numbers were the same as the night before, and I did not believe them.
Six weeks.
Forty-three days, if I counted from yesterday, which I had.
Forty-three days until the quarter rent came due and the figures in the credit column would need to outpace the figures in the debit column by eleven pounds, eight shillings, and fourpence.
I knew the sum the way I knew the creak of the third stair and the draft beneath the taproom door--it was simply part of the building.
I closed the ledger and set it on the shelf above the flour bin where it lived between uses.
The kitchen was cold.
The fire I had built ten minutes ago was still working its way through the kindling, not yet hot enough to take the chill off the flagstones.
I could see my breath if I breathed hard enough, so I did not breathe hard.
I pulled my sleeves down over my wrists and went to the range to check the draw.
The flue was clear.
I had cleaned it on Sunday and it would hold for another week.
I set the kettle on the hob and crossed through the passageway to the taproom.
The fire there was yesterday's ash.
I knelt, raked it out, and built a new one--paper, kindling, two splits of beech from the stack Jem kept by the back wall.
The beech was drier than the elm and caught faster.
I did not waste elm on the morning fire.
The taproom smelled of last night's ale and tallow and the cold particular smell of a room that had been shut up with its own breath overnight.
I opened the small window at the far end two inches, no more.
The October air came in sharp and clean and I let it work while I moved behind the bar to count bottles.
Three of the good brandy.
Seven of the ordinary.
Gin adequate.
Ale: two barrels tapped, one reserve in the cellar.
The reserve would want broaching by Saturday if the coaching traffic held.

The accounts from last night were where I had left them, weighed down with the smooth stone I used as a paperweight--a river stone, grey, that my mother had kept on this bar for as long as I could remember.
I ran the column.
Four shillings ninepence from the taproom.
Six shillings eightpence from two dinners and the rooms.
One shilling threepence from stabling.
Total receipts for the day: twelve shillings eightpence.
Against that, the coal delivery, the kitchen stores, and Nan's wages for the week, which I owed her tomorrow.
I set the accounts aside.
The window had done its work.
I shut it.
The passage to the yard was dark, and I went through it by feel--hand on the left wall, three steps, then the latch of the back door.
Outside, the morning was grey-white.
Frost rimmed the horse trough and the edges of the cobbles.
Jem was in the stable yard already, his back to me, straightening a halter on its hook with his one hand.
He did not turn around.
The tack was in order because Jem's tack was always in order, and the stable doors were latched, and the yard was swept.
I looked, confirmed what I expected to confirm, and went back inside.
Nan arrived through the kitchen door a few minutes later, pins in her hair not yet set, apron already tied.
She passed me without a word and took her place at the bar.
I heard her lift the stone, check the accounts sheet, set it down again.
Then the sound of a cloth being wrung into the bucket.
She was wiping the bar top.
We had done this before.
Many hundreds of times.
The London coach was late.

This was not unusual, but I had been listening for it since half seven and it was nearly nine when I heard the change in sound from the road--the particular heavy rhythm of a full team at a trot slowing for the turn.
I went to the yard.
It was running short.
Two passengers where the way-bill said four.
The first was a woman of perhaps forty-five, well-dressed, furious about something, holding a trunk by its remaining handle while the split hinge gaped open like a broken jaw.
The second was a man in a dark coat who wanted nothing but to get inside and be left alone, and who managed this without my help.
The coachman climbed down stiffly and stood stretching his back while Jem appeared beside the horses without having been called.
I directed Jem to the trunk.
He took it with a glance at the hinge that communicated his opinion of whoever had packed it.
The woman watched her trunk depart and turned her displeasure on me.
"That hinge was perfectly sound when I left London," she said.
"Your roads have shaken it apart."
"The room is at the top of the stairs, first on the left," I said.
"There is hot water.
I will have the hinge seen to within the hour."
She opened her mouth, reconsidered, and went inside.
The coachman had not moved.
He was a man of about fifty, heavy through the shoulders, with the permanently weathered complexion of a person who has spent thirty years facing into the wind.
"The road above Hatfield," he said.
"North stretch, past the toll."
"The ruts."
"It's worse than ruts.
There's a section where the surface has broken through entirely.
Six yards, maybe eight.
I nearly lost a wheel."
"Was it marked?"
"A branch across the road.
That was all."
"I will send word to the turnpike trust this afternoon."
He nodded.
It was not gratitude--it was the acknowledgment of a man who had discharged his duty and could move on.
"Will you eat?"
I asked.
"No time.
I'm forty minutes behind as it is."
He climbed back up.
Jem had already changed the lead pair.

The coach pulled out of the yard and the sound of it diminished down the road until there was nothing left but the ordinary morning quiet of the inn: Jem's boots on the cobbles, the settling of the horses, the creak of the sign above the front door turning in a wind I could not feel at ground level.
Nan had been wiping the same stretch of bar through all of this.
I saw the cloth pause when the yard was clear, then resume.
I noted it.
Said nothing.
The chandler came at eleven.
He was a broad man named Hadwell with clean hands and a careful way of placing his delivery crate on the kitchen table that was meant to communicate the value of its contents.
Twelve dozen tallow candles, wrapped in paper, smelling of rendered fat.
"Fourpence ha'penny the dozen this month," he said.
I set down the knife I had been using to trim the wick of the kitchen lamp.
"It was fourpence last month."
"Tallow's gone up."
"Tallow has gone up a farthing the pound since March.
You have raised your price a ha'penny the dozen four times since then.
That is twopence the dozen above what the cost warrants."
He shifted the crate an inch to the left on the table, as though it might leave with him.
"I've other customers on this road who pay what I ask and don't require an accounting lesson."
"You have six customers on this stretch between Hatfield and Baldock.
Three of them buy fewer than four dozen a month.
The Angel at Baldock buys in quantity from a supplier in Hitchin.
That leaves me and the Feathers at Welwyn, and Mrs.
Pryce at the Feathers told me last Tuesday she is considering making her own."
Hadwell looked at the crate.
He looked at me.
"Fourpence farthing," I said.
"That's barely above my cost."
"It is a farthing above your cost, and you know it, and I will take twelve dozen a month through the winter, which is more than the Feathers takes in a quarter."
He stood there.
I waited.
The fire popped behind me.
Somewhere in the stable yard, a horse stamped.
"Fourpence farthing," he said.
He left.
The candles stayed.
I wrote the adjusted price in the margin of the delivery note and set it with the accounts.
The ink was not yet dry when I moved on to the kitchen stores, tallying what was needed for the evening meal against what was in the larder.
The coverture calculation came then, the way it always came--not as a thought I chose to have but as a fact that arrived alongside the other facts: the candle price, the rent, the diminishing margin.
If I married, the inn passed to my husband.

The lease, the income, the negotiation I had just conducted and the ones that would follow it--all of it would belong to a man who might be shrewd or might be a fool and over whom I would have no authority whatever.
The law was not complicated.
I had understood it since I was old enough to understand the ledger.
I moved on.
He came around the back, as the sign asked.
Young--twenty, perhaps, or less.
Thin in the way of a man who has been thin for a long time, not the way of a man who was born to it.
His coat was adequate.
His boots were not.
The welt of the left boot had separated from the sole along the outside edge, and the right was heading the same way.
He stood outside the kitchen door without knocking.
I saw him through the window--the pause, the assessment, the particular stillness of a person calculating whether he would be welcome enough to knock.
I opened the door.
He straightened.
He did not speak first, which told me something about him.
"Have you eaten?"
I said.
"Not since yesterday, ma'am.
Morning."
"Kitchen, not the taproom.
Sit there."
He came in and sat where I pointed, at the end of the kitchen table farthest from the door to the passageway.
I cut bread and ladled broth from the pot on the range.
It was yesterday's broth--mutton bone, turnip, onion--reheated, perfectly sound.
I set it in front of him with a spoon.
He ate.
Not desperately, but steadily, the way a man eats who has learned to eat when food is available and not to waste the opportunity.
He finished the bread.
He finished the broth.
He set the spoon down parallel to the edge of the bowl.
"Thank you, ma'am."
"Where are you headed?"
"North," he said.
"My mother's people are in Lincolnshire."
He stood, and I saw his hand go briefly to the table edge to steady himself, and then he was upright and the moment passed.
He went out through the kitchen door, and I watched him cross the yard to the road, and then I closed the door and took the bowl to the basin and washed it and set it with the others.
The afternoon passed in the ordinary way of afternoons at the White Hound when no coach was due and the guests had settled or gone.

Two men in the taproom had been sitting too long over their second pints, and something about the prior night's boxing match at Barnet had tipped from disagreement into the kind of noise that precedes breakage.
I went in.
"Gentlemen.
You will lower your voices or you will settle your account and leave.
Those are the options."
They lowered their voices.
Nan, behind the bar, set down the glass she had been holding and said nothing.

The gap between the afternoon coach and the evening trade was the inn's dead time, and I used it as I always used it: accounts, provisions, the room on the second floor that wanted fresh linen, the kitchen prepared for supper.
Nan at the bar.
Jem outside.
The work.
I did not stop, because the work did not stop, and because the alternative to working was thinking, and thinking was a luxury that cost more than I could afford.
I locked up alone, as I always did.
The last guest settled by half nine.
The taproom fire banked down to coals.
I stood for a moment with my hand on the mantelpiece, watching the last colour leave the embers.
Then the bar--cloth over the taps, glasses accounted for, the stone on the accounts.
The kitchen: range damped, surfaces wiped, the morning's bread dough set to prove overnight under a cloth.
The cellar hatch: locked, key on the hook by the passage door.
I went out to the yard for the final circuit.
The stable doors were latched.
Jem had settled the horses--I could hear their breathing through the walls, the slow shuffle of hooves on straw.
The night was cold and very clear.
Above the roofline, more stars than I had attention for.
On the second floor of the inn, a lit shape at Bridget's window.
I did not look long.
My hands at the end of the day: reddened from cold water and the cleaning, the knuckles rough, a small cut on the index finger where the edge of Hadwell's delivery note had caught the skin.
It was the invoice that had cut me.
I noticed this without stopping to account for it.
I came back to the kitchen.
The fire was down to almost nothing, and the room held that particular silence of a space that has been used hard and is now finished with its day.
Everything in order.
Everything accounted for.
The ledger on its shelf.
The accounts under the stone.

The morning's tasks already assembling themselves in my mind--Jem would need to look at the loose board on the mounting block, and the flour was running lower than I liked, and the woman with the broken trunk would want breakfast early if she was catching the southbound coach.
The letter was on the table.
It had not been there at supper.
Someone had brought it--Nan, most likely, who collected the post from the village--and set it down without remark.
Stainforth's seal on the envelope.
His handwriting on the direction, small and very even.
Miss D.
Dale, The White Hound, Great North Road.
I picked it up.
I held it.
I turned it over once.
I did not open it.
I had known it was coming since the last quarter.

I had known it the way I knew the draught beneath the taproom door and the creak of the third stair--it was part of the building, part of what the building cost, and I had been moving faster ever since, as though speed alone could outrun the arithmetic.
I set the letter down on the table, seal up, and looked at it.
"Well," I said to the room.
"There it is."
No one heard me.
The fire ticked as it cooled.
Outside, the sign creaked once in the wind, and then the inn was quiet.
I checked the ledger twice because the first time the numbers were worse than I remembered, and the second time they were exactly the same.
Six weeks.
Perhaps seven, if the weather held and the coaches kept running full.

The column on the right-hand side of the page -- what came in -- and the column on the left -- what went out -- had been drawing toward each other all autumn like two dogs circling in a yard, and I did not care for what would happen when they met.
I closed the book and set my hand flat on its cover, as if the figures might try to crawl out while my back was turned.
The kitchen fire had burned down to a dull orange crust in the night.
I knelt and raked the ashes forward, laid kindling crosswise the way my mother had taught me, and blew until the flame caught.
The floorboards were cold through my stockings.
I had come downstairs without shoes -- a habit I ought to break, and would not.
The kitchen was mine at this hour in a way it was not once the day began, and I did not wish to announce my arrival to it.
I filled the kettle and hung it on the crane.
Checked the bread bin: two loaves from yesterday, still good enough for toast, not good enough for the table.
The butter crock was down by a third.
I had noted this already in the ledger but I noted it again now, with my hands, pressing the cloth cover down and feeling the level beneath.
My fingers were stiff.
The windows were rimed at their edges, a thin crust of frost that caught no light because there was no light yet to catch.
The taproom fire took longer.

The grate had not been properly cleared the night before -- my own fault -- and I spent several minutes on my knees with the ash bucket, scraping out the cold mass of yesterday's fuel before I could lay a new one.
The air in the taproom was thick and stale, carrying the ghost of pipe smoke and spilled ale.
I opened the small window behind the bar and let the cold pour in.
Better cold than foul.
Bar stock: I counted bottles by feel in the dimness.
The gin was lower than it ought to be, which meant I had poured more generously than I intended last night or someone had helped himself after hours.
I set the bottle at the front of the shelf where I would see it clearly later and moved on.
The cask of ordinary ale was two-thirds full.
The strong ale, barely tapped.
No one was drinking the strong ale this month.
The price was not dear but people's pockets were, and they chose accordingly.
I tallied the previous night's take against the chalkboard behind the bar.
The figures matched.
One evening's income would not have impressed anyone, but it was correct, and being correct was the only victory available at six o'clock in the morning.
The stable yard was grey when I looked out the back door.
Jem was there already, straightening a length of tack on the hook beside the mounting block.
He did not look up.
His one hand moved with the deliberate precision I had grown accustomed to, the stump of his left arm bracing the leather against the post while his right hand worked the buckle.
I watched him for a moment -- not because he needed watching, but because the sight of a person doing useful work before being asked to do it was a comfort I had not learned to take for granted.
I pulled the door shut and went back inside.
Nan came through the kitchen a few minutes later, pins in her hair not yet properly set, her apron already tied.
She took her place behind the bar without a word and began wiping down the counter with a rag she must have picked up from the shelf on her way through, because I had not put one out.
We had done this before.
Many hundreds of times.
The London coach was late.
This was not unusual.

What was unusual was that it arrived carrying two passengers instead of the expected four, and both of them came through the front door with expressions that suggested the Great North Road had personally offended them.
The first was a stout woman in a travelling cloak who carried a trunk with a split hinge.
She set this down in the hallway with the air of a person presenting evidence at a trial.
The second was a thin man in a brown coat who said nothing and went directly upstairs.
"This has been like this since Barnet," the woman said, pointing at the trunk.
"I cannot be expected to travel the length of England with my belongings falling into the road."

"Jem," I said, and he was there -- I do not know how he heard from the yard, but he always did -- and took the trunk by its leather handles, tilting it so the broken hinge held shut under its own weight.
He carried it toward the stairs without comment.
The woman opened her mouth to say something further, reconsidered, and followed him.
The coachman had climbed down and was standing in the yard, stamping his feet against the cold.
He was a man I had seen many times -- Gibbs, or Gibbon -- the regular driver on the Tuesday route.
"Road's breaking up past Hatfield," he said when I came out.
"Ruts deep enough to lose a wheel.
You'll want to warn anyone heading north this afternoon."
"I will.
How far past Hatfield?"
"Mile and a half, perhaps two.
Where the road crosses the stream bed.
The rain's done for it."
He blew into his hands.
"If the trust doesn't send someone to relay gravel before the frost sets in hard, you'll be pulling coaches out of ditches all winter."
"I'll send word to the surveyor.
You've twenty minutes if you want something hot."
He nodded and went inside.
I could have given him more than twenty minutes.
I could have given him an hour.
But the coach had a schedule, and the schedule was not mine to adjust, and neither of us had time to pretend otherwise.
The coachman went.
The passengers had disappeared into their rooms or the dining room.
Jem took the trunk upstairs and returned to the yard.
The small bustle of arrival passed through the inn and out again like a breath, and the building settled.
Nan was behind the bar, wiping the same surface she had already wiped, her eyes on the doorway through which the last of the morning's activity had gone.
I noticed it.
Said nothing.
The chandler arrived at half past ten, which was his custom on Tuesdays.
He was a man called Fitchett, narrow-shouldered, with a careful way of setting down his crate of candles that suggested he wanted full credit for the effort of carrying them.
He had a ledger of his own, smaller than mine, which he consulted as he stood in the kitchen doorway, though I suspected he had memorized the figure before he left his shop.
"Tallow per dozen, one and tenpence," he said.
"It was one and seven last month."
"Cost of tallow's gone up.
Everyone's paying more."
"Everyone on this stretch of road is paying one and seven, Mr Fitchett.
I spoke to Mrs Beale at the Red Hart on Saturday and she confirmed it."
A pause.
He had not expected me to have spoken to Mrs Beale.
He adjusted the crate on his hip.
"One and nine."
"One and seven."
"Miss Dale, I cannot sell below my cost."
"Your cost for rendered tallow is ninepence per dozen, and has been since August.
I know because your carter told Jem when he was drunk, and Jem does not forget figures.
One and seven gives you tenpence clear, which is exactly what you were making in June when you were cheerful enough about the arrangement."
Fitchett stared at me.
I stared back.
The kitchen was very quiet.
Somewhere behind me the kettle shifted on its crane with a small metallic sound.
"One and eight," he said.
"One and seven.
And I'll take an extra two dozen this month, which you may tell anyone who asks."
He set the crate down on the kitchen table.
He made a note in his ledger.
He did not look at me as he did it.
"Pleasure doing business, Miss Dale."
I did not reply.
He let himself out through the kitchen door, and I listened to his boots on the yard stones until the sound of them was gone.
I wrote the adjusted price in the margin of the delivery note.
One and seven.
The ink blurred slightly where my pen pressed too hard.

I set the note aside and began counting candles into the storage box, and somewhere between the eighth and the ninth my mind did what it did when the numbers pressed in -- it ran the calculation I had made before, the one that sat beneath all the other calculations like the foundation beneath a floor.
The lease was mine so long as I held it alone.
If I married, everything transferred.
The inn, the income, the forty years my family had poured into this place.
One signature in a church register and it became some man's property, to run or ruin or sell as he chose.
This was not a grievance.
It was arithmetic.
I set the ninth candle into the box and reached for the tenth.
I saw him through the window before he knocked.
Young -- younger than Jem, younger than the coachman -- with a thin face and a coat that had once been military issue, though someone had torn the insignia from the sleeve.
His boots were coming apart where the upper met the sole, the welt splitting along both sides so that his stockings showed through.
He stood outside the kitchen door with his hand raised, not yet touching the wood.
He was looking at the door the way a man looks at a thing he is not certain he is permitted to approach.
He knocked.
I opened it.
He had a narrow, weather-darkened face and hair that had been cut badly and not recently.
His eyes moved past me to the kitchen -- the fire, the kettle, the table with its candles and ledger -- and came back to my face.
"Have you eaten?"
I said.
"Not today."
He paused, as if deciding whether more honesty would help or hurt.
"Not yesterday, properly."
"Kitchen, not taproom.
Sit there."
I pointed to the bench by the hearth.
He came in and sat where I told him.
He did not remove his coat.
I cut bread from yesterday's loaf and ladled broth from the pot that had been on the fire since morning.
I set both in front of him with a spoon and nothing else, because ceremony was not what he needed and I did not have it to spare.
He ate.
Not fast, which surprised me.
Men who had not eaten in two days usually ate as though the food might be taken away.
This one ate steadily, deliberately, like a man who was rationing his own hunger.
When he finished he set the spoon across the bowl and sat with his hands on his knees.
"Thank you," he said.
His voice was quiet and had the particular flatness of someone who has recently stopped expecting things.
"Where are you headed?"
"North."
He hesitated.
"Huntingdon, if I can make it."
I nodded.
He stood, and I saw him glance at the bread on the table, and then stop himself from glancing at it.
I cut a second piece and held it out.
He took it.
"The road's bad past Hatfield," I said.
"Keep to the verge where you can."
He went out through the kitchen door.
I watched him cross the yard and turn north along the lane, the bread in his hand, the broken boots dark against the frost-hardened mud.
I closed the door and took the bowl to the basin and washed it.
I dried it.
I set it back on the shelf.
The afternoon was a slow one.

In the taproom, two men who had been sitting since midday found something to disagree about -- I never learned what -- and their voices began to climb in the way that voices climb when men have been still too long and the ale has given their grievances a shape.
"Gentlemen," I said from the doorway.
"You'll settle it outside or you'll settle it now, but you will not settle it in my taproom."
They settled it now.
Nan watched from behind the bar with her cloth in her hand and did not need to move.
The hours between the coach's departure and the evening meal were the hours that belonged to the building itself.
No one arrived.
No one left.
Nan polished glasses.
Jem was outside -- I could hear the rhythmic scrape of a rake on cobblestones.

I sat in the kitchen with the ledger open and the candles counted and the evening menu worked out in my head: what we had, what would stretch, what could not be made to stretch no matter how I managed it.
The kitchen fire cracked and settled.
I closed the ledger and went upstairs to check the rooms.
Room four wanted airing.
Room seven had a cracked pane that would need boarding before the cold deepened.

I noted both and moved on, running my hand along the banister as I came down the stairs -- a gesture that had no practical purpose but that I had been performing since I was tall enough to reach, and that my mother had performed before me, and that I was not willing to examine for what it meant.
Evening came down quickly.
The last of the light went grey, then blue, then dark.
The guests who remained had eaten and retired.
The fire in the taproom was low, the coals orange beneath a fine white skin of ash.
I stood before it for a moment, then closed the grate.
The bar was tallied.
Nan had gone upstairs an hour ago.
The kitchen was clean -- the pots on their hooks, the knives in the drawer, the range shut down, the kettle empty and cool.
I moved through the closing routine the way I had done it every night for two years, and every other night for the ten years before that when my mother was alive and I was learning the sequence.
Taproom fire: coals safe, no open flame.
Cellar hatch: bolted.
Front door: locked, key on the nail.
Stable yard: quiet.
I stepped outside for a moment and stood in the cold.
Jem had settled the horses.
I could hear one of them shifting in its stall, a slow heavy sound that carried in the stillness.
On the second floor, a light burned behind Bridget's window.
The faint shape of her behind the glass -- seated, watchful.
I did not look long.
She was there.
She was always there.
I went back inside and shut the door.
My hands, when I looked at them in the kitchen lamplight, were reddened from cold water and cleaning.
There was a small cut on my right index finger -- the edge of Fitchett's delivery note, which I had not noticed at the time.
The paper had been coarser than I expected.
I examined the cut without interest and let my hand drop.
The letter was on the kitchen table.

It had not been there when I cleared the table before dinner, which meant it had been delivered to the front door while I was upstairs checking rooms, and Nan had set it in the kitchen for me, and I had been moving through the building all evening with this thing sitting here, waiting.
I picked it up.
The seal was a dull red -- Stainforth's seal, the one he used for correspondence with tenants, different from his magistrate's seal.
I knew both.
His handwriting on the direction was small and slanted and very regular, the hand of a man who did not waste ink.
I turned the envelope over once.
The paper was heavy.
Good paper.
He did not economize on paper.
I set the letter down on the table.
I did not open it.
I had known it was coming.
I had known since the last quarter's rent was received without acknowledgment -- no note of receipt, no confirmation, just silence where there had always been at least a formal line.
The silence had been louder than any letter.
I had been moving faster ever since, though I could not have said toward what.
The kitchen was empty.
The fire was down to its last coal.
The inn around me was silent with the particular silence of a place that has worked hard and is done.
"Right, then," I said.
No one heard me.
I turned down the lamp.
I checked the ledger twice because the first time I did not believe the numbers, and the second time I did.
Six weeks.
That was what remained between the White Hound and the next quarter's rent, and between the next quarter's rent and the conversation I did not intend to have with myself about what came after.
I closed the book and set my hand flat on the cover as though the figures might shift if left unattended.
They would not.
Numbers did not rearrange themselves out of sympathy.
I had learned this from my mother, who had learned it from hers, and the lesson had not improved with repetition.
The kitchen was cold.
The fire I had built twenty minutes earlier was still finding its courage, the coals ticking and settling beneath the first true flames.

I could see my breath if I turned toward the window, where the glass was rimed at its edges with a fine, persistent frost that had been there every morning this week and would be there every morning for the next several months.
October had no business being this cold.
I pulled my sleeves down over my wrists and went to check the bar stock.
The taproom was dark and smelled of last night's ale and the particular staleness of a room where men had sat too long.
I opened the shutter on the nearest window to let in enough grey light to work by and ran my eye along the casks.
The small beer was adequate.
The porter was low -- I would need to speak to the brewer before Friday.
The gin was untouched, which meant either that last night's guests had been unusually abstemious or that Nan had watered it again, and I suspected the latter, and I did not blame her.
I tallied the previous evening's take against what was in the cashbox.
The numbers agreed, which was a small mercy.
I wiped down the counter where someone had left a sticky ring the size of a saucer, checked that the chairs were pushed in, and moved to the second fireplace.
This one I built more carefully than the kitchen fire, because the taproom was the room that paid for everything else, and a cold taproom was an empty one.
The wood was damp.

I stacked it with the driest pieces on the inside and the greenest on the outside where the draught from the chimney would season them over the course of the morning, and I used the last of the kindling without thinking about it and then stood up and thought about it.
I would need to send Jem to split more before the evening.
I added this to the list I kept in my head, which was the only list I had ever found entirely reliable.
The staircase boards were cold underfoot as I climbed to check the second-floor landing.
Two rooms occupied, both doors shut, no sound from within.
The linen on the unoccupied beds had been turned yesterday.

The washstand in room four had a crack in the basin that I had noticed three days ago and not yet replaced, because the replacement basin cost one and fourpence and one and fourpence was one and fourpence.
I noted it again and went back downstairs.
Through the kitchen window I could see Jem in the stable yard.

He was straightening tack on the wall hooks, working with his one hand and the stump of the other in the efficient, unhurried way that meant he had been up for some time and had already seen to the horses.
He did not look toward the house.
He did not need to.

The morning required the tack to be straight and the horses fed and the yard swept, and Jem attended to what the morning required without being asked, which was the quality I valued most in him and the one I would never embarrass us both by naming.
I went back to the kitchen and put the kettle on.
Nan came through the back door a few minutes later with her pins not yet set and her apron already tied.
She crossed to the bar without a word, took her place, and began laying out the breakfast things.
We had done this before.
We had done this six mornings out of seven for three years, and the rhythm of it was so fixed that any interruption would have been more conspicuous than the routine itself.
I heard her set out the bread board, the butter crock, the knives.
The small sounds of a house preparing to be of use.
The London coach was late, which was not unusual.

What was unusual was that it was also short -- two passengers instead of the expected four, and both of them in the kind of temper that comes from being rattled over bad road in a cold coach for the better part of three hours.
The first was a man who said nothing and wanted only to be shown to a room.
Nan took him.
The second was a woman of perhaps fifty with a trunk that had a split hinge and a great deal to say about it.
"The clasp gave way at Hatfield," she told me, holding the damaged trunk as though presenting evidence in a court of law.
"The coachman offered no assistance whatsoever."

"Jem," I said, and Jem was there, which he had been since the coach pulled into the yard, and he took the trunk from her hands with a nod that conveyed both competence and the absolute minimum of social engagement.
The woman watched her trunk leave with the expression of someone who was not yet finished being aggrieved but had temporarily lost the object of her grievance.
I directed her to the dining room, where Nan had already set out breakfast, and she went.
The coachman had come down from the box and was stamping his boots in the yard.
He was a man I knew by sight -- Fenton, who drove the Tuesday and Friday route -- and he wanted a word.
"Road north of Hatfield is gone to pieces," he said.
"Ruts past the axle in two places.
I'll not answer for the springs if it's left another week."
"The turnpike trust meets Thursday.
I'll send word to Harding."
"Harding won't do a damn thing."
"Harding will do a damn thing if I tell him his coaches are losing passengers to the Baldock road.
Which they are."
I handed him a cup of ale, which was what he had actually come for.
"Two passengers today, Fenton."
He drank, wiped his mouth, and set the cup down.
"Aye.
Well."
He touched his hat and went back to the coach, and that was the end of it.
He had his route and I had mine, and neither of us had time for more.
The yard cleared.
The coach pulled away with a sound of wheels and harness that I could have identified blind -- the particular rattle of Fenton's rig, which wanted a new linchpin on the off side.
Jem took the woman's trunk inside.
Nan was behind the bar, wiping down the counter with one eye on the door through which the guests had gone.
I noticed.
I said nothing.
The chandler arrived at half past ten with his cart and his monthly delivery and his new price.
"Tenpence the dozen," he said, setting the first box of tallow candles on the kitchen table as though the matter were already settled.
I did not pick up the box.
"It was ninepence last month."
"Tallow's gone up."
"Tallow has gone up a farthing the pound since March.
Your price has gone up a penny the dozen four times in seven months.
That is not the same arithmetic."
He looked at me with the expression of a man who had hoped this would be easier.
I knew his expression well.
I had been seeing it for seven months.
"I've costs, Miss Dale."
"You have costs.
And I know what they are, Mr Flood, because you supply every establishment on this stretch of road and they all talk to one another.
You pay fourpence halfpenny the pound for tallow from Barnet.
You sell to the Red Lion at eightpence the dozen.
You sell to the George at eightpence the dozen.
You would like to sell to me at tenpence the dozen because I am one woman with one inn and you believe I have no other source.
But I do have another source.
I can buy direct from Barnet and make my own, and I have done it before, and the only reason I have not done it recently is that your candles are better than mine and we both know it."
He said nothing for a moment.
Then: "Ninepence ha'penny."
"Ninepence.
Same as last month.
Same as next month."
He exhaled through his nose.
He left the candles.
He took his money.
He went.
The door closed behind him.
I stood in the kitchen with the delivery note in my hand and wrote the adjusted price in the margin: ninepence.
The pencil point caught the edge of the paper and I felt it but did not look at my hand.
There was the afternoon to manage and the evening after that, and the chandler's ninepence was ninepence I would not have to find somewhere else, and that was the whole of what it meant.
I carried the candles to the storeroom.
Somewhere between the storeroom and the kitchen -- between one task and the next, in the gap where thought sometimes slipped in uninvited -- it came to me as it always did.
The ledger.
The rent.
The chandler's price edging up and my margin edging down, and all of it weighed against the fact that none of it would be mine to fight for if I were any man's wife.
The lease was in my name.
The law was not.
I had done this calculation before.
I did not dwell on it.
I went to check the dining room.
He came around the back, as the sign on the gate asked.
I saw him through the kitchen window before he knocked -- young, thin, standing outside the door with the particular stillness of a man who was deciding whether he was welcome enough to try.
His coat was too large for him and had been too large for whoever owned it before him.
His boots were coming apart at the welt, the left sole separating from the upper in a way that meant he had been walking a long time on wet ground.
He was perhaps twenty.
He was not threatening.
He was not sure.
He raised his hand to knock and I opened the door before his knuckles reached the wood.
"Have you eaten?"
I said.
He looked at me.
His eyes were older than his face.
"Not recent."
"Kitchen.
Not the taproom."
I stepped back and he understood and came in and sat where I pointed, which was the bench nearest the range.
I set out what the kitchen had: bread from this morning, broth from last night reheated, a piece of cheese that was harder than I would have served to a paying guest but was food and he was hungry.
He ate without speaking and without haste, which told me he had been hungry long enough to know that eating too fast would make him sick.
When the bowl was empty he set down the spoon and looked at the table.
"Thank you, ma'am."
"Where are you headed?"
"North," he said.
He did not name a town.
I cleared the bowl and the plate and he stood and went out through the kitchen door and I closed it behind him.
The latch caught.
I washed the bowl and set it on the rack and wiped the table where he had sat and went to see what Nan needed for the evening.
In the taproom, two men who had been sitting since midday had found something to disagree about.
I could hear the pitch of it rising as I came through the doorway -- not yet a fight, but the particular frequency that preceded one, when voices go tight and chairs begin to scrape.
"Gentlemen," I said.
"You'll settle it outside or you'll settle it nowhere, but you will not settle it in my house."
They settled it nowhere.
Nan, behind the bar, had not moved.
She did not need to.
The afternoon passed the way afternoons at the White Hound passed when there was no coach due and no crisis to manage -- which is to say, it passed in work.
I reset the rooms that needed resetting.
I checked the kitchen stores against what we would need for the evening meal and made a list that was shorter than I wanted and longer than I could afford.
Nan polished glasses.
Jem split kindling.
The light outside went from grey to the colour of old pewter and then, slowly, to the colour of nothing at all.
I locked up alone.
This was not unusual.
This was every night.
The last guests settled or gone, the last fire checked, the bar tallied, the kitchen closed down.

I moved through the inn's closing routine the way I had moved through it hundreds of times -- taproom first, where the fire was down to coals and the chairs were pushed in and the floor wanted sweeping but would get it in the morning.
The cellar hatch: locked.
The front door: bolted.
The dining room: cleared, the shutters drawn.
I checked the kitchen range and closed the damper halfway for the night.
The stable yard was quiet.
Jem would have settled the horses.
I could see the line of the stable roof against what was left of the sky, and beyond it the second-floor windows of the inn.
A light behind the glass in Bridget's room -- the shape of her, sitting at the window, watching the yard below as she watched it every evening.
I did not look long.
She was there.
She was watching.
I had seen it too many times for it to need anything from me.
I came back inside and stood in the kitchen.
My hands at the end of the day were reddened from the cold water and the cleaning, and there was a small cut on my index finger where the edge of the chandler's delivery note had caught the skin.
I noticed it the way I noticed everything at this hour -- with the flat attention of a body that had been in use since before dawn and was nearly finished.
The letter was on the table.
It had not been there this morning.
Someone -- Nan, or the afternoon post -- had left it beside the ledger, and I had not seen it until now, or I had seen it and had not let myself know that I had seen it.
Stainforth's seal on the envelope.
His handwriting on the direction.
I picked it up.
I held it.
I turned it over once and felt the weight of it, which was the weight of good paper and sealing wax and nothing more.
I did not open it.
I had known it was coming since the last rent quarter.

I had known it the way I knew when the porter was running low or the chimney wanted sweeping -- not because anyone told me, but because I paid attention, and the signs were there if you were willing to read them.
I had been moving faster ever since.
The chandler's price.
The short coaches.
The six weeks in the ledger.
All of it the same current, and this letter the place where it surfaced.
I set it down on the table beside the closed ledger.
I stood in the kitchen with my cut hand and my reddened fingers and the inn locked and quiet around me.
"Right, then," I said.
No one heard it.
There was no one to hear.
I checked the ledger twice because the first time I could not make the six come out any different from the five, and I wanted it to be wrong.
It was not wrong.
Six weeks to the quarter.

I knew it already, the way you know bad weather is coming from the colour of the sky before you look at the glass, but there is a difference between knowing and seeing the numbers laid out in your own hand.
The candle had burned down to a stub.
I had lit it early because the kitchen was still dark, the windows rimed at their edges with the cold, and the fire not yet hot enough to throw good light.
The wax pooled on the edge of the table near my wrist.
I closed the ledger.
The fire first.
I raked the coals from last night's bank and fed in kindling, then two splits of ash, setting them so the draught would catch.

There is a way to build a kitchen fire that gives you heat in ten minutes and a way that gives you heat in thirty, and I had not used the slow way since I was twelve and my mother stood behind me and told me to do it again.
The wood caught.
I left the door of the firebox cracked and moved to the taproom.
The taproom fire was dead.
I cleaned the grate, laid the fire fresh, and lit it.
The room smelled of last night's ale and tallow and the particular staleness of a space that has held too many bodies and not enough air.
I opened the small window above the settle to clear it, though the cold came in like water.
I checked the bar stock: two casks of ordinary, one of best bitter, the gin nearly out, the brandy adequate.
I tallied what remained against last night's take.
The numbers matched.
They always matched.

I had been doing this since I was fifteen and Nan was not yet born and my mother stood where I stood and said, Count it twice, Dinah, and if it doesn't match, count it again, because ale does not walk out on its own legs.
I pulled my sleeves down over my wrists.
The cold was in the walls now.
It would not come out until April.
There was a broken latch on the window of room six that I had noted two days ago and not yet mended.
There was a stain on the ceiling of the dining room where the lead flashing above had let in rain during the last storm.
There was a board in the upstairs corridor that had begun to give underfoot.
I noted all of it, as I noted it every morning, and set it against what could be done today with the hands and hours available.
I went out the back.
Jem was in the stable yard.
He had the big bay's harness across the rail and was working saddle soap into the leather with his one hand, the stump braced against the post for purchase.
The yard was swept.
The water trough was full.
He did not look up when I came out, and I did not speak.

The morning was cold and the cobbles were dark with damp and Jem had been at this since before I came down, which I knew because the soap was already warm in its tin and you cannot warm saddle soap in October without time and effort.
I went back inside.
Nan came through the kitchen door a few minutes later.
Her pins were not set yet but her apron was on and tied, and she went to the bar and began wiping it down with the rag she kept under the counter.
She did not say good morning.
Neither did I.
We had done this before.
Many hundreds of times.
The efficiency was the greeting.
The London coach was late.

I heard it before I saw it, the way you always hear them first on the Great North Road: iron on gravel, the driver's shout, the particular grinding protest of a vehicle that has been running hard since Barnet and wants everyone to know about it.
I was at the front door before the wheels stopped.
Two passengers, not four.
That was short.
The first was a man in a brown coat who stepped down without looking at anyone and went straight for the dining room as though he had been here before and did not require direction.
The second was a woman with a trunk.
The trunk had a split hinge.
The leather had pulled away from the brass and the lid sat crooked, held shut by a length of rope the coachman or someone had tied in haste.
The woman was perhaps forty, well dressed, and had the particular expression of a person who has been nursing a grievance for fifteen miles and intends to see it settled.
"That trunk was perfectly sound when I left London," she said.
"Jem," I said.
He was there.
I had not called him and had not heard him come, but he was there, and he took the trunk by its good handle and carried it inside without comment.

The woman watched him and then looked at me as though she were about to say something further about the trunk, but I had already turned to the coachman and whatever she saw in the efficiency of the transfer seemed to satisfy her, because she followed Jem inside.
The coachman wanted a word.
He was a big man with a red face and hands that looked like they had been holding reins since birth.
"Road's breaking up north of Hatfield," he said.
"Half a mile past the Wrestler's.
Ruts a foot deep in places."
"It was bad a fortnight ago," I said.
"Worse now?"
"Worse.
I nearly lost a wheel."
"I'll send word to the turnpike trustees."
He looked at me the way men sometimes looked at me when I said something practical, as though he had expected something else and was recalibrating.
"Do that," he said.

He went in for his ale and his ten minutes, and I let him have them because a coachman who loses a wheel on the Great North Road is a coachman who does not stop at your inn on the return, and ten minutes was a cheap price for his goodwill.
The passengers went upstairs or to the dining room.
Jem took the woman's trunk to her room.
The yard cleared.
Through the doorway I could see Nan behind the bar, cloth in hand, her eyes on the front door.
She had been watching through all of it.
I noted this.
I said nothing.
The chandler came at half past ten.

His name was Burrell and he had a cart and a boy and thirty dozen tallow candles wrapped in paper and packed in a crate that the boy set down in the kitchen doorway with the careful blankness of someone who has been told not to speak.
Burrell had a slate with the price marked on it.
He held it out to me the way a man holds out a card he thinks will win.
"Fourpence ha'penny the dozen," he said.
"It was fourpence last month."
"Tallow's gone up."
"Tallow has not gone up.
Tallow is the same price it was in August.
I buy from Hale's in Welwyn and I know what he charges you."
Burrell's face did not change.
He was a man who had learned not to show it when a negotiation turned.
"Cost of carriage," he said.
"Your carriage cost has not changed since you bought that horse in June.
She's the same horse and this is the same road."
"Fourpence farthing, then."
"Fourpence."
He looked at me.
I looked at him.

He had the option of loading his candles back onto the cart and taking them to the Red Lion at Stevenage, where the landlord would pay fourpence ha'penny without blinking because the landlord at the Red Lion did not know what Hale's charged for tallow and had never thought to ask.
But the Red Lion was six miles further on, and six miles was an hour and a half with a loaded cart, and Burrell's boy was cold and Burrell's horse was not getting younger, and we both knew it.
"Fourpence," he said.
I counted out the money.
Burrell took it, touched his hat, and went.
The boy carried the crate inside.
The door closed.
The kitchen was quiet.
I picked up the delivery note and wrote 4d./doz.

in the margin where Burrell had written his price, and the edge of the paper caught the side of my index finger and opened a thin line of red that I did not notice until I saw the mark it left on the page.
There was a thought that came at moments like this, when the numbers were fresh and the margins tight and the silence in the kitchen let it in.
If I married, none of this would be mine to negotiate for.

The ledger, the lease, the four farthings I had just held against a man who thought he could take them from me because he could: all of it would pass to a husband along with the right to stand in this doorway and say fourpence.
It was not a new thought.
I had done the calculation before, and the answer had not changed.
I cleared the delivery note from the table and went to check the dining room.
He came around the back, as the sign on the road asked.
I saw him through the kitchen window before he knocked: young, thin, standing on the step with the particular stillness of someone deciding whether he would be welcome enough to try.
His coat was army issue, the grey-brown broadcloth worn to nothing at the elbows.
His boots were coming apart where the upper met the sole, the stitching pulled loose and the welt separating so that you could see the pale line of his stocking beneath.
He was perhaps twenty.
He stood with his weight on both feet, arms at his sides, looking at the door.
I opened it.
He took half a step back.
"Ma'am."
"Have you eaten?"
He thought about lying.
I watched him think about it.
Then he said, "Not since yesterday morning."
"Kitchen," I said.
"Not the taproom."
"Yes, ma'am."
I sat him at the table and put in front of him what the kitchen had: bread, half a bowl of broth from the stockpot that had been on since morning, a piece of cheese.
He ate quickly and without looking up, his hands cupped around the bowl as though someone might take it.
The broth was not hot.
He did not care.
When the bread was gone he wiped the bowl with his finger and then sat still.
"Thank you," he said.
"Where are you headed?"
"North," he said.
He named a place I did not know, somewhere in Leicestershire or Nottinghamshire.
He said it quietly, as though the name were not quite real to him yet.
He stood.
He touched his forehead.
He went.
I cleared the bowl and the plate and put them in the basin.
I wiped the table where he had sat.
The kitchen door was still open and the cold came through it.
I closed it and turned back to the work.
The taproom trouble came in the middle of the afternoon, when the hours are long and the ale has been sitting in men too idle to use it well.
Two guests near the window had got loud over something I did not catch and did not need to.
One had his hand flat on the table and the other had pushed his chair back.
"That's enough," I said.
"Take it outside or settle it, but you will not break my furniture."
They looked at me.
The one with his hand on the table opened his mouth, thought better of it, and picked up his glass.
The other pulled his chair in.
Nan, behind the bar, had not moved.
She did not need to.
The afternoon stretched.
The inn between rushes is the inn at its truest: no coaches, no commotion, just the work that has to be done whether anyone sees it or not.
Nan at the bar.
Jem outside.
I went through the accounts again, reset the rooms that needed resetting, checked the kitchen stores against what was needed for the evening meal.
The board in the upstairs corridor gave under my foot as I passed it.
I would need Jem to look at it tomorrow.

There was never enough time and there was always more to be done and the doing of it was the thing that held the day in place, one task to the next, each one small and specific and necessary and leading without pause to the one that followed.
Evening came on early, the way it does in late October, the light going grey and then gone.
The last guests settled.
The dining room cleared.
The kitchen fire burned down.
I checked the bar with Nan.
The take was adequate.
Not good.
Adequate.

She untied her apron and folded it and set it under the counter where she always set it and went upstairs without a word, because words at the end of a day like this one were just more weight and neither of us had the strength to carry them.
I moved through the inn's closing routine alone.
Taproom fire down to coals.
Cellar hatch locked, the bolt stiff in the cold, my fingers numb around it.
The kitchen: range damped, surfaces wiped, the stockpot set to the side of the hob for morning.
I checked the front door, the side door, the kitchen door.
I went out to the yard.
The stable was quiet.
Jem would have settled the horses and gone to his room above the tack store.
The cobbles were wet.
The air smelled of cold stone and horse and the particular darkness of an English autumn night when there is no moon.
I looked up.
On the second floor, behind the glass of Bridget's window, there was a lit shape.
She was there.
Watching.
The light flickered as though she had shifted in her chair or turned her head.
I did not look long.
I came back inside and locked the kitchen door.
My hands at the end of the day were red from the cold water and the cleaning, the knuckles rough, a thin cut on my index finger where the edge of Burrell's delivery note had caught me.
The cut had stopped bleeding hours ago.
It was the invoice that had done it.
The letter was on the kitchen table.
I had not seen it when I came in, or I had seen it and not let myself register it, but there it was: cream-coloured paper, sealed with the dark red wax I knew.
The handwriting on the direction was precise, slanted slightly to the right, each letter formed with the care of a man who believed his penmanship reflected his character.
Mr Phineas Stainforth.
I picked it up.
I held it.
I turned it over once.
The seal was unbroken, the wax smooth under my thumb.
I set it down on the table.
I did not open it.
I would not open it tonight.
I had known it was coming.

I had known since the last quarter when the rent went out three days late and no answer came and no answer was itself an answer, because Stainforth was a man who replied to everything promptly and silence from a man like that was not silence but preparation.
I had been moving faster ever since.
Counting more carefully.
Holding Burrell to his fourpence.
Closing the ledger and opening it again as though the numbers might rearrange themselves into something more forgiving.
The kitchen was empty.
The fire was out.
The letter sat on the table in the dark.
"Well then," I said.
I checked the ledger twice because the first time the numbers were worse than I remembered and I wanted to be certain I had not carried a figure wrong.
I had not.
Six weeks and two days to the quarter, and the margin between what I held in reserve and what Mr Stainforth's agent would expect was narrowing to something I could feel in my teeth.
I wrote the total at the foot of the column, set down the pen, and closed the book.
The kitchen was cold.
The fire had been banked overnight and I had built it up twenty minutes ago, but the chimney drew badly when the wind came from the north and this morning the wind was doing exactly that.
I could hear it testing the casements in the dining room, that particular low moan that meant the putty on the northeast window had cracked again.
I would deal with it after breakfast.
I pulled my sleeves down over my wrists and went to check the taproom.
The taproom fire I built from scratch.
