I set the pot down on the hearth with the cloth over its handle, the way she liked it, so the spout would not drip on the tiles.
I asked after her knee.
She told me about her knee.

I told her I would send Nan up with a hot brick after dinner, and she said she did not need a hot brick, and I said she would have one regardless, and by the time I kissed her forehead and took the tray away I had put what she had said behind a door in a part of my head I did not intend to visit today.
I went down the back stairs with the tray.
I returned the cups to the scullery.
I washed them myself because the good china did not go in with the rest.
I dried them.
I put them back on Bridget's shelf.

I went into the kitchen and took up the list I had been working from since dawn, and I crossed off *cellar* and *latches* and *yard* and *Stainforth,* and I added *fence post* in the margin in pencil, and I did not look at the letter on the table, which I had still not put away.
By the time Nan had brought the taproom shutters in and banked the fire and gone up to bed, it was past eleven, and the yard was quiet, and the cold had set hard enough to crack a bucket.
I bolted the front door.
I took the lantern into the kitchen and set it on the sill.
I was about to blow it out when the knock came.
Three knocks.
Not hurried.
Not drunk.
A man who knew he was asking at an hour when he should not have been.
I drew the bolt back and opened the door a hand's width.
A dog looked at me first.
A grey-brindled lurcher with a long nose and an expression of worried patience, sitting on the step with its tail across its paws.
Then the man: tall, tired, a cloak that had been a good cloak once, and boots that had walked from somewhere a long way off.
The leather was good.
The leather was finished.
He had his hat in his hand, which told me something about him that I did not have the energy to examine.
"Forgive the hour," he said.
His voice was lower than I had expected and more careful.
"I was hoping for work, or a place to sleep.
Either will do.
I can pay for the bed if I must."
I looked at the dog.
The dog leaned against his leg.
"I'm full inside," I said, which was not true, and he knew it, and did not press.
"There's clean straw in the second stable, the box at the far end.
You and the dog may have it till morning.
Come to the kitchen door at six and we'll talk about the work."
"Thank you."
"Don't thank me yet.
The wind gets under the door and the cat will try to sleep on your face."
The corner of his mouth moved.
It was not quite a smile.
It was the shape a smile takes in a man who has forgotten how to wear one at short notice.
"I'll take my chances with the cat."
"Stable's across the yard.
There's a lantern by the mounting block if you need it."
"I'll manage."

He touched the brim of his hat to me, though it was in his hand and not on his head, which is the gesture of a man who is used to a hat being there, and he turned and went down the step with the dog at his heel, and I shut the door and drew the bolt.
I ought to have gone to bed.
I had been awake since four.
The cut on my finger was throbbing, and my jaw was sore from the morning, and there was a ledger still to balance at the kitchen table.
I took up the lantern to carry it upstairs.
At the kitchen window I stopped.
I was not watching him.
I was checking the yard, as I did every night, because a woman who runs a coaching inn alone learns to look at her yard before she sleeps.
The moon was high enough to put the stable roof in outline and the paddock fence in silhouette and the man in shape rather than detail.
He had the lantern.
He had set it on the mounting block.

He was bent at the stable door, his hand at the hinge, and he moved the door once on it and then again, listening to it, and then he took something from his pocket — a pin, a nail, I could not see — and he worked at the hinge until the door swung true.
He closed it.
He opened it.
He closed it again.
Then he went to the paddock fence.
The corner post that Stainforth had laid his hand on that morning.
The post that leaned an inch and a half out of true.
He did not lay his hand on it.

He put his shoulder to it and his palms flat on the rail and he rocked it, once, to find the play, and then he walked round to the far side and pressed his knee into the earth at its base, and he worked the post upright with his whole weight behind it until it stood clean against the sky.
He drove a stone in at the foot with his boot heel.
He tested it.
He set the top rail back on its peg.
He tested the rail.
He stood back from the fence and looked at it for a long moment in the way a man looks at a job to see whether it has been done.
The dog sat by the mounting block, watching him.
He bent and picked up the lantern.

I watched his hand close around the handle, and his other hand go to the small of his back as he straightened, the small stiff movement of a man with something wrong in one of his legs that he had decided not to attend to.
He took the lantern into the stable.
The yard went dark except for the square of warmer light under the stable door.
I turned from the window.
I blew out my own lantern.
I set it on the sill.
The cut on my finger was still bleeding, a little, under the linen.
I pressed my thumb to it and went up to bed.
The ledger sat open to the page I had been avoiding for a week, and the numbers on it had not improved overnight.
Six weeks, near enough, before the quarter's rent came due, and the column under income did not agree with the column under expenditure in the way I needed it to.
I added the figures a third time, because a third time was what I gave myself before I was allowed to close the book.
They came out the same.
I wanted a cup of tea I did not have time to make.
I closed the ledger and set it on the shelf above the flour crock, where Nan would not see it and ask.
The kitchen fire I had already built up; it was the taproom that wanted me now.
I went through, sleeves pushed back, and knelt to the grate.
The inn was cold in the particular way of a building that had given its warmth to strangers all week and been left to cool between coaches.
Frost rimed the insides of the window corners.
I laid kindling.
I struck the flint.
The first shaving caught, and I fed it with the patience the thing required, which was not very much if you knew what you were doing and a great deal if you did not.
Bar stock next.
Porter: two barrels, one broached.
Small beer: sufficient.
Brandy: low.
I noted it on the slate.
Candles would be a conversation I intended to have this morning, and I did not intend to lose it.
My sleeves had ridden up.
I pulled them down over my wrists and went out into the yard to look at the weather.
Jem was already there.
He had the tack across the trestle and was working the strap of a bridle between his remaining hand and the stump of the other, bracing the buckle against the bench and drawing the leather through.
He had taught the stump to do the work of the other hand over a year of patient invention, and he did not like to be watched doing it.
I did not watch.
I looked at the sky, which was a sky, and I looked at the cobbles, which had a skin of frost on them, and I went back inside.
Nan came in through the kitchen door five minutes later, pins half in, apron tied, and took her place behind the bar without saying good morning.
We had been saying good morning to each other for seven years, and we had lately agreed, without discussion, that we could stop.
The London coach was late.
This was not news.
What was news was that it was short, and the coachman's temper with it.
Two passengers got down where four ought to have, and one of them had a trunk with a split hinge that was already gaping by the time Jem reached it.
She was the sort of woman who made opinions into weather.
The hinge, the road, the hour, the fact that the sign on the road from Hatfield was ill-placed and had misled her late husband once in 1807: all of it, apparently, my affair.
"Ma'am," I said, when she had reached a natural breath.
"Jem will have the hinge mended before you are upstairs.
Mrs.
Hollis in room four is vacating.
I will put you there.
There is hot water in ten minutes and breakfast in twenty."
She opened her mouth to argue and then, reading my face, shut it.
"Thank you," she said, surprised into civility.
"Mind the second step," I said.
"It sings."
The coachman wanted me next.
He was a big man gone grey around the jaw, and he smelled of horse and the particular damp of a man who had been on the box since four.
"Miss Dale," he said.
"The road above Hatfield is a disgrace."
"I believe you."
"Ruts to the axle.
I nearly lost a wheel."
"I'll send word to the surveyor this week.
I owe him a letter anyway."
"It wants more than a letter."
"It will have a letter from me, which he dislikes, and a visit from my cousin-by-marriage at the quarter session, which he dislikes more.
Will that do for now?"
He looked at me under his brows.
"Aye.
That'll do."
"Good.
Nan has coffee in the taproom.
Two minutes.
I haven't more."
He went.

The yard cleared as a yard clears when a thing is over: trunks through the side door, passengers up the stairs, Jem leading the team toward the stable with the split-hinge trunk balanced under his arm as if it weighed nothing, which it did not, if you were Jem.
Nan wiped the bar with one eye on the door through the whole of it.
I saw her do it.
I said nothing.
She would not have thanked me for the notice.
Mr.
Partlet arrived at ten with his tallow.
I had been negotiating with Mr.
Partlet for four years, in which time he had raised his price four times, three of them in the last seven months.
He knew his margins.
I knew them better.
He also knew I knew, which was the part of the arrangement that kept our conversations civil.
"Miss Dale," he said, setting the crate on the table and taking off his hat with the slow courtesy that meant he was about to ask for more than I wished to give.
"Mr.
Partlet.
How is Mrs.
Partlet?"
"Indifferent, thank you.
It's her knees."
"Give her my respects.
What are you charging me for the dozen?"
He named a figure.
I let it sit in the air between us, where it could be observed.
"That is sixpence above September."
"Tallow's gone up."
"Tallow has not gone up sixpence a dozen to anyone else between here and Baldock.
I had a word with Mr.
Easton at the Cock last Sunday."
He had the grace not to pretend surprise.
"Mr.
Easton takes a smaller order."
"Mr.
Easton takes half my order and pays fourpence less the dozen.
I can do arithmetic, Mr.
Partlet.
So can you."
"It's a fair price for the quality."
"It is a price," I said.
"I will pay you last month's, plus a penny, and not a farthing more.

You will sell me the dozen because I take more candles than anyone else on this stretch of road and because you do not wish to drive back to Hitchin with a full cart explaining to your wife why you did not sell them."
He looked at the crate.
He looked at me.
The side of his mouth did the small movement that meant he had decided before he spoke.
"Last month's plus a penny."
"Thank you."
He counted the candles out.
I counted the coins.
He touched his hat at the door and went, and the door shut behind him with the decent small click of a deal that has been completed without anyone calling anyone a name.
I allowed myself one breath of private pleasure, the sort a person takes after lifting something heavy and setting it down without dropping it on her foot.
*A good morning's work, Dinah.
And it is not yet eleven.* I set the candles in the cupboard and stood a moment with my hand on the shelf.
The ledger, the rent, the candles, the road, the coachman, the trunk: all of it came back, in the quiet of the cupboard, to the one fact I refused to let sit in the front of my mind for long.
If I married, none of these negotiations would be mine to make.
The lease would be my husband's.
The ledger would be my husband's.
Mr.
Partlet would have tipped his hat to my husband and charged him sixpence above September, and my husband, who would not know Mr.
Easton at the Cock, would have paid it.
I had refused two men already on those grounds.
I had liked one of them well enough to miss him for a fortnight.
I closed the cupboard.
The next task was the larder, and the next task was the one that got done.
He came round the back, as the painted sign on the yard gate asked them to.
I saw him through the kitchen window before he knocked, because I see the yard from the kitchen as a matter of practice.
He was young.
Thin inside a coat that had been made for a larger man.
His boots had given up at the welt on the left foot and were working on the right.
He stood at the step without raising his hand, assessing whether he was welcome enough to knock, and arriving, I could see, at no answer.
I opened the door.
"Have you eaten?"
I said.
"Not recent, ma'am."
"Kitchen, not taproom.
You will sit at that end of the table where you will not be in Nan's way.
You will not come through into the front."
"Yes, ma'am."
I gave him bread and the end of last night's broth, which was thicker than broth had any business being and the better for it.
I set down a spoon and a cup of small beer.
He sat.
He ate with the slow care of a man who has learned, recently, that eating too fast costs him the meal.
He held the spoon with both hands, as my father had the winter he was ill.
I turned to the stockpot so that I was not watching him.
"Where are you headed?"
I said, over my shoulder.
"North, ma'am.
Nottingham, if I can make it.
I've a sister there."
"The road is bad above Hatfield.
Keep to the verge where you can."
"Thank you, ma'am."
He finished.
He stood.
He set the spoon down exactly square to the bowl, as if squareness mattered, and I suppose for him it did.
"Thank you," he said again, at the door.
"I'll not forget it."
"Mind how you go."
He went.
I stood at the sink a moment with my hands on the rim of the basin.
I was sorry about the boots.
I was sorry he was somebody's, and I did not let myself finish the sentence.
The stockpot wanted stirring.
I stirred it.
The afternoon moved the way afternoons move between coaches.
Two men in the taproom near one o'clock took offence at each other over a question about a horse that neither of them owned.
I went through.
"Gentlemen," I said.
"Not in this room."
They looked at me.
"Not in this room," I said again, in the voice my mother had used on drovers.
"Or not in this inn."
They found, upon consideration, that they had not been quarrelling after all.
Nan, behind the bar, did not look up from the glass she was polishing.
She had known I would not need her.
I had known she would be there if I had.
The inn was quiet.
It was always quiet between coaches.

I did the accounts at the kitchen table, reset the two vacated rooms on the first floor, spoke to Cook about the evening joint, and carried a scuttle of coal up the back stairs because Piers was not yet hired and the scuttle was not going to carry itself.
By six the evening coach had come and gone.
By nine the taproom had thinned.
By half past ten the last guest had been given his candle and sent up, and the fire in the taproom was a low red bed of coals that would hold until morning.
I did my circuit.
Taproom fire: down to coals, guard set.
Cellar hatch: bolted.
Back door: barred.
Kitchen fire: banked.
Stable yard: quiet.
Jem had been through; the horses were settled and the lamp in the tack room was out.
Second floor: the line of doors dark under the doors, except for the small warm seam at the turn of the passage where Aunt Bridget's window gave onto the yard.
I crossed the cobbles to the stable door and back, and when I looked up I could see her shape behind the glass, as I always could.
I did not look long.
She would be watching me the same as she watched everything, and she had done it for enough years that neither of us needed to remark upon it.
I set the bolt on the front door last.
It was a heavy bolt and the fit had stiffened in the cold.
I leaned my shoulder to it and felt it go home.
I stood a moment in the passage with my hand on the iron.
My palms smarted.
The right had a small cut across the pad of the index finger from the sharp edge of Mr.
Partlet's delivery note, which I had not noticed taking, and there was dried blood at the base of the nail.
I turned the hand in the candlelight.
A small thing.
It had been a long day.
I was tired, and the inn was quiet around me, and there was no one in any of the rooms I loved who was mine, and I let myself notice that for the length of one held breath before I moved on.
The letter was on the kitchen table.
I had seen it there when I came through at nine, and I had walked past it twice on purpose.
Now there was nothing else to do and nowhere else to be, and I picked it up.
Stainforth's seal.
His hand on the direction, which I knew as well as I knew my own.
I turned the letter over once, which changed nothing.
I broke the seal.
*Miss Dale,* he had written, in the cramped even script of a man who considered himself reasonable, *I write to you in the hope that we may bring a long-standing matter to a civil conclusion.

It has been represented to me by a gentleman of good standing that the lease of the White Hound might be put to more profitable use under different management, and I am minded to give the suggestion serious consideration.
My nephew, Mr.
Edmund Stainforth, is prepared to take the premises at Lady Day, with terms that would allow you a reasonable sum for the goodwill and fixtures.
I have a buyer.

I do not doubt that you will see the advantage to all parties of a prompt and orderly transfer.* *I ask that you attend me at Whitcombe on the fifteenth of November, at eleven o'clock, to discuss the particulars.
I trust you will not require me to repeat the invitation.* *Yr obedient servant,* *P.
Stainforth* I read it twice.
The second time I read it slowly, because I wanted to be certain of what he had written and what he had not.
He had not mentioned my mother.
He had not named the grounds.
He had not said *vagrant* or *public nuisance*, which meant he was keeping those in reserve.
He had said *buyer*, and he had said *Lady Day*, and he had given me three weeks to come to his house and be told how to lose my life politely.
I set the letter on the table.
I smoothed it flat with the side of my hand.
The cut on my finger had opened again.
I put the finger in my mouth, which was what my mother had done, and which had always annoyed me, and I stood in the kitchen and thought.
"Mr.
Stainforth," I said aloud, to the empty room, in a voice that was quite steady and quite my own, "you have written to the wrong woman."
Chapter One
The White Hound
The ledger was open on the kitchen table at a quarter to five, because there was no other hour when I could count a column in peace.
Six weeks.
That was the figure I had come to, and the figure did not grow kinder the second time I added it.
Six weeks and one day, if I gave myself the benefit of the doubt, which I didn’t ordinarily do.
Rent quarter fell at Christmas.
Whatever was owed at Christmas had to be in the rent-box by Christmas, and no creditor in Hertfordshire had ever done me the courtesy of being mistaken about a date.
I closed the ledger.
There was no sum to be reached by staring, and my mother had told me, often enough that it lodged: work the figures once, then work the inn.
The kitchen held the cold of a room whose fire had been banked seven hours.
I pulled my sleeves down over my wrists and went to build up the grate.
The window above the sink was rimed at its edges.
My breath showed when I bent to the embers, which I disliked.
Breath in a kitchen was untidy.
What I wanted, at five in the morning of a Tuesday in October, was a quarter-hour longer with the coals before the inn began to want me in six places at once.
I gave myself the ten minutes I could afford instead of the quarter-hour I preferred.
The fire caught.
I fed it in the careful order my mother had taught me and I had taught myself.
When I could leave it without watching it, I did.
The taproom came next.
I laid the fire there and lit it from a splint off the kitchen.
I counted the ale casks in the bar and found them at the number I had left them at.
That was not a thing to be taken for granted in October.
Men on the road had been hungry long enough to muddle the difference between begging and helping themselves, and I had learned to count whatever could walk.
The bar stock I checked by touch as much as sight, because the light was still poor and the stock was in the places I had put it.
Beer cellar.
Wine cellar.
Spirits lock-box.
Glassware shelf.
Everything at the count I had left it.
Alice, the chambermaid, had left me a note on a folded scrap about a broken pane in the second-floor passage window.
She had papered it for the night.
Jem would glaze it in the morning.
She had drawn a small rectangle on the note to show me which pane, which was Alice all over.
She was fourteen and had been with us eighteen months, and she wrote as neatly as a clerk.
That was more than I could say for either of the men on the payroll.
I tallied the night’s receipts against the cash-box and was pleased, in a small and practical way, that the accounts ran true to within a shilling and ninepence.
That was the ninepence the chambermaid had taken for soap out of the petty, and she had written it on the scrap by the box, as was proper.
I set the soap-shilling aside.
I went to check the cellar door.
I went to check the back door.
I opened the yard door, because the morning was what it was and the inn couldn’t be opened from inside.
Jem was in the yard already, as he was always in the yard already, straightening a bridle I hadn’t asked him to straighten.
He did not look up when I came to the step.
I did not call to him.
We had done this a thousand mornings.
He knew I was at the door; he knew I wouldn’t keep him.
Nan came through the kitchen a few minutes later with her pins not yet set in her hair and her apron already on, which was the proper order of Nan’s priorities.
She nodded at me.
She went to the bar.
She began wiping down the counter with the rag I had told her, twice, to replace.
This was not a battle I intended to fight at six in the morning.
The London coach came in at a quarter past seven, which was twenty minutes late and two passengers short.
I knew it was two short before the door opened, because the roof of the coach was light.
A full coach sat heavier on its springs.
I had listened for coaches coming off the high road for most of my life.
I had learned to tell a coach’s weight by the sound it made at the gate.
Jem had the horses’ heads before the wheels had stopped turning.
I had the coach door.
The first passenger down was a woman in a grey bonnet who had begun her complaint before her boots touched the yard.
“The hinge on my trunk,” she said, “is split.”
“I see it is, madam.
Jem will take it to the shed and mend it before your onward coach.
Tea in the dining room in the meanwhile?”
“The hinge is split.”
“It is,” I said.
“And it will be mended.
Tea is in the dining room.”
She had expected to be indignant in the yard.
I had offered her the chance to be indignant indoors, which was warmer.
She took it.
She was, I noted, the sort of woman who would be tolerable by the time the second cup was poured.
I had met her sort often enough not to be wrong about her.
I sent her through with Nan to seat her by the window where the sun would be by ten.
Indignant women were, in my experience, more tractable once warmed by actual sunlight than by any argument I could make.
The dining room was set for six.
By the time Nan had her in a chair and a teapot in her hands, she would have forgotten the specifics of her grievance in favour of its general outline.
By the time the onward coach came, she would be describing me to anyone who would listen as a perfectly capable woman.
The second passenger was a man of about sixty.
He spoke to no one.
He took a room-key from me with a nod and went up the stairs with a carpet-bag in one hand and his own quiet in the other.
I wished him a small private well, as I did all men who paid their rooms without conversation, and I turned to the coachman.
The coachman had the look of a man who wanted his two minutes more than he wanted his ale.
“Road’s bad above Hatfield,” he said.
“Wheel ruts a foot deep in places.
Lost a mailbag off the back going through.”
“Did you find it?”
“Aye.
But if you’ve passengers booked for the eleven, they’ll walk the last mile.”
“Thank you.
I’ll send word to the parish about the road.”
“Much good it’ll do you.”
“Probably none.
But I’ll send it.”
He gave me a small tilt of the head that might have been a laugh in a man with more time for laughing, and went to see to his horses.
The yard emptied.
I counted the coach out of the gate.
A coach that left the yard and did not reach the road was a coach that had become a yard problem.
This one made the turn, and I heard it take the post-road within thirty seconds.
Jem took the split trunk to the shed.
The passengers had gone upstairs or to the dining room.
The trunk would be back mended by half past two.
The Norwich coach came through at three, and any trunk that went to the shed before noon came back by half past two.
Jem understood the trade.
Nan had kept one eye on the door throughout and hadn’t needed to be called.
She caught my look.
I caught hers.
I went on to the kitchen.
Mr Pargeter the chandler came at half past nine with a case of tallow candles and a price I had not agreed to.
“Sixpence farthing the dozen,” he said, setting the case on the back step.
“Prices have moved, Miss Dale.”
“They have.
Yours more than most.”
I dried my hands on my apron and came out to him.
“That’s the fourth time in seven months, Mr Pargeter.
I’m beginning to think the tallow is moving along with you.”
He gave me the smile he had learned was meant to look apologetic.
“Hard season.
Beef’s up.”
“Beef’s up a penny in the hundredweight.
Your tallow’s up threepence in the dozen.
One of us has the arithmetic wrong, and it isn’t me.”
He looked at me.
He looked at the case.
He looked, very briefly, at the empty road behind him.
That was the tell of a man considering whether he had anywhere better to take candles at a quarter to ten on a Tuesday in October.
He did not.
The Black Bull bought from Highfield out of St Albans.
The George at Baldock used rush-lights for the bar and wax for the rooms and never touched tallow at all.
I knew this because it was my business to know it, and Mr Pargeter knew I knew it.
I let the sentence sit.
The yard was quiet behind him.
A sparrow had come down from the stable eaves onto the paving and was picking at something the midday coach had dropped.
Mr Pargeter watched me.
I waited.
A tallow-chandler was a man whose year had four good months and eight thin ones.
The thin ones were the months you survived by knowing which house would take your candles at your price.
I was not going to be the house that took his candles at his price.
He knew that now.
I had refused his first rise in the spring, and his second in July, and his third in September.
This was the fourth.
Three of the four refusals had been conducted over the same back step in the same tone of voice.
On each occasion Mr Pargeter had behaved as though he had not been refused on the three previous.
That was the form of the negotiation.
I did not enjoy it.
I also did not allow myself to dislike it, because to dislike a negotiation was to do it badly, and I had never been taught to do any work of the inn badly.
The sparrow flew off.
“Five and three-ha’pence,” he said.
“Five even.
And I’ll take three dozen instead of two.”
He did the multiplication behind his eyes.
I watched him do it.
The chandler was a close man with a close man’s habits, and I owed him no prettiness in the watching.
“Right,” he said.
“Five even.
Three dozen.”
“Leave them on the step.
Nan will count them in.”
He left them on the step.
He touched his hat, which was a courtesy he did not ordinarily pay me, and went back down the yard to his cart.
I watched him to the gate.
My mother had taught me to watch a man out of the yard if there had been money on the step between you.
I had never known her to be wrong about a chandler.
I went back to the kitchen and washed my hands.
Four pennies and a farthing, across three dozen candles, that I had not meant to save.
I allowed myself, in the privacy of the basin, one small satisfaction on the occasion of having done that particular thing well.
Four pennies and a farthing wouldn’t buy a pension.
It would buy tomorrow’s eggs.
And, if I was being truthful with myself at the basin, the smaller thing it bought was the quieter satisfaction of having been underestimated by a man who had known me nine years.
It didn’t do to take too much pride in a small victory over a candle-man.
The small victories were the whole of what I had.
The ledger, the rent, the chandler’s price: all of it counted against the single fact that none of it was mine in any way the law would recognise.
Let me marry, and the White Hound passed by the same Tuesday post to whatever husband I had selected.
This was why I had said no to Mr Eveleigh two years ago, and no again to the young Reverend Hibbert last spring, who had taken it better than he needed to.
There were easier trades than this one; I was not in the market for any of them.
A man came around the back of the inn a little past noon.
I saw him through the kitchen window before he knocked, because he did not knock immediately.
He stood on the step with his hands at his sides and looked at the door with the face of a man trying to decide whether he was welcome enough to knock on it.
He was young.
His coat was the grey that had once been another colour.
His boots were coming apart at the welt of the right foot; I could see the flash of paler cloth where a stocking showed through.
He settled his cap against his chest.
He knocked.
I opened the door.
“Have you eaten?”
I said.
“Not today, ma’am.”
“Kitchen, not taproom.
The bench by the window.
Bread and broth, whatever’s going.”
“Thank you, ma’am.”
He took his cap off and sat where I pointed.
He kept his hands between his knees while I ladled.
I went to the stockpot on the range and lifted the lid.
The stock was deeper than it had been at noon.
I had put a chicken carcass in at ten for the evening’s service, and it had given up what it had to give.
I ladled a bowl three-quarters full and took a piece of the morning’s bread from the rack, the heel, because the heel was mine to give and no one would miss it.
I carried the bowl to him.
He looked at the bread for a moment before he took it up.
He ate with the care of a man who had learned, somewhere, that eating too fast was its own punishment.
I cut him a second slice without asking.
He looked up.
“Where are you headed?”
I said.
“Lincoln, ma’am.
My mother’s sister.”
“That’s a week on foot.”
“Aye.”
He didn’t elaborate.
I didn’t press.
When he had finished the broth and mopped the bowl with the second piece of bread, he stood and put his cap back on.
He said thank you again.
He said God bless, and he meant it.
I opened the back door for him, because his hands were occupied with his cap.
“God speed,” I said, because that was what one said.
He went.
I stood at the door after it was shut.
His boots, I thought.
His boots were not going to take him to Lincoln.
I knew that, and he knew it, and I had fed him bread and broth that wouldn’t carry him any further than tomorrow morning.
That was what I felt, standing there.
He had a week’s walking ahead of him on boots that would not last a day.
I had given him what I could give him.
It had not been enough.
He was also somebody’s son, and I minded that too, although I didn’t intend to dwell on it.
I minded it for about half a minute.
Then I went back to the stockpot and took the knuckle-bone out of it because it was done.
I set the pot back.
I did not think about his boots again until the evening.
Two farmers had gone the wrong distance into a bottle in the taproom after the midday coach.
They were now arguing about the price of barley in a tone that was beginning to carry.
I went in.
Nan was behind the bar, and she lifted one eyebrow at me as I came through, which was her way of saying she had it and preferred not to.
“Gentlemen,” I said.
“The barley price is what the broker pays, not what we argue about over my ale.
Any voice raised in this room past the next minute will leave it on its own two feet.
Sit down.”
They sat down.
I went back to the kitchen.
The afternoon did itself, which was the best an afternoon could do in October.
I made up the first-floor rooms for the evening’s custom and sent Nan to the village for more salt, because we were always running out of salt.
The gap between coaches was the only hour of the day when I could hear myself think.
The thought I had, when I let myself have one, was that the knuckle-bone had been generous of me, and I had done it anyway.
That was the thought.
I moved on.
At eight I sent Nan home.
At nine Jem came in from the yard to tell me the horses were settled and the coach-house bolts drawn, and I told him to go, and he went.
At a quarter to ten I began the circuit.
The taproom fire I banked to coals.
I bolted the cellar hatch and damped the kitchen range.
The dining room I walked through with the lamp and found nothing out of place, which was Nan’s doing.
I drew the great bolt across the front door.
The back door I left for last.
I checked the back corridor for anything the staff had left out.
A bucket, a coat, a wet rag over a chair-back.
Nothing out of place.
Nan had at least learned, in the three years she had been with me, that a coaching inn cleaned for the following morning and not for the previous evening.
She had not always understood this.
She had come to it, and the business of teaching her had taught me as much as it had taught her about how much patience was a form of arithmetic.
My hands were raw by that point in the day.
Reddened from the cold water in the scullery, and from the cleaning, and from the wind through the kitchen window when Nan had left it open again by the bread.
There was a small cut on the side of my right index finger that I had taken off the edge of Mr Pargeter’s delivery note when I signed it, and forgotten.
It stung now, in the cold.
I held the finger to my mouth for half a breath and went on.
The inn rested.
That was the word for it.
A coaching inn at ten at night in October has a quiet of its own.
Twenty rooms mostly full.
Fires down.
Horses quiet in the stalls.
It is a quiet like no other building in the world, and I had lived inside the sound of its resting for all my life.
I stood at the bottom of the back stairs with the lamp and listened to it.
It made the same sound it had made the night before, and the night before that.
Every night since I had been tall enough to be the one who carried the lamp.
The hall was dark above.
Bridget’s door at the end of the upper corridor had no light beneath it.
That meant she had taken her lamp to her window where she sat most nights, and that was Bridget’s business and not mine.
The bolts were drawn.
The fires were down.
The inn was full.
There was nobody in the house I needed to speak to, and nobody in the house I could have called down if I had.
It was the hour, I allowed myself to notice, when I would have liked somebody to be there to say good night to.
That was all.
I noticed it.
I did not sit down with it.
I crossed the yard one last time to check the taproom chimney against the sky.
A fire banked wrong showed itself as a brightness against the night an hour before it showed itself in the room.
My mother had taught me that, and I had never stopped doing it.
The chimney was quiet.
Bridget’s window was lit as I crossed back.
It was lit most nights.
The shape of her at it was the shape I had seen a thousand times.
I did not look up long.
The letter was on the kitchen table when I came back in.
I had not seen it when I went out, because I hadn’t gone back through the kitchen after Nan had gone, and the afternoon post must have come in between.
Nan must have set it there.
It had Stainforth’s seal on it, and Stainforth’s handwriting on the direction: Miss D.
Dale, the White Hound, Stevenage Road.
I set the lamp down beside it.
I turned the letter over once in my hands.
I picked up the kitchen knife, because I had never carried a letter-opener in a kitchen in my life, and I broke the seal with the edge of it.
I did not sit down to read.
I stood at the table with the lamp close, which was how I read all correspondence that required an answer.
A man who wrote to me from a desk was not a man I was going to read from a chair.
He wrote, as he wrote everything, with the courtesy of a man confident he was doing one a kindness.
He requested a meeting on Wednesday next, the 6th of November, at my earliest convenience.
The matter of the White Hound’s lease had become, in his phrasing, pressing.
He had received an offer for the premises from a party in London, who proposed to establish his nephew in the trade, and the offer was, in his professional judgment, both generous and final.
He had no wish to see the matter proceed without the consideration of my own circumstances, which he understood to be considerable.
He remained hopeful, nonetheless, that an equitable arrangement might yet be reached between us.
Should he not hear from me by Monday fortnight, he would be obliged to regard my silence as a release of any further claim upon the lease.
I read it twice, standing over the table with the lamp close.
The ink, under the lamp, looked as if it had been bled into the paper rather than drawn on it.
The second time I read the phrase equitable arrangement, I made a sound that was not quite a laugh.
An equitable arrangement with Mr Stainforth had always meant, in my experience, an arrangement by which Mr Stainforth was made comfortable and I was made grateful.
I was not going to be grateful for the loss of the White Hound to his nephew.
I had seen the nephew’s face twice.
I had resolved on neither occasion to commit his name to memory.
I set the letter down flat on the table.
The seal had broken clean.
Monday fortnight.
Eleven days.
Eleven days to answer the letter, and eleven days to decide in what temper I meant to answer it, which were two different counts on the same clock.
He had a buyer.
He had a price.
He had, in his own estimation, the law and the custom of the county and the run of his own certainty.
And he had given me eleven days to find a reason for him to change his mind.
There were eleven days.
There was the lease.
There was me.
And I had spent the evening locking up an inn that by Christmas might not be mine to lock.
I folded the letter.
I put it in the drawer below the knife where I kept correspondence that required answering.
I blew out the lamp.
Then, because the room was empty, I said it aloud to the kitchen.
I used a voice I would not have used in the hearing of any soul who drew breath.
“Wednesday it is, Mr Stainforth,” I said.
“Bring your buyer.”
The letter sat where I had left it, opened, refolded, opened again.
Stainforth's hand was the kind that had been taught by a master and then improved by money.
Every loop closed.
Every line ran true.
He wished, at my convenience, to discuss the terms.
I knew what at my convenience meant.
It meant today.

The kitchen was cold because I had not stirred the fire, and I had not stirred the fire because I had been sitting at the table with my hands flat on the wood and the arithmetic running through me like a draft under a door.
Six weeks to the next quarter.
Forty pounds owed and twenty-eight in the strongbox.
Twelve to find by the first week of December, and a man on the road from Hertford who could turn that twelve into nothing if he chose.
He would not choose, today.
Today he would be courteous.
Today was the wind, not the cliff.
The ledger was where I had left it last night.
I did not open it.
The numbers were behind my eyes whether I looked at them or not.
My finger had bled into the seam of the apron pocket.
I had cut it on a hoop nail two evenings ago and forgotten about it the way one forgets the weather, which is to say it kept reminding me.
I sucked the side of it, tasted iron, and stood up.
The fire took on the second match.
The kettle went on the hook.
I put bread on the board for Nan and turned the loaf so the cut side faced down, the way Patience had shown me when I was eight and convinced that bread was a thing one simply ate.
Then I went into the taproom and made the inn ready for inspection.
I swept what did not need sweeping.
I wiped the bar with a cloth that had wiped it last night.

I went down into the cellar with a candle and counted casks I had counted on Saturday, and I did it because if Mr Stainforth ran his eye along my taproom floor and found a curl of ash from the grate I would have given him something, and I had decided some weeks ago that I would give him nothing he had not paid for.

By the time I heard the carriage I was at the front door with my hands clean and my apron straight and the bone-deep certainty that I had already lost the morning's first round, because waiting for him on my own threshold was a posture he had chosen for me without saying a word.
He stepped down from the carriage and came up the path with the unhurried walk of a man who had never been late to anything that mattered.
"Miss Dale."
"Mr Stainforth."
"How good of you to receive me at such short notice."
He pulled off his gloves a finger at a time and folded them into one hand.
His coat was the kind of dark wool that costs what a coaching inn earns in a fortnight, and it carried with it the particular warm smell of good cloth in cold air.
"I trust your aunt is well."
"She is, thank you."
"And the road from Hatfield was a credit to the parish.
One forgets, in town, how passable the country can be in October."
"We are fortunate in our weather."
He smiled.
It was a small smile, exactly proportioned to the exchange.
"May I come in?"
I stood aside.
He did not say thank you, because thanking a tenant for the use of one's own door would have collapsed the architecture he had walked in carrying.
"I so rarely have the chance," he said, looking up at the lintel as if noticing the inn for the first time, "to see the place properly.
Would you indulge me?"
"Of course."
He walked into the taproom ahead of me, which was also a thing he had chosen.
I let him.
Patience had taught me that you do not contest the small ground when the large ground is what you mean to keep.
He moved along the bar with one hand trailing the rail.
He stopped at the window and tested the latch with his thumb, lifting it and setting it back.
He bent at the cellar door and ran his thumb along the upper hinge, where I had oiled it on Sunday, and his thumb came away clean and he looked at the clean thumb for a moment before he straightened.
"How is your drainage, in the cellar?"
"Sound.
We laid new gravel in the spring."
"And your supply?
You take your ale from Welwyn still?"
"From Welwyn.
Mr Pratchett delivers on Tuesdays."
"And the coaching companies.
Are they satisfied?"
"They are."
He waited, the way a man waits for a servant to elaborate.
I let the wait happen.
Patience had taught me that too.
Give him the number, not the explanation.
Give him the answer to the question he asked, and not the question he might have asked next.
"Sixteen rooms let last week," I said, when the silence had stopped being his and become mine, "of the twenty.
Three coaches a day on the up road, two on the down.
I can show you the book if you wish."
"Oh, I should not dream of troubling you."
He had no intention of looking at the book.
The book was where the answers were, and he had not come to see the answers.
He had come to see the inn.
We went down the cellar stair.
He noted the casks.
He noted the gravel I had told him about, and bent and put a finger to the floor, and lifted his finger and considered it.
He did not ask another question for the length of the cellar, and I did not offer one.
We came back up.

He admired the woodwork on the dining-room door, which was original, and the brass on the dining-room fender, which was not, and he admired both with the same attention, which told me what his admiration was worth.
In the passage to the yard he paused at the kitchen entry and looked in.
Nan was at the range with her back to us.
He looked at her the way a man looks at a piece of furniture he is not yet sure he means to keep.
"Out the back?"
he said.
"This way."
The stable yard had a frost on it that had not lifted, and our breath came out white.
The mended half of the fence stood square.
The unmended half listed where the post had taken last winter's weight and never quite recovered.
Stainforth walked to the post and put his gloved hand on the top of it and rocked it gently, the way one rocks a tooth.
"A pity," he said.
"It will be done before the month is out."
"I do not doubt it."
He let go of the post.
"Miss Dale, may I speak frankly?"
"You may speak as you wish, Mr Stainforth.
I cannot guarantee what I shall hear."
The corner of his mouth moved.
He liked that, in the way a man likes a coin he was not expecting to find in his pocket.
Then he set the smile down.

"An establishment of this size," he said, looking past me at the stable doors, "with the traffic it now carries, and the kind of trade we are seeing on the road since the summer, might benefit from —" He did not finish.
He was offering me the end of the sentence, the way one offers a child a sweet, to see if she will reach.
I did not reach.
He let the unfinished sentence stand a moment longer, then folded it neatly away.
"I only mean," he said, "that the demands upon a single proprietor must be considerable.
The parish has been remarking upon it."
"The parish remarks upon a great many things."
"It does."
"My mother used to say the parish is a creature with one mouth and no ears."
"Your mother," he said, "was a remarkable woman."
He meant it as an offering.
He meant it as the small soft thing one places on the table before raising the larger one.
I took it for what it was.
"She was.
She is missed."
"By more than yourself, I should imagine."
He looked at me then, properly, for the first time that morning.
His eyes were a pale grey and very clean.
"I should be sorry to see anything happen to the White Hound that might diminish its standing.
I think you know that."
"I know what you have said."
"Then we understand one another."
"We understand the words, Mr Stainforth.
I do not think we understand the same thing by them."
I had not meant to say it as cleanly as that.
The sentence had come out a half-inch sharper than the one I had drafted in my head, and I felt it land.
He did not flinch.
He did not even pause.
He inclined his head a quarter of an inch, as though I had pointed out a small error in his reckoning, and accepted the correction without conceding the sum.
"Quite," he said.
"Quite so.
Well.
I have taken enough of your morning."
He walked me back through the passage at the same unhurried pace.
At the door he drew on his gloves a finger at a time, in the reverse of the order in which he had removed them.
"You keep the place very well, Miss Dale.
I have always said so."
"Thank you."
"Do give my regards to your aunt."
"I shall."
I watched the carriage to the bend in the road, and past the bend, and a little after that to be sure.
Then I closed the door.
I leaned my shoulder against it and let out a breath I had been carrying since I heard the wheels on the gravel.
My jaw ached.
I unclenched it and the ache stayed.
The cut on my finger had opened again.
I had not noticed when.
Bridget had seen the carriage.
Of course she had.
Her window looked down over the yard and Bridget had not missed a carriage in the boulevard du Cange — no, in the White Hound's yard — in twenty-six years.
The good china was already out when I came up the stair.

The teapot was on the hob and the cups were on the little table by the window, and the room smelled of lavender and tea and the particular dryness of old wool blankets that had been Bridget's smell for as long as I had known her.
The fire was high.
It always was.
I did not argue about her coal.
"Sit down, child."
I sat.
She poured.
The good cup came to me with its old chip on the rim turned away, because Bridget had been turning the chip away from guests for so long she could not stop doing it for me.
"Did he take his gloves off?"
"He did."
"Slowly?"
"Slowly."
"Mm."
She drank.
I drank.
The tea was strong enough to stand a spoon in and she had put a finger of milk into mine because she knew I took it that way and did not need to ask.
"Your mother," Bridget said, "had a man in here once.
Before your time.
Greville.
Owned the land before Stainforth's father bought it off him in '99."
"I know the name."
"He wanted the stable yard expanded.
Twice the stalls, he said.
Twice the trade.

Patience walked him round the yard same as you walked Stainforth this morning, and at the end of it she said to him, Mr Greville, the drainage will not bear it, and if I put twice the horses on this ground I shall have a yard of standing water by Michaelmas, and you will have an inn nobody stops at.
And he said, Mrs Dale, you are a stubborn woman.
And she said, I am, Mr Greville.
Thank you for noticing."
I smiled into the cup.
I could hear my mother saying it.
I could hear the dry note at the end of the thank you.
"She knew," Bridget said, "what to hold.
She was good at knowing what to hold."
"She was."
Bridget set her cup down.
The chip on the rim caught the light.
"Holding on and holding back are not the same thing, Dinah."
The room did not change.
The fire ticked.
The tea steamed.
Somewhere below, Nan dropped a pan and swore at it and the swear came up through the floorboards small and far away.
I picked up the teapot.
"More?"
"A little."
I poured for her.
I poured for myself.
My hand was steady, which surprised me.
I set the pot down and watched the steam come off the surface of the cup.
"Did he stand at the cellar door long?"
Bridget said.
"Long enough."
"Mm."
We finished the tea.

She talked about the apothecary's boy who had come to deliver her drops and stayed too long at the door asking about Nan, and I let her talk because Bridget talking about Tobias Meade was Bridget being kind, and I had run out of room for the other kind of kindness this morning.
I went down the stair.
I shut the kitchen door behind me.
I did not think about what she had said, because thinking about it was a thing I could do later, when I had the time, and time was a thing I had never had.
The day went the way days go.
Dinner went out.
The plates came back.

Nan and I scrubbed and dried and set out for tomorrow, and Jem came in from the yard with a list of small repairs and we agreed which would be done this week and which would wait, and the fire in the taproom was banked and the front bolt slid home and the inn arranged itself for sleep around me as it had every night for two years.
I was crossing the taproom with the lamp when the knock came.
It was not a coachman's knock.
A coachman knocks with the side of his fist and keeps knocking.
This was three taps with the knuckles, evenly spaced, and then nothing.
I drew the bolt and opened the door a hand's breadth.
A man.
Tall.
Standing back from the threshold, not crowding it.
A dog at his heel — long-legged, grey-brindled, sat without being told.
The man's boots had walked a long way.
They were good leather once.
They were not good leather now.
"Forgive the hour."
His voice was low and careful.
The voice of a man who had learned to make it do what he wanted.
"We're shut."
"I see that.
I'd ask a corner of your stable for the night, if you can spare it.
The dog won't trouble the horses.
I can pay for it in the morning, or in work, whichever suits."
I looked at him.
Thirty seconds is enough for most men.
He was not drunk; the consonants were too clean.
He was not dangerous in any of the ways I had learned to recognise; his hands were where I could see them, and the dog was the kind of dog that does not sit still for a man it does not trust.
He was tired.
He was very tired.
The kind of tired that has been tired for months.
"The stable's open.
Empty stall at the back, on the left, has clean straw.
There's a bucket by the trough."
"Thank you."
"We talk in the morning.
Not before."
"Understood."
He touched the brim of his hat — once, brief — and turned.
The dog rose with him as though they had agreed on it years ago.
I shut the door and slid the bolt.

I went through to the kitchen and set the lamp down and looked out of the window into the yard, because I looked out into the yard every night before bed, and the man was in it, and that was a fact about the yard tonight I needed to take account of.
He had the dog settled against the wall of the stable, out of the wind.
He stood a moment with his hand on the dog's head.
Then he went to the stable door and tried the hinge and the hinge gave, and he stood looking at it.
He did not call for tools.
He went round to the wood pile by the kindling shed and came back with a stone in his hand.
He set the hinge pin with the stone, two careful taps, and tried the door again, and it sat true.
He turned then, and looked at the fence.
The crooked post.
He walked to it.

He set his shoulder against it and rocked it the way Stainforth had rocked it that morning, and then he went down on one knee in the frost and worked his hand into the dirt at its base and packed the loose earth back round it, and packed it again, and rose and pressed the post upright with the flat of his hand and held it there until the ground had taken the weight.
He stood a moment, looking at the post, his hand still on it.
I turned from the window and put out the lamp.
The letter was folded on the kitchen table where I had left it, because I had not wanted it near the ledger and I had not wanted it near the bread.
Stainforth's hand was the kind that had been taught by a good tutor and corrected by a better one.
Every downstroke as obedient as a servant.
He wished to discuss the terms.
He wrote *the terms* as though the terms were a creature of their own, and he were only its custodian, kind enough to walk it over on a lead.
I knew the arithmetic.
I had known it since Michaelmas.

The next rent quarter was due on the twenty-fifth of December, and between now and then the inn would have to earn one hundred and twelve pounds clear, which meant a full coach in most nights and two full on market days, which meant weather we would not get and luck we had not been having.
Stainforth's visit was six weeks early, which was the whole of his courtesy.
A man who meant to take something did not wait for the last hour.
He arrived when the taking could still be called a conversation.
The fire was banked low and the kettle was cold.
My hands were the hands I had gone to bed with: the knuckles cracked red from the cellar air, and the cut on the pad of my index finger still open enough to catch on the muslin when I reached for it.
I did not reopen the ledger.
The numbers were where I had left them.
I got up and laid the fire.

• • • By nine I had swept the taproom twice, wiped down the bar until the oak showed its grain, checked the cellar for damp and the cellar stair for the loose tread that had been loose since August, and taken a rag to the window latch in the passage where last winter's paint had started to blister.
None of it wanted doing this morning.
All of it wanted doing.

I was setting the inn the way my mother used to set a table for the vicar — nothing better, nothing different, only every fork at its right angle and the salt where a man could reach it without asking.
A house that gave him nothing to correct.
Nan came through with the breakfast plates stacked up her arm and looked at the rag in my hand and the bucket by the door, and did not say a word.
She was twenty-one and she could read a room faster than most people could read a bill.
She set the plates down, took the rag from me, and went to do the bar rail a third time herself.
"He'll be here by eleven," I said.
"I know," said Nan.

• • • I heard the carriage before I saw it — the soft four-wheeled roll of a gentleman who paid to keep his springs in order, not the rattle of the post coaches we fed and turned round in twenty minutes.
By the time I reached the front step he was already on the gravel, and his man was already walking the horse.
Stainforth's coat was good wool, cut close, and smelling faintly of cedar where it had hung in a press that knew its business.
Next to it the inn's doorway looked like what it was: whitewash that wanted fresh, a boot scraper worn to a shine by thirty years of boots.
He took off his hat.
His hair was iron grey at the temples and combed with the care of a man who did not like surprises.
"Miss Dale."
He inclined his head.
"Forgive the hour."
"Mr Stainforth."
"I hope you had my note."
"I had it."
"And Mrs Dale, she is well?"
"My aunt keeps very well.
Thank you."
He drew off his gloves slowly, one finger at a time, and folded them together in his left hand as though he meant to hold them for the length of the visit.
He did not give them to me.
He did not ask after my day.
He stood on my step with his gloves in his hand and looked past my shoulder at the passage, as if the inn were a thing he had heard described and was now politely verifying.
"A wretched road up from Hatfield," he said.
"Quite rutted."
"It has been a wet autumn."
"So it has.
So it has."
He smiled, a small, symmetrical smile that cost him nothing.
"I wonder, Miss Dale — I so rarely have the chance to see the place properly — if I might impose on you to walk the premises.
Not for any formal purpose.
Only for my own interest."
I stood in my doorway a moment longer than civility required, and he waited for me to stand aside, as patient as a man waiting for a cat to move off a chair he had decided to sit in.
"Of course," I said, and stood aside.
• • • He walked the taproom the way a man walks a horse he is thinking of buying.
He did not touch the tables.
He touched the bar.
He ran two fingers along the underside of the oak, where a poor carpenter would have left splinters and where my grandmother's carpenter had not.
He seemed pleased that he could find no splinter, and also, I thought, faintly disappointed.
"Your drainage in the cellar," he said.
"Holds, does it?"
"It holds."
"Even in the wet?"
"Even in the wet.
The floor is tiled to fall to the drain at the north wall.
My mother had it done in the year six."
"Ah.
Your mother."
He paused at that.
"A formidable woman, by all accounts."
"By all accurate ones."
He gave a thin laugh at that and did not look at me.
He opened the cellar door.
The hinge was new — I had put it on myself in June, because the old one had begun to drop and the door caught on the flagstone.
He found the hinge with his thumb, and ran his thumb up the length of it, from the plate to the pin, feeling the set of the screws.
He did not need to do that.
Nothing asked him to do that.
He did it, and then he looked at me, and then he closed the door.
"Very sound," he said.
"Thank you."
"The coaching companies.
I understand the Edinburgh Mail still stops with you."
"Four nights a week.
And the Leeds, and the York day coach."
"And they are satisfied."
"They are satisfied, or they would not stop."
"Quite.
Quite."
He walked to the window and ran a finger along the latch and drew the finger back and looked at the pad of it.
There was no dust.
He had not expected any.
"And the rooms?"
"Twenty.
Seventeen let last Wednesday.
Twelve on Thursday.
A slow Friday.
The book is on the bar if you would like to see it."
"I would not presume."
"It is no trouble."
"Another time, perhaps."
He turned from the window.
"I confess I am always impressed, Miss Dale, when I come here.
One hears — one hears, you understand, I do not say one believes — one hears that the house is run on thinner ice than is comfortable.
And then one arrives, and the bar is clean, and the hinge is sound, and the book is full, and one feels rebuked for listening."
"You should not listen," I said.
"We are very well."
I gave him the answer in the number of words it wanted, and not one more.
It is how Patience taught me to handle a man who came to argue a price — you give him the number.
You do not give him the reasoning.
If he wants the reasoning he may buy it by asking.
He did not ask.
• • • Outside, the stable yard was cold enough to show our breath.
Jem was at the far end, settling the Leeds team for their morning feed.
He did not look up at us, which was his form of greeting and his form of refusal at once.
Stainforth did not greet him.
One does not greet an ostler one does not know.
This is the kind of thing men like Stainforth do not have to be told.
He walked the yard.

He came to the fence at the paddock corner where the post had gone crooked in last week's frost, the top rail loose at its joint, and he touched the post, and tested it with the weight of his palm, and did not right it.
"This wants a hand," he said.
"It wants half an hour of one."
"Mm."
He did not take his palm off the post.
"Miss Dale, may I speak plainly."
"You may speak however you prefer."
"An inn of this size" — he said it as though measuring a coat — "an inn of this size might benefit from —" He did not finish the sentence.
He left it in the cold between us for me to pick up, and when I did not, he smiled as if I had confirmed something for him.
"From?"
I said.
"From a firmer hand on certain matters.
The yard.
The suppliers.
The parish — you will know there has been talk about the soldiers on the road, and the feeding of them, and what that draws to a respectable stop.
Nothing serious.
Only talk.
But talk is how trouble begins, and it is easier borne by a household with — let us say — more than one shoulder to set against it."
I felt the cold come up the back of my neck the way it comes up when a fire has gone out behind you and you have not noticed.
I did not look away from him.
I had been hearing this sentence in one form or another since I was fifteen years old.
I did not need it finished.
I knew the end of it as well as I knew the cut on my finger.
"The yard has been held by a woman's hand for forty-four years, Mr Stainforth.
My grandmother's, then my mother's, now mine.
It has not fallen down yet."
He considered the fence post.
He did not flinch.
A man who flinched could be met.
A man who absorbed was another matter.
"No," he said.
"No, it has not.
And I hope very much, Miss Dale, that it will not.
Truly.
I mean that."
He took his hand off the post.

"I only wish to say — and I would not say it if I did not respect your mother's memory — that the terms of the lease come up for review in the new year, and it is my duty as landlord to see that the parish is served.
I am sure we understand each other."
"I think we do."
"Good."
He smiled again, warmer than he had smiled all morning.
"I shall not trespass on your day any further.
You keep this place very well, Miss Dale.
Anyone can see it."
It was the compliment a man gives a tenant he intends to replace, and he knew I knew it, and he gave it anyway, because the giving of it was also the visit.
He put on his gloves.
He found his carriage.
I stood on the step until the wheels turned out of the yard and onto the road and the sound of them was lost in the sound of the rooks in the elm.
Then I went inside and shut the door.
• • • I set my forehead against the cold wood for the count of three and then I straightened.
My jaw ached.
I had been holding it for two hours without knowing I was holding it.

• • • Bridget's room was at the top of the back stair and it was warm before you reached the door — the one constant warm place in the inn from October to April, because Bridget kept her fire, and I did not argue with her about the coal.
I had stopped arguing with her about the coal when I was eight.
She was in her chair by the window with the good china already set on the table and the pot under the knitted cosy she had made in 1803.
The cosy had been new when I was fourteen.
The china had been in the family since before any of us could remember, and she used it, as she had always used it, because there was no one we were keeping it for.
"Sit down, girl," she said.
I sat.
She poured.
Her hands were knotted at the knuckles and she held the pot with both of them, and she did not spill.
She had seen the carriage.
She had been at the window when it came and at the window when it went.
She did not ask me what Stainforth had wanted.
Bridget never asked a question she already had the answer to.
"He touched the cellar hinge," I said.
I had not meant to say it.
"Did he."
She handed me the cup.
The cup was warm already.
"Your mother had a landlord before him.
Greville.
This was in the year four, five.
You were a child."
"I remember Greville."
"Do you."
"The red face."
"The red face, yes.
He wanted the stabling expanded.
He had a nephew in Baldock with a notion about a larger yard.
He wrote your mother three letters and came twice.
The second time he brought a surveyor."
She drank her tea and set the cup down.
"Your mother knew the drainage in the yard would not bear it.
The low end floods in a wet March — you know this.
So she refused him.
She refused him flat, on paper, with a copy kept.
And the third letter never came, because Greville had a stroke at the Angel in Ware and that was the end of Greville."
"I don't remember the third letter not coming."
"You would not.
You were seven."
She looked at me over the rim of the cup.
"I mention it because your mother refused Greville for the right reason, which was the drainage.
She was always refusing for the right reason.
It was her particular gift.
She could tell a stone wall from a man, which is more than most of us manage."
I drank my tea.
The room smelled of lavender and old wool and the particular sweetness of the linseed Bridget used on her writing box.
I had sat in this room as a child while Patience worked the bar downstairs, and my shoulders dropped an inch whether I wished them to or not.
"And now," Bridget said, "there is Stainforth."
"There is Stainforth."
"And you will refuse him for the right reason."
"I will refuse him for every reason I have."
She smiled a small, Irish smile that had nothing soft in it.
"That is my girl.
That has always been my girl."
She turned the cup in its saucer.
"Dinah."
"Yes."
"Holding on and holding back are not the same thing."
I reached for the teapot.
"Is this one cold?
I'll go down and —" "It is not cold."
"I'll go down anyway.
Nan is short-handed with the Leeds coach."
"Mm," said Bridget.
She did not press me.
She never pressed me.
She said what she had come to say, and whether I had heard it was my problem, not hers.
She picked up her cup again, and I set mine down, and I kissed the top of her white head where the hair was thinnest, and I went.
On the stair I put the sentence away.

I put it in the place I put things that I would not be thinking about today, and I shut the lid on it, and I went back down to the kitchen and started the dough for the evening's bread, because we were short by a loaf and I had said nothing to Nan about it and it was my fault, not hers.

• • • By ten at night the last coach had gone through, the taproom was empty but for Jem's mug on the end of the bar where he had left it out of habit and an apology, and I was drawing the bolt on the front door when someone knocked on it from the outside.
Not hard.
Not the knock of a man who thought he was owed an answer.
Three even raps, spaced the way a man knocks when he would rather not have troubled you.
I opened it on the chain.
A man stood on the step with a dog at his knee.
Tall — I had to look up a little, and I am not short.
His coat had walked a long way.
His boots had walked further.
They were good leather, once, and now they were the colour of the lane after rain and worn so thin at the toe that I could see where the stitching was giving.

The dog was a lurcher, long-legged, grey-brindled, and it sat when he had not told it to sit, and it watched me with an expression I might have called worried if I had been in the habit of assigning expressions to dogs.
"Madam," he said.
His voice was low and even, and tired.
"I am sorry for the hour.
I would not ordinarily — I wondered if you had work, or a bed for the night.
I can pay for one.
I would rather earn the other."
"Both tonight or one?"
"Whichever you have."
He did not smile.
He did not lean on the doorpost.
He stood straight in the cold as though standing straight were what he did, and waited for me to decide.
The dog leaned against his leg.
I read him in thirty seconds, which is the length of time reading a man at a door takes if you have been doing it since you were fourteen.
Not drunk.
Not dangerous.
Not a problem I was going to solve tonight.
"The stable," I said.
"There's clean straw in the end stall and a blanket on the hook.
The dog goes with you.
We'll talk in the morning."
"Thank you."
"Breakfast is at six.
If you're not in the yard by seven you've missed me."
"I will be in the yard."
I unhooked the chain long enough to point him round to the side gate, and he went, and the dog went after him without being called.
I shut the door.
I drew the bolt.
• • • I should have gone up.

Instead I went through to the kitchen, because the kitchen window gave onto the yard and because I checked the yard every night before bed — the stable door, the pump, the coal — and because there was no reason not to look as well tonight as any other night.
He was in the yard by the stable door.
The dog had already lain down against the step with its chin on its paws.
He set his pack against the wall, and he did not go in.

He stood a moment with his hand on the stable door, and then he ran his palm down the edge of it to the hinge, and found the screw that had been loose since September, and tightened it a quarter turn with his thumb against the head of it, because he had no tool and it would hold until morning.
Then he crossed the yard to the paddock fence.
He set his shoulder against the crooked post where Stainforth had put his hand that afternoon, and he shifted it straight, working it in the frozen ground until it took.
He lifted the loose rail back onto its joint.
He put both hands on the top of the post, and leaned, testing it, and leaned again, and took his hands off.
The post stood.
I turned from the window.
I banked the kitchen fire.
I went up to bed.
The London coach came in forty minutes late and two passengers short, which meant the coachman was already talking before the wheels had stopped turning.
I went out to meet it.
The yard was cold, the cobbles dark from last night's rain, and my breath came in short clouds as I crossed to the step.
Jem was at the horses before I reached the coach door, which was where he was supposed to be and where he always was without being told.
"Road above Hatfield," the coachman said, climbing down.
His name was Aldous.
He'd been running this route four years and never wasted a word.
"Three inches of mud from Welwyn to the toll gate.
We took twenty minutes off the schedule and still came in behind."
"Same stretch as September?"
"Worse."
"I'll note it."
He nodded and went to his horses.
The two passengers who had made it were a woman of middle age in a grey travelling cloak and a younger man whose hat was pulled low and whose jaw was set tight.
The woman went straight toward the door without looking at me.
The man came last and then stopped and looked back at the boot.
"That trunk," he said.
I looked.
The hinge on the near corner had split, and the lid stood open a finger's width, held only by the rope the guard had lashed across it.
"I'll have Jem see to it," I said.
"It was locked when I handed it over in London."
"The road above Hatfield is three inches of mud.
Your trunk is intact.
You've lost a hinge."
He looked at me.
He was waiting for something—an apology, or an argument.
I offered neither.
"I'll want a room with a bolt," he said.
"You'll have one."
He went inside.
Jem was already there, hands on the rope, working it loose without being asked.
The guard had the mail bag down.
Aldous was at the trough.
The woman in grey was through the door.
I stayed until the last of it was settled.
Aldous came back around the rear of the coach, hands in his coat pockets.
"Same stretch will be impassable by December.
Tell Barker if you see him."
"Barker came through Tuesday.
He knows."
He nodded once.
That was the end of it.
The yard cleared in the way it always did: not at once, but in pieces, one thing finishing and then the next until there was only mud and wheel ruts and the smell of horse.
Jem went through the door with the trunk balanced on his shoulder.
The passengers were upstairs or headed to the dining room.
The coachman was gone.
I went back inside.
Nan was at the bar.
She had been pulling a cloth across the same length of counter for longer than the wood required, which was how I knew she had been watching the yard.
I did not say anything about it.
She did not say anything about anything.
I went through to the office.
Hollis came an hour later, earlier than his usual Monday, and that alone told me something.
He had his delivery cart outside and his boy with him, and he set the first box of candles on the counter before he had said good morning.
"Prices have come up," he said.
"Tallow's dearer now than it was at summer."
"How much dearer."
"Sixpence the dozen above what we agreed in March."
I knew what he paid for tallow.
I knew what he charged at the Falcon in Hatfield and the Cock at Welwyn, because Barker talked and the girl from the Cock came in on Sundays.
This was the fourth time since March he had arrived naming a new price.
Sixpence above our agreed rate was not the market.
It was what he wanted to see if I would pay.
"You charged the Falcon fourpence above March in September," I said.
"You're asking me sixpence."
"Different quantities."
"Same quantities.
I've kept the record."
He looked at the box on the counter.
He looked at me.
"Fourpence and a half."
"Fourpence," I said.
"Same as the Falcon.
And you'll be back next month."
He left the candles and went out to his boy.
I carried the first box through to the storeroom and set it on the shelf above the October account.
Four increases since March.
This one I had held.
The rent was due in eleven days.
The ledger balanced, barely, because I had managed every line of it myself.
If I had a husband, the inn would be his.
The ledger, the candles, the argument with Hollis, the note about the Hatfield road—all of it would pass from my hands by law and by the ordinary course of things.
I set the second box on top of the first and went back out to the bar.
Nan had stopped pretending about the counter and was drawing ale for the man from the coach, who had come down from his room and apparently found his temper somewhere on the stairs.
There was the dining room to check and the afternoon coach to account for.
I went to the dining room.
Chapter One: The Forger's Daughter
I could forge anything.
Signatures in three hands---copperplate, clerk's scrawl, that loose flourish gentlemen used when they signed away fortunes.
Seals with the right weight of wax; too much and it looked new, too little and it looked desperate.
Letters of reference that smelled like attics and old leather; I knew seventeen ways to age paper and three to make ink fade just right.
The letter under my hands was a gentleman's introduction to a shipping firm in Bristol.
Simple work.
The kind Thomas charged twenty pounds for because desperation had a fixed price in Seven Dials.
Dawn was grey through the shop window; coal smoke made everything the color of old copper.
I worked by candlelight even with the sun rising---better for seeing the watermark, that faint tracery that separated my work from a hemp rope at Newgate.
The paper was good stock; Thomas had sources for that, men who worked at the mills and understood the economics of silence.
I'd matched the seal to the original Thomas kept in the third drawer; pressed it in red wax that I'd mixed myself, just enough vermillion to catch light without looking fresh.
Looking at the finished letter, I felt that old lift of pride---wrong, probably, that satisfaction in work that could get us both hanged.
"Veri."
My father's voice from the doorway.
I didn't look up.
"Almost done."
"Leave it.
We have---" He stopped.
Started again.
"Someone's coming."
That made me look.
Thomas Blackwood was a forger; a good one; the kind Seven Dials whispered about when the Fleet Street printers needed something special.
He'd taught me everything---how to read a hand, how to match ink, how to lie with paper and wax and confidence.
Fifty-three years old and he'd never been caught; not once; but his hands shook now when the creditors called.
He wasn't shaking.
His face had gone---no, wrong word.
His face was plaster-white, that particular shade I associated with fear the way other girls associated it with weddings.
I set down my pen.
"Who?"
"Don't know his name.
But he sent word yesterday through Mick Flynn."
That was bad.
Mick Flynn ran a flash house in St.
Giles; the kind of place where cutpurses drank and housebreakers planned work and everyone understood that law was something that happened to other people.
If someone sent word through Flynn, they weren't ordinary clients.
Three exits in this room.
The door Thomas stood in.
The window that opened onto the alley---two-story drop, but there was a rain barrel.
The passage behind the false wall that led to the cellar.
I'd counted them a thousand times; part of how I worked; always knowing where to run.
"He's coming at dawn?"
"He's coming now."
I looked at the letter on my desk, at the careful lines of false reference and forged regard.
Twenty pounds for this.
Forty if the client was desperate.
Death if we were caught.
"Put it away," Thomas said.
I did.
Blotted the signature---Henry Carstairs, shipping merchant, a man who'd never existed but whose hand I knew better than my own---and slid the letter into the drawer with seventeen others.
Evidence enough to hang us both; but we'd always worked from the shop; always kept our life and our work in the same three rooms because rent was dear and secrets were expensive.
The knock came.
Not loud.
Not aggressive.
Three taps, perfectly spaced, the kind of knock that suggested the person on the other side had knocked on many doors and knew exactly how to make it sound like they belonged.
Thomas looked at me.
I looked back.
We'd had this conversation before---without words, just that exchange of glances that said run or stay, fight or fold, trust this or cut our losses.
He nodded.
Once.
I was staying.
Thomas crossed to the door; his hand steady now; that particular steadiness that came from decades of lying.
He opened it.
The man who entered wore Mayfair tailoring in a Seven Dials dawn.
Wrong.
Everything about him wrong for this place, this time, this kind of business.
His coat was superfine---I knew fabric the way other girls knew fashion---and his boots were polished to that mirror-shine that required a valet.
He carried a walking stick; the handle caught what light the candle gave; silver, probably real, the kind of thing that would get a man murdered three streets over.
But he walked into our shop like he owned it.
Like he owned Seven Dials and everyone in it.
"Mr.
Blackwood."
His voice was officer-class.
That particular accent that came from the right schools and the right regiment and never having to wonder where the next meal was coming from.
"Thank you for seeing me."
Thomas said nothing.
