I watched him do the calculation I'd done myself---this man was dangerous; but turning him away might be more dangerous; we needed money; but some money came with a rope attached.
"And this must be your daughter."
The man's gaze found me.
I was still at my desk; still wearing my work clothes; ink on my fingers despite the rag I'd used.
My hair was pinned back with the same pins I'd been using for three years; bent in places but too expensive to replace.
I'd been working since midnight and probably looked it.
But I met his eyes.
He was handsome---that distant, cold kind of handsome that came from good bones and better breeding.
Forty-five, maybe.
Dark hair going grey at the temples in that way that looked distinguished on men and old on women.
His face was unreadable; a perfect mask of polite interest; the kind of expression that gave away nothing while seeing everything.
"My daughter helps with---" Thomas started.
"With the work.
Yes.
I'm aware."
The man smiled.
It was the smile of a hanging judge who enjoyed his job.
"Miss Blackwood.
A pleasure."
I didn't correct him on the Miss---I'd never been formally acknowledged, never had that luxury---just nodded.
"May I?"
He gestured to the chair across from my desk.
Thomas looked at me.
I looked at the man's boots---expensive, yes, but with mud from Seven Dials streets.
He'd walked here.
That was either confidence or stupidity, and he didn't look stupid.
"Sit," I said.
He did.
Placed his walking stick across his knees; those perfect knees in their perfect trousers; and looked at me like I was a curiosity.
A specimen.
Something to study.
"I have a proposition," he said.
"One that requires someone with your particular talents."
I waited.
Thomas had taught me that too---never speak first when someone is buying lies.
"There's a house party," the man continued.
"At Kelmarsh Park.
The Duke of Kelmarsh's estate in Northamptonshire.
Week-long affair.
Very exclusive.
Very observed."
I knew about house parties the way I knew about peacocks---both existed, both were expensive, neither had anything to do with me.
"There will be a guest," he said.
"An Italian contessa.
Contessa Oriana Castelfranco.
She'll be traveling from Venice.
Letters of introduction.
Aristocratic connections.
Fluent Italian, of course."
Of course.
I'd been teaching myself Italian for two years---street Latin and opera phrases and anything else I could steal from the books Thomas brought home.
My accent was probably terrible but better than nothing.
"Unfortunately," the man said, and his smile widened, "the Contessa will not be attending."
Silence.
I understood.
Of course I understood.
I'd been understanding the unspoken language of crime since I was eight years old.
"You want me to impersonate her."
"Very good, Miss Blackwood."
"Why?"
"The Duke has something I need.
Documents in his private study.
I need them retrieved.
Carefully.
Without suspicion."
"And you need a thief who speaks Italian."
"I need someone who can play a role.
Who can forge a life as easily as she forges a letter.
Who can walk into Kelmarsh Park as a contessa and walk out with what I require."
I looked at Thomas.
His face was careful---too careful.
That blank expression he wore when magistrates asked questions.
"No," I said.
The man's eyebrows rose.
"I haven't mentioned the payment."
"Don't care about the payment.
This is---" I searched for a word.
"Mad.
I can't pass for a contessa.
I've never been north of Camden.
I don't know the first thing about---"
"You know everything about being someone you're not."
His voice was quiet.
Final.
"That's what forgery is, Miss Blackwood.
Creating truth from lies.
You've been doing it all your life."
"On paper.
Not---"
"I'll provide everything you need.
Documentation.
History.
Training.
You'll have a week to prepare.
Mrs.
Fielding will coach you---she's an expert in deportment, speech, all those little aristocratic habits.
You'll know everything the real Contessa knows.
You'll be perfect."
"And if I'm caught?"
"You won't be."
"But if I am?"
His smile didn't change.
"Then you'll hang.
Along with your father.
I have enough evidence in my possession to ensure that."
The room was very quiet.
Thomas's hand found the edge of the doorframe.
Knuckles white.
"You're blackmailing us," I said.
Because calling things by their names was sometimes all you had left.
"I'm offering you employment.
Very well-paid employment.
Fifty pounds for the week.
More if you successfully retrieve the documents."
Fifty pounds.
We owed sixty-two to various creditors; three of them the breaking-fingers kind; one of them worse.
Fifty pounds would clear most of that.
Let us breathe.
Let us work without looking over our shoulders.
But this wasn't work.
This was walking into a duke's house and playing aristocrat and stealing from someone who probably had the power to have us both transported.
"I need to think about it," I said.
"No."
The man stood.
"You need to say yes.
Because I've taken the liberty of ensuring your father's arrest on forgery charges.
He's expected at Newgate this afternoon.
Unless, of course, you agree to my terms."
Everything stopped.
I looked at Thomas.
Thomas looked back.
His face was that terrible empty calm.
"You're lying," I said.
"I rarely lie, Miss Blackwood.
It's so much easier to simply arrange reality to suit my purposes."
He reached into his coat---I tensed, but he only pulled out papers.
Set them on my desk.
"There's your documentation.
The Contessa's history.
Her letters of introduction.
A miniature portrait for reference---you do look rather alike, which is fortunate.
And the address where Mrs.
Fielding will meet you tomorrow at noon."
I didn't touch the papers.
The man picked up his walking stick.
Gave me that hanging-judge smile.
"You have twelve hours to prepare yourself, Miss Blackwood.
After that, Mrs.
Fielding will begin your transformation.
One week from today, you'll travel to Kelmarsh Park.
You'll arrive as Contessa Oriana Castelfranco.
You'll retrieve the documents I've specified.
And you'll leave with your father's life intact and fifty pounds richer."
"And if I refuse?"
"You won't refuse.
Because you love your father.
And because---" He paused at the door.
"Because you're curious.
About that world.
Those people.
That life you've spent your whole life forging but never living."
He was right.
God help me, he was right.
He left.
The door closed.
The room was grey dawn and coal smoke and the particular silence that came after disaster.
Thomas sat down.
Not gracefully---just sat, like his legs had given out.
"It's a trap," I said.
"Of course it's a trap."
"We should run."
"Where?"
He laughed, but it was glass breaking.
"Veri, I'm fifty-three.
I've got bad knees and worse lungs and three creditors who'll find me anywhere in London.
You're twenty-four and the most talented forger I've ever trained.
Between us, we've got maybe forty pounds and one chance."
"One chance to get hanged."
"Or one chance to clear the debt and start clean."
I looked at the papers on my desk.
At the miniature portrait lying face-up.
The Contessa was beautiful---dark hair like mine, similar bone structure, but her face had never known hunger.
Never counted exits.
Never wondered if the next knock was magistrates.
"I could be anyone," I said.
Out loud this time.
"That's my gift."
"And your curse."
Thomas's voice was rough.
"Your mother used to say that.
That you'd be anything you chose."
I looked at him.
Really looked.
At his greying hair and his forger's hands and the stoop in his shoulders that came from thirty years bent over a desk.
At the man who'd taught me everything except how to live any other way.
"You'll go to Newgate if I don't do this."
"Yes."
"And if I do this and fail, we both hang."
"Probably."
I picked up the miniature portrait.
Studied the Contessa's face.
Her serene expression.
Her perfect aristocratic bearing.
Everything I'd never been and never could be.
Except.
Except I could forge anything.
"Tell me about the client," I said.
"Who is he?"
"Don't know.
Calls himself the Sphinx.
Deals in information.
Blackmail, mostly.
Very connected.
Very dangerous."
"The Sphinx."
I tested the name.
It fit.
Riddles and secrets and impossible questions.
I set down the portrait.
Looked at my ink-stained fingers.
At the work I'd been doing when the knock came.
At the letter of recommendation that would free some desperate merchant from his gambling debts and cost us nothing but skill and risk.
And I thought about my mother.
Catherine Blackwood, dead twelve years now.
Consumption and poverty and Seven Dials winters.
She'd taught me to read when I was four---taught me with stolen books and candle-stubs and that fierce determination that I be more than her circumstances.
That I be educated.
That I be capable.
That I be better.
"You're meant for more than this," she'd said.
Over and over, until it became prayer or prophecy or both.
"You're meant for more."
I'd never believed her.
But standing at the window now, looking toward Mayfair and Belgravia and all those glittering places I'd only ever seen from Seven Dials streets, I wondered.
If maybe.
Just maybe.
I could forge a contessa as easily as I forged a signature.
I could walk into that world wearing silk instead of threadbare muslin.
I could see---just for a week---what it felt like to be someone else.
Someone better.
Someone who belonged.
"I'll do it," I said.
Thomas exhaled.
"Veri---"
"I'll do it.
But not for the money.
Not even for you."
I turned from the window.
Met his eyes.
"I'll do it because I want to know.
If I can.
If I'm good enough.
If all these years of forging other people's lives means I can forge my own."
"That's not forging.
That's lying."
"What's the difference?"
He didn't answer.
Maybe there wasn't an answer.
Maybe the whole of Seven Dials was built on that question---the difference between survival and sin, between what you had to do and what you chose to be.
I picked up the papers the Sphinx had left.
The Contessa's history.
Her letters.
The address for Mrs.
Fielding.
"In seven days," I said, "I'll be a contessa.
Or I'll be dead."
Thomas stood.
Crossed to me.
Put his forger's hands on my shoulders.
"Your mother would be proud."
"My mother would be horrified."
"Both those things can be true."
He kissed my forehead.
Left the room.
Left me standing there with a dead woman's life in my hands and my own future balanced on the edge of a lie.
I looked in the cracked mirror propped against the wall.
Studied my face.
My dark eyes and my sharp cheekbones and my Seven Dials pallor.
Tried to imagine myself in silk.
In jewels.
In that world of house parties and dukes and casual wealth.
"Buongiorno," I said to my reflection.
The accent was terrible.
"Mi chiamo Contessa Oriana Castelfranco."
The words felt like forgery.
Like truth.
Like the best lie I'd ever told.
Outside, Seven Dials was waking.
The costermongers and the pickpockets and the girls who sold what they had to because selling anything else required capital.
The world I'd known all my life.
The world I was about to leave---temporarily, dangerously, possibly fatally.
I touched the miniature portrait again.
The Contessa's face stared back, serene and distant.
"I could be you," I whispered.
"I could be anyone."
And somewhere in the grey dawn, in a room that smelled of ink and secrets, I became someone else.
I became the Counterfeit Contessa.
The London coach came in twenty minutes late and two passengers short, which I already knew from the yard boy's face before the wheels had stopped turning.
I was at the door before the coachman had handed down the second passenger.

There were four in all: a wool merchant I recognised from the autumn run, his face dark with something that had nothing to do with the cold; a woman in grey travelling alone who descended carefully, testing each step; a clergyman who went straight past me as though I were a post; and a young man in a new coat who stood looking at his trunk with an expression that prepared me for trouble.
The trunk had a split hinge.
One corner of the lid had buckled outward, and the strap across it was doing work the hinge should have done.
The young man said, "Your man dropped it."
"Let's see what we have," I said.
Jem was already there.
He had not been there a moment before and I had not called him; he was simply there, with his hands on the trunk before the young man could say anything further.
I watched him test the hinge with his thumb.
"Came to it already split," Jem said, not looking up.
"The leather's dried clear through.
See how it's cracked along the fold?"
The young man looked.
The cracking was there, plain enough.
"I'll have Watts look at it this afternoon," I said.
"He'll have it right before the evening.
If the goods are undamaged, the repair costs nothing."
He wanted to argue.
I could see it gathering in him.
But there was nothing in what I'd said to argue with, and after a moment he let it go and turned toward the door.
Jem lifted the trunk and took it toward the back passage.
The coachman caught me before I turned back to the others.
His name was Briggs and he was a careful man, not given to complaint.
"North road above Hatfield," he said.
"There's a section coming loose before the Stanborough turn.
Six feet, maybe eight.
I took it slow but the next rain will finish it."
"I'll send word to the surveyor's office today."
"Aye."
He looked at his horses.
"That's all."
The yard emptied by degrees.
The wool merchant went to the dining room still wearing his dark expression.
The woman in grey went upstairs with the chambermaid.
The clergyman had already vanished.
The young man followed when he saw Jem carry his trunk through the back.
The horses went to the stable in pairs, their breath hanging white in the cold air.
Briggs climbed back to his box and the coach went through to the far yard.
The silence after a coach arrival is not a quiet silence.
It is the silence of a room that has just stopped being loud.
I stood a moment in the doorway and watched the last of the mud settle in the wheel-ruts.
Behind me I heard Nan moving at the bar, the clink of a glass set down and taken up again.
She had been watching the whole of it through the serving hatch, her cloth going in slow circles on the counter.
She did not say anything and I did not turn around.
The chandler came just before eleven.
His name was Perrin.
He had held the account six years, and in that time I had paid him on the first of every month without exception.
He set his delivery down in the passage and named his price, and the price was higher.
I said, "That's the fourth rise since March."
"Tallow's up across the county.
I'm not the only one."
"You're charging the King's Arms at Welwyn sixpence less per dozen."
A pause.
He had not expected that.
"Different quantities," he said.
"I take more than they do."
I let that sit for a moment.
"I pay on time and I don't send things back.
That's worth something to a man carrying three accounts that don't."
I knew two of the three by name.
He knew I knew.
"I'll pay what I paid in September."
He looked at the candles.
He looked at me.
"Split the difference," he said.
"September's price," I said.
He left the candles.
I carried the tally book through to the back room and wrote the figure down.
The rent had gone up in August.
The coal price had gone up before that.
Every number I wrote came back to the same fact: every lease, every account, every supplier on this road would belong to a husband if I had one, and the inn along with them.
I would have no more standing to negotiate than the hall table.
I noted the figure and closed the book.
In the passage, Watts was already at the young man's trunk with a strip of new leather and a pot of paste.
The hinge, as Jem had said, had been dry for months.
Chapter One: The Forger's Daughter
The Earl of Pemberton's signature required three things: confidence in the downstroke, hesitation on the capital P, and complete disregard for the fact that the Earl had been dead for six months.
I pressed the seal into red wax—not too hot, which made it glossy and obvious, but cooled just enough to catch light the way old seals did.
The letter beneath my hands was a recommendation for a merchant's son.
Fifteen pounds, which would keep us in coal for two months and maybe convince Mrs.
Hartley downstairs that we'd pay February's rent.
"That's Pemberton's third son you've gotten positions for."
I didn't look up.
Thomas had a way of appearing in doorways without sound, which made him excellent at forgery and terrible at fatherhood.
"Fourth.
The second son got two positions.
Different names, different cities."
"Christ."
But he was smiling.
"Your mother would have—"
"Don't."
The smile vanished.
We had rules, Thomas and I.
Don't talk about Mother.
Don't talk about the life before Seven Dials.
Don't count how many years we'd been doing this or how many more we could manage before someone noticed the pattern.
I blotted the signature—Thomas Pemberton, who'd never existed but whose handwriting I knew better than my own—and held the letter to the light from our single window.
Dawn was happening somewhere above the smoke, turning everything the color of old pennies.
The watermark showed through perfect.
Another ghost successfully documented.
"We've got company coming."
Thomas's voice had changed.
Flat now.
The voice he used when bailiffs knocked.
I set down the letter.
"Who?"
"Don't know.
Message came through Mick Flynn last night."
That stopped my hands completely.
Mick Flynn ran the Pewter Crown, which wasn't a pub so much as a gathering place for people who made their living in ways that required never being remembered.
If someone sent word through Flynn, they were either desperate or dangerous.
"What did the message say?"
"Special client.
Dawn.
Come alone."
Thomas touched his coat pocket, checking for the knife he always carried.
"Might be nothing."
"Might be magistrates."
"Magistrates don't send warnings."
True.
Magistrates kicked in doors and sorted through the debris afterward.
This was something else.
Something that wanted us nervous and waiting.
I looked at our shop—calling it that gave it more dignity than it deserved.
One room with a bed behind a curtain, a desk where I worked, shelves holding our stock: paper of seven different weights, ink in four colors, wax in six.
The tools of our trade, which was lying and getting paid for it.
Three exits.
I'd counted them so many times they'd become automatic.
The door Thomas stood in.
The window that opened onto a two-story drop, but there was a barrel below if you got desperate.
The false panel behind the shelves that led to the cellar, and from there to the tunnels that ran under half of Seven Dials like veins under skin.
"I'm staying," I said.
"Veri—"
"If they're coming for us, running won't help.
And if they're really a client, we need the money."
We needed more than money.
We owed sixty-two pounds across five different creditors, three of whom had threatened to break Thomas's fingers if we didn't pay by month's end.
The other two had threatened worse, in ways that didn't require specifics.
Thomas rubbed his face.
He looked old suddenly, though he was only fifty-three.
Forgery aged you the way worry did, etching itself into the lines around your eyes until you couldn't remember what you'd looked like when you still believed in things like safety.
"I'm making tea," he said, which meant yes, you can stay, but I don't like it.
While the kettle boiled on our ancient stove, I cleaned ink from under my fingernails and tried to shake the feeling that had settled into my chest.
Not quite fear.
Something sharper.
The sense that the world was about to tilt and I'd need to be ready.
"Buongiorno," I said to my reflection in the window glass.
"Mi chiamo Contessa Oriana Castelfranco."
"Your accent's getting better."
Thomas handed me tea in a chipped cup.
"Why Italian?"
"Why not?"
But we both knew.
I'd been teaching myself for two years now, stealing grammar from books Thomas brought home, memorizing opera phrases from the singers who worked the flash houses.
Learning Italian because it was beautiful and useless and everything Seven Dials wasn't.
Learning it because my mother had once said I was meant for more than this, and I'd never figured out if she meant more than poverty or more than survival or just more than her.
The knock came at exactly six o'clock.
Not loud.
Not aggressive.
Three taps, perfectly spaced, the kind of knock that said I know you're listening and I can afford to be patient.
Thomas set down his tea.

I stood, brushing wrinkles from my dress—useless gesture; the dress was three years old and wrinkles were permanent—and tried to look like someone who had conversations with dangerous people regularly.
Thomas opened the door.
The man who entered wore money.
Not just expensive clothes, though his coat was definitely superfine and his boots had that mirror shine that required a valet.
He wore money the way other people wore skin, like it was so fundamental to his existence that removing it would leave him naked.
Wrong.
Everything about him wrong for Seven Dials, for dawn, for our shop.
His walking stick had a silver handle that would get him murdered three streets over.
His cravat was tied in some complicated arrangement I didn't have words for.
He looked at our room the way a naturalist might look at an interesting species of beetle.
"Mr.
Blackwood."
His voice was officer-class, the kind of accent that came from good schools and better breeding.
"Thank you for receiving me."
Thomas said nothing.
I watched him do the calculation—turn this man away and risk his displeasure, or let him stay and risk whatever he'd brought with him.
The man's gaze found me.
"And this must be your daughter."
I was still at my desk, ink on my fingers despite the washing, hair pinned with bent pins because new ones cost money.
I'd been working since midnight and looked it.
His eyes were grey-green.
Cold.
The color of Thames water in winter.
"She helps with the business," Thomas said carefully.
"I'm aware."
The man smiled, which somehow made him more dangerous.
"Miss Blackwood.
May I sit?"
I gestured to the chair across from my desk.
He sat, placed his walking stick across his knees with the precision of someone who'd never knocked anything over accidentally in his life.
"I have a proposition," he said.
"One that requires your particular talents."
I waited.
Thomas had taught me that—never speak first when someone's buying lies.
"There's a house party.
Kelmarsh Park in Northamptonshire.
Week-long affair.
The Duke of Kelmarsh is hosting twenty guests, all very exclusive, all very observed."
I knew about house parties the way I knew about peacocks—they existed, they were expensive, they had nothing to do with me.
"There will be a guest," he continued.
"An Italian contessa.
Contessa Oriana Castelfranco.
She's traveling from Venice with letters of introduction, aristocratic connections, fluent Italian."
I understood before he finished.
The way you understand when someone's about to hit you, that split-second awareness before impact.
"Unfortunately," he said, "the Contessa will not be attending."
The room was very quiet.
Outside, Seven Dials was waking—costermongers calling, someone singing badly, the constant background noise of people trying to survive another day.
"You want me to impersonate her."
"Very good, Miss Blackwood."
He sounded pleased, like I was a student who'd correctly identified a Latin conjugation.
"The Duke has something I need.
Documents in his private study.
They need to be retrieved carefully, without suspicion."
"I can't—" I started.
"You can forge anything."
He pulled papers from his coat, set them on my desk.
"Letters of introduction.
The Contessa's history.
A miniature portrait for reference—you do look rather alike.
And the address where Mrs.
Fielding will meet you.
She'll coach you in deportment, speech, all those aristocratic habits you'll need."
I looked at the papers.
At the miniature portrait lying face-up.
The Contessa was beautiful—dark hair like mine, similar bone structure, but her face had never counted exits or measured the weight of desperation.
"And if I'm caught?"
"You won't be."
"But if I am?"
His smile didn't change.
"Then you'll hang.
Along with your father.
I have enough evidence to ensure it."
Thomas's hand tightened on the doorframe.
White knuckles.
"You're blackmailing us," I said, because naming things was sometimes all you had.
"I'm offering employment.
Fifty pounds for the week.
More if you succeed."
Fifty pounds.
Enough to clear most of our debts.
Enough to breathe.
Enough to maybe, possibly, almost be safe.
But this wasn't forgery.
This was walking into a duke's house and playing aristocrat and stealing from someone who could have us both transported for the presumption.
"I need to think—"
"No."
He stood.
"You need to say yes.
Because your father is expected at Newgate this afternoon.
Unless you agree to my terms."
Everything stopped.
Thomas's face was empty.
That terrible calm he got when things were very, very bad.
"You're lying," I said.
"I rarely lie, Miss Blackwood."
He picked up his walking stick.
"It's so much easier to arrange reality.
You have twelve hours to prepare.
Mrs.
Fielding will begin your transformation tomorrow at noon.
One week from today, you'll travel to Kelmarsh Park.
You'll arrive as Contessa Oriana Castelfranco.
You'll retrieve my documents.
And you'll leave with your father's life intact and fifty pounds richer."
"And if I refuse?"
"You won't."
He paused at the door.
"Because you're curious.
About that world.
Those people.
That life you've spent your whole life forging but never living."
The bastard was right.
He left.
The door closed.
The room filled with grey light and the particular silence that came after disaster.
Thomas sat down heavily.
"It's a trap."
"Obviously."
"We should run."
"Where?"
I laughed, but it sounded wrong.
"You're fifty-three with bad knees.
I'm twenty-four with ink under my fingernails.
Between us we have forty pounds and enemies everywhere."
"We have each other."
"We have debts."
I picked up the miniature portrait.
Studied the Contessa's face—her serene expression, her casual wealth, her complete ignorance that somewhere in Seven Dials, a forger's daughter was about to steal her entire life.
"Your mother—" Thomas started.
"Don't."
But I was thinking about her anyway.
Catherine Blackwood, dead twelve years, who'd taught me to read with stolen books and desperate hope.
Who'd said I was meant for more and then died before explaining what more looked like.
I touched the papers on my desk.
Letters written in Italian.
The address for Mrs.
Fielding.
An entire life laid out like a forgery waiting to be completed.
"I'll do it," I said.
"Veri—"
"Not for the money.
Not even for you."
I looked at him.
"I'll do it because I want to know if I can.
If all these years of forging other people's lives means I can forge my own."
"That's not forging.
That's lying."
"What's the difference?"
He didn't answer.
Maybe there wasn't one.
Maybe the whole of Seven Dials was built on that question—survival or sin, necessity or choice, who you had to be versus who you chose to become.
Thomas stood.
Crossed to me.
Put his forger's hands on my shoulders.
"She would be proud."
"She would be horrified."
"Both can be true."
He kissed my forehead and left me alone with a dead woman's life in my hands and my future balanced on the edge of a lie.
I looked in the window glass.
Tried to see myself in silk instead of threadbare cotton.
In jewels instead of bent pins.
In that world of house parties and dukes where fifty pounds was pocket money.
"Mi chiamo Contessa Oriana Castelfranco," I whispered.
The accent was still terrible.
The words felt like forgery.
Like truth.
Like the best lie I'd ever told.
Outside, Seven Dials woke fully.
The pickpockets and costermongers, the girls who sold what they had to because selling anything else required capital.
The world I'd known all my life.
The world I was about to leave—temporarily, dangerously, possibly fatally.
I touched the portrait one last time.
The Contessa stared back, serene and distant and completely unaware that in seven days, I would become her.
Or die trying.
The letter had been sitting on the kitchen table since half past five that morning, and I had not looked at it again because I did not need to.
I knew the shape of the thing.
Stainforth's hand was the sort of hand that signed leases and pew rents and letters to the parish, slanted just enough to suggest education, never enough to suggest haste.
He wished to discuss the terms.
He would call upon me this afternoon, if convenient.
Everything about the letter was civil, and every civil word in it was a boot set down an inch closer to my door.
Six weeks to the quarter.
Forty-two days.
I had done that arithmetic on the back of a bill of lading the night before, and the numbers had not changed overnight, because numbers did not.
I had seven pounds nine shillings in the cash box and another eleven owed me by the Highflyer and the Regulator between them, neither of which paid before the month's end.
The rent, when it came due, would be forty.
I knew what I could squeeze from the taproom in the next forty-two days, and I knew what I could not.
What I could not was forty pounds.
My hands were on the table.
The right one still had the split on the index finger from yesterday's cask, a clean cut that had scabbed overnight and would open again the first time I lifted anything heavier than a tray.
I put the kettle on.
The ledger was where I had left it.
I did not open it.
There was nothing in the ledger that would not be in the ledger this afternoon, and whatever Stainforth wanted to see, he would not see it on my face first.
I did the morning faster than the morning needed.
I swept the taproom and wiped the bar and took the cellar stairs two at a time to check the tap on the October ale, which did not need checking.
I wiped the brass on the coaching clock.
I put fresh sand in the spittoons.
None of it was for him.
All of it was for him.
Nan came down at seven and took one look at me and said nothing, which was one of the kindnesses I had come to rely on in her.
She tied her apron and went to the kitchen.
I heard her begin the bread.
His carriage was on the road before ten.
I heard it at the bend by the elms, the particular check of a coachman who knew a yard and was slowing for it, and I was at the door before the wheels stopped.
Stainforth climbed down without hurry.

His coat was the colour of wet slate and cut by a man who had been paid not to cut it like anyone else's, and the wool of it, even from the step, carried the smell of good wool, which is to say of money kept dry.
"Miss Dale."
"Mr Stainforth."
"How good of you to receive me.
I trust Mrs Dale is well?
Your aunt, I should say.
Forgive me."
"She is well.
Thank you."
"And the road?
I found it better than last month.
They have mended the stretch by the mill."
"So I am told."
He drew off his gloves, finger by finger, and folded them against his palm, and held them in one hand for the rest of the conversation, as if to have put them down would have conceded something.
I stood in my own doorway and did not invite him past it, and he did not ask.
He stood on the step and looked past me into the taproom with an expression of mild, pleasant interest, which is the expression a man wears when he is counting.
"A raw morning."
"Yes."
"I so rarely have the chance to see the place properly, Miss Dale.
Would you indulge me?"
It was not a request.
It was the shape of a request laid over something else, and we both knew which shape was underneath.
I stepped back from the door.
"As you like."
He walked the taproom floor first.
He did not stride; he moved at the pace of a man who had the afternoon.
He paused at the bar rail and set his hand flat on it, as though testing the grain, and then he ran his thumb along the inside edge where the wood had worn silky from twenty years of elbows.
He looked up at the beams.
He looked at the hearth.

He looked at the window latch and tried it with two fingers, and it held, because I had oiled the latches myself in September, and then he tried it again, because a latch that held once might not hold twice.
"Well kept."
"Thank you."
"Your mother kept it so."
"She did."
"And you after her.
Remarkable."
I did not answer that.

My mother used to say that a woman who argued with a compliment was a woman who did not yet know what it had cost her, and I had learned that lesson at thirteen across a counter full of mutton, watching her tell a butcher his price was fair and then pay him exactly what she had meant to pay.
Give them the number, she had said later, not the explanation.
The explanation is what they are fishing for.
He moved toward the cellar door.
"May I?"
"The step's worn.
Mind your foot."
He opened the door and stood a moment at the head of the stair, and then he bent and ran his thumb along the hinge.
Not the handle.
The hinge.
He tested the pin with his nail.
He did this as naturally as a man checks his own watch.
"Drainage?"
"To the soakaway at the back.
It was cut in '03.
It takes what we put in it."
"In wet years?"
"In wet years also."
"And your supplier for the October is still Howland's?"
"It is."
"A good house."
"Yes."
"You take, what, two firkins a week through this season?"
"Three, when the London mails are running.
Two otherwise."
"And the rooms?
You let, on average?"
"Twelve a night through autumn.
Fourteen on a Saturday."
He nodded at each answer, small and courteous, the way a clerk nods at figures he is not writing down because he will remember them without.
He did not ask me anything he did not already half know.
He was not learning the inn.
He was confirming it.
I gave him the numbers and not the explanation, and when he paused as though to leave room for the explanation, I let the room stay empty.
We went out into the yard.
The yard was the yard.
The muck had frozen in ridges overnight where Jem had not yet raked it, and the light was thin and grey and did not flatter anything.
Stainforth walked the length of the stabling without speaking, which was its own kind of speech.
At the fence where the paddock met the road he stopped.
The post at the corner had shifted in last winter's frost and had been leaning since, and the top rail had worked its peg loose in August, and I had meant, and meant, and meant.
He put his hand on the post.
He did not push it.
He only rested his hand against it, as a man rests his hand against a piece of furniture in a house he is considering taking.
"An inn of this size," he said, and left the sentence there, in the cold, for me to pick up.
I did not pick it up.
"You were saying, Mr Stainforth."
"Only that an inn of this size might benefit from a steadier hand on certain matters.
The outbuildings.
The yard.
Small things.
A woman alone cannot be expected to mind every post and rail."
"The post will be set by Sunday."
"I do not doubt it."
"Then we are agreed."
He smiled, briefly, without warmth and without coldness.
It was the smile of a man who had been smiled at a great deal in his life and had learned the use of it.
"Miss Dale.
I think very well of you.
I hope you know that.
I think very well of what your mother built here, and of what you have kept.
I came today only to speak of the lease, and of what might be best for the parish, which is a thing I must consider whether I wish to or not."
"The lease is in good standing."
"It is."
"The rent will be paid at quarter day."
"I have every confidence."
He said this and he meant it, and that was the worst of it.
He did have every confidence.
He had every confidence because he had already worked out what forty pounds did to seven pounds nine, and he had the patience of a man who did not need to win the conversation today.
He only needed to have had it.
I heard myself say, "You will have your rent, sir.
And the post will be straight.
Was there anything else?"
It came out sharper than I had meant.
A quarter of an inch sharper.
I watched him absorb it without a flinch, the way a good wall absorbs a knock, and I knew at once that I had given him more than he had given me.
"Nothing else.
Thank you for your time.
The inn is very well kept, Miss Dale.
Truly."
He drew his gloves back on, finger by finger, and climbed into his carriage.
I stood in the yard until the wheels turned at the elms, and then I stood a moment longer, because I did not trust my hands yet to do anything small.
My jaw ached.
I had been holding it.

I unclenched it, and the back of my neck went hot, and I walked to the pump and put my wrist under the water until the cut on my finger stung and the stinging gave me something to think about that was not him.
Then I went upstairs.
Bridget's door was open the width of a hand, which was how she left it when she had seen something from her window and wished to be found.
The good china was out.
It was always out now, and had been since the day she decided, somewhere in her seventieth year, that she was finished saving crockery for a funeral she had already attended in her head.

The room smelled of lavender and of tea and of the particular mustiness of wool blankets that have been folded and unfolded for fifty years, and I sat down in the chair across from her, and my shoulders dropped, and I did not know I had done it until she poured.
"Drink it while it's hot, child."
"Yes."
She did not ask.
She had seen the carriage.
She had seen me in the yard.
She had seen Stainforth put his hand on the fence post, which I had not known she could see from her window, and which she had seen anyway, because Bridget saw what she meant to see.
She drank.
She set her cup down with both hands, because her hands were not what they had been.
"Greville," she said.
"What about him?"
"Before Stainforth.
Before you were born, nearly.
The last landlord but one.
He wanted your mother to double the stabling.
Said the coaching trade would only grow, said she was throwing money away by not building.
He came with plans.
He had a man of his own who would do it for a price he called fair."
"And she refused."
"She refused.
The yard wouldn't take it, she said.
The drainage would foul by Michaelmas and the horses would founder by Christmas, and then where would he be with his doubled stabling.
She was right.
She was almost always right about the ground under her feet."
"Well, then."
"Well, then.
Greville went away and he came back.
He came back twice a year for four years, and each time she gave him the same answer in the same words, and each time he went away thinking he had nearly had her."
"And?"
"And one day he stopped coming, because he had died, and his son had no taste for it, and that was that.
Your mother buried three landlords, child.
She held on to this place through every one of them."
"Then I will do the same."
Bridget looked at me.
She had a way of looking that was not sharp, exactly, but that arrived at you from further off than you had expected, as though she had been considering you from the other side of her life.
"Holding on and holding back are not the same thing, Dinah."
I reached for the teapot.
"Shall I warm yours?"
"You shall not.
I have not finished it."
"Then I shall warm mine."
I poured.
My hand was steady, which was a small grace I granted myself.

The tea went into the cup and the steam went up, and Bridget watched me do it, and said nothing further, because she had said what she had come upstairs to say, and whether I took it in was not her afternoon's business.
"The post wants setting before Sunday," I said.
"I told him Sunday."
"Then I expect you will set it."
"I will."
I drank the tea.

I kissed her on the top of her head, where the hair was very fine and very white, and I went down the stairs and I did not think about what she had said, because there was no room for it in the afternoon, and the afternoon was what I had.
By nine the taproom had emptied.

By ten the fire was banked and the bolt was in my hand at the front door, and my feet hurt in the particular way that meant I had been on them since before light, and I was counting stairs to my bed when the knock came.
Two knocks.
Measured.
Not loud.
I drew the bolt and opened the door the breadth of my shoulder.
A man.
Tall.
His hat was in his hand, which was the first thing I noticed, because the men who did not take off their hats were the men I did not let past the threshold.
A dog sat at his heel, long-legged and grey-brindled, with a face like a creature that had been given a job and was not sure of its hours.
His boots were good leather worn past good, the kind of boots that had been bought in a shop once and had walked out of their price.
"Ma'am.
I'm looking for work, or a bed, or both, if you can spare either."
His voice was low and careful, pitched to a tired woman at a late door.
"The inn is shut."
"Yes, ma'am."
"The stable is dry.
There's clean straw in the end stall, and water at the pump.
I'll not take a penny from you and I'll not give you a penny, and we'll talk in the morning about the rest."
"Thank you."
"The dog stays with you."
"He would anyway."
I looked at him for another half a breath.
He was not drunk.
He was not dangerous in any way I could read at a door at ten o'clock at night, and I had learned to read a door at ten o'clock at night by the time I was fifteen.
He was tired to the bone.
So was I.
It could wait.
"Round the side.
Jem will be in the loft.
Don't wake him."
"No, ma'am."
He put his hat back on and stepped off the flag, and the dog rose with him and went.
I shot the bolt.
I went through to the kitchen and damped the range for the night and, because I did every night, looked out through the window at the yard to make sure the yard was as I had left it.
It was not.
He was crouched at the fence.
The crooked post.

He had the dog sitting three paces off, patient as a churchwarden, and he was working the base of the post with his hands, clearing the frozen muck from round it with the side of his boot, and then he lifted.

He lifted the post clean out of the hole, set it aside, and knelt, and felt the hole with his fingers for what was in it, and took a stone from the pile by the trough and bedded it under where the post would go.
He set the post back.

He pushed it true with his shoulder, and held it, and kicked earth round its foot, and tamped the earth with his heel, and then with his hand on the top of the post he rocked it to see if it would rock, and it did not.
I watched his hands.
Not his face.
Not his shoulders.
His hands, bare in the cold, doing the thing I had told Stainforth would be done by Sunday, on a Tuesday night, by a stranger who had not been asked.
He moved to the top rail next, and found the loose peg, and worked it in with the heel of his hand.
I turned from the window.
I went up the stairs to my bed.
The letter sat on the kitchen table where I had left it last night, unopened, beside the salt.
I had promised myself I would not let it keep me from sleeping, and I had kept that promise by not reading it.
Which was, I understood now, its own kind of sleeplessness.
I cut the seal with the edge of my thumbnail.
Stainforth's hand was what it always was: small, even, entirely without flourish.
A gentleman who does not waste ink on a leaseholder.
He would call today, between the hours of ten and noon, upon a matter concerning the renewal.
He remained my obedient servant.
I read it twice.
Then I put it down next to the ledger, smoothed it flat under my palm, and went to find my apron.
"Is that the letter?"
Nan said from the doorway.
"It is."
"And?"
"He'll be here before noon."
I tied the apron strings twice at the back, the way my grandmother had done, because a single knot worked itself loose by dinner.
"Sweep the taproom proper.
Not the quick sweep.
The proper one."
"Yes, ma'am."
"And leave the ledger where it is."
Nan looked at the ledger on the table and then at me, and then she went to fetch the broom without saying anything, which was one of the many reasons I had hired her.
I checked the fire.
I checked the bread.
I put the kettle on because the kettle being on was what a working kitchen looked like, and I wanted him to walk into a working kitchen.
I did not change my dress.
Changing my dress for Phineas Stainforth would have been a concession, and I did not mean to concede anything before he had even climbed out of his gig.
--- He arrived at a quarter past ten.
The gig was dark green, very clean, and drawn by a bay that had been brushed that morning.
A single groom held the reins, a young man I did not know, who looked at the front of the inn with the mild contempt of a servant borrowed for the day.
Stainforth's boots struck the flagstones of the yard in that measured way I remembered from the two previous occasions he had called.
My grandmother used to say you could tell a landlord by how he entered a yard, and that the worst ones entered as though they already owned the flagstones.
My grandmother had received his father, once, standing in this same doorway with her hands on her apron, and had afterwards described him, in the kitchen, as a man who counted his own buttons.
I had carried this forward as a practical instruction: these are men who count.
Be ready to be counted.
"Miss Dale."
"Mr Stainforth.
You had good weather for the drive."
"I did.
A clear morning is a pleasant thing at this season."
He did not take off his hat until he was inside the hall, and then he set it on the side table with the brim turned up, the way a man does who expects to pick it up again quite soon.
The coat was good wool, very dark, cut two seasons ago but cut well.
"I hope I have not called at an inconvenient hour."
"You named the hour, sir."
"So I did."
The faintest movement at the side of his mouth.
"Forgive me.
One falls into civilities."
"Will you take tea?"
"Thank you, no.
I mean to be brief."
He had not come to be brief.
Men who mean to be brief do not arrive with a letter the night before.
"Then perhaps you will tell me how I may be of service."
"I had hoped, if the morning allows it, to walk through the premises.
It has been some time since I saw the inn properly, and a landlord who does not see his property is an inattentive landlord."
He said this with the air of a man apologising for his diligence.
"A quarter of an hour, no more."
"Of course."
I had known he would ask.
I had known, and still the word *premises* hit me somewhere under the ribs.
I put my hands together at my waist so that he could not see me close them.
"Shall we begin with the taproom?"
--- He walked through my inn as though he were reading it.

The taproom first, where he stopped at the near end and looked at the beams, and then at the hearth, and then at the long bench under the window, and did not say anything for long enough that I understood he wished me to hear him not saying anything.
He laid two fingers briefly on the edge of a table.
He moved on.
"The cellar stair is through here, I believe."
"Yes."
He went down the cellar stair ahead of me, which no guest had ever done, and which I permitted because the alternative was to stand alone at the top of the stair while he went down.
He paused at the foot.
He put his hand on the cellar door's hinge, the lower one, the one that sticks in damp weather and that Jem has been meaning to see to since Michaelmas.
He moved the door a quarter inch on the hinge.
He let it go.
"A little stiff."
"It wants oil.
Jem will see to it this week."
"Ah.
Your ostler."
He considered the door a moment longer, as though the door might have more to tell him.
"He is a capable man, I understand."
"He is."
"Missing an arm."
"The lower part of one."
"Remarkable, what a determined fellow can do."
"Yes."
He went up the stair before me.

I had never known a man not to stand back at a stair and let a woman pass; it was the sort of thing Stainforth would never fail at on a morning call, and the sort of thing he would permit himself to forget inside a property he considered, in the abstract, already his.
At the first-floor landing he spoke without turning round.
"Twenty rooms, I think."
"Twenty, yes."
"And your occupancy this past quarter?"
"Sixteen on average.
Eighteen through the autumn fair.
Twelve in the week after Christmas."
"You have the figures to hand."
"I have them in the ledger on the kitchen table.
You are welcome to see them."
"I do not doubt you, Miss Dale."
He smiled without moving the rest of his face.
"I merely remark upon your command of them."
We did not go into any of the bedchambers.
He glanced along the passage, noted the door at the end, and turned back toward the stair.

A man who already knows what is inside a room does not need to open it; a man who wishes the woman beside him to feel that her rooms are his to open on another occasion does not need to open it either.
I could not tell which man he was being.
It did not, in the event, matter.
The passage to the stable yard was the last of it.
He paused at the door into the yard, hand on the frame, and looked out at the cobbles and the stalls and the fence along the kitchen-garden wall.
Jem was at the far end with a horse; he did not look up.
A good ostler knows when not to look up.
"The post is leaning," Stainforth said.
"Yes."
He stepped out into the yard, crossed to the crooked post, and set two fingers against the top of it.
The post moved a quarter inch toward him.
He let it go.
"A small matter."
"Jem means to reset it this week."
"Jem means to do a great deal, it seems."
*And a man in a very good coat means to count my hinges before lunch,* I thought, and I did not say it.
I thought also that my hands were cold, which is the body's way of reminding a woman that she is working harder than she looks.
He turned from the post and faced me across two yards of cobble.
"Miss Dale, I shall be plain."
"Please."
"The lease comes up at the Lady Day quarter.
I have been, as you know, content to leave matters as they stand for some years, out of a proper respect for your late mother.
But I am a trustee as well as a landlord, and the parish takes an interest in a house of this size upon the London road."
"The parish has made no complaint."
"No.
Not yet."
He did not raise his voice.
He had no reason to.
"There is, however, a question of succession.
A house at this crossroads will outlive any one tenant.
It is reasonable for the parish to ask where it will stand in ten years, in twenty.
A lease held in a single pair of hands, without settlement or successor named, is a matter the vestry will wish to consider."
"The lease is in my name, Mr Stainforth.
It was in my mother's before me."
"Indeed.
And at renewal the terms may be reviewed.
I have a nephew, a steady young man of good habits, who has expressed an interest in a house of business such as this.
I mention it to you in confidence, as the matter will want time."
"How much time."
"The quarter.
Perhaps a little beyond.
I should not wish you to be hurried."
"I am obliged for the consideration."
"You understand, I trust, that I raise this as a kindness.
A woman in your position may find a suitable arrangement in the meanwhile.
Many do."
"Many do."
He inclined his head half an inch.
He had what he came for, which was the knowledge that I now knew what he had.
He had lost nothing.
I had held every inch of ground I stood on, which was not the same as gaining any.
"I shall write again before the quarter."
"I shall look for the letter."
He crossed back to the passage, through the hall, to the front step.
His hat went on in the doorway.
The groom brought the gig forward without being called; good servants have the instincts of well-trained dogs.
"Good morning, Miss Dale."
"Good morning, Mr Stainforth."
The gig turned in the yard and went out under the arch, and the sound of the wheels on the road carried clearly for longer than it ought to have done.
I stood on the flagstones a moment.
Then I went inside, because standing on the flagstones was what he would have wanted me to do, and I would not give him that either.

--- The stair up to Bridget's rooms has eleven treads, and the third from the top is warped, and I have been climbing it long enough that my foot knows to lift a half-inch higher on that step without my telling it to.
She did not ask me what had happened.
She was sitting where she sat every morning, in the chair by the window that looked down into the yard, and the tray was already set.
"Sit."
"Aunt."
"Sit down, child.
The tea is poured."
The good china.

Always the good china, because Bridget had decided in 1802 that she would not die with unused china in the cupboard, and she had not yet died, and the china was by now a little chipped at the rim, because use wears things.
She handed me the cup with hands that were knotted at every joint and steady on the handle.
"Green gig," she said.
"Yes."
"Same groom as last time?"
"A new one."
"Hm."
She sipped.
"Well.
He's bought a second servant since we saw him last.
Good.
It means he's borrowing."
"Or that the first one left him."
"Or that."
She looked at me over the rim of her cup.
Her accent was gentler than it had been when I was small, but it rose at the edges when she was amused.
"Did he touch the hinge?"
"He did."
"And the post?"
"And the post."
"Of course he did."
She set her cup down.
"His father used to run a finger along the top of the mantelpiece.
For the dust, do you see.
I watched him do it once and I thought, well, here is a man who has decided to be disappointed before he has sat down.
This one is the same man with better manners."
"He was civil."
"They are always civil.
Civility is how they do it."
She reached and took my hand, briefly, and let it go.
"Drink your tea, Dinah.
You look as though you haven't sat down since Tuesday."
"I haven't."
"Well, sit now."
I drank.
The tea was very hot, and I had not realised until I tasted it how badly I had wanted something hot.
Bridget watched the yard through the window, because that was what she did, and did not watch me, because that was also what she did.
"He named a successor," I said.
"Did he?"
"A nephew."
"Of course a nephew."
"He gave me the quarter."
"That is generous of him, in his own accounting."
She did not look away from the window.
"And what will you do?"
"I will keep the books clean and the rooms full and give him no ground he can stand on at the vestry."
"Yes.
That is what you will do during the day."
I set the cup down.
"Don't, Aunt."
"Dinah."
"Please."
She turned her head then, and she looked at me with the particular attention of a woman who has earned, at seventy-two, the right not to apologise for what she is about to say.
"Your mother held this inn with both hands for fourteen years, and I loved her, and I watched her.
And I will tell you what I have been waiting these two years to tell you, because you are old enough now to hear it and because that man has just driven out of the yard.
There is a difference between holding on and holding back, child.
Your mother did not know it.
I would like you to know it before it costs you what it cost her."
The kitchen clock below us struck the half.
I heard it through the floor.
"I am holding on to the inn," I said.
"I know you are."
"That is not the same."
"I know it isn't."
She did not press.
She never pressed.
She had said the thing, and she would let the thing sit where it was.
"Finish your tea."
I finished my tea.
I set the cup on the tray, and I stood, and I smoothed my apron over my skirt because my hands wanted something to do.
"I have the accounts to go over before supper."
"Then go and do them."
"Aunt."
"Go, Dinah.
I have sewing."
She did not have sewing.
She had the window and the yard and whatever she had been thinking before I came up.

I kissed the top of her head, which smelled of the lavender water she had used since I was a child, and I went down the stair, and on the third step from the top my foot lifted, and I felt the line she had said move inside me like a coin dropped into a pocket I had meant to keep empty.
I did not take it out to look at.
I left it where it had fallen, and I went back down to the work.
--- The afternoon went.
Nan tended the bar.
Jem was in the yard with a pair of post-horses from a gentleman bound for Baldock.
The weather turned early; a thin cold rain came on by four, and I had the lamps lit before five because the kitchen windows had gone slate-coloured and there was no use pretending otherwise.
I did the accounts.
I settled the butcher.
I ate standing up.
--- The knock came at the kitchen door, not at the front.
It was past eight.

I had the lantern in my hand because I had been on my way to the pantry for onions, and when I opened the door the lantern lit him before anything else did: a tall man on the step, a long dark coat that had seen rain before this rain, boots that had been good once and were nearly through at the toe, and at his heel a lean grey dog that kept its head low and its eyes on me without moving any other part of itself.
"Ma'am."
"Yes."
"I'm looking for work, if there's any, and a place out of the rain for the night.
I can pay for the night if I cannot work for it."
His voice was quiet and not at all servile.
He did not step closer.
He did not pull off his hat until he had finished the sentence, which was a small thing, and I noticed it the way I notice small things.
I was very tired.
There had been a man in a good coat in my yard this morning, and a line in Bridget's parlour that I had not yet taken out of my pocket, and I did not want, tonight, to sit down with another question.
"The stable's warm," I said.
"There's clean straw at the back, past the bay mare.
You can have it until morning.
I'll not promise work until I've seen you in daylight."
"That's fair."
"There's bread on the sill of the kitchen window in half an hour.
Take it or don't."
"Thank you, ma'am."
He said a word then that might have been his name, offered flat and short the way a man offers a coin he is not sure you will accept, and I did not repeat it, and I did not ask him to.
The dog shifted its weight against his leg.
The rain ran off the brim of his hat onto the step.
Vagrants in this weather were as regular as the almanac; my mother used to say you could set your clock by the turn of the year and the knock at the door.
"The stable's through the passage.
The second door on the left opens into the yard."
"I'll find it."
He touched the brim of his hat, and he turned, and the dog turned with him as though they had agreed on it long before either of them reached the step.
I shut the door.
I leaned my forehead a moment against the wood, because there was no one in the kitchen to see me do it, and then I went and got my onions.
--- I was paring the onions at the kitchen window when I saw him again.
The window looked down the length of the yard toward the stable.
The rain had thinned to a mist.
He had set the dog in the doorway of the stable with a folded coat under it, and he had come back out into the yard because something had caught his eye on the way in.
He was at the cellar door, which stood in the lee of the kitchen wall.

He had taken the hinge between his fingers, the lower one, the one Stainforth had moved that morning, and he was working it up and down with a patience that had nothing to do with showing anyone anything.
After a minute he stepped back, went into the stable, came out with a small tin, and oiled the hinge, and worked it again, and shut the door, and opened it, and shut it.
It sat true.
Then he crossed to the crooked post at the corner of the kitchen-garden wall.
He stood and looked at it a moment.
He set his shoulder against it, and he shifted his weight, and he moved the post upright in its footing and packed the stones in around the base with his boot.
He did not make a performance of it.
He did not look toward the house.
I stood at the window with the knife in my hand and the onion half pared on the board, and I looked at his hands.
They were working hands, dark with rain and whatever the hinge had left on them, steady at the post, steady at the stones.
He set the last stone with his palm.
I turned back to the onion, and I cut it, and I set the pieces in the bowl.

The letter was on the kitchen table where I had left it last night, and the seal was still unbroken, and the cup of tea I had set beside it to give myself courage had gone cold and scummed over, which served me right.
I broke the seal.
Stainforth wrote as he spoke.
Three sentences, the middle one doing the work.
He would call at the White Hound today, between the hours of eleven and one, to discuss matters pertaining to the lease and to the inn's continued accommodation of irregular persons.
He hoped I would make myself available.
He signed himself as always.
I read it twice.
The second time was to see whether I had invented the word *irregular*, because it was the sort of word I would have invented for him, and he had saved me the trouble.
"Is that him, then?"
Nan said, coming through with the ashes in a pan.
"That's him."
"What time?"
"Any time that suits him."
"Of course."
She tipped the ashes out.
"I'll do the taproom first.
You'll want it swept."
"I'll want the ledger on the table," I said.
"Open to the quarter.
He can look at it or not, as he chooses."
Nan nodded once and went back out.
She had been at the inn seven years and did not waste words when she understood a situation, which was nearly always.

I set the letter face down beside the ledger, put the kettle back on, and went to find a clean apron because the one I had on had a smear of soot at the hip from the range, and I would not receive Stainforth with a smear at the hip.
I did not examine the business of the apron.
I tied it and went to look at the taproom.
The taproom was already in order.
Nan had been at it before breakfast.

I straightened a settle that did not need straightening and checked the state of the window-glass, and looked at the room as Stainforth would look at it — not as a traveller, but as a man measuring rent.
The light was good.
The boards were clean.
The fire was laid but not lit, because it was not cold enough yet to justify the wood.
I laid it anyway.
It made the room look occupied.
Back in the kitchen I opened the ledger to Michaelmas and set it square on the table.
I pushed the letter to one side and set the inkwell at the top of the page.
If he wanted to see my numbers, he would see them.
If he wanted to comment on them, I would let him, and I would not explain.
The gig came through the yard gate a little before noon.
One horse, a neat bay.
A single groom, who did not dismount.
Stainforth handed down his gloves to the groom and stepped across the flagstones to the main door, and the first crunch of his boots carried through the open kitchen window.
I went to receive him at the door.
"Miss Dale."
"Mr Stainforth.
Good day to you."
"Good day.
A fine dry one, for the season."
"It is.
Will you come through?
The taproom is warmer than the hall."
"Thank you."
His coat was a very good wool, close-fitted, the cuffs showing no wear.
The hat he handed me was new within the year.

I took it and set it on the hook by the door where my grandmother had set the hats of his father, when his father had called, which his father had done twice a year for the last ten years of his life.
"I trust your aunt is well," Stainforth said.
"Well enough.
Thank you."
"And your people."
"All in good health."
"Excellent."
Two exchanges and we had arrived at the taproom.
He looked at the laid fire and did not remark on it.
He set his stick against the settle.
"I shan't detain you long, Miss Dale.
I should like to walk through the premises, if I may.
A matter of the lease renewal, which, as you are aware, falls at Lady Day."
"Of course."
"Shall we begin here, then."
He began, though the *shall we* was the shape of the thing and not the substance of it.
He moved along the wall to the fireplace and set his hand on the lintel beam.
He did not press.
He set the hand there, took it away, looked at his fingers as though for dust, and found none.
"A good old beam."
"It is."
"Oak, I should think."
"Oak.
My grandmother's time."
"Quite."
He went next to the cellar door.
I went with him because leaving him to the cellar alone was not to be thought of.
He bent at the latch and set a finger against the lower hinge.
"This sticks in damp weather, I imagine."
"In wet weather.
Jem sees to it."
"Jem is your ostler."
"He is."
"A useful man, I've no doubt."
"He is."
He straightened.
He did not open the cellar door.
It was not the cellar he had come to see; it was the hinge, which he had now registered, and he was satisfied.
We went up the stair to the first-floor landing.
He touched the newel post at the turn.
He did not touch the rail.
"How many rooms, Miss Dale."
"Twenty.
Sixteen chambered at present, the four small ones at the back shut up since August."
"Shut up for what reason."
"I hadn't call to open them.
Trade has been steady but not full."
"Steady but not full."
He repeated the phrase as though it might be a fact or might be an opinion, and he had not yet decided.
"And the takings for the quarter?"
"On the table in the kitchen, open to the page, if you wish to see them."
"I shall, presently.
And your custom — coaches as before?"
"The Edinburgh mail, the Baldock, the York through-coach three days the week.
Private traffic as it comes."
"And the parish — no complaints that have come to you."
"None that have come to me."

"I ask," he said, and here was the register, the civil measured one I had been waiting for, "because there has been some remark in vestry about the number of discharged men who have taken shelter here in recent months.
I do not raise it as an accusation.
Merely as a concern for the parish, which you will understand I am obliged to register."
"They take bread in the kitchen and move on, Mr Stainforth.
They sleep in the stable when the stable is empty of horses and not when it isn't.
I have not had a theft or a disturbance in nine months."
"I am gratified to hear it."
"I should hope so."
He looked at me, briefly, and then he went on along the landing, and I went with him.

It occurred to me, with the dry clarity that comes when a person has not quite enough sleep and far too much to lose, that I was walking through my own house behind a man in a very good coat who was counting my hinges.
The absurdity was exact.
It did not make him less dangerous.
It made him more tiresome.
We went out by the back passage to the stable yard.
Jem was not in the yard.
He was in the far stall with the roan mare and had the sense not to come out.
Stainforth stopped at the fence post by the water trough.
The one that had come loose in August, that Jem had been meaning to reset before the frost, and which I had been meaning to remind him about and had not.
He did not touch it with his hand.
He set the end of his stick against it and tested the give.
"This wants reseating."
"It does."
"Before winter, I should think."
"Before winter, yes."
"Miss Dale."
He turned to me with the stick still resting against the post.
"I shall be plain with you, because I believe plainness is a kindness.
The lease falls at Lady Day.
I have, as you know, discretion at renewal.
I have held that discretion in your favour for four years, on the strength of your mother's tenancy and in regard for the difficulty of your position.
I do not propose to continue to hold it indefinitely."
"No."
"There is a view within my family that the lease on a coaching inn of this standing is better held by a man.
I do not offer this view as my own preference.
I offer it as a fact of the circumstances in which we find ourselves.

A successor of my choosing — a younger man, a man of the family — would take the lease on terms favourable to the parish and to the establishment, and would look to make certain improvements which the present tenancy has not found it convenient to undertake."
"I see."
"I say this now so that you have the quarter before you to consider your position.
I do not require an answer today."
"I shouldn't have given you one today."
"No.
I did not suppose you would."
He took the stick away from the post.
The post did not move; the stick did.
"I shall look at the ledger, if I may, before I go."
"Of course."
He looked at the ledger for eleven minutes.
I counted the minutes on the kitchen clock because I had nothing else to do with them, and because counting was the thing my mother had taught me to do when I wanted to throw something.
He turned three pages.
He did not ask a single question.
He closed the ledger and rested his hand on the cover as though he had read a letter from a friend.
"Your accounts are admirably kept, Miss Dale."
"Thank you."
"I shall write again before Lady Day."
"I shall expect it."
He took his hat from the hook.
He set it, adjusted the brim, and inclined his head.
"Good day to you."
"Good day, Mr Stainforth."
The gig went out of the yard the way it had come in.

I stood in the kitchen doorway until the crunch of the wheels had gone off down the lane, and then I went back inside and picked up the ledger, and set it on the shelf above the range where it lived when it was not in use, and then I picked it up again and set it back on the table, open to the page, because I did not want it out of sight.
Then I went up the stairs to Bridget.
The third stair from the top warped in November and creaked when you trod it square.
I trod it square.
I did not want to go up softly.
I wanted her to hear me coming.
"Come in, child," she said, before I had knocked.
Her window gave on to the yard.
She had been at it since breakfast; she had seen the gig come and the gig go, and she did not need to be told what had passed between.
The teapot was already on the tray — the good china, the blue-and-white with the chipped saucer she would not throw out — and she was pouring.
"Sit yourself down."
"Bridget."
"Sit."
I sat.
She handed me the cup.
Her hands were bad with the damp; the pour was careful and slow, and she did not apologise for it and I did not offer to take the pot.
"He stayed the hour, then."
"A little less."
"Did he touch the cellar hinge."
"He touched the cellar hinge."
"He touched it for his father, too."
She sat back in her chair, the one by the window with the worn patch on the arm where her right hand lived.
"His father was a worse man and a better-mannered one.
Drink your tea."
I drank.
"Lady Day?"
"Lady Day."
"And a man of the family waiting in the wings."
"So he tells me."
"He would tell you.
He likes a timetable.
Gives him the pleasure of watching the clock."
"Bridget."
"I'm not making a speech, girl.
Drink your tea."
I drank my tea.

The cup was hot through the china and I held it with both hands, and for a moment I was not the woman who had walked through her own inn behind Phineas Stainforth; I was a girl of eleven at this same table, and Bridget had poured then, too, and had not made a speech then either.
"Your mother," she said.
"Yes."
"Your mother held on to this place through worse than this man and his nephew.
She held on with both hands and both feet and her teeth for good measure."
She took a sip.
"And there is a thing I should have told her forty years ago and never did, and I will tell you now because you are sitting in front of me and she is not."
"Bridget."
"Holding on and holding back are not the same thing, Dinah.
Your mother never learned the difference.
It is not a thing you inherit.
It is a thing you choose.
And you have been choosing the one when you thought you were choosing the other for rather a long while now."
I set the cup in the saucer.
The chipped one.
The chip was at the four-o'clock position and I had known it since I was seven.
"I'll think on it," I said.
"You will not," she said, not unkindly.
"You'll set it aside and do the evening service.
But the thought will sit where I've put it, and that's enough for one afternoon."
"I've a great deal to do."
"I know you have."
I stood.
I took the cup with me to the tray and set it down, and I took her empty one and set it beside mine, and I did not kiss her forehead because we did not do that, and she did not ask me to.
"Send Nan up later," she said.
"I'll want a bit of supper."
"I'll send her."
The third stair creaked going down as it had going up.
I had thought about asking Jem to plane it, once, and had not, because the creak was useful; it told me when a guest was coming down at an hour they had no business on the stairs.
In the kitchen I put the kettle on again and did the next thing.
I wrote out the orders for the brewer.
I spoke to Nan about the two chambermaids and about the linen that wanted turning.
I did not set the ledger back on the shelf.
I left it on the table, open, because the table was where it lived now, and I was not going to shift it to suit a man who had gone.
The afternoon went the way afternoons go.
The weather thinned.

By four the light had begun to go blue at the edges, and by five Nan had lit the lamps at the taproom end, and a thin rain came on with a colder wind behind it and Jem was in and out of the yard with the horses for the Baldock coach, which was late as the Baldock coach usually was.
I ate standing at the range and did not remember, afterward, what I had eaten.
The knock came at the kitchen door a little after eight.
Not the main door.
Not the taproom.
The kitchen door, which opens on the yard, and which is the door a man uses when he has worked out that the main door will turn him away.
I took the lantern from its hook and opened the door on the chain, and then, because of what I saw, I took the chain off and opened it the rest.
A man stood in the rain.
Tall.
A long dark coat, soaked at the shoulders, and boots that had been good boots and were now walked past pity.
A dog at his heel, long-bodied, quiet, keeping close to the man's left leg.
I could not see the man's face under the hat-brim.
I did not try.
"Good evening," he said.
"Good evening."
"I was told at the green that you sometimes had work for a man passing through.
I'd take a night's shelter for it if you had the work.
The stable would do."
His voice was tired and steady and not servile.
The dog sat down on the flagstone and looked up at me and did not beg.
"I haven't work tonight," I said.
"I've a stable with dry straw in the end stall and a pump in the yard.
You can have that till morning.
I'll not decide past that tonight."
"That will do.
Thank you."
"There's bread on the scrubbed table inside the tack room.
Take what you want.
Don't let the dog in the kitchen."
"He won't come in where he's not asked."
"Good."
He touched the brim of his hat.
He did not offer a name.
He turned and went across the yard toward the stable with the dog following at his heel, and I shut the door and put the chain back on and hung the lantern up.
I was tired.
I had been tired at breakfast; I was tireder now.
I did not want another thing to decide tonight.
I was, as my mother used to say, at the end of my useful hours, and past the end was where mistakes got made.

The stranger could sleep on straw until daylight and I could sort him out then with a morning's wits about me, and if that was soft I would live with being soft for one evening in a year that had not asked me to be.
I went back to the range and finished scouring the pan I had left.
The kitchen window gave on the yard, and the lantern the stranger carried moved across the flagstones in a slow path toward the stable door, and I watched it without meaning to.
He set the lantern down inside the stable.
I could see its light in the door-gap.
He came back out.

He went to the stable door and lifted it, the way a man lifts a door that has dropped on its hinge, and he set his shoulder to it and eased the pin back in place — the hinge that stuck in wet weather, the hinge Jem had not got to.
Then he went across to the fence post by the trough.
He did not look at it long.
He took his weight against it, rocked it free of the wet earth, and reseated it square.
He tamped the ground at the foot of it with the heel of his boot.
He did not look up at the kitchen window.
He had not seen me.
He went back to the stable and the dog went with him and the door shut behind them both.
I finished the pan.
I set it on the rack.

I stood at the window with the cloth still in my hand and I watched the stable door a moment longer, and what I noticed — what came to me last, after the hinge and the post and the quiet economy of a tired man doing two small pieces of work before he slept — was his hands.
They had moved at the post with the sureness of hands that had done harder work than that, and worse, and had not forgotten how.
I set the cloth down on the rail above the range and turned back to the kitchen.
The London coach came in forty minutes late and two passengers short.
I was in the yard when it turned under the arch, and I could see from the set of Dobbins's shoulders that it had been a hard run.
He brought the team down and called to me before he was properly stopped.
"Road above Hatfield's cut up bad, Mrs.
Dale.
Three inches of mud and worse where it narrows past the mill."
"How far past the mill?"
"Half a mile, then it eases.
But loaded, you'll feel it."
"I'll send word to the Hare."
That was enough.
He nodded and turned back to his team.
Two of the four passengers got down in a temper.
The first, a heavyset man in a damp coat, wanted to know why the journey had taken three hours longer than advertised.
I told him the road was responsible, and the road was not mine.
He wanted to complain further and I let him have his say, then asked whether he required a room or the dining room.
He required the dining room.
I sent him in.
The second passenger had a trunk.
It came down from the boot badly, one of the leather hinges split along the strap, the whole side of it gaping.
The passenger, a woman of perhaps forty with a good wool travelling dress and a look that suggested she had learned to expect things to go wrong, stood over it and waited.
"We can bind that today," I told her.
"There's leather and rivets in the tack room.
Jem will see to it before you travel on."
"And if it opens on the road?"
"It won't.
Not with a rivet through both sides."
I met her eye.
"I've had trunks mended here before.
This is a straightforward repair."
She looked at the trunk, then at me.
"Very well."
Jem was already there.
I hadn't called him.
He crouched beside the trunk and had his hand on the hinge before the woman had finished speaking, and she went indoors, and that was the end of it.
The coachman came round once more before he took the team through to the stables.
"One more thing, Mrs.
Dale.
Coming through Hatfield we passed two men on horseback asking whether anyone had seen a young woman travelling alone.
Couldn't say what she looked like, only that she had a bandbox and a green cloak."
I thought of the two missing passengers.
"Where did they ask?"
"At the toll.
Constables, they looked like.
Or close to it."

He touched his hat and went.
The yard took perhaps ten minutes to clear after that.

The cobbles were wet and the yard smelled of horse and cold mud and the particular sharpness of October mornings when the wind comes off the north fields.

Nan was behind the bar, wiping glasses.
She had been there when the coach came in and she was there still, working through the rack with her back half-turned, but I had seen her watching.
I said nothing.
There was nothing to say.

Norris, who had been supplying the White Hound since before I took over the lease, and who had a workshop in the town and supplied four other inns on this road that I knew of.

Dale."

This morning."

He picked up his pen.

I sat down at the desk and opened the ledger.

veered off.

Reservation.

Stones rose in a neat cone.

Fresh as a scraped knee.
He lifted one stone, turned it, set it down the way he had found it.

Edges that had not learned wind.
Faces sharp where there should be a roundness from years of rain.

He kept his hands loose.
Men shot quicker when they believed you held answers.
