he said to Cass.

He sank a finger in.
Sharp jags in the crumbs.

One of the privates shifted his rifle.

Old cut.

Sand fell.
In that thin void he saw a line of dust darker than the rest.
Shovel smear.
He brought his fingers out and held them up.
Grit glinted where quartz had scraped him clean.
He showed the captain his palm.

Pike looked without looking.
He had a way of moving his eyes as if that was enough.
He spoke to Sergeant Daughtry.
“Make note that Mr.
Calder claims disturbance of federal markers.”
“Yes, sir,” Daughtry said.
His eyes had the dull shine of a stockman’s spade.

Rosa asked.

“What kind of sickness?”
she asked.
“That is not your concern,” he said.

Beg?”
“We read the earth,” Cass said.

Pike’s smile did not move.
“Ah.
You are one of those romantic surveyors.
Shadows and sticks.

Calder.

Cass looked at the sky.
Noon had already slid past but not by much.
The sun still cast short things.
He found a straight willow shoot laying with the other camp litter the soldiers had dropped.
He sunk one end into crack and let the other point straight up.
“You see that rock on the shelf,” he said.

“Captain Pike,” she said.

No smell of life on his skin.

dies.

It was not belief.

Pike nodded to Daughtry.

The board read in paint.
Military reservation.
No stock.
No cutting.
No fires.
Violators will be arrested.
A dragonfly sketched a blue loop and returned to the true seam under the shelf where water still sang, faint and hidden.

He squatted and listened.
He heard three notes.
The drip that counts days.
The faint run through stone veins.
The whisper that water makes when it has a place to go.
He stood and faced everyone, his shoulders square.
He was tired of the small talk that men use when they wish to eat time.
“I will walk this boundary at noon in three days,” he said.

Noon in three.

The guard remains.

Eliseo slid from his saddle and stepped toward him.

Cass put his hand on Eliseo’s breastbone and pushed once, slow.

Cass smiled with one side of his mouth.

The captain looked at the young private with the honest eyes.
He looked at Daughtry.
He looked at Tala, who had not shifted her feet.

Cass nodded once.

No one laughed.
The soldiers moved off a few paces and pretended to be busy while they listened.
Pike tied a blue ribbon to the stake and made a neat square knot.
He believed in the square of things.
It comforted him when the land would not.
Rosa took a breath that loosened her shoulders.
“Thank you,” she said.
She did speak to Cass as if he had given her a gift.

spat again.
“He rides with the Army now and likes a payday.

He could do it without anyone seeing it done.
Then he decided not to.
He let the wrong cone stand where it stood.
The lie needed witnesses to end it with grace.

Cass brought the mare down without sliding the stones that held the trail.
Dust lifted in a prayer.
The cattle milled short and then settled.

A horsefly landed and flew off quick, as if it had touched a skillet.

“Three days,” she said.
“We do not sleep in those days.

Cass looked up through the leaves.
Heat bent the world a little.
A hawk sat the blue and made a tight circle.
He remembered a day in a different uniform when he had guided a column to high ground, and a captain with a different name had held a paper that said ride here.
He remembered a young man who had wanted to be right as often as he was brave.

Metal can be a liar when it is stretched by men who want it to say a number they can live with.

A link with a flat on one side told him a story of a blacksmith who had worked hot and tired one night.
He liked that story.
Tala appeared in the doorway.
She had dust on her cheekbone and a nick on a knuckle.

“It has done for years,” Cass said.

Eliseo threw a piece of apple at a post and missed.
“I will carry the saw,” he said.
“You will carry it.
you will not swing it until we have words to cover the cut,” Rosa said.
He nodded and looked anywhere but at her.
Cass lifted the chain and coiled it again.

Leaves tossed a brighter underside.
The day’s heat settled into the kind of slow that asks men to decide what sort of men they are.
In three days he would plant a pole where a spring had taught patience to stone.

“Three days,” he said, and the word felt like a saddle cinch pulled snug.

Rosa cleaned a tin pan at the pump with a kind of prayer in the way she scrubbed.
Tala wrapped a rag around her knuckle and watched the door as if trouble could be seen in the dust.
Eliseo took the saw down and tested a tooth with his thumb and bled a little and did not flinch.
Cass stepped into the yard and let the sun find his face.
He looked at the mesa and saw the anvil rock taking light on its crown.

He felt a weight shift inside him.
Not dread.
Not joy.
Work settling into place.
“Three days,” he said again, to make sure the world knew he meant it.
The mare lifted her head and flicked an ear.
A bee worked the apple blossoms late for reasons of its own.

Then the sun would teach.
Men would choose whether to learn.
Cass found a straight stick and set it by the door so he would not forget the feel of grain in his hand.

Weather.
Light sliding along stone.

They rode toward the spring as the sun rose.
Men fell in behind without being told.

He stood without speaking.
The wind ran a finger along the rim of his hat and moved on.
A bee found the seam and told its friends.
The telling brought more life than any word on paper ever had.
Pike shifted once.
The clerk cleared his throat and held his pen like a weapon.
Eliseo shifted the saw and breathed like a man getting to the first rise in a day’s ride.
Rosa stared at the shelf without blinking.
Tala watched everyone and everything and also nothing at all.
The shadow shortened.
It steadied.
It reached, thin as truth, toward the notch on the anvil rock.
Cass did not look at faces.
He looked at stone.
When the line touched the notch, he spoke one word.
“Now.”
He did not raise his voice.
He did not have to.
Men leaned forward as if the world had whispered to them by name.
The pole’s shadow kissed the notch and lay quiet.
The cone sat a hand’s width east of where it belonged.
Somewhere below, where the false trough had baked in the sun, a horsefly landed, tasted dust.
lifted away as if it had remembered something important too late.
Cass breathed out.
He did not look at the captain yet.
He looked at the spring and saw the ring on the stone as clear as a woman’s hand.
“I will reset your cone,” he said.
“I will do it gentle.
After we move your stake.”
He picked up the first stone and waited in case anyone wished to make a fool of himself in front of the sky.
No one moved.
He smiled without showing teeth and began.

THE LAST RETREAT
Chapter One: The White Hound
The grate was dead.
I rebuilt it.
Whoever had banked it last night had done a pitiful job of it.
I didn’t waste the time to wonder who.
There were only three of us and the odds were even enough.
Forty years of coaching traffic had worn the flagstones uneven.
Forty years had smoked the ceiling beams to the colour of old bone.
The taproom had six tables, a bar of elm I’d sanded myself after Jem pointed out that the old pine had gone soft enough to splinter.
The ceiling was low enough that any man over six feet ducked on instinct when he crossed the threshold.
The bar top was good now.
Smooth, the grain running even, the knots sealed against spilled ale.
I’d worked it on a Tuesday in March because March is the dead month on the Great North Road.
There had been nothing else pressing except the damp patch above the third window and seventeen other things I couldn’t fix without spending money I didn’t have.
I’d done the bar instead.
The damp patch was still there.
The lease hung on its nail behind the bar, where my grandmother had put it in the year I was born.
Stainforth’s name was at the top of it.
Abel Dale’s name below that, though Abel Dale had been dead sixteen years and had never, in any practical sense, run a single day of this inn.
My name was nowhere on it.
Three women had kept the White Hound standing through two wars, a failed harvest, and my father’s inability to keep his accounts and none of our names were on the lease.
I noticed the nail needed straightening.
I straightened it.
I hung the lease back on it and turned to get the bread going.
Nan came in at half past five tying her cap and saying, without preamble and without looking up from the strings, “The coach company’s switching agents.
I heard it last night from Dawes at the Bull.
A Chipping Norton man, apparently.
There’ll be new rates.”
“The new rates — up or down.”
“Up.”
She tied the final bow, tucked a strand of hair that wouldn’t behave, and reached past me for the apron on the hook.
“Dawes said the Hatfield coach is already paying sixpence more a head.”
“Dawes is a gossip.”
“Dawes is a gossip who hasn’t been wrong yet.”
She pulled the apron over her head and turned to face me.
“I’m only saying.”
I cracked the first egg against the rim of the bowl.
The second.
“We always adjust.”
Nan said it pleasantly.
The morning coach arrived at seven with nine passengers and a coachman in a temper about the state of the road past Stevenage.
The yard became itself when a coach came in.
Jem was already at the horses and the lead pair were haltered and the first trunk was down from the roof.
The passengers were stepping out blinking into the cold and the coachman was calling for water and Nan was there with the manifest.
The yard smell was horse and leather and dead October leaves.
“The left rear wheel wants looking at,” Jem said, when I came past with a trunk for the luggage room.
He said it to the wheel.
I already knew.
I’d heard it come in.
“How bad is it.”
“It won’t make York.”
“I’ll tell him before he loads back up,” I said.
“I’ll tell him.”
“Tell him before he loads back up or we’ll be having a worse conversation.”
Jem went back to the wheel.
The coachman’s name was Hartley and he was working himself toward a scene about the trunk.

It belonged to a woman travelling to Biggleswade, was the size of a small cottage, and was currently in my luggage room because Hartley had declined to carry it up himself on account of it being, in his opinion, the woman’s own business to make arrangements for her own property.
I waited until he’d finished.
“Mr Hartley.
It’s the coachman’s responsibility to the first interior door.”
Hartley looked at me.
Hartley opened his mouth.
I looked at him until he closed it.
He picked up the trunk.
The woman from Biggleswade had requested the trunk be brought to her room, immediately, and had communicated this request with confidence.
I arranged for it.

She said the room was cold, which it was not — I had laid the fire myself — and that the sheets wanted airing, which they did not, and that she hoped the establishment would be rather more attentive than it had yet appeared.
I said I hoped so too.
She gathered as much composure as she could locate and swept into the room.
I closed the door behind her with exquisite care.
The chandler came at eleven.
His name was Murchett.

He’d supplied the White Hound for four years, and for the first three of those years the arrangement had been satisfactory, and for the fourth it had become an occasion for him to stand in my kitchen rearranging his sample box and telling me that costs had risen.
He set the box on the table.
He looked at the window.
He put his hands in his coat pockets and then took them out again.
“It’s the tallow,” he said.
“It’s the prices out of London.”
“You told me that in August.
How much worse.”
He told me.
He looked at the window again when he said it.
I went to the shelf and took down the ledger.
I opened it on the table between us, my finger on the column for October last year, which showed me his margin at the old rate and showed me, more importantly, that I knew what his margin was.
“Mr Murchett.”
“Miss Dale.”
“I can pay the August rate and I can go to Baldock.”
“Baldock’s too far.
Fourteen miles.”
“Eleven.
I’ve done it.
I can send Jem.”
He was quiet for a moment.
His hand settled on the counter, not quite gripping it.
He looked at the ledger.
He looked at me.
He said, “I might manage to hold at the September figure.
Given the volume you take.”
“August,” I said.
He picked up the sample box.
He moved it six inches to the left and back again.
“August, then.
Miss Dale.”
“Thank you, Mr Murchett.”
The ledger went back on the shelf.
My hands were tight on it when I set it down.

The two men in the taproom had been at the bench by the fire since the late-morning coach came in, which made it three hours, and in that time they had consumed enough of the ordinary ale to make the dispute about who had scuffed whose boot feel considerably more significant than it actually was.
The taller one had the other’s collar by the time I came through the door.
A stool scraped.
I knew the sound of a stool scraping.
“Put him down,” I said.
The tall one sat down.
His companion rubbed his collar and looked at my face and decided against it.
One of them muttered something into his ale.
I heard it and chose not to.
I went back behind the bar.

Jem was in the far corner of the room, leaning on the wall with his arms crossed and he looked at me and I looked at him, and that look contained everything: the frequency of it, the tedium of it, the question of how men managed to make a quarrel about a boot into an occasion requiring a woman to stand in a doorway like an army.

He came to the kitchen door at half past three, just after the afternoon coaches had gone through and before the evening rush, when the yard was quiet and the smell of the stockpot had been working at the air for two hours.
He knocked.
Quietly, and then again.
I opened it.
The collar on his coat was old infantry, but it had been let out at the shoulders.
His boots were repaired, the toe-stitching recent, the heel leather not — someone had done what they could for them, and it showed.
He stood straight in the doorway, his hands at his sides, his eyes at my shoulder rather than my face.
He asked if there was work.
I looked at him for thirty seconds.
“I’ve a floor wants sweeping in the luggage room,” I said.
“The broom is on the left side of the door.
When you’re done, come in.”
He swept the floor.
I set bread on the table and ladled a bowl of stockpot beside it and said nothing while I shaped the next morning’s loaves, and he ate, and neither of us made a show of it.
After a while, he said, “The road was frozen past Stevenage.”
“It’s been this cold since Sunday.”
He nodded.
He ate the last of the bread.
He didn’t say it was good, and I didn’t say anything about giving it, and we were both satisfied with this.
He finished the bread and thanked me and went.
I watched his boots go through the kitchen door and then they were gone, and the yard was empty, and the afternoon light was already failing.

The bolt on the front door had stuck — the frame around it swelled with the autumn damp every year — and required a firm shoulder and a particular angle; I leaned and pushed and felt it give with a scrape of iron on iron.

The window in the taproom that had never quite hung straight caught in its frame when I pulled it and let in a thread of cold air past the latch, as it always did, until I reached up and eased the top corner into the groove.
I snuffed the last candle and the smell of tallow hung in the air for half a minute after.
I wiped down the bar.
It was already clean — Nan had done it after the last customers went — but I wiped it anyway, the cloth moving in the same circles, the elm smooth under my hands.
There was a gouge near the far end, an inch long, just where the bar curved.
I ran my thumb over it.
A keg, I thought.
Thursday’s delivery.
The bottom rim of the big barrel, the way Jem tilts it when he’s bringing it through alone — he tilts it rather than carry it, which is the sensible solution, but it catches the corner sometimes.
I’d have to talk to him about the Thursday delivery.
Whether he could manage the heavy cask, whether we needed to ask for the smaller measure.
The lease was on its nail.
My grandmother had held this place for twenty years through a husband’s death and the mill closures and the bad winter of ‘84.
There was no passing traffic for a week and she’d fed the staff from the cellar stores and not lost a single booking.
My mother had finished the dinner service the night she died.
And me.
I wrung out the cloth.
I hung it on the hook.
The hook was one my mother put in.
The letter was on the shelf beside the ledger, where I’d set it when it arrived that afternoon.
I’d seen the seal before I’d seen the direction, and I’d set it on the shelf and gone back to the afternoon’s business, and I’d been knowing ever since.
Stainforth’s seal.
His man had brought it.
I looked at it for a moment.
I picked it up.
The wax was smooth under my thumb, the device pressed clean.
I set the letter on the shelf beside the ledger.
I took the candle and went to bed.
The letter was on the table where I had left it, face up, his handwriting small and even and courteous as the handwriting of a man who had never in his life had to write anything urgent.
Mr Stainforth wished to discuss the terms.
He hoped the hour would be convenient.
He remained, as ever, my obedient servant.
I had read it twice last night and once at four this morning, and I did not intend to read it again.
The kitchen was cold.
The fire had not yet taken.

I laid the sticks the way my mother had laid them, smaller to larger, breath of air between, and struck the flint harder than I needed to because my hands were stiff and the cut on my index finger had opened again in the night.
Six weeks until the quarter's rent.

Sixty-eight pounds, eleven shillings, and the coaching office's receipt for October not yet paid out because the Royal Mail paid slow and paid late and considered a woman's patience one of the perquisites of the arrangement.
I knew the arithmetic.
I had known it since September.
Stainforth's letter was only the wind at my back, and I had been bracing against wind all autumn.
The ledger was still on the table where I had shut it last night.
I did not open it.
I knew what was in it.
I drank my tea standing up.
Then I went and did the morning.
I swept the taproom until the boards showed pale at the edges.
I wiped down the bar rail.
I checked the cellar stair for the loose tread and checked the barrels for the weep we'd mended last week and found it dry.
I turned the bread in the larder.
I set Nan to the upstairs fires.
I did every task a little harder than it needed to be done, which was how I knew I was afraid.
My mother used to say fear was a useful servant and a miserable master.
She said a great many things.
Most of them I heard now in my own voice.
I heard the carriage before I saw it.
A private carriage at walking pace, no outrider, harness in good order.
The wheels on our gravel made a cleaner sound than the mail coaches did, because the mail coaches came loaded and his came empty but for him.
I met him in the doorway of my own inn.
"Miss Dale."
He removed his hat.
"I hope I have not come at an inconvenient hour."
"Not at all, Mr Stainforth."
"And Mrs Dale — your aunt.
She keeps well?"
"She does.
Thank you for asking."
His coat was dark green wool, cut close, and smelled faintly of cedar and the good kind of tobacco.
He drew off his gloves one finger at a time and folded them together and held them in his left hand.
He did not look past me into the taproom, which was the courtesy of a man who intended to look at it at length later.
"A raw morning," he said.
"It will rain before noon."
"You think so?"
"The sky is flat and the wind has dropped.
It will rain."
He smiled slightly at that, as if I had confirmed something pleasant about the countryside.
"I shall not keep you long.
I so rarely have the chance to see the place properly, and I find I am negligent in my duties as landlord if I do not, from time to time, take advantage of an hour.
You will indulge me, I hope."
He was not asking.
I stepped back and let him in.
He walked the taproom the way a man walks a field he is thinking of buying.
He did not hurry.
He stopped once at the long table by the window and ran his thumb along the grain, where the oak had silvered from decades of elbows.
He stopped again at the bar.
He put his hand on the rail, not to lean, simply to put it there.
He looked up at the beam and then down at the boards under his boot.
"Oak," he said.
"Yes."
"Original to the building?"
"As far as I know."
"Your grandmother's time."
"Before that."
He nodded, as though I had given him a number he could enter into a column.
"How many rooms do you let in an average week, Miss Dale?"
"Eighteen, this time of year.
Twenty in summer."
"And the coaching trade?
The Edinburgh mail still comes through?"
"Every night but Sunday.
The Leeds and York three times a week.
The Glasgow, twice."
"And they are satisfied, your coaching companies?
The drivers, the passengers?"
"The companies pay on the nail.
The drivers come back.
If they were not satisfied they would not."
"Admirable."
He moved on.
He opened the cellar door.

I had checked it at six and it was clean and dry and the barrels were racked the way my mother had taught me to rack them, smallest to largest, left to right, the spigots all at the same height so you could feel your way in the dark.
He did not go down.
He ran his thumb along the hinge, where Jem had oiled it yesterday, and then along the jamb, where the wood had swelled with the autumn damp.
He asked about the drainage.
I told him about the French drain my grandmother had put in in 1789.
He asked who supplied our ale.
I told him Foulkes of Hitchin, on a three-year contract, with two years still to run.
He asked whether we took our candles from the chandler in the village or bought in bulk from Hertford.
I told him Hertford, by the gross, and did not add that we paid three ha'pence less that way.
He did not ask, and I did not volunteer.
Give them the number, my mother had said, and not the explanation.
The explanation is where they find the crack.
He asked the same sort of question about the bed linen, the stabling contracts, the number of hands I employed in the kitchen.
I answered each in the fewest words the question required, and then I waited, with my hands folded in front of my apron, for the next one.
He was methodical.
I will give him that.
He was also, in his own way, enjoying himself, though he would have considered enjoyment the wrong word.
He considered himself to be taking an interest.
"Shall we step out to the yard?"
he said at last, as if the idea had just come to him.
"I should like to see the stabling.
One hears such reports of your stabling, Miss Dale."
I fetched my shawl.
The yard was the colour of wet pewter.
The wind had not yet dropped to nothing, but it was thinking about it.
Jem was at the far end with a gelding on a short rein, and he glanced up at us once and glanced down again and said nothing, which was Jem's way of saying a great deal.
Stainforth walked the length of the fence.
At the corner, where the post leaned three degrees out of true and the rail had come loose from its peg, he stopped.
He put his gloved hand on the top of the post and pressed.
The post gave, the little that rotten posts give.
"Ah," he said.
"It's on the list."
"I do not doubt it.
You keep a list, I am sure."
"I do."
He left his hand on the post a moment longer.
Then he took it off and looked at me, not unkindly.
"Miss Dale.
Forgive me.
You will think I am stepping out of my place, and perhaps I am.

But I wonder, sometimes, whether an establishment of this size — a coaching inn, on a road of this traffic, with the responsibilities that attach to such a house — whether it might not benefit from —" He let the sentence go.
He did not hurry to finish it.

He waited for me to finish it for him, which I would not, or to ask him to finish it, which I would not, or to show, by a movement of the face, that I had understood what he was not saying, which was the only part of the exchange I could not entirely prevent.
"From?"
I said, because silence would have been a kind of answer.
"From a steadier hand at the helm, let us say.
In these difficult seasons.
One reads such unhappy reports of inns on the Great North Road.
Vagrancy.
Disorder.
Soldiers.
I should be very sorry to hear the White Hound spoken of in such a way.
Very sorry."
"The White Hound is not spoken of in such a way."
"Not yet."
"Mr Stainforth.
The books are in order.
The rent has been paid on the day, every quarter, for forty-four years.
The coaching companies renew on the terms they renewed on under my mother and under my grandmother.
If you have a complaint, I should prefer to hear it plainly."
It came out a degree sharper than I had meant it to.
I felt it leave my mouth and I did not call it back.
He did not flinch.
He did not even blink.
He received the sentence the way a wall receives a thrown pebble, and his face rearranged itself into something still more civil.
"My dear Miss Dale.
I have no complaint.
I have only an interest.
As your landlord, as a magistrate, as a neighbour — an interest.
We shall speak again, I hope, when the terms come to be reviewed in the spring.
In the meantime —" He glanced at the leaning post and then past it to the stable roof, which was sound, and then at me.
"You keep the place very well.
Very well indeed.
Your mother would be proud."
He put his hat on.
"Good day."
"Good day, Mr Stainforth."
I watched his carriage down the lane until it turned at the elm and was gone.
Then I stood where I was for a count of ten, because if I moved any sooner I would have moved too fast.
My jaw ached.
I unclenched it.
The cut on my finger had opened again inside my glove.
I went in and took the kettle off the hob and put it back on because my hands wanted something to do.
Bridget's door was open when I got to the top of the stairs.
It always was.
The fire was up, the room smelt of lavender and old books and the wool of the blanket over her knees, and the good china was on the small table by the window, two cups, the pot already drawn.
She did not look round.
"Sit down, child."
"I've only a minute."
"Sit down."
I sat.
My shoulders dropped without my permission.
She poured.
Her hands were brown and spotted and her knuckles were bad and the pot trembled a little and none of it mattered.
She had been pouring tea in this room since I was four years old.
"He stayed an hour," she said.
"Fifty-five minutes."
"And he touched things."
"Yes."
"Mm."
She pushed my cup across.
"Greville used to do that.
Before your time.

Your mother had him half an afternoon one autumn, walking the yard with his hand on everything, and at the end of it he wanted to double the stabling and she said no, because the drainage would not take it, and he said she was a woman and would not understand the drainage, and she said that was as may be, but the drainage was still the drainage."
"What did he do?"
"Sulked.
Died.
His son was easier."
She sipped.
"She saw him off, your mother.
She knew when to hold her ground and she knew when the ground wasn't worth holding.
That was the trick of it."
"I held my ground."
"You did."
"I was civil."
"You were."
She set her cup down.

She looked at me with her one good eye and her one clouded one, and for a moment I was eleven years old and she was telling me my mother would be down in a minute, and my mother was not going to be down in a minute, and both of us had known it.
"Dinah.
Holding on and holding back are not the same thing."
I reached for the pot, though my cup was full.
"This tea is stewed," I said.
"It isn't."
"It will be by the time I come back up."
"You won't come back up today.
You've the supper to do and the Leeds at nine."
"Then it will be stewed tomorrow."
She let me have it.
She let me have all of it.
She picked up her cup again and looked out of the window at the yard, where the light was going, and she said, in her ordinary voice, "Send Nan up when she has a minute.
I have a stocking she can darn that I cannot."
"I will."
I kissed the top of her head on the way past.
Her hair smelt the way it had always smelt.

I shut the door behind me, softly, because there was no call to slam it, and I went down the stairs and back to the kitchen and put on my apron and did not think about what she had said, because there was the supper to do, and the Leeds at nine, and a man was coming with the chandler's account in the morning, and I had no time for what she had said, and that was an end to it.
The Leeds came and went.
The taproom emptied by half past ten.

I banked the fire and turned the lamps down and shot the bolt on the front door and stood a moment in the passage listening to the house settle, which it did in the same order every night: the stair creak, the pantry door, the cat.
Then the knock.
Not loud.
Two, and a pause, and one.
I opened the top half of the door.
He was tall.
That was the first thing, because I had to look up, and I do not often have to.
His hat was in his hand.
His coat had been a good coat once and was still, in the bones of it, a good coat.
His boots had walked a long way; the leather was soft to nothing at the instep.
A dog sat at his left heel, long-legged, grey-brindled, ears up, watching me with a worried patience that looked like it was the dog's usual expression.
"Forgive the hour," he said.
His voice was low and measured and tired.
"I am looking for work, or for a bed in a stable, or both, if you can spare them.
I can pay for the bed.
I would rather work for it."
I looked at him.
I looked at the dog.
I looked at the boots.
Not drunk.
Not dangerous.
Not a thing I had to settle tonight.
"The stable's dry," I said.
"Second stall on the left is empty.
There's straw and a horse blanket on the peg.
The pump's in the yard.
Come to the kitchen door at six and we'll talk about the rest."
"Thank you."
"Has the dog a name?"
"Sapper."
"Keep him out of the chickens."
"He won't trouble the chickens."
"They all say that."
The corner of his mouth moved.
It was not a smile.
It was the place where a smile would have been, in a man less tired.
"Six," he said.
"Six."

I shut the door and shot the bolt and went through to the kitchen, because I always checked the yard from the kitchen window before I went up, and I was not going to change the order of my night for a stranger at the gate.
He was at the pump.
He filled a bucket and set it down for the dog and waited while the dog drank.
Then he took the bucket to the stable and came out without it.

He stopped at the stable door and ran his hand along the top of it, and I thought, not again, not tonight — and then he reached up and lifted the door a quarter-inch on its hinge and set it back, and the small wrongness in it that I had heard every evening for a month was gone.
He stood a moment, listening, as if to be sure.
He walked the length of the fence.
At the corner post he stopped.
He set his shoulder to it and tried it, the way Stainforth had tried it, and it gave him the same answer.
He put his hat on the rail.
He knelt.

He scraped the wet leaves back from the foot of the post with the edge of his hand, and found the stone that had shifted, and worked it out, and took up a larger one from the pile Jem kept by the gatepost, and set it in, and packed the earth back round it with the heel of his hand, and stood up, and pushed the post, and the post did not move.
He picked up his hat.
He put it on.
He went into the stable, and the dog went in after him, and the door closed behind them without a sound.
I stood at the window with my hand flat against the sill.
The cut on my finger had stopped bleeding.
I turned from the window and went upstairs to bed.

The letter had been on the kitchen table all night, and in the morning I opened it standing up, because if I sat down I would have to stand again to do the next thing, and the next thing was the fire.
Stainforth's hand.
Narrow, even, the ink good.
He would call today between eleven and one, with my convenience very much in mind.
He regretted the short notice.
He did not regret it enough to have sent yesterday.

I read it twice, and then I read the last line a third time, because the last line was the one that mattered: he wished to walk the premises before Michaelmas, so that the question of the renewal might be approached in an orderly way.
Orderly.
I set the letter down on the ledger, lined up the corner of the paper with the corner of the book, and went to the grate.
"Was that his seal?"
Nan said from the doorway, a basket of linen on her hip.
"It was."
"When?"
"Before one."
She looked at the clock, then at the ledger, then at me.
"I'll do the taproom floor again."
"You did it yesterday."
"I'll do it again."
I did not argue with her.

I banked the fire, pinned my hair tighter, and put on the clean apron instead of the working one, then took it off and put the working one back on, because a clean apron at eight in the morning would tell him I had dressed for him, and I had not.
I had dressed for the day.
He would arrive during the day.
The two facts did not require me to confuse them.
The ledger I left where it was.
I would not hide my accounts from him.
He was welcome to see what four years of a woman's management looked like, down to the farthing.

I set the ink at the ledger's right hand, because my grandmother had kept her ink on the right, and I had kept it on the right since I was nine, and I was not going to move it today for a man in a good coat.
"Mrs.
Bridget saw the gig come down the Baldock road last autumn," Nan said, not quite looking at me.
"She'll see it today."
"She will."
"She'll want to know."
"She'll know.
She won't have to be told."
Nan nodded and went away with the linen.
I set the kettle, swept the stoop myself because sweeping the stoop was a thing I could do with my own hands, and waited.
He came at a quarter past eleven.
A gig, a single groom, the dry clear light of a morning that had promised rain and failed to deliver it.

I heard the wheels on the flagstones before I saw the hat, and by the time the hat was in the yard I was at the door with my hands folded in front of me in the way Patience had stood at this door for every landlord's call I could remember.
The posture was hers.
I had inherited it as I had inherited the ink-stand and the crooked third stair and the lease.
"Miss Dale."
"Mr.
Stainforth."
His coat was very good wool, a dark blue-green I did not know the name of.
He took off his hat without flourish.
His boots were clean; his groom had been set to hold the reins, which meant we would not be offering the groom tea.
He looked at the façade of the inn the way a man looks at a horse he is thinking of buying.
"A dry morning," he said.
"I had expected rain."
"It held off.
We were glad of it.
The yard dries slowly."
"Your sign wants paint."
"It does.
It's on the spring list."
"I am glad to hear there is a list."
He said it pleasantly.
It was the pleasantness that was the thing.
I stepped back and opened the door wider, because leaving him on the stoop was worse than letting him inside, and inside was my house, and I could walk it beside him.
"Will you come through?"
"Thank you."
He came through.
In the taproom he set his hat on the long table, not on a peg, and I registered the hat without looking at it.
The taproom was swept.
The fire was low and clean.
The bottles behind the bar were dusted.
Nan had done her work and then done it again, and he walked the length of the room and looked at the beams above the bar without comment and then turned to me.
"Twenty rooms, Miss Dale."
"Twenty."
"Full through the summer, I understand."
"Full enough.
We turned away seven coaches in August for want of beds.
I have the dates in the ledger if you want them."
"I am sure you have."
A pause.
"The cellar."
I took him to the cellar.
The door sticks in damp weather; Jem had been meaning to set the hinge since Lammas, and the hinge had not been set, because the yard fence had been worse, and I had chosen the fence.
Stainforth laid his gloved hand on the hinge and opened the door halfway and let it rest there, and did not remark on the stick.
He went down three steps and looked at the casks and came up again.
"Your father kept this dry," he said.
"My mother kept it dry.
My father was a farrier."
"Forgive me.
Your mother."
"She learned it from my grandmother."
"A long tenure."
"Forty-four years, this Michaelmas."
He touched the hinge a second time on the way out, closing the door with a care that was almost courtesy.
I registered the second touch as I had registered the first.
A man in a good coat, counting hinges.
I had the irrelevant thought that if he were going to itemise my fixtures he might at least have brought a pencil.
The stair.
He went up ahead of me, because a gentleman does not climb behind a woman on a narrow stair, and I let him, because my refusal would have cost more than it was worth.
The third tread warped in winter; he put his weight on it and it gave its small sound and he did not look down.
On the first-floor landing he laid his hand on the newel post and left it there while he spoke.
"The parish, Miss Dale.
There have been complaints."
"From whom?"
"From a number of sources.
The number of demobilised men you have taken in through the yard.
The broth.
The back door."
His hand stayed on the newel.
"I have defended the practice.
It is Christian.
But the parish is uneasy.
A woman alone at an inn on the Great North Road, feeding strangers at her kitchen door, is spoken of."
"The men are fed, and they go on."
"They do.
And then others come."
"They do."
"My nephew, when he takes a wife, will want an establishment that is not spoken of in the parish."
There it was.
Not his nephew by name; a nephew.
A man, not spoken of in the parish.
I took one breath in through my nose and counted to two, which was my grandmother's count, not my mother's.
My mother had counted to three.
"The lease renews at Michaelmas next," I said.
"It does."
"The terms have been met each quarter since my mother signed them.
The rent is current.
The repairs are current.
The condition of the premises you may see for yourself."
"I am seeing it."
He took his hand off the newel.
"You understand, Miss Dale, that the discretion at renewal is mine."
"I understand it."
"I should prefer the lease to be held by a man.
I say that plainly because I believe plainness is a kindness.
A man could carry the trade into a better account of itself, and the parish would rest, and the house would be what your grandmother intended it to be, which was a going concern."
"It is a going concern."
"It is a going concern run by a woman.
Those are not the same thing to the vestry."
"They are the same thing in the ledger."
He inclined his head, as if I had made a neat remark at dinner.
"Shall we see the yard?"
We saw the yard.
Jem had taken the two nearest horses out on purpose, which I understood and was grateful for.
Stainforth walked the line of the stable, laid his gloved hand on the post that leans, said nothing about the lean, and walked back.
He did not touch the post twice.
He had touched the hinge twice.

I did not know what to make of the arithmetic of his touches, and I did not intend to make anything of it, and I registered it anyway, because a woman who registers nothing dies in the kitchen with the ladle in her hand.
At the gig he put on his hat.
"I shall write before Michaelmas."
"I shall expect the letter."
"Good day, Miss Dale."
"Good day, Mr.
Stainforth."
He climbed up.
The groom let go of the reins.

The wheels went over the flagstones, and then they were gone, and the yard was quiet, and I stood where he had left me for the count of five, which was longer than I meant, and then I went inside and up the stairs to Bridget, because if I stood where he had left me for the count of six I would stand there all day.
Fifteen treads.
The third from the top warps; I went round it as I had gone round it since I was a girl, on the left side where the nail holds.
Bridget's door was on the latch.
She had left it on the latch because she had seen the gig.
"Come in, pet."
She was in the chair by the window.
Her hands were on the arms of the chair.
The tea tray was already set, the good china out, because what were we saving it for, she would say, the funeral of a stranger.
The pot was under the cosy.
A plate of seed-cake Nan must have brought up yesterday.
"Shut the door."
I shut it.
"Sit."
I sat.
She poured.

Her hands shook a little on the handle of the pot; they had shaken a little for two years now, and the tea went into the cup without a drop on the saucer, because Bridget had been pouring tea from that pot since before I was born, and the shake did not yet know more than the hand.
"Blue coat," she said.
"Green.
Dark green."
"Green, then.
And his nephew?"
"Not by name.
A man.
Not spoken of in the parish."
"Ah."
She pushed the cup toward me.
"Drink."
I drank.
The tea was strong, the way she liked it; the way Patience had liked it.
I had not drunk tea this strong in my own kitchen in months, because I drank it on my feet and wanted it weak enough to swallow fast.
"He touched the hinge twice," I said, and did not know I was going to say it until I had.
"The cellar one."
"Yes."
"It sticks."
"I know."
"Jem knows."
"I know he knows."
She looked at me over the rim of the cup.
Her eyes are very pale now, paler than they were, but they see.
They have always seen.
"Your mother," she said, "was the most careful woman I ever knew.
Do you know what she was careful of?
Not the inn.
The inn took care of itself in her hands, the way a good horse takes care of itself in the hands of a person who knows horses.
She was careful of herself.
She kept herself back.

She kept herself back from Abel, who did not deserve it and would not have noticed, and she kept herself back from you, which she regretted at the end, and she kept herself back from me, and she kept herself back from the one or two men after Abel who would have done for her, because she had decided that holding on to this place meant holding back from everything else."
A pause, the length of one breath.
"Holding on and holding back, Dinah, are not the one thing.
Your mother thought they were.
She was wrong."
Her accent had come up under the last sentence, the Wexford under the Hertford, the way it did when she was in earnest.
I put my cup down on the saucer and the china made its small sound.
"I have an inn to run before Michaelmas," I said.
"You have."
"I have not got time for philosophy this morning, Aunt."
"You have not."
"Thank you for the tea."
"You are welcome to it."
I stood.
She did not stand; she had stopped standing to see people out about a year ago, and I had stopped expecting her to.
She watched me to the door.

I had the thought at the door, and did not turn with it, that she had said the thing she had been working up to saying, and that she had said it cleanly, and that she had not softened it with an embrace or a hand on my sleeve, because she knew me, and she knew that softening would have let me out of it, and she did not want to let me out of it.
I went down the stairs thinking about the renewal, because the renewal was the thing I could hold in my hands.
The other thing I would carry with me and work alongside.
Afternoon into evening went the way afternoons into evenings go at an inn on the Great North Road.
A coach from the south at three, another from the north at half past four, a private chaise at six with a gentleman who wanted his own sheets and got ours.
Nan at the bar.
Jem in the yard with the lamps.
The weather turned: a thin rain came in from the west, and the wind with it, and I had the yard lamps lit early and the taproom lamps earlier.

By eight the sky was black and the rain was steady, and I was in the kitchen with my sleeves pushed up, scalding the milk for the morning's porridge, because if I was going to be a woman who stood in her own kitchen I was going to be a woman who had porridge at dawn.
The knock came at the yard gate a little before nine.
Not the main door.
Not the taproom.
The yard gate, which meant a man on foot.
I took the lantern and went.
He was tall.
That was the first thing: taller than the gate, so the top of his shoulder cleared the top board.
The rain was on his coat, which had been good once and had been walked in hard.
A dog at his heel, long-legged, low, grey in the lantern light.
His hat was in his hand, which told me something, though I was too tired tonight to say what.
"Ma'am."
A voice low, not servile; a man used to speaking to people and used to not speaking more than he had to.
"I'm looking for work.
A night's shelter, if you've got it.
I can pay for the shelter if you can't spare the work."
"What do you do?"
"Horses.
Walls.
Most things."
"Where have you come from?"
"London, the last stretch.
Before that, further."
I looked at him in the lantern light.
He did not fidget under the looking.
The dog did not fidget either.
I was tired.
I did not want a new question tonight.
I had had my day's allowance of questions, and this was not one I had the wit left to answer well.
"The stable's dry at the north end," I said.
"There's straw.
There's a blanket on the nail by the tack room door.
You can sleep there tonight.
We'll speak in the morning about the work."
"Ma'am."
"Supper's bread and cheese at the kitchen door in half an hour.
Tell the girl Dinah said."
"Thank you."
"The dog stays with you.
He doesn't come in the yard past the mounting block."
"He won't."
He put his hat back on.

He touched the brim, not to flourish, only to settle it against the rain, and he went round to the north end of the stable with the dog at his heel, and I shut the yard gate and slid the bolt and went back inside.
The kitchen was warm.
The milk had not caught.
I stirred it down off the heat and set it to cool and wiped my hands on my apron and looked out through the window over the sink, which gave on the yard.
He had the lantern I had left by the mounting block.
He had the dog settled on a rag by the stable door; the dog lay down once, got up, turned twice, lay down again.

He set the lantern on the block and went to the stable door, and he took the hinge in his hand, the hinge Stainforth had not touched, the lower one that sticks, and he felt along the pin with his thumb and lifted the door a little on its frame and set it back, and the stick was gone.

He walked along to the yard fence then, to the post that leans, the one Jem has been meaning to reset since Lammas, and he squatted by it and put his shoulder against it and rocked it once to feel the give, and then he packed stones at its foot with his hands, two, three, four stones, fitting them the way a man fits stones who has done it before, and he stood up and pushed the post with the flat of his hand and the post held.
His hands moved quickly in the lantern light.
I watched them a moment longer, and then I turned back to the milk.
The ledger lay open under my hand, and the sum at the bottom of the page had not improved overnight.
I had rather hoped it might.
The fire in the kitchen range was new-built and making a serious effort; the rest of the inn was cold in the way old buildings are cold before dawn, which is to say thoroughly, and with opinions.
I added the column again.
Six weeks until the quarter's rent was due, and the till at present was about four pounds short of pretending otherwise.
I shut the ledger.
I pulled my sleeves down over my wrists.
One can do a great many sums in one's head while also checking the state of the bar stock and the last of the evening's tallies, and I had learned to do most of them without moving my lips.
My mother had insisted on that.
A woman who counted aloud, she said, was a woman who was telling everyone in the room what she had.
The kitchen fire wanted a fresh log.
I gave it one.
The taproom fire was down to ash and I built it up from coal and a twist of newsprint, which I prefer because it burns quickly and does not smell of promises.
Last night's accounts: twenty-two covers, eleven beds, one dispute over a chamber pot that I did not propose to record in writing.
The barrels in the cellar: two full, one three-quarters, one I would have to tap by Thursday.
The windows at the front were rimed at the edges; I pressed the pad of my thumb to the glass and the frost went to water under it and then back to frost again almost at once.
I did not like the numbers.
I did not have to like them.
I had only to live with them, and I had been living with worse since I was eleven.
In the yard Jem was already at the tack.

He had the bridle over the stump and the buckle in his right hand and he was working the strap through with the patience of a man who had long since stopped being surprised by the shape of his own arm.
He did not look up.
He did not need to.
I had taught myself, over the months, not to hover at that doorway with any expression on my face that might be mistaken for concern.
Concern, in Jem's vocabulary, was a thing one paid in wages.
Nan came through the kitchen door with two pins in her mouth and her apron already on and a look of someone who had argued with her hair and won on points.
She nodded at me.
I nodded back.
She went to the bar.
We had done this perhaps a thousand times.
The coach was late, which was not news, and running two passengers short, which was.
A split-hinged trunk came off the roof with a complaint from its owner that arrived before the trunk did.
"If your man so much as drags it," said the lady, "I shall have the maker's name from him and write to them directly."
"My man," I said, "will carry it over his shoulder.
Jem?"
Jem was already there.

He lifted the trunk as though it were a child and took it inside without remark, and the lady, who had been prepared for a longer engagement, found herself without opposition and went, a little disoriented, toward the dining room.
The coachman wanted his word.
He had the look of a man who had been cold for six hours and intended to share the experience.
"The road above Hatfield," he said.
"How bad."
"Bad enough that I've lost a spring.
I'll want an hour and a smith if you've got one."
"I've a smith at Codicote who'll come if I send Jem.
You'll have your hour.
Tea in the taproom.
Two minutes."
"Miss Dale —" "Two minutes," I said.
"I've a chandler due at ten who believes he can charge me what he charges the posting house at Welwyn, and I should like to disabuse him before you leave."
He laughed, which I had not intended, and took his tea.
By half past nine the yard was empty again.
Jem had the trunk in the hall.
Nan was wiping the bar with one eye on the door, as she always did when a stranger was upstairs, and I noted it and said nothing, because saying it would have embarrassed us both.
Mr.
Hollis the chandler arrived at ten exactly, which is the only punctual thing about him.
He set his box on the table and named a price.
"Ninepence the dozen," he said.
"It was sevenpence ha'penny in March."
"Tallow's up."
"Tallow was up in March.
You raised me then too."
"Miss Dale, I've six other houses on this road and every one of them pays ninepence."
"Mr.
Hollis, you have four other houses on this road, the Bell at Welwyn renders its own, and the Red Lion has been buying from Baldock since Michaelmas because you quarreled with Mr.
Pettifer about his gatepost.
That leaves you and me and two inns that do a quarter of my trade."
I did not raise my voice.
I did not need to.
"I'll pay you eightpence.
You'll leave the candles.
You'll come again next month, and we will have this conversation again, and I expect we'll both enjoy it more if we start nearer the figure we mean to end on."
He looked at me.
I looked at him.
There is an art, in these matters, to not looking pleased with oneself.
"Eightpence," he said.
"Eightpence."
He set the candles down with slightly more force than was necessary and took his coin and went.
I listened to the yard door close.
I allowed myself, privately, the smallest possible smile.
I had not lost a fight with Mr.
Hollis yet, and I did not intend to start today.
I carried the candles through to the pantry.
Somewhere between the shelf and the door I let myself think the thought that always came after the chandler, because the chandler was only the start of the list and the list had a bottom line.
If I married, the candles would be his.
The ledger would be his.
The arguing with Mr.
Hollis would be his, and Mr.
Hollis would charge him ninepence, and the lease would be in a name that was not Dale, and I would be a woman who had once run an inn.
I had refused Mr.

Lacey two Augusts ago and the farmer at Knebworth the summer before that, and I had liked neither of them enough to regret it, and I had liked them both enough to know that the liking was not the point.
The point was the ledger.
The point was always the ledger.
I set the candles on the shelf and went back to the kitchen.
He was at the back door before I saw him, and then I saw him through the window and he had not yet knocked.
He was young — younger than Nan, I thought, but it was hard to be sure, because hunger ages a face and then undoes the aging all at once when it smiles, and he was not smiling.
His coat was too large.
His boots were coming apart at the welt on the left side; I could see the pale line of his stocking through the gap.
He stood with his hands at his sides and he was deciding whether to knock.
I opened the door before he could.
"Have you eaten."
"Not today, ma'am."
"When last."
"Yesterday morning.
A bit of bread."
"Kitchen," I said.
"Not the taproom.
You'll sit at that table and you'll eat what I give you and you'll not trouble the guests.
Do you agree."
"Yes, ma'am."
I ladled broth and cut bread and set both down and a spoon with them.
He thanked me and sat.
He held the spoon in both hands, as my father had the winter he was ill.
He ate slowly, which I took for good manners, and then more quickly, which I took for the truth.
When the bowl was empty I gave him a second.
He looked at me as though he had not expected it, and then he looked at the bowl.
"Where are you going," I said.
"North, ma'am.
There's a cousin at Grantham."
"Grantham's a long road from here."
"Yes, ma'am."
I said nothing about the war.
He said nothing about the war.
When he had finished he wiped the spoon on the edge of the bowl and set both down square to the edge of the table and stood up.
He thanked me again.
He went out the way he had come.
I shut the door.
I went to the stockpot.
I was thinking about his boots.
I was thinking about the way he had set the spoon square to the table, as though the table were the Army's and had to be left as he found it.
I was thinking that he was somebody's son and had sat at somebody's table once and had been taught, and that the teaching had held through whatever had happened in between.
I was thinking, briefly and without permission, that I was tired, and that a stockpot is a thing one can manage when one is tired, and I was grateful for it.
I stirred the pot.
I added a little salt.
I moved on.
The midday rush came and went.
Two drovers argued in the taproom over a wager neither of them remembered making, and their voices began to climb toward the kind of pitch that ends in broken glass.
"Gentlemen," I said, from the doorway.
"You'll settle it outside or you'll settle it tomorrow.
You will not settle it here."
They looked at me.
Nan, behind the bar, did not move.
I did not need her to move.
"Tomorrow," said one of them, after a moment, and the other nodded into his cup, and that was the end of it.
The afternoon went quiet.
The inn was quiet.
It was always quiet between coaches, and I had learned to use the hour as my mother had used it — for the books, for the rooms, for the kitchen list for the evening.
Jem was in the yard.
Nan was at the bar with a novel under the counter that she thought I did not know about.
I did the accounts.
I reset the rooms on the first floor.
I spoke to Cook about mutton.
By six the evening coach had come and gone and by ten the taproom was down to three and by eleven the three had gone to bed.
I walked the inn.
I checked the taproom fire, which was down to coals and safe.
I locked the cellar hatch.
I looked into the yard and heard nothing, which meant Jem had seen to the horses, because Jem's yard was quieter than any yard I had ever kept alone.
My hands at the end of the day were not pretty.
The knuckles were red from cold water, and there was a small cut on my right index finger from the edge of Mr.
Hollis's delivery note, which I had not noticed when he gave it to me and had noticed afterward every time I wrote anything.
A paper cut from a man who had tried to charge me ninepence.
It seemed about right.
I crossed the yard one last time.
The lamp at Bridget's window was lit, and the shape behind it was Bridget, and Bridget was watching, as she did.
I did not look long.
She had seen me cross this yard ten thousand times and neither of us required a performance of it.
I bolted the front door.
I set the bar.

The sound the bar makes in its cradle is one of the sounds I know best in the world, and standing there at the end of a day, with the inn behind me breathing and the fire down to coals and every one of us where we ought to be, I allowed myself — briefly — to notice that I was alone.
Not lonely, exactly, which is a larger word.
Only alone, in a house full of people, which is what I had arranged.
I went back to the kitchen.
The letter was on the table where Nan had put it.
I had seen it when I came in after the coach and I had chosen not to see it, which is a thing one can do with a letter for a few hours but not indefinitely.
The seal was Stainforth's.
The handwriting on the direction was his clerk's — I knew the clerk's hand; he had written to me twice before, once about a drainage ditch and once about the question of the sign.
I sat down.
I turned the letter over once.
I broke the seal.
He had a buyer.
That was the first thing, and he had put it in the second line, which was the mark of a man who had rehearsed the placement.
His nephew, Mr.

Gilbert Stainforth, proposed to take on the lease of the White Hound at its next renewal, with the intention, the letter said, of raising the establishment to a standard more in keeping with the character of the road.

He would be pleased, in the interim, to meet with me at his house in Knebworth on the fourth of November to discuss the terms upon which I might be persuaded to surrender the remainder of my lease in advance of the Michaelmas quarter.
He named a sum.
The sum was not ungenerous, for a man who meant to have the inn for nothing within eighteen months and knew it.
A more fashionable establishment.
I read that phrase twice.

My grandmother had built this inn out of a husband's death and a young widow's refusal to be sent back to her father's house, and my mother had kept it through a war and a drunk, and I had held it through two years alone, and Mr.
Phineas Stainforth proposed to make it more fashionable.
For his nephew.
Who had, I happened to know, been sent down from Cambridge for a matter involving a horse and a bet.
The fourth of November.
Eleven days.
I set the letter down.
I flattened it against the wood with the heel of my hand, because paper that has been folded in a pocket does not lie flat on its own, and I had a dislike of documents that did not lie flat.
My finger stung where the cut was.
I looked at the cut and at the seal and at the date written in the clerk's careful hand.
"Eleven days, Mr.
Stainforth," I said, to the empty kitchen and the coals and the cat that was not there.
"Let us see what your nephew is made of."
Bow Down

Early in 1880, in spite of a well-founded suspicion as to the advisability of perpetuating that race which has the sanction of the Lord and the disapproval of the people, Hedvig Volkbein, a Viennese woman of great strength and military beauty, lying upon a canopied bed of a rich spectacular crimson, the valance stamped with the bifurcated wings of the House of Hapsburg, the feather coverlet an envelope of satin on which, in massive and tarnished gold threads, stood the Volkbein arms­ gave birth, at the age of forty-five, to an only child, a son, seven days after her physician predicted that she would be taken.

Turning upon this field, which shook to the clatter of morning horses in the street beyond, with the gross splendour of a general saluting the flag, she named him Felix, thrust him from her, and died.
The child's father had gone six months previously, a victim of fever.

Guido Volkbein, a Jew of Italian descent, had been both a gourmet and a dandy, never appearing in public without the ribbon of some quite unknown distinction tinging his buttonhole with a faint thread.

He had been small, rotund, and haughtily timid, his stomach protruding slightly in an upward jutting slope that brought into prominence the buttons of his waistcoat and trousers, marking the exact centre of his body with the obstetric line seen on fruits-the inevitable arc produced by heavy rounds of burgundy, schlagsahne, and beer.
The autumn, binding him about, as no other season, with racial
memories, a season of longing and of horror, he had called his weather.

Then walking in the Prater he had been seen carrying in a conspicuously clenched fist the exquisite handkerchief of yellow and black linen that cried aloud of the ordinance of 1468, issued by one Pietro Barbo, demanding that, with a rope about its neck, Guido's race should run in the Corso for the amusement of the Christian populace, while ladies of noble birth, sitting upon spines too refined for rest, arose from their seats, and, with the red-gowned cardinals and the Monsignori, applauded with that cold yet hysterical abandon of a people that is at once unjust and happy, the very Pope himself shaken down from his hold on heaven with the laughter of a man who forgoes his angels that he may recapture the beast.
This memory and the handkerchief that accompanied it had
wrought in Guido (as certain flowers brought to a pitch of florid ecstasy no sooner attain their specific type than they fall into its decay) the sum total of what is the Jew.

He had walked, hot, incautious and damned, his eyelids quivering over the thick eyeballs, black with the pain of a participation that, four centuries later, made him a victim, as he felt the echo in his own throat of that cry running the Piazza Montanaro long ago, 'Roba vecchia!'-the degradation by which his people had survived.

Childless at fifty-nine, Guido had prepared out of his own heart for his coming child a heart, fashioned on his own preoccupation, the remorseless homage to nobility, the genuflexion the hunted body makes from muscular contraction, going down before the impending and inaccessible, as before a great heat.
It had made Guido, as it was to make his son, heavy with impermissible blood.
And childless he had died, save for the promise that hung at the Christian belt of Hedvig.

Guido had lived as all Jews do, who, cut off from their people by accident or choice, find that they must inhabit a world whose constituents, being alien, force the mind to succumb to an imaginary populace.
When a Jew dies on a Christian bosom he dies impaled.
Hedvig, in spite of her agony, wept upon an outcast.
Her body at that moment became the barrier and Guido died against that wall, troubled and alone.
In life he had done everything to span the impossible gap; the saddest and most futile gesture of all had been his pretence to a Barony.

He had adopted the sign of the cross; he had said that he was an Austrian of an old, almost extinct line, producing, to uphold his story, the most amazing and inaccurate proofs: a coat of arms that he had no right to and a list of progenitors (including their Christian names) who had never existed.
When Hedvig came upon his black and yellow handkerchiefs he had said that they were to remind
him that one branch of his family had bloomed in Rome.
He had tried to be one with her by adoring her, by imitating her goose­ step of a stride, a step that by him adopted, became dislocated and comic.
She would have done as much, but sensing something in him blasphemed and lonely, she had taken the blow as a Gentile must-by moving toward him in recoil.
She had believed whatever he had told her, but often enough she had asked: 'What is the matter?'-that continual reproach which was meant as a continual reminder of her love.
It ran through his life like an accusing voice.
He had been tormented into speaking highly of royalty, flinging out encomiums with the force of small water made great by the pressure of a thumb.
He had laughed too heartily when in the presence of the lower order of title, as if, by his good nature, he could advance them to some distinction of which they
dreamed.

Confronted with nothing worse than a general in creaking leather and with the slight repercussion of movement common to military men, who seem to breathe from the inside out, smelling of gunpowder and horse flesh, lethargic yet prepared for participation in a war not yet scheduled (a type of which Hedvig had been very fond), Guido had shaken with an unseen trembling.
He saw that Hedvig had the same bearing, the same though more condensed power of the hand, patterned on seizure in a smaller mould, as sinister in its reduction as a doll's house.
The feather in her hat had been knife-dean and quivering as if in an heraldic wind; she had been a woman held up to nature, precise, deep-bosomed and gay.
Looking at the two he had become confused as if he were about to receive a reprimand, not the officer's, but his wife's.

When she danced, a little heady with wine, the dance floor had become a tactical manoeuvre; her heels came down staccato and trained, her shoulders as conscious at the tips as those which carry the braid and tassels of promotion; the turn of her head held the cold vigilance of a sentry whose rounds are not without apprehension.
Yet Hedvig had done what she could.
If ever there was a massive chic she had personified it­ yet somewhere there had been anxiety.
The thing that she had stalked, though she herself had not been conscious of it, was Guido's assurance that he was a Baron.
She had believed it as a soldier 'believes' a command.
Something in her sensitory predicament-upon which she herself would have placed no value-had told her much better.
Hedvig had become a Baroness without question.

In the Vienna of Volkbein's day there were few trades that welcomed Jews, yet somehow he had managed, by various deals in household goods, by discreet buying of old masters and first editions and by money changing, to secure for Hedvig a house in the Inner City, to the north overlooking the Prater, a house that, large, dark and imposing, became a fantastic museum of their encounter.

The long rococo halls, giddy with plush and whorled designs in gold, were peopled with Roman fragments, white and disassociated; a runner's leg, the chilly half-turned head of a matron stricken at the bosom, the blind bold sockets of the eyes given a pupil by every shifting shadow so that what they looked upon was an act of the sun.
The great salon was of walnut.
Over the fireplace hung impressive copies of the Medici shield and, beside them, the Austrian bird.
Three massive pianos (Hedvig had played the waltzes of her time with the masterly stroke of a man, in the tempo of her blood, rapid and rising
-that quick mannerliness of touch associated with the playing of the
Viennese, who, though pricked with the love of rhythm, execute its demands in the duelling manner) sprawled over the thick dragon's-blood pile of rugs from Madrid.
The study harboured two rambling desks in rich and bloody wood.
Hedvig had liked things in twos and threes.
Into the middle arch of each desk silver-headed brads had been hammered to form a lion, a bear, a ram, a dove, and in their midst a flaming torch.

The design was executed under the supervision of Guido who, thinking on the instant, claimed it as the Volkbein field, though it turned out to be a bit of heraldry long since in decline beneath the papal frown.

The full length windows (a French touch that Guido thought handsome) overlooking the park were curtained in native velvets and stuffs from Tunis, and the Venetian blinds were of that peculiarly sombre shade of red so loved by the Austrians.

At this point exact history stopped for Felix who, thirty years later, turned up in the world with these facts, the two portraits and nothing more.

What had formed Felix from the date of his birth to his coming to thirty was unknown to the world, for the step of the wandering Jew is in every son.

No matter where and when you meet him you feel that he has come from some place-no matter from what place he has come-some country that he has devoured rather than resided in, some secret land that he has been nourished on but cannot inherit, for the Jew seems to be everywhere from nowhere.

From the mingled passions that made up his past, out of a diversity of bloods, from the crux of a thousand impossible situations, Felix had become the accumulated and single-the embarrassed.
His embarrassment took the form of an obsession for what he termed 'Old Europe': aristocracy, nobility, royalty.
He spoke any given title with a pause before and after the name.
Knowing circumlocution to be his only contact, he made it interminable and exacting.

He felt that the great past might mend a little if he bowed low enough, if he succumbed and gave homage.

In nineteen hundred and twenty he was in Paris (his blind eye had kept him out of the army), still spatted, still wearing his cutaway, bowing, searching, with quick pendulous movements, for the correct thing to which to pay tribute: the right street, the right cafe, the right building, the right vista.
